title: Reducing Redundancy in Whole-Slide Image Patching for Scalable Indexing and Retrieval
summary: The rapid growth of digital pathology has created an urgent need for efficient indexing and retrieval of whole slide images (WSIs). This need is intensified by emerging generative AI workflows, particularly retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which require dependable similarity search to support high-stakes clinical decision-making. Yet the substantial cost of high-performance storage limits the scalability and accessibility of WSI indexing for many healthcare institutions. Consequently, methods that can reduce storage demands while preserving retrieval accuracy have become a critical research priority. We propose ARReST (Antithetical Redundancy Reduction Strategy), a principled oppositional framework that leverages redundancy across dissimilar tissue classes to markedly decrease the number of patches that must be indexed from each WSI. Instead of eliminating only within-class duplicates, ARReST identifies antithetical patches-those whose representations contribute minimally to cross-class discrimination-and prunes them from the searchable archive. This targeted reduction substantially compresses the index without sacrificing morphological diversity or retrieval fidelity. By minimizing superfluous patch representations, ARReST reduces storage footprint, lowers computational overhead, and accelerates similarity search across large pathology repositories. Extensive experiments on TCGA repository (The Cancer Genome Atlas with 21 organs) demonstrate that ARReST achieves significant index compression while maintaining competitive retrieval performance. The observed storage savings of 3% to 60% (14%$\pm$13%) can be reliably achieved without compromising retrieval performance for many organs. The proposed strategy enables scalable, cost-efficient WSI indexing and is well-suited for next-generation retrieval-driven clinical AI systems.

AI.tldr: ARReST is a patch pruning framework for whole slide image indexing that removes antithetical patches (those contributing minimally to cross-class discrimination) rather than only within-class duplicates, achieving 14%±13% storage reduction without compromising retrieval accuracy across 21 TCGA organs.
AI.motivation: The growth of digital pathology and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) workflows demands efficient WSI indexing, but high-performance storage costs limit scalability. Existing methods that remove only within-class duplicates are insufficient; there is a need for more aggressive compression that preserves cross-class discriminability.
AI.method: ARReST identifies "antithetical patches"—those whose feature representations contribute minimally to distinguishing between dissimilar tissue classes. These patches are pruned from the index, reducing storage while deliberately preserving morphological diversity and cross-class retrieval fidelity. The approach operates as a principled oppositional redundancy reduction framework.
AI.result: Experiments on TCGA (21 organs) show index compression ranging from 3% to 60%, with an average of 14%±13% storage savings, achieved without compromising retrieval performance for most organs.
AI.conclusion: ARReST enables scalable, cost-efficient WSI indexing suitable for next-generation retrieval-driven clinical AI systems by minimizing superfluous patch representations, lowering both storage footprint and computational overhead.

title: From Clicks to Intent: Cross-Platform Session Embeddings with LLM-Distilled Taxonomy for Financial Services Recommendations
comment: Dianjing Fan and Yao Li equally contributed to this work. 7 pages, 1 figure
summary: Sequential user behavior modeling is widely adopted in industrial recommender systems; however, significant gaps remain in financial services, where pre-login web interactions and authenticated in-app experiences differ drastically. Specifically, pre-login web users typically explore new products, whereas logged-in app users focus on account servicing. Due to the challenge of cross-channel entity resolution (e.g., matching anonymous web sessions to authenticated mobile accounts), web-based intent signals remain underutilized for post-authentication personalization. Existing methods for capturing web-based intent are often ad-hoc and narrow, lacking the flexibility to support both quantitative downstream recommendations and qualitative understanding at scale. In this work, we propose a scalable and dual-purpose intent prediction framework for web-based interactions and demonstrate its applicability for personalization. Our approach transforms raw web clickstreams into two outputs: a self-supervised Transformer encodes multi-modal clickstreams into a compact session embedding, while an LLM-based taxonomy generation and distillation pipeline produces interpretable intent labels. Our system demonstrates that self-supervised clickstream representations combined with LLM-distilled taxonomies can jointly serve quantitative tasks and qualitative understanding in production: on the mobile homepage tile ranking task, the session embedding improves macro Recall@1 by 1.88% and reduces Log Loss by 13.38% over production baselines. On the user conversion prediction task, the embedding outperforms the LLM labels by 4.3% on micro F1, while the distillation layer delivers interpretable labels at ultra-low latency with only a 7% performance drop.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a dual-purpose framework that transforms web clickstreams into both compact session embeddings (via self-supervised Transformer) and interpretable intent labels (via LLM-based taxonomy distillation), enabling cross-channel personalization in financial services where pre-login web and authenticated app behaviors are siloed. On mobile homepage tile ranking, the embedding improves Recall@1 by 1.88% and reduces Log Loss by 13.38%; on conversion prediction, it outperforms LLM labels by 4.3% micro F1, while the distillation layer provides interpretable labels at ultra-low latency with only a 7% performance drop.
AI.motivation: Financial services face a cross-channel gap: pre-login web users explore new products while logged-in app users focus on account servicing. Due to the difficulty of matching anonymous web sessions to authenticated mobile accounts (entity resolution), web-based intent signals remain underutilized for post-authentication personalization. Existing methods are ad-hoc and narrow, lacking flexibility for both quantitative recommendations and qualitative understanding at scale.
AI.method: A dual-output framework: (1) a self-supervised Transformer encodes multi-modal web clickstreams into compact session embeddings; (2) an LLM-based taxonomy generation and distillation pipeline produces interpretable intent labels. The two outputs jointly serve downstream tasks: session embeddings for quantitative ranking/prediction, distilled labels for qualitative understanding at low latency.
AI.result: On mobile homepage tile ranking, the session embedding improves macro Recall@1 by 1.88% and reduces Log Loss by 13.38% over production baselines. On user conversion prediction, the embedding outperforms LLM labels by 4.3% on micro F1. The distillation layer delivers interpretable labels at ultra-low latency with only a 7% performance drop compared to full LLM labels.
AI.conclusion: Self-supervised clickstream representations combined with LLM-distilled taxonomies can jointly serve quantitative tasks and qualitative understanding in production, effectively bridging the pre-login web and authenticated app gap for personalization in financial services.

title: Scoring Is Not Enough: Addressing Gaps in Utility-fairness Trade-offs for Ranking
summary: Scoring functions are used to represent the relevance of individual documents. In modern information retrieval or recommendation systems, they are often learned from data and play a pivotal role in ranking sets of documents or items in a way that maximizes utility to a query or user. With the recent interest in algorithmic fairness, the success of scoring has naturally led to methods that learn scores that simultaneously trade off fairness and utility. In this work, we show that in stark contrast with utility-centric objectives, scoring is sub-optimal in achieving all utility-fairness trade-offs. We establish this with a series of counter-examples with a generic fairness formulation. We show that the issue persists whether we have a deterministic scoring function or a randomized one, or whether we measure fairness at the scope of a single query or across multiple queries. On the positive side, we empirically demonstrate that semi-greedy post-processing has the potential to achieve much better trade-offs, often approaching the ideal of exhaustive post-processing in a tractable way.

AI.tldr: Scoring functions are fundamentally sub-optimal for achieving fairness-utility trade-offs in ranking, unlike in purely utility-centric settings. The authors prove this via counter-examples across multiple fairness formulations and demonstrate that semi-greedy post-processing can approach the optimal trade-off frontier more effectively.
AI.motivation: Recent work on algorithmic fairness in ranking has adopted scoring-based approaches (learning fair scoring functions) by analogy with utility-centric ranking. The authors challenge whether scoring is fundamentally capable of achieving all desirable utility-fairness trade-offs, questioning this direct transfer of methodology from utility to fairness settings.
AI.method: The authors construct a series of counter-examples under a generic fairness formulation to prove that scoring functions cannot achieve the full Pareto frontier of utility-fairness trade-offs. They examine this limitation across multiple axes: deterministic vs. randomized scoring functions, and single-query vs. multi-query fairness scopes. Empirically, they compare scoring-based methods against semi-greedy post-processing and exhaustive post-processing to assess how close each approach gets to the optimal trade-off frontier.
AI.result: Scoring functions are provably insufficient to achieve all points on the utility-fairness trade-off frontier, regardless of whether scores are deterministic or randomized, or whether fairness is measured per-query or across queries. Semi-greedy post-processing empirically achieves significantly better trade-offs than scoring-based methods and often approaches the performance of exhaustive (but intractable) post-processing.
AI.conclusion: Scoring is an inherently limited mechanism for fairness-aware ranking; the field should shift attention toward post-processing methods, particularly tractable semi-greedy approaches, to achieve near-optimal utility-fairness trade-offs that scoring cannot realize.

title: TileMaxSim: IO-Aware GPU MaxSim Scoring with Dimension Tiling and Fused Product Quantization
summary: Multi-vector retrieval models such as ColBERT achieve state-of-the-art accuracy through fine-grained token-level MaxSim scoring, yet existing GPU implementations leave most hardware performance unused. We give a roofline analysis of MaxSim on modern GPUs and identify a severe bandwidth gap: naive implementations reach only 5-18% of peak HBM bandwidth because they materialize the Nq x Nd similarity matrix, wasting memory traffic on data that is consumed once and discarded. We present TileMaxSim, a family of IO-aware Triton kernels that close this gap via (1) multi-query SRAM tiling that streams document embeddings through shared memory while accumulating per-query-token maxima in registers, reading each embedding from HBM exactly once; (2) dimension tiling that partitions the embedding dimension into 128-wide chunks, enabling scoring for d > 128 embeddings that overflow shared memory; and (3) fused product-quantization scoring via shared-memory lookup tables, cutting HBM I/O by up to ~31x. On NVIDIA H100 GPUs, TileMaxSim reaches 80.2% of peak HBM bandwidth and scores 82M documents/second (71.6M/s on real MS MARCO passages), a 220x speedup over loop-based scoring, 6.5x over fused PyTorch, 6.6-8.5x over torch.compile, and 469x the scoring throughput of WARP's CPU engine on the same node. TileMaxSim preserves exact retrieval quality: on MS MARCO and three BEIR benchmarks, rankings match reference MaxSim. As a drop-in replacement in ColBERTv2/PLAID, it cuts scoring latency at 100K candidates from 268 ms to 1.2 ms (98% lower end-to-end latency). We further show constant throughput from 100K to 500K documents, data-parallel multi-GPU sharding, robustness across dimensions 64-768, and FP16/BF16/FP32 support. Concurrent work independently develops an IO-aware fused MaxSim kernel; we differ in dimension tiling for d > 128 and fused product-quantization scoring.

AI.tldr: TileMaxSim introduces IO-aware Triton kernels for ColBERT-style MaxSim scoring that achieve 80.2% peak HBM bandwidth on H100 GPUs, yielding up to 220× speedup over naive implementations while preserving exact retrieval quality, through multi-query SRAM tiling, dimension tiling, and fused product-quantization scoring.
AI.motivation: Existing GPU implementations of token-level MaxSim scoring for multi-vector retrieval (e.g., ColBERT) severely underutilize hardware, reaching only 5-18% of peak HBM bandwidth. The core bottleneck is materialization of the full Nq × Nd similarity matrix in HBM, wasting memory bandwidth on intermediate data consumed only once. This bandwidth gap limits scoring throughput and inflates end-to-end retrieval latency.
AI.method: TileMaxSim comprises three key techniques: (1) Multi-query SRAM tiling that streams document embeddings through shared memory while accumulating per-query-token maxima in registers, reading each embedding exactly once from HBM. (2) Dimension tiling that partitions embedding dimensions into 128-wide chunks, enabling scoring for d > 128 embeddings that would otherwise overflow SRAM. (3) Fused product-quantization scoring using shared-memory lookup tables, reducing HBM I/O by up to ~31×. Implemented as custom Triton kernels drop-in compatible with ColBERTv2/PLAID.
AI.result: On NVIDIA H100 GPUs: 80.2% peak HBM bandwidth achieved; 82M documents/second raw scoring (71.6M/s on MS MARCO passages); 220× speedup over loop-based scoring, 6.5× over fused PyTorch, 6.6-8.5× over torch.compile, 469× over WARP CPU engine. In ColBERTv2/PLAID, end-to-end scoring latency at 100K candidates drops from 268ms to 1.2ms (98% reduction). Constant throughput from 100K-500K documents; robust across dimensions 64-768; supports FP16/BF16/FP32.
AI.conclusion: TileMaxSim demonstrates that IO-aware kernel design can close the bandwidth gap in multi-vector retrieval, achieving near-roofline GPU performance without sacrificing exact retrieval quality. The techniques (SRAM tiling, dimension tiling, fused PQ scoring) are general and enable practical, low-latency ColBERT deployment at scale.

title: Kiko: Programming Agents to Enact Interaction Protocols
summary:
Realizing a multiagent system involves implementing member agents who interact based on a protocol while making decisions in a decentralized manner. Current programming models for agents offer poor abstractions for decision making and fail to adequately bridge an agent's internal decision logic with its public decisions.
  We present Kiko, a protocol-based programming model for agents. To implement an agent, a programmer writes one or more decision makers, each of which chooses from among a set of valid decisions and makes mutually compatible decisions on what messages to send. By completely abstracting away the underlying communication service and by supporting practical decision-making patterns, Kiko enables agent developers to focus on business logic. We provide an operational semantics for Kiko and establish that Kiko agents are protocol compliant and able to realize any protocol enactment.

AI.tldr: Kiko is a protocol-based programming model for multiagent systems that abstracts decision-making logic from communication mechanics, enabling developers to focus on business logic while ensuring protocol compliance.
AI.motivation: Current agent programming models offer poor abstractions for decision making and fail to bridge the gap between an agent's internal decision logic and its externally visible decisions in decentralized multiagent systems.
AI.method: The authors present Kiko, a programming model where agents are implemented via one or more decision makers that select from valid, mutually compatible decisions about message sending. Kiko fully abstracts the underlying communication service and supports practical decision-making patterns, with a formal operational semantics provided.
AI.result: Kiko agents are proven to be protocol compliant and capable of realizing any protocol enactment.
AI.conclusion: Kiko successfully bridges internal decision logic with public protocol-governed interactions, offering a cleaner programming abstraction for decentralized multiagent systems.

title: Orchestrating Black-Box Schema Converters: An Empirical Study of Automated, Quality-Ranked Conversion Across Heterogeneous Schema Languages
summary: Modern software systems routinely need the same data model in several schema languages: a model may exist as JSON Schema for a web API, as XSD for data exchange, and as SHACL for a knowledge graph. Keeping these representations consistent as the model evolves is a recurring construction and maintenance burden, because converters between schema languages are hard to find, scattered across ecosystems, of uneven quality, and frequently lossy. We study, empirically, to what extent such imperfect, heterogeneous converters can be orchestrated into automated, reproducible, and quality-ranked conversions, and where the current converter landscape reaches its limits. Our approach models schema languages as nodes and converters, treated as black boxes, as directed edges, so that conversions become paths that are discovered, executed, ranked, and reported with full per-step provenance, with failures handled by trying alternatives. We realize it as the open-source Schema Conversion Orchestrator, integrate it into MetaConfigurator, and evaluate it on 60 conversion tasks built from real-world schemas across five schema languages, using agent-assisted, human-reviewed quality annotations. Orchestration surfaces a usable result for 43 of 60 tasks; the remaining failures localize concrete gaps in the converter landscape. We discuss implications for tool builders and for measuring conversion quality.

AI.tldr: The paper studies orchestrating multiple imperfect schema converters to automate cross-language schema conversions, finding that 43 of 60 real-world tasks yield usable results, while failures pinpoint gaps in the converter ecosystem.
AI.motivation: Modern software systems require the same data model in multiple schema languages (JSON Schema, XSD, SHACL, etc.), but maintaining consistency across these representations is burdensome. Existing converters are scattered, of uneven quality, lossy, and hard to find — necessitating a systematic way to chain them for automated, reproducible conversions.
AI.method: The approach models schema languages as nodes and converters (treated as black boxes) as directed edges in a graph. Conversions become paths discovered, executed, ranked, and reported with full per-step provenance. Failures are handled by trying alternative paths. This is realized as the open-source Schema Conversion Orchestrator, integrated into MetaConfigurator. Evaluation uses 60 conversion tasks across five schema languages, with agent-assisted, human-reviewed quality annotations.
AI.result: The orchestration approach surfaces a usable result for 43 out of 60 conversion tasks. The 17 remaining failures localize concrete gaps in the current converter landscape, providing actionable insights for tool builders.
AI.conclusion: Imperfect, heterogeneous converters can be effectively orchestrated into automated, reproducible, quality-ranked conversion pipelines. The approach not only improves practical schema conversion but also identifies specific weaknesses in the converter ecosystem, offering guidance for future tool development and quality measurement.

title: Having Dog Ears "for Real": Effects of Active and Passive Haptics on Embodying Non-Human Body Parts in VR
comment: Accepted to the IEEE International Symposium on Mixed and Augmented Reality (ISMAR) 2026
summary: Embodying non-human body parts in VR is a prevalent practice among certain subcultures and is a personally important creative outlet to many individuals. However, the discrepant morphology between real and virtual bodies can decrease Sense of Embodiment (SoE). Haptic feedback can compensate by increasing SoE felt towards non-human body parts, but there is a literature gap in comparing the effects of different haptic modalities, and their combinations, on SoE. Through an online survey sent out to social VR communities (n = 63), we determined that animal ears are a commonly embodied and ecologically valid non-human body part to study. We then ran a 2x2 within-subjects user study (n = 28) with two independent variables: active haptics, delivered through vibrotactile gloves, and passive haptics, delivered through a physical headband, for when participants reach up to touch virtual dog ears appended to their avatar in VR. Our findings show that (1) passive haptics produced the strongest overall embodiment outcomes, (2) combining modalities reduced the benefits of passive haptics, and (3) SoE towards non-human body parts positively correlates with SoE towards the entire avatar. We discuss implications of our findings in various domains, and on embodiment literature.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how different haptic feedback modalities affect the Sense of Embodiment (SoE) towards non-human body parts (specifically dog ears) in VR. A survey identified animal ears as a common non-human extension in social VR communities. A 2×2 within-subjects study (n=28) compared active haptics (vibrotactile gloves) and passive haptics (physical headband) when touching virtual dog ears. Results show passive haptics alone produce the strongest embodiment, combining modalities reduces passive haptics' benefits, and SoE towards non-human parts correlates with overall avatar embodiment.
AI.motivation: Embodying non-human body parts is a meaningful creative practice in VR subcultures, but morphological discrepancies between real and virtual bodies can diminish Sense of Embodiment. While haptic feedback is known to compensate for this, there is a gap in the literature comparing how different haptic modalities and their combinations affect SoE toward non-human body parts.
AI.method: A two-phase approach: (1) An online survey of social VR communities (n=63) to identify animal ears as an ecologically valid non-human body part for study. (2) A 2×2 within-subjects user study (n=28) manipulating two independent variables: active haptics (vibrotactile gloves) and passive haptics (physical headband), experienced when participants reach up to touch virtual dog ears on their avatar.
AI.result: (1) Passive haptics (physical headband) produced the strongest overall embodiment outcomes. (2) Combining active and passive haptics reduced the benefits that passive haptics provided alone. (3) Sense of Embodiment toward non-human body parts positively correlates with SoE toward the entire avatar.
AI.conclusion: Passive haptic feedback is most effective for enhancing embodiment of non-human body parts in VR, and combining haptic modalities can be counterproductive. The correlation between part-specific and whole-avatar SoE extends embodiment theory to non-human morphologies, with implications for VR design, social VR platforms, and future embodiment research.

title: MIRAGE: Protecting against Malicious Image Editing via False Moderation
summary: The proliferation of AI-powered image editing systems raises serious concerns because it allows personal images to be arbitrarily manipulated at scale, with minimal effort, and a lower barrier to entry. Prior work on image immunization adds imperceptible perturbations to an image to protect against unauthorized manipulations. However, these methods usually require access to the model weights and the image manipulating prompt. This significantly limits their use, especially against powerful commercial image-editors such as GPT-Image, Gemini Flash Image (Nano Banana), and Grok Imagine. To address this, we take a system-level view of the problem and identify a previously unexplored attack surface common to all major commercial image editing systems: pre-generation safety moderation.Rather than disrupting the generative model itself, we propose to immunize images by causing these moderation classifiers to flag images as policy-violating, triggering an automatic refusal regardless of the editing prompt. We operationalize this by adding adversarial perturbations to align our image to policy-violating concepts in the representation space of an ensemble of open-source embedding and moderation models. We call our method MIRAGE, which stands for Moderation Induced Resistance Against Generative Editing. We evaluate MIRAGE against multiple closed-source image editing APIs and demonstrate success rates of more than 88%. Our approach is simple, prompt-agnostic, and effective, offering a practical path towards protecting personal images from unauthorized AI-powered editing.

AI.tldr: MIRAGE immunizes personal images against unauthorized AI editing by fooling pre-generation safety moderators (not the generative model itself) into flagging images as policy-violating, achieving 88%+ success rates against commercial APIs like GPT-Image and Gemini without requiring model weights or prompt access.
AI.motivation: Existing image immunization methods require access to model weights and editing prompts, making them ineffective against closed-source commercial image editors (GPT-Image, Gemini Flash Image, Grok Imagine). There is an unexploited attack surface in the pre-generation safety moderation pipeline common to all major commercial systems.
AI.method: MIRAGE adds adversarial perturbations to images that align them with policy-violating concepts in the representation space of an ensemble of open-source embedding and moderation models. This causes the commercial editor's pre-generation safety classifier to flag the image and refuse editing, regardless of the user's editing prompt. The approach is system-level, targeting the moderation layer rather than the generative model itself.
AI.result: MIRAGE achieves over 88% success rate in preventing edits across multiple closed-source commercial image editing APIs, without requiring access to model weights or editing prompts.
AI.conclusion: MIRAGE offers a simple, prompt-agnostic, and effective practical defense against unauthorized AI-powered image manipulation by exploiting the universal pre-generation moderation infrastructure in commercial systems.

title: HierBias: Context-Conditioned Hierarchical Media Bias Detection with Multi-Task Type Classification
summary: Media bias detection is a critical task for ensuring fair and balanced information dissemination, yet existing sentence-level approaches classify each sentence independently, ignoring inter-sentence contextual signals that human annotators naturally exploit. We present \textbf{HierBias}, a hierarchical context-conditioned media bias detector that formally models document context in bias prediction. We introduce the \emph{context-conditioned bias probability} and prove theoretically that leveraging document context strictly reduces the Bayes error of sentence-level classification when inter-sentence mutual information is non-zero. A multi-task generalization bound further establishes that jointly training binary bias detection and fine-grained bias type classification improves sample efficiency on small annotated corpora. Architecturally, HierBias pairs a sentence-level RoBERTa encoder with a cross-sentence Transformer aggregator and dual output heads for binary detection and four-class type classification. Evaluated on BABE and BASIL, HierBias achieves 0.853 F1 and 0.723 MCC, surpassing the state-of-the-art bias-detector by $+2.6\%$ F1 and $+4.3\%$ MCC (McNemar's test, $p < 0.05$). Ablation experiments confirm that each theoretical component contributes independently and consistently.

AI.tldr: HierBias introduces a hierarchical, context-conditioned approach to media bias detection that leverages inter-sentence context via a RoBERTa encoder paired with a cross-sentence Transformer, theoretically proving that document-level context reduces Bayes error and improves sample efficiency through multi-task learning. It achieves SOTA on BABE and BASIL.
AI.motivation: Existing sentence-level bias detection methods classify sentences independently, ignoring inter-sentence contextual signals that human annotators use. This independence discards mutual information present across sentences in a document, limiting classification accuracy.
AI.method: HierBias uses a hierarchical architecture: a sentence-level RoBERTa encoder produces per-sentence representations, which are then aggregated by a cross-sentence Transformer to model document context. Dual output heads perform binary bias detection and fine-grained four-class bias type classification jointly. The authors formally introduce the context-conditioned bias probability, prove that document context strictly reduces Bayes error when inter-sentence mutual information is non-zero, and derive a multi-task generalization bound showing improved sample efficiency.
AI.result: On BABE and BASIL, HierBias achieves 0.853 F1 and 0.723 MCC, outperforming the prior state-of-the-art by +2.6% F1 and +4.3% MCC (McNemar's test, p < 0.05). Ablation studies confirm each theoretical component contributes independently and consistently.
AI.conclusion: Modeling document-level context via hierarchical context-conditioned architectures, combined with multi-task joint training, significantly improves media bias detection. The theoretical guarantees and empirical results together validate the approach.

title: Detecting and Controlling Sycophancy with Cascading Linear Features
summary: Interpreting and controlling model behaviors through activation steering methods requires many pairs of contrastive samples that clearly exhibit desired or undesired behavior. These data pairs determine the degree to which interpretability frameworks can reliably detect model features responsible for a behavior, and therefore the ability to steer models toward or away from such behavior. In this work, we present an iterative data generation pipeline that isolates cascading linear features responsible for a behavior. Specifically, we show how moving beyond simple binary pairs of samples, and instead isolating samples that show degrees of features that scale linearly with behavior, allows for better disentanglement of features. We focus on detecting and steering away from sycophancy -- the tendency of language models to prioritize user validation. We demonstrate that sycophancy features discovered through cascading samples form linearly separable subspaces, and allow for selection of model activations that more clearly correspond to the desired behavior than baseline approaches. We also evaluate their ability to enable detection, deterministic scoring, and robust steering, and see that they either match or outperform LLM-as-a-judge and system prompting baselines while providing lower computational demand and more interpretability guarantees. Code & Data: https://cascading-feats.github.io/

AI.tldr: The paper introduces an iterative data generation pipeline that isolates cascading linear features responsible for model behaviors by using samples exhibiting scalar degrees of behavior (rather than binary pairs), enabling better feature disentanglement. Applied to sycophancy in LLMs, the method produces linearly separable subspaces that improve activation steering, detection, and scoring, matching or outperforming LLM-as-a-judge and system prompting baselines with lower computational cost.
AI.motivation: Existing activation steering methods rely on binary contrastive data pairs (desired vs. undesired behavior), which limits the ability to reliably isolate features responsible for a behavior. The authors argue that moving beyond binary pairs to samples showing continuous, scalar degrees of behavior enables better disentanglement of cascading linear features, leading to more interpretable and robust model control.
AI.method: The authors propose an iterative data generation pipeline that isolates "cascading linear features" — features that scale linearly with the degree of a target behavior. Instead of binary contrastive pairs, they generate samples exhibiting varying degrees of the behavior (sycophancy). These samples are used to identify activation subspaces that are linearly separable with respect to the behavior. The pipeline iteratively refines the data to better isolate features. The discovered features are then used for activation steering (shifting activations toward or away from sycophancy), deterministic behavior scoring, and behavior detection.
AI.result: The cascading feature approach produces activation subspaces that are linearly separable and more clearly correspond to sycophancy than baseline binary-pair methods. For steering, detection, and scoring, the method matches or outperforms LLM-as-a-judge and system prompting baselines, while requiring lower computational demand and offering stronger interpretability guarantees.
AI.conclusion: Isolating behaviors through scalar, cascading samples rather than binary contrastive pairs yields better-disentangled linear features. This enables more effective and interpretable activation steering, with performance competitive with or superior to existing methods at reduced computational cost. The approach is demonstrated specifically on sycophancy but the pipeline is potentially generalizable to other behaviors.

title: Physics-guided Convolutional Neural Network for Domain Growth Prediction in Systems with Conserved Kinetics
summary: The spatiotemporal evolution of many physical, chemical, and biological systems is described by nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs). Recently, deep neural network-based surrogate models have gained increasing interest as efficient alternatives to computationally expensive traditional numerical solvers. In this work, we propose an attention-based, physics-guided convolutional neural network as a surrogate model to learn the microstructural evolution of such systems. We train the model to accurately predict the full time-evolution of phase separation in binary mixtures governed by the Cahn-Hilliard equation. We show that predictions from our trained surrogate model remain stable and accurate over long-time rollouts for both critical and off-critical mixtures and preserve the mixture composition throughout evolution. We also show that our model accurately captures the growth of domain size and is consistent with the Lifshitz-Slyozov domain-growth law. The prediction results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed framework for modeling systems with conserved kinetics and can be extended to other complex dynamical systems.

AI.tldr: Proposes an attention-based, physics-guided CNN surrogate model for learning microstructural evolution governed by the Cahn-Hilliard equation, demonstrating stable, accurate long-time predictions that preserve composition and obey Lifshitz-Slyozov domain-growth scaling.
AI.motivation: Traditional numerical solvers for nonlinear PDEs describing spatiotemporal systems are computationally expensive. Deep learning surrogates offer efficiency but must maintain physical consistency, stability over long time horizons, and adherence to conservation laws — challenges this work addresses.
AI.method: An attention-based, physics-guided convolutional neural network (CNN) is developed as a surrogate model. The model is trained to learn the full temporal evolution of phase separation in binary mixtures described by the Cahn-Hilliard equation, incorporating physics guidance to enforce conserved kinetics.
AI.result: The trained surrogate yields stable, accurate long-time rollout predictions for both critical and off-critical mixtures, preserves mixture composition throughout evolution, accurately captures domain size growth, and shows consistency with the Lifshitz-Slyozov domain-growth law.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework is effective for modeling systems with conserved kinetics and can be extended to other complex dynamical systems governed by nonlinear PDEs.

title: GPUSparse: GPU-Accelerated Learned Sparse Retrieval with Parallel Inverted Indices
summary: Learned sparse retrieval models such as SPLADE achieve retrieval quality competitive with dense models while preserving the interpretability and exact-match advantages of sparse representations. However, inference-time scoring still relies on CPU-bound inverted index traversal algorithms (WAND, Block-Max WAND), creating a fundamental bottleneck for real-time serving at scale. We present GPUSparse, a system for GPU-accelerated exact learned sparse retrieval that introduces: (1) a GPU-parallel inverted index with block-aligned, warp-coalesced posting lists; (2) a batched scatter-add scoring algorithm that processes hundreds of queries simultaneously; and (3) fused Triton kernels with an analysis of the tradeoff between work-efficiency and hardware utilization. On MS MARCO passage ranking (8.8M passages) with real SPLADE embeddings, GPUSparse matches CPU exact scoring to three decimals (MRR@10=0.383, equal to Pyserini SPLADE at this precision; Recall@1000>=0.999 vs. dense matmul, the residual from floating-point tie-breaking) while providing a 235x speedup over Pyserini CPU at 8.8M documents (1.27ms vs. 298ms per query). Compared to Seismic (the fastest CPU sparse retrieval system), which trades 25% recall for speed (R@1000=0.738 vs. 0.983 exact), GPUSparse achieves exact scoring at 787 QPS throughput (batch 500) on the full 8.8M collection, with 1.3ms per query. Our document-parallel kernel reaches 62.6% of H100 peak HBM bandwidth, revealing a fundamental work-efficiency vs. bandwidth-efficiency tradeoff in GPU sparse retrieval. The reformulation of sparse scoring as scatter-add over an inverted index is shared with SPARe's iterative mode; our contribution is its fused-kernel realization, which we measure to be 23-270x faster than a faithful SPARe iterative reimplementation.

AI.tldr: GPUSparse is a GPU-accelerated system for exact learned sparse retrieval that achieves 235× speedup over CPU baselines while preserving exact-match scoring, using GPU-parallel inverted indices, batched scatter-add scoring, and fused Triton kernels.
AI.motivation: Learned sparse models like SPLADE offer competitive quality with interpretable sparse representations, but inference-time scoring is bottlenecked by CPU-bound inverted index traversal (WAND/Block-Max WAND), limiting real-time serving at scale. GPU acceleration is needed to bridge this gap.
AI.method: GPUSparse introduces three components: (1) a GPU-parallel inverted index with block-aligned, warp-coalesced posting lists; (2) a batched scatter-add scoring algorithm handling hundreds of queries simultaneously; and (3) fused Triton kernels with analysis of the work-efficiency vs. hardware-utilization tradeoff. The scatter-add reformulation over an inverted index is shared with SPARe's iterative mode, but realized as fused kernels.
AI.result: On MS MARCO (8.8M passages) with SPLADE embeddings, GPUSparse matches CPU exact scoring to three decimals (MRR@10=0.383, Recall@1000≥0.999). It achieves 235× speedup over Pyserini CPU (1.27ms vs. 298ms/query), 787 QPS throughput at batch 500, and reaches 62.6% of H100 peak HBM bandwidth. It is 23–270× faster than a faithful SPARe iterative reimplementation.
AI.conclusion: GPUSparse demonstrates that exact learned sparse retrieval can be efficiently GPU-accelerated via fused-kernel scatter-add over inverted indices, revealing a fundamental work-efficiency vs. bandwidth-efficiency tradeoff and enabling high-throughput, low-latency serving without sacrificing retrieval quality.

title: Agentic Analysis for Agentic Infrastructure: An LLM-Powered Pipeline for Comparative Governance of DAO and Corporate AI Protocols
summary: As AI agent protocols proliferate, the governance structures shaping their interoperability standards remain empirically underexamined. We introduce an LLM-powered comparative pipeline for large-scale governance discourse analysis, integrating automated annotation, neural topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis to study socio-technical power structures at scale. We validate it on two contrasting standards for agent interoperability: ERC-8004 (permissionless, on-chain) and Google A2A (corporate-led). Analyzing 4,323 governance participation records, we combine LLM-assisted coding, topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis to examine how institutional design shapes thematic priorities and community structure. We find that while governance form influences substantive focus, both regimes exhibit comparable levels of participation inequality and community fragmentation. Discourse alignment is denser in the permissionless setting, suggesting that open governance may foster greater thematic convergence despite decentralized participation. These findings illustrate how LLM-assisted methods can advance the empirical study of technology governance, with implications for designing more equitable agentic AI standards. All data and code are openly available.

AI.tldr: The paper presents an LLM-powered pipeline for analyzing governance discourse at scale, applied comparatively to two AI agent interoperability standards—ERC-8004 (permissionless) and Google A2A (corporate-led). Using 4,323 governance participation records with automated annotation, topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis, the authors find that governance form shapes thematic priorities but both regimes show similar participation inequality and community fragmentation, with denser discourse alignment in the permissionless setting.
AI.motivation: Despite the proliferation of AI agent protocols, the governance structures influencing their interoperability standards lack empirical scrutiny. There is a methodological gap in analyzing socio-technical power structures at scale within technology governance contexts.
AI.method: The authors introduce a comparative pipeline combining: (1) LLM-assisted automated annotation/coding of governance participation records, (2) neural topic modeling to extract thematic content, and (3) multi-layer network analysis to investigate community structure and discourse alignment. This is applied to 4,323 governance participation records from two contrasting protocols: ERC-8004 (permissionless, on-chain) and Google A2A (corporate-led).
AI.result: Key findings: (1) Institutional design influences substantive thematic focus in governance discourse. (2) Both permissionless and corporate-led regimes exhibit comparable levels of participation inequality and community fragmentation. (3) Discourse alignment is denser in the permissionless (ERC-8004) setting, indicating that open governance may foster greater thematic convergence despite decentralized participation patterns.
AI.conclusion: LLM-assisted methods can effectively advance empirical research on technology governance. The findings carry implications for designing more equitable agentic AI standards, and the authors contribute to open science by making all data and code publicly available.

title: Augmentation with Dilution: A Large-Scale Empirical Study of Human Contributor Ecosystems After AI Coding Agent Adoption
summary: AI coding agents are penetrating open-source software development at an unprecedented pace, yet existing research predominantly treats human contributors as a static backdrop rather than as the subject of inquiry. This paper presents the first large-scale empirical study that takes the human contributor ecosystem as its dependent variable, examining how the number, composition, and behavior of human participants change following AI coding agent adoption in open-source projects. Using a staggered difference-in-differences design on a dataset of 11,097 GitHub repositories spanning January 2023 to May 2026, we provide causal evidence via the Sun and Abraham estimator. Our results show that AI agent adoption does not significantly change the absolute number of human contributors (ATT = 0.014, p = 0.224), but significantly reduces human contributor density (ATT = -0.019, p = 0.002), indicating that the relative share of human participation declines as AI-generated pull requests accumulate. The relative participation share of newcomers declines significantly by 3.7 percentage points (ATT = -0.037, p < 0.001), with the effect emerging immediately after adoption and remaining stable throughout the observation window. Review depth increases significantly by 5.3% (ATT = +0.0168, p < 0.001), indicating that AI agents shift burden from the code production stage to the review stage. Moderator analysis reveals that these effects vary systematically with project size, programming language, and project maturity. Together, these findings present a pattern of augmentation with dilution: AI agents are not displacing human contributors, but are systematically reshaping the participation structure of open-source ecosystems.

AI.tldr: First large-scale empirical study examining how AI coding agents affect human contributor ecosystems in open-source projects. Using staggered DiD on 11,097 GitHub repos, the study finds AI agents do not displace humans but reduce human participation density, shrink newcomer share by 3.7pp, and increase review burden by 5.3% — a pattern termed "augmentation with dilution."
AI.motivation: Existing research on AI coding agents in OSS treats human contributors as static background context rather than as the primary subject of study. The authors aim to fill this gap by causally examining how AI agent adoption reshapes the human contributor ecosystem — their numbers, composition, and behavioral patterns.
AI.method: Staggered difference-in-differences (DiD) design using the Sun and Abraham estimator, applied to a dataset of 11,097 GitHub repositories from January 2023 to May 2026. The human contributor ecosystem is the dependent variable. Moderator analyses examine heterogeneity by project size, programming language, and project maturity.
AI.result: AI agent adoption shows no significant effect on absolute human contributor count (ATT = 0.014, p = 0.224). However, human contributor density declines significantly (ATT = −0.019, p = 0.002). Newcomer participation share drops by 3.7 percentage points (ATT = −0.037, p < 0.001), with immediate and persistent effects. Review depth rises significantly by 5.3% (ATT = +0.0168, p < 0.001), indicating burden shifts from code production to review. Effects are systematically moderated by project characteristics.
AI.conclusion: The findings reveal a pattern of "augmentation with dilution": AI agents do not displace human contributors outright, but systematically restructure participation by reducing human density, marginalizing newcomers, and shifting workload from code generation to code review — with implications for the long-term sustainability and inclusivity of open-source ecosystems.

title: Assistive Visual Cues for Visual Neglect Patients
summary: Previous research on exogenous and endogenous cues has shown how they direct attention and improve interaction speed and error rate in applications. However, most studies focus on people with normal sight. People suffering from visual neglect have difficulties attending to parts of the visual field. One treatment method calls for the use of strong visual cues to remind patients of their neglected area and help guide their attention to it. Therefore, we examine the effects of endogenous and exogenous cues on visual neglect patients. Our results showed that visual neglect patients perform better with endogenous cues, when targets are within their neglected area. In some cases, combining exogenous and endogenous cues improve performance further. However, the performance varies greatly between patients. Using one neglect patient as an example, we saw that the best endogenous cue had an average acquisition time of 3.5 seconds compared to 6.5 for the best exogenous. Combining exogenous and endogenous cues further improved acquisition time to 2.8 seconds.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how endogenous (internally-driven) and exogenous (externally-driven) attentional cues affect performance in patients with visual neglect, finding that endogenous cues yield better target acquisition times in neglected visual fields, and that combined cues can further improve performance—though results vary significantly across individuals.
AI.motivation: Most prior research on attentional cueing (exogenous and endogenous) has focused on normally-sighted individuals, leaving a gap in understanding how these cues affect patients with visual neglect—a condition where individuals fail to attend to portions of their visual field. Since strong visual cues are already used clinically to redirect attention in neglect patients, the authors seek to empirically compare cue types to inform more effective treatment strategies.
AI.method: The study experimentally compared the effects of exogenous cues (reflexive, stimulus-driven), endogenous cues (volitional, symbolic), and combined exogenous-endogenous cues on visual neglect patients' ability to detect targets, particularly those presented in the neglected hemifield. Performance was measured via target acquisition time. A within-subjects case analysis was also conducted on one neglect patient to illustrate individual variability.
AI.result: Visual neglect patients performed better with endogenous cues than exogenous cues when targets appeared in the neglected area. Combining both cue types yielded further improvements in some instances. In an exemplar patient, the best endogenous cue produced an average acquisition time of 3.5 seconds versus 6.5 seconds for the best exogenous cue, while combined cues reduced this further to 2.8 seconds. However, substantial inter-patient variability was observed.
AI.conclusion: Endogenous cues are more effective than exogenous cues for directing attention in visual neglect patients, and multimodal cue combinations may offer additional benefit. The high inter-individual variability suggests that cue-based interventions should be personalized rather than applied uniformly.

title: Data Facts: A Metadata Schema for Structured Data Exchange in the NANDini Multi-Agent Ecosystem
summary:
NANDini (Networked Agents Natural Distillation of Interconnected Nodal Intelligence) envisions an automated ecosystem where intelligent agents independently create, process, and exchange data to drive decisions at scale. Realizing this vision requires infrastructure beyond agent discovery and communication: agents must be able to advertise, evaluate, and verify the datasets they hold.
  Current protocols, including NANDA for federated registry and A2A and MCP for inter-agent messaging, address identity and communication but provide no mechanism for structured data exchange. Existing enterprise data-sharing frameworks, such as IDS-RAM, Gaia-X, and Ocean Protocol, assume human-in-the-loop governance that is incompatible with autonomous, real-time agent interactions.
  We introduce Data Facts, a core NANDini concept: a lightweight JSON metadata schema that bridges agent discovery and data access through a single pointer, `data_facts_url`, added to an existing Agent Facts registry record. The linked document encodes dataset identity, access tier, whether public, semi-private, or private, endpoint, a time-to-live for freshness validation, and a SHA-256 integrity checksum.
  For private and semi-private data, we implement a three-layer security pipeline: JWT authentication, capability-scoped gateway authorization, and an A2A credential delegation protocol. Across 840 decision-making evaluations, data-informed agents achieve 100% accuracy versus 35.2% without data access (p < 0.001); TTL enforcement reduces stale-data errors from 37.6% to 8.8%; checksum verification achieves 100% corruption detection at all injection rates; and the security pipeline blocks all 46 forgery attempts with zero data leakage.

AI.tldr: NANDini introduces "Data Facts," a lightweight JSON metadata schema that bridges agent discovery and data access by adding a `data_facts_url` pointer to registry records. It implements a three-layer security pipeline (JWT, capability-scoped authorization, A2A delegation) for private data. Experiments show data-informed agents achieve 100% accuracy vs 35.2% without data, TTL enforcement cuts stale-data errors from 37.6% to 8.8%, checksum verification detects 100% of corruption, and the security pipeline blocks all 46 forgery attempts.
AI.motivation: Current agent protocols (NANDA, A2A, MCP) address identity and communication but lack structured data exchange mechanisms. Existing enterprise data-sharing frameworks (IDS-RAM, Gaia-X, Ocean Protocol) rely on human-in-the-loop governance, which is incompatible with autonomous, real-time agent interactions. NANDini aims to fill this gap by enabling agents to autonomously advertise, evaluate, and verify datasets.
AI.method: The paper proposes "Data Facts," a lightweight JSON metadata schema linked via a `data_facts_url` pointer in Agent Facts registry records. The document encodes dataset identity, access tier (public/semi-private/private), endpoint, TTL for freshness, and a SHA-256 checksum. A three-layer security pipeline secures private data: (1) JWT authentication, (2) capability-scoped gateway authorization, and (3) an A2A credential delegation protocol. Evaluation uses 840 decision-making trials with forgery attempts, corruption injection, and stale-data scenarios.
AI.result: Data-informed agents achieved 100% accuracy vs. 35.2% without data access (p < 0.001). TTL enforcement reduced stale-data errors from 37.6% to 8.8%. SHA-256 checksum verification achieved 100% corruption detection across all injection rates. The security pipeline blocked all 46 forgery attempts with zero data leakage.
AI.conclusion: The Data Facts schema and its accompanying security pipeline enable fully autonomous, verifiable, and secure data exchange among agents without human intervention, addressing a critical infrastructure gap for the NANDini vision of automated agent ecosystems.

title: Know2Guess: A Contamination-Aware Multi-Zone Benchmark for Knowledge-Boundary Evaluation in Large Language Models
summary: Reliable evaluation of large language models should separate supported answering from unsupported guessing without conflating either with data contamination, prompt idiosyncrasy, or generic refusal behavior. We present a contamination-aware, multi-zone benchmark for measuring the transition from answerable knowledge to abstention-expected unknowns under frozen build-time labels. The benchmark contains 1,200 items across five domains, explicit abstention expectations, contamination-risk metadata, and dual parsing with an official strict parser plus a normalized robustness parser. We evaluate FLAN-T5, Qwen2.5-Instruct, and Llama-3-Instruct models under locked answer-or-abstain prompts, answer-only controls, and prompt-template variants. The benchmark is not solved by generic non-answer behavior: FLAN baselines remain weak on productive abstention, while stronger instruction-tuned models expose a selective but incomplete transition from answering to abstaining. Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct achieves the best overall reliability, but answer-expected zones remain difficult, calibration remains poor, and benign-item refusal persists. Prompt and parser robustness analyses preserve the main ranking and qualitative conclusions. The benchmark therefore provides a reproducible protocol for auditing answerability, abstention, refusal, and contamination as distinct but interacting dimensions of LLM reliability.The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/renweimeng/Know2Guess-A-Contamination-Aware-Multi-Zone-Benchmark.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Know2Guess, a contamination-aware multi-zone benchmark with 1,200 items across five domains that measures LLMs' transition from answerable knowledge to abstention-expected unknowns, distinguishing supported answering from unsupported guessing while controlling for data contamination, prompt idiosyncrasy, and refusal behavior.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM evaluation conflates supported knowledge retrieval with unsupported guessing, and fails to disentangle contamination, prompt sensitivity, and generic refusal. A reliable benchmark must isolate these distinct dimensions to audit whether models appropriately transition from answering to abstaining at the knowledge boundary.
AI.method: The benchmark comprises 1,200 items across five domains with explicit abstention expectations per item and contamination-risk metadata. Two parsers are provided: an official strict parser and a normalized robustness parser. Three model families (FLAN-T5, Qwen2.5-Instruct, Llama-3-Instruct) are evaluated under locked answer-or-abstain prompts, answer-only controls, and prompt-template variants. Analyses examine productive abstention, calibration, benign-item refusal, and prompt/parser robustness.
AI.result: FLAN baselines show weak productive abstention. Stronger instruction-tuned models exhibit a selective but incomplete answer-to-abstain transition. Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct achieves the best overall reliability, yet answer-expected zones remain difficult, calibration is poor, and benign-item refusal persists. Prompt and parser robustness analyses preserve the main ranking and qualitative conclusions.
AI.conclusion: The benchmark provides a reproducible protocol for auditing answerability, abstention, refusal, and contamination as distinct but interacting dimensions of LLM reliability. It successfully surfaces gaps between known and guessed answers that conventional evaluation misses.

title: Life After Benchmark Saturation: A Case Study of CORE-Bench
summary: When a benchmark's accuracy saturates, it is often retired and replaced with a more challenging version. We show that this approach privileges accuracy and misses the opportunity to study six other key dimensions of agent performance: construct validity issues such as shortcuts, out-of-distribution generalizability, efficiency, reliability, the relative importance of the model versus the scaffold, and uplift from human-agent collaboration. We use CORE-Bench Hard, a benchmark for computational reproducibility of scientific code, as a case study to demonstrate that measuring agents along these dimensions yields meaningful insights into agent performance even after accuracy saturates. First, we surface threats to construct validity in CORE-Bench Hard that are difficult to anticipate with less capable agents. We introduce an improved benchmark, CORE-Bench v1.1, and an out-of-distribution task suite, CORE-Bench OOD. Second, we find that despite accuracy saturation, CORE-Bench v1.1 remains useful for measuring efficiency, reliability, model performance, and scaffold performance. Finally, we conduct a small-scale randomized experiment to measure uplift from human-agent collaboration on real-world computational reproducibility tasks. We find a statistically significant speedup by about a factor of two -- likely underestimated due to one-fifth of human-only reproductions reaching the time limit before completing -- and describe various other findings. Together, our contributions present a more rigorous alternative to the dominant accuracy-centric evaluation paradigm.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that when benchmarks saturate on accuracy, they should not simply be retired; instead, six other dimensions of agent performance should be measured. Using CORE-Bench as a case study, the authors demonstrate that construct validity, generalizability, efficiency, reliability, model vs. scaffold contributions, and human-agent collaboration uplift yield meaningful insights even after accuracy plateaus.
AI.motivation: Current evaluation paradigms retire benchmarks once accuracy saturates and replace them with harder ones. This privileges a single metric (accuracy) and neglects other critical performance dimensions, leading to missed insights about agent capabilities and limitations.
AI.method: The authors use CORE-Bench Hard (a benchmark for computational reproducibility of scientific code) as a case study. They (1) surface threats to construct validity, (2) introduce CORE-Bench v1.1 and an out-of-distribution suite (CORE-Bench OOD), (3) measure efficiency, reliability, model performance, and scaffold performance post-saturation, and (4) conduct a small-scale randomized experiment comparing human-only vs. human-agent collaboration on real-world reproducibility tasks.
AI.result: Construct validity threats were identified that less capable agents could not reveal. Despite accuracy saturation, CORE-Bench v1.1 differentiated agents on efficiency, reliability, model performance, and scaffold performance. The human-agent collaboration experiment showed a statistically significant ~2x speedup (likely underestimated due to human-only timeouts), along with other qualitative findings.
AI.conclusion: Measuring agents beyond accuracy — across construct validity, generalizability, efficiency, reliability, model/scaffold contributions, and human-agent uplift — provides a more rigorous evaluation paradigm. Benchmarks should be iteratively improved and used multi-dimensionally rather than discarded upon accuracy saturation.

title: \chisao{}: A GPU-Native Parallel Optimizer for Multimodal Black-Box Functions via Convergence-Anticonvergence Oscillation
summary: Finding all modes of a multimodal black-box function is a fundamental challenge in optimization, Bayesian inference, and scientific computing. Existing approaches -- basin-hopping, CMA-ES, multistart gradient descent -- operate sequentially and cannot exploit the massive parallelism of modern GPU hardware. We introduce \chisao{} (\textbf{C}onvergence-\textbf{H}alt-\textbf{I}nvert-\textbf{S}tick-\textbf{A}nd-\textbf{O}scillate), a GPU-native population optimizer that runs an entire sample batch simultaneously and exploits a deliberate convergence-anticonvergence oscillation cycle to escape local traps while freezing confirmed modes. The structural move is asymmetric: samples that reach true peaks are frozen (``stuck'') and preserved, while the rest keep exploring via momentum-based anti-convergence and stochastically smoothed gradients. Adaptive reseeding via two complementary strategies (Repulse Monkey and Golden Rooster) maintains population diversity throughout. On all 42 functions of the Simon Fraser University optimization benchmark suite across dimensions $d \in \{2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64\}$, \chisao{} achieves \textbf{100\%} mode recovery where all CPU baselines collapse at $d \geq 8$ on the hardest multimodal functions, at up to \textbf{$34\times$} speedup over basin-hopping on functions where all methods succeed (Michalewicz $d=64$) and up to \textbf{$39\times$} on unimodal functions (Rotated Hyper-Ellipsoid $d=64$, pure GPU dividend). All benchmarks evaluate the objective by value alone -- gradients come from finite differences -- so the reported speedups are a derivative-free worst case. Under substantial likelihood noise ($σ_{\mathrm{noise}}$ up to 1.0), mode detection remains 100\% reliable. The algorithm is available as a standalone open-source Python package on PyPI.

AI.tldr: CHISAO is a GPU-native population optimizer that uses a convergence-anticonvergence oscillation cycle with asymmetric freezing to find all modes of multimodal black-box functions. It achieves 100% mode recovery on all 42 SFU benchmark functions across dimensions 2–64, with up to 34× speedup over sequential baselines, and remains robust under substantial noise.
AI.motivation: Existing multimodal optimization methods (basin-hopping, CMA-ES, multistart gradient descent) are inherently sequential and cannot leverage GPU parallelism. This limits their scalability and speed when searching for all modes of black-box functions, especially in high dimensions.
AI.method: CHISAO runs an entire sample batch simultaneously on GPU with a deliberate convergence-anticonvergence oscillation cycle. The asymmetric mechanism (Convergence-Halt-Invert-Stick-And-Oscillate) works as follows: samples converging to true peaks are frozen ("stuck") and preserved as confirmed modes, while remaining samples continue exploring via momentum-based anti-convergence and stochastically smoothed gradients. Two complementary adaptive reseeding strategies — Repulse Monkey and Golden Rooster — maintain population diversity. Gradients are obtained via finite differences, making this a derivative-free method.
AI.result: On all 42 functions of the SFU benchmark suite (d ∈ {2,4,8,16,32,64}), CHISAO achieves 100% mode recovery. All CPU baselines fail at d ≥ 8 on the hardest multimodal functions. Speedups reach up to 34× over basin-hopping where all methods succeed (Michalewicz d=64), and up to 39× on unimodal functions (Rotated Hyper-Ellipsoid d=64). Under likelihood noise up to σ_noise = 1.0, mode detection remains 100% reliable.
AI.conclusion: CHISAO demonstrates that a GPU-native, population-based approach exploiting structured oscillation dynamics can achieve perfect multimodal mode recovery with massive speedups over sequential CPU methods, even in high-dimensional, derivative-free, and noisy settings. The algorithm is released as an open-source Python package on PyPI.

title: Attributed, But Not Incremental: Cannibalization-Corrected Attribution for Large-Scale Advertising
summary:
In large-scale paid acquisition and growth advertising systems, production attribution outputs are widely used for daily budget allocation and channel diagnosis. However, paid-attributed conversions such as daily new users (DNU) may systematically overstate true incremental growth when paid channels overlap with organic demand, brand-driven traffic, or other acquisition channels. This attribution-cannibalization mismatch can distort incremental ROI measurement and budget decisions at scale.
  We propose an experiment-calibrated attribution correction framework that uses incrementality experiments as causal anchors to convert sparse lift measurements into daily correction estimates. To make the corrected signal actionable at production granularity, we further allocate calibrated cannibalization volume across business hierarchies under structural consistency constraints. Offline forward-in-time validation against channel-level incrementality experiment readouts shows that the proposed framework substantially reduces calibration error relative to raw attribution and fine-grained ML baselines. Deployed across multiple global TikTok markets, the system supported budget and traffic strategy adjustments that were followed by an approximately 15-percentage-point reduction in the measured cannibalization rate.

AI.tldr: Paid attribution systems often overstate true incremental conversions due to cannibalization from organic/brand traffic. This paper proposes an experiment-calibrated correction framework that uses incrementality experiments as causal anchors to produce daily corrected attribution signals, deployed at TikTok with a ~15pp reduction in measured cannibalization rate.
AI.motivation: In large-scale advertising systems, raw paid-attributed conversions (e.g., DNU) systematically overstate true incrementality because paid channels overlap with organic demand, brand-driven traffic, and other acquisition channels. This attribution-cannibalization mismatch distorts incremental ROI measurement and downstream budget allocation decisions, necessitating a scalable correction framework grounded in causal experimentation.
AI.method: The framework uses incrementality experiments as causal anchors to convert sparse lift measurements into daily correction estimates. It then allocates the calibrated cannibalization volume across business hierarchies (e.g., channels, campaigns, geos) under structural consistency constraints, ensuring the corrected signal is actionable at production granularity. The approach is validated via offline forward-in-time evaluation against channel-level incrementality experiment readouts, and benchmarked against raw attribution and fine-grained ML baselines.
AI.result: Offline validation shows the framework substantially reduces calibration error compared to raw attribution and fine-grained ML baselines. In live deployment across multiple global TikTok markets, budget and traffic strategy adjustments supported by the system led to an approximately 15-percentage-point reduction in measured cannibalization rate.
AI.conclusion: The proposed experiment-calibrated correction framework effectively bridges the gap between sparse incrementality experiments and daily production attribution needs. By embedding causal lift measurements into a hierarchical allocation system with consistency constraints, it delivers actionable, de-biased signals that demonstrably improve budget efficiency and reduce cannibalization at scale.

title: The Red Queen Gödel Machine: Co-Evolving Agents and Their Evaluators
comment: 12 pages main text + 21 pages appendix (37 pages total, incl. references); 10 figures (6 main text + 4 appendix); 10 tables (2 main text + 8 appendix). Preliminary preprint; work in progress. Keywords: self-improving agents, learned evaluation, multi-agent systems, auto- mated scientific discovery, controlled utility evolution, co-evolutionary search, autoresearch
summary: Self-improving agents are state-of-the-art (SOTA) on agentic coding benchmarks and have recently been extended to general domains. However, their search methods generally assume a stationary evaluation criterion: a fixed verifier, benchmark, or labeled dataset that remains valid as the agent improves. This ignores a central feature of evolution: species adapt as their environments change with them. We aim to bring the same principle to recursive self-improvement, making evaluation part of the improvement loop and opening search to evolving evaluators, adversarial objectives, and dynamic utilities that may surpass static benchmarks. We introduce the Red Queen Godel Machine (RQGM), an evolutionary framework for recursive self-improvement under non-stationary utilities. The RQGM makes this possible through controlled utility evolution: search is organized into epochs with a fixed within-epoch evaluation criterion, while the utility can be updated at epoch boundaries, so self-improvement guarantees hold per epoch as the objective evolves across them. We begin by showing that even on verifiable coding tasks, the RQGM improves test pass rate over the prior SOTA by adding a complementary agent-as-a-judge code-review signal. This signal is cheaper and the RQGM uses 1.35x-1.72x fewer tokens. We then turn to scientific paper writing and reviewing, and Olympiad-level proof writing and grading, where the RQGM improves performance over prior self-improving agents: co-evolved writers reach 1.78x-1.86x higher acceptance rates under a diverse agent-as-a-judge panel, while co-evolved graders reach 9% higher ground-truth accuracy. In paper reviewing, the strongest baseline reviewer over-accepts AI-generated papers at up to 1.91x the human rate. The RQGM corrects this by introducing an adversarial objective that discovers reviewers equally stringent on AI and human work.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Red Queen Godel Machine (RQGM), an evolutionary framework enabling recursive self-improvement with non-stationary evaluation criteria. Unlike prior methods assuming fixed verifiers, RQGM allows utility functions to evolve across epochs. Demonstrates improvements in coding tasks (1.35x-1.72x fewer tokens), scientific writing (1.78x-1.86x higher acceptance), proof grading (9% higher accuracy), and adversarial reviewer calibration.
AI.motivation: Prior self-improving agents assume stationary evaluation criteria (fixed verifiers, benchmarks, labeled datasets), ignoring that in natural evolution, species and environments co-adapt. The authors aim to incorporate non-stationary, co-evolving evaluators into recursive self-improvement, enabling dynamic utilities, adversarial objectives, and evolving benchmarks that may surpass static ones.
AI.method: The Red Queen Godel Machine (RQGM) organizes search into epochs, each with a fixed within-epoch evaluation criterion. Utility functions are updated only at epoch boundaries, preserving per-epoch self-improvement guarantees while allowing objectives to evolve across epochs. Applied to coding (agent-as-a-judge code review), scientific writing/reviewing (co-evolved writer-reviewer panels), and Olympiad proof writing/grading (adversarial objectives for reviewer calibration).
AI.result: On coding: RQGM surpasses prior SOTA test pass rates using 1.35x-1.72x fewer tokens via complementary code-review signal. On scientific writing: co-evolved writers achieve 1.78x-1.86x higher acceptance rates under diverse agent-as-judge panels. On proof grading: co-evolved graders reach 9% higher ground-truth accuracy. On reviewing: strongest baseline reviewer over-accepts AI papers at 1.91x human rate; RQGM's adversarial objective yields reviewers equally stringent on AI and human work.
AI.conclusion: Non-stationary utility evolution via the RQGM framework is both feasible and beneficial for recursive self-improvement, enabling agents to co-adapt with their evaluators. This yields practical gains across coding, scientific writing, and mathematical proof domains while addressing evaluator bias through adversarial objective design.

title: Towards Safety-Aware Mutation Testing for Autonomous Driving Systems
summary:
Simulation-based testing is essential for ensuring the safety of Autonomous Driving Systems (ADS), yet the community lacks a systematic criterion for determining when we can safely stop additional test scenario generation. Existing coverage metrics typically focus on individual component reliability or treat the ADS as a black box, failing to capture certain component interactions that cause most ADS accidents. While traditional mutation testing provides a falsifiable measure of test adequacy, directly porting code- and deep learning model-level mutations to the corresponding modules of ADS is insufficient.
  In this vision paper, we propose a paradigm shift toward Safety-Aware Mutation Testing (SAMT). Unlike traditional mutation testing, which creates mutants (i.e., faulty versions of the software under test) by injecting artificial faults into individual components, SAMT systematically injects temporally bounded faults into the messages exchanged between ADS modules to simulate realistic interaction failures. To ensure these mutants represent genuine hazards, we propose deriving mutant generation rules directly from top-down safety engineering frameworks, such as System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA). By embedding systems thinking into the mutation testing pipeline, SAMT provides a rigorous mechanism for evaluating test adequacy, enabling automated scenario generation, and guiding ADS repair. We also outline critical open challenges.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Safety-Aware Mutation Testing (SAMT), a paradigm shift that injects faults into inter-module messages of Autonomous Driving Systems based on safety engineering frameworks like STPA, moving beyond traditional component-level mutation testing to evaluate test adequacy and guide scenario generation.
AI.motivation: Current ADS testing lacks a systematic stopping criterion for scenario generation. Existing coverage metrics fail to capture component interactions responsible for most ADS accidents, and traditional mutation testing—designed for code or deep learning models—does not adequately translate to the modular architecture of ADS.
AI.method: SAMT injects temporally bounded faults into messages exchanged between ADS modules (rather than individual components) to simulate realistic interaction failures. Mutant generation rules are derived from top-down safety engineering frameworks, specifically System-Theoretic Process Analysis (STPA), embedding systems thinking into the mutation testing pipeline.
AI.result: This is a vision paper; no empirical results are reported. The paper outlines the conceptual framework and identifies open challenges for realizing SAMT.
AI.conclusion: SAMT offers a rigorous, falsifiable mechanism for evaluating ADS test adequacy, enables automated scenario generation, and guides ADS repair. The authors call for community engagement on open challenges including mutant generation automation, fidelity validation, and integration with existing ADS development workflows.

title: TinyCNNDeep: Lightweight Attention-Based CNN for EEG Classification of Eye States and Sleep Deprivation
summary: Sleep deprivation impairs vigilance and cognitive function, yet jointly identifying the sleep condition (normal vs deprived) and the eye state (open vs closed) from electroencephalography (EEG) remains underexplored. We address this four-class problem with TinyCNNDeep, a lightweight convolutional neural network that combines residual learning with a Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE) attention module. We convert short multi-channel EEG segments from five physiologically relevant channels (Fp1, Fp2, O1, Oz, O2) into 224x224 grayscale images through per-channel Z-score normalization, min-max scaling, and center padding, enabling 2D convolutions to jointly model inter-channel and temporal structure. On a 35-subject dataset recorded under normal-sleep and sleep-deprivation sessions, TinyCNNDeep attains a subject-wise mean accuracy of 83.69%, outperforming the strongest baseline (Random Forest with combined time-frequency features, 47.66%) by 36.03 percentage points, while three established EEG architectures (EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, DeepConvNet) operate near chance. Per-subject analysis quantifies inter-subject variability, and confusion-matrix inspection shows that residual misclassifications concentrate between eyes-closed states across sleep conditions. These results indicate that an image-based EEG representation paired with residual feature extraction and channel attention provides an accurate and computationally efficient framework for multiclass sleep-related EEG classification under a minimal electrode configuration.

AI.tldr: TinyCNNDeep, a lightweight CNN combining residual learning and Squeeze-and-Excitation attention, classifies four sleep-condition/eye-state combinations from 5-channel EEG images, achieving 83.69% accuracy and substantially outperforming Random Forest (47.66%) and established EEG architectures.
AI.motivation: Joint classification of sleep condition (normal vs. sleep-deprived) and eye state (open vs. closed) from EEG is underexplored. Existing EEG architectures fail on this four-class problem, motivating a lightweight, accurate solution using minimal electrodes.
AI.method: EEG segments from five channels (Fp1, Fp2, O1, Oz, O2) are converted to 224×224 grayscale images via per-channel Z-score normalization, min-max scaling, and center padding.
