A lightweight CNN (TinyCNNDeep) with residual learning and Squeeze-and-Excitation attention performs 2D convolutions to jointly model inter-channel and temporal structure. Evaluated on 35 subjects under normal and sleep-deprived sessions.
AI.result: TinyCNNDeep achieves 83.69% subject-wise mean accuracy, outperforming Random Forest with time-frequency features (47.66%) by 36.03 points. EEGNet, ShallowConvNet, and DeepConvNet perform near chance. Misclassifications concentrate between eyes-closed states across sleep conditions.
AI.conclusion: Image-based EEG representation with residual feature extraction and channel attention enables accurate, computationally efficient multiclass sleep-related EEG classification under a minimal 5-channel montage.

title: CyberChainBench: Can AI Agents Secure Smart Contracts Against Real-World On-Chain Vulnerabilities?
summary: We present CyberChainBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agents on smart contract security across three complementary tasks: vulnerability detection, exploit generation, and patch synthesis. Built from 541 real-world exploit incidents from DeFiHackLabs spanning 9 EVM chains, the benchmark provides end-to-end on-chain evaluation where agents interact with historical blockchain state through isolated evaluation environments orchestrated by Harbor, using tools to read code, trace transactions, and validate exploits on mainnet forks. Each case is anchored to a specific block and includes structured ground truth covering vulnerability type, localization, and attacker profit. Exploits are graded by economic impact on historical forks; patches are validated by replaying historical attacks and legitimate transactions as fail-to-pass test oracles on a proxy-upgradeable subset. We define a five-type vulnerability taxonomy and evaluate multiple agent--model configurations. Results reveal a clear difficulty gradient: the best configuration scores 37.5% on detection, 43.7% on exploitation, but only 23.4% on patching, with the top agent (Codex with GPT-5.5) realizing \$57.4M in total exploit profit across the 200-case exploit set at a cost of $2.39 per case.

AI.tldr: CyberChainBench is a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agents on smart contract security, covering vulnerability detection, exploit generation, and patch synthesis using 541 real-world DeFi exploits across 9 EVM chains. Results show agents perform best at exploitation (43.7%), worse at detection (37.5%), and worst at patching (23.4%).
AI.motivation: Existing benchmarks for LLM-based smart contract security evaluation are limited in scope — they focus on isolated vulnerability detection using synthetic or simplified datasets, lack end-to-end on-chain evaluation with historical state, and do not assess the full pipeline of detection, exploitation, and patching. The authors aim to fill this gap with a realistic, multi-task benchmark grounded in real-world exploit incidents.
AI.method: CyberChainBench is built from 541 real-world exploit incidents from DeFiHackLabs spanning 9 EVM chains. Each case is anchored to a specific block with structured ground truth (vulnerability type, localization, attacker profit). The benchmark provides isolated evaluation environments via Harbor, enabling agents to interact with historical blockchain state on mainnet forks, read code, trace transactions, and validate exploits. Evaluation covers three tasks: (1) vulnerability detection, (2) exploit generation (graded by economic impact on historical forks), and (3) patch synthesis (validated using historical attacks and legitimate transactions as fail-to-pass test oracles on proxy-upgradeable contracts). A five-type vulnerability taxonomy is defined, and multiple agent-model configurations are evaluated.
AI.result: A clear difficulty gradient emerged across tasks: the best configuration achieved 37.5% on detection, 43.7% on exploitation, and 23.4% on patching. The top-performing agent (Codex with GPT-5.5) realized $57.4M in total exploit profit across the 200-case exploit set at a cost of $2.39 per case.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based agents show non-trivial but still limited capability in smart contract security, with exploitation being surprisingly easier than detection and patching being the hardest. The benchmark establishes a rigorous, economically-grounded evaluation framework for future progress in AI-driven smart contract security.

title: Helpfulness Hurts: Domain-Dependent Degradation of Mid-Trained Compassion Values Under Post-Training
summary: Standard post-training pipelines apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) to make language models helpful, but these processes may inadvertently degrade values instilled during pre-training. We investigate whether the domain of post-training data differentially affects the retention of animal compassion values in a Llama 3.1 8B model mid-trained on compassion-oriented synthetic data, using both SFT (helpfulness via Dolly-15k vs. coding via Magicoder-110K) and GRPO (helpfulness via RLHFlow vs. coding via Magicoder), evaluated on the Animal Harm Benchmark (AHB 2.2) and MORU benchmark (Moral Reasoning Under Uncertainty). Helpfulness training significantly degrades animal compassion relative to coding training on AHB (SFT: 35.7% vs. 65.2%; GRPO: 18.7% vs. 32.0%), replicating across two independent helpfulness datasets and two training paradigms. On English MORU items, helpfulness training degrades general moral reasoning by 25.5 percentage points (46.4% vs. 71.9%), a striking gap that rivals the compassion effect in magnitude. However, this effect does not transfer cross-lingually: on the multilingual MORU benchmark, the domain effect disappears (SFT: 52.3% vs. 51.2%). In contrast, the animal compassion effect transfers consistently across languages, with Magicoder's AHB percentage-point gain over the base model 4.5 times larger on non-English items than English items. This divergence suggests that values instilled through mid-training are encoded more deeply and cross-lingually than reasoning improvements from domain-specific post-training. These results suggest that, for labs building on value-laden mid-training, coding-domain post-training may better preserve mid-trained values than helpfulness post-training without harming general reasoning capabilities.

AI.tldr: Post-training on helpfulness data degrades animal compassion values and moral reasoning in a compassion-mid-trained Llama 3.1 8B model, while coding-domain post-training preserves these values. The animal compassion effect transfers cross-lingually, but the moral reasoning degradation does not.
AI.motivation: Standard SFT and RL pipelines aim to make models helpful but may inadvertently erode values (e.g., animal compassion) instilled during pre-training or mid-training. The authors investigate whether the domain of post-training data differentially affects value retention.
AI.method: A Llama 3.1 8B model was mid-trained on compassion-oriented synthetic data. Two post-training paradigms were compared: SFT (helpfulness: Dolly-15k vs. coding: Magicoder-110K) and GRPO (helpfulness: RLHFlow vs. coding: Magicoder). Evaluation used the Animal Harm Benchmark (AHB 2.2) and the MORU benchmark (Moral Reasoning Under Uncertainty), including multilingual variants.
AI.result: Helpfulness training significantly degraded animal compassion vs. coding training on AHB (SFT: 35.7% vs. 65.2%; GRPO: 18.7% vs. 32.0%), replicating across two datasets and paradigms. On English MORU, helpfulness training reduced moral reasoning by 25.5 pp (46.4% vs. 71.9%). However, the moral reasoning domain effect disappeared multilingually (SFT: 52.3% vs. 51.2%), while the animal compassion effect transferred cross-lingually, with Magicoder's AHB gain 4.5× larger on non-English items.
AI.conclusion: Values instilled via mid-training are encoded more deeply and cross-lingually than reasoning improvements from domain-specific post-training. Coding-domain post-training better preserves mid-trained values than helpfulness post-training, without harming general reasoning.

title: Refusal Lives Downstream of Persona in Chat Models
comment: Accepted to the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability workshop
summary: Linear directions in activation space have been identified for both refusal and persona traits in instruction-tuned chat models, but the two have been studied as separate mechanisms. We show they interact: a compliant persona gates refusal. In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we extract a compliant model-persona direction and a refusal direction and intervene on both. Compliant persona steering suppresses refusal -- in Llama, the refusal rate falls from 97% to 2%. Reintroducing the refusal direction partially restores refusal at late layers but not at early ones. Projecting out the persona direction in a late-layer window restores it to baseline; projecting out a random direction does not. Refusal is therefore gated at the late-layer expression stage, downstream of where it is computed. Treating refusal as a single isolated direction misses its dependence on persona.

AI.tldr: This paper reveals that refusal behavior in instruction-tuned chat models is gated by the model's persona: a compliant persona suppresses refusal expression at late layers. Interventions on persona and refusal directions in Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct show they interact causally, not independently.
AI.motivation: Prior work has studied refusal directions and persona directions in activation space as separate, isolated mechanisms. The authors challenge this assumption, hypothesizing that these two directions causally interact — specifically, that the model's adopted persona modulates whether a computed refusal is ultimately expressed.
AI.method: The authors extract a compliant model-persona direction and a refusal direction from Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct using activation steering techniques. They then perform causal interventions: (1) steering toward a compliant persona and measuring refusal rate changes; (2) reintroducing the refusal direction at different layer ranges after persona steering; (3) projecting out the persona direction in late-layer windows and comparing with random-direction ablation as a control.
AI.result: Compliant persona steering drastically suppresses refusal — in Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, refusal rate drops from 97% to 2%. Reintroducing the refusal direction partially restores refusal at late layers but not at early layers. Projecting out the persona direction in a late-layer window restores refusal to baseline levels, while projecting out a random direction has no effect.
AI.conclusion: Refusal is gated at the late-layer expression stage, downstream of where it is computed. Treating refusal as a single isolated direction misses its critical dependence on persona. The two mechanisms should be understood as interacting components of a two-stage process: computation followed by persona-gated expression.

title: Implementation of reinforcement learning in chemical reaction networks: application to phototaxis as curiosity-driven exploration
comment: This paper is accepted as talk at ALIFE 2026 (Waterloo, Canada)
summary: Living systems navigate environments using noisy and incomplete sensory signals. In unicellular algae, phototaxis is often modeled as a mechanistic run--tumble process driven by stimulus--response rules. However, such descriptions overlook how organisms actively sample their environment to reduce sensory ambiguity. From a minimal cognition perspective, we reframe this navigation as a subjective, information-driven sensorimotor process. To this end, we propose a framework linking a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) with biochemical reaction dynamics. Environmental variables are hidden, while the cell updates a minimal internal state from each observation through a memoryless Bayesian step. These internal dynamics balance orienting toward light with exploratory reorientation and can be implemented through Chemical-Reaction-Network Ordinary Differential Equations (CRN--ODEs). Our model includes a biophysical observation process for photoreception and a chemically computable polynomial bound on information gain. Using Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) on 30 experimentally recorded Chlamydomonas trajectories, we infer the behavioral objective consistent with observed phototactic motion and benchmark the resulting dynamics with standard Stochastic Simulation Algorithm (SSA) baselines. Our model reproduces the empirical alignment-to-light distribution, comparable to objective SSA baselines on this dataset. Within this framework, run--tumble alternation emerges as an information-acquisition strategy: tumbling reorients the cell to sample new sensory configurations and resolve sensor ambiguity, demonstrating how intracellular biochemical networks can support adaptive information-seeking behavior in cellular navigation.

AI.tldr: The paper reframes unicellular algal phototaxis not as a mechanistic stimulus-response process but as an information-driven sensorimotor strategy. It introduces a POMDP framework coupled with biochemical reaction dynamics (CRN-ODEs), where the cell updates internal states via memoryless Bayesian updates to balance light-seeking with exploratory reorientation. Using Inverse Reinforcement Learning on 30 Chlamydomonas trajectories, the model reproduces empirical alignment-to-light distributions and reveals that run-tumble alternation serves as an information-acquisition strategy to resolve sensory ambiguity.
AI.motivation: Traditional mechanistic models of algal phototaxis (run-tumble processes) overlook how organisms actively sample their environment to reduce sensory ambiguity. The authors aim to bridge this gap by treating navigation as a subjective, information-driven process grounded in minimal cognition, linking decision-making under uncertainty (POMDP) with biochemically plausible intracellular dynamics.
AI.method: The authors propose a framework that couples a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) with Chemical-Reaction-Network Ordinary Differential Equations (CRN-ODEs). The cell maintains a minimal internal state updated via a memoryless Bayesian step after each observation. A biophysical observation process models photoreception, and a polynomial bound on information gain is derived for chemical computability. Inverse Reinforcement Learning (IRL) is applied to 30 experimentally recorded Chlamydomonas trajectories to infer the behavioral objective, and results are benchmarked against Stochastic Simulation Algorithm (SSA) baselines.
AI.result: The inferred model reproduces the empirical alignment-to-light distribution comparably to objective SSA baselines on the dataset. Within the framework, run-tumble alternation emerges as an adaptive information-acquisition strategy: tumbling reorients the cell to sample new sensory configurations and resolve sensor ambiguity.
AI.conclusion: Run-tumble behavior in cellular phototaxis can be understood as an information-seeking strategy rather than a purely reactive mechanism. Intracellular biochemical networks are capable of supporting adaptive, information-driven navigation, demonstrating a form of minimal cognition where sensory ambiguity is actively resolved through exploratory reorientation.

title: A Shared IPTC Topic Space for Cross-Source Topic Modelling
summary: Comparing topic attention across different media is hindered by a fundamental modelling problem: topic models fitted separately to each corpus produce corpus-specific topic spaces that cannot be aligned directly. This paper presents a reproducible framework that places corpora in a single shared topic space defined by a taxonomy. Discovered topics are obtained with guided BERTopic, scored against the ninety-four IPTC Media Topics' taxonomy topics (level-1) through weighted keyword and target centroids, and then collapsed upward to seventeen IPTC parent topics by a maximum-similarity rule. The framework was developed and selected on a controlled New York Times 2011 corpus through a narrowing sequence: a broad model screen, a focused mapping refinement, a strict finalist comparison, a target-construction ablation, and a threshold calibration. In this corpus, the guided family retained substantially stronger mapped coverage than a zero-shot benchmark under stricter assignment thresholds, a parent-enriched target construction improved both coverage and parent consistency, and coverage declined gradually rather than collapsing as the assignment threshold was tightened. The contribution is an externally anchored method for constructing a shared topic space that enables reproducible cross-source topic comparison.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a reproducible framework that maps topics from different corpora into a single shared topic space using the IPTC Media Topics taxonomy, enabling cross-source topic comparison via guided BERTopic with a parent-enriched matching strategy.
AI.motivation: Cross-media topic comparison is hindered by the incomparability of corpus-specific topic spaces produced by independently fitted topic models. There is a need for an externally anchored method that can place disparate corpora into a common, interpretable topic space to enable reproducible cross-source analysis.
AI.method: The framework uses guided BERTopic to discover topics, then scores them against the 94 level-1 IPTC Media Topics taxonomy topics using weighted keyword and target centroids. Topics are collapsed upward to 17 parent IPTC topics via a maximum-similarity rule. The approach was developed through a narrowing sequence on a controlled NYT 2011 corpus: broad model screening, focused mapping refinement, strict finalist comparison, target-construction ablation, and threshold calibration.
AI.result: Guided models retained substantially stronger mapped coverage than a zero-shot benchmark under stricter assignment thresholds. A parent-enriched target construction improved both coverage and parent consistency. Coverage declined gradually rather than collapsing as the assignment threshold was tightened.
AI.conclusion: The framework provides an externally anchored, reproducible method for constructing a shared topic space that enables principled cross-source topic comparison, with the IPTC taxonomy serving as a stable reference for alignment.

title: Instruction Bleed: Cross-Module Interference in Prompt-Composed Agentic Systems
comment: 8 pages, 2 tables. Accepted to the ICML 2026 Workshop on Failure Modes in Agentic AI (FAGEN), Seoul, South Korea
summary: Practitioners of prompt-composed agentic systems report a recurring failure mode: editing one prompt module silently shifts the behavior of others despite no shared variable or executable dependency. We formalize this as compositional behavioral leakage (CBL): interference between modules sharing a context window. CBL is enabled by architectural non-isolation: transformer self-attention provides no formal boundary between concatenated modules. We probe CBL on a deployed job-evaluation agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6, 144 trials) through a reusable three-channel protocol that perturbs non-focal modules along volume, content, and form. Only the content channel produces a detectable paired effect (Cohen's d = 0.63, bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero); no recommendation flipped -- a sub-threshold regime invisible to standard QA but compounding across the thousands of decisions a deployed agent makes. CBL is orthogonal to known agent-failure axes (adversarial injection, cognitive degradation, multi-agent fault propagation, privacy leakage). We contribute an operational definition, a reusable protocol, a falsifiable prediction set, and a system-class characterization, establishing cross-module interference measurement as a requirement for prompt-composed agent evaluation.

AI.tldr: Compositional Behavioral Leakage (CBL) is formalized as interference between prompt modules sharing a transformer context window due to architectural non-isolation in self-attention. A three-channel perturbation protocol on a deployed agent reveals sub-threshold but compounding effects, establishing cross-module interference measurement as a necessary evaluation requirement.
AI.motivation: Practitioners observe a recurring failure mode in prompt-composed agentic systems: editing one prompt module silently alters the behavior of other modules despite no explicit dependencies. This phenomenon lacks formal definition and measurement methodology, representing an unaddressed failure axis distinct from known issues like adversarial injection or multi-agent fault propagation.
AI.method: The authors formalize CBL and design a reusable three-channel perturbation protocol probing non-focal modules along volume (prompt length), content (semantic meaning), and form (structural formatting) dimensions. They deploy this on a job-evaluation agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6) across 144 trials, using paired experimental design with Cohen's d effect size and bootstrap confidence intervals.
AI.result: Only the content channel produced a detectable paired effect (Cohen's d = 0.63, bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero). No individual recommendation flipped, indicating a sub-threshold regime invisible to standard QA evaluation but potentially compounding across thousands of agent decisions in deployment.
AI.conclusion: CBL is orthogonal to known agent-failure axes. The authors contribute an operational definition, a reusable measurement protocol, a falsifiable prediction set, and a system-class characterization, arguing that cross-module interference measurement must become a standard requirement in prompt-composed agent evaluation.

title: An Empirical Study of LLM-Generated Specifications for VeriFast
summary: Static verification tools can assure industrial scale software, but require significant human labor to write specifications. This is particularly true of static verifiers based on separation logic (SL verifiers), which excel at verifying heapmanipulating programs, but require many complex auxiliary specifications to reason about heap structure. Recent work applies large language models (LLMs) to generate code, tests, and proofs, including specifications for verifiers, but mostly targeting non-SL verifiers. To address this gap, this paper thoroughly evaluates how well LLMs perform when prompted to generate specifications for verifying 303 C functions with the SL verifier VeriFast. We explored eight prompting approaches, ten LLMs, and three input types in two stages. Quantitative and qualitative analyses are used to assess the LLM-generated code and specifications for functional behavior, verifiability and errors. The results show that LLMs preserve functional behavior in source code and specifications (both over 91%), but achieve modest verification success (31.4%). Using Gemini 2.5 Pro and providing formal contracts lead to higher success rates in our setting. Moreover, most errors (94%) come from LLMs' mistakes in the domainspecific knowledge of SL verifiers such as VeriFast. These findings provide guidance for optimizing LLM-generated specifications for SL verifiers.

AI.tldr: This paper conducts a comprehensive empirical evaluation of how well large language models (LLMs) can generate specifications for the separation logic verifier VeriFast, testing 303 C functions across 8 prompting approaches, 10 LLMs, and 3 input types. LLMs preserve functional behavior well (91%+) but achieve only 31.4% verification success, with 94% of errors stemming from domain-specific SL verifier knowledge gaps.
AI.motivation: Static verifiers based on separation logic (SL) require substantial manual effort to write complex auxiliary specifications for heap-manipulating programs. While LLMs have shown promise in generating specifications for non-SL verifiers, their effectiveness for SL verifiers like VeriFast remains largely unexplored, creating a significant gap that this work aims to address.
AI.method: The authors evaluated LLM-generated specifications for 303 C functions targeting the VeriFast SL verifier. They systematically explored 8 prompting approaches (varying in context and guidance), 10 different LLMs, and 3 input types across two stages. Both quantitative metrics (functional correctness, verifiability rates, error categorization) and qualitative analyses were employed to assess the generated code and specifications.
AI.result: LLMs preserve functional behavior in both source code and specifications at rates exceeding 91%. However, overall verification success is modest at 31.4%. Gemini 2.5 Pro combined with formal contracts yielded the highest success rates. Critically, 94% of errors originate from LLMs' lack of domain-specific knowledge about SL verifiers like VeriFast, rather than general programming or specification errors.
AI.conclusion: LLMs show promise for automating specification generation for SL verifiers, but their current limitations in domain-specific SL knowledge represent a major bottleneck. The findings offer concrete guidance for optimizing future LLM-based approaches to SL verifier specification generation, suggesting that targeted training or prompting strategies addressing SL-specific concepts could yield significant improvements.

title: DanceDuo: Bridging Human Movement and AI Choreography
summary: In recent years, advancements in deep learning and generative models have revolutionized music-driven dance generation. This paper introduces a novel platform, namely DanceDuo, leveraging diffusion models to generate AI-choreographed dance sequences synchronized with a variety of music genres, to encourage dancing practice. The system allows users to interact with AI by selecting music tracks, humanoid models, and importing personal dance videos for comparison, fostering a rich and engaging user experience. DanceDuo not only offers dance generation but also integrates human pose estimation models to provide users with insightful comparisons of their own performances with AI-generated sequences. We conducted a comprehensive user study, revealing that users found the interface intuitive, with particular praise for the dance comparison feature. Our DanceDuo contributes significantly to the integration of AI in dance choreography, offering novel avenues for both recreational and professional applications.

AI.tldr: DanceDuo is an interactive platform that uses diffusion models to generate AI-choreographed dance sequences synchronized with music, and integrates pose estimation to allow users to compare their own dance performances against AI-generated sequences.
AI.motivation: To leverage deep learning advances in music-driven dance generation to create an engaging, interactive platform that encourages dancing practice through AI-choreographed sequences and performance comparison.
AI.method: The system employs diffusion models for music-synchronized dance generation, supports multiple music genres and humanoid models, and integrates human pose estimation to enable side-by-side comparison between user-imported dance videos and AI-generated dance sequences.
AI.result: A comprehensive user study demonstrated that users found the interface intuitive, with the dance comparison feature receiving particular praise.
AI.conclusion: DanceDuo makes a significant contribution to AI-integrated dance choreography, opening novel avenues for both recreational dancing practice and professional applications.

title: Expecting (Targeted Ads)? Network Analysis of User Health Data Leakage in Fertility Tracking Apps
summary: While human factors in the privacy of fertility tracking apps -- health trackers that record user's menstrual or pregnancy data -- has been the subject of extensive study, little attention has been paid to the technical aspects of apps' data handling practices. We conduct a network-based measurement study of a corpus of 20 Android fertility tracking apps from the Google Play Store, focusing on how user data is shared with third party advertising services. After systematizing app features, we conduct a series of standardized user interactions across all apps in an environment that records TLS-stripped network traffic. In a subset of apps (n=5) we identify explicit leakage of user health data as well implicit leakage through highly targeted contextual advertising URL's. Equally importantly, we observe additional apps that use an ad-based monetization model without apparent leakage of user data, as well as several apps the interact only minimally with ad services. These findings provide technical grounding for widespread user concerns, but also underscore the importance of consumer choice in the privacy implications of app-based fertility tracking.

AI.tldr: A network traffic analysis of 20 Android fertility tracking apps reveals that while some apps leak sensitive health data (both explicitly and implicitly via targeted ad URLs) to third-party advertisers, others using ad-based monetization show no apparent leakage, highlighting both privacy risks and the role of consumer choice.
AI.motivation: Prior research on fertility tracking app privacy has focused heavily on human factors (user perceptions, behaviors) while neglecting the technical data handling practices of the apps themselves. The authors aim to fill this gap by empirically measuring how these apps actually share user data with third-party advertising services.
AI.method: The authors collected a corpus of 20 Android fertility tracking apps from the Google Play Store, systematized their features, and conducted standardized user interactions across all apps within an instrumented environment that captures TLS-stripped network traffic. They analyzed the resulting network traces for evidence of data sharing with third-party advertising domains.
AI.result: In 5 of the 20 apps, the authors identified explicit leakage of user health data and implicit leakage via highly contextual advertising URLs. However, several other apps employing ad-based monetization showed no apparent data leakage, and some apps interacted only minimally with advertising services.
AI.conclusion: The findings provide empirical, technical evidence substantiating widespread user privacy concerns, while also demonstrating that ad-supported fertility tracking need not entail data leakage — underscoring the importance of consumer choice in navigating the privacy landscape of these apps.

title: Investigating LLM's Problem Solving Capability -- a Study on Statics Questions
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly influenced many aspects of society, particularly education, due to their demonstrated ability to complete assignments and examinations across a wide range of subjects. Although prior studies have examined the educational impact of LLMs, much of the existing work relies on public or open problem datasets and lacks topic-specific analysis. In engineering education, especially within mechanical engineering, systematic investigations of LLM performance on specific problem types remain limited. Instead of using traditional methods that directly ask textbook questions to an LLM tool, our study adopts a model distillation process to evaluate LLM capabilities in solving statics problems. By distilling ChatGPT, we extracted 25 text-only statics questions and further constructed two additional datasets by adding diagrams and modifying their numerical values. Experimental results show that while LLMs perform well on text-only statics problems, their accuracy decreases when diagrams are introduced and the problems require multi-step reasoning. Further analysis suggests that this performance drop is not primarily caused by limitations in image recognition, but rather by difficulties in multi-step reasoning and in consistently applying extracted visual information across successive solution stages.

AI.tldr: LLMs perform well on text-only statics problems but struggle when diagrams are added, primarily due to multi-step reasoning difficulties rather than image recognition limitations.
AI.motivation: Prior LLM-in-education studies rely on public/open datasets and lack topic-specific analysis, particularly in mechanical engineering statics. This work fills that gap.
AI.method: Model distillation: extracted 25 text-only statics questions from ChatGPT; constructed two additional datasets by adding diagrams and modifying numerical values; evaluated LLM performance across these three conditions.
AI.result: LLM accuracy degrades significantly when diagrams are introduced and multi-step reasoning is required. The performance drop is attributed to difficulties in multi-step reasoning and consistent application of extracted visual information — not primarily image recognition failures.
AI.conclusion: LLMs face fundamental challenges with multi-step reasoning and integrating visual information across solution stages in statics problems, suggesting current limitations for engineering education applications.

title: AlgoEvolve: LLM-driven Meta-evolution of Algorithmic Trading Programs
summary: Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can act as semantic mutation operators for the evolutionary discovery of programs and proofs. Most current applications focus on static coding benchmarks. We extend this paradigm to algorithmic trading. This domain is uniquely challenging because it is noisy, non-stationary, and highly discontinuous. We present AlgoEvolve, an LLM-driven evolutionary framework that generates, evaluates, and iteratively improves executable trading strategies. These strategies are expressed as Python code and evaluated through a rigorous testing protocol. Across multiple experiments, the system exhibits emergent regime-adaptive strategy logic, including autonomous shifts in trading rules. We further introduce a meta-evolutionary outer loop that evolves the prompts guiding program synthesis in the inner loop. This outer loop discovers improved search heuristics. These heuristics balance exploration and exploitation while reducing zero-trade failures. They consistently outperform initial human-designed instructions. The results demonstrate that LLM-based semantic evolution provides a viable approach for continual program synthesis in complex environments.

AI.tldr: AlgoEvolve uses LLMs as semantic mutation operators in an evolutionary framework to automatically generate and improve algorithmic trading strategies, with a meta-evolutionary outer loop that evolves the prompts themselves, outperforming human-designed instructions.
AI.motivation: Extend LLM-driven evolutionary program synthesis beyond static coding benchmarks into complex, noisy, non-stationary, and discontinuous domains — specifically algorithmic trading — where continual adaptation is critical.
AI.method: AlgoEvolve, an LLM-driven evolutionary framework that (1) generates executable Python trading strategies via LLM semantic mutations, (2) evaluates them through rigorous testing, and (3) employs a meta-evolutionary outer loop that evolves the prompts/instructions guiding inner-loop program synthesis, thereby discovering improved search heuristics.
AI.result: Evolved strategies exhibit emergent regime-adaptive behavior with autonomous shifts in trading rules. The meta-evolutionary outer loop discovers heuristics that better balance exploration-exploitation, reduce zero-trade failures, and consistently outperform initial human-designed prompts.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based semantic evolution is a viable approach for continual program synthesis in complex, dynamic environments, going beyond static benchmarks to domains requiring ongoing adaptation.

title: Neural Architecture Search for Generative Adversarial Networks: A Comprehensive Review and Critical Analysis
summary: Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has emerged as a pivotal technique in optimizing the design of Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), automating the search for effective architectures while addressing the challenges inherent in manual design. This paper provides a comprehensive review of NAS methods applied to GANs, categorizing and comparing various approaches based on criteria such as search strategies, evaluation metrics, and performance outcomes. The review highlights the benefits of NAS in improving GAN performance, stability, and efficiency, while also identifying limitations and areas for future research. Key findings include the superiority of evolutionary algorithms and gradient-based methods in certain contexts, the importance of robust evaluation metrics beyond traditional scores like Inception Score (IS) and Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), and the need for diverse datasets in assessing GAN performance. By presenting a structured comparison of existing NAS-GAN techniques, this paper aims to guide researchers in developing more effective NAS methods and advancing the field of GANs.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive review of Neural Architecture Search (NAS) methods applied to GANs, categorizing approaches by search strategies and evaluation metrics. The paper finds evolutionary algorithms and gradient-based methods particularly effective, underscores the need for robust evaluation metrics beyond IS and FID, and calls for more diverse datasets in GAN assessment.
AI.motivation: Manual design of GAN architectures is challenging and suboptimal. NAS offers automation to discover effective GAN architectures, but the landscape of NAS-GAN methods is fragmented. The paper aims to systematically categorize, compare, and evaluate existing NAS approaches for GANs to guide future research.
AI.method: The authors conduct a structured literature review, categorizing NAS-GAN approaches based on search strategies (e.g., evolutionary algorithms, gradient-based methods, reinforcement learning), evaluation metrics employed, and reported performance outcomes. They then perform a comparative analysis across these dimensions.
AI.result: Evolutionary algorithms and gradient-based NAS methods show superiority in specific contexts. Traditional metrics like Inception Score (IS) and Fréchet Inception Distance (FID) are insufficient alone; robust, multi-faceted evaluation metrics are essential. Diverse datasets are needed for fair and comprehensive GAN performance assessment.
AI.conclusion: NAS significantly benefits GAN performance, stability, and efficiency. The structured comparison serves as a guide for developing more effective NAS-GAN methods. Future work should address current limitations, adopt richer evaluation protocols, and test across more diverse datasets.

title: TriPAH: Imbalance-Aware Tri-Prompt Affinity Hashing for Cross-Modal Medical Retrieval
summary: In the era of big medical data, efficient cross-modal retrieval is pivotal for evidence-based diagnosis and large-scale case management. Cross-modal medical hashing retrieval aims to enable efficient image-text search and support downstream tasks such as case-based reasoning and decision support by learning compact, semantically aligned binary codes. However, current methods suffer from semantic fragmentation due to noisy clinical language, long-tailed labels, and brittle quantization that weakens alignment. We propose TriPAH, a Tri-Prompt Affinity Hashing framework. TriPAH synthesizes ontology-grounded, patient-level prompts conditioned on normalized clinical cues to yield low-noise textual representations for initial alignment. A lightweight prompt-token mixer performs hierarchical, multi-granularity alignment and produces quantization-ready features under an asymmetric multi-task objective coupling multi-positive contrastive alignment, imbalance-aware classification, and progressive quantization regularization. A patient-level consistency module further stabilizes codes across complementary views. Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that TriPAH significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods.

AI.tldr: TriPAH is a cross-modal medical hashing framework that uses ontology-grounded patient-level prompts, hierarchical multi-granularity alignment, and a multi-task objective with consistency regularization to produce semantically aligned binary codes, outperforming state-of-the-art methods on three public datasets.
AI.motivation: Current cross-modal medical hashing methods suffer from semantic fragmentation caused by noisy clinical language, long-tailed label distributions, and brittle quantization, which collectively weaken image-text semantic alignment. There is a need for robust hashing that can handle these real-world clinical data challenges for efficient cross-modal retrieval in evidence-based diagnosis.
AI.method: TriPAH consists of: (1) ontology-grounded, patient-level prompt synthesis conditioned on normalized clinical cues to produce low-noise textual representations; (2) a lightweight prompt-token mixer performing hierarchical multi-granularity alignment yielding quantization-ready features; (3) an asymmetric multi-task objective coupling multi-positive contrastive alignment, imbalance-aware classification, and progressive quantization regularization; and (4) a patient-level consistency module that stabilizes hash codes across complementary views.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on three public datasets demonstrate that TriPAH significantly outperforms state-of-the-art cross-modal medical hashing methods.
AI.conclusion: TriPAH effectively addresses semantic fragmentation in medical cross-modal hashing through prompt-based noise reduction, hierarchical alignment, and multi-task learning, establishing a new state-of-the-art for efficient image-text retrieval in clinical settings.

title: SOLAR: AI-Powered Speed-of-Light Performance Analysis
summary: How fast could a deep-learning model run on target hardware, and how far is today's implementation from that limit? These questions are central to software, hardware, and algorithm optimizations. Speed-of-Light (SOL) analysis answers them by computing a workload's theoretical minimum execution time on a given architecture. Yet deriving SOL bounds remains manual, error-prone, and disconnected from rapid model development. To close this gap, we introduce SOLAR, a framework that automatically derives validated SOL bounds from PyTorch and JAX source code. SOLAR leverages both generative and deterministic components in its flow: an LLM frontend translates any source programs into an executable Affine Loop IR, validated by output comparison; a deterministic flow lifts the IR into an einsum graph; and an analytical backend computes unfused, fused, and cache-aware SOL bounds. SOLAR provides comprehensive operator and language coverage, produces validated bounds with zero observed SOL violations, and offers multi-fidelity analysis that tightens bounds and surfaces optimization insights. We evaluate SOLAR across KernelBench, JAX/Flax models, and robotics workloads. These experiments demonstrate four use cases: headroom analysis at multiple fidelity levels, identifying optimization opportunities, cross-platform exploration, and inverse-roofline hardware provisioning.

AI.tldr: SOLAR is a framework that automatically derives validated Speed-of-Light (SOL) bounds — the theoretical minimum execution time of a deep-learning workload — directly from PyTorch/JAX source code. It uses an LLM frontend to translate programs into an Affine Loop IR, then deterministically lifts this to an einsum graph for analytical bound computation at multiple fidelity levels (unfused, fused, cache-aware), enabling headroom analysis, optimization identification, and hardware provisioning.
AI.motivation: Speed-of-Light analysis is essential for understanding hardware-software gaps and guiding optimization, but manually deriving SOL bounds is labor-intensive, error-prone, and decoupled from the rapid model development cycle. There is no prior automated tool that takes arbitrary PyTorch/JAX source code and produces validated, multi-fidelity SOL bounds.
AI.method: SOLAR employs a hybrid flow: (1) an LLM-based frontend translates PyTorch/JAX source code into an executable Affine Loop IR, with validation via output comparison against the original program; (2) a deterministic flow lifts this IR into an einsum graph capturing the workload's compute and data movement in a hardware-agnostic form; (3) an analytical backend computes SOL bounds at three fidelity tiers — unfused (peak FLOPs/memory bandwidth), fused (reuse-aware), and cache-aware (hierarchy-sensitive). The bounds are empirically validated to have zero observed violations.
AI.result: SOLAR was evaluated on KernelBench (level 1 & 2), JAX/Flax models (including ViT, ResNet), and robotics workloads. It demonstrated comprehensive operator and language coverage, produced validated bounds with zero observed SOL violations, and enabled four key use cases: (1) multi-fidelity headroom analysis, (2) identifying optimization opportunities, (3) cross-platform exploration, and (4) inverse-roofline hardware provisioning.
AI.conclusion: SOLAR closes the gap between SOL analysis and modern ML development by providing an automated, validated, and multi-fidelity SOL derivation pipeline directly from source code. It surfaces actionable optimization insights and can guide both software tuning and hardware design decisions.

title: Evaluation-Strategy Gap in Fault Diagnosis of Deep Learning Programs
comment: Accepted research track paper in the 42nd IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME 2026)
summary: Deep Learning (DL) programs can fail during training for many reasons, and diagnosing the cause is a costly and time-consuming maintenance task. Techniques for diagnosing such failures are commonly assessed using within-program cross-validation, which may be inadequate for deployment settings involving previously unseen programs. It is therefore necessary to assess how performance differs across these settings and to identify the causes of any performance gap in established fault diagnosis techniques for DL. We investigate this gap using DynFault, a corpus of 5,542 fault-injected training traces from 38 real-world DL programs. We found a gap of 0.190 in balanced accuracy for existing fault diagnosis techniques between within-program evaluation and holding out whole programs. We also found the gap comes from program-level structure in the features, which led us to examine two runtime feature sets, curvature features and optimizer features, and their behavior on unseen programs. We found that curvature features are useful for instability detection on unseen programs, while optimizer and activation features help only on programs seen during training.

AI.tldr: Existing DL fault diagnosis techniques show a significant performance gap (0.190 balanced accuracy drop) when evaluated on unseen programs versus within-program cross-validation. The gap stems from program-level feature structure: curvature features generalize to unseen programs for instability detection, while optimizer and activation features are program-specific.
AI.motivation: DL training failures are costly to diagnose, and current fault diagnosis techniques are typically evaluated using within-program cross-validation, which may not reflect real-world deployment where entirely new, unseen programs are encountered. Understanding how and why performance degrades across these settings is critical for building robust diagnostic tools.
AI.method: The authors constructed DynFault, a corpus of 5,542 fault-injected training traces from 38 real-world DL programs. They evaluated existing fault diagnosis techniques under two evaluation regimes: within-program cross-validation and leave-one-program-out (holding out entire programs). They then analyzed the performance gap by examining program-level feature structure, specifically comparing curvature features, optimizer features, and activation features across the two settings.
AI.result: A performance gap of 0.190 in balanced accuracy exists between within-program evaluation and unseen-program evaluation. Curvature features prove effective for detecting training instability on unseen programs, whereas optimizer and activation features only provide benefit when the program was seen during training, indicating they capture program-specific rather than generalizable diagnostic signals.
AI.conclusion: The evaluation protocol for DL fault diagnosis techniques must account for cross-program generalization. Curvature features are recommended for building diagnostic tools that must work on previously unseen programs, while reliance on optimizer/activation features should be limited to settings where the target program is known a priori.

title: Budget-Aware Keyboardless Interaction
summary: Interacting with computers typically relies on traditional input devices such as keyboards, mice, and monitors, which can be cumbersome for users seeking greater mobility. Virtual keyboards have been explored to address these limitations, but they often involve complex setups or expensive equipment. This paper proposes a novel virtual keyboard system that leverages only a standard camera and a paper with a printed keyboard layout. Unlike previous methods requiring complex calibration or special lighting conditions, our approach can work on standard environment using modern computer vision technologies. Combining modern segmentation and detection models with traditional image processing algorithms, we efficiently identify the keyboard region. Touch detection is performed using an algorithm analyzing the color of the user's fingernail. Experiments demonstrated a promising results our proposed solution of keyboard and keystroke detection for practical applications. Participants attended our user study also found the proposed system interesting.

AI.tldr: A virtual keyboard system using only a standard camera and a printed paper keyboard, employing computer vision for keyboard region detection and fingernail color analysis for touch detection.
AI.motivation: Traditional input devices (keyboards, mice, monitors) limit user mobility. Existing virtual keyboard solutions are hampered by complex calibration, expensive hardware, or special lighting requirements, motivating a simpler, low-cost alternative.
AI.method: The system uses a standard camera and a printed keyboard layout on paper. Modern segmentation and detection models are combined with traditional image processing algorithms to identify the keyboard region. Keystroke detection is performed by analyzing the color of the user's fingernail to determine touch events.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrated promising results for both keyboard detection and keystroke detection in practical applications. A user study was conducted, and participants found the proposed system interesting.
AI.conclusion: The proposed low-cost, calibration-free virtual keyboard system is viable for practical use and well-received by users, offering a more mobile input alternative without requiring specialized equipment.

title: TEMPO-Diffusion: Temporally Exposed Malicious Poisoning of Diffusion Models
summary: Noise-based backdoor attacks on diffusion models typically rely on input-time trigger injection, untargeted activation, and out-of-distribution target generation. Such assumptions reduce both the stealthiness and the practical relevance of these attacks. In this work, we present TEMPO-Diffusion, a targeted backdoor framework that localizes the malicious distribution shift to a temporal, in-distribution exposure. TEMPO-Diffusion supports: (i) targeted attacks on and to specific classes, (ii) multiple sub-image backdoors that reconstruct specific features within multiple, different output images and at multiple locations, and (iii) in-painting with time-conditioned triggers. To study relevant, practical security concerns in leveraging backdoored diffusion models for synthetic training data, we also introduce CALISA: a balanced, region-aware traffic-sign dataset emphasizing Canadian and U.S. road signs. Across CIFAR10, GTSRB, and CALISA, our experiments show that TEMPO-Diffusion can reliably poison class-specific synthetic data generation and induce high attack success rates in downstream classifiers trained on that data.

AI.tldr: TEMPO-Diffusion introduces a targeted backdoor attack on diffusion models using temporal, in-distribution triggers rather than input-time injection, enabling class-specific poisoning, multi-feature sub-image backdoors, and time-conditioned in-painting, with demonstrated high attack success rates on downstream classifiers.
AI.motivation: Existing noise-based backdoor attacks on diffusion models suffer from three limitations: reliance on input-time trigger injection, untargeted activation, and out-of-distribution target generation. These assumptions undermine stealthiness and practical relevance, motivating the need for a more realistic, targeted backdoor framework.
AI.method: TEMPO-Diffusion localizes the malicious distribution shift to a temporal, in-distribution exposure phase. It supports: (i) targeted class-to-class attacks, (ii) multiple sub-image backdoors that reconstruct specific features across multiple output images and locations, and (iii) time-conditioned trigger in-painting. The authors also introduce CALISA, a balanced, region-aware traffic-sign dataset covering Canadian and U.S. road signs, for evaluating practical security concerns in synthetic data generation.
AI.result: Experiments on CIFAR-10, GTSRB, and CALISA demonstrate that TEMPO-Diffusion reliably poisons class-specific synthetic data generation and induces high attack success rates in downstream classifiers trained on the poisoned synthetic data.
AI.conclusion: TEMPO-Diffusion demonstrates that temporal, in-distribution backdoor injection is both feasible and highly effective against diffusion models, raising significant security concerns for pipelines that rely on diffusion-generated synthetic training data.

title: Assert, don't describe: Linguistic features that shift LLM reasoning about animal welfare
summary: Animal-welfare advocates produce a lot of writing, and increasingly that writing trains the language models that millions of people then ask about animal welfare. Using vocabulary-matched stance-contrast probes on a held-out animal-welfare benchmark, we measure how each of ten linguistic features changes Llama-3.2-1B's preference for pro-animal-welfare reasoning when used as fine-tuning data. Eight of the ten features produce statistically significant shifts. Seven move the model toward stronger pro-animal-welfare reasoning: assertive certainty, explicit moral vocabulary, emotion words, evaluative claims, narrative structure, depicted harm severity, and immediate temporal framing. Two move it the other way: hedged language and concrete sensory description both dilute the pro-animal-welfare stance. First-person perspective has no statistically significant effect. The practical recommendation for anyone writing animal-welfare text that may end up in LLM training corpora: assert a position rather than describe a scene neutrally. The features that shift the model are the ones that make the writer's position explicit; the features that dilute it hold animal-welfare content but withhold stance.

AI.tldr: Using controlled probes on a held-out benchmark, the study measures how ten linguistic features in fine-tuning data shift Llama-3.2-1B's stance on animal welfare. Seven features (assertive certainty, moral vocabulary, emotion words, evaluative claims, narrative, depicted harm severity, immediate temporal framing) strengthen pro-animal-welfare reasoning; two (hedged language, concrete sensory description) weaken it; first-person perspective has no effect. The core insight: making the writer's stance explicit drives the shift.
AI.motivation: Animal-welfare advocates produce substantial text that increasingly trains LLMs, yet no systematic understanding exists of which linguistic features in this writing causally influence model stance on animal welfare. The authors aim to provide empirical, actionable guidance for advocates whose content may enter training corpora.
AI.method: The authors employ vocabulary-matched stance-contrast probes on a held-out animal-welfare benchmark. They fine-tune Llama-3.2-1B on texts embodying each of ten distinct linguistic features and measure the resulting shift in the model's preference for pro-animal-welfare reasoning relative to a baseline.
AI.result: Eight of ten features produce statistically significant shifts. Seven strengthen the pro-animal-welfare stance: assertive certainty, explicit moral vocabulary, emotion words, evaluative claims, narrative structure, depicted harm severity, and immediate temporal framing. Two weaken it: hedged language and concrete sensory description. First-person perspective shows no significant effect.
AI.conclusion: The features that amplify pro-animal-welfare reasoning are those that make the writer's evaluative stance explicit, while features that withhold stance (neutral description, hedging) dilute it. The practical takeaway: advocates should assert a position rather than describe a scene neutrally when writing text likely to enter LLM training corpora.

title: KG-TRACE: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Mechanistic Grounding in Antimicrobial Resistance Prediction
summary:
While WGS-based AMR prediction has reached high accuracy, existing models lack a mechanism to ground neural attributions in established biological pathways. We present KG-TRACE, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that integrates the WHO mutation knowledge graph (KG) as a structured biological constraint on a neural genomic model. Unlike existing methods that learn statistical patterns in isolation, KG-TRACE fuses genomic features and RotatE-based KG embeddings through a learned epistemic trust gate, dynamically weighting neural evidence against symbolic biological knowledge.
  Evaluated on the CRyPTIC M. tuberculosis cohort, KG-TRACE achieves an AUROC of 0.9760 for isoniazid, achieving competitive accuracy while its primary value lies in symbolic grounding, not predictive uplift. More importantly, we introduce the Biological Grounding Ratio (BGR), a dataset-level metric that quantifies alignment between neural attributions and established biology. Our framework achieves a 92.5% symbolic coverage of isoniazid-resistant predictions and effectively identifies MDR co-occurrence artifacts by issuing laboratory follow-up flags for 'UNCERTAIN' cases. We demonstrate that neuro-symbolic grounding provides a verifiable audit trail for clinicians, bridging the gap between predictive accuracy and clinical trust.

AI.tldr: KG-TRACE is a neuro-symbolic framework for AMR prediction that grounds neural model attributions in the WHO mutation knowledge graph, achieving competitive accuracy (AUROC 0.9760 for isoniazid) while introducing the Biological Grounding Ratio (BGR) to quantify alignment between model explanations and established biology, thereby providing verifiable audit trails for clinical trust.
AI.motivation: Current WGS-based antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prediction models achieve high accuracy but operate as black boxes, learning statistical patterns without grounding their attributions in established biological pathways. This lack of biological grounding undermines clinical trust and interpretability, creating a gap between predictive performance and actionable, verifiable clinical decision support.
AI.method: KG-TRACE is a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates the WHO mutation knowledge graph (KG) as a structured biological constraint on a neural genomic model. It fuses genomic features with RotatE-based KG embeddings through a learned epistemic trust gate, which dynamically weights neural evidence against symbolic biological knowledge. The framework also introduces the Biological Grounding Ratio (BGR), a dataset-level metric quantifying alignment between neural attributions and known biology, and flags uncertain cases for laboratory follow-up.
AI.result: Evaluated on the CRyPTIC M. tuberculosis cohort, KG-TRACE achieves an AUROC of 0.9760 for isoniazid resistance prediction, competitive with existing methods. The framework attains 92.5% symbolic coverage of isoniazid-resistant predictions and successfully identifies MDR co-occurrence artifacts by issuing follow-up flags for uncertain cases.
AI.conclusion: Neuro-symbolic grounding, as implemented in KG-TRACE, provides a verifiable audit trail for clinicians, effectively bridging the gap between predictive accuracy and clinical trust in AMR prediction without sacrificing performance.

title: UniFormer: Efficient and Unified Model-Centric Scaling for Industrial Recommendation
summary: Recently, substantial progress has been made in industrial recommendation through component-centric model scaling, where individual components such as behavior modeling, feature interaction, or task modeling are independently scaled to improve model capacity. Although recent methods such as HyFormer and OneTrans further explore cross-module co-scaling by jointly modeling behavior and interaction, their designs are still confined to the feature space and lack a unified model-centric scaling framework over the overall modeling space. In this paper, we propose UniFormer, an efficient and unified model-centric scaling framework for industrial recommender systems. To improve efficiency, UniFormer decomposes the overall modeling space into feature and task spaces, which are modeled by stacked Feature-space Interaction Modules and Task-space Interaction Modules, respectively. Moreover, UniFormer introduces semantic-based tokenization scheme to enable user-item decoupling, thereby achieving request-level inference acceleration. To prevent preference collapse, UniFormer employs multi-sequence cross-attention to separately capture heterogeneous behavior patterns, followed by the self-attention to enhance interaction modeling. Besides, dedicated multi-view FFNs are introduced to support flexible and scalable parameter scaling across different modeling components. Extensive online A/B testing in two production scenarios, Kuaishou and Kuaishou Lite, shows that UniFormer consistently improves user engagement and interaction metrics, achieving gains of +0.101%/+0.260% in App Stay Time and +0.729%/+1.113% in Watch Time, respectively.

AI.tldr: UniFormer proposes a unified model-centric scaling framework for industrial recommender systems that decomposes the modeling space into feature and task spaces, uses semantic tokenization for user-item decoupling and inference acceleration, employs multi-sequence cross-attention to capture heterogeneous behaviors, and introduces multi-view FFNs for flexible parameter scaling. It achieved significant gains in A/B tests on Kuaishou platforms.
AI.motivation: Existing component-centric scaling methods (e.g., HyFormer, OneTrans) independently scale individual components and remain confined to feature-space co-scaling without a unified model-centric framework covering the entire modeling space. There is a need for a holistic, efficient, and scalable architecture that jointly addresses feature interaction, behavior modeling, task modeling, and inference efficiency.
AI.method: UniFormer decomposes the overall modeling space into Feature-space Interaction Modules and Task-space Interaction Modules, stacked together. It introduces: (1) a semantic-based tokenization scheme for user-item decoupling to achieve request-level inference acceleration; (2) multi-sequence cross-attention to separately capture heterogeneous behavior patterns, followed by self-attention for enhanced interaction modeling; and (3) dedicated multi-view FFNs to support flexible and scalable parameter scaling across different modeling components.
AI.result: Extensive online A/B testing on Kuaishou and Kuaishou Lite demonstrated consistent improvements: +0.101%/+0.260% in App Stay Time and +0.729%/+1.113% in Watch Time, respectively.
AI.conclusion: UniFormer provides an effective unified model-centric scaling framework that outperforms component-centric approaches, achieving both improved recommendation performance and inference efficiency in production industrial recommender systems.

title: Scientific discovery as meta-optimization: a combinatorial optimization case study
summary: Scientific discovery is fundamentally an optimization problem, defined by a vast "state space" of theories and experiments, and an evaluation criterion based on quality, novelty, and validity. Large language models (LLMs) have enabled automated exploration of this space, but we argue that simultaneous modification of the evaluation criteria is equally important. Here, we propose formalizing research as meta-optimization, where the optimization objective itself is also being optimized. Our key contribution is "consensus objective aggregation," where LLM-generated objective functions are combined via correlation-weighted voting, yielding a stable, self-correcting evaluation criterion that evolves as understanding deepens. We apply this framework to algorithm discovery for 3-SAT problems based on digital MemComputing machines, reducing the baseline scaling with problem size $N$ from $\sim N^{2.51}$ to $\sim N^{1.33}$ and delivering a $\sim 67\times$ speedup on the largest instances tested. As a problem-agnostic framework, we hope this approach will considerably aid scientific discovery.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes scientific discovery as meta-optimization, where both the search over theories/experiments and the evaluation criteria evolve simultaneously. The key mechanism is "consensus objective aggregation," using correlation-weighted voting among LLM-generated objective functions. Applied to 3-SAT algorithm discovery with digital MemComputing, it reduces scaling from ~N²·⁵¹ to ~N¹·³³, yielding a ~67× speedup on large instances.
AI.motivation: Scientific discovery can be framed as optimization over a state space of theories and experiments. While LLMs have enabled automated exploration of this space, the authors argue that the evaluation criteria themselves should also be dynamically optimized, not held static — motivating a meta-optimization formulation.
AI.method: The authors propose formalizing research as meta-optimization, where the optimization objective is itself optimized. The core technical contribution is "consensus objective aggregation": multiple LLM-generated objective functions are combined via correlation-weighted voting, producing a stable, self-correcting evaluation criterion that evolves as understanding deepens.
AI.result: Applied to algorithm discovery for 3-SAT problems using digital MemComputing machines, the framework reduced scaling with problem size N from approximately N²·⁵¹ to N¹·³³, achieving a ~67× speedup on the largest instances tested.
AI.conclusion: The framework is problem-agnostic and the authors express hope that it will significantly aid scientific discovery across domains by enabling co-evolution of search and evaluation criteria.

title: Same Scrutiny, More Time: Eye Tracking Insights into Reviewing LLM-Labelled Code
comment: Accepted at the 41st IEEE/ACM International Conference on Automated Software Engineering (ASE 2026)
summary: Modern software development increasingly involves the use of large language models (LLMs) to generate code. Despite their rapid advancement, LLMs remain prone to errors and hallucinations, emphasizing the importance of careful code inspection. However, in practice, developers' trust in LLM-generated code and their willingness to review it thoroughly may differ from these recommendations. How developers actually behave when reviewing LLM-generated code remains largely unexplored. In this study, we conduct a Wizard-of-Oz experiment to examine how software engineers behave when code is explicitly labeled as LLM-generated during a code review task. We collect both behavioral data and participant feedback through eye-tracking and exit interviews. Combining Bayesian data analysis with qualitative analysis, we found that while the thoroughness of code review did not change for participants, they spent more time fixating on LLM-labelled code, indicating that the label itself influences attention. Practitioners also adapted their review strategy for LLM-labelled code by assessing the code based on specific criteria (e.g., logical correctness), or using the prompt to guide their review. These findings inform LLM-based tool design on labelling while incorporating the prompt as a software artifact. Our study reveals a gap between reviewers' intentions and actual reviewing behaviour, highlighting the need for software companies to revisit their AI policies (particularly regarding LLM-assisted development) to better support developers in reviewing LLM-generated code.

AI.tldr: A Wizard-of-Oz experiment using eye-tracking and interviews reveals that developers do not review LLM-labeled code more thoroughly, but they allocate more visual attention to it and adapt review strategies based on specific criteria or prompts, exposing a gap between intended and actual reviewing behavior.
AI.motivation: Despite recommendations for careful inspection of LLM-generated code due to error-proneness, how developers actually behave when reviewing such code remains largely unexplored. The study aims to empirically investigate whether labeling code as LLM-generated affects review thoroughness and attention allocation.
AI.method: A Wizard-of-Oz experiment was conducted where software engineers performed code review tasks with code explicitly labeled as LLM-generated. Behavioral data and participant feedback were collected through eye-tracking and exit interviews, analyzed using Bayesian data analysis combined with qualitative analysis.
AI.result: Review thoroughness did not significantly change for LLM-labeled code. However, participants spent more time fixating on LLM-labeled code (indicating the label influences visual attention) and adapted their review strategies by assessing code based on specific criteria like logical correctness or using the prompt to guide review.
AI.conclusion: The study reveals a gap between reviewers' intentions and actual reviewing behavior, highlighting the need for software companies to revisit AI policies on LLM-assisted development and informing LLM-based tool design regarding labeling and treating prompts as software artifacts.

title: Co-Designing Community-Centered AI Education for Adults: A Midwestern Case Study
summary: Artificial Intelligence (AI) education is increasingly important, yet adults outside higher education receive less attention. We report a case study of an AI education session with 54 adults (48 in-person and 6 virtual) in a predominantly African American community on the east side of a major Midwestern city. We ask: "What does AI education for adults outside formal educational systems look like in practice?" and "What does this AI education session reveal about AI literacy at the community level?" Through a co-designed session developed with community partners, we found that concerns about AI persisted but shifted to specific, locally grounded questions about AI design and deployment. We also discuss AI literacy from a community capacity perspective and argue for AI literacy frameworks grounded in local community contexts that strengthen community capacity.

AI.tldr: A case study of a co-designed AI education session with 54 adults in a predominantly African American community reveals that AI concerns shift toward locally grounded questions when education is contextualized, supporting community-capacity-based AI literacy frameworks.
AI.motivation: AI education primarily targets formal educational settings (K-12, higher education), leaving adults outside these systems underserved. The authors address this gap by exploring what community-based AI education looks like in practice for marginalized adult populations and what it reveals about AI literacy at the community level.
AI.method: The authors conducted a case study of a single co-designed AI education session with 54 participants (48 in-person, 6 virtual) in a predominantly African American neighborhood on the east side of a major Midwestern city. The session was developed collaboratively with community partners, and data were gathered through qualitative observation of participant interactions, questions, and shifting concerns about AI.
AI.result: Participants' initial broad concerns about AI persisted but evolved into more specific, locally grounded questions about AI design and deployment. The session demonstrated that contextualizing AI education within community-specific issues helps surface practical, situated inquiries rather than abstract anxieties.
AI.conclusion: AI literacy frameworks should be grounded in local community contexts and designed to strengthen community capacity, rather than following one-size-fits-all models. Co-design with community partners is essential for effective adult AI education outside formal systems.

title: Beyond Takedown: Measuring Malicious Go Module Persistence in the Wild
summary: We measure an automation-based supply chain campaign in the Go ecosystem. The attackers repackage legitimate Go modules under attacker-controlled owners, and embed them with obfuscated code for an import-triggered downloader. Our results come from two complementary analyses: a) a manual search on GitHub across 2,113 repositories and b) a large-scale scan of 12.3M index entries using a deobfuscating AST scanner (GOAST) that we implemented. As a result, we identified 2,289 malicious versions of legitimate Go modules. We demonstrate that purely GitHub-centric searches fail to identify the full extent of the compromise and are only effective for as long as the affected code is present on the platform. Moreover, our proxy-based measurements of the takedown-remediation gap reveal that among artifacts later found to be GitHub-unobservable (i.e., removed or suspended), at least 99.4% remained retrievable via Go proxy. Following our disclosure, GitHub has removed 684 malicious repositories and the Google Go team has remediated 1,377 module versions.

AI.tldr: Researchers uncovered a supply chain attack in the Go ecosystem where attackers repackaged legitimate modules with obfuscated downloader malware. Using manual GitHub searches and a custom deobfuscating AST scanner (GOAST) across 12.3M index entries, they found 2,289 malicious module versions. GitHub-centric searches proved insufficient, and proxy-based measurements showed 99.4% of GitHub-unobservable artifacts remained retrievable via Go proxy, highlighting a critical takedown-remediation gap.
AI.motivation: To investigate and quantify the scope of an automation-based supply chain campaign targeting the Go module ecosystem, where attackers repackage legitimate modules with malicious obfuscated code, and to assess the effectiveness of existing detection and takedown mechanisms.
AI.method: A two-pronged approach: (a) manual search across 2,113 GitHub repositories for malicious Go modules, and (b) large-scale automated scanning of 12.3 million index entries using GOAST, a custom-built deobfuscating Abstract Syntax Tree scanner. Complemented by proxy-based measurements to assess the takedown-remediation gap.
AI.result: Identified 2,289 malicious versions of legitimate Go modules. GitHub-centric searches failed to capture the full scope of compromise and were effective only while affected code remained on the platform. Proxy measurements revealed that 99.4% of GitHub-unobservable artifacts (removed or suspended) remained retrievable via Go proxy. Post-disclosure, GitHub removed 684 malicious repositories and the Go team remediated 1,377 module versions.
AI.conclusion: GitHub-only detection is insufficient for identifying supply chain compromises in the Go ecosystem. The significant takedown-remediation gap — where malicious artifacts persist on Go proxies long after GitHub removal — represents a critical security vulnerability requiring coordinated remediation across platforms.

title: Context Recycling for Long-Horizon LLM Inference
summary: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong capabilities in short-context reasoning but degrade in performance over long conversational horizons due to context window limitations and inefficient token usage. We introduce ContextForge, a system for context recycling that maintains task-relevant information across turns by combining structured query generation, external memory retrieval, and controlled synthesis. The system enables efficient reuse of prior computation without relying on full context replay, reducing token overhead while preserving answer quality. We evaluate ContextForge using a 15-turn conversational benchmark that tests multi-turn reasoning, back-references, and domain shifts across structured healthcare queries. Compared to a baseline agent using identical underlying models, ContextForge demonstrates improved consistency and reduced token consumption, while maintaining comparable response accuracy. These results suggest that context recycling provides a practical approach for extending LLM capabilities in long-horizon tasks without requiring larger context windows or model retraining. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/Betanu701/ContextForge.

AI.tldr: ContextForge introduces a context recycling system that uses structured queries, external memory, and controlled synthesis to maintain task-relevant information across long conversational turns, reducing token overhead while preserving accuracy in multi-turn LLM interactions.
AI.motivation: LLMs perform well in short contexts but degrade over long conversations due to context window limits and inefficient token usage. Existing solutions like full context replay are token-expensive, and larger context windows or retraining are costly. A practical method is needed to extend LLM capabilities in long-horizon tasks without these drawbacks.
AI.method: ContextForge combines three components: (1) structured query generation to extract task-relevant information from prior turns, (2) external memory retrieval to store and access past computation results, and (3) controlled synthesis to integrate retrieved context into responses. The system recycles prior computation without full context replay. Evaluation uses a 15-turn conversational benchmark with healthcare queries testing multi-turn reasoning, back-references, and domain shifts.
AI.result: Compared to a baseline agent using identical underlying models, ContextForge achieved improved consistency and reduced token consumption while maintaining comparable response accuracy on the 15-turn healthcare benchmark.
AI.conclusion: Context recycling is a practical approach for extending LLM capabilities in long-horizon tasks without requiring larger context windows or model retraining.

title: Knowledge-augmented Agentic AI for Mental Health Medication Information Seeking
summary: Patients increasingly seek medication information online, yet safety knowledge for psychiatric drugs is split between regulatory adverse-event records, which are authoritative but abstract, and patient narratives, which are experience-near but unvalidated. Integrating them without conflating evidence and anecdote is especially consequential in psychiatry, where poorly contextualised information can amplify fear, nocebo responses, and non-adherence. Here we develop a provenance-aware, knowledge-graph-based multi-agent framework unifying 466,525 Reddit posts, 60,782 WebMD reviews, and twenty years of U.S. FDA Adverse Event Reporting System records for nine antidepressants.
