A large-language-model entity-recognition pipeline benchmarked against physician annotations reached highest F1 scores of 0.969 for medications and 0.973 for conditions. The two community platforms were far more concordant with each other (overlap up to a Jaccard similarity of 0.905) than with regulatory reports, indicating that patient-generated data form a partly independent safety signal. For sertraline, many adverse events appeared in community sources hundreds of days before the corresponding FDA date. A Neo4j knowledge graph grounded in ATC-N, ICD-10, and MedDRA vocabularies preserves provenance, keeping every claim traceable and regulatory facts distinct from patient experience. These results establish source-aware integration as a route to more auditable psychiatric medication information, with usefulness and patient benefit to be tested prospectively.

AI.tldr: A multi-agent framework integrates FDA adverse event records with patient-generated data from Reddit and WebMD into a provenance-aware knowledge graph. Patient platforms show high mutual concordance but differ substantially from regulatory reports, forming an independent safety signal. A graph-based architecture preserves source traceability, enabling auditable psychiatric medication information.
AI.motivation: Psychiatric medication safety knowledge is bifurcated: FDA adverse event records are authoritative but abstract, while patient narratives are experiential but unvalidated. Conflating these sources risks amplifying fear, nocebo responses, and non-adherence in psychiatry. A source-aware integration framework is needed to preserve evidence provenance while leveraging both data types.
AI.method: A provenance-aware, knowledge-graph-based multi-agent framework was developed. It unifies three data sources: 466,525 Reddit posts, 60,782 WebMD reviews, and 20 years of FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) records for nine antidepressants. An LLM-based entity-recognition pipeline was benchmarked against physician annotations (F1: 0.969 for medications, 0.973 for conditions). A Neo4j knowledge graph grounded in ATC-N, ICD-10, and MedDRA vocabularies preserves source provenance. Jaccard similarity quantified concordance between platforms; temporal analysis assessed signal timing relative to FDA dates.
AI.result: The LLM pipeline achieved F1 scores of 0.969 (medications) and 0.973 (conditions). Reddit and WebMD showed high concordance (Jaccard similarity up to 0.905), both differing substantially from FAERS, indicating patient-generated data constitutes a partly independent safety signal. For sertraline, many adverse events appeared in community sources hundreds of days before the corresponding FDA reporting date.
AI.conclusion: Source-aware integration via a provenance-preserving knowledge graph enables more auditable psychiatric medication information. The framework demonstrates that patient-generated data provide a complementary, temporally earlier safety signal distinct from regulatory reports. Prospective testing of usefulness and patient benefit remains necessary.

title: Necessary but Not Sufficient: Temperature Control and Reproducibility in LLM-as-Judge Safety Evaluations
summary: LLM-as-judge ("grader") components are now standard in evaluation harnesses, including safety evaluations where a pass/fail verdict may gate downstream deployment decisions. A widespread assumption is that setting the grader's sampling temperature to 0 makes grading deterministic. We test this assumption against a real safety-evaluation codebase (Japan AISI's open-source aisev) and show it fails on two levels. First, the harness invokes its grader without setting temperature or seed; the underlying provider silently applies its default of 1.0, so items near the decision boundary flip pass/fail across identical runs (per-item disagreement up to ~50% over 20 runs). Second, pinning temperature=0 reduces but does not eliminate flips: across 690 API calls spanning two providers, three model tiers, and five sampling configurations, 1-2 of 7 borderline items remain non-reproducible even under forced greedy decoding (top_k=1). Claude Opus 4.7/4.8 has since deprecated temperature entirely, rendering the primary mitigation inapplicable to newer model generations. These findings expose a structural gap: evaluation harnesses that report single-run verdicts without variance or grader-disagreement metrics can present noise as a safety property. We release a reproduction harness (690 calls, 7 conditions) and recommend that harnesses treat grader disagreement as a first-class health metric alongside the scores themselves.

AI.tldr: LLM-as-judge evaluators exhibit non-deterministic pass/fail verdicts even when temperature is set to 0, undermining the reliability of safety evaluations used for downstream deployment decisions. The authors demonstrate this across multiple providers and model tiers, showing that 1-2 of 7 borderline items remain non-reproducible under greedy decoding.
AI.motivation: Safety evaluations increasingly gate deployment decisions via LLM-as-judge graders, yet the widespread assumption that temperature=0 guarantees deterministic grading is untested against real codebases. Failures in reproducibility could mean noise is mistaken for genuine safety properties.
AI.method: The authors audit Japan AISI's open-source aisev harness. First, they identify that the harness omits temperature/seed settings, causing the provider default (1.0) to silently apply. Second, they conduct 690 API calls across two providers, three model tiers, and five sampling configurations (including temperature=0 with top_k=1) to measure per-item disagreement rates over 20 identical runs on borderline safety items.
AI.result: Under default settings, per-item pass/fail disagreement reaches ~50% over 20 runs for items near the decision boundary. Pinning temperature=0 reduces but does not eliminate flips: 1-2 of 7 borderline items remain non-reproducible even with greedy decoding (top_k=1). Claude Opus 4.7/4.8 has deprecated temperature entirely, making the primary mitigation inapplicable to newer models.
AI.conclusion: There is a structural gap in evaluation harnesses that report single-run verdicts without variance metrics. The authors recommend treating grader disagreement as a first-class health metric alongside scores, and release a reproduction harness (690 calls, 7 conditions) to support this practice.

title: TRUST: Item-Calibrated Interval Evidence for Temporal Session-Based Recommendation
summary: Temporal signals have been widely used in session-based recommendation to infer user interest. Existing temporal session-based recommenders primarily rely on absolute interval values, implicitly assuming that the same interval carries similar interest signals across items. However, we empirically find that this assumption does not hold: each item has its own interval distribution, so an interval should be interpreted relative to the item it belongs to. Based on this observation, we propose TRUST, a framework that evaluates each observed interval relative to the empirical interval distribution of the corresponding item. Specifically, we propose a score function to guide global neighbor sampling, session graph encoding, and final interest aggregation. Experiments on public datasets show that TRUST consistently improves over representative temporal and non-temporal baselines, and plug-in experiments further show that the proposed scoring function can improve existing temporal session recommenders as a model-agnostic method. Component-wise ablations further show that calibrating the temporal signals within each module, rather than removing the module itself, consistently improves neighbor sampling, session graph encoding, and interest aggregation.

AI.tldr: TRUST is a session-based recommendation framework that reinterprets temporal intervals relative to each item's own empirical interval distribution, rather than treating absolute intervals uniformly across items. It introduces a score function to calibrate neighbor sampling, session graph encoding, and interest aggregation, yielding consistent improvements over baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing temporal session-based recommenders assume that identical time intervals between interactions carry similar interest signals across all items. The authors empirically demonstrate this assumption fails: each item exhibits its own interval distribution, meaning an interval's significance should be interpreted relative to the item. This motivates a relative, item-aware temporal calibration approach.
AI.method: TRUST (Temporal Relative Understanding for Session-based recommendaTion) evaluates each observed interval against the empirical interval distribution of the corresponding item. A score function is designed to guide three core modules: (1) global neighbor sampling, (2) session graph encoding, and (3) final interest aggregation. The scoring is model-agnostic and can be plugged into existing temporal session recommenders.
AI.result: Experiments on public datasets show TRUST consistently outperforms representative temporal and non-temporal baselines. Plug-in experiments reveal the scoring function improves existing temporal session recommenders when used as a model-agnostic enhancement. Component-wise ablation confirms that calibrating temporal signals within each module (rather than removing modules) consistently boosts performance in neighbor sampling, graph encoding, and interest aggregation.
AI.conclusion: Interpreting temporal intervals relative to item-specific distributions is critical for session-based recommendation. TRUST provides an effective, modular, and model-agnostic approach to achieve this calibration, with strong empirical validation across datasets and ablations.

title: Semantic Early-Stopping for Iterative LLM Agent Loops
comment: 7 pages, 5 figures, 4 tables. Open implementation, machine-checked theory, and reproducible harness: github.com/SahilShrivastava-Dev/semantic-halting-problem
summary: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) loops, for example a Writer that drafts and a Critic that revises, are almost always terminated by a fixed iteration cap (max_iterations). This is a syntactic kill-switch: it is blind to whether the answer is still improving, so it over-spends tokens on easy inputs and truncates hard ones. We study semantic early-stopping: the loop halts when consecutive draft embeddings stop changing in meaning (cosine distance with a patience window) and the answer's measured quality stops improving. Our work makes three contributions. First, an honest theoretical footing: we prove deterministic termination and well-definedness and machine-check these claims, while treating the convergence of the distance sequence as an empirically tested conjecture rather than a (previously over-claimed) Banach contraction. Second, a judge-efficient evaluation protocol: we generate each question's full trajectory once, replay every stopping policy over the identical drafts, and cache every LLM-judge call, yielding a strictly paired efficiency-versus-quality comparison at low cost; we further separate operational tokens (charged to a policy) from evaluation tokens (a measurement instrument). Third, an empirical study on multi-hop retrieval-augmented question answering (HotpotQA). On the 60-question test split, a judge-free semantic stopper reduces operational tokens by 38% relative to max_iterations at parity quality (Delta-IS = -0.004, p = 0.81), whereas the full quality-gated variant is counter-productive because its per-round judging dominates cost. An oracle that selects the best round attains +0.115 Information Score over every practical policy (p ~ 4e-11), reframing the problem from "when to stop" (easy) to "which round is best" (open).

AI.tldr: The paper proposes semantic early-stopping for multi-agent LLM loops, replacing fixed iteration caps with a method that halts when consecutive draft embeddings converge (cosine distance) and quality stops improving. It provides formal termination proofs, a judge-efficient evaluation protocol using cached trajectories, and empirical results on HotpotQA showing 38% token reduction at parity quality with a judge-free stopper, while revealing that quality-gated stopping is counterproductive due to judging overhead.
AI.motivation: Current multi-agent LLM systems (e.g., Writer-Critic loops) rely on a fixed iteration cap (max_iterations) as a termination condition — a syntactic kill-switch blind to whether answers are still improving. This wastes tokens on easy inputs and truncates hard ones. The authors argue for semantically meaningful, adaptive stopping based on answer convergence and quality.
AI.method: The approach uses: (1) Semantic early-stopping based on cosine distance between consecutive draft embeddings with a patience window to detect meaning convergence; (2) A quality-gated variant that additionally checks whether measured answer quality stops improving; (3) A judge-efficient evaluation protocol that generates a full trajectory once, replays all stopping policies over identical drafts, and caches LLM-judge calls, separating operational tokens from evaluation tokens; (4) Formal proofs of deterministic termination and well-definedness, machine-checked, treating distance convergence as an empirical conjecture rather than a Banach contraction.
AI.result: On HotpotQA (60-question test split), the judge-free semantic stopper achieves 38% reduction in operational tokens relative to max_iterations at parity quality (Delta-IS = -0.004, p = 0.81). The full quality-gated variant is counterproductive because per-round judging costs dominate. An oracle selecting the best round attains +0.115 Information Score over all practical policies (p ≈ 4e-11), reframing the problem from "when to stop" to "which round is best."
AI.conclusion: Semantic early-stopping — particularly the judge-free variant — is a viable and cost-effective alternative to fixed iteration caps for multi-agent LLM loops. The oracle result reframes the core challenge: identifying the best round is an open problem more impactful than deciding when to stop. The evaluation protocol also provides a low-cost, strictly paired methodology for future stopping-policy research.

title: ConcoLixir: Reactive LLM Discovery Oracles for Python Concolic Testing
summary: Concolic testing combines concrete execution with symbolic constraint solving, but Python programs expose recurring limits. Library calls can cause symbolic variables to downgrade to concrete values. Regular expressions, checksums, parsers, and other semantic operations can be hard to solve, and exploration can plateau on already covered paths. We present ConcoLixir, a reactive LLM extension for Python concolic execution. The LLM acts as a discovery oracle, not a replacement for the solver or a correctness oracle. It generates initial seeds, proposes concrete inputs after solver failures, and targets uncovered code when coverage stalls. Each candidate is executed concolically, and only observed coverage and collected path constraints guide later exploration. Across synthetic, real-world, and library targets, ConcoLixir improves mean line coverage over the baseline concolic tester without an LLM oracle by 8.6, 15.1, and 17.0 percentage points. The gains are strongest near semantic barriers and library boundaries, and the full evaluation costs \$1.63 in API charges. These results show that bounded LLM discovery can complement symbolic reasoning without replacing it.

AI.tldr: ConcoLixir augments Python concolic execution with a reactive LLM oracle that generates seeds, proposes inputs when solvers fail, and targets uncovered code during coverage plateaus, achieving 8.6–17.0 pp coverage gains across benchmarks at a total API cost of $1.63.
AI.motivation: Python concolic testing faces recurring limits: symbolic variables downgrade to concrete values across library calls, semantic operations (regex, checksums, parsers) are hard for solvers, and exploration stalls on already-covered paths. Existing approaches cannot bridge these gaps without sacrificing soundness or scalability.
AI.method: ConcoLixir integrates an LLM as a discovery oracle (not a solver replacement or correctness oracle) into a Python concolic execution framework. The LLM serves three reactive roles: (1) generating initial seeds to bootstrap exploration, (2) proposing concrete inputs when the constraint solver fails on hard semantic barriers, and (3) targeting uncovered code when coverage plateaus. Every LLM-generated candidate is executed concolically, and only observed coverage and collected path constraints guide subsequent exploration, preserving the soundness of the concolic engine.
AI.result: Across synthetic, real-world, and library targets, ConcoLixir improves mean line coverage over the baseline concolic tester (no LLM) by 8.6, 15.1, and 17.0 percentage points respectively. Gains are concentrated near semantic barriers and library boundaries. The full evaluation incurs only $1.63 in LLM API charges.
AI.conclusion: Bounded LLM discovery can effectively complement symbolic reasoning without replacing it. The reactive, oracle-style integration preserves the concolic engine's soundness while overcoming its practical limitations at semantic and library boundaries, all at negligible cost.

title: An exploratory behavioral and electroencephalographic study of artificial intelligence-assisted learning modes in high school students
summary: As artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly integrating into education, concerns have emerged regarding its potential implications on cognitive engagement and problem-solving behavior. However, existing research largely treats AI exposure as a binary condition (AI vs. no-AI), with limited differentiation between interaction modalities and post-exposure effects. This study investigates whether distinct AI interaction modes (Tutor, Collaborator, Solver) influence frontal EEG spectral activity. Electroencephalography (EEG) data and quantified behavioral metrics were recorded from 48 study participants (24 males, 24 females; ages 14-18) across two counterbalanced quizzes in a within-subject design. Statistical analyses included Friedman tests, repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t-tests, and effect size calculations. Behavioral changes were mathematically analyzed in an observation matrix of three characteristics -Initiation, Processing, and Stress-measured on an ordinal scale. Each mode showed significant differences in all three behavioral measures. Descriptive EEG patterns in AI interaction mode were observed, and the possibility of short-term carryover effects of AI was explored. Although the EEG data did not reach statistical significance, the patterns observed across the three AI interaction modes warrant further investigation. This study provides preliminary behavioral evidence and investigative electrophysiological observations, exploring possible AI-interaction-mode-based differences in neural activity and behavior, while establishing a replicable framework for future human-AI interaction studies.

AI.tldr: This study examines how three distinct AI interaction modes (Tutor, Collaborator, Solver) affect EEG frontal spectral activity and behavioral metrics in adolescents. While behavioral differences were significant across modes, EEG patterns were descriptive but not statistically significant, with possible carryover effects warranting further study.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-in-education research treats AI exposure as a binary condition (AI vs. no-AI), failing to differentiate between interaction modalities or examine post-exposure effects. This limits understanding of how specific AI interaction types may differentially impact cognitive engagement and problem-solving.
AI.method: A within-subject design with 48 participants (ages 14-18, gender-balanced) completed two counterbalanced quizzes under three AI interaction modes: Tutor, Collaborator, and Solver. Frontal EEG spectral activity and behavioral metrics (Initiation, Processing, Stress) were recorded. Statistical analyses included Friedman tests, repeated-measures ANOVA, paired t-tests, and effect sizes.
AI.result: All three behavioral measures showed statistically significant differences across AI interaction modes. Descriptive EEG patterns were observed for each mode, and potential short-term carryover effects were explored. However, electrophysiological differences did not reach statistical significance.
AI.conclusion: The study provides preliminary behavioral evidence and exploratory electrophysiological observations suggesting that AI interaction modality may differentially influence cognitive and behavioral outcomes. It establishes a replicable framework for future human-AI interaction research while highlighting the need for larger studies to confirm EEG trends.

title: Hybrid privacy-aware semantic search: SVD-truncated document geometry and CKKS-encrypted query reranking under a restricted threat model
summary:
Dense embeddings power semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, but embedding-inversion attacks can reconstruct source text from a vector: when a vector database leaks, the documents behind it leak too. The textbook defences are extremes - encrypting the whole search homomorphically is sound but too slow at million-document scale, while privacy noise degrades ranking long before it protects. We study a middle path exploiting the asymmetry between the static collection and the dynamic query. The collection is protected geometrically: each vector is truncated onto a lower-dimensional SVD subspace and rotated by a secret orthogonal transform known only to the owner. The query is protected cryptographically: it is reranked under CKKS homomorphic encryption, so an honest-but-curious server never sees the query or the scores. CKKS parameters come from a small offline benchmark.
  We prove a tight lower bound on the reconstruction error of any attacker confined to the protected subspace. On one million documents and five encoders the scheme preserves ranking quality (slightly improving it on strong encoders, as a linear denoiser) at sub-second latency, and an off-the-shelf inversion attack on the protected space collapses to the noise floor. We then test stronger adversaries: a known-plaintext attacker recovers the rotation by orthogonal Procrustes from about as many leaked pairs as the retained dimension; the public product-quantization codes preserve most nearest-neighbour structure; and random-projection, calibrated-noise and BEIR baselines show the truncation is an encoder-dependent accuracy cost, not a free denoiser. We state the limits: query confidentiality is cryptographic, but document protection is an empirical obfuscation layer (SVD truncation plus a secret rotation), not a cryptographic primitive, and we delimit the threat model for each claim.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid privacy-preserving dense retrieval scheme: document vectors are protected via SVD truncation and a secret orthogonal rotation (geometric obfuscation), while query vectors are protected by CKKS homomorphic encryption for reranking. This balances efficiency and privacy, maintaining ranking quality on million-document scales with sub-second latency.
AI.motivation: Existing privacy defenses for dense vector search are polar extremes: fully homomorphic encryption over the entire collection is sound but prohibitively slow at scale, while differential privacy noise degrades ranking quality before providing meaningful protection. The authors seek a middle ground exploiting the natural asymmetry between a static document collection and dynamic queries.
AI.method: Document protection: Each document embedding is projected onto a lower-dimensional SVD subspace and rotated by a secret orthogonal matrix known only to the data owner. Query protection: The query is processed under CKKS homomorphic encryption; the server reranks candidates blindly, never seeing the plaintext query or relevance scores. A small offline benchmark tunes the CKKS parameters. The scheme is analyzed theoretically with a tight lower bound on reconstruction error for subspace-confined attackers, and empirically against inversion attacks, known-plaintext attacks (orthogonal Procrustes), product quantization leakage, and various baselines.
AI.result: On one million documents across five encoders, ranking quality is preserved (slightly improved for strong encoders via a linear denoising effect) at sub-second latency. Off-the-shelf inversion attacks collapse to the noise floor in the protected space. However, a known-plaintext attacker can recover the secret rotation via orthogonal Procrustes given leaked pairs roughly equal to the retained dimension. Public product-quantization codes preserve most nearest-neighbor structure. Truncation incurs an encoder-dependent accuracy cost, not a free denoising gain.
AI.conclusion: Query confidentiality is cryptographically guaranteed via CKKS; document protection is an empirical obfuscation layer (SVD truncation + secret rotation), not a cryptographic primitive. The threat model is explicitly delimited for each claim, and the approach represents a pragmatic trade-off between the extremes of full homomorphic encryption and noise-based privacy.

title: Reducing Conversational Escalation in Large Language Model Dialogue with Nonviolent Communication Constraints
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in emotionally charged situations involving interpersonal conflict, frustration, and distress. While prior safety research has focused on preventing explicit harms such as toxic or policy-violating content, less attention has been paid to conversational behaviors that may unintentionally escalate conflict. In this paper, we investigate whether LLMs can be guided toward more de-escalating dialogue behavior through lightweight prompt-level constraints derived from Nonviolent Communication (NVC). We reformulate NVC principles as process-oriented guidelines that discourage blame attribution, emphasize attention to users' emotional experiences, and encourage clarification before advice. Using a dual-agent simulation framework across multiple instruction-tuned models and user resistance levels, we show that NVC-constrained prompting consistently reduces conversational escalation and stabilizes interactions with highly resistant users. These results suggest that simple communication constraints can meaningfully improve the trustworthiness of LLM dialogue in conflict-prone settings.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates whether lightweight, prompt-level constraints based on Nonviolent Communication (NVC) can guide LLMs toward de-escalating dialogue behavior in conflict-prone settings, finding that NVC-constrained prompting consistently reduces conversational escalation and stabilizes interactions with resistant users.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in emotionally charged situations involving interpersonal conflict, yet prior safety research has focused on preventing explicit harms (toxicity, policy violations) rather than unintentional conversational escalation. There is a gap in understanding how to guide LLMs toward de-escalating behaviors.
AI.method: The authors reformulate NVC principles as process-oriented prompt-level guidelines (discouraging blame attribution, emphasizing emotional experience, encouraging clarification before advice). They evaluate these constraints using a dual-agent simulation framework across multiple instruction-tuned models with varying levels of user resistance.
AI.result: NVC-constrained prompting consistently reduces conversational escalation and stabilizes interactions, even with highly resistant users, across all tested instruction-tuned models.
AI.conclusion: Simple, lightweight communication constraints derived from NVC can meaningfully improve the trustworthiness of LLM dialogue in conflict-prone settings, offering a practical and scalable approach to conversational safety beyond traditional toxicity prevention.

title: Accelerating Skill Assessment in Chess: A Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System
comment: Accepted at the IEEE Conference on Games (IEEE CoG) 2026
summary: Rating systems such as Elo serve as the gold standard for matchmaking in competitive chess. However, they inherently suffer from response lag due to their exclusive reliance on match outcomes, neglecting the granular quality of gameplay. Nevertheless, incorporating move-by-move information into rating adjustments presents a significant challenge given the substantial noise and the vastness of the game-state space. To address this, we propose the Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System (DD-Elo), a novel skill assessment framework inspired by the drift diffusion model (DDM) from cognitive neuroscience. By modeling skill expression as a decision-making process, our model integrates move-level data to capture rapid skill fluctuations. We provide a rigorous mathematical derivation proving that DD-Elo maintains a bounded deviation from the traditional Elo system, ensuring theoretical alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DD-Elo adapts to skill changes faster than Elo. Our findings suggest that DD-Elo offers an explainable, highly responsive, and backward-compatible solution for chess rating ecosystems. The implementation code is publicly available at https://github.com/Aquila-zhou1/DD-Elo .

AI.tldr: DD-Elo integrates move-level gameplay data into the Elo rating system using a drift-diffusion model from cognitive neuroscience, enabling faster adaptation to skill changes while maintaining theoretical alignment and backward compatibility with traditional Elo.
AI.motivation: Traditional Elo rating systems suffer from response lag because they rely solely on match outcomes, ignoring the rich move-by-move information that reflects granular skill quality. Incorporating such data is challenging due to noise and vast game-state spaces.
AI.method: The authors propose DD-Elo, which models skill expression as a drift-diffusion decision process. Move-level data is integrated to capture rapid skill fluctuations. A rigorous mathematical derivation proves bounded deviation from traditional Elo, ensuring theoretical consistency.
AI.result: Extensive experiments show that DD-Elo adapts to skill changes significantly faster than the standard Elo system.
AI.conclusion: DD-Elo provides an explainable, highly responsive, and backward-compatible rating solution for chess ecosystems, with code publicly available.

title: Clue-Guided Money Laundering Group Discovery
summary: Money Laundering Group Discovery (MLGD) aims to identify hidden criminal groups and recover their complete structures in large-scale financial networks. Existing graph anomaly detection methods mainly produce node-level risk alerts, while global group discovery methods passively search for suspicious groups over the whole network. Both are mismatched with real Anti-money-laundering (AML) investigations, where analysts usually start from a concrete clue and gradually expand the investigation to recover the responsible group. To address this gap, we propose Clue-Guided Group Discovery (CGGD), where a laundering group is progressively recovered from an initial clue set through analyst interaction. We further propose Clue2Group, a framework that first constructs a compact local investigation context to reduce noise and preserve chain-like and cycle-like laundering structures. It then estimates a clue-conditioned local risk field with a multi-semantic local-temporal GNN, and finally integrates risk, structural, and prior-pattern evidence to recover a coherent laundering group. Experiments on two large-scale AML benchmarks show that Clue2Group provides a practical clue-driven analysis framework for AML investigations, offering a feasible step toward bridging the gap between graph-based AML research and real investigation workflows.

AI.tldr: Clue2Group introduces Clue-Guided Group Discovery (CGGD), a framework that progressively recovers money laundering groups from initial clue sets through analyst interaction, using a local-temporal GNN and multi-evidence integration. It bridges the gap between node-level anomaly detection and real AML investigation workflows, demonstrating effectiveness on two large-scale benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing graph-based AML methods suffer from a critical mismatch with real-world investigations: node-level anomaly detection only produces risk alerts without group structure recovery, while global group discovery passively searches the entire network. Real AML analysts operate clue-driven — starting from concrete leads (e.g., suspicious accounts) and iteratively expanding to uncover the full criminal network. The paper addresses this gap by formalizing a clue-guided, analyst-in-the-loop group discovery paradigm.
AI.method: The Clue2Group framework operates in three stages: (1) **Local investigation context construction** — extracts a compact subgraph around the clue set that reduces noise while preserving chain-like and cycle-like laundering structural motifs; (2) **Clue-conditioned local risk field estimation** — employs a multi-semantic local-temporal GNN to estimate the likelihood that each candidate node belongs to the same laundering group as the clues; (3) **Multi-evidence group recovery** — integrates risk scores, structural coherence, and prior-pattern knowledge to assemble the final coherent laundering group through analyst interaction loops.
AI.result: Experiments on two large-scale AML benchmark datasets demonstrate that Clue2Group effectively recovers laundering groups from initial clues, outperforming alternative approaches in both group recovery quality and practical usability. The framework provides a feasible step toward operationalizing graph-based AML research for real investigation workflows.
AI.conclusion: Clue2Group successfully bridges the gap between graph-based AML detection and real investigative procedures by formalizing Clue-Guided Group Discovery. Its progressive, interactive framework aligns with how analysts actually work, making it a practical tool for anti-money laundering investigations while opening new directions for human-in-the-loop graph mining in financial crime domains.

title: NOVA: A Verification-Aware Agent Harness for Architecture Evolution in Industrial Recommender Systems
summary:
Industrial advertising recommender models are continuously improved through architecture evolution. Upgrades such as RankMixer, TokenMixer-Large, and MixFormer show that better structures remain a key source of quality and business gains. Yet developing such upgrades in production is expert-intensive and difficult to scale. Existing automation is insufficient: AutoML mainly tunes hyper-parameters, while effective gains often require cross-module changes under strict constraints; generic LLM coding agents optimize for runnable code, but runnable code does not imply a valid recommender architecture. Candidates may pass local tests while causing silent failures that degrade performance.
  We present NOVA, a level-aware agent harness for verification-aware architecture evolution. NOVA uses an architecture gradient, an SGD-inspired, non-differentiable update signal that aggregates prior modifications, verification diagnostics, metric feedback, and trajectory memory to guide the next modification. A verification cascade checks structure semantics, local executability, offline effectiveness, and online impact; invalid candidates are blocked early, with failure patterns recorded as forbidden directions. L1--L4 task-level control matches automation to task complexity and risk, routing high-risk tasks to Copilot for human oversight. Deployed in an industrial advertising system, NOVA achieves the highest effective pass rate on L2 ScaleUp and L3 Literature-to-Production tasks (54.5% and 60.0%), reduces silent failures compared with coding-agent baselines, and shortens one literature-to-production cycle by over 13x in human-attended time. In online A/B testing, the selected L3 candidate improves GMV on three pCVR objectives by +1.25%, +1.70%, and +2.02%, while reducing pCVR bias by 58.8%, 66.7%, and 37.3%.

AI.tldr: NOVA is a level-aware agent framework for automated recommender architecture evolution that uses an "architecture gradient" signal, multi-stage verification cascades, and L1-L4 task-level control to safely automate architecture modifications. Deployed in production advertising systems, it achieves 54.5-60% effective pass rates on complex tasks, reduces silent failures, and delivers +1.25-2.02% GMV gains in online A/B tests.
AI.motivation: Industrial advertising recommender models require continuous architecture evolution for quality gains, but developing such upgrades is expert-intensive and hard to scale. Existing AutoML approaches focus narrowly on hyper-parameter tuning, while generic LLM coding agents optimize for runnable code rather than valid recommender architectures, leading to silent failures that degrade performance but pass local tests. A system is needed that can automate cross-module architectural changes under strict production constraints while preventing silent failures.
AI.method: NOVA introduces four key mechanisms: (1) An "architecture gradient" — an SGD-inspired non-differentiable update signal that aggregates prior modifications, verification diagnostics, metric feedback, and trajectory memory to guide iterative modifications. (2) A verification cascade that checks structure semantics, local executability, offline effectiveness, and online impact sequentially, blocking invalid candidates early and recording failure patterns as forbidden directions. (3) L1-L4 task-level control routing automation based on task complexity and risk, escalating high-risk tasks to human Copilot oversight. (4) Integration with production advertising systems for end-to-end deployment.
AI.result: NOVA achieves a 54.5% effective pass rate on L2 ScaleUp tasks and 60.0% on L3 Literature-to-Production tasks, outperforming coding-agent baselines while reducing silent failures. It shortens one literature-to-production cycle by over 13× in human-attended time. In online A/B testing, the selected L3 candidate improves GMV on three pCVR objectives by +1.25%, +1.70%, and +2.02%, while reducing pCVR bias by 58.8%, 66.7%, and 37.3%.
AI.conclusion: NOVA demonstrates that verification-aware, level-aware automation with architecture gradients can effectively scale recommender architecture evolution in production. By combining structured verification cascades with human oversight for high-risk tasks, it overcomes the limitations of both AutoML and generic coding agents, delivering significant business metrics improvements while maintaining safety.

title: Quantum Mutant Equivalence via Transpilation
summary: Mutation testing evaluates test suite quality by introducing artificial faults (mutants) and checking whether tests detect (kill) them. A central challenge is the equivalent mutant problem: some mutants are syntactically different from the original program but semantically identical to it and therefore cannot be killed by any test. If left unidentified, such mutants waste testing effort and distort mutation scores. In quantum software, mutation testing is increasingly used, but the equivalent mutant problem remains unsolved. A recent study generated more than 700,000 quantum circuit mutants and found that roughly half survived the available tests, making it unclear whether these survivors reflect weak tests or semantic equivalence. We propose Transpiler-Based Equivalence (TBE), a lightweight approach that identifies equivalent quantum mutants by transpiling original and mutated circuits under the same configuration and comparing their resulting OpenQASM code. We evaluate TBE on 348,299 surviving mutants, 92,011 of which are equivalent; TBE identifies 29,536 of them (32.1%) as equivalent while achieving 100% precision and 82% accuracy.

AI.tldr: TBE identifies equivalent quantum mutants by transpiling original and mutated circuits and comparing the resulting OpenQASM code, achieving 100% precision on 348K surviving mutants.
AI.motivation: Quantum software mutation testing faces the equivalent mutant problem—many surviving mutants may be semantically identical to the original rather than indicating weak tests. A prior study found ~50% of 700K+ quantum circuit mutants survived, but it is unclear whether this is due to inadequate tests or equivalence.
AI.method: Transpiler-Based Equivalence (TBE): transpile both original and mutated quantum circuits under identical configuration, then compare the resulting OpenQASM representations. Identical transpiled outputs indicate semantic equivalence.
AI.result: Evaluated on 348,299 surviving mutants (of which 92,011 are ground-truth equivalent). TBE identified 29,536 equivalent mutants (32.1% recall) with 100% precision and 82% overall accuracy.
AI.conclusion: TBE is a lightweight, high-precision method for detecting equivalent quantum mutants, though its 32% recall suggests many equivalent mutants require more sophisticated analysis beyond transpiler-based comparison.

title: HiLSVA: Design and Evaluation of a Human-in-the-Loop Agentic System for Scientific Visualization
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents enable natural language interaction for scientific visualization (SciVis). Still, prior systems have essentially prioritized autonomy over human analytical control, thereby limiting transparency and human oversight. We present HiLSVA, a human-in-the-loop agentic system that supports mixed-initiative SciVis workflows. HiLSVA integrates a plan-first multi-agent architecture with explicit human oversight, stepwise provenance tracking, and learn-at-test-time adaptation from user feedback. The system supports fluid handoff between humans and agents through both natural language and direct manipulation of visualizations, while sandboxed execution ensures safe, reproducible workflows. In doing so, HiLSVA reframes agentic SciVis as a collaborative process that augments, rather than replaces, human analytical reasoning. We evaluate HiLSVA through representative case studies and a controlled user study with twelve participants of varying expertise across multiple autonomy settings. Results show that mixed-initiative interaction improves task completion, user control, and workflow transparency across different levels of user expertise, while revealing a tradeoff between execution efficiency and human oversight. These findings highlight the importance of human-centered design in agentic SciVis and guide the development of future collaborative visualization systems. We encourage readers to explore our demo video, case studies, and source code at https://hilsva.github.io/.

AI.tldr: HiLSVA is a human-in-the-loop agentic system for scientific visualization that combines a plan-first multi-agent architecture with explicit human oversight, provenance tracking, and test-time adaptation, reframing LLM-driven SciVis as a collaborative mixed-initiative process rather than autonomous automation.
AI.motivation: Prior LLM-based scientific visualization agents prioritize autonomy over human analytical control, resulting in limited transparency and insufficient human oversight. There is a need for systems that augment rather than replace human reasoning in SciVis workflows.
AI.method: HiLSVA integrates (1) a plan-first multi-agent architecture, (2) explicit human oversight mechanisms, (3) stepwise provenance tracking, (4) learn-at-test-time adaptation from user feedback, (5) fluid human-agent handoff via natural language and direct manipulation, and (6) sandboxed execution for safe, reproducible workflows. Evaluation was conducted through representative case studies and a controlled user study with twelve participants across varying expertise levels and multiple autonomy settings.
AI.result: Mixed-initiative interaction improved task completion, user control, and workflow transparency across all expertise levels. A tradeoff emerged between execution efficiency and human oversight — greater human control reduced raw speed but improved outcomes and trust. The user study validated benefits across multiple autonomy settings.
AI.conclusion: Human-centered design is critical in agentic scientific visualization. HiLSVA demonstrates that mixed-initiative collaboration between humans and LLM agents enhances analytical workflows, and the findings provide guidance for future collaborative visualization systems.

title: Verifying Intent and Harm: A Unified Defense Against LLM-Generated Threats
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in interactive applications, yet they remain vulnerable to adversarial interactions that induce harmful, deceptive, or policy-violating outputs. Existing defenses typically analyze either user prompts or generated outputs, but not both. However, many real-world attacks exploit a separation between adversarial intent expressed in the prompt and actionable harm manifested only in the response. As a result, prompt-only and response-only defenses frequently miss unsafe interactions that appear benign when viewed from either side in isolation. We present a verification-centric defense framework that jointly evaluates prompt intent and response harm before an LLM response is delivered to a user. The framework employs specialized analysts for intent and harm assessment together with a Judge for conflict resolution. We formalize a threat model for prompt-response attacks and evaluate the framework across five threat categories: jailbreaks, prompt injection, phishing, cyber abuse, and harmful content. Experiments on multiple benchmark datasets show that jointly verifying prompt intent and response harm consistently outperforms single-sided defenses and single-agent reasoning baselines. Across threat categories, the framework improves average F1 from 0.90 for the strongest applicable baselines to 0.95 while reducing the average attack success rate to 4.1 percent. Compared with a Single-Agent+CoT baseline, it improves average F1 from 0.87 to 0.95 and reduces the false positive rate on benign-sensitive requests from 0.12 to 0.06. We further evaluate architecture-aware adaptive attacks in which the attacker knows the verifier structure and attempts to bypass individual verification components. Our results suggest that prompt-response verification provides a practical foundation for securing LLM applications against evolving adversarial threats.

AI.tldr: A joint prompt-response verification framework uses specialized intent and harm analysts with a conflict-resolving Judge to defend LLMs against adversarial interactions, achieving 0.95 F1 and reducing attack success rate to 4.1%, outperforming single-sided defenses.
AI.motivation: Existing LLM defenses analyze either user prompts or generated outputs in isolation. However, real-world attacks exploit the gap between adversarial intent in the prompt and harm manifested only in the response, causing prompt-only and response-only defenses to miss unsafe interactions that appear benign from either side alone.
AI.method: A verification-centric defense framework with three components: (1) an Intent Analyst that assesses adversarial intent in the prompt, (2) a Harm Analyst that evaluates harmful content in the generated response, and (3) a Judge that resolves conflicts between the two analysts. The framework operates before responses are delivered to users. A formal threat model for prompt-response attacks is defined, and evaluation spans five threat categories: jailbreaks, prompt injection, phishing, cyber abuse, and harmful content. Architecture-aware adaptive attacks, where the attacker knows the verifier structure, are also tested.
AI.result: The joint framework improves average F1 from 0.90 (strongest applicable baselines) to 0.95 and reduces attack success rate to 4.1%. Against a Single-Agent+CoT baseline, F1 improves from 0.87 to 0.95, and false positive rate on benign-sensitive requests drops from 0.12 to 0.06. The framework remains effective under adaptive attacks targeting individual verification components.
AI.conclusion: Prompt-response verification provides a practical and robust foundation for securing LLM applications against diverse and evolving adversarial threats, with consistent improvements over single-sided and single-agent approaches.

title: Low Resource Multimodal Translation of Nepali Spoken Words into Emotion-Conditioned Sign Language Avatars
summary: Sign language communication systems, that integrate emotional expression remain underexplored, particularly for low-resource languages. This pilot study presents NEST-V1 (Nepali Emotion and Speech Transformer - Version 1), a proof-of-concept multimodal framework that demonstrates the feasibility of generating emotion-conditioned Nepali Sign Language avatars from spoken input. As a preliminary investigation, we focus on four common Nepali words ("thank you", "hello", "house", "me") across three emotional states (happy, neutral, sad) to validate our core technical approach. Our lightweight architecture employs a shared acoustic encoder for simultaneous Automatic Speech Recognition and emotion classification, achieving 81.1% ASR accuracy and 79.21% emotion recognition accuracy on a dataset of 600 labeled audio samples from 50 speakers. The system demonstrates 37% parameter efficiency compared to separate model architectures while maintaining a lightweight footprint with only 22.1M parameters suitable for edge deployment. This pilot work establishes the technical foundation for emotion-aware sign language translation in low-resource settings and provides a scalable framework for future expansion to larger vocabularies and more diverse emotional expressions. Our preliminary results indicate the viability of real-time, emotionally expressive sign language communication systems for the hearing-impaired community, with clear pathways for enhancement in subsequent development phases.

AI.tldr: NEST-V1 is a proof-of-concept multimodal framework that generates emotion-conditioned Nepali Sign Language avatars from spoken input, using a shared acoustic encoder for joint ASR and emotion classification, achieving ~80% accuracy on both tasks with only 22.1M parameters.
AI.motivation: Sign language communication systems integrating emotional expression are underexplored, especially for low-resource languages like Nepali. There is a need for emotion-aware sign language translation to better serve hearing-impaired communities in such settings.
AI.method: A lightweight multimodal architecture with a shared acoustic encoder that simultaneously performs Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) and emotion classification. The system maps four Nepali words across three emotional states (happy, neutral, sad) to sign language avatars. Evaluated on 600 labeled audio samples from 50 speakers.
AI.result: Achieved 81.1% ASR accuracy and 79.21% emotion recognition accuracy. The shared encoder design yields 37% parameter efficiency compared to separate architectures, with a total of only 22.1M parameters suitable for edge deployment.
AI.conclusion: The pilot study validates the feasibility of real-time, emotionally expressive sign language communication for low-resource languages. It establishes a scalable technical foundation for future expansion to larger vocabularies and more diverse emotional expressions.

title: Governing Actions, Not Agents: Institutional Attestation as a Governance Model for Autonomous AI Systems
summary: Autonomous AI agents may begin to perform consequential, irreversible actions such as clinical prescribing and production software deployment. This paper observes that human institutions have governed powerful autonomous actors not by monitoring their reasoning but by requiring independently attested evidence at the point of consequential action. We formalise this institutional pattern as a computational governance model for AI agent systems. Under the proposed model, an agent retains full autonomy over planning and reasoning but holds no execution authority over designated high-risk actions. Execution is conditional on preconditions that are each independently attested by a separate authoritative source, cryptographically bound to a declared intent, and evaluated by a deterministic policy. Decisions are recorded in a tamper-evident log amenable to independent re-verification. We present a proof-of-concept implementation and illustrate the model with examples from software deployment and clinical prescribing.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a computational governance model for autonomous AI agents where high-risk actions require independently attested evidence from separate authoritative sources before execution, rather than relying on monitoring the agent's internal reasoning. The model uses cryptographic binding, deterministic policy evaluation, and tamper-evident logging.
AI.motivation: Autonomous AI agents are beginning to perform consequential, irreversible actions (e.g., clinical prescribing, production software deployment). The authors argue that monitoring an agent's internal reasoning is insufficient for governing such actions. Instead, they draw on an institutional pattern from human society: governing powerful autonomous actors through independently attested evidence at the point of consequential action, rather than by scrutinizing their decision-making process.
AI.method: The authors formalize a governance model where: (1) agents retain full autonomy over planning and reasoning but have no execution authority for designated high-risk actions; (2) execution is conditional on preconditions independently attested by separate authoritative sources; (3) these attestations are cryptographically bound to a declared intent; (4) a deterministic policy evaluates whether conditions are met; (5) all decisions are recorded in a tamper-evident log amenable to independent re-verification. A proof-of-concept implementation is presented.
AI.result: The paper presents a proof-of-concept implementation demonstrating the feasibility of the proposed governance model, illustrated through examples in software deployment and clinical prescribing domains.
AI.conclusion: Human institutions have long governed powerful actors through ex ante attested evidence rather than ex post reasoning analysis. Applying this same institutional pattern computationally — via cryptographic attestations, deterministic policies, and tamper-evident logs — offers a viable governance framework for constraining autonomous AI agents at the point of consequential action without limiting their reasoning autonomy.

title: Federated Hash Projected Latent Factor Learning
summary: Hash Learning (HL) is an efficient representation learning approach that maps real-valued data into compact binary representations. Traditional HL methods typically require users to upload personal data to a central server, which is incompatible with increasingly stringent data security regulations. Federated Learning (FL) provides a decentralized paradigm for learning globally optimal models without centralizing private data. However, most FL methods rely on transmitting large-scale real-valued gradient information, leading to high communication overhead and potential privacy risks. Integrating HL into FL is a promising solution. Nevertheless, existing HL methods suffer from limited representational capacity of binary codes, which may degrade model accuracy. To address this challenge, we propose a Federated Hash Projected Latent Factor (FHPLF) model. FHPLF introduces three key innovations: (a) replacing real-valued gradient matrices with binary gradient-like matrices, significantly reducing computation, storage, and communication costs while enhancing privacy protection; (b) leveraging Projected Hamming Distance for similarity modeling, which captures the importance of individual binary bits to improve representation capability; and (c) proposing a Secure Binary Gradient Reassembly and Privacy-Enhanced Upload (SBG-PEU) strategy to further reduce the risk of user interaction leakage during transmission. Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets demonstrate that FHPLF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art HL and FL methods, achieving a favorable trade-off among accuracy, efficiency, and privacy preservation.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes FHPLF, a federated hash learning model that replaces real-valued gradients with binary gradient-like matrices, uses Projected Hamming Distance for improved similarity modeling, and employs a secure binary gradient reassembly strategy. It achieves superior accuracy-efficiency-privacy trade-offs compared to existing methods.
AI.motivation: Traditional hash learning requires centralized data upload, violating data security regulations. Federated learning transmits large real-valued gradients, causing high communication overhead and privacy risks. Existing hash learning methods have limited binary code representational capacity, degrading model accuracy when integrated with FL. The paper aims to address all three issues simultaneously.
AI.method: FHPLF introduces three innovations: (a) binary gradient-like matrices replace real-valued gradients to cut computation/storage/communication costs and enhance privacy; (b) Projected Hamming Distance captures per-bit importance for richer similarity modeling; (c) Secure Binary Gradient Reassembly and Privacy-Enhanced Upload (SBG-PEU) strategy mitigates user interaction leakage during transmission.
AI.result: Extensive experiments on four real-world datasets show FHPLF consistently outperforms state-of-the-art hash learning and federated learning methods, achieving a favorable trade-off among accuracy, efficiency, and privacy preservation.
AI.conclusion: FHPLF effectively integrates hash learning into federated learning, overcoming representational capacity limitations through binary gradient compression and projected Hamming distance, while SBG-PEU further secures transmission. It provides a viable solution for privacy-preserving, communication-efficient hash learning in decentralized settings.

title: Knowledge-Based Pull Requests: A Trusted Workflow for Agent-Mediated Knowledge Collaboration
summary: AI coding agents are changing the bottleneck in software collaboration: code is increasingly cheap, while understanding intent, negotiating scope, and governing long-term project responsibility remain costly. This paper proposes \emph{Knowledge-Based Pull Requests} (KPR), a trusted workflow for agent-mediated software collaboration across trust boundaries, including open source, enterprise, vendor, contractor, and customer-driven settings. In KPR, an external collaborator's local code, tests, and cleaned agent interaction trace are treated as knowledge sources rather than as the default merge candidate. Agents distill these sources into a human-confirmed knowledge package and render it into reviewer-facing forms such as design memos, risk checklists, test plans, or implementation briefs. A project-owned inner trusted coding agent then regenerates candidate code inside the receiving project's environment under repository context, engineering conventions, tests, and security policy. KPR therefore separates two decisions that traditional pull requests often collapse: whether the knowledge should enter the project, and whether a particular implementation should be merged. We contribute the KPR workflow, a candidate artifact schema, a cost-accounting view, a collaboration gateway architecture, a minimal controlled simulation pilot over seven merged public pull requests, and an evaluation agenda. The pilot shows that KPR packages can be instantiated from real PR material and stress-tested under description ablation, diff ablation, and synthetic poisoned-patch conditions. We position KPR as an empirically testable workflow: its value depends on whether auditable extraction, transformation, and project-side regeneration reduce the cost of understanding and reworking high-context external changes.

AI.tldr: KPR proposes a workflow where external contributions are treated as knowledge sources rather than direct merge candidates. A project-owned agent extracts, distills, and regenerates code, separating the decision to accept knowledge from the decision to merge a specific implementation, aiming to reduce the cost of understanding and governing high-context external changes.
AI.motivation: As AI coding agents make code generation increasingly cheap, the real bottleneck in software collaboration shifts to understanding intent, negotiating scope, and governing long-term responsibility—especially across trust boundaries (open source, enterprise, vendor, contractor). Traditional pull requests conflate two decisions: whether external knowledge should enter the project and whether a particular implementation should be merged.
AI.method: The KPR workflow: (1) external collaborator submits local code, tests, and cleaned agent interaction traces as knowledge sources; (2) agents distill these into human-confirmed knowledge packages (design memos, risk checklists, test plans, implementation briefs); (3) a project-owned inner trusted coding agent regenerates candidate code under the receiving project's environment, conventions, and policies. The paper contributes a workflow definition, artifact schema, cost-accounting view, collaboration gateway architecture, and a minimal controlled pilot over seven merged public PRs tested under description ablation, diff ablation, and synthetic poisoned-patch conditions.
AI.result: The pilot demonstrates that KPR packages can be instantiated from real PR material and stress-tested under multiple adversarial conditions. The workflow is positioned as empirically testable, with value hinging on whether auditable extraction, transformation, and project-side regeneration reduce understanding and rework costs.
AI.conclusion: KPR offers a structured alternative to traditional PR workflows for the era of agent-mediated development, decoupling knowledge acceptance from code merging. Its adoption depends on empirical validation that the extraction-regeneration pipeline meaningfully lowers the cost of handling high-context external contributions across trust boundaries.

title: Reviving Reflection-in-Action: Instilling Designerly Thinking in AI-Supported Ideation through Multimodal Prompting
summary: Current AI-powered creativity support tools (AI-CSTs) primarily use text prompting to generate solution-oriented outputs. However, the potential value of multimodal prompting in designer-AI interaction, specifically the introduction of productive friction to encourage iteration and reflection, has not been fully explored. To address this, we developed SketchifAI, a prototype AI-CST, and evaluated it with design students. In a mixed-methods, within-participants study, we examined how different input modalities (text, sketch, and sketch-plus-tags) affected design students' perceived ability to express their intent, their perception of creativity support, and their divergent thinking performance. Our preliminary findings suggest that the sketch modality tended to enhance fluency, with inconclusive evidence for differences in variety, originality, or quality compared to text modality. Yet, paradoxically, participants showed a strong preference for text prompting. We discuss how AI tools might be designed to reintroduce reflection-through-sketching, ensuring that designer-AI interaction supports, rather than erodes, essential design skills in students.

AI.tldr: A study comparing text, sketch, and sketch-plus-tags input modalities in an AI creativity support tool (SketchifAI) with design students, finding that sketching enhanced fluency but users paradoxically preferred text prompting.
AI.motivation: Current AI-CSTs rely predominantly on text prompting for solution-oriented outputs. The authors identify a gap: multimodal prompting — particularly sketching — could introduce productive friction that encourages iteration and reflection in the designer-AI interaction, yet this potential remains underexplored.
AI.method: The authors developed SketchifAI, a prototype AI-CST, and conducted a mixed-methods, within-participants study with design students. They compared three input modalities — text, sketch, and sketch-plus-tags — measuring perceived intent expression, creativity support perception, and divergent thinking performance.
AI.result: Preliminary findings indicate the sketch modality tended to enhance fluency (quantity of ideas). Evidence for differences in variety, originality, or quality between modalities was inconclusive. Paradoxically, participants showed a strong subjective preference for text prompting despite sketching's fluency benefits.
AI.conclusion: AI tools should be designed to reintroduce reflection-through-sketching, ensuring that designer-AI interaction supports rather than erodes essential design skills in students. The preference paradox suggests a need to bridge the gap between what designers find comfortable (text) and what fosters deeper creative processes (sketching).

title: Lessons from the Adoption and Deprecation of the Privacy Sandbox Web APIs
summary: While several web actors have been trying to reduce web tracking for years, it remains unclear how to achieve both desirable levels of utility and privacy. In 2019, Google launched the Privacy Sandbox initiative to balance that trade-off and find privacy alternatives to common use cases such as advertising. Yet, in late 2025, Google canceled the project and deprecated most of the newly introduced APIs. Despite its end, the Privacy Sandbox represents a unique opportunity to learn about how the ecosystem reacted to the proposed changes and make observations about why and how it failed. In this paper, we present a longitudinal measurement and analysis study of the Privacy Sandbox APIs to characterize their adoption and deprecation over the past seven years by different web actors. Leveraging historical HTTP Archive crawls and public Chrome telemetry data, we offer the largest study of its kind into the prevalence of each Privacy Sandbox feature, during their entire respective lifetime (5+ years for some), on popular websites (CrUX top 100k), and as experienced by Chrome users during their browsing journey. Our results showcase an adoption that remained limited and uneven across the years; only few web actors implemented very specific APIs, and in disparate manners. We motivate our interpretation of these results by considering the incentives (interest, resources, timeline, etc.) and risks (potential trade-offs, privacy violations, and legal exposure, etc.) for these actors. Finally, our analysis also yields actionable recommendations for the next generation of web privacy proposals. More broadly, the Privacy Sandbox illustrates the limitations and disparities across browsers of ``fix it in the browser'' remedies: today, tracking and third-party cookies limitations in Chrome still remain largely opt-in, while they have been enabled by default on other browsers like Brave, Firefox, or Safari.

AI.tldr: A seven-year longitudinal study of Google's Privacy Sandbox initiative reveals limited, uneven adoption of its APIs by web actors. The authors analyze HTTP Archive crawls and Chrome telemetry data to characterize the project's failure, attribute it to misaligned incentives and risks, and offer recommendations for future web privacy proposals, highlighting the shortcomings of browser-based privacy fixes.
AI.motivation: Despite years of effort across the web ecosystem to reduce tracking, balancing utility (particularly advertising) with privacy remains unsolved. Google's Privacy Sandbox represented a major, high-profile attempt to address this trade-off, but its 2025 cancellation provides a rare, natural experiment. The authors aim to systematically understand why and how it failed by empirically measuring adoption patterns across its entire lifetime, thereby extracting lessons to inform the next generation of web privacy standards.
AI.method: The study employs a longitudinal measurement approach spanning seven years, combining two large-scale data sources: (1) historical HTTP Archive crawls to analyze Privacy Sandbox API prevalence on the CrUX top 100k popular websites, and (2) public Chrome telemetry data to capture real-world exposure as experienced by Chrome users during browsing. The analysis covers the entire lifetime of each Privacy Sandbox feature (5+ years for some APIs) and characterizes adoption by different web actor categories, examining both the extent and manner of implementation.
AI.result: Adoption of Privacy Sandbox APIs remained limited and highly uneven throughout their lifetimes. Only a small subset of web actors implemented specific APIs, and implementations varied substantially in how they were deployed. The authors interpret these findings through the lens of actor incentives (interest, resources, timelines) and risks (privacy trade-offs, potential violations, legal exposure), concluding that the initiative failed to align these factors sufficiently to drive broad ecosystem participation.
AI.conclusion: The Privacy Sandbox's failure illustrates fundamental limitations of "fix it in the browser" approaches: while browsers like Brave, Firefox, and Safari have enabled tracking protections and third-party cookie restrictions by default, Chrome's limitations remained largely opt-in, revealing disparities in how browser-based remedies are deployed. The authors distill actionable recommendations for future web privacy proposals, emphasizing the need for better incentive alignment across the ecosystem.

title: Where Larger Models Excel: The Primacy of Constraint-Guided Reasoning
summary: Larger language models consistently outperform smaller ones on reasoning benchmarks, yet the reasoning differences underlying this gap remain underexplored. Across benchmarks in mathematics, physics, chemistry, and programming, we observe stable performance gaps: averaged over datasets, Qwen3-32B outperforms Qwen3-8B by 6.43%, while GPT-OSS-120B exceeds GPT-OSS-20B by 7.38%. To study the reasoning differences behind these gains, we develop AdvCluster, an automated framework that identifies questions where the larger model shows a stable advantage, extracts fine-grained advantage descriptions from paired reasoning traces produced by larger and smaller models, and organizes them through semantic clustering with quantitative evaluation and selection guided by a reviewer model. Our analysis yields a systematic taxonomy of larger model reasoning advantages, spanning both common advantages that recur across domains and specialized advantages associated with particular domains. Across these patterns, a recurring theme is Constraint-Guided Reasoning: larger models are better at identifying explicit and implicit constraints, organizing them into structured reasoning, and using them to rule out infeasible paths and verify intermediate steps.

AI.tldr: Larger language models outperform smaller ones by 6–7% across STEM benchmarks. This paper develops AdvCluster to automatically extract and cluster fine-grained reasoning advantages from paired model outputs, revealing a systematic taxonomy where "Constraint-Guided Reasoning" — the ability to identify, structure, and verify constraints — emerges as a core differentiator.
AI.motivation: While the performance gap between larger and smaller LMs on reasoning benchmarks is well-documented, the specific reasoning differences that produce this gap are underexplored. The authors aim to move beyond aggregate scores to understand *how* larger models reason differently.
AI.method: AdvCluster: an automated three-stage framework that (1) identifies questions where the larger model holds a stable performance advantage over the smaller model, (2) extracts fine-grained advantage descriptions from paired reasoning traces (comparing how both models solve the same problem), and (3) organizes these descriptions via semantic clustering, with quantitative evaluation and selection guided by a reviewer model to build a systematic taxonomy.
AI.result: A systematic taxonomy of reasoning advantages was produced, categorized into (a) common advantages recurring across domains (math, physics, chemistry, programming) and (b) specialized advantages tied to specific domains. The dominant cross-cutting theme identified is Constraint-Guided Reasoning.
AI.conclusion: Larger models' reasoning superiority is not monolithic but decomposable into identifiable patterns. Constraint-Guided Reasoning — better identification of explicit/implicit constraints, structured organization, and constraint-based verification/elimination — is the recurring mechanism behind the performance gap, suggesting a promising direction for improving smaller models.

title: COrigami: An AI Pipeline for Co-Designing Flat-Foldable Visually Recognisable Origami
summary: While generative AI has achieved remarkable success in solving problems with verifiable solutions, generating physical art that satisfies both strict geometric constraints and subjective visual aesthetics remains a challenge. This paper presents an approach to tackle these difficulties in the domain of computational origami, a mathematically rigid environment that grounds artistic design within the equations of flat foldability. We present COrigami, an end-to-end AI-driven pipeline that assists the design cycle by generating crease patterns from natural language. Our pipeline involves generating a semantic stick figure, computing a base packing, solving for a flat-foldable crease pattern, shaping the flat-folded crease pattern, and refining the generated model using reinforcement learning driven by an autonomous aesthetic evaluation loop. Our system acts as a highly effective collaborative assistant, generating structural starting points that human artists can further expand and shape. By integrating algorithmic optimisation with autonomous aesthetic critique, this work demonstrates how AI systems can satisfy multi-objective physical constraints to enable reliable, mathematically grounded co-creativity.

AI.tldr: COrigami is an end-to-end AI pipeline that generates flat-foldable origami crease patterns from natural language descriptions, combining geometric constraint solving with reinforcement learning-based aesthetic refinement to serve as a collaborative design assistant for artists.
AI.motivation: Generative AI excels at problems with verifiable solutions but struggles with tasks requiring both strict mathematical constraints (e.g., flat-foldability) and subjective visual aesthetics. Computational origami provides an ideal testbed because it grounds artistic design within rigorous mathematical equations, yet no existing system bridges natural language input to physically valid, aesthetically pleasing origami designs.
AI.method: The COrigami pipeline proceeds in five stages: (1) generating a semantic stick figure from natural language input, (2) computing a base circle packing that satisfies local foldability, (3) solving for a globally flat-foldable crease pattern using the packing constraints, (4) shaping the flat-folded form, and (5) refining via reinforcement learning with an autonomous aesthetic evaluation loop that iteratively critiques and improves the visual quality of the output.
AI.result: The system reliably produces structurally valid, flat-foldable crease patterns that respond to natural language prompts, acting as an effective collaborative assistant that provides human artists with mathematically sound starting points for further creative elaboration.
AI.conclusion: By integrating algorithmic optimization with autonomous aesthetic critique, the work demonstrates that AI systems can satisfy multi-objective physical constraints, enabling reliable, mathematically grounded human-AI co-creativity in domains where both verifiable correctness and subjective quality matter.

title: Statistical and Structural Approaches to Algorithmic Fairness
summary: Modern machine learning systems have outgrown their origins as isolated predictive constructs, evolving into complex socio-technical architectures that actively mediate human opportunity. As algorithms increasingly determine access to economic and social opportunities, it has become widely recognized that these systems are deeply embedded with the structural inequalities and prejudices of their environments. The field of algorithmic fairness emerged in response to the growing recognition that models optimized for predictive accuracy can systematically disadvantage marginalized groups. Early mitigation strategies, however, rested on fragile simplifications that limited their effectiveness in complex socio-technical environments. This thesis identifies and addresses two fundamental limitations of contemporary fairness paradigms: the reliance on deterministic point estimates for auditing and the treatment of individuals as isolated entities devoid of structural context.

AI.tldr: This thesis critiques two foundational limitations in algorithmic fairness: the use of deterministic point estimates in auditing, and the atomistic treatment of individuals stripped of structural context. It argues that modern ML systems are socio-technical architectures that mediate opportunity and embed structural inequality, requiring more nuanced fairness paradigms.
AI.motivation: Modern machine learning systems have evolved from isolated predictive models into complex socio-technical architectures that actively gatekeep access to economic and social opportunities. These systems embed structural inequalities and prejudices from their environments, and models optimized solely for predictive accuracy can systematically disadvantage marginalized groups. Early fairness mitigation strategies relied on fragile simplifications that prove inadequate in real-world socio-technical settings, motivating the need for more robust paradigms.
AI.method: The thesis identifies and addresses two specific limitations of contemporary fairness approaches: (1) the reliance on deterministic point estimates for auditing fairness, and (2) the treatment of individuals as isolated entities lacking structural context. The work proposes to move beyond these simplifications, though the abstract does not specify the precise technical interventions or alternative frameworks developed.
AI.result: The abstract is framed as a problem identification and thesis overview rather than reporting empirical results. It identifies two fundamental weaknesses in existing fairness paradigms — deterministic point-estimate auditing and decontextualized individual treatment — and positions these as the core problems the thesis addresses. Specific findings or experimental outcomes are not detailed in this abstract.
AI.conclusion: Contemporary fairness paradigms are limited by their reliance on deterministic point estimates for auditing and their atomistic treatment of individuals. Addressing these two limitations is essential for developing algorithmic fairness approaches that can function effectively within the complex socio-technical realities in which modern ML systems operate.

title: A Deterministic Control Plane for LLM Coding Agents
comment: 45 pages, 9 figures, 13 tables. Dataset and reproduction scripts: Zenodo DOI 10.5281/zenodo.20780913. Ancillary files include report.json, organizations.txt, and figure-reproduction scripts
summary:
