LLM coding harnesses grant agents broad file and shell access, yet the configuration layer that steers them -- rules files, agent definitions, IDE-specific markdown -- is largely unmanaged. A prevalence study of 10,008 public GitHub repositories (n=6,145 agent config files) finds that agent configurations propagate as undeclared shared components: 10.1% of tracked paths are SHA-256 exact duplicates across independent repositories (fork-adjusted, threshold-independent), with 75.5% of clone pairs crossing organisational boundaries. Two further patterns are indicative: configurations are rarely revised (58% single-commit; 0.4 vs 0.6 commits/month age-normalised against CI/CD workflows), and rarely declare permission boundaries (<1% of agent configs vs 33% of Actions workflows, n=31 true positives).
  We propose a deterministic control plane above the harness that maps one-to-one to these gaps. Rel(AI)Build treats agent definitions as a managed supply chain (SHA-256 content addressing, HMAC-stamped lockfiles, hash-chained audit logs); enforces tiered permissions and attack-derived blocklists before LLM invocation; gates feature work through a phase state machine with requirement-to-file-to-test traceability; compiles a single canonical definition to seven IDE targets; and detects prompt drift via Jaccard similarity. Conformance tests on injected violations confirm each mechanism enforces its stated invariant; developer outcomes remain future work. Governance of this layer must be deterministic and tool-agnostic -- not delegated to further LLM orchestration.

AI.tldr: LLM coding agents suffer from unmanaged, copy-pasted configuration files that lack permission boundaries and are rarely revised. A study of 10,008 GitHub repos reveals widespread config duplication across org boundaries and minimal security hardening. Rel(AI)Build proposes a deterministic control plane with content-addressed supply chain management, tiered permissions, blocklists, phase-gated workflows, multi-target compilation, and prompt drift detection to address these gaps.
AI.motivation: LLM coding agents are granted broad file and shell access, but their configuration layer (rules files, agent definitions, IDE-specific markdown) is largely unmanaged. This creates a security blind spot where agent configurations propagate as undeclared shared components without permission boundaries, revision history, or supply chain integrity. The motivation is to quantify this problem empirically and propose a deterministic governance layer that closes these gaps without delegating control to further LLM orchestration.
AI.method: The paper combines an empirical prevalence study with a systems design contribution. The study analyzes 10,008 public GitHub repositories containing 6,145 agent config files, measuring SHA-256 exact duplication rates (fork-adjusted, threshold-independent), cross-organizational clone pairs, commit frequency (age-normalized against CI/CD workflows), and permission boundary declarations. The systems contribution, Rel(AI)Build, introduces: (1) SHA-256 content addressing with HMAC-stamped lockfiles and hash-chained audit logs for supply chain integrity; (2) tiered permissions and attack-derived blocklists enforced pre-invocation; (3) a phase state machine with requirement-to-file-to-test traceability; (4) canonical definition compilation to seven IDE targets; (5) prompt drift detection via Jaccard similarity. Conformance tests validate each mechanism against injected violations.
AI.result: The prevalence study reveals: 10.1% of tracked config paths are SHA-256 exact duplicates across independent repositories, with 75.5% of clone pairs crossing organizational boundaries. Configurations are rarely revised (58% single-commit; 0.4 vs 0.6 commits/month when age-normalized against CI/CD workflows). Fewer than 1% of agent configs declare permission boundaries, compared to 33% of GitHub Actions workflows (n=31 true positives). Conformance testing confirms each Rel(AI)Build mechanism enforces its stated invariant against injected violations.
AI.conclusion: The configuration layer governing LLM coding agents constitutes an unmanaged supply chain with demonstrable security weaknesses: rampant cross-organizational duplication, near-absent permission declarations, and stagnant revision practices. A deterministic, tool-agnostic control plane like Rel(AI)Build can systematically address these gaps through content addressing, permission enforcement, and phase-gated governance. Critically, governance of this layer must remain deterministic and not be delegated to further LLM orchestration. Developer outcome studies remain as future work.

title: Invisible Impact of Empathy on Behavioral Change: Isolating the Effect of Empathy in Long-term Physical Activity Coaching Chatbot Interactions
comment: Shortened version of paper accepted into CUI Short paper and WIP
summary: Current dialogue systems, powered by large language models, often treat empathy as essential without assessing its true impact, especially in behavior change, where motivation and adherence often depend on subtle user-chatbot dynamics. We examine this assumption by building three WhatsApp physical-activity (PA) coaching chatbots that differ only in empathy level and evaluating them in a six-week within-subject study (N = 13). Participants struggled to distinguish between the empathy conditions, and the non-empathetic version was often rated as more engaging and useful. However, higher-empathy variants were still associated with a larger overall average increase in step counts and faster improvement in intention to follow advice. These results suggest empathy's role is nuanced: it may be hard for lay users to identify explicitly, but it can still shape motivation and trust that support sustained change. We interpret this pattern through the Elaboration Likelihood Model's peripheral route. We highlight design implications for building next-generation PA coaching chatbots that balance effectiveness with human-like connection.

AI.tldr: A six-week within-subject study (N=13) tested three WhatsApp physical-activity coaching chatbots differing in empathy level. Users struggled to distinguish empathy conditions, often preferring the non-empathetic version for engagement, yet higher-empathy variants produced larger step-count increases and faster intention improvement — suggesting empathy operates peripherally (via the Elaboration Likelihood Model) rather than through explicit user recognition.
AI.motivation: Current dialogue systems treat empathy as universally essential without empirical validation of its actual impact. In behavior-change domains like physical-activity coaching, motivation and adherence hinge on subtle user-chatbot dynamics, yet whether empathy genuinely improves outcomes remains unexamined. The authors challenge this assumption directly.
AI.method: Three WhatsApp-based physical-activity coaching chatbots were built, differing only in empathy level (non-empathetic, moderate, high). A six-week within-subject study was conducted with 13 participants, collecting both subjective ratings (engagement, usefulness, perceived empathy) and objective behavioral measures (step counts, intention to follow advice).
AI.result: Participants could not reliably distinguish between empathy conditions, and the non-empathetic chatbot was frequently rated more engaging and useful. However, higher-empathy variants were associated with a larger overall average increase in step counts and faster improvement in intention to follow advice — a dissociation between explicit preference and implicit behavioral impact.
AI.conclusion: Empathy's role in behavior-change chatbots is nuanced: lay users may not explicitly recognize it, yet it shapes motivation and trust through peripheral-route processing (Elaboration Likelihood Model), supporting sustained change. Design implications include balancing effectiveness with human-like connection without over-indexing on explicit user preference for empathy.

title: What Browsers Do in the Shaders: A Measurement Study of WebGPU Privacy
summary:
WebGPU lets ordinary web pages run GPU workloads through a validated programming model. Validation protects memory safety, but shared browser, driver, OS, and GPU state can still expose privacy-relevant signals. We present WGPULens, a framework for measuring those signals across controlled scenarios, browser-native co-residency, a participant field study, public page loads, and mitigation policies. Our framework separates measurements: controlled scenarios support leakage, boundary, and mitigation claims; participant runs support deployment, compatibility, and fingerprintability; and a Tranco crawl measures WebGPU exposure in real-world pages.
  Our controlled results identify persistent pipeline compilation state as the clearest surface. Cold/warm pipeline probes reveal prior compilation state across selected origin, profile, and browser placements. Controlled browser/native experiments also show native GPU activity can be inferred from browser-visible observables under labeled workloads. Other resource probes provide weaker positive results and negative controls.
  The participant field study shows active WebGPU behavior is highly distinctive within the sample, with deterministic components stable within runs and lower exact stability across repeated visits. A page-load crawl finds WebGPU use mainly as adapter probing and static support code, with no observed page-load shader, pipeline, queue, query, or map activity. Mitigation pilots identify source-level key separation as a proxy for evaluating pipeline-cache partitioning. Overall, WGPULens shows that WebGPU privacy analysis must be surface-specific: browsers need to measure which GPU state crosses which boundary, which browser-visible signals reveal it, and what the corresponding mitigations cost.

AI.tldr: WGPULens is a measurement framework that systematically identifies privacy leakage surfaces in WebGPU, finding that persistent pipeline compilation state is the clearest fingerprinting vector, while real-world WebGPU usage remains minimal.
AI.motivation: WebGPU exposes GPU compute to web pages with memory safety guarantees, but shared state across browser, driver, OS, and GPU layers may leak privacy-relevant signals. No systematic measurement framework existed to quantify what leaks, across which boundaries, and under what conditions.
AI.method: A multi-tier measurement framework spanning: (1) controlled lab scenarios isolating leakage surfaces across origin, profile, and browser placements; (2) a participant field study measuring deployability and fingerprintability of active WebGPU workloads; (3) a Tranco top-list crawl assessing real-world WebGPU exposure; and (4) mitigation pilots testing source-level key separation as a proxy for pipeline-cache partitioning.
AI.result: Pipeline compilation state emerged as the dominant leakage surface — cold/warm probes reliably detected prior compilation. Browser-visible observables could infer native GPU activity under labeled workloads. In the field study, active WebGPU behavior was highly distinctive with stable deterministic components within runs but lower exact stability across revisits. The Tranco crawl found WebGPU use limited to adapter probing and static support code, with zero observed shader, pipeline, queue, query, or map operations on page load. Mitigation experiments demonstrated source-level key separation as a viable evaluation proxy for pipeline-cache partitioning.
AI.conclusion: WebGPU privacy analysis requires a surface-specific approach: browsers must systematically measure which GPU state crosses which boundary, which browser-visible signals reveal it, and what mitigations cost — rather than treating WebGPU as a monolithic privacy threat.

title: From Lexicon to AI: A Structured-Data Pipeline for Specialized Conversational Systems in Low-Resource Languages
summary: Low-resource languages face a critical challenge in AI development: creating specialized conversational systems without access to massive training corpora. We present a systematic methodology for transforming structured linguistic resources into specialized AI systems, demonstrating that expert-curated lexical databases can serve as effective foundations for conversational AI development. Our approach converts Hindi WordNet into 1.25 million diverse instruction-response pairs, fine-tunes a 12B-parameter language model using resource-efficient LoRA with 4-bit quantization. Evaluation through a Hindi language learning chatbot demonstrates that structured-knowledge-based systems achieve superior pedagogical effectiveness (91.0 vs. 79.4-83.6 for general-purpose models) while maintaining competitive semantic performance and exceptional consistency. The complete pipeline demonstrates a proof-of-concept methodology using Hindi for developing specialized AI systems for any languages with WordNet resources. This work addresses the critical gap in AI accessibility for low-resource languages, offering a practical alternative to corpus-intensive approaches and potentially enabling specialized AI development for the hundreds of languages with existing WordNet resources.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a methodology to convert structured lexical resources (Hindi WordNet) into specialized conversational AI systems for low-resource languages. Using LoRA fine-tuning with 4-bit quantization on a 12B-parameter model, the approach generates 1.25M instruction-response pairs. A Hindi learning chatbot built with this method achieved 91.0% pedagogical effectiveness versus 79.4-83.6% for general-purpose models, demonstrating a scalable, corpus-efficient alternative for languages with existing WordNet resources.
AI.motivation: Low-resource languages lack the massive training corpora required for developing specialized conversational AI systems. The authors aim to bridge this accessibility gap by leveraging existing structured linguistic resources (WordNets) as an alternative to data-intensive approaches, enabling specialized AI development for hundreds of underrepresented languages.
AI.method: The methodology converts Hindi WordNet — a structured lexical database — into 1.25 million diverse instruction-response pairs. These are used to fine-tune a 12-billion-parameter language model via Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) combined with 4-bit quantization for resource efficiency. The resulting system is evaluated as a Hindi language learning chatbot against general-purpose models.
AI.result: The WordNet-based system achieved 91.0% pedagogical effectiveness, significantly outperforming general-purpose models (79.4-83.6%). It maintained competitive semantic performance and demonstrated exceptional consistency, validating structured-knowledge-based approaches as viable alternatives to corpus-intensive methods.
AI.conclusion: Expert-curated lexical databases like WordNet can serve as effective foundations for specialized conversational AI in low-resource languages. The pipeline offers a proof-of-concept that generalizes to any language with existing WordNet resources, addressing the critical gap in AI accessibility and offering a practical, scalable alternative to data-hungry approaches.

title: The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards
comment: Authors are listed alphabetically by their first names
summary: A classical intuition holds that verifying a solution is easier than producing one. For today's coding agents, this intuition is being inverted: as foundation models develop stronger reasoning capabilities and engineering harnesses grow more sophisticated, generating complex candidate solutions is no longer difficult -- reliably verifying them has become the harder problem. Every verifier we can build is only a proxy for human intent, never the intent itself. This makes verification subject to a twofold difficulty: first, intent is underspecified by nature, making it inherently hard to faithfully check whether it has been fulfilled; second, during model training, optimization widens the gap between proxy and intent -- manifesting as reward hacking or signal saturation. To address this, we characterize the quality of verification signals along three dimensions -- scalability, faithfulness, and robustness -- and argue that achieving all three simultaneously is the central challenge. We further study four reward constructions: a test verifier for general coding tasks, a rubric verifier for frontend tasks, the user as verifier for real-world agent tasks, and an automated agent verifier for long-horizon tasks. Across different task types and policy capability levels, we conduct in-depth analysis and experiments on the core challenges of reward design and how to more effectively leverage reward signals. Experiments show that targeted verification design can effectively suppress reward hacking, improve task completion quality, and achieve significant gains across multiple internal and public benchmarks. These experiences collectively point to a core observation: no fixed reward function can remain effective as policy capability continues to grow; and verification must co-evolve with the generator.

AI.tldr: As coding agents grow stronger at generating solutions, verification becomes the bottleneck. The paper argues that all verifiers are imperfect proxies for human intent, subject to underspecification and optimization-induced degradation (reward hacking). It proposes evaluating verification along scalability, faithfulness, and robustness, explores four reward constructions across task types, and concludes that verification must co-evolve with the generator as policy capability improves.
AI.motivation: The classical intuition that verification is easier than generation is being inverted for modern coding agents. As foundation models become more capable at producing complex candidate solutions, reliably verifying those solutions has become the harder problem. This stems from a twofold difficulty: (1) human intent is inherently underspecified, making faithful verification difficult by nature; (2) optimization during training widens the gap between proxy verifiers and true intent, manifesting as reward hacking or signal saturation. The paper is motivated by the need to systematically understand and address these verification challenges.
AI.method: The authors characterize verification signal quality along three dimensions: scalability, faithfulness, and robustness, arguing that simultaneously achieving all three is the central challenge. They then study four distinct reward constructions: (1) a test verifier for general coding tasks, (2) a rubric verifier for frontend tasks, (3) the user as verifier for real-world agent tasks, and (4) an automated agent verifier for long-horizon tasks. Across these settings and varying policy capability levels, they conduct in-depth analysis and experiments on reward design challenges.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that targeted verification design can effectively suppress reward hacking, improve task completion quality, and yield significant gains across multiple internal and public benchmarks. The results validate that careful attention to verification signal design is critical for maintaining alignment between proxy rewards and true intent as policy models improve.
AI.conclusion: The central observation is that no fixed reward function can remain effective as policy capability continues to grow. Verification must co-evolve with the generator — as models become more capable, verification mechanisms must be continually refined to avoid reward hacking and maintain faithfulness to human intent.

title: Topology-Informed Neural Networks for Flood Detection in Optical and Synthetic Aperture Radar Imagery
summary: Floods frequently impact regions around the world. Rapid and accurate flood detection is crucial for emergency response and timely mitigation of human and economic loss. The expanding availability of satellite data and advances in artificial intelligence have enhanced monitoring of environmental hazards, but many flood events remain challenging to detect because cloud cover obscures optical satellite imagery. Rambour et al. introduced the SEN12-FLOOD dataset and extracted per-image features using a ResNet-50 convolutional neural network backbone, then fed these features into a gated recurrent unit network to show that temporal information can substantially improve accuracy compared to single-image baselines. More recently, Chamatidis et al. showed that a vision transformer can achieve strong performance with popular convolutional architectures. However, these models typically function as opaque black boxes, making it difficult to interpret their decision boundaries, learned features, and internal reasoning, especially in safety-critical domains like remote sensing. In contrast, topological data analysis (TDA) provides a mathematically grounded framework for capturing global structural features of data. TDA has emerged as a powerful tool for analyzing complex imagery, especially imagery with geometrically interpretable structures, of which floods are a prime candidate. In this work, we systematically evaluate topological descriptors for flood detection using the open-source SEN12-FLOOD dataset. By extracting topological features from each image and incorporating them into neural networks, we demonstrate that topological descriptors carry meaningful flood signals independently and complement existing networks to yield more robust and interpretable flood detection systems.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates topological data analysis (TDA) descriptors for satellite-based flood detection, demonstrating that topological features carry independent flood signals and complement existing neural networks, yielding more robust and interpretable flood detection systems on the SEN12-FLOOD dataset.
AI.motivation: Existing deep learning flood detection models (CNNs, RNNs, vision transformers) act as opaque black boxes, making decision boundaries and internal reasoning difficult to interpret — a critical limitation in safety-sensitive remote sensing applications. Meanwhile, floods exhibit geometrically interpretable structures well-suited to topological analysis.
AI.method: The authors systematically evaluate topological descriptors for flood detection using the SEN12-FLOOD dataset. Topological features are extracted from each satellite image and incorporated into neural network architectures, both as standalone signals and as complementary inputs alongside existing learned features.
AI.result: Topological descriptors carry meaningful flood signals independently and, when combined with existing neural networks, yield more robust and interpretable flood detection performance compared to conventional black-box approaches.
AI.conclusion: TDA provides a mathematically grounded, interpretable framework that enhances flood detection reliability. Integrating topological features with deep learning models offers a promising direction for safety-critical remote sensing applications where model transparency is essential.

title: ProvenAI: Provenance-Native Traces of Evidence in Generated Answers
summary: Retrieval-augmented systems routinely present citations alongside generated answers, yet a citation does not confirm that the corresponding source meaningfully shaped the output. This paper introduces ProvenAI, a framework that decomposes transparency in multi-hop question answering into three independently measurable layers: answer correctness, citation fidelity against benchmark supporting evidence, and per-document influence under leave-one-resource-out intervention. Targeting the HotpotQA distractor benchmark through a seven-stage pipeline covering data normalisation, retrieval indexing, citation-aware answer generation, attribution auditing, ablation-based influence estimation, batch evaluation, and interactive inspection, ProvenAI evaluates 7,405 validation examples drawn from a canonical corpus of 509,300 passages. The system achieves 53.53% answer accuracy alongside a mean citation-fidelity score of 71.55%, and a worked example surfaces what we call the citation-influence gap: a clean citation audit co-occurring with a profile in which one cited source registers only weak influence while seven uncited sources demonstrably shift the output. We formalise the relationship between the implemented surface proxy and a token-level KL-divergence target through a stated faithfulness condition, ground the framework in causal-mediation analysis and database-provenance theory, and discuss how the three measurement layers compose with cryptographic provenance architectures emerging in autonomous scientific discovery. ProvenAI establishes that meaningful transparency in retrieval-grounded QA requires traceable links across retrieved, cited, and behaviourally influential evidence as three distinct, independently measured layers.

AI.tldr: ProvenAI introduces a three-layer transparency framework for retrieval-augmented QA—answer correctness, citation fidelity, and per-document influence via leave-one-resource-out ablation—evaluated on HotpotQA, revealing a "citation-influence gap" where clean citations coexist with weak actual influence from cited sources.
AI.motivation: Existing retrieval-augmented systems display citations alongside answers, but citation presence alone does not guarantee that cited sources meaningfully shaped the generated output. The authors aim to decompose transparency into independently measurable layers to expose discrepancies between what is cited and what is causally influential.
AI.method: A seven-stage pipeline: (1) data normalization, (2) retrieval indexing over 509,300 passages, (3) citation-aware answer generation, (4) attribution auditing for citation fidelity against benchmark evidence, (5) ablation-based influence estimation using leave-one-resource-out intervention, (6) batch evaluation on 7,405 HotpotQA distractor examples, and (7) interactive inspection. The framework is grounded in causal-mediation analysis and database-provenance theory, with a formal faithfulness condition linking surface proxies to token-level KL-divergence targets.
AI.result: On 7,405 HotpotQA validation examples, ProvenAI achieves 53.53% answer accuracy and 71.55% mean citation-fidelity score. A worked example reveals the citation-influence gap: a citation audit appears clean while one cited source shows only weak influence, yet seven uncited sources demonstrably shift the output when ablated.
AI.conclusion: Meaningful transparency in retrieval-grounded QA requires traceable links across three distinct, independently measured layers: retrieved evidence, cited evidence, and behaviorally influential evidence. The framework composes with emerging cryptographic provenance architectures for autonomous scientific discovery.

title: Are LLMs Ready for Anti-Pattern Detection in Microservice Architectures?
summary: Microservice systems are prone to recurrent architectural anti-patterns (APs) that hinder maintainability, evolvability, and operational quality. Most existing AP detection approaches rely on static analysis and handcrafted rules, which can be effective but are often tool-dependent, limited to explicitly encoded detection logic, and difficult to adapt to heterogeneous repositories. In this paper, we investigate whether large language models (LLMs) are ready to support architectural anti-pattern detection in microservice architectures through a prompt-based analysis pipeline over static repository artifacts. We evaluate three general-purpose LLMs on a curated benchmark of microservice repositories annotated with 16 architectural anti-patterns, and compare their performance against the state-of-the-art static-analysis tool MARS using a uniform evaluation protocol based on precision and recall. Our results show that LLMs can provide useful support for anti-pattern detection, achieving competitive performance on several anti-patterns, especially when the relevant evidence is local, heterogeneous, or semantically rich. At the same time, they exhibit clear limitations on anti-patterns that require explicit structural or cross-service dependency evidence, where static analysis remains more reliable. These findings suggest that LLMs are not yet a replacement for traditional analyzers, but already represent a promising complementary aid for architectural assessment in microservice systems.

AI.tldr: This paper evaluates whether large language models can detect architectural anti-patterns in microservice systems by analyzing static repository artifacts via prompts. Comparing three LLMs against the static-analysis tool MARS on a curated benchmark of 16 anti-patterns, results show LLMs are competitive for semantically rich, local, or heterogeneous patterns but fall short on those requiring explicit structural or cross-service dependencies, positioning LLMs as complementary aids rather than replacements for traditional analyzers.
AI.motivation: Existing AP detection tools rely on handcrafted rules and static analysis, making them tool-dependent, limited to explicitly encoded logic, and difficult to adapt across heterogeneous repositories. The authors investigate whether LLMs can overcome these limitations through flexible, prompt-based analysis.
AI.method: The authors construct a prompt-based analysis pipeline that feeds static repository artifacts to three general-purpose LLMs. They curate a benchmark of microservice repositories annotated with 16 architectural anti-patterns and evaluate LLM performance using precision and recall, comparing results against the state-of-the-art static-analysis tool MARS under a uniform evaluation protocol.
AI.result: LLMs achieve competitive performance on anti-patterns where evidence is local, heterogeneous, or semantically rich, but exhibit clear limitations on anti-patterns requiring explicit structural or cross-service dependency evidence — cases where static analysis (MARS) remains more reliable.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are not yet a replacement for traditional static analyzers but already serve as a promising complementary aid for architectural assessment in microservice systems, suggesting a hybrid approach may be optimal.

title: From Content to Strategy: Understanding the Motivations, Processes, and Impacts of AI-Guided Communication
summary: Artificial intelligence-mediated communication (AI-MC) is conceptualized as applying AI to augment or generate message content (Hancock et al., 2020). However, advances in generative AI have expanded its use beyond generating content to guiding individuals' communication strategies, that is, AI-guided communication, yet theoretical and empirical understandings of this emerging use pattern and its consequences remains limited. To address this gap, this study conducted 26 in-depth interviews with individuals who have used AI to develop their communication strategies. Findings suggest participants strongly preferred using AI to analyze challenging scenarios in close relationships, because it fostered self-reflection, eased emotions, prevented conflict escalation, offered multiple perspectives, and provided a safe, nonjudgmental space for self-disclosure. Participants also stated that AI-guided communication enhanced their empathy and communication skills, though some voiced self-doubt and worried about losing their uniqueness. Views on long-term relational impact were mixed, depending on perceived usefulness of AI for resolving short-term interpersonal challenges.

AI.tldr: This interview study explores how individuals use generative AI not just to produce messages, but to guide their communication strategies in close relationships. Participants valued AI for analyzing challenging scenarios, fostering self-reflection, and providing a safe space, but expressed mixed feelings about long-term impacts on relational authenticity and self-identity.
AI.motivation: While AI-mediated communication (AI-MC) has been conceptualized primarily as AI augmenting or generating message content, recent advances in generative AI have enabled a new, understudied use pattern: AI-guided communication, where AI shapes users' communication strategies. Theoretical and empirical understanding of this emerging phenomenon and its relational consequences remains limited, motivating this exploratory study.
AI.method: The authors conducted 26 in-depth interviews with individuals who had experience using AI to develop their communication strategies, employing a qualitative approach to capture participants' lived experiences, perceptions, and concerns.
AI.result: Participants strongly preferred using AI to analyze challenging scenarios in close relationships. Key benefits included fostering self-reflection, easing negative emotions, preventing conflict escalation, offering multiple perspectives, and providing a safe, nonjudgmental space for self-disclosure. AI-guided communication was perceived to enhance empathy and communication skills. However, some participants experienced self-doubt and worried about losing their uniqueness. Views on long-term relational impact were mixed, contingent on whether AI was seen as useful for resolving short-term interpersonal challenges.
AI.conclusion: AI-guided communication represents a distinct and consequential evolution of AI-MC. While users appreciate its reflective and strategic benefits, concerns about authenticity, identity, and long-term relational effects highlight tensions that warrant further theoretical development and empirical investigation.

title: Adaptive Evaluation of Out-of-Band Defenses Against Prompt Injection in LLM Agents
summary: Recent work (2024 to 2026) has converged on a strategy for defending tool-using LLM agents against indirect prompt injection: rather than training the model to refuse malicious instructions, enforce security outside the model with a deterministic policy that mediates the agent's actions. Systems such as CaMeL, FIDES, Progent, RTBAS, and FORGE realize this with capabilities, information-flow labels, and reference monitors, and several report near-elimination of attacks on the AgentDojo benchmark. We make two contributions. First, we organize these out-of-band defenses as instances of classical integrity protection (Biba), reference monitoring, and least privilege, yielding a structured comparison of what they do and do not cover. Second, we warn that every one of them is validated only on static benchmarks (a fixed set of injection attempts), the same methodology that made in-band defenses look strong until adaptive, defense-aware attacks broke twelve of them at over 90% success; we specify the threat model and protocol an adaptive evaluation requires. We then run that protocol as an independent reproduction and extension of Progent's own adaptive-attack analysis, on AgentDojo, with an open-weight agent (Qwen2.5-7B) self-hosted on a single H200, a setting its authors did not test. Averaged over three runs, the defense held: Progent cut mean attack success roughly sixfold (25.8% to 4.2%), and a hand-crafted adaptive attack did not raise it (2.6%). This is one small-scale data point on a weak model with a single black-box attack template; a stronger optimized (white-box GCG) attack remains open. The result is consistent with, but does not establish, the hypothesis that deterministic out-of-band enforcement is a harder target for an adaptive attacker than in-band detection.

AI.tldr: Recent defenses against indirect prompt injection in LLM agents use deterministic, out-of-band enforcement (capabilities, information-flow labels, reference monitors) rather than model-level refusal training. The paper systematizes these defenses under classical security principles (Biba integrity, reference monitoring, least privilege) and critiques their evaluation methodology. The authors then independently reproduce and extend Progent's adaptive-attack analysis, finding that Progent reduces attack success ~6× and resists an adaptive attack, though stronger white-box attacks remain untested.
AI.motivation: Twofold: (1) Multiple recent out-of-band defenses (CaMeL, FIDES, Progent, RTBAS, FORGE) have been proposed independently but lack systematic comparison under a unified security framework. (2) All these defenses are validated only on static benchmarks — the same flawed methodology that previously made in-band defenses appear robust until adaptive, defense-aware attackers broke 12 of them at >90% success. The authors aim to both organize the defense landscape and demonstrate what proper adaptive evaluation entails.
AI.method: First, the authors taxonomize out-of-band defenses as instances of Biba integrity protection, reference monitoring, and least privilege, producing a structured comparison of coverage gaps. Second, they specify a threat model and adaptive evaluation protocol, then execute it as an independent reproduction of Progent on AgentDojo using Qwen2.5-7B (open-weight, self-hosted on a single H200) — a setting Progent's original authors did not test. They measure attack success rate (ASR) over three runs under both static and hand-crafted adaptive attacks.
AI.result: Progent reduced mean attack success rate from 25.8% (undefended) to 4.2% (~6× reduction). A hand-crafted adaptive attack did not increase ASR (2.6%). The authors emphasize this is a small-scale data point on a weak model with a single black-box template; a stronger white-box (GCG) adaptive attack remains open. The result is consistent with — but does not confirm — the hypothesis that deterministic out-of-band enforcement is harder for adaptive attackers than in-band detection.
AI.conclusion: Deterministic, out-of-band enforcement grounded in classical OS security principles appears promising against indirect prompt injection, and may be more resistant to adaptive attacks than in-band defenses. However, current evaluation practices are insufficient: the field must adopt adaptive, defense-aware threat modeling and evaluation protocols. Stronger white-box attacks against these defenses remain an open challenge.

title: Dynamic-dLLM: Dynamic Cache-Budget and Adaptive Parallel Decoding for Training-Free Acceleration of Diffusion LLM
summary: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) offer a promising alternative to autoregressive models, excelling in text generation tasks due to their bidirectional attention mechanisms. However, their computational complexity scales on the order of L cubed with the sequence length L. This poses significant challenges for long-sequence and real-time applications, primarily due to the lack of compatibility with key-value caching and the non-autoregressive nature of denoising steps. Existing acceleration methods rely on static caching or parallel decoding strategies, which fail to account for the dynamic behavior of token properties across layers and decoding steps. We propose Dynamic-dLLM, a training-free framework that enhances dLLM inference efficiency through two components: Dynamic Cache Updating (DCU), which adaptively allocates cache-update budgets based on layer-wise token dynamics, and Adaptive Parallel Decoding (APD), which dynamically calibrates decoding thresholds to balance generation quality and efficiency. Extensive experiments on models like LLaDA-8B-Instruct, LLaDA-1.5, and Dream-v0-7B-Instruct across benchmarks such as MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval demonstrate that Dynamic-dLLM significantly improves inference speed. It attains an average speedup exceeding 3 times while maintaining performance. Dynamic-dLLM outperforms state-of-the-art acceleration methods and provides a plug-and-play solution for efficient dLLM deployment without compromising performance. The code is available at https://github.com/TianyiWu233/DYNAMIC-DLLM.

AI.tldr: Dynamic-dLLM is a training-free inference acceleration framework for diffusion LLMs that combines adaptive cache updating and dynamic parallel decoding to achieve >3x speedup without performance loss.
AI.motivation: Diffusion LLMs (dLLMs) suffer from O(L³) computational complexity with sequence length, making them impractical for long-sequence and real-time applications. Existing acceleration methods (static caching, parallel decoding) ignore the dynamic behavior of token properties across layers and decoding steps.
AI.method: Two components: (1) Dynamic Cache Updating (DCU) — adaptively allocates cache-update budgets based on layer-wise token dynamics; (2) Adaptive Parallel Decoding (APD) — dynamically calibrates decoding thresholds to balance generation quality and efficiency. Both are training-free and plug-and-play.
AI.result: Experiments on LLaDA-8B-Instruct, LLaDA-1.5, and Dream-v0-7B-Instruct across MMLU, GSM8K, and HumanEval benchmarks show >3x average inference speedup while maintaining performance. Outperforms state-of-the-art acceleration methods.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic-dLLM provides an effective, plug-and-play solution for efficient dLLM deployment, overcoming the KV-cache incompatibility and non-autoregressive limitations of diffusion LLMs without sacrificing generation quality.

title: How Do Tool-Augmented LLM Agents Perform on Real-World Energy Analytics Tasks?
summary:
Agentic benchmarks have emerged across general-purpose and domain-specific settings, including finance, coding, law, and drug discovery, yet energy-domain evaluations remain largely limited to static knowledge recall. This is a critical gap for a sector that requires live data retrieval, specialized regulatory and market knowledge, and multi-step quantitative reasoning under real-world constraints.
  We present an empirical study of tool-augmented LLM agents on real-world energy market analytics tasks. Our evaluation environment includes 243 expert-curated problems across three categories: (1) Market Data Retrieval and Analysis, (2) Knowledge Retrieval and Interpretation, and (3) Advanced Quantitative Modeling and Decision Analytics. Tasks include price and demand analysis, tariff impact modeling, asset revenue and returns estimation, hedging strategy analysis, and optimization modeling, with problems spanning multiple difficulty levels.
  Agents are equipped with a configurable suite of domain tools, including live electricity market APIs for major U.S. ISOs, regulatory docket search, utility tariff databases, asset optimization models, and retrieval-augmented generation over energy market documents. We assess agent responses using a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol that scores approach correctness, answer accuracy, attribute alignment, and source validity, with category-aware routing to match scoring criteria to question type. We evaluate both closed-source and open-source LLMs, providing a comparative analysis of how model capability and domain tooling interact in a high-stakes professional domain. Key artifacts are publicly released to support reproducibility and future research.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces an empirical evaluation of tool-augmented LLM agents on real-world energy market analytics, addressing the gap in agentic benchmarks for the energy domain. Using 243 expert-curated problems across three task categories—market data retrieval, knowledge retrieval, and advanced quantitative modeling—agents are equipped with domain tools (live ISO APIs, tariff databases, regulatory search, optimization models, RAG). Evaluation employs a multi-dimensional protocol scoring approach correctness, answer accuracy, attribute alignment, and source validity, comparing both closed-source and open-source LLMs.
AI.motivation: Existing agentic benchmarks cover general-purpose and domain-specific settings (finance, coding, law, drug discovery), but energy-domain evaluations remain limited to static knowledge recall. The energy sector uniquely demands live data retrieval, specialized regulatory and market knowledge, and multi-step quantitative reasoning under real-world constraints, creating a critical evaluation gap.
AI.method: The authors construct an evaluation environment with 243 expert-curated problems spanning three categories: (1) Market Data Retrieval and Analysis, (2) Knowledge Retrieval and Interpretation, and (3) Advanced Quantitative Modeling and Decision Analytics. Agents are equipped with configurable domain tools including live electricity market APIs for major U.S. ISOs, regulatory docket search, utility tariff databases, asset optimization models, and RAG over energy market documents. A multi-dimensional evaluation protocol scores responses on approach correctness, answer accuracy, attribute alignment, and source validity, with category-aware routing to match scoring criteria to question type. Both closed-source and open-source LLMs are evaluated.
AI.result: The paper provides a comparative analysis of how model capability and domain tooling interact in high-stakes professional energy market tasks. Key artifacts are publicly released for reproducibility. Specific quantitative results are not detailed in the abstract.
AI.conclusion: Tool-augmented LLM agents show promise for real-world energy market analytics, but the interaction between model capability and domain-specific tooling is critical. The public release of benchmarks and artifacts aims to spur further research in this underexplored, high-stakes domain.

title: A General Framework for Learning Algebraic Properties from Cayley Graphs using Graph Neural Networks
summary: A Graph Neural Network (GNN) framework for predicting the solvability of finite groups from their Cayley graph representations was introduced in [1]. In the present work, we generalize this approach and develop a property-independent framework for learning algebraic properties of finite groups directly from Cayley graphs. As representative case studies, we consider abelianity, nilpotency, and solvability. Using a common GNN architecture and training pipeline, we investigate the extent to which algebraic structure can be recovered from graph-based representations alone. Results on a collection of finite groups drawn from several families demonstrate that the framework successfully learns and distinguishes multiple algebraic properties from their associated Cayley graphs. These findings suggest that substantial algebraic information is encoded in graph representations and can be extracted through GNNs. More broadly, the proposed framework provides a proof of concept for applying graph representation learning to the study of algebraic properties of finite groups.

AI.tldr: A property-independent GNN framework is developed to learn multiple algebraic properties (abelianity, nilpotency, solvability) of finite groups directly from Cayley graphs, demonstrating that substantial algebraic structure is encoded in graph representations and can be reliably extracted.
AI.motivation: Prior work showed GNNs can predict solvability from Cayley graphs, but was limited to a single property. This paper asks: can a unified, property-independent GNN framework learn and distinguish multiple algebraic properties from the same graph representations?
AI.method: A common GNN architecture and training pipeline is applied to Cayley graphs of finite groups from several families. The framework is tested on three binary classification tasks: abelianity, nilpotency, and solvability, using the same graph-based input representation across all tasks.
AI.result: The framework successfully learns and distinguishes all three algebraic properties across diverse families of finite groups, showing that Cayley graphs encode substantial algebraic information recoverable by GNNs.
AI.conclusion: Cayley graph representations preserve rich algebraic structure that GNNs can extract in a property-agnostic manner. This serves as a proof of concept for broader application of graph representation learning to algebraic property prediction in finite groups.

title: Extracting Problem and Method Sentence from Scientific Papers: A Context-enhanced Transformer Using Formulaic Expression Desensitization
summary: Billions of scientific papers lead to the need to identify essential parts from the massive text. Scientific research is an activity from putting forward problems to using methods. To learn the main idea from scientific papers, we focus on extracting problem and method sentences. Annotating sentences within scientific papers is labor-intensive, resulting in small-scale datasets that limit the amount of information models can learn. This limited information leads models to rely heavily on specific forms, which in turn reduces their generalization capabilities. This paper addresses the problems caused by small-scale datasets from three perspectives: increasing dataset scale, reducing dependence on specific forms, and enriching the information within sentences. To implement the first two ideas, we introduce the concept of formulaic expression (FE) desensitization and propose FE desensitization-based data augmenters to generate synthetic data and reduce models' reliance on FEs. For the third idea, we propose a context-enhanced transformer that utilizes context to measure the importance of words in target sentences and to reduce noise in the context. Furthermore, this paper conducts experiments using large language model (LLM) based in-context learning (ICL) methods. Quantitative and qualitative experiments demonstrate that our proposed models achieve a higher macro F1 score compared to the baseline models on two scientific paper datasets, with improvements of 3.71% and 2.67%, respectively. The LLM based ICL methods are found to be not suitable for the task of problem and method extraction.

AI.tldr: To overcome small-scale dataset limitations in extracting problem and method sentences from scientific papers, the authors propose formulaic expression (FE) desensitization data augmenters, a context-enhanced transformer, and evaluate LLM-based in-context learning, achieving macro F1 improvements of 3.71% and 2.67% on two datasets.
AI.motivation: Scientific paper annotation is labor-intensive, producing small-scale datasets that cause models to overfit to specific formulaic expressions (FEs) and suffer from poor generalization. The authors aim to address this by increasing dataset scale, reducing FE dependence, and enriching sentence-level information.
AI.method: Three complementary approaches: (1) FE desensitization-based data augmenters that generate synthetic training data while masking or replacing formulaic expressions to reduce superficial pattern reliance; (2) a context-enhanced transformer that uses surrounding context to weight word importance in target sentences and filter contextual noise; (3) evaluation of LLM-based in-context learning (ICL) methods as an alternative paradigm for the extraction task.
AI.result: The proposed models outperform baselines, achieving macro F1 score improvements of 3.71% and 2.67% on two scientific paper datasets. LLM-based ICL methods were found unsuitable for problem and method extraction.
AI.conclusion: FE desensitization augmentation and context-enhanced transformers effectively mitigate small-data challenges in scientific sentence extraction. LLM-based ICL is not a viable alternative for this specific task, highlighting the continued need for specialized models.

title: CLIR: Liveness-Driven and Structure-Aware Fuzzing for the Cranelift Compiler
summary:
Modern compilers are complex software systems that must correctly translate high-level programming languages into machine code across multiple architectures. Cranelift, a fast and modern compiler backend originally developed for WebAssembly and recently adopted as an experimental backend for Rust, has gained increasing importance due to its superior compilation speed compared to LLVM and comprehensive multi-architecture support, including x86-64, AArch64, s390x, and RISCV64. However, despite decades of development in compiler testing, testing Cranelift still presents unique challenges, including (1) constructing valid IR under the strict enforcement of SSA form, (2) generating sequences with sufficient computational density to stress backend components, and (3) balancing broad backend coverage with efficient root cause analysis across heterogeneous architectures.
  To address these challenges, we propose CLIR, a differential testing framework that integrates a syntax-preserving hierarchical generation strategy to guarantee SSA validity, a liveness-guided instruction refinement mechanism to maximize computational density, and a diagnosis-guided cross-architecture adaptation scheme to facilitate efficient root cause analysis across heterogeneous backends. Our comprehensive evaluation demonstrates that CLIR significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines, detecting 8x, 24x, and 8x more unique bugs than cranelift-fuzzgen, wasm-smith, and WASMaker, respectively, while RustSmith uncovered no bugs. Consequently, within 72 hours of testing, CLIR discovered 24 bugs spanning all target architectures, with 21 confirmed and 9 fixed.

AI.tldr: CLIR is a differential testing framework for the Cranelift compiler backend that uses syntax-preserving hierarchical generation, liveness-guided instruction refinement, and diagnosis-guided cross-architecture adaptation to uncover bugs. It found 8x, 24x, and 8x more unique bugs than existing tools, discovering 24 bugs in 72 hours across all target architectures.
AI.motivation: Cranelift, a fast compiler backend used for WebAssembly and Rust, presents unique testing challenges: (1) constructing valid IR under strict SSA enforcement, (2) generating computationally dense instruction sequences to stress backend components, and (3) balancing broad architecture coverage with efficient root cause analysis across heterogeneous backends (x86-64, AArch64, s390x, RISCV64). Existing tools inadequately address these challenges.
AI.method: CLIR employs three key techniques: (1) a syntax-preserving hierarchical generation strategy to guarantee SSA validity of generated IR, (2) a liveness-guided instruction refinement mechanism to maximize computational density in test sequences, and (3) a diagnosis-guided cross-architecture adaptation scheme that enables efficient root cause analysis across heterogeneous backends.
AI.result: CLIR detected 8x, 24x, and 8x more unique bugs than cranelift-fuzzgen, wasm-smith, and WASMaker respectively. RustSmith found no bugs. Within 72 hours, CLIR discovered 24 bugs across all four target architectures, with 21 confirmed and 9 already fixed.
AI.conclusion: CLIR significantly advances compiler testing for Cranelift by effectively addressing the unique challenges of SSA validity, computational density, and cross-architecture diagnosis. Its superior bug-finding capability demonstrates the importance of tailored testing strategies for modern compiler backends.

title: Modeling Adaptive Visual Search in Semantically Hierarchical Layouts
summary: This paper introduces a computational cognitive model to investigate how information grouping impacts visual search, a key consideration in user interface design. The model uses computational rationality to view user behavior as an adaptation to cognitive and task constraints. Our work highlights that humans use hierarchical task representations, exploiting semantic and visual structures to improve search efficiency within the constraints of the visual system. We validate this model with data from two human studies focused on visual search and semantic categorization, demonstrating that semantic grouping improves search performance when it aligns with spatial grouping. Our model replicates task durations and eye movement patterns. By improving understanding of how hierarchical memory structures are utilized in human cognition, the model extends previous visual search models. We showcase our model in the rapid prototyping and evaluation of semantic visual groupings within user interface wireframes, suggesting a pathway toward applications in more complex, real-world interface design.

AI.tldr: A computational cognitive model using computational rationality demonstrates how hierarchical task representations exploiting semantic and visual structures improve visual search efficiency. Validated with human studies, the model replicates task durations and eye movements and is applied to rapid prototyping of UI wireframes.
AI.motivation: Understanding how information grouping impacts visual search is critical for user interface design, yet existing visual search models do not adequately capture how humans exploit hierarchical memory structures combining semantic and spatial information to improve search efficiency under cognitive and task constraints.
AI.method: The paper introduces a computational cognitive model grounded in computational rationality, framing user behavior as optimal adaptation to cognitive and task constraints. The model incorporates hierarchical task representations that leverage both semantic and visual structures. It is validated against data from two human studies involving visual search and semantic categorization tasks.
AI.result: The model successfully replicates empirical task durations and eye movement patterns. Semantic grouping improves search performance when aligned with spatial grouping. The model is demonstrated in rapid prototyping and evaluation of semantic visual groupings within UI wireframes.
AI.conclusion: Hierarchical memory structures that integrate semantic and visual groupings significantly enhance visual search. The computational rationality framework offers a principled way to model this behavior, extends prior visual search models, and provides a practical pathway for evaluating interface designs in real-world applications.

title: DKVE: Decentralized Key Validation for End-to-End Encrypted Messaging
summary:
End-to-end encrypted messaging systems depend on authentic public key distribution to prevent man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks. Current solutions present a stark trade-off: out-of-band (OOB) verification provides strong security but lacks scalability for large contact lists, while key transparency (KT) systems enable automated verification at high storage costs and operational complexity.
  We propose DKVE, a protocol that validates public keys through privacy-preserving cross-validation within users' social graphs. When obtaining a contact's public key from a key server, clients query mutual contacts to verify they hold the same key, combining Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (OPRF) and Oblivious Key-Value Stores (OKVS) to preserve privacy of both queries and contact lists. DKVE employs a Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) to aggregate responses and detect server misbehavior with user-configurable error bounds.
  We evaluate DKVE through simulations on real social network datasets, demonstrating DKVE can detect MitM attacks with exceeding 97% for strong-to-moderate-tie networks. The remaining 3% of cases require validation through alternative methods such as KT and OOB verification. Our proof-of-concept implementation confirms feasibility for background operation on commodity hardware, in terms of the latency and bandwidth.
  As DKVE can reduce the frequency of KT queries by two orders of magnitude, it enables fundamental architectural shifts: KT directories can migrate from fast but space-inefficient Merkle trees to space-efficient data structures like RSA accumulators. While DKVE cannot replace existing methods entirely -- suffering from bootstrapping problems and degraded performance on weak-tie networks -- it provides a practical complementary key validation mechanism, making secure messaging more deployable for billion-user systems.

AI.tldr: DKVE is a privacy-preserving protocol that validates public keys by cross-checking them through mutual contacts in a user's social graph, using OPRF and OKVS to protect privacy, and SPRT for statistical attack detection. It achieves >97% MitM detection on strong-tie networks and can reduce key transparency queries by two orders of magnitude, serving as a practical complement to existing key distribution verification methods.
AI.motivation: Current public key distribution for end-to-end encrypted messaging faces a trade-off: out-of-band (OOB) verification is secure but unscalable for large contact lists, while key transparency (KT) systems offer automation at high storage cost and operational complexity. The authors seek a practical middle ground that leverages social graph structure for scalable, privacy-preserving key validation.
AI.method: DKVE introduces a cross-validation protocol where clients, upon fetching a contact's public key from a key server, query mutual contacts to verify key consistency. It combines Oblivious Pseudorandom Functions (OPRF) and Oblivious Key-Value Stores (OKVS) to ensure queries and contact lists remain private. A Sequential Probability Ratio Test (SPRT) aggregates responses to statistically detect server misbehavior with user-configurable error bounds.
AI.result: Simulations on real social network datasets show DKVE detects MitM attacks with >97% success in strong-to-moderate-tie networks. The remaining ~3% of cases need fallback methods (KT or OOB). A proof-of-concept implementation confirms feasibility on commodity hardware regarding latency and bandwidth. DKVE can reduce KT query frequency by two orders of magnitude, enabling KT directories to adopt space-efficient structures like RSA accumulators instead of Merkle trees.
AI.conclusion: DKVE is not a full replacement for existing methods — it has bootstrapping problems and weakened performance on weak-tie networks — but it offers a practical complementary mechanism that makes secure messaging more deployable at billion-user scale by drastically reducing reliance on costly KT infrastructure.

title: Thinking Like a Scientist? A Structural Study of LLM-Generated Research Methods
summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to guide research methodology, yet their default methodological tendencies under minimal prompting remain unclear. Here, we prompt GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.2 with an LLM-extracted research question from each of 1,000 recent arXiv computer-science papers and compare the resulting methodology suggestions against a paper-derived experimental inventory. Since we provide only the research question, the differences we measure reflect initial suggestions and not how optimal those suggestions are. We extract structured method features from both sources, map them into a shared taxonomy, and quantify divergence across multiple taxonomy dimensions including model provider, dataset task type, and evaluation metric type. The strongest imbalance appears in provider choice, with Jensen-Shannon divergence about 3-5x larger than any other taxonomy dimension. Other/Academic single-occurrence models are underrepresented by 23-24 percentage points, while reused academic/community models are slightly overrepresented (4-6pp). LLMs also suggest a much narrower range of methods overall: the effective number of model entities contracts from 1,232 to 59-96, and inter-LLM rank correlations (0.55-0.68) generally exceed LLM-to-paper correlations (0.33-0.56), so the distortions are largely shared across models. Popularity baselines, BM25 retrieval calibration, and paper-level similarity tests confirm that the outputs are query-specific responses, but filtered through a narrower set of options. Researchers who rely on LLM suggestions without cross-checking therefore risk narrowing their methodological search space toward a more concentrated default.

AI.tldr: This paper probes whether contemporary LLMs exhibit biased, narrowed methodological recommendations when minimally prompted with only a research question. GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.2 were given 1,000 CS research questions; their suggested methods diverged sharply from real paper inventories — especially in model provider choice (JSD 3-5× larger than other dimensions) — and the effective number of recommended model entities collapsed from 1,232 to 59–96, with distortions largely shared across LLMs.
AI.motivation: As researchers increasingly rely on LLMs to shape methodology, it is critical to know whether these models harbor systematic, convergent biases in their default suggestions — biases that could silently narrow the methodological search space if left unchecked.
AI.method: The authors prompted three frontier LLMs with research questions extracted from 1,000 recent arXiv CS papers. They extracted structured method features (model provider, dataset task type, evaluation metric) from both LLM outputs and the original paper metadata, mapped them into a shared taxonomy, and quantified divergence via Jensen-Shannon divergence, effective entity counts, rank correlations, BM25 retrieval calibration, and paper-level similarity tests. Only the research question was provided, isolating default tendencies rather than optimality.
AI.result: Provider choice showed the strongest imbalance (JSD 3–5× greater than other dimensions). Other/Academic single-occurrence models were underrepresented by 23–24 pp, while reused academic/community models were overrepresented by 4–6 pp. The effective number of model entities shrank from 1,232 (papers) to 59–96 (LLMs). Inter-LLM rank correlations (0.55–0.68) exceeded LLM-to-paper correlations (0.33–0.56), indicating shared distortion. BM25 and similarity tests confirmed outputs are query-specific but drawn from a far narrower repertoire.
AI.conclusion: LLMs, under minimal prompting, funnel methodological suggestions toward a concentrated set of defaults — particularly a restricted set of model providers — creating a risk that researchers who do not cross-check will unknowingly narrow their methodological search space.

title: What We are Missing in Multimodal LLM Evaluation?
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process diverse inputs, e.g., text, images, audio, and video, and generate textual responses. While their capabilities have advanced rapidly, evaluation of such models has not kept pace. Most existing evaluation benchmarks are limited to isolated tasks and reveal little about whether a model integrates information across modalities. We examine current means for evaluating MLLMs and review the existing benchmark taxonomy to identify gaps, including temporal-spatial coherence, physical world understanding, multimodal consistency, and selective attention. Addressing these gaps is essential for measuring real progress in multimodal intelligence and exposing capability boundaries.

AI.tldr: Current MLLM evaluation benchmarks are limited to isolated tasks and fail to assess cross-modal integration. The paper identifies four key gaps in existing benchmarks: temporal-spatial coherence, physical world understanding, multimodal consistency, and selective attention, arguing that addressing these is essential for measuring genuine progress in multimodal intelligence.
AI.motivation: While MLLM capabilities have advanced rapidly, evaluation methods lag behind. Existing benchmarks focus on isolated unimodal or simple multimodal tasks, revealing little about whether models truly integrate information across modalities. This creates a critical disconnect between claimed capabilities and measured performance.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic review of current MLLM evaluation approaches and the existing benchmark taxonomy. Through this analysis, they identify and characterize four fundamental gaps in current evaluation frameworks.
AI.result: Four critical gaps in MLLM evaluation were identified: (1) temporal-spatial coherence — assessing understanding of time and space relationships across modalities; (2) physical world understanding — evaluating grasp of physical laws, causality, and commonsense reasoning; (3) multimodal consistency — measuring alignment and coherence across different input modalities; and (4) selective attention — testing a model's ability to focus on relevant cross-modal information while ignoring distractors.
AI.conclusion: Addressing the identified gaps is essential for measuring real progress in multimodal intelligence and for exposing the true capability boundaries of MLLMs. Without more comprehensive, integration-focused benchmarks, the field risks overestimating model capabilities.

title: Fast LeWorldModel
summary: Joint-Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs), including recent LeWorldModel (LeWM), have become a promising foundation for reconstruction-free visual world models. For visual planning, however, LeWM evaluates candidate action sequences by repeatedly applying a local one-step latent transition model. This autoregressive rollout makes planning computationally expensive and exposes the predicted trajectory to accumulated latent errors as the horizon grows. We propose Fast LeWorldModel (Fast-LeWM), a fast latent world model that replaces repeated local rollout with action-prefix prediction. Given the current latent and a candidate action sequence, Fast-LeWM encodes its prefixes and predicts the future latents reached after executing those prefixes in parallel. By making action prefixes the basic prediction unit, Fast-LeWM directly models action effects accumulated to different extents over multiple horizons. This prefix-level supervision forces the model to learn how states continuously evolve under different action prefixes, rather than only fitting one-step state transitions. During planning, the predictor can use the last prefix token from the encoded action sequence to evaluate the corresponding future latent without explicitly rolling through each intermediate imagined state. Across multiple tasks, Fast-LeWM improves average success over LeWM while substantially reducing planning time, achieving lower open-loop latent loss whose growth becomes significantly slower as the rollout horizon increases.

AI.tldr: Fast-LeWM accelerates visual planning by replacing autoregressive latent rollout with parallel action-prefix prediction, where prefixes of candidate action sequences directly predict future latents, reducing computational cost and accumulated errors.
AI.motivation: Existing LeWM uses iterative one-step latent transitions for planning, which is computationally expensive and suffers from compounding latent errors as the rollout horizon grows. A more efficient, parallelizable alternative is needed.
AI.method: Fast-LeWM encodes prefixes of a candidate action sequence and predicts the future latents reached after executing those prefixes — all in parallel. It treats action prefixes as the fundamental prediction unit and applies prefix-level supervision so the model learns continuous state evolution under different action prefixes, rather than only one-step transitions. At planning time, the last prefix token directly yields the corresponding future latent without intermediate rollouts.
AI.result: Fast-LeWM improves average success rate over LeWM across multiple tasks, substantially reduces planning time, and achieves lower open-loop latent loss whose growth rate is significantly slower as rollout horizon increases.
AI.conclusion: Modeling action prefixes as the basic prediction unit enables fast, parallel latent prediction that mitigates compounding errors and reduces computational burden, making Fast-LeWM a more efficient and accurate visual world model for planning.

title: Utilizing Cognitive Signals Generated during Human Reading to Enhance Keyphrase Extraction from Microblogs
summary: Microblogging platforms generate massive amounts of short, noisy, and dispersed user content, making automatic keyphrase extraction (AKE) an important but challenging task. Prior studies have used eye-tracking signals to improve microblog-based AKE because such signals reflect readers' attention to salient words. However, eye tracking alone is limited by physiological, acquisition, and feature-decoding constraints. To address this issue, we investigate whether electroencephalogram (EEG) signals can complement eye-tracking signals for AKE. Using the ZuCo cognitive language processing corpus, we select 8 EEG features and 17 eye-tracking features and incorporate them into microblog-based AKE models. To reduce possible distortion of cognitive signals by model structures, we inject these features into the input of the soft-attention layer and the query vectors of the self-attention layer. We then evaluate different combinations of cognitive signals across AKE models. The results show that cognitive signals produced during reading consistently improve AKE performance, regardless of feature combinations and model architectures. EEG features bring the largest gains, while combining EEG and eye-tracking features yields performance between the two individual signal types, suggesting partial complementarity but also possible redundancy or noise. These findings indicate that EEG signals provide useful cognitive evidence for microblog-based AKE and that multimodal cognitive signals deserve further investigation.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using EEG signals alongside eye-tracking to improve automatic keyphrase extraction (AKE) from microblogs. Results show EEG yields the largest gains, while combining both signals shows partial complementarity but possible redundancy.
AI.motivation: Microblog AKE is challenging due to short, noisy text. Eye-tracking has been used to capture reader attention for salient words, but it suffers from physiological, acquisition, and decoding limitations. The authors explore whether EEG can complement eye-tracking to provide richer cognitive evidence for AKE.
AI.method: Using the ZuCo corpus, 8 EEG and 17 eye-tracking features are extracted and injected into AKE models at two points: the input of the soft-attention layer and the query vectors of the self-attention layer (to minimize model-induced distortion). Different feature combinations are evaluated across multiple AKE architectures.
AI.result: Cognitive signals consistently improve AKE performance across all feature combinations and model architectures. EEG features alone produce the largest gains. The EEG+eye-tracking combination yields intermediate performance (between each signal alone), suggesting partial complementarity but also redundancy or noise.
AI.conclusion: EEG signals provide useful cognitive evidence for microblog AKE. Multimodal cognitive signals (EEG + eye-tracking) warrant further investigation to better understand their complementarity and to mitigate redundancy.

title: To Run or Not to Run: Analyzing the Cost-Effectiveness of Code Execution in LLM-Based Program Repair
comment: Accepted to the ACM SIGSOFT International Symposium on Software Testing and Analysis (ISSTA 2026). 23 pages
summary: LLM-based agents for program repair are increasingly built on a "generate-run-revise" paradigm, iteratively executing tests to evaluate and refine patches. This execution-based approach has become standard practice in state-of-the-art systems. However, executions can be time-consuming and expensive, yet their impact on these agents remains underexplored. In this paper, we conduct a two-stage empirical study over execution behavior in LLM-based program repair. To characterize execution behavior at scale, we first analyze 7,745 agent traces from SWE-bench leaderboard submissions. Second, we evaluate 3,000 end-to-end repair attempts across 200 SWE-bench instances and three agents (Claude Code, Codex, and the open-source OpenCode) under four execution paradigms, which allows for a fine-grained comparison of performance and cost. Our analysis reveals three key observations: (1) Code execution is used across all agents and models analyzed, with an average of 8.8 test runs per task. Execution behavior varies substantially across agents and models, with frequency ranging from 2 to 19 per task, and late-stage executions consistently achieve higher success rates than early-stage ones. (2) Execution restrictions have little effect on repair success: on commercial agents with SOTA models the resolve-rate gap between Prohibited and Unrestricted is only 1.25 percentage points and not statistically significant, while Prohibited saves substantial token and wall-clock cost. (3) Execution benefit is concentrated rather than uniform. These patterns suggest that current agents apply execution indiscriminately, paying its cost on instances where it provides little benefit. Execution, therefore, should be treated as a resource with an explicit cost-benefit tradeoff, not a default capability.

AI.tldr: An empirical study of 7,745 agent traces and 3,000 repair attempts reveals that LLM-based program repair agents use code execution indiscriminately (avg 8.8 test runs/task), yet restricting execution barely affects repair success (only 1.25pp gap) while saving substantial cost. The authors argue execution should be treated as a resource with explicit cost-benefit tradeoffs rather than a default.
AI.motivation: Current LLM-based program repair agents rely on a "generate-run-revise" paradigm where test execution is standard practice. However, executions are time-consuming and expensive, and their actual impact on repair outcomes remains underexplored. The authors aim to characterize execution behavior at scale and determine whether execution restrictions meaningfully affect repair success.
AI.method: A two-stage empirical study: (1) Large-scale analysis of 7,745 agent traces from SWE-bench leaderboard submissions to characterize execution behavior patterns across agents and models. (2) Controlled evaluation of 3,000 end-to-end repair attempts across 200 SWE-bench instances using three agents (Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode) under four execution paradigms (Unrestricted, Prohibited, and two intermediate conditions), enabling fine-grained performance-cost comparison.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Code execution is universal across all agents/models, averaging 8.8 test runs per task, with high variance (2–19) across agents. Late-stage executions consistently outperform early-stage ones. (2) Execution restrictions have minimal impact: the resolve-rate gap between Prohibited and Unrestricted on SOTA commercial agents is only 1.25pp and not statistically significant, while Prohibited saves substantial token and wall-clock costs. (3) Execution benefit is concentrated on specific instances rather than uniformly distributed, yet agents apply execution indiscriminately across all instances.
AI.conclusion: Current LLM-based repair agents overuse code execution, incurring costs even on instances where it provides negligible benefit. Execution should be reconceptualized as a resource governed by explicit cost-benefit tradeoffs rather than treated as a default, always-on capability.

title: 'A bit of chaos and madness': The AI Assessment Scale and the work of assessment reform
summary:
Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has intensified pressure on universities to redesign assessment while maintaining integrity, equity, and validity. Structured frameworks such as the Artificial Intelligence Assessment Scale (AIAS) offer one response, but evidence of how staff experience their implementation remains limited. This qualitative study examines AIAS implementation at a private international university in Vietnam and a public university in the United Kingdom. Data from five focus groups with 30 academic staff were analysed using hybrid thematic analysis, with Critical AI Literacy used as a sensitising concept. Six themes were developed: recognising and integrating AI, facilitating conditions, building capacity, pathways to adoption, ethics in practice, and reframing pedagogy.
