Cliff's delta advantages of +0.79 to +0.90 (stakeholder count) and +0.65 to +0.93 (uncertainty score) persist for three of four generators against the matched-budget control. Section ablation confirms each improvement is attributable to its corresponding sub-instruction. Textual-gradient descent further improves the scaffold. A cross-family training judge outperforms an in-family judge on all measured axes. The debate protocol converts a 6% standoff into 95% full consensus (calibration set) and achieves 100% combined convergence (replication set).
AI.conclusion: NoT provides a lightweight, training-free method to externalize stakeholders, consequences, and uncertainty in LLM moral reasoning, producing auditable traces suitable for dependable agentic deployment. The structured scaffold generalizes across models and vendors, and synergizes with debate protocols for consensus-building.

title: AgentX: Towards Agent-Driven Self-Iteration of Industrial Recommender Systems
comment: Authors are listed alphabetically by their first name
summary:
Recommendation algorithm iteration is moving from an artisanal, engineer-bound process toward an industrialized research loop, but this transition remains blocked by a structural execution bottleneck: the idea-to-launch cycle still depends on human engineers to generate hypotheses, modify production code, launch A/B experiments, and attribute online results. Innovation therefore scales linearly with headcount rather than compounding with evidence, compute, and accumulated experimental knowledge. We present AgentX, a production-deployed multi-agent system that fundamentally restructures this production function. AgentX operates as a self-evolving development engine: it autonomously generates, implements, evaluates, and learns from recommendation experiments at a scale and pace that no manual workflow can sustain.
  The system orchestrates four tightly coupled stages in a closed loop. A Brainstorm Agent synthesizes evidence from historical experiments, system architecture, data analysis, and external research into ranked, executable proposals. A Developing Agent translates each proposal into production-ready code through repository-grounded generation and multi-dimensional reliability verification. An Evaluation Agent conducts safe online rollout with guardrail-vetoed A/B judgment, converting both successes and failures into structured knowledge assets. A Harness Evolution layer (SGPO) then distills execution trajectories into semantic-gradient updates that continuously sharpen the agents themselves -- making the system not merely automated, but self-improving.

AI.tldr: AgentX is a production-deployed multi-agent system that autonomously generates, implements, evaluates, and learns from recommendation algorithm experiments in a closed loop, overcoming the manual bottleneck that limits innovation scaling in industrial recommender systems.
AI.motivation: Recommendation algorithm development is constrained by a structural bottleneck: the idea-to-launch cycle depends on human engineers for hypothesis generation, code modification, A/B testing, and result attribution. This causes innovation to scale linearly with headcount rather than compounding with accumulated evidence and compute. The goal is to break this bottleneck by automating the entire research loop.
AI.method: AgentX consists of four tightly coupled stages in a closed loop: (1) Brainstorm Agent synthesizes historical experiments, system architecture, data analysis, and external research into ranked executable proposals; (2) Developing Agent translates proposals into production-ready code with repository-grounded generation and multi-dimensional reliability verification; (3) Evaluation Agent conducts safe online A/B experiments with guardrail-vetoed judgment, converting outcomes into structured knowledge; (4) Harness Evolution layer (SGPO) distills execution trajectories into semantic-gradient updates that continuously self-improve the agents.
AI.result: AgentX restructures the recommendation production function, enabling autonomous experiment generation, implementation, and evaluation at a scale and pace unattainable by manual workflows. The system is not merely automated but self-improving through the SGPO mechanism.
AI.conclusion: By closing the full idea-to-launch loop with self-evolving agents, AgentX transforms recommendation algorithm iteration from a linear, headcount-bound process into a compounding, self-improving research engine deployed in production.

title: ATGBuilder: Feature-Assisted Graph Learning for Activity Transition Graph Construction with Seed Supervision
summary: Android applications are organized around activities that provide visual Graphical User Interface (GUI) containers that host the UI and handle user interaction events. Activity Transition Graphs (ATGs) have been widely used to model apps' GUI navigation. However, the construction of high-quality ATGs is challenging: ATGs based on static analysis may miss acceptable transitions and may extract infeasible ones; while dynamically explored ATGs can yield incomplete transitions. Recent learning-based approaches can treat ATG construction as a seed-supervised link-prediction task. However, the use of activity-layout and widget-trigger information for ATG construction remains limited. We propose ATGBuilder, a feature-assisted graph-learning approach for seed-supervised ATG construction. ATGBuilder uses a Large Language Model (LLM) to summarize UI activity metadata from layouts into compact textual functionality summaries. ATGBuilder explicitly models widget-trigger information into the edge attribute: It then uses an auxiliary widget-attribute reconstruction objective on this information during model training. ATGBuilder's performance was evaluated across a series of ablations on the frontmatter corpus, and an experiment on benchmark using manually-checked ground-truth ATGs. Experiments on multiple benchmarks show that ATGBuilder significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods. We further demonstrate its effectiveness by improving automated GUI exploration tools through better navigation guidance.

AI.tldr: ATGBuilder is a feature-assisted graph-learning approach that leverages LLM-generated activity functionality summaries and explicit widget-trigger edge attributes to construct high-quality Activity Transition Graphs from seed transitions, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art methods.
AI.motivation: Existing ATG construction methods are limited: static analysis yields infeasible transitions and misses acceptable ones, dynamic exploration produces incomplete graphs, and learning-based approaches underutilize activity-layout semantics and widget-trigger information. A method that better exploits these underused signals is needed.
AI.method: ATGBuilder frames ATG construction as a seed-supervised link-prediction task. It uses an LLM to summarize UI activity metadata from layouts into compact textual functionality descriptions. Widget-trigger information is explicitly modeled as edge attributes, and an auxiliary widget-attribute reconstruction objective is employed during training to reinforce this signal.
AI.result: ATGBuilder significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods across multiple benchmarks, validated by ablation studies on the frontmatter corpus and experiments using manually-checked ground-truth ATGs. It also improves automated GUI exploration tools through better navigation guidance.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly incorporating LLM-based activity functionality summaries and widget-trigger edge attributes into a graph-learning framework yields substantially more accurate ATG construction, with practical downstream benefits for automated GUI exploration.

title: Continuous Behavioral Synthesis for Adaptive Health Dashboards: An LLM-Mediated Architecture Integrating Explicit Preference, Spatial Reorganization, and Attention Allocation Signals
summary: The engineering of adaptive user interfaces has traditionally relied on either rule-based systems encoding designer intuitions about user needs or machine learning approaches requiring substantial historical data before achieving effective personalization. We present a technical architecture that leverages Large Language Models as behavioral synthesis engines to enable immediate adaptation from sparse, heterogeneous user signals. Our system integrates three distinct behavioral channels, i) explicit micro-feedback on individual interface elements, ii) spatial priority inferred from manual widget reorganization through drag-and-drop interaction, iii) and attentional investment measured through dwell time during hover events, within a structured prompt engineering framework that continuously regenerates dashboard layouts while maintaining explanatory coherence. The architecture addresses the technical challenge of translating low-level interaction patterns into high-level design decisions through a layered prompt construction methodology that separates temporal context determination, behavioral signal extraction, explicit preference enforcement, and user profile synthesis. The approach combines manually specified behavioral interpretations and temporal heuristics with LLM-mediated synthesis, enabling the reconciliation of multiple simultaneous signals that would be difficult to encode through explicit rules alone. We demonstrate the system through an instantiation in the personal health monitoring domain, including an analytical evaluation of adaptation behavior across multiple scenarios and a working implementation managing fourteen distinct health metrics across seven widget visualization modalities. The evaluation compares profile-driven initialization, multi-signal behavioral adaptation, and presents the resulting interfaces through representative post-adaptation screenshots.

AI.tldr: A system using LLMs as behavioral synthesis engines to adapt UI dashboards in real-time from sparse user signals (explicit feedback, drag-and-drop reorganization, hover dwell time), demonstrated in a personal health monitoring domain with 14 health metrics and 7 widget types.
AI.motivation: Traditional adaptive UI engineering suffers from a dichotomy: rule-based systems are brittle and encode designer assumptions, while ML approaches require large historical datasets before achieving effective personalization. Neither can handle immediate adaptation from sparse, heterogeneous signals.
AI.method: A layered prompt construction framework translates low-level interactions into high-level design decisions via four stages: temporal context determination, behavioral signal extraction, explicit preference enforcement, and user profile synthesis. Three behavioral channels feed the system: explicit micro-feedback, spatial priority (drag-and-drop reorganization), and attentional investment (hover dwell time). An LLM synthesizes these signals through structured prompts incorporating manually specified behavioral interpretations and temporal heuristics.
AI.result: The system was instantiated in a personal health monitoring dashboard managing 14 health metrics across 7 widget visualization modalities. Evaluation included analytical assessment of adaptation behavior across multiple scenarios and profile-driven initialization comparisons, with results presented through post-adaptation screenshots.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can serve as effective behavioral synthesis engines for adaptive interfaces, reconciling multiple simultaneous interaction signals that would be difficult to encode through explicit rules alone, while maintaining explanatory coherence through structured prompt engineering.

title: TGHE: Template-based Graph Homomorphic Encryption for Privacy-Preserving GNN Inference in Edge-Cloud Systems
comment: 7 pages, 3 figures, 3 tables. Accepted at IEEE ICWS 2026
summary: Existing homomorphic encryption (HE)-based GNN systems adopt a graph-centric paradigm that couples per-query cost to global graph size, limiting evaluations to at most ~20k nodes and making them incompatible with dynamic, large-scale financial graphs. We propose TGHE (Template-based Graph Homomorphic Encryption), an ego-centric framework that resolves this by exploiting a template phenomenon: local computation trees in transaction graphs converge into a small set of structural shapes. TGHE canonicalizes ego-graphs at the edge and packs structurally identical trees into shared CKKS ciphertexts for SIMD-parallel encrypted inference, with two long-tail optimizers (Approximate Template Fitting and Topology Collapse) ensuring full SIMD coverage. On DGraphFin (3.7M nodes, 4.3M edges), TGHE-Collapse achieves a 66.9x speedup over the sequential encrypted baseline with less than 0.002 AUC loss.

AI.tldr: TGHE proposes an ego-centric framework for encrypted GNN inference that exploits structural template convergence in transaction graphs, enabling SIMD-packed CKKS homomorphic evaluation on large-scale graphs (3.7M nodes) with 66.9x speedup and negligible accuracy loss.
AI.motivation: Existing HE-based GNN systems use a graph-centric paradigm where per-query cost scales with global graph size, capping evaluations at ~20k nodes and preventing deployment on dynamic, large-scale financial transaction graphs.
AI.method: TGHE adopts an ego-centric paradigm that canonicalizes ego-graphs at the edge and packs structurally identical computation trees into shared CKKS ciphertexts for SIMD-parallel encrypted inference. Two long-tail optimizers — Approximate Template Fitting and Topology Collapse — ensure full SIMD coverage by handling rare or irregular structural shapes.
AI.result: On the DGraphFin dataset (3.7M nodes, 4.3M edges), TGHE-Collapse achieves a 66.9x speedup over the sequential encrypted baseline while incurring less than 0.002 AUC loss.
AI.conclusion: The template-based ego-centric approach decouples encrypted inference cost from global graph size, making privacy-preserving GNN inference practical on real-world financial graphs at scale.

title: ConflictScore: Identifying and Measuring How Language Models Handle Conflicting Evidence
summary: Existing metrics for factuality and faithfulness evaluate whether an answer is supported or contradicted by its grounding documents, but they fail to capture when both supporting and contradicting evidence coexist. We introduce ConflictScore, a novel metric that quantifies how well a model's response acknowledges conflicting evidence in its grounding documents. Our framework decomposes responses into atomic claims, labels each claim against each grounding document, and then aggregates these labels into two complementary measures: ConflictScore-Count (CS-C), the proportion of claims exhibiting conflicts, and ConflictScore-Ratio (CS-R), the balance between supporting and contradicting evidence. We develop ConflictBench, a benchmark covering diverse forms of conflicts such as ambiguity, contradiction, and divergent opinions, to systematically evaluate our metric. Experiments show that ConflictScore effectively detects overconfident claims across domains and can serve as a corrective feedback mechanism that improves truthfulness on TruthfulQA.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces ConflictScore, a metric that quantifies how well a model acknowledges conflicting evidence in grounding documents, where both supporting and contradicting information coexist. It also presents ConflictBench, a benchmark for evaluating this capability across diverse conflict types.
AI.motivation: Existing factuality and faithfulness metrics only assess whether an answer is supported or contradicted by grounding documents, but fail to handle cases where both types of evidence coexist. This gap means models can appear factual while ignoring contradictory evidence, leading to overconfident or misleading responses.
AI.method: The framework (1) decomposes responses into atomic claims, (2) labels each claim against each grounding document as supporting, contradicting, or neutral, and (3) aggregates labels into two metrics: ConflictScore-Count (CS-C), the proportion of claims exhibiting conflicts, and ConflictScore-Ratio (CS-R), the balance between supporting and contradicting evidence. ConflictBench is developed with diverse conflict types including ambiguity, contradiction, and divergent opinions.
AI.result: ConflictScore effectively detects overconfident claims across domains and can serve as a corrective feedback mechanism that improves truthfulness on the TruthfulQA benchmark.
AI.conclusion: ConflictScore fills a critical evaluation gap by measuring response-level conflict awareness, and demonstrates practical utility both as an evaluation metric and as a feedback signal for improving model truthfulness.

title: Geometry-Aware MCTS for Extremal Problems in Combinatorial Geometry
summary: We study certain extremal problems in combinatorial geometry that ask about configurations of points in an $n \times n$ grid that satisfy strict, global geometric constraints. Classical exact solvers suffer from combinatorial explosion for these types of problems, and standard reinforcement learning and transformer-based models struggle with the sparse reward "validity cliff" and quadratic token-consumption limits. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose a Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework. Our approach strictly enforces geometric constraints through incremental updates to the feasible action space. For constraints about collections of collinear points, like those that occur in the classic No-Three-in-Line problem (Max-N3IL), this mechanism reduces the constraint checking complexity from $O(n^3)$ to $O(n^2)$. To improve search efficiency, we exploit geometric symmetries in two ways: canonical pruning during node expansion to reduce the branching factor, and symmetric batch transitions to accelerate the discovery of promising configurations. We perform extensive experiments and establish new best-known computational results on five out of six of the problems that we considered. Notably, for Max-N3IL we find configurations of size roughly $1.8 n$ for grids of size $82 \le n \le 119$. For the Smallest Complete Set problem, we find configurations of size roughly $0.95 n$, providing new upper bounds within the tested grids. This work establishes Geometry-Aware MCTS as a highly adaptable framework for discovering novel configurations in combinatorial geometry.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework for solving extremal combinatorial geometry problems (e.g., No-Three-in-Line) on n×n grids. It introduces incremental feasibility updates dropping constraint-checking from O(n³) to O(n²), plus symmetry-based pruning and batch transitions. The method achieves new state-of-the-art results on five of six benchmark problems.
AI.motivation: Classical exact solvers suffer combinatorial explosion on point-configuration problems under strict global geometric constraints (e.g., no three collinear points). Reinforcement learning and transformer models fail due to sparse-reward "validity cliffs" and quadratic token consumption. A framework is needed that enforces geometric constraints efficiently while exploring the massive search space intelligently.
AI.method: A Geometry-Aware MCTS framework with three key components: (1) Incremental feasible-action-space updates that enforce geometric constraints during tree traversal, reducing collinearity-checking complexity from O(n³) to O(n²). (2) Canonical pruning via geometric symmetries (reflections, rotations) during node expansion to cut the branching factor. (3) Symmetric batch transitions that apply symmetric transformations to discovered promising states, accelerating convergence to high-quality configurations.
AI.result: New best-known results on 5 of 6 benchmark problems. For Max-No-Three-in-Line (Max-N3IL), configurations of size ≈1.8n were found for grids 82 ≤ n ≤ 119, surpassing prior records. For the Smallest Complete Set problem, configurations of size ≈0.95n yielded improved upper bounds within tested grid sizes.
AI.conclusion: Geometry-Aware MCTS is a highly adaptable and effective framework for discovering novel extremal configurations in combinatorial geometry, outperforming classical solvers and learning-based methods by integrating domain-specific geometric constraints directly into the search process.

title: High-Probability PL-SGD with Markovian Noise: Optimal Mixing and Tail Dependence
summary:
We study first-order methods for smooth objectives satisfying the Polyak-Łojasiewicz (PL) condition when gradient samples are generated by an exogenous Markov chain. In the light-tailed setting, prior uniform-in-time high-probability bounds for ordinary Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) under a standard growth envelope scale as $\widetilde{O}(t_{mix}^2/k)$, leaving a gap with the $\widetilde{O}(t_{mix}/k)$ expectation bounds. We close this gap using a lag-blocking argument to establish a uniform high-probability guarantee with a leading stochastic term of $\widetilde{O}(t_{mix}/(k+K_0))$ under geometric mixing. We prove this linear dependence on the mixing time is optimal via a matching $Ω(σ^2 t_{mix}/k)$ lower bound on a quadratic objective driven by a persistent two-state chain.
  We then extend this framework to heavy-tailed Markovian gradients satisfying a stationary finite-$p$-moment condition, $p \in (1,2]$. We design an all-samples clipped block method that uses every Markov transition while mitigating Markovian bias. Under a transition budget $T$, this algorithm achieves a high-probability stochastic error of $\widetilde{O}(σ_p^2(t_{mix}/T)^{2(p-1)/p})$. We establish a matching lower bound by reducing PL optimization to heavy-tailed mean estimation for a sticky Markov chain. Ultimately, this work tightly characterizes the optimal polynomial dependence on mixing time for light-tailed PL-SGD, and the optimal heavy-tail exponent and effective-sample-size dependence in the robust regime.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes tight high-probability convergence bounds for SGD under the Polyak-Łojasiewicz condition with Markovian gradient noise. In the light-tailed setting, it closes a gap between expectation and high-probability rates via a lag-blocking argument, achieving optimal linear mixing-time dependence. In the heavy-tailed regime (finite p-th moment, p∈(1,2]), it designs a clipped block method and proves matching upper and lower bounds on the optimal heavy-tail exponent and effective-sample-size dependence.
AI.motivation: Prior high-probability bounds for SGD with Markovian gradients under the PL condition exhibited suboptimal quadratic dependence on mixing time (Õ(t_mix²/k)), creating a gap relative to expectation bounds (Õ(t_mix/k)). The work aims to close this gap and extend the analysis to heavy-tailed settings, where robust optimization under Markovian dependence remains poorly understood.
AI.method: For light-tailed gradients under geometric mixing, the authors employ a lag-blocking argument that partitions the Markov chain trajectory into nearly independent blocks separated by lag intervals, establishing a uniform high-probability bound. A matching lower bound is proved using a quadratic objective driven by a persistent two-state Markov chain. For heavy-tailed gradients with finite p-th moment (p∈(1,2]), they design an all-samples clipped block method that processes every Markov transition while controlling Markovian bias via clipping, and prove a matching lower bound by reducing PL optimization to heavy-tailed mean estimation on a sticky Markov chain.
AI.result: Light-tailed: Uniform high-probability bound of Õ(t_mix/(k+K₀)) under geometric mixing, with a matching Ω(σ²t_mix/k) lower bound — establishing optimal linear mixing-time dependence. Heavy-tailed: High-probability stochastic error of Õ(σ_p²(t_mix/T)^{2(p-1)/p}) using the clipped block method, with a matching lower bound — tightly characterizing the optimal heavy-tail exponent and effective-sample-size dependence.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a complete characterization of optimal rates for PL-SGD under Markovian gradients: linear mixing-time dependence is both sufficient and necessary for light-tailed settings, and the exponent 2(p-1)/p is optimal in the heavy-tailed robust regime. The lag-blocking and all-samples clipped block methods are practical algorithmic contributions that achieve these optimal rates.

title: On the Reproducibility of Quantum Software Defect Datasets: A Case Study of Bugs4Q
comment: 10 pages plus 2 pages of references. Accepted to the Replication and Negative Results (RENE) Track of ICSME 2026
summary: The reproducibility of software defect datasets is essential for obtaining reliable and comparable research results. Zhu et al. have shown that defect datasets such as Defects4J suffer from reproduction failures (i.e., reported bugs become non-reproducible) as time passes since their creation. However, it remains unclear whether these findings generalize to quantum software defect datasets. We therefore conduct a replication study of the prior work using Bugs4Q, a widely used dataset of real-world bugs in quantum programs. Our analysis includes 77,700 quantum program executions of 37 Bugs4Q artifacts across 21 core-library versions. The experimental results showed that the reproducibility of Bugs4Q dropped from 62.2% on Qiskit v0.20.1 to 16.2% on v2.3.1, the latest version as of April 1, 2026. A manual inspection of the root causes further indicated that 93.6% of the failures were dependency-related. While these findings are consistent with those of the prior work, we also observed differences. In particular, most reproduction failures in Bugs4Q cannot be resolved merely by adjusting dependency versions; instead, they require source-code modifications such as migrating import paths and API invocations. Based on this observation, we curated Bugs4Q-Robust, a patched version of Bugs4Q to restore reproducibility. Bugs4Q-Robust increases reproducibility from 16.2% to 78.4% on Qiskit v2.3.1. Our findings highlight the importance of continuous dataset maintenance in the rapidly evolving quantum software ecosystem.

AI.tldr: A replication study on the Bugs4Q quantum software defect dataset reveals that bug reproducibility drops sharply from 62.2% to 16.2% across Qiskit versions, primarily due to dependency-related failures requiring source-code changes. The authors introduce Bugs4Q-Robust, restoring reproducibility to 78.4%.
AI.motivation: Prior work by Zhu et al. demonstrated that classical defect datasets like Defects4J suffer from reproduction failures over time. However, it remains unknown whether this phenomenon generalizes to quantum software defect datasets. This motivates a replication study to assess the reproducibility of Bugs4Q across evolving quantum library versions.
AI.method: The authors replicated the prior methodology using the Bugs4Q dataset, executing 77,700 quantum program runs across 37 Bugs4Q artifacts and 21 versions of the Qiskit core library (v0.20.1 through v2.3.1). They measured reproducibility rates, manually inspected root causes of failures, and categorized them — particularly distinguishing dependency-related failures from other causes. Based on these findings, they curated Bugs4Q-Robust by applying source-code patches (e.g., migrating import paths and API invocations) to restore reproducibility.
AI.result: Reproducibility of Bugs4Q declined from 62.2% (Qiskit v0.20.1) to 16.2% (Qiskit v2.3.1). Among failures, 93.6% were dependency-related. Unlike classical datasets where version pinning often suffices, most Bugs4Q failures required explicit source-code modifications (import path and API migration). Bugs4Q-Robust achieved 78.4% reproducibility on the latest Qiskit version.
AI.conclusion: The reproducibility decay observed in classical defect datasets also applies to quantum software datasets, confirming the generalizability of Zhu et al.'s findings. However, the nature of failures differs: quantum datasets require active source-code maintenance rather than simple dependency version adjustments. The introduction of Bugs4Q-Robust underscores the need for continuous dataset curation in fast-evolving quantum software ecosystems.

title: What Holds Back Brain-Computer Interfaces? Uncovering Challenges and Opportunities in BCI-controlled Games for Cerebral Palsy Rehabilitation
summary: Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) offer promising avenues for cerebral palsy (CP) rehabilitation at home and in the clinic, using games that promote engagement and sustained training effort. Nonetheless, the design constraints of BCI-based CP rehabilitation remain unclear, especially how individuals with CP experience a sense of control through BCI, and how they experience computer-mediated game assistance. To address this gap, we present preliminary clinical and user perspectives on BCI-based CP rehabilitation, drawing on in-clinic insights from a CP therapist and experiential accounts from ten individuals with CP engaging with BCI game prototypes. Sporadic help in BCI games eased monotony, but also fostered doubts regarding agency. The therapist saw BCI rehabilitation as complementary to traditional training, facilitating the transition from playful exercises to autonomous, self-managed training. We outline key challenges and opportunities to inform and empower further design and research of BCI training for CP.

AI.tldr: This paper presents preliminary clinical and user perspectives on BCI-based rehabilitation for cerebral palsy, revealing tensions between game assistance and user agency, and outlining design challenges and opportunities for BCI training systems.
AI.motivation: The design constraints of BCI-based CP rehabilitation are poorly understood, particularly regarding how individuals with CP experience a sense of control through BCI and how they perceive computer-mediated game assistance.
AI.method: The study gathered qualitative data through in-clinic insights from a CP therapist and experiential accounts from ten individuals with CP who engaged with BCI game prototypes.
AI.result: Sporadic help in BCI games reduced monotony but raised doubts about user agency. The therapist viewed BCI rehabilitation as complementary to traditional training, aiding the shift from playful exercises to autonomous self-managed training.
AI.conclusion: The paper outlines key challenges and opportunities to inform future design and research of BCI-based training for cerebral palsy, emphasizing the need to balance assistance with preserving user agency.

title: The Fungible Reserve Standard: A Deterministic Framework for Encoding Carrying Costs in Asset-Backed Tokens
summary: The tokenization of real-world assets (RWAs) has emerged as a transformative application of blockchain technology, with market projections estimating trillions of dollars in tokenized assets within the coming decade. However, a fundamental challenge remains unaddressed: physical assets such as precious metals, stored commodities, and warehoused goods incur structural negative carry -- custody, insurance, and audit costs that accumulate over time. While existing tokenization models have successfully established the market for digital gold and treasuries, they typically manage operational costs at the issuer level. The FRS introduces a framework to bring these economics directly on-chain, avoiding mechanisms such as token rebasing that compromise fungibility and composability with decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols. This paper proposes the Fungible Reserve Standard (FRS), a deterministic token design framework that encodes carrying costs transparently into on-chain logic. The FRS introduces an asset-per-token variable q(t) that decreases according to a predefined annualized carrying cost rate, coupled with a supply reconciliation mechanism that preserves holder balances and ERC-20 composability. While mathematically inspired by the daily expense ratio accrual in traditional asset management -- which often embed centralized profit margins -- the FRS design specifically encodes actual operational carrying costs to provide pure institutional-grade accounting clarity without compromising DeFi compatibility. The framework is asset-agnostic and applicable to any real-world asset with positive, predictable holding costs.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes the Fungible Reserve Standard (FRS), an on-chain tokenization framework that transparently encodes real-world asset carrying costs (custody, insurance, audit) into a time-decaying asset-per-token variable q(t), preserving ERC-20 composability without token rebasing.
AI.motivation: Physical RWAs incur structural negative carry — custody, insurance, and audit costs that accumulate over time. Existing tokenization models manage these costs off-chain at the issuer level or use rebasing mechanisms that compromise fungibility and DeFi composability. The FRS aims to bring these economics directly on-chain in a transparent, deterministic manner.
AI.method: The FRS introduces a deterministic token design with a time-dependent asset-per-token variable q(t) that decays at a predefined annualized carrying cost rate. A supply reconciliation mechanism preserves holder balances and ERC-20 composability, avoiding rebasing. The model is mathematically inspired by daily expense ratio accrual in traditional asset management but encodes only actual operational costs.
AI.result: The framework is asset-agnostic and applicable to any RWA with positive, predictable holding costs. It provides institutional-grade accounting clarity while maintaining full DeFi compatibility.
AI.conclusion: FRS offers a transparent, on-chain solution for encoding carrying costs into tokenized RWAs, bridging the gap between traditional asset management cost structures and DeFi composability requirements, without compromising fungibility.

title: When Agents Meet Electric Bus Fleet Operations: Pricing Behavior, Trade-offs, and Policy Implications in an Aggregator Framework
summary: Agentic systems are changing how complex operational tasks are coordinated, introducing a new paradigm for connecting heterogeneous data sources and automating processes. Electric bus fleets provide a relevant test case. Their operation requires continuous coordination between service reliability, battery state-of-charge, charger availability, electricity prices, route-energy uncertainty, and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) opportunities. This paper proposes an agentic aggregator framework that streamlines this decision environment by coupling an optimization-based electric bus scheduling model with supervisory agents for disturbance detection, tariff adaptation, and schedule evaluation. The optimization core enforces physical feasibility across routes, chargers, batteries, and V2G exchanges, while the agentic layer interprets changing operating conditions, triggers real-time re-optimization when needed, and defines how flexibility value is allocated between the aggregator and the public transport operator (PTO). A realistic depot case study evaluates day-ahead and real-time operations under profit-based and operation-based coordination modes, considering service delays, route-energy deviations, electricity price shocks, and combined disturbances. The results show that agentic aggregation can support adaptive fleet-grid coordination by maintaining feasible schedules, activating re-optimization selectively, and improving the use of charging and V2G flexibility. However, they also reveal a critical trade-off: the same agentic capability that reduces operational complexity can extract value from the PTO when configured around profit-oriented pricing. These findings suggest that agentic aggregators can become useful for managing electric bus V2G operations, but their deployment in public-fleet contexts requires transparent coordination modes, auditable tariff-setting, and explicit value-sharing rules.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an agentic aggregator framework that couples optimization-based electric bus scheduling with supervisory agents to manage V2G operations, demonstrating that while agentic aggregation improves fleet-grid coordination, it also introduces a risk of value extraction from the PTO under profit-oriented configurations, necessitating transparent governance mechanisms.
AI.motivation: Electric bus fleet operations face complex, continuous coordination challenges across service reliability, battery state-of-charge, charger availability, electricity prices, route-energy uncertainty, and V2G opportunities. Existing approaches lack an integrated framework that can adapt to real-time disturbances while balancing physical feasibility and economic objectives. The paper aims to explore whether agentic systems can streamline this decision environment effectively.
AI.method: The authors develop an agentic aggregator framework with a two-layer architecture: (1) an optimization-based electric bus scheduling core that enforces physical feasibility across routes, chargers, batteries, and V2G exchanges; and (2) a supervisory agentic layer for disturbance detection, tariff adaptation, and schedule evaluation. The framework is tested via a realistic depot case study under profit-based and operation-based coordination modes, with disturbances including service delays, route-energy deviations, electricity price shocks, and combined events, evaluated in both day-ahead and real-time operations.
AI.result: Agentic aggregation supports adaptive fleet-grid coordination by maintaining feasible schedules, selectively activating re-optimization, and improving charging and V2G flexibility utilization. However, a critical trade-off emerges: profit-oriented pricing configurations enable the aggregator to extract value from the PTO, revealing that the same agentic capability that reduces operational complexity can also create adverse distributional outcomes.
AI.conclusion: Agentic aggregators hold significant promise for managing electric bus V2G operations, but their deployment in public-fleet contexts demands transparent coordination modes, auditable tariff-setting processes, and explicit value-sharing rules to prevent inequitable value extraction from public transport operators.

title: EVOM: Agentic Meta-Evolution of Actor-Critic Architectures for Reinforcement Learning
summary: In actor-critic reinforcement learning, network architectures are typically manually designed. Automating this design is challenging because each candidate must be trained before evaluation, and the design space is open-ended. To address these challenges, we introduce EVOM, an agentic meta-evolution framework for discovering high-performance actor-critic architectures. We frame architecture search as a bi-level optimization: an inner loop trains weights via the low-fidelity proximal policy optimization (PPO), while an outer loop drives meta-evolution by iteratively refining architecture programs. Crucially, this outer loop is powered by an LLM-based design agent that operates purely as an architecture designer, completely decoupled from policy execution and environment control. Experiments reveal that EVOM outperforms the manually designed baseline, an LLM-guided random search, and the state-of-the-art LLM-guided programmatic policy search method MLES, delivering superior performance on Ant-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4. Ablation studies validate that both the meta-evolution loop and the LLM Design Agent are indispensable for final performance.

AI.tldr: EVOM introduces an agentic meta-evolution framework that uses an LLM-based design agent in a bi-level optimization loop to automatically discover high-performance actor-critic architectures for reinforcement learning, outperforming manually designed baselines and existing search methods.
AI.motivation: Manual design of actor-critic network architectures is labor-intensive and suboptimal. Automating this search is difficult because (1) each candidate architecture requires full training before evaluation, and (2) the architectural design space is open-ended. Existing methods lack an efficient, principled way to navigate this vast space.
AI.method: EVOM frames architecture search as bi-level optimization: the inner loop trains network weights using a low-fidelity PPO algorithm, while the outer loop performs meta-evolution by iteratively refining architecture programs. The outer loop is driven by an LLM-based design agent that acts solely as an architecture designer — fully decoupled from policy execution and environment control. This agent proposes, mutates, and recombines architectural programs across evolutionary generations.
AI.result: EVOM outperforms the manually designed baseline, an LLM-guided random search, and the state-of-the-art LLM-guided programmatic policy search method MLES on Ant-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4 benchmarks. Ablation studies confirm that both the meta-evolution loop and the LLM Design Agent are individually indispensable for achieving the final performance gains.
AI.conclusion: The agentic meta-evolution framework effectively automates actor-critic architecture discovery, with the LLM design agent and evolutionary outer loop both proving essential. This approach opens a promising direction for automated neural architecture search in reinforcement learning.

title: Smaller Models, Unexpected Costs: Trade-offs in LLM Quantization for Automated Program Repair
comment: Accepted for publication in the Research Papers Track of the 42nd IEEE International Conference on Software Maintenance and Evolution (ICSME 2026), 14-18 September 2026, Benevento, Italy
summary:
Language Models (LLMs) are powerful toolsand have been increasingly adopted for complex software engineering tasks. As the number of parameters increases, results can often be improved, but this also imposes substantialmemory requirements. While quantization effectively reduces thememory footprint, its overall impact is often summarized onlyby benchmark scores, which mask changes in model behaviorand non-functional overheads. In this work, we conduct anempirical evaluation of LLM quantization using AutomatedProgram Repair (APR), a complex task in software engineering.We analyze 13 quantization configurations spanning differentbit-widths, methods, and target components (weights and KVcache) across six representative LLMs, evaluated on two APRbenchmarks (HumanEval-Java and Defects4J).
  Our findings reveal that base and quantized models can provide different sets of repaired problems with little overlap, whileretaining a comparable number of repaired problems. Althoughquantization successfully reduces memory footprints by up to85%, it increases both inference time and energy consumption,which we attribute to suboptimal hardware utilization. OurPareto trade-off analysis shows that 48% of the configurationsevaluated are strictly dominated by alternatives. Rather thanidentifying a superior quantization method, our findings highlightthat the trade-offs between effectiveness, memory footprint,and energy efficiency are sensitive to the underlying modelarchitecture and the complexity of the task.

AI.tldr: This paper empirically evaluates how LLM quantization (13 configurations across 6 models) affects Automated Program Repair performance. Key findings: quantized and base models repair different sets of problems with little overlap; quantization reduces memory by up to 85% but increases inference time and energy consumption due to suboptimal hardware utilization; 48% of configurations are Pareto-dominated; trade-offs are highly sensitive to model architecture and task complexity.
AI.motivation: LLM quantization's impact is typically summarized only through benchmark scores, masking behavioral changes and non-functional overheads (inference time, energy). Prior work lacks a nuanced, multi-dimensional analysis of how quantization affects complex software engineering tasks like APR.
AI.method: Empirical evaluation of 13 quantization configurations (varying bit-widths, methods, and target components: weights and KV cache) applied to 6 representative LLMs. Evaluation conducted on two APR benchmarks: HumanEval-Java and Defects4J. Pareto trade-off analysis performed across effectiveness, memory footprint, and energy efficiency.
AI.result: Base and quantized models repair different problem sets with minimal overlap, despite comparable total counts. Memory footprint reduced by up to 85%. However, inference time and energy consumption increase due to suboptimal hardware utilization. Pareto analysis reveals 48% of configurations are strictly dominated. No single superior quantization method emerged; trade-offs depend on model architecture and task complexity.
AI.conclusion: Quantization for LLMs in APR involves complex, architecture- and task-dependent trade-offs that cannot be captured by accuracy benchmarks alone. Practitioners must consider effectiveness, memory, and energy jointly when selecting quantization strategies.

title: Floor Raiser or Ceiling Limiter? Differential Storytelling Outcomes with a Child-Centric GenAI System Across Individual Differences
summary: Generative AI (GenAI) holds promise for democratizing creative literacy, yet whether it benefits all children equally remains unclear. Using a child-centric GenAI storytelling system for children aged 7-12, we conducted a mixed-methods within-subjects experiment (N = 40, Grades 2-6) comparing GenAI-assisted and traditional storyboard conditions. Three findings emerged. First, the GenAI-assisted condition was associated with a floor-raising convergence pattern, with the quality gap narrowing by 83.5%, driven by lower-end support and upper-end constraint mechanisms. This convergence was dimension-selective, improving creativity and richness while leaving coherence and narrative structure tied to baseline performance. Second, younger children more often selected semantically distant keywords while older children preferred semantically closer ones, although engagement orientation varied across individuals regardless of age. Third, image regeneration was positively associated with structural quality dimensions, though this association was attenuated after baseline control. We propose mechanism-contingent scaffolding as a design principle for adaptive GenAI storytelling systems serving diverse children.

AI.tldr: A study with 40 children (Grades 2–6) found that GenAI-assisted storytelling produced a floor-raising effect, narrowing the quality gap by 83.5% — boosting creativity and richness but not coherence or narrative structure. Younger children chose semantically distant keywords; older children chose closer ones. Image regeneration correlated with structural quality but not after controlling for baseline. The authors propose mechanism-contingent scaffolding for adaptive GenAI storytelling systems.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether Generative AI benefits all children equally in creative literacy contexts, addressing the equity implications of GenAI tools for diverse young learners.
AI.method: A mixed-methods within-subjects experiment (N=40, ages 7–12, Grades 2–6) using a child-centric GenAI storytelling system, comparing GenAI-assisted versus traditional storyboard conditions.
AI.result: (1) A floor-raising convergence pattern: the quality gap narrowed by 83.5% via lower-end support and upper-end constraint; effects were dimension-selective (creativity and richness improved, coherence and narrative structure did not). (2) Younger children favored semantically distant keywords; older children favored semantically closer ones; engagement orientation varied individually regardless of age. (3) Image regeneration positively associated with structural quality, but the association attenuated after baseline control.
AI.conclusion: GenAI-assisted storytelling has a selective floor-raising effect rather than universal benefit. The authors propose mechanism-contingent scaffolding — tailoring GenAI support to specific cognitive mechanisms — as a design principle for adaptive storytelling systems that serve diverse children equitably.

title: DroidBreaker: Practical and Functional Problem-Space Attacks on Machine-Learning Android Malware Detectors
summary: Adversarial APKs are Android applications modified in the problem space to evade machine-learning malware detectors. In this work, we first show that, despite claims, existing problem-space attacks remain largely impractical. Most techniques leverage software transplantation to inject entire benign modules, introducing many side-effect features and often causing build-time failures. Fine-grained methods that inject only a narrow subset of components exhibit limited effectiveness, while those that also use obfuscation rely on brittle bytecode rewriting, producing APKs that are syntactically valid but semantically unusable. Prior work further overestimates attack success rates by running smoke tests that only validate installation and basic execution, without assessing whether the modified APK still preserves its intended behavior. To overcome these limitations, we present DROIDBREAKER, a practical (build-safe) and functional (semantics-preserving) problem-space attack framework that provides: (i) query-efficient white- and black-box attacks by manipulating only the APK components most influential to the target model; (ii) a set of fine-grained, build-safe manipulations (including injection and obfuscation of API calls, app modules, permissions, and URLs) with minimal side effects; and (iii) a semantics-preserving functionality test that enforces runtime equivalence by comparing execution logs and API-level traces between the initial and the modified APK. Evaluated on a recent corpus of Android applications, DROIDBREAKER achieves high evasion rates with few queries and minimal side effects in both white-box and black-box settings, and drastically reduces detections by commercial malware scanners hosted on VirusTotal.

AI.tldr: Existing problem-space attacks on Android malware detectors are largely impractical due to build failures, semantic breakage, and overestimated success rates. The authors propose DROIDBREAKER, a practical, build-safe, semantics-preserving attack framework that achieves high evasion rates with minimal queries and side effects against both ML-based and commercial malware detectors.
AI.motivation: Prior problem-space adversarial attacks on Android APKs suffer from three critical flaws: (1) coarse-grained transplantation methods cause build-time failures and excessive side-effect features; (2) fine-grained methods have limited effectiveness; (3) success rates are overestimated because evaluation relies only on smoke tests (installation/basic execution) without verifying semantic equivalence—i.e., whether the modified APK still performs its intended malicious behavior.
AI.method: DROIDBREAKER introduces: (i) query-efficient white-box and black-box attacks that manipulate only the most influential APK components; (ii) a suite of fine-grained, build-safe manipulations—including injection and obfuscation of API calls, app modules, permissions, and URLs—designed to minimize side effects; and (iii) a semantics-preserving functionality test that enforces runtime equivalence by comparing execution logs and API-level traces between original and modified APKs.
AI.result: Evaluated on a recent Android application corpus, DROIDBREAKER achieves high evasion rates with few queries and minimal side effects in both white-box and black-box settings, and significantly reduces detection by commercial malware scanners on VirusTotal.
AI.conclusion: DROIDBREAKER demonstrates that practical, build-safe, and semantics-preserving problem-space attacks are feasible, setting a new benchmark for evaluating the robustness of Android malware detectors against realistic adversarial threats.

title: AnySimLite: A Lightweight Few-Shot Similarity Encoder for On-Device Speech-Adjacent Classification
summary: To minimize privacy concerns and inference latency on edge devices like smartphones, lightweight on-device models remain important for end-user applications. Many of these applications involve natural language classification, but deploying multiple specialized models creates a memory footprint challenge. We investigate: Can a single lightweight architecture solve multiple Speech-Adjacent (SA) classification tasks through reduction to a nuanced text similarity formulation? We propose AnySimLite, a lightweight similarity encoder that combines word-level and character-level channels. Together with a dataset transformation strategy, we evaluate AnySimLite across multiple SA classification tasks and show that it consistently achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) or SOTA-competitive performance in few-shot settings while maintaining a low memory footprint. Even in the worst case, the performance drop remains below 7% while using $<\frac{1}{250}^{\mathrm{th}}$ of the model size of the SOTA qLLaMA_LoRA-7B baseline.

AI.tldr: AnySimLite is a lightweight dual-channel (word + character) similarity encoder that unifies multiple speech-adjacent NLP classification tasks via a text similarity formulation, achieving near-SOTA few-shot performance with under 1/250th the model size of a 7B-parameter baseline.
AI.motivation: Deploying multiple specialized on-device models for different natural language classification tasks creates a memory footprint challenge on edge devices. The authors aim to determine whether a single lightweight architecture can handle multiple speech-adjacent classification tasks while preserving privacy and reducing inference latency.
AI.method: The authors propose AnySimLite, a lightweight similarity encoder with word-level and character-level dual channels, paired with a dataset transformation strategy that reformulates diverse speech-adjacent classification tasks into a unified text similarity problem.
AI.result: AnySimLite consistently achieves state-of-the-art or SOTA-competitive performance in few-shot settings across multiple SA tasks. Worst-case performance drop remains below 7% compared to much larger models, while using less than 1/250th the model size of the qLLaMA_LoRA-7B baseline.
AI.conclusion: A single lightweight similarity encoder with dual-channel encoding and a unified similarity formulation can effectively replace multiple specialized models for SA classification tasks, offering a practical solution for resource-constrained on-device deployment.

title: Unbiased Canonical Set-Valued Oracles Via Lattice Theory
summary: A non-agentic "oracle" AI that estimates probabilities of future events faces a self-reference problem: once its answer is learned and acted upon, it can change the very probability it was asked to report. One response, advocated for the Scientist AI programme, is to ask only counterfactual questions, evaluated as if the answer had no influence. We observe that such answers tend to become irrelevant the moment they are learned, precisely because their premise is then false. We therefore explore a self-referential alternative in which the oracle reports not a single probability but a credal set that is simultaneously unbiased and self-consistent with the consequences of being learned. The naive self-consistency requirement is satisfied by too many sets (including the useless answer $[0,1]$), so the problem is to single out a canonical, nontrivial member. We do so with the Knaster--Tarski fixed-point theorem on the complete lattice of closed credal sets, taking the least fixed point of a suitably defined isotone operator; a variant instead reports the least fixed point that contains every self-consistent point estimate. We prove existence, self-consistency, and nonemptiness, show that the construction collapses to the classical point answer for non-performative questions, and that for a binary event the canonical answer is, under a natural hull-factoring assumption, an interval. The development is purely lattice-theoretic and extends unchanged from a binary event $B$ to an arbitrary random variable $X$, with $P(B\mid A,C)$ replaced by the conditional law $\mathcal{L}(X\mid A,C)$. We close with open questions, including whether the interval characterization itself survives that generalization.

AI.tldr: This paper addresses the self-reference problem in oracle AI by proposing a lattice-theoretic framework where the oracle reports a credal set (rather than a single probability) that is both unbiased and self-consistent. Using the Knaster-Tarski fixed-point theorem, it identifies a canonical least fixed point as the answer, which collapses to the classical point estimate for non-performative questions and yields an interval for binary events under a natural hull-factoring assumption.
AI.motivation: Oracle AIs that estimate event probabilities suffer from performative self-reference: once the answer is learned and acted upon, the underlying probability distribution may change, invalidating the original estimate. The Scientist AI counterfactual approach dodges this by assuming the answer has no influence, but this makes answers irrelevant the moment they are learned. The paper seeks a self-referential alternative that produces answers which remain meaningful even after being incorporated into the world's dynamics.
AI.method: The authors model the problem on the complete lattice of closed credal sets (sets of probability measures). They define an isotone (monotone) operator that captures the self-consistency requirement and apply the Knaster-Tarski fixed-point theorem to obtain the least fixed point, which serves as the canonical oracle answer. A variant reports the least fixed point containing all self-consistent point estimates. The framework is purely lattice-theoretic and extends from binary events to arbitrary random variables by replacing conditional probabilities with conditional laws.
AI.result: The construction provably exists, is self-consistent, and nonempty. For non-performative questions, it collapses to the classical point-valued conditional probability. For a binary event under a hull-factoring assumption, the canonical answer is shown to be an interval. The paper leaves open whether the interval characterization generalizes to arbitrary random variables.
AI.conclusion: The proposed credal-set oracle resolves the self-reference problem by reporting the least fixed point of an isotone operator on the lattice of closed credal sets. This yields nontrivial, self-consistent answers that reduce to classical probabilities in the non-performative case. Several open questions remain, including generalization of the interval result beyond binary events, treatment of full conditional probabilities, and extension to credal sets over joint distributions of the event and the oracle's output.

title: Mesh-RL: Coupled subgrid reinforcement learning
summary: Reinforcement learning in large or sparse-reward environments suffers from slow temporal-difference reward propagation, as value information spreads only locally across the state space. We propose Mesh-RL, a spatial domain-decomposition framework inspired by the finite element method and domain decomposition theory, which partitions the environment into overlapping subgrids and enforces boundary-consistent temporal-difference updates. Such an approach enables localized learning while ensuring globally coherent value propagation. Unlike hierarchical or model-based approaches, Mesh-RL accelerates long-range credit assignment without modifying the reward function, Bellman operator, or introducing explicit planning mechanisms. We evaluate Mesh-RL on hazard-dense grid-world environments with varying geometries and mesh resolutions. Across Q-learning, SARSA, and Dyna-Q, Mesh-RL consistently improves convergence speed, cumulative reward, and learning stability. Higher mesh resolutions sustain exploration, prevent premature convergence, and substantially accelerate value propagation to distant states. While Dyna-Q already benefits from internal planning, it still achieves additional gains under structured decomposition. Overall, Mesh-RL introduces a principled spatial domain-decomposition mechanism for accelerating temporal-difference learning. Our framework bridges finite element method-inspired boundary-consistency techniques from scientific computing with reinforcement learning to improve sample efficiency in sparse-reward environments. We will release source code of the study.

AI.tldr: Mesh-RL proposes a spatial domain-decomposition framework inspired by finite element methods that partitions environments into overlapping subgrids with boundary-consistent TD updates, accelerating value propagation in sparse-reward settings without modifying the reward function or Bellman operator.
AI.motivation: Reinforcement learning in large or sparse-reward environments suffers from slow temporal-difference reward propagation, as value information spreads only locally across the state space. Existing solutions like hierarchical RL or model-based planning introduce additional complexity; the authors seek a principled way to accelerate long-range credit assignment without altering the core RL components.
AI.method: Mesh-RL partitions the environment into overlapping spatial subgrids (inspired by finite element method domain decomposition) and enforces boundary-consistent temporal-difference updates. Each subgrid learns locally, but boundary consistency constraints ensure globally coherent value propagation across the entire state space.
AI.result: Evaluated on hazard-dense grid-worlds with varying geometries and mesh resolutions across Q-learning, SARSA, and Dyna-Q, Mesh-RL consistently improved convergence speed, cumulative reward, and learning stability. Higher mesh resolutions sustained exploration, prevented premature convergence, and accelerated value propagation to distant states. Even Dyna-Q, which already benefits from planning, achieved additional gains.
AI.conclusion: Mesh-RL introduces a principled spatial domain-decomposition mechanism that bridges finite element method-inspired boundary-consistency techniques with RL, improving sample efficiency in sparse-reward environments without modifying the reward function, Bellman operator, or introducing explicit planning.

title: Beyond Objects
summary: A core principle of object orientation -- that the functionality of a system can be partitioned amongst objects that correspond to individuals in the problem domain -- has influenced how software has been specified, designed and implemented for more than fifty years. Later developments in software engineering sought to build on this principle. But in fact this partitioning is neither natural nor straightforward, and the problems that these later developments sought to mitigate -- the fragmentation and conflation of functionality -- were often, in fact, the inevitable consequences of this founding principle. An easier path to addressing these problems therefore starts by going back, abandoning object orientation, and replacing it with an alternative approach that decouples the individuals of the problem domain from the modules that partition functionality.

AI.tldr: Object orientation fundamentally partitions functionality by problem-domain individuals, but this founding principle inevitably causes fragmentation and conflation of functionality. The paper argues that later software engineering developments merely mitigated symptoms rather than addressing the root cause, and proposes abandoning object orientation in favor of decoupling domain individuals from functional modules.
AI.motivation: The author contends that the core principle of object orientation — aligning software modules with individuals in the problem domain — is neither natural nor straightforward. Subsequent software engineering approaches (e.g., aspect-oriented programming, design patterns) attempted to fix the resulting problems of fragmented and conflated functionality, but these problems are inherent to the object-oriented paradigm itself. The motivation is to expose this root cause and advocate for a fundamental paradigm shift.
AI.method: This is a conceptual/critical essay that traces the historical influence of object orientation over fifty-plus years, identifies the structural flaws inherent in its founding principle (fragmentation and conflation of functionality), and demonstrates that later software engineering remedies failed because they treated symptoms rather than the underlying cause. The paper then proposes an alternative approach: decoupling domain individuals from the modules that partition functionality.
AI.result: The analysis concludes that the problems of fragmentation and conflation of functionality — which later software engineering developments sought to mitigate — were inevitable consequences of object orientation's founding principle. Abandoning object orientation and decoupling domain individuals from functional modules offers an easier path to resolving these problems.
AI.conclusion: Rather than continuing to patch object orientation with ever more sophisticated remedies, the field should abandon the paradigm entirely. The path forward lies in an approach that separates the representation of problem-domain individuals from the modular partitioning of system functionality.

title: Urban Context and Travel Experience Events: An Exploratory Comparison of Two German Cities
summary: The presented study investigates events influencing public transportation experience in both urban (Hamburg) and rural (Tuttlingen) areas in Germany, with the aim of identifying events that affect travel experience and as a result travel behavior. Using a mobile application, 21 participants in Tuttlingen and 70 participants in Hamburg tracked everyday trips, providing real-time evaluations of travel experiences along with situational data. Multi-level regression analyses were applied to assess the impact of events such as punctuality, capacity offer, information about public transportation and others on the ontrip experience. Results indicate that a sufficient public transportation capacity offer has the strongest positive effect in Tuttlingen, whereas a lack of punctuality and low personal well-being have the strongest negative effects. In Hamburg, a lack of punctuality and a negative information event have the largest impacts. These identified effects provide a foundation for decision-making and measures to improve local public transportation.

AI.tldr: A mobile app-based study in Hamburg (urban) and Tuttlingen (rural), Germany, with 91 participants used multi-level regression to identify key events affecting public transport experience. Punctuality and information quality were critical in Hamburg, while capacity offer and punctuality were most impactful in Tuttlingen, alongside personal well-being.
AI.motivation: To identify specific events that influence the on-trip experience and consequent travel behavior in both urban and rural public transportation contexts, providing an empirical basis for targeted service improvements.
AI.method: 91 participants (70 Hamburg, 21 Tuttlingen) tracked everyday trips via a mobile application, providing real-time evaluations of travel experience and situational data. Multi-level regression analyses were applied to assess the impact of various events (punctuality, capacity offer, information provision, etc.) on on-trip experience.
AI.result: In Tuttlingen (rural), sufficient capacity offer had the strongest positive effect; lack of punctuality and low personal well-being had the strongest negative effects. In Hamburg (urban), lack of punctuality and negative information events had the largest impacts on experience.
AI.conclusion: The identified event-experience relationships provide an evidence-based foundation for decision-makers to prioritize and implement targeted measures for improving local public transportation quality in both urban and rural settings.

title: MergeLLL: A Hierarchical Divide-and-Conquer Framework for LLL-Based Lattice Reduction
summary:
Lattice basis reduction algorithms have various applications in computational number theory and lattice-based cryptography, but their complexity increases rapidly with the dimension. Motivated by the divide-and-conquer strategy of merge sort and incorporating PotLLL-style deep insertions during recombination, MergeLLL is proposed. In this framework, a lattice basis is split into sub-bases, local reductions are performed independently, and the full basis is reconstructed through hierarchical merging.
  The approach is focused on improving local lattice structure first before global basis properties are refined, resulting in enhanced Gram-Schmidt orthogonality and numerical stability, while overall computational cost is reduced. The method is naturally parallelizable, allowing efficient multicore and distributed execution. It is shown that the reduction and merging steps preserve the lattice structure through unimodular transformations and achieve logarithmic parallel depth. In experiments on subset-sum and NTRU-derived lattices, improvements over classical lattice reduction algorithms are demonstrated, including better orthogonality, a reduced number of expensive swap operations, and an improved Hermite factor, indicating higher-quality reduced bases.

AI.tldr: MergeLLL is a parallelizable, divide-and-conquer lattice basis reduction algorithm that splits a lattice basis into sub-bases, reduces them independently, and hierarchically merges them using PotLLL-style deep insertions, achieving better orthogonality, fewer swaps, and improved Hermite factors compared to classical LLL.
AI.motivation: Classical lattice basis reduction algorithms scale poorly with dimension. The authors are motivated by the divide-and-conquer paradigm (analogous to merge sort) to develop a framework that reduces computational cost, improves numerical stability, and enables parallel execution.
AI.method: MergeLLL splits the lattice basis into sub-bases, applies local reductions independently, then reconstructs the full basis through hierarchical merging with PotLLL-style deep insertions. The merging steps use unimodular transformations, preserving lattice structure while achieving logarithmic parallel depth.
AI.result: Experiments on subset-sum and NTRU-derived lattices show improvements over classical algorithms: enhanced Gram-Schmidt orthogonality, fewer expensive swap operations, and improved Hermite factors — all indicating higher-quality reduced bases.
AI.conclusion: The MergeLLL framework effectively combines divide-and-conquer parallelism with deep insertion strategies to produce higher-quality reduced bases at lower computational cost, offering a practical advancement for large-dimension lattice reduction in cryptography and number theory.

title: Soft Token Alignment for Cross-Lingual Reasoning
summary: Multilingual large language models often produce inconsistent reasoning and answers for semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. Prior work suggests that intermediate representations can be relatively language-agnostic, but generation becomes increasingly language-specific as models commit to discrete output tokens. This is problematic because language-specific lexical choices can cause semantically equivalent reasoning paths to diverge across languages. These divergences motivate searching for a cross-lingual alignment signal that is less tied to any single vocabulary item or script. We propose SOLAR, an auxiliary objective for supervised fine-tuning that aligns soft-token representations across languages, using English as a pivot. Soft tokens are probability-weighted mixtures over the vocabulary embeddings, yielding continuous representations that can aggregate information from semantically related tokens across languages. We then align each non-English soft-token summary to its English counterpart in the shared embedding space. Across four multilingual reasoning benchmarks, SOLAR improves accuracy by up to +17.7 points over the base model and +3.8 over standard supervised fine-tuning, with the largest gains on low-resource languages. SOLAR also strengthens final-layer cross-lingual similarity and substantially reduces language-cluster separability, suggesting that aligning soft-token representations helps preserve shared semantic structure during multilingual reasoning.

AI.tldr: SOLAR introduces an auxiliary training objective that aligns soft-token (probability-weighted vocabulary embedding) representations across languages during supervised fine-tuning, using English as a pivot, to reduce cross-lingual reasoning divergence and improve multilingual consistency.
AI.motivation: Multilingual LLMs exhibit inconsistent reasoning and answers for semantically equivalent prompts in different languages. While intermediate representations are relatively language-agnostic, the decoding stage becomes increasingly language-specific, causing semantically equivalent reasoning paths to diverge across languages. A cross-lingual alignment signal is needed that operates below the level of discrete lexical choices.
AI.method: SOLAR proposes an auxiliary objective during supervised fine-tuning that aligns soft-token representations across languages. Soft tokens are defined as probability-weighted mixtures over vocabulary embeddings, yielding continuous representations that aggregate semantically related information across languages. Using English as a pivot, each non-English soft-token summary is aligned to its English counterpart in the shared embedding space.
AI.result: Across four multilingual reasoning benchmarks, SOLAR improves accuracy by up to +17.7 points over the base model and +3.8 points over standard supervised fine-tuning, with the largest gains observed on low-resource languages. It also strengthens final-layer cross-lingual similarity and substantially reduces language-cluster separability.
AI.conclusion: Aligning soft-token representations helps preserve shared semantic structure during multilingual reasoning, suggesting that continuous, probability-weighted representations can effectively bridge cross-lingual reasoning gaps without being tied to any single vocabulary item or script.

title: Estimating Uncertainty in Classifier Performance with Applications to Large Language Models and Nested Data
summary: Researchers increasingly use text classification--supervised models or large language models--to measure constructs from natural language, providing metrics such as recall and precision as evidence of their validity. Yet, though these metrics are point estimates subject to sampling variation, measures of uncertainty are inconsistently reported alongside them. Further, when they are reported, they are often estimated with methods that are not appropriate when relevant labelled datasets are small or performance is high. To increase and improve confidence interval reporting in the field, this paper evaluates confidence interval methods for performance metrics under conditions typical of social science text classification: small to moderate sample sizes, infrequent constructs, and texts nested within individuals. Across simulations, default methods such as the Wald interval and the basic percentile bootstrap are the least accurate, with coverage sometimes far below the nominal 95% level. Accuracy is improved with the use of Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap (which is particularly relevant to the calculation of F1). When texts are nested within individuals, we demonstrate that adjustment for both effective N and the appropriate degrees of freedom is necessary for producing accurate analytic intervals. Among bootstrap intervals, the hierarchical bootstrap is more accurate than the cluster bootstrap when individuals produce a moderate number of texts but overly conservative when individuals produce only a few. By providing guidance to the field on appropriate interval estimation, we aim to improve the transparency of machine learning applications, and to encourage greater attention to the validation sample size at the design stage.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates confidence interval methods for text classification performance metrics under realistic social science conditions (small samples, rare constructs, nested data). Default methods like Wald intervals and basic bootstrap perform poorly, while Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap improve coverage. For clustered texts, hierarchical bootstraps outperform cluster bootstraps with moderate within-cluster sample sizes. The work aims to improve reporting standards and design-stage attention to validation sample sizes.
AI.motivation: In social science text classification, performance metrics (recall, precision, F1) are reported as point estimates without measures of sampling uncertainty. When uncertainty is reported, methods are often inappropriate given the typical conditions: small to moderate labeled datasets, infrequent constructs, and texts nested within individuals. This erodes the transparency and credibility of machine learning measurement in the social sciences.
AI.method: The authors conduct simulation studies varying sample sizes, construct prevalence, and clustering structures. They systematically compare confidence interval methods: Wald, Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson (analytic intervals); basic percentile bootstrap, cluster bootstrap, hierarchical bootstrap, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap (for F1). Coverage rates at the nominal 95% level are the primary evaluation criterion. They also examine adjustments for effective N and degrees of freedom when texts are nested within individuals.
AI.result: Default Wald intervals and basic percentile bootstraps yield coverage substantially below 95%, especially with small samples or high performance. Agresti-Coull, Wilson, and Clopper-Pearson intervals improve coverage markedly. The novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap is particularly effective for F1. Under clustering, adjusting for effective N and degrees of freedom is essential for accurate analytic intervals. The hierarchical bootstrap outperforms the cluster bootstrap with moderate texts-per-individual but becomes overly conservative when individuals contribute few texts.
AI.conclusion: Researchers should abandon default Wald intervals and naive bootstraps. Instead, they should adopt Agresti-Coull/Wilson/Clopper-Pearson for analytic intervals and pseudo-count regularized bootstraps for F1. When data are nested, effective N and degrees-of-freedom corrections are necessary. The hierarchical bootstrap is recommended except when within-cluster N is very small. The field must attend to validation sample size at the study design stage to ensure reportable uncertainty.

title: EMA-FS: Accelerating GBDT Training via Gain-Informed Feature Screening
summary:
Gradient Boosted Decision Trees (GBDT), exemplified by LightGBM, spend a dominant fraction of training time -- typically 65-70% -- constructing per-feature histograms. Existing approaches such as random feature subsampling (feature_fraction) discard features without regard for their predictive utility. We propose EMA-based Feature Screening (EMA-FS), an algorithm-level optimization that maintains an exponential moving average (EMA) of per-feature split gains across boosting iterations and, after a short warmup, restricts histogram construction to the top-K features ranked by historical gain. Unlike random subsampling, EMA-FS is informed: it retains high-gain features while screening out low-gain ones.
