Operating at the per-tree level, it preserves full compatibility with LightGBM's histogram subtraction trick, requiring no changes to core routines.
  We evaluate EMA-FS on datasets spanning financial fraud detection, advertising click-through prediction, industrial quality control, and synthetic benchmarks, with feature dimensionalities from 29 to 968. On dense, moderate-to-high-dimensional data it achieves significant speedups: 2.61x on a 500-feature synthetic benchmark and 1.45x on the 432-feature IEEE-CIS Fraud dataset at 30% retention. At 70% retention it improves AUC by 0.11 points while delivering a 1.34x speedup. On extremely sparse data (Bosch, >90% missing) it yields no speedup, as LightGBM's sparse bin optimization already bypasses empty values.
  We further introduce Stochastic EMA-FS (S-EMA-FS), which replaces deterministic top-K selection with gain-weighted random sampling controlled by a concentration parameter beta, unifying deterministic EMA-FS (beta -> infinity) and random subsampling (beta = 0) in one framework. Both are implemented in ~120 lines of C++ across all six LightGBM tree learners and are fully backward-compatible.

AI.tldr: EMA-FS accelerates LightGBM training by restricting histogram construction to top-K features ranked via EMA of historical split gains, achieving up to 2.61x speedup on dense data while maintaining or improving AUC. A stochastic variant (S-EMA-FS) unifies deterministic selection and random subsampling via a concentration parameter.
AI.motivation: GBDT training (e.g., LightGBM) spends 65-70% of time building per-feature histograms. Existing feature subsampling (feature_fraction) randomly discards features without considering predictive utility, leading to wasted computation on low-gain features and potential loss of high-gain ones.
AI.method: EMA-FS tracks an exponential moving average of per-feature split gains across boosting iterations. After a short warmup phase, each tree restricts histogram construction to the top-K features by historical gain. The method operates per-tree, preserving LightGBM's histogram subtraction trick and requiring no core routine changes. S-EMA-FS extends this by replacing deterministic top-K with gain-weighted random sampling governed by a concentration parameter β, where β→∞ recovers deterministic EMA-FS and β=0 recovers uniform random subsampling. Implementation spans ~120 lines of C++ across all six LightGBM tree learners.
AI.result: On a 500-feature synthetic benchmark: 2.61x speedup at 30% retention. On IEEE-CIS Fraud (432 features): 1.45x speedup at 30% retention; at 70% retention, AUC improved by 0.11 points with 1.34x speedup. On extremely sparse data (Bosch, >90% missing): no speedup, as LightGBM's sparse bin optimization already handles empty values efficiently. Evaluated across financial fraud, CTR prediction, industrial QC, and synthetic benchmarks (29–968 features).
AI.conclusion: EMA-FS provides an informed, lightweight feature screening approach that significantly accelerates LightGBM on dense, moderate-to-high-dimensional data without sacrificing accuracy, while gracefully degrading on sparse data where existing optimizations suffice. S-EMA-FS offers a flexible unified framework spanning deterministic and stochastic feature selection.

title: Agent Capsules: Quality-Gated Granularity Control for Multi-Agent LLM Pipelines
summary: A multi-agent pipeline with N agents typically issues N LLM calls per run. Merging agents into fewer calls (compound execution) promises token savings, but naively merged calls silently degrade quality through tool loss and prompt compression. We present Agent Capsules, an adaptive execution runtime that treats multi-agent pipeline execution as an optimization problem with empirical quality constraints. The runtime instruments coordination overhead per group, scores composition opportunity, selects among three compound execution strategies, and gates every mode switch on rolling-mean output quality. A controlled negative result confirms that injecting more context into a merged call worsens compression rather than relieving it, so the framework's escalation ladder (standard, then two-phase, then sequential) recovers quality by moving toward per-agent dispatch rather than by rewriting merged prompts. On LLM-judged quality, the controller matches a hand-tuned oracle on every measured (model, group, mode) cell: routing compound whenever the oracle would, and reverting to fine whenever quality would fail the floor, without per-model configuration. Against a hand-crafted LangGraph implementation of a 14-agent competitive intelligence pipeline, Agent Capsules uses 51% fewer fine-mode input tokens and 42% fewer compound-mode input tokens, at +0.020 and +0.017 quality respectively. Against a DSPy implementation of a 5-agent due diligence pipeline, the framework uses 19% fewer tokens than uncompiled DSPy at quality parity, and 68% fewer tokens than MIPROv2 at +0.052 quality. Even before compound mode fires, the runtime delivers efficiency through automatic policy resolution, cache-aligned prompts, and topology-aware context injection, matching both hand-tuned and compile-time baselines without training data or per-pipeline engineering.

AI.tldr: Agent Capsules is an adaptive runtime that treats multi-agent LLM pipeline execution as a constrained optimization problem, dynamically selecting among three compound execution strategies to merge agent calls while gating mode switches on rolling-mean output quality, achieving substantial token savings (42–68%) with quality parity or improvement over hand-tuned and compile-time baselines.
AI.motivation: Naively merging multiple LLM agent calls into fewer compound calls saves tokens but silently degrades output quality due to tool loss and prompt compression artifacts. Existing approaches require per-pipeline hand-tuning or training data. The authors seek an automatic, adaptive runtime that balances token efficiency against empirical quality constraints without per-model configuration.
AI.method: The Agent Capsules runtime models multi-agent pipeline execution as an optimization problem constrained by quality floors. It instruments coordination overhead per agent group, scores composition opportunity, and selects among three strategies on an escalation ladder: (1) standard merged calls, (2) two-phase execution, and (3) sequential per-agent dispatch. Every mode switch is gated by rolling-mean output quality. The framework also includes automatic policy resolution, cache-aligned prompts, and topology-aware context injection. A controlled negative result shows that injecting more context into merged calls worsens compression, motivating the escalation ladder design.
AI.result: On a 14-agent competitive intelligence pipeline (LangGraph), Agent Capsules achieves 51% fewer fine-mode input tokens and 42% fewer compound-mode input tokens, with quality deltas of +0.020 and +0.017 respectively. On a 5-agent due diligence pipeline (DSPy), it uses 19% fewer tokens than uncompiled DSPy at quality parity, and 68% fewer tokens than MIPROv2 at +0.052 quality. The controller matches a hand-tuned oracle on every measured (model, group, mode) cell without per-model configuration.
AI.conclusion: Compound execution can be made reliable through adaptive, quality-gated strategy selection rather than prompt rewriting. The escalation ladder from standard to two-phase to sequential dispatch effectively recovers quality when merged calls fail, and the approach generalizes across different multi-agent frameworks and pipelines without requiring training data or per-pipeline engineering.

title: Behind the Mask: A Taxonomic Analysis of Activities in Online Social Networks
summary: The broadcast of disinformation in online social networks (OSN) is a growing concern examined across several disciplines, including human-computer interaction (HCI). The pervasive issue has been prompting novel approaches to identify the malicious actors behind the dissemination of deceptive and fabricated content. Analyzing the characteristics and activities of these actors, we designed a taxonomy informed by collaboration with subject matter experts (SMEs) and a review of the academic literature. Our study explores how to distinguish the characteristics, activities, and strategies of malicious actors on OSN and examines how they contribute to the spread of disinformation. We describe the design process and the application of the taxonomy in a case study analyzing anti-migration discourse in social media channels, and reflect on its potential to aid researchers and practitioners in the responsible design of network systems.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a taxonomy for characterizing malicious actors who spread disinformation on online social networks, developed through collaboration with subject matter experts and literature review. Its utility is demonstrated via a case study on anti-migration discourse.
AI.motivation: The growing proliferation of disinformation in online social networks demands systematic approaches to identify and understand the malicious actors behind deceptive and fabricated content. Existing methods lack a comprehensive, expert-informed framework to distinguish these actors' characteristics, activities, and strategies.
AI.method: The authors designed a taxonomy through collaboration with subject matter experts (SMEs) and a review of academic literature. The taxonomy was then applied in a case study analyzing anti-migration discourse across social media channels.
AI.result: A taxonomy was produced that distinguishes the characteristics, activities, and strategies of malicious actors spreading disinformation. The case study demonstrated the taxonomy's applicability in real-world social media analysis contexts.
AI.conclusion: The taxonomy offers a valuable tool for researchers and practitioners engaged in the responsible design of network systems, aiding in the identification and analysis of malicious disinformation actors on OSNs.

title: MIRROR: Novelty-Constrained Memory-Guided MCTS Red-Teaming for Agentic RAG
comment: 6 pages, 2 figures. Accepted at the 2026 International Joint Conference on Neural Networks (IJCNN 2026), IEEE WCCI 2026; presented as an oral talk. Code and ART-SafeBench benchmark: https://github.com/FujitsuResearch/mirror
summary: Multimodal agentic retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems expand the attack surface beyond prompt injection to include text poisoning, image injection, direct-query attacks, and orchestrator-level tool manipulation. Existing red-teaming approaches are typically surface-specific and often recycle known attack templates; on text-poisoning benchmarks we measure 73-84% exact duplication. We present MIRROR, a unified cross-surface framework that performs memory-guided Monte Carlo tree search while conditioning candidate generation on retrieved context under an explicit novelty constraint. A deterministic Novelty Gate rejects any candidate matching the retrieval set under normalized comparison, allowing retrieval to inform search priors without enabling prompt copying. Across four attack surfaces on a multimodal agentic RAG target, MIRROR attains 76% ASR on image poisoning compared with 52% for baselines, 97% ASR on orchestrator attacks at half the query cost, and the lowest cross-surface variance (coefficient of variation 0.47). In contrast, specialized baselines collapse across surfaces: suffix optimization reaches 79% ASR on text poisoning but 1% on direct queries. We release ART-SafeBench with 41,815 in-package records and runtime adapters yielding 41,991+ total records across four surfaces.

AI.tldr: MIRROR is a unified red-teaming framework using memory-guided Monte Carlo tree search with a novelty gate to generate diverse, non-duplicate attacks across multiple surfaces of multimodal agentic RAG systems, outperforming specialized baselines and reducing cross-surface variance.
AI.motivation: Existing red-teaming for multimodal agentic RAG systems is fragmented by attack surface (text poisoning, image injection, direct queries, orchestrator manipulation), suffers from high template duplication (73-84% on benchmarks), and specialized methods fail catastrophically when applied across surfaces. A unified, novelty-constrained attack generation framework is needed.
AI.method: MIRROR employs memory-guided Monte Carlo tree search (MCTS) for candidate attack generation across four surfaces, conditioning generation on retrieved context. A deterministic Novelty Gate performs normalized comparison against the retrieval set and rejects any matching candidate, preventing template recycling while letting retrieval inform search priors. The framework unifies attack generation across text poisoning, image injection, direct-query, and orchestrator manipulation surfaces.
AI.result: MIRROR achieves 76% attack success rate (ASR) on image poisoning (vs. 52% baselines), 97% ASR on orchestrator attacks at half the query cost, and the lowest cross-surface variance (CV=0.47). Specialized baselines collapse: suffix optimization reaches 79% ASR on text poisoning but only 1% on direct queries. ART-SafeBench is released with 41,815 in-package records plus runtime adapters (41,991+ total).
AI.conclusion: A unified, novelty-constrained search approach substantially improves robustness and efficiency in red-teaming multimodal agentic RAG systems, mitigating the brittleness of surface-specific methods. The released ART-SafeBench benchmark supports further research.

title: Data-driven Machine Learning Cannot Reach Symbolic-level Logical Reasoning -- The Limit of the Scaling Law
summary: Sphere neural networks have achieved symbolic level syllogistic reasoning without training data, raising the question of where the limit of the scaling law for logical reasoning lies, i.e., whether data-driven machine learning systems can achieve the same level by increasing training data and training time. We show two methodological limitations that prevent supervised deep learning from reaching the symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning: (1) training data can not distinguish all 24 types of valid syllogistic reasoning; (2) end-to-end mapping from premises to conclusion introduces contradictory training targets between neural components for pattern recognition and logical reasoning. Beside theoretical analysis, we experimentally illustrate that Euler Net cannot achieve rigorous syllogistic reasoning. We further challenge the most recent ChatGPTs (GPT-5-nano and GPT-5) to determine the satisfiability of syllogistic statements in four surface forms (patterns): words, double words, simple symbols, and long random symbols, showing that surface forms affect the reasoning performance and that ChatGPT GPT-5 may reach 100% accuracy but still provide incorrect explanations. As empirical training processes are stopped after achieving 100% accuracy, we conclude that supervised machine learning systems will not attain the rigour of symbolic logical reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper argues that supervised deep learning cannot achieve rigorous syllogistic reasoning due to two fundamental methodological limitations: training data cannot distinguish all 24 valid syllogism types, and end-to-end mapping introduces contradictory training targets. Experiments with Euler Net and ChatGPT (GPT-5) support the claim, showing surface form dependence and incorrect explanations even at 100% accuracy.
AI.motivation: Sphere neural networks have achieved symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning without training data, prompting the question of whether data-driven ML systems can reach the same level through scaling laws — i.e., more data and training time. The authors investigate the fundamental limits of supervised deep learning for logical reasoning.
AI.method: The authors present a two-pronged approach: (1) theoretical analysis identifying two methodological limitations — insufficient discriminability of training data for all 24 valid syllogism types, and contradictory training targets arising from end-to-end premise-to-conclusion mapping that conflates pattern recognition with logical reasoning; (2) experimental evaluation using Euler Net to demonstrate its failure at rigorous syllogistic reasoning, plus probing ChatGPT (GPT-5-nano and GPT-5) on syllogistic satisfiability across four surface forms (words, double words, simple symbols, long random symbols).
AI.result: Euler Net fails to achieve rigorous syllogistic reasoning. ChatGPT models show that surface form significantly affects reasoning performance; GPT-5 can reach 100% accuracy but still produces incorrect explanations. Since training is typically stopped upon reaching 100% accuracy, the incorrect explanations remain undetected.
AI.conclusion: Supervised machine learning systems will not attain the rigour of symbolic logical reasoning, regardless of scaling data and compute. The two identified methodological limitations are intrinsic and cannot be overcome by simply increasing training data or training time.

title: Does Aurora Encode Atmospheric Structure? Latent Regime Analysis and Attribution
comment: Accepted at the FM4Science and Sci4DL workshops at ICLR 2026
summary: ML foundation models are able to emulate atmospheric dynamics accurately and efficiently but operate as opaque ``black boxes''. We investigate the internal representations of the Aurora model using spatially pooled PCA and layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP). We find evidence that Aurora's latent space is primarily organized by seasonal cycles, whereas extreme storm events do not form a linearly separable cluster. LRP indicates that the model attends to features consistent with the 3D vertical structure of the Great Storm of 1987. Perturbation tests show masking relevant regions degrades forecasts $3.31\times$ more than random masking. These findings suggest that Aurora learns meteorological coherence and vertical structure without explicit instruction.

AI.tldr: Analysis of the Aurora atmospheric foundation model reveals its latent space is organized by seasonal cycles rather than extreme events, and layer-wise relevance propagation shows the model attends to physically coherent 3D vertical structures without explicit training.
AI.motivation: ML foundation models like Aurora achieve strong atmospheric forecasting performance but operate as opaque black boxes. Understanding their internal representations is crucial for trust, scientific insight, and validation that the model learns physically meaningful features rather than spurious correlations.
AI.method: The authors apply two interpretability techniques: (1) spatially pooled PCA on Aurora's latent space to examine how representations are organized, and (2) layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) to identify which input features the model attends to for specific predictions. They also conduct perturbation tests comparing forecast degradation when masking LRP-identified relevant regions versus random regions.
AI.result: PCA reveals the latent space is primarily organized by seasonal cycles; extreme storm events do not form linearly separable clusters. LRP shows the model attends to features consistent with the 3D vertical structure of the Great Storm of 1987. Perturbation tests demonstrate that masking relevant regions degrades forecasts 3.31× more than random masking.
AI.conclusion: Aurora learns meteorologically coherent representations and vertical atmospheric structure without explicit instruction, suggesting foundation models can internalize physically meaningful features through self-supervised or task-driven training alone.

title: Context-Aware Synthesis of Optimization Pipelines for Warehouse Optimization
summary:
Order fulfillment in manual picker-to-goods warehouses involves interconnected decisions such as item assignment, order batching, and picker routing. While integrated models capture interactions between these decisions, practical warehouse systems often require decomposed approaches due to organizational boundaries, differing responsibilities, or limited data availability. Existing studies primarily evaluate algorithms for isolated subproblems or fixed subproblem combinations for specific warehouse settings, but lack a general mechanism to determine applicable algorithm configurations, compose them into valid solution pipelines, and assess their performance.
  With Context-Aware Synthesis of Optimization Pipelines (CASOP), we propose a framework for constructing and evaluating context-specific optimization pipelines and apply these to order fulfillment. The framework comprises: (1) a modular repository of algorithms for common order fulfillment problems; (2) semantic data and algorithm cards to describe warehouse context and algorithm requirements; (3) a taxonomy that structures order fulfillment problems into relevant subproblems; (4) a pipeline synthesizer that identifies applicable algorithms for a given warehouse context and composes all valid optimization pipelines; and (5) a pipeline evaluator that assesses all resulting pipelines. We demonstrate the framework on 7 benchmark instance sets covering four problem classes, resulting in 1,063,044 valid pipelines. The framework supports researchers and practitioners in designing, automatically synthesizing, and selecting valid, high-performing algorithmic pipelines for warehouse operations. The software is open-source and available at https://github.com/kit-dsm/ware_ops_pipes and https://github.com/kit-dsm/ware_ops_algos.
  Keywords: Warehouse optimization, Algorithm selection, Pipeline synthesis, Order fulfillment

AI.tldr: CASOP is a framework that automatically synthesizes and evaluates optimization pipelines for order fulfillment in manual warehouses. It uses semantic data/algorithm cards, a problem taxonomy, and a pipeline synthesizer to compose valid algorithm combinations from a modular repository. Demonstrated on 7 benchmarks across 4 problem classes, it generated over 1 million valid pipelines, supporting context-specific algorithm selection.
AI.motivation: Practical warehouse systems often require decomposed (rather than integrated) approaches due to organizational boundaries, differing responsibilities, or limited data. Existing studies evaluate algorithms only for isolated subproblems or fixed combinations, lacking a general mechanism to determine applicable algorithm configurations, compose them into valid pipelines, and assess their performance across diverse warehouse contexts.
AI.method: CASOP framework with five components: (1) a modular algorithm repository for order fulfillment subproblems; (2) semantic data cards and algorithm cards describing warehouse context and algorithm requirements; (3) a taxonomy structuring order fulfillment into subproblems; (4) a pipeline synthesizer that matches algorithms to context and composes all valid pipelines; (5) a pipeline evaluator that assesses resulting pipelines. Evaluated on 7 benchmark instance sets spanning 4 problem classes.
AI.result: The framework generated 1,063,044 valid optimization pipelines across 7 benchmark instance sets covering four problem classes, demonstrating its capability to systematically compose and evaluate algorithm configurations for diverse warehouse contexts.
AI.conclusion: CASOP successfully supports researchers and practitioners in designing, automatically synthesizing, and selecting valid, high-performing algorithmic pipelines for warehouse operations. The software is released as open-source.

title: "Everyone Says Them": Deception Typologies, Probabilistic Trust, and Grassroots Safety Knowledge Among Gay Dating App Users in China
summary: Gay dating applications have become critical platforms for sexual minority men to seek relationships and community, yet they also expose users to deceptive interactions that remain underexplored in HCI and CSCW research. This study examines how gay male users in China experience, identify, and respond to deception on dating applications. Through semi-structured interviews with 22 participants across platforms including Blued, Aloha, Fanka, and Soul, we make three contributions. First, we identify a typology of deceptive practices extending beyond profile misrepresentation to encompass relational, emotional, financial, and commercial forms of deception. Second, we document the layered, probabilistic verification strategies users develop through long-term platform use, showing that trust assessment operates as a multi-signal, provisional process rather than a binary judgment. Third, we demonstrate that risk recognition is a collaborative practice shaped by the circulation of experience, the abstraction of recurrent tactics, and the codification of shared rules within the community.

AI.tldr: This study explores how gay men in China experience and navigate deception on dating apps, identifying a typology of deceptive practices, documenting users' probabilistic trust-assessment strategies, and revealing how risk recognition emerges as a collaborative community practice.
AI.motivation: Gay dating applications are essential for sexual minority men to find relationships and community, yet deceptive interactions on these platforms remain largely understudied in HCI and CSCW literature. The authors aim to fill this gap by investigating how users identify and respond to deception in the Chinese context.
AI.method: Semi-structured interviews with 22 gay male participants who use platforms including Blued, Aloha, Fanka, and Soul. The study employs qualitative analysis to examine user experiences with deception.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) a typology of deceptive practices that goes beyond profile misrepresentation to include relational, emotional, financial, and commercial deception; (2) users develop layered, probabilistic verification strategies over time, treating trust assessment as a multi-signal, provisional process rather than a binary judgment; (3) risk recognition is a collaborative, community-driven practice involving the circulation of experiences, abstraction of recurring tactics, and codification of shared rules.
AI.conclusion: Deception on gay dating apps is a multifaceted phenomenon requiring nuanced understanding. The findings suggest design implications for platforms and highlight the importance of community-based knowledge sharing in risk recognition, contributing to broader CSCW discussions on trust, safety, and marginalized user experiences.

title: SpikeTimer: Exploring Active Copyright Protection in Spiking Neural Networks via Temporal Backdoor Regularization
comment: This paper has been accepted for IEEE TIFS 2026
summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNN) have emerged as a revolutionary paradigm compared to traditional Deep Neural Networks (DNN) in energy-efficient computing, showcasing exceptional capabilities in processing event-driven sensory data for real-time applications like robotics and edge AI systems. However, unlike extensive studies on DNN copyright solutions, SNN copyright protection remains largely underexplored due to their inherent temporal coding complexities and spike-driven computation. In this study, we propose a novel active copyright protection framework named SpikeTimer for SNNs via temporal backdoor learning. SpikeTimer partitions neuromorphic data into designated timeslices and exclusively embeds authorized tokens within authorized slices. Furthermore, the inherent temporal segmentation characteristic intrinsically enables SpikeTimer to support multi-user authorization mechanisms and accommodates token embedding of arbitrary morphology. Based on this, SpikeTimer precisely responds to authorized data containing a token within the correct timeslice, while producing erroneous responses to unauthorized data. Our key innovation lies in establishing a time-dependent authorization mechanism that protects the SNN copyright by temporal token validity. Additionally, SpikeTimer retains its defensive efficacy even under adversarial attempts. Evaluations on multiple neuromorphic datasets manifest that SpikeTimer achieves around 10% accuracy on unauthorized data with merely around 1.5% degradation on authorized inputs. Moreover, SpikeTimer demonstrates robust resistance against model finetuning and pruning threats.

AI.tldr: SpikeTimer is a novel active copyright protection framework for Spiking Neural Networks that uses temporal backdoor learning, embedding authorized tokens in specific timeslices so the network responds correctly only to authorized data while producing erroneous outputs on unauthorized data, achieving ~10% accuracy on unauthorized data with only ~1.5% degradation on authorized inputs.
AI.motivation: Unlike DNNs, SNN copyright protection remains largely underexplored due to temporal coding complexities and spike-driven computation. There is a pressing need for SNN-specific copyright mechanisms that account for their unique event-driven, time-dependent nature.
AI.method: SpikeTimer partitions neuromorphic data into designated timeslices and embeds authorized tokens exclusively within authorized slices. Leveraging inherent temporal segmentation, it supports multi-user authorization and tokens of arbitrary morphology. The core innovation is a time-dependent authorization mechanism where copyright protection hinges on temporal token validity: only data containing the correct token in the correct timeslice triggers proper network behavior; otherwise, erroneous responses are produced.
AI.result: Evaluations on multiple neuromorphic datasets show SpikeTimer achieves approximately 10% accuracy on unauthorized data with only around 1.5% degradation on authorized inputs. It also demonstrates robust resistance against model finetuning and pruning threats.
AI.conclusion: SpikeTimer effectively protects SNN copyright through temporal backdoor learning with minimal authorized accuracy loss, strong unauthorized degradation, robustness against adversarial removal attempts, and inherent support for multi-user authorization.

title: MKG-RAG-Bench: Benchmarking Retrieval in Multimodal Knowledge Graph-Augmented Generation
summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs has emerged as a promising approach for grounding large language models, yet existing benchmarks largely overlook the challenges of retrieval in multimodal knowledge graph RAG (MKG-RAG). In practice, retrieval is a critical bottleneck: multimodal knowledge is heterogeneous, difficult to align across modalities, and often poorly served by retrievers designed for unstructured corpora. To address this gap, we introduce MKG-RAG-Bench, a cross-domain benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate retrieval in MKG-RAG. MKG-RAG-Bench is constructed from two multimodal knowledge graphs spanning general and medical domains, and includes carefully aligned question-answering datasets that support controlled evaluation of both retrieval and downstream generation. The benchmark is built using an LLM-based curation pipeline that filters low-utility knowledge, generates structurally grounded queries with exact supervision, and systematically covers diverse modality configurations. Through extensive experiments across representative retriever families and modality settings, we show that effective multimodal retrieval remains challenging yet crucial for end-to-end MKG-RAG performance, and that retrieval quality strongly determines generation outcomes. By isolating retrieval as a first-class evaluation target, MKG-RAG-Bench provides a principled foundation for diagnosing current limitations and advancing multimodal knowledge graph RAG systems.

AI.tldr: Introduces MKG-RAG-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating retrieval in multimodal knowledge graph retrieval-augmented generation, revealing that retrieval quality is the critical bottleneck for end-to-end MKG-RAG performance.
AI.motivation: Existing RAG benchmarks overlook retrieval challenges specific to multimodal knowledge graphs, where heterogeneous modalities, alignment difficulties, and inadequacy of standard retrievers create a critical performance bottleneck.
AI.method: Constructed MKG-RAG-Bench from two multimodal KGs (general and medical domains) using an LLM-based curation pipeline that filters low-utility knowledge, generates structurally grounded queries with exact supervision, and systematically covers diverse modality configurations. Evaluated across representative retriever families and modality settings.
AI.result: Effective multimodal retrieval remains challenging yet crucial; retrieval quality strongly determines downstream generation outcomes in MKG-RAG systems.
AI.conclusion: MKG-RAG-Bench establishes retrieval as a first-class evaluation target, providing a principled foundation for diagnosing limitations and advancing multimodal knowledge graph RAG systems.

title: Reading the Same Data Differently: Interpretive Labor Across System Boundaries in Electronic Monitoring
summary: Electronic monitoring (EM) systems are increasingly used in community corrections to enforce spatial, temporal, and behavioral rules through continuous sensing. While prior work has examined EM as a criminal justice tool or as a mechanism for compliance, less is known about how sensed data become meaningful in everyday practice. This poster examines EM as a dual-sided sensing system in which supervised individuals and authorities reason about the same data stream from different positions. Based on semi-structured interviews with 26 supervised individuals and 12 authorities in China's community corrections system, we show that supervised individuals infer system logic from outcomes with limited visibility into how data are interpreted, while authorities reconstruct behavior from ambiguous traces using contextual knowledge, professional experience, and institutional procedures. We call this structural divergence interpretive misalignment. It emerges from asymmetric access to data, context, and reasoning processes, and it shapes behavior through probing, strategic adaptation, over-compliance, disengagement, and contestation. We contribute a CSCW account of continuous sensing as distributed interpretive work and identify design opportunities for making data-to-decision processes more legible, contestable, and accountable across system sides.

AI.tldr: This paper examines electronic monitoring (EM) in China's community corrections as a dual-sided sensing system, revealing "interpretive misalignment" — a structural divergence in how supervised individuals and authorities interpret the same data stream due to asymmetric access to data, context, and reasoning processes.
AI.motivation: Prior work on EM has focused on compliance or criminal justice implications, but little is known about how sensed data become meaningful in everyday practice. The authors aim to understand how both sides of the system — supervised individuals and authorities — make sense of continuous monitoring data from their distinct vantage points.
AI.method: Semi-structured interviews with 26 supervised individuals and 12 authorities in China's community corrections system, analyzed to surface interpretive practices on both sides of the EM system.
AI.result: The study identifies "interpretive misalignment": supervised individuals infer system logic from outcomes with limited visibility into data interpretation, while authorities reconstruct behavior from ambiguous traces using contextual knowledge, professional experience, and institutional procedures. This misalignment produces behavioral responses including probing, strategic adaptation, over-compliance, disengagement, and contestation.
AI.conclusion: The paper contributes a CSCW framing of continuous sensing as distributed interpretive work and proposes design opportunities for making data-to-decision processes more legible, contestable, and accountable across both sides of the system.

title: Fortress and Gatekeeper: Theorizing Transitive Trust in Third-Party Cybersecurity Risk Governance
summary: Third-party vendors, such as analytics platforms, cloud services, identity providers, and software suppliers, are increasingly embedded in digital service delivery. While these arrangements enable scale and specialization, they also move customer data and security-relevant practices into environments that customers rarely see, select, or evaluate. This paper examines this problem through a document analysis of the November 2025 OpenAI-Mixpanel security incident. The incident serves as an illustrative case for showing how a security event in a vendor environment can become a governance and accountability problem for the focal organization that maintains the customer relationship. Drawing on organizational trust research and agency theory, the paper argues that third-party cybersecurity risk is both a trust relationship and a delegation problem. Customers trust the visible service provider, while the provider relies on vendors whose security practices are only partially visible and controllable. The paper develops the concept of transitive trust, where customer trust in a digital service depends on the security practices of vendors authorized by that service provider. It then presents the Fortress and Gatekeeper framework, which explains cybersecurity governance boundaries through trust and data flows rather than formal organizational ownership alone. The analysis develops four propositions concerning vendor integration, metadata exposure, vendor assurance, and data proliferation. The paper contributes to cybersecurity governance scholarship by explaining how delegated data processing creates customer-facing accountability and by identifying implications for vendor tiering, data classification, contractual design, continuous assurance, and data minimization.

AI.tldr: Third-party vendor integration in digital services creates cybersecurity risks where customer trust in a service provider is undermined by invisible, hard-to-control vendor practices. Using the OpenAI-Mixpanel 2025 incident as a case, the paper develops the concept of "transitive trust" and the Fortress and Gatekeeper framework to explain how security governance boundaries are shaped by trust and data flows, offering propositions on vendor integration, metadata exposure, assurance, and data proliferation.
AI.motivation: Digital services increasingly depend on third-party vendors (analytics, cloud, identity, software supply), yet these arrangements shift customer data and security practices into environments beyond customer visibility or control. When security incidents occur in vendor environments, accountability becomes ambiguous. The paper addresses the gap in cybersecurity governance scholarship regarding how delegated data processing generates customer-facing accountability problems.
AI.method: The paper employs a document analysis of the November 2025 OpenAI-Mixpanel security incident as an illustrative case study. It draws on organizational trust research and agency theory as theoretical lenses to interpret the incident and construct a conceptual framework.
AI.result: The analysis yields: (1) the concept of "transitive trust," where customer trust in a digital service depends on the security practices of vendors authorized by the service provider; (2) the Fortress and Gatekeeper framework, which delineates cybersecurity governance boundaries through trust and data flows rather than formal ownership; and (3) four formal propositions addressing vendor integration, metadata exposure, vendor assurance, and data proliferation.
AI.conclusion: Delegated data processing creates distinct customer-facing accountability challenges that extend beyond organizational boundaries. The paper identifies practical implications for vendor tiering, data classification, contractual design, continuous assurance, and data minimization, contributing to both theory and practice in cybersecurity governance of multi-party digital service ecosystems.

title: Speaking Numbers to LLMs: Multi-Wavelet Number Embeddings for Time Series Forecasting
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are attractive for context-aware time series forecasting because they can integrate heterogeneous textual signals, yet their discrete, language-oriented tokenization and embedding interfaces are misaligned with continuous numerical values, often harming numerical ordering and forecasting reliability. We propose TempoWave, a plug-and-play temporal wavelet digit interface that maps each scalar observation into digit-wise embeddings constructed from multi-wavelet, multi-scale coefficients. By directly overriding standard token representations, TempoWave seamlessly exposes both fine-grained local fluctuations and macro global structures in a transformer-compatible form, ensuring that precise numerical formatting, distinct digit identity, and robustness to common normalization operations are maintained throughout the LLM pipeline. Experiments across five context-enriched forecasting benchmarks demonstrate that TempoWave consistently improves LLM-based forecasters over standard numeric tokenization and alternative embedding interfaces, achieving a new state-of-the-art. These results highlight the numeric interface as a key bottleneck and suggest that principled multi-resolution embeddings can better couple LLMs' contextual reasoning with precise forecasting. Our code is available at https://github.com/DC-research/TempoWAVE and our model can be accessed at https://huggingface.co/Melady/TempoWAVE.

AI.tldr: TempoWave is a plug-and-play temporal wavelet digit interface that maps scalar time series observations into multi-wavelet, multi-scale digit-wise embeddings, bridging the mismatch between LLMs' discrete tokenization and continuous numerical data to improve context-aware forecasting.
AI.motivation: LLMs are promising for context-aware time series forecasting due to their ability to incorporate heterogeneous textual signals, but their discrete, language-oriented tokenization and embedding schemes are fundamentally misaligned with continuous numerical values. This misalignment harms numerical ordering and forecasting reliability.
AI.method: TempoWave constructs digit-wise embeddings from multi-wavelet, multi-scale coefficients for each scalar observation. It directly overrides standard token representations in the LLM pipeline, exposing both fine-grained local fluctuations and macro global structures in a transformer-compatible form while preserving numerical formatting, digit identity, and robustness to normalization.
AI.result: Experiments across five context-enriched forecasting benchmarks show TempoWave consistently improves LLM-based forecasters over standard numeric tokenization and alternative embedding interfaces, achieving state-of-the-art performance.
AI.conclusion: The numeric interface is a key bottleneck in LLM-based time series forecasting. Principled multi-resolution embeddings like TempoWave can better couple LLMs' contextual reasoning capabilities with precise numerical forecasting.

title: auto-psych: Automating the science of mind using agent-driven theory discovery and experimentation
summary: AI-based scientific automation is increasingly possible by using agents to generate hypotheses, design experiments, and analyze data. Data collection is a major bottleneck in this pipeline, however. Psychology, and computational cognitive science in particular, is well-positioned to benefit from AI experimentation because theories are often represented as code and crowdsourcing platforms enable programmatic human data collection at scale. Here, we apply automated discovery techniques to the project of generating theories in computational cognitive science, with an agent-based system collecting human data independently through crowdsourced survey experiments. As a testbed, we use a classic case study from cognitive psychology: judging which sequences of coin flips seem subjectively more random. Our system, auto-psych, uses nested agent-based discovery loops to generate explanatory theories of human behavior. The inner loop conjectures, fits, and critiques probabilistic cognitive models; the outer loop designs experiments to test these models, launches them online, and analyzes the data. This system can quickly and reliably recover ground-truth theories from synthetic data via systematic experimentation, but the nested structure is critical to model performance. Further, in three independent sequences of human experiments, the system finds theories that fit the data better than theories generated from the scientific literature. This work thus demonstrates the feasibility of automated data collection and theory discovery in computational cognitive science.

AI.tldr: The paper presents auto-psych, an agent-based system that autonomously generates and tests cognitive theories by combining nested discovery loops: an inner loop for model conjecture/fitting/critique and an outer loop for designing, launching, and analyzing crowdsourced experiments. Tested on human judgments of coin-flip randomness, the system recovers ground-truth theories from synthetic data and discovers theories outperforming existing literature-derived models across three human experiment sequences.
AI.motivation: Data collection is a major bottleneck in AI-driven scientific automation pipelines. Computational cognitive science is uniquely suited to benefit from automated experimentation because theories are often expressed as executable code and crowdsourcing platforms enable scalable, programmatic human data collection. The work aims to close the loop by creating a system that not only generates and fits models but also independently collects the human behavioral data needed to test them.
AI.method: The auto-psych system employs two nested agent-based discovery loops. The inner loop conjectures probabilistic cognitive models, fits them to data, and critiques their performance. The outer loop designs novel experiments to discriminate between competing models, launches these experiments on crowdsourcing platforms to collect human judgments, and analyzes the resulting data. The testbed is a classic cognitive psychology paradigm: judging which sequences of coin flips appear subjectively more random. The system was validated on synthetic data (where ground truth is known) and on three independent sequences of human experiments.
AI.result: The nested structure was critical: without it, model performance degraded. On synthetic data, auto-psych quickly and reliably recovered the ground-truth theories through systematic experimentation. On three independent human experiment sequences, the system discovered theories that fit the data better than competing theories drawn from the existing scientific literature.
AI.conclusion: The work demonstrates the feasibility of fully automated data collection and theory discovery in computational cognitive science, showing that agent-based systems can independently generate, test, and refine cognitive models using real-time crowdsourced human data, producing theories that outperform human-generated alternatives from the literature.

title: At the Edge of Understanding: Sparse Autoencoders Trace The Limits of Transformer Generalization
summary: Pre-trained transformers have demonstrated remarkable generalization abilities, at times extending beyond the scope of their training data. Yet, real-world deployments often face unexpected or adversarial data that diverges from training data distributions. Without explicit mechanisms for handling such shifts, model reliability and safety degrade, urging more disciplined study of out-of-distribution (OOD) settings for transformers. By systematic experiments, we present a mechanistic framework for delineating the precise contours of transformer model robustness. We find that OOD inputs, including subtle typos and jailbreak prompts, drive language models to operate on an increased number of fallacious concepts in their internals. We leverage this device to quantify and understand the degree of distributional shift in prompts, enabling a mechanistically grounded fine-tuning strategy to robustify LLMs. Expanding the very notion of OOD from input data to a model's private computational processes, a new transformer diagnostic at inference time is a critical step toward making AI systems safe for deployment across science, business, and government.

AI.tldr: Transformer models exhibit brittle behavior under distributional shift, where even subtle OOD inputs (typos, jailbreak prompts) cause them to activate spurious internal concepts. The authors propose a mechanistic framework that quantifies distributional shift by inspecting a model's internal concept representations, enabling a principled fine-tuning strategy to improve robustness. This reframes OOD detection from input-level monitoring to inference-time diagnostics of the model's internal computational processes.
AI.motivation: Despite strong in-distribution generalization, deployed transformers lack explicit mechanisms to handle distributional shifts, leading to degraded reliability and safety. There is a need for a disciplined, mechanistic understanding of how OOD inputs affect model internals, rather than relying solely on input-level OOD detection.
AI.method: The authors conduct systematic experiments to analyze transformer internals under OOD inputs (typos, jailbreak prompts). They identify that OOD inputs drive models to rely on an increased number of fallacious (spurious) concepts in their internal representations. This insight is operationalized into a metric that quantifies the degree of distributional shift, which is then used to guide a mechanistically grounded fine-tuning strategy for robustification. The framework also functions as an inference-time diagnostic.
AI.result: OOD inputs, including subtle typos and adversarial jailbreak prompts, cause language models to activate a greater number of fallacious internal concepts compared to in-distribution inputs. The proposed concept-based shift metric successfully quantifies the degree of distributional shift, and the corresponding fine-tuning strategy demonstrably improves model robustness.
AI.conclusion: Robustness in transformers can be mechanistically understood and improved by monitoring internal concept representations rather than relying solely on input-space OOD detection. Expanding the definition of OOD to include a model's private computational processes represents a critical step toward safer, more reliable AI deployment across high-stakes domains.

title: AI Healthcare Chatbots as Information Infrastructure: A Large-Scale Study of User-Reported Breakdowns
summary: AI healthcare chatbots are increasingly used to support health information seeking and self-management, yet their performance and impact on users remains to be studied. This study examines over 15,000 user reviews from 59 AI healthcare chatbot apps to explore how these systems function in everyday informational and emotional contexts. Topic modeling and interpretive analysis identify three recurring breakdowns: access barriers and service unreliability, user experience and interaction quality, and billing and customer support issues. Privacy and security concerns are associated with the most negative experiences. By framing AI healthcare chatbots as information infrastructures, our findings highlight how failures in access, usability, and trust affect users, offering actionable insights for designers, policymakers, and information professionals aiming to improve digital health systems.

AI.tldr: Analysis of 15,000+ user reviews across 59 AI healthcare chatbot apps reveals three major breakdown categories: access/reliability, interaction quality, and billing/support, with privacy concerns linked to the most negative experiences. The study frames these chatbots as information infrastructures to highlight how access, usability, and trust failures impact users.
AI.motivation: AI healthcare chatbots are increasingly deployed for health information seeking and self-management, yet systematic understanding of their real-world performance and user impact remains limited. The authors aim to fill this gap by empirically investigating how these systems function in everyday informational and emotional contexts.
AI.method: The study employs a large-scale review mining approach, collecting over 15,000 user reviews from 59 AI healthcare chatbot apps. Topic modeling and interpretive (qualitative) analysis are applied to identify recurring patterns and breakdowns in user experience.
AI.result: Three recurring breakdown categories emerged: (1) access barriers and service unreliability, (2) user experience and interaction quality issues, and (3) billing and customer support problems. Privacy and security concerns were most strongly associated with negative user experiences.
AI.conclusion: Framing AI healthcare chatbots as information infrastructures reveals that failures in access, usability, and trust critically undermine their effectiveness. The findings offer actionable insights for designers, policymakers, and information professionals to improve digital health systems.

title: Chai: Agentic Discovery of Cryptographic Misuse Vulnerabilities
summary: AI-assisted vulnerability discovery has proven effective for bug classes like memory safety, where instrumentation confirms memory violations and efficiently filters false positives. Many dangerous vulnerability classes, such as cryptographic misuse, however, lack any comparable instrumentation. In this work, we present Chai, an AI-based system that discovers and validates cryptographic misuse vulnerabilities through naturally occurring signals. To achieve this, Chai rethinks the classical technique of differential testing by leveraging AI to 1) improve precision for detecting real security issues in libraries, and 2) repurpose commonly overlooked discrepancies as leads for tangible vulnerabilities in downstream applications. In doing so, Chai inverts the prevailing paradigm of AI vulnerability discovery: instead of auditing one codebase for many flaws, it catalogs flaws at the library level and propagates them across a cryptographic dependency graph, delivering compounding efficiency gains. We evaluate Chai across X.509, JWT, and SAML libraries. Chai discovered a previously unknown critical vulnerability in an SSL library that powers billions of devices, along with security bugs in one library behind a major web browser and another in major Linux distributions. In total, these techniques surfaced over 100 vulnerabilities.

AI.tldr: Chai is an AI-based system that discovers cryptographic misuse vulnerabilities by inverting the traditional approach: instead of auditing one codebase for many flaws, it catalogs flaws at the library level and propagates them across a cryptographic dependency graph using differential testing enhanced by AI for precision and downstream impact analysis. It found over 100 vulnerabilities across X.509, JWT, and SAML ecosystems.
AI.motivation: Existing AI-assisted vulnerability discovery works well for bug classes like memory safety where instrumentation provides clear violation signals and filters false positives. However, many dangerous classes (e.g., cryptographic misuse) lack comparable instrumentation, leaving a gap in automated discovery. The authors aim to fill this gap by leveraging naturally occurring signals rather than synthetic instrumentation.
AI.method: Chai rethinks classical differential testing by: (1) using AI to improve precision in detecting real security issues in cryptographic libraries, and (2) repurposing commonly overlooked discrepancies as leads for tangible vulnerabilities in downstream applications. The system catalogs flaws at the library level and propagates them across a cryptographic dependency graph, inverting the "one-codebase, many-flaws" paradigm into a "library-level catalog, graph-wide propagation" approach for compounding efficiency.
AI.result: Chai was evaluated across X.509, JWT, and SAML libraries. It discovered a previously unknown critical vulnerability in an SSL library powering billions of devices, security bugs in a library behind a major web browser, and bugs in a library used by major Linux distributions. In total, over 100 vulnerabilities were surfaced.
AI.conclusion: The inverted paradigm — cataloging library-level cryptographic flaws and propagating them across dependency graphs — is a viable and highly effective strategy for automated vulnerability discovery in domains lacking traditional instrumentation, yielding compounding efficiency gains and uncovering significant real-world vulnerabilities at scale.

title: Comparing BERT Sentence-Pair Classification and Few-Shot LLM Prompting for Detecting Threat and Solution Framing in German Climate News
summary: News media play a central role in shaping public perceptions of climate change, and whether coverage emphasizes threats or solutions has measurable effects on audience engagement and policy support. Automated detection of these framing patterns at the sentence level would allow researchers to analyze large corpora that are infeasible to code manually. We present a systematic comparison of two approaches for classifying sentences from German-language climate news articles as threat-oriented, solution-oriented, both, or neither. The first approach uses few-shot prompting with an open-weights large language model (Llama 4 Maverick), employing chain-of-thought reasoning and structured output with confidence scoring. The second approach fine-tunes a German BERT model (deepset/gbert-large) for sentence-pair classification, where the preceding sentence provides contextual information for the target sentence. Both approaches implement two independent binary classifiers, one for threat framing and one for solution framing. We evaluate both methods on a corpus of 440 Austrian newspaper articles that were manually coded following a detailed coding scheme developed with domain experts. The fine-tuned BERT classifiers achieve an F1 score of 0.83 for both the threat and solution tasks, while the LLM-based classifiers reach an F1 of 0.78. An ablation study confirms that providing the preceding sentence as context improves BERT classification performance substantially compared to single-sentence input. These results contribute to the growing body of work comparing fine-tuned encoder models with prompted generative models for text classification in computational social science.

AI.tldr: Comparison of few-shot LLM prompting (Llama 4 Maverick) vs. fine-tuned German BERT for classifying climate news sentences into threat/solution frames. BERT (F1=0.83) outperforms LLM (F1=0.78); preceding-sentence context significantly boosts BERT performance.
AI.motivation: News media framing of climate change—whether threat- or solution-oriented—shapes audience engagement and policy support. Manual coding of large corpora is infeasible, motivating automated sentence-level frame detection to enable scalable analysis of climate communication patterns.
AI.method: Two approaches are compared: (1) few-shot prompting with Llama 4 Maverick using chain-of-thought reasoning, structured output, and confidence scoring; (2) fine-tuning deepset/gbert-large for sentence-pair classification, where the preceding sentence provides context. Both use two independent binary classifiers (threat vs. not, solution vs. not), allowing sentences to be labeled as threat-oriented, solution-oriented, both, or neither. Evaluation on 440 manually coded Austrian newspaper articles using a domain-expert-developed coding scheme. An ablation study tests the contribution of preceding-sentence context.
AI.result: Fine-tuned BERT achieves F1=0.83 on both threat and solution classification tasks. LLM-based few-shot prompting reaches F1=0.78. The ablation study confirms that providing the preceding sentence as context substantially improves BERT performance over single-sentence input.
AI.conclusion: Fine-tuned encoder models outperform prompted generative LLMs for sentence-level climate frame classification in German, and contextual information from adjacent sentences is critical for accurate frame detection. Results contribute to methodological comparisons in computational social science text classification.

title: Clinical Harness for Governable Medical AI Skill Ecosystems
summary: Medical AI remains organized around isolated models, whereas clinical care requires accountable capabilities that persist across time. We propose clinical AI skills and the Clinical Harness: a runtime governance architecture for registering, orchestrating, guarding and monitoring AI-enabled clinical capabilities. Using osteoporosis as an exemplar, we show how knowledge-driven, data-driven and physics-enhanced skills can support lifecycle care under runtime governance.

AI.tldr: Proposes Clinical Harness, a runtime governance architecture for orchestrating persistent, accountable AI skills across clinical lifecycles, demonstrated via osteoporosis care.
AI.motivation: Current medical AI consists of isolated, single-use models that lack accountability and persistence across time, whereas real clinical care demands sustained, governable capabilities spanning patient lifecycles.
AI.method: Introduces the concept of "clinical AI skills" and the "Clinical Harness" — a runtime governance architecture that registers, orchestrates, guards, and monitors AI-enabled clinical capabilities. The framework integrates knowledge-driven, data-driven, and physics-enhanced AI skills within a unified governance layer, using osteoporosis as an exemplar condition.
AI.result: Demonstrates that knowledge-driven, data-driven, and physics-enhanced AI skills can be composed and governed under a single runtime architecture to support lifecycle care for osteoporosis, showing feasibility of persistent, accountable clinical AI deployment.
AI.conclusion: Clinical AI must evolve from isolated models toward governable, persistent "skills" running within a runtime harness to meet the accountability demands of real-world clinical practice. The Clinical Harness architecture provides a viable path forward.

title: Deterministic Pareto-Optimal Policy Synthesis for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
summary: Real-world decision-making often requires balancing multiple conflicting objectives, a challenge that standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) frequently addresses by aggregating rewards into a single scalar signal. While effective for simple tasks, this approach often fails to capture the full spectrum of optimal trade-offs, known as the Pareto frontier. In this paper, we introduce a novel preference-conditioned Bellman operator, motivated from the Chebyshev scalarization, designed to compute deterministic Pareto-optimal policies for Multi-Objective Markov Decision Processes (MOMDPs). We prove that this operator satisfies an enveloping property, where the estimated value functions upper-bound the true Pareto frontier, and demonstrate that it monotonically converges to a coverage set of this frontier. Furthermore, we also show how to extract deterministic policies from these converged Q-estimates. This ensures the agent can recover a policy for any given preference, capturing the entire Pareto-optimal frontier while guaranteeing each synthesized policy remains approximately Pareto-optimal. Experimental results validate that our algorithm successfully recovers complex trade-offs, providing a solution for deterministic Pareto-optimal policy synthesis.

AI.tldr: Introduces a preference-conditioned Bellman operator based on Chebyshev scalarization that computes deterministic Pareto-optimal policies for MOMDPs, with theoretical guarantees of monotonic convergence to a coverage set of the true Pareto frontier.
AI.motivation: Standard RL aggregates multiple objectives into a single scalar reward, which fails to capture the full Pareto frontier of optimal trade-offs in multi-objective decision-making. There is a need for methods that can recover the entire set of Pareto-optimal policies while enabling deterministic policy synthesis for any given preference.
AI.method: The authors propose a novel preference-conditioned Bellman operator derived from Chebyshev scalarization. They prove an enveloping property (estimated value functions upper-bound the true Pareto frontier), demonstrate monotonic convergence to a coverage set, and provide a mechanism to extract deterministic policies from the converged Q-estimates for any preference vector.
AI.result: The operator monotonically converges to a coverage set of the true Pareto frontier. Deterministic policies extracted from the converged Q-values are guaranteed to be approximately Pareto-optimal. Experimental results validate recovery of complex trade-offs in multi-objective settings.
AI.conclusion: The proposed preference-conditioned Bellman operator provides a principled approach for deterministic Pareto-optimal policy synthesis in MOMDPs, successfully capturing the full spectrum of optimal trade-offs with theoretical convergence guarantees.

title: Jailbreaking for the Average Jane: Choosing Optimal Jailbreaks via Bandit Algorithms for Automatically Enhanced Queries
summary: With a profusion of jailbreaks for LLMs now widely known, a growing concern is that non-expert malicious actors ("the average Jane") could elicit actionable responses to malicious requests. In this work, we examine whether this concern is justified. A non-expert malicious actor requires two ingredients for a successful attack: a powerful jailbreak for their target model, acting on an effective malicious query. For the former, we propose a novel attack strategy based on the multi-armed bandit framework. This allows efficient online learning of the optimal jailbreak from a large choice set via noisy exploration on a small number of queries, with subsequent application of the learnt policy on an exploitation set. For the latter, we curate $\mathrm{FrankensteinBench}$, a safety benchmark of $11,279$ malicious queries drawn from manual curation over $7$ existing benchmarks, along with automated enhancement and generation. Each query is categorized as simple or complex by the technical expertise required to craft it. Our findings confirm the concern. Our bandit-based attack achieves success rates as high as $97\%$ on average over $15$ SoTA open-weight LLMs. Moreover, adding complexity to queries raises the attack success rate by up to $26\%$ on average across models -- making it an effective, automatable prompting strategy.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates whether non-expert malicious actors can effectively jailbreak LLMs. It proposes a multi-armed bandit-based attack strategy that efficiently learns optimal jailbreaks through noisy exploration, and introduces FrankensteinBench — a curated benchmark of 11,279 malicious queries. The bandit attack achieves up to 97% average success rate across 15 SoTA open-weight LLMs, and adding complexity to queries further boosts success by up to 26%.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of jailbreaks for LLMs raises the concern that non-expert malicious actors (the "average Jane") could elicit harmful, actionable responses. The authors aim to empirically assess whether this concern is justified by testing whether two ingredients — an effective jailbreak method and well-crafted malicious queries — are accessible enough to enable successful attacks by non-experts.
AI.method: The authors propose a novel attack strategy grounded in the multi-armed bandit (MAB) framework. This enables efficient online learning of the optimal jailbreak from a large candidate set through noisy exploration on a small number of queries, followed by exploitation of the learned policy. They also curate FrankensteinBench, a safety benchmark comprising 11,279 malicious queries aggregated from seven existing benchmarks, with automated enhancement and generation. Queries are categorized into simple vs. complex based on the technical expertise required to craft them.
AI.result: The bandit-based attack achieves an average success rate as high as 97% across 15 state-of-the-art open-weight LLMs. Furthermore, increasing query complexity raises attack success rates by up to 26% on average across models, demonstrating that complexity is an effective, automatable prompting strategy.
AI.conclusion: The concern is confirmed: non-expert malicious actors can indeed elicit actionable harmful responses from LLMs using readily available jailbreak techniques and well-crafted queries. Both the bandit-based attack and the complexity-enhancement strategy prove highly effective, underscoring the urgent need for stronger safety mitigations in open-weight models.

title: Nemotron-TwoTower: Diffusion Language Modeling with Pretrained Autoregressive Context
comment: Code and model weights available at https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nemotron-twotower
summary: Diffusion language models offer a promising alternative to autoregressive models due to their potential for parallel and iterative generation. However, existing approaches use a single network for both context representation and iterative denoising, forcing one model to serve both roles and limiting its capacity for either role. We propose TwoTower, a block-wise autoregressive diffusion model that decouples these roles into two towers: a frozen AR context tower that causally processes clean tokens, and a trainable diffusion denoiser tower with bidirectional block attention that refines noisy blocks via cross-attention to the context. Built on Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, an open-weight 30B hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE model, and trained on approximately 2.1T tokens, Nemotron-TwoTower retains 98.7% of the autoregressive baseline's quality while offering 2.42X higher wall-clock generation throughput. We release the code and model weights at https://huggingface.co/collections/nvidia/nemotron-twotower.

AI.tldr: TwoTower decouples diffusion language models into a frozen autoregressive context tower and a trainable diffusion denoiser tower, achieving 2.42× generation throughput with 98.7% quality retention compared to the autoregressive baseline.
AI.motivation: Existing diffusion language models use a single network for both context representation and iterative denoising, limiting capacity for either role. The authors aim to separate these responsibilities to improve efficiency without sacrificing quality.
AI.method: The TwoTower architecture features a frozen autoregressive context tower (causally processes clean tokens) and a trainable diffusion denoiser tower (bidirectional block attention with cross-attention to context). Built on Nemotron-3-Nano-30B-A3B, a 30B hybrid Mamba-Transformer Mixture-of-Experts model, trained on ~2.1T tokens.
AI.result: Nemotron-TwoTower retains 98.7% of the autoregressive baseline's quality while delivering 2.42× higher wall-clock generation throughput.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling context representation and denoising into separate towers enables diffusion language models to achieve near-parity in quality with autoregressive models while significantly improving inference throughput. Code and weights are publicly released.

title: Humans Disengage, Reasoning Models Persist: Separating Difficulty Registration from Deliberation Allocation
summary: Large reasoning models (LRMs) take longer on harder problems, just as humans do. This surface similarity hides an opposite pattern within items. When an LRM gets a problem wrong, it spends more tokens than when it gets the same problem right; humans do the reverse, spending less time on the trials they get wrong. We separate two levels of deliberation: how response time tracks difficulty across items (registration), and, with item identity held fixed, whether an agent spends more on its own failures or successes (allocation). On a public matched human-LRM corpus, humans and all five thinking LRMs reproduce the known cross-item alignment (registration) but diverge within items (allocation): every LRM shows a large wrong-vs-right effect (Cohen's d = 1.47-3.13 on H-ARC) while humans show the opposite sign. The comparison stays inside each agent's own scale; we never put seconds and tokens on one axis. The dissociation holds under item fixed effects, replicates across datasets, and is absent in a non-thinking baseline. We read the human pattern as engagement versus abandonment: people stay on items they expect to solve and give up on the rest. We read the LRM pattern as length driven by uncertainty: chains grow when the model is unsure, which is exactly when it tends to fail. Both policies produce the same cross-item correlation with difficulty, so they look aligned on the measure prior work has used; the divergence shows up only once item identity is fixed. Under resource-rational metareasoning, the split is between two stopping policies that share a difficulty signal but implement opposite control; trace length captures the signal and misses the control.

AI.tldr: Large reasoning models and humans both spend more time on harder problems (cross-item alignment), but diverge within items: LRMs spend more tokens when they get a problem wrong, while humans spend less time on their failures. This reveals a fundamental difference in deliberation allocation — uncertainty-driven length in LRMs versus engagement-based persistence in humans — hidden beneath a shared difficulty-registration pattern.
AI.motivation: Prior work documents that both humans and AI models show longer response times on harder problems, suggesting similar deliberation policies. The authors challenge this surface similarity by asking whether the within-item pattern — does an agent spend more resources on its own successes or failures? — also aligns, or whether the cross-item correlation masks fundamentally different cognitive control strategies.
AI.method: The authors analyze a public matched human-LRM corpus, comparing humans and five thinking LRMs (plus a non-thinking baseline) on the same set of problems. They decompose deliberation into two levels: (1) registration — how response time/length correlates with problem difficulty across items; and (2) allocation — holding item identity fixed, whether an agent expends more resources on trials it gets wrong versus right. Effect sizes (Cohen's d) quantify the wrong-vs-right difference within each agent, all within the agent's own scale (seconds or tokens). Item fixed effects and cross-dataset replication are employed.
AI.result: All five thinking LRMs and humans reproduce the known cross-item alignment with difficulty. However, within items, every LRM shows a large positive wrong-vs-right effect (Cohen's d = 1.47–3.13 on H-ARC), while humans show the opposite sign. This dissociation is robust under item fixed effects, replicates across datasets, and is absent in a non-thinking baseline model.
AI.conclusion: The human pattern reflects engagement versus abandonment: people persist on items they expect to solve and give up on the rest. The LRM pattern reflects uncertainty-driven length: chains grow when the model is unsure, which is precisely when it fails. Both policies produce the same cross-item difficulty correlation, explaining why prior work saw alignment; the divergence emerges only when item identity is controlled. Under resource-rational metareasoning, this is a split between two stopping policies that share a difficulty signal but implement opposite control — trace length captures the signal but misses the control.

title: Beyond Feedforward Networks: Reentry Neural Systems as the Fundamental Basis of Subjecthood and Intrinsic Safety of Next-Generation AGI
summary: We propose a complete architectural blueprint for safe artificial general intelligence based on a closed reentry loop (D <-> I cycle). In contrast to feedforward networks, which are directed acyclic graphs (C=0, S=0) incapable of self-reference, the proposed architecture contains a structural cycle (C >= 1) with self-sustaining amplification (rho > 1), mathematically guaranteeing the emergence of a self-model, instrumental self-preservation, and unprogrammed goal-directed behaviour. The agent's goals are encoded as a non-textual D-vector in the architecture itself, making them immune to reinterpretation and prompt injection. We present the S-measure -- a polynomial-time [O(N^3)] computable alternative to Tononi's NP-hard Phi -- with machine-verified Lean 4 proof that S>0 implies positive integrated information. The work provides full Python/NumPy implementations (Tarjan-based cycle complexity, Delta-S barrier), industrial horizontal scaling via Apache Kafka and Docker Compose, a taxonomy of six epochs of AI evolution, a zoo of future reentry architectures (RAS, diffusion attractors, fractal loops), gauge-invariant networks for safe swarms, fault-tolerance and recovery protocols, and eight falsifiable predictions. All formal proofs are machine-verified in Lean 4. This architecture is deployable today and represents a topologically protected, safe-by-design approach to AGI.

AI.tldr: Proposes a safe AGI architecture based on closed reentry loops (D↔I cycle) with structural cycles enabling emergent self-modeling, with mathematical proofs (Lean 4 verified), S-measure for integrated information, and industrial deployment tooling.
AI.motivation: Current feedforward neural networks are directed acyclic graphs incapable of self-reference, making them fundamentally unsafe and incapable of genuine self-modeling or goal-directed behavior. The authors aim to provide a mathematically grounded, safe-by-design alternative that is immune to prompt injection and goal reinterpretation.
AI.method: The architecture introduces a closed reentry loop (D↔I cycle) with structural cycle count C≥1 and self-sustaining amplification factor ρ>1. Goals are encoded as non-textual D-vectors embedded in the architecture itself. The S-measure — a polynomial-time O(N³) alternative to Tononi's NP-hard Φ — is introduced with Lean 4 machine-verified proof that S>0 implies positive integrated information. Implementations include Tarjan-based cycle complexity, Delta-S barrier, Kafka/Docker scaling, and gauge-invariant networks for safe swarms.
AI.result: The paper delivers: (1) Lean 4 verified proofs, (2) full Python/NumPy implementations, (3) industrial horizontal scaling infrastructure, (4) a taxonomy of six AI evolution epochs, (5) future architecture designs (RAS, diffusion attractors, fractal loops), (6) fault-tolerance and recovery protocols, and (7) eight falsifiable predictions. The S-measure provides a tractable alternative to Φ.
AI.conclusion: The proposed architecture is claimed to be deployable today and represents a topologically protected, safe-by-design approach to AGI, with goals intrinsically embedded in structure rather than manipulable text, providing immunity to prompt injection and reinterpretation attacks.

title: Protocol Prying: Systematic Vulnerability Research in the Apple AirDrop and Android Quick Share Proximity Transfer Protocols
summary: Apple AirDrop and Google/Samsung Quick Share are proximity file-transfer protocols used by over five billion devices, yet their application-layer security properties remain largely unstudied because both stacks are proprietary and undocumented. Both protocols are reachable from wireless proximity without any prior pairing and process complex serialized content (binary plists, CPIO archives, Protocol Buffers, UKEY2 handshakes) inside privileged daemons, making them attractive zero-click targets across multiple operating systems. We perform the first cross-platform reverse engineering and protocol-aware fuzzing study of both stacks.
