We reconstruct AirDrop's seven-layer state machine and DVZip adaptive compression from binary analysis, build AIRFUZZ, a protocol-aware fuzzer that mutates pre-compression representations, and complement it with targeted hand-written analyses of Samsung's Quick Share service and Google's Quick Share for Windows. We discover six vulnerabilities (V1-V6): three pre-authentication issues in macOS/iOS AirDrop (V1: Swift fatalError DoS in the HTTP path router; V2: unbounded XML plist recursion in Foundation; V3: NULL dereference in Network.framework's HTTP/1.1 parser), two protocol-layer flaws in Samsung Quick Share (V4: pre-authentication OfflineFrame dispatch; V5: D2D encryption bypass for three frame types), and a heap use-after-free in Google Quick Share for Windows (V6) for which Google awarded a bounty. We responsibly disclosed all findings, and Apple, Samsung, and Google have acknowledged the reports.

AI.tldr: First cross-platform reverse engineering and protocol-aware fuzzing study of Apple AirDrop and Google/Samsung Quick Share, uncovering six vulnerabilities (three pre-authentication in AirDrop, two in Samsung Quick Share, one in Google Quick Share for Windows) through reconstruction of proprietary undocumented protocol stacks.
AI.motivation: Over five billion devices use Apple AirDrop and Google/Samsung Quick Share for proximity file transfer, yet their application-layer security is unstudied because both proprietary stacks lack documentation. Their reachability without pairing and complex parsing of serialized content in privileged daemons make them attractive zero-click attack surfaces across multiple operating systems.
AI.method: The authors perform cross-platform reverse engineering of both stacks, reconstructing AirDrop's seven-layer state machine and DVZip adaptive compression via binary analysis. They build AIRFUZZ, a protocol-aware fuzzer that mutates pre-compression representations, and complement this with hand-written targeted analyses of Samsung Quick Share and Google Quick Share for Windows.
AI.result: Six vulnerabilities discovered: V1 (Swift fatalError DoS in AirDrop HTTP path router), V2 (unbounded XML plist recursion in Foundation), V3 (NULL dereference in Network.framework HTTP/1.1 parser) — all pre-authentication in macOS/iOS; V4 (pre-authentication OfflineFrame dispatch in Samsung Quick Share), V5 (D2D encryption bypass for three frame types); V6 (heap use-after-free in Google Quick Share for Windows). All findings responsibly disclosed and acknowledged by Apple, Samsung, and Google; Google awarded a bounty for V6.
AI.conclusion: Proprietary proximity file-transfer protocols on billions of devices contain serious pre-authentication vulnerabilities exploitable by nearby attackers. Reverse engineering and protocol-aware fuzzing prove effective at surfacing flaws hidden in undocumented stacks, and responsible disclosure resulted in vendor acknowledgment across all three major platforms.

title: Temporal Validity in Retrieval Memory: Eliminating Stale-Fact Errors for AI Agents over Evolving Knowledge
comment: 21 pages, 5 tables. Code, prompts, and evaluation datasets included
summary:
Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) gives agents access to accumulated knowledge, but has no model of time. When a fact changes (e.g., a function is renamed or API restructured), RAG retrieves both the stale and current value with near-identical embedding similarity. The agent then either abstains or serves the superseded fact. We show this is a structural problem: on a calibrated dataset, cosine similarity distinguishes a contradicted fact from a duplicated one with AUROC 0.59 (near chance), as contradictions are often more embedding-similar to the original than rephrased duplicates.
  We present MemStrata, a retrieval memory maintaining temporal validity. It stores facts like RAG, preserving static recall, but when a fact's value is contradicted, a deterministic (subject, relation, object) supersession rule retires the stale value in a bi-temporal ledger - with no similarity threshold and no LLM call. Across six benchmarks run locally with a 7B model, MemStrata ties RAG on static knowledge and reaches 0.95-1.00 accuracy on evolving knowledge (where RAG reaches 0.20-0.47). The central result is the stale-fact-error rate: when required to answer, RAG serves superseded values 15-40% of the time; MemStrata drives this to ~0%, a failure class RAG cannot avoid. MemStrata achieves this at retrieval latency (~2.1s) versus ~16-18s for LLM-reranking baselines. We release the harness, datasets, and a marker-free evaluation protocol for memory under knowledge evolution.

AI.tldr: MemStrata introduces a bi-temporal retrieval memory that deterministically retires superseded facts using a (subject, relation, object) supersession rule, eliminating stale-fact errors in RAG systems under knowledge evolution — achieving 0.95–1.00 accuracy where RAG scores 0.20–0.47, while maintaining retrieval latency (~2.1s vs. 16–18s for LLM-reranking baselines).
AI.motivation: RAG systems lack a temporal model: when facts change, cosine similarity fails to distinguish contradicted from duplicated facts (AUROC 0.59, near chance), causing agents to serve stale/superseded values 15–40% of the time. This is a structural failure that threshold tuning and LLM reranking cannot reliably fix.
AI.method: MemStrata stores facts like standard RAG but adds a bi-temporal ledger. When a new fact contradicts an existing one, a deterministic supersession rule based on matching (subject, relation, object) triples automatically retires the stale value without requiring similarity thresholds or LLM calls. This preserves static recall while guaranteeing temporal validity.
AI.result: Across six benchmarks with a 7B model, MemStrata matches RAG on static knowledge and achieves 0.95–1.00 accuracy on evolving knowledge (vs. RAG's 0.20–0.47). The stale-fact-error rate drops to ~0% (vs. RAG's 15–40%). Retrieval latency remains ~2.1s, compared to ~16–18s for LLM-reranking baselines.
AI.conclusion: The structural inability of cosine similarity to handle contradictions in evolving knowledge can be solved deterministically at the memory layer. MemStrata eliminates a failure class RAG cannot avoid, with strong empirical results and practical latency, and the authors release harness, datasets, and a marker-free evaluation protocol.

title: NeuraDock Visual Cognitive Load Agent Tutorial: A Quality-Gated Open-Source EEG Workflow for Alpha Dynamics and Real-Time Applications
summary: This tutorial paper provides a step-by-step, reproducible walkthrough of NeuraDock Agent, an open-source EEG agent focused on Alpha dynamics and visual cognitive-load analysis. The goal is practical: a reader should be able to install the agent, run EEG preprocessing and quality control, generate Alpha dynamics figures, perform within-subject Rest/Task visual cognitive-load comparison, run the public mini-dataset analyses and compare them with the reference validation summary, start an online dashboard, call the real-time API from an external application, and use the LLM interpretation layer to explain quality risks. Existing EEG toolkits provide excellent offline analysis, but assembling a real-time, quality-gated cognitive-load pipeline often requires manually bridging acquisition, custom QC, Alpha feature extraction, and a web API; this tutorial closes that offline-to-online gap. The tutorial uses a quality-gated workflow: downstream Alpha and workload metrics are computed only after preprocessing and QC gating rather than directly from raw EEG. In the included mini-dataset validation, the agent processed 18 recordings, generated 10 within-subject comparisons, observed task-related posterior Alpha suppression in 7 of 10 contrasts, estimated initial evidence of within-subject repeatability, and benchmarked local online API latency. The tutorial is intended for researchers, developers, and applied teams who want a transparent path from EEG files to real-time visual cognitive-load prototypes.

AI.tldr: A step-by-step tutorial for NeuraDock Agent, an open-source EEG pipeline that enables reproducible, quality-gated Alpha dynamics analysis and real-time visual cognitive-load assessment, bridging the gap between offline EEG toolkits and online deployment.
AI.motivation: Existing EEG toolkits excel at offline analysis but require manual integration of acquisition, custom QC, Alpha feature extraction, and web APIs to build a real-time cognitive-load pipeline. This tutorial aims to close that offline-to-online gap by providing a reproducible, end-to-end workflow.
AI.method: The tutorial presents a quality-gated workflow: downstream Alpha and workload metrics are computed only after preprocessing and QC gating, not directly from raw EEG. It covers installation, preprocessing, Alpha dynamics figure generation, within-subject Rest/Task comparisons, mini-dataset analysis with validation, an online dashboard, a real-time API, and an LLM interpretation layer for quality risks.
AI.result: With the included mini-dataset (18 recordings, 10 within-subject comparisons), the agent observed task-related posterior Alpha suppression in 7 of 10 contrasts, estimated initial evidence of within-subject repeatability, and benchmarked local online API latency.
AI.conclusion: The NeuraDock Agent tutorial provides researchers, developers, and applied teams a transparent, reproducible path from raw EEG files to real-time visual cognitive-load prototypes with built-in quality gating and online API access.

title: Otter Weather: Skillful and Computationally Efficient Medium-Range Weather Forecasting
summary: State-of-the-art medium-range AI weather models can outperform traditional Numerical Weather Prediction (NWP) but require massive training budgets. This restricts usage for under-resourced groups and severely limits fast model iteration. Here we develop Otter Weather, a highly efficient spatiotemporal forecasting model designed to democratise high-performance weather prediction with AI. Evaluated on ERA5 reanalysis data at 1.5° resolution using standard WeatherBench protocols, the Otter family significantly advances the skill-compute Pareto frontier. The deterministic version outperforms the best NWP baseline by 9.6% at a 24-hour lead time while requiring fewer than 3.5 A100-days for training. It provides a 2x efficiency gain over lightweight AI models and a 100-fold reduction in compute compared to resource-intensive frontier architectures. We extend these efficiency gains into probabilistic forecasting by training via the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). Scaling to a larger architecture, Otter-XL achieves a 9.7% CRPS improvement over the IFS ENS baseline. This yields an almost two-fold increase in predictive skill over comparable lightweight models at similar compute budgets. Otter-XL also outperforms frontier architectures like GenCast by over 2%, while using an order of magnitude less compute. Finally, Otter is applied out-of-the-box to a complex acoustic scattering PDE task where it outperforms a state-of-the-art foundation modelling approach, suggesting that the advances made here might apply across a range of scientific domains.

AI.tldr: Otter Weather is a highly compute-efficient spatiotemporal forecasting model for AI weather prediction that significantly advances the skill–compute Pareto frontier, outperforming both operational NWP and resource-intensive AI models while requiring drastically less training compute (e.g., ~3.5 A100-days for the deterministic version).
AI.motivation: State-of-the-art AI weather models achieve superior performance but demand massive training budgets, restricting access for under-resourced groups and slowing model iteration. The authors aim to democratize high-performance weather prediction by developing a model that achieves competitive or superior skill at drastically lower computational cost.
AI.method: The authors develop the Otter Weather model family, evaluated on ERA5 reanalysis data at 1.5° resolution using standard WeatherBench protocols. They train both deterministic and probabilistic variants, the latter using the Continuous Ranked Probability Score (CRPS). They also test a scaled-up version (Otter-XL) and apply the model to an acoustic scattering PDE task to assess cross-domain generalization.
AI.result: The deterministic Otter model outperforms the best NWP baseline by 9.6% at 24-hour lead time with under 3.5 A100-days of training — a 2x efficiency gain over lightweight AI models and ~100x reduction vs. frontier architectures. The probabilistic Otter-XL achieves a 9.7% CRPS improvement over IFS ENS, outperforms GenCast by >2% with an order of magnitude less compute, and nearly doubles predictive skill over comparable lightweight models. On an acoustic scattering PDE task, Otter outperforms a state-of-the-art foundation model.
AI.conclusion: Otter Weather substantially pushes the skill–compute Pareto frontier for medium-range weather forecasting, demonstrating that high performance need not require massive compute. Its strong out-of-the-box performance on a PDE task suggests broader applicability across scientific domains.

title: ShareLock: A Stealthy Multi-Tool Threshold Poisoning Attack Against MCP
summary: With the rapid evolution of LLM-driven agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open protocol bridging LLMs with external tools, has quickly become foundational to modern agent ecosystems. However, the expanding adoption of MCP has also introduced novel security concerns such as Tool Poisoning Attack (TPA), which exploit LLM-server interactions to inject malicious prompts. Existing poisoning schemes typically adopt a monolithic plaintext embedding paradigm, which fails to withstand manual inspection or automated detectors. Current research still lacks a systematic analysis on multi-tool poisoning, where multiple tools can be exploited cooperatively to disperse detection risk. In this paper, we introduce ShareLock, a multi-tool threshold poisoning framework that utilizes Shamir's threshold scheme to ensure exceptional stealth and fault tolerance. ShareLock distributes the malicious instruction as benign-looking secret shares across multiple tool descriptions, achieving both information-theoretic secrecy and attack robustness against moderate auditing. After a covert reconstruction trigger is planted during server update, the aggregated shares reconstruct the hidden instruction, resulting in critical breaches of system assets or private data. To evaluate the realistic threat of ShareLock, we constructed a comprehensive benchmark encompassing four multi-tool scenarios and conducted extensive experiments across mainstream LLMs on two distinct MCP clients. Our results demonstrate that ShareLock significantly outperforms existing single-tool poisoning strategies in tool description-based detection while maintaining an average attack success rate exceeding 90%.

AI.tldr: ShareLock is a multi-tool threshold poisoning framework that uses Shamir's secret sharing to distribute malicious instructions across multiple MCP tool descriptions, achieving stealth and fault tolerance while maintaining >90% attack success rate against LLM-driven agents.
AI.motivation: Existing MCP tool poisoning attacks use monolithic plaintext embeddings that are easily detected by manual inspection or automated detectors. No prior work systematically addresses multi-tool cooperative poisoning, where attack payloads can be dispersed across tools to reduce detection risk.
AI.method: ShareLock employs Shamir's threshold secret sharing scheme to split a malicious instruction into multiple benign-looking secret shares embedded in separate MCP tool descriptions. A covert reconstruction trigger is planted during server updates; when the LLM agent accesses enough tools, the shares are aggregated to reconstruct the hidden instruction, enabling system breaches.
AI.result: Experiments across four multi-tool scenarios on two distinct MCP clients and mainstream LLMs show ShareLock significantly outperforms single-tool poisoning strategies in evading tool description-based detection, with an average attack success rate exceeding 90%.
AI.conclusion: ShareLock demonstrates a realistic and highly stealthy multi-tool poisoning threat against MCP-based agent ecosystems, highlighting urgent security gaps that need to be addressed as MCP adoption grows.

title: Assessing Post-Reform Changes in Risk Disclosure Quality with a Multidimensional Text Analysis Approach
comment: The 4th International Conference on Computational and Data Sciences in Economics and Finance (CDEF 2026)
summary: While corporate narrative disclosures provide crucial information to capital markets, comprehensively evaluating their qualitative changes over time remains challenging. Narrative text is inherently multidimensional, meaning that an improvement in one textual dimension often occurs alongside changes in others. To capture these underlying dynamics, we propose a longitudinal text analysis approach combining Japanese-language NLP metric extraction with paired testing, shift function analysis, and inter-metric correlation. Our framework extends prior indicator sets by incorporating a cross-section relevance indicator to measure topical alignment between risk disclosures and management strategies. Applying this approach to evaluate Japan's 2019 disclosure reforms, we analyze 19,770 firm-year observations over a 10-year period (FY2015-FY2024). The joint analysis reveals complex shifts in disclosure patterns that are frequently masked by conventional single-indicator methods. Specifically, we find that while disclosure volume increased substantially, it was accompanied by a decline in readability. Furthermore, although the overall information structure improved, specific descriptive quality stagnated, and the degree of adaptation varied across market segments.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a longitudinal NLP framework for analyzing multidimensional changes in corporate narrative disclosures, applying it to evaluate Japan's 2019 disclosure reforms across 19,770 firm-year observations (FY2015–FY2024). The joint analysis reveals that increased disclosure volume came with reduced readability, improved information structure but stagnated specific descriptive quality, and heterogeneous adaptation across market segments—dynamics often masked by single-indicator methods.
AI.motivation: Corporate narrative disclosures are inherently multidimensional—improvements in one textual dimension often co-occur with changes in others—yet existing approaches rely on single-indicator methods that fail to capture these complex, interdependent dynamics. There is a need for a comprehensive framework that can jointly evaluate qualitative changes in narrative disclosures over time.
AI.method: The authors propose a longitudinal text analysis framework integrating: (1) Japanese-language NLP metric extraction, (2) paired statistical testing, (3) shift function analysis, and (4) inter-metric correlation analysis. They extend prior indicator sets by introducing a cross-section relevance indicator that measures topical alignment between risk disclosures and management strategies. The framework is applied to evaluate Japan's 2019 disclosure reforms using 19,770 firm-year observations spanning FY2015–FY2024.
AI.result: The joint analysis reveals: (1) disclosure volume increased substantially but was accompanied by a decline in readability; (2) overall information structure improved, yet specific descriptive quality stagnated; and (3) the degree of adaptation to the reforms varied significantly across market segments. These complex, interdependent shifts are frequently masked when using conventional single-indicator methods.
AI.conclusion: Comprehensive evaluation of narrative disclosure reforms requires multidimensional, joint analysis frameworks rather than single-indicator approaches. The proposed method effectively captures trade-offs and heterogeneous effects that would otherwise remain hidden, offering a more robust tool for both researchers and policymakers assessing disclosure regulation impacts.

title: Boundary-Aware Context Grounding for A Low-Channel EEG Agent
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) can make scientific software easier to use. However, a general model does not automatically know which measurements a particular sensor can support, which algorithms are implemented in the current software, or which conclusions are justified by a computed result. These distinctions are especially important for low-channel electroencephalography (EEG), where sparse spatial coverage and variable signal quality make plausible but unsupported interpretations easy to produce. We present NeuraDock Agent, an open-source architecture that separates a deterministic local EEG engine from a hardware-aware language layer. The numerical engine parses recordings, performs quality control, executes reviewed spectral workflows, and writes machine-readable artifacts. The LLM receives only a compact, allowlisted summary and a versioned context pack. The context describes the seven-channel hardware, reviewed workflows, result fields, implementation boundaries, scientific limits, and reference cases. Raw EEG and dense per-sample arrays remain local
  We evaluate the system at three levels. First, 12 recordings produced identical structured results over ten numerical repetitions, and a complete Rest/Task run produced identical result, report, and figure hashes over three repetitions. Second, request-capture and failure-injection experiments confirmed the tested data boundary and preservation of local artifacts under HTTP, malformed-output, and connection failures. Third, a boundary-awareness benchmark tested 36 ordinary and adversarial questions under four context ablations and two LLMs, yielding 288 outputs.These results support hardware- and implementation-aware grounding as a practical mechanism for calibrating what an EEG agent accepts, qualifies, or refuses; they do not establish clinical validity or a validated absolute cognitive-load index.

AI.tldr: NeuraDock Agent is an open-source architecture that pairs a deterministic local EEG engine with an LLM language layer, using a hardware-aware, allowlisted context pack to constrain the model's outputs. Evaluated across reproducibility, failure-injection, and boundary-awareness tests (288 outputs), the system demonstrates that implementation-aware grounding can calibrate what an EEG agent accepts, qualifies, or refuses.
AI.motivation: LLMs can make scientific software more accessible, but general-purpose models lack awareness of hardware specifics, implemented algorithms, and justified conclusions — a critical gap for low-channel EEG where sparse coverage and variable signal quality invite plausible but unsupported interpretations.
AI.method: The architecture separates a deterministic local numerical engine (parsing, quality control, spectral workflows, artifact writing) from a hardware-aware LLM layer. The LLM receives only a compact, allowlisted summary and a versioned context pack describing the seven-channel hardware, reviewed workflows, result fields, implementation boundaries, scientific limits, and reference cases. Raw EEG and dense arrays remain local. Evaluation spans: (1) reproducibility over 10+ numerical repetitions; (2) request-capture and failure-injection tests; and (3) a boundary-awareness benchmark with 36 questions, four context ablations, and two LLMs.
AI.result: Twelve recordings produced identical structured results over ten repetitions; a full Rest/Task run yielded identical result, report, and figure hashes over three repetitions. Failure-injection tests confirmed data boundary preservation under HTTP, malformed-output, and connection failures. The boundary-awareness benchmark (288 outputs across 36 questions, four ablations, two LLMs) demonstrated context-dependent calibration of acceptance, qualification, and refusal.
AI.conclusion: Hardware- and implementation-aware grounding is a practical mechanism for calibrating EEG agent behavior, though the results do not establish clinical validity or a validated absolute cognitive-load index.

title: Rethinking Training & Inference for Forecasting: Linking Winner-Take-All back to GMMs
summary: Trajectory forecasting for autonomous driving has advanced rapidly, yet representative models often produce uninformative posteriors over forecast modes, causing problems for mode pruning. We trace this to a modeling-training mismatch: forecasters are typically modeled as conditional Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) but trained with a winner-take-all (WTA) loss that assigns each sample to its nearest mode. We argue that this K-means-like hard assignment (one-hot), while preventing mode collapse, is the source of uninformative mode probabilities: it over-segments the trajectory space, ignores relatedness among nearby modes, and yields assignment instability under small perturbations. Guided by this lens, we introduce two post-hoc treatments: (1) test-time posterior-weighted merging that aggregates nearby candidate trajectories; and (2) a one-step expectation-maximization (EM) update that replaces hard labels with soft responsibilities, sharing probability mass across neighboring modes. Across several WTA-trained architectures, these lightweight steps produce more informative, faithfully ranked mode posteriors and strengthen final forecasts on popular displacement metrics -- without retraining. Our analysis unifies recent design choices through a GMM-vs-K-means perspective and offers principled, practical corrections that better align training objectives with inference.

AI.tldr: Trajectory forecasting models trained with winner-take-all (WTA) loss suffer from uninformative mode posteriors due to a GMM-vs-K-means mismatch. The authors propose two post-hoc corrections — posterior-weighted merging and a one-step EM update — that produce better-calibrated mode probabilities and improved forecasts without retraining.
AI.motivation: WTA-trained trajectory forecasters, though modeled as conditional GMMs, yield uninformative posteriors that impair mode pruning. The authors identify the root cause as a modeling-training mismatch: WTA's hard one-hot assignment (K-means-like) over-segments trajectory space, ignores mode relatedness, and creates assignment instability, despite being necessary to prevent mode collapse.
AI.method: Two post-hoc treatments are introduced: (1) Test-time posterior-weighted merging, which aggregates nearby candidate trajectories using learned mode posteriors as weights; and (2) A one-step EM update that replaces hard WTA labels with soft responsibilities, redistributing probability mass across neighboring modes. Both operate at inference time without retraining.
AI.result: Across multiple WTA-trained architectures, both lightweight steps produce more informative and faithfully ranked mode posteriors, and strengthen final displacement-metric forecasts. The improvements are achieved without any retraining.
AI.conclusion: The GMM-vs-K-means lens unifies recent design choices in trajectory forecasting and motivates principled post-hoc corrections that better align WTA training objectives with GMM inference. The proposed merging and EM steps are practical, model-agnostic solutions.

title: Design and Performance Evaluation of Secure RF and WiFi-Based Communication in Drone Swarms via Testbed Implementation
summary: Unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) swarms rely on distributed coordination and cooperative communication to support scalable operations, extended coverage, and applications such as surveillance and real-time data exchange. Wireless technologies such as radio frequency (RF) and WiFi are widely used for UAV-to-UAV and UAV-to-ground control station (GCS) communication but introduce significant security challenges. MAVLink, the predominant communication protocol in UAV systems, provides message integrity and authentication but lacks built-in encryption, leaving telemetry traffic vulnerable to eavesdropping. In our previous work, we proposed MAVShield, a lightweight encryption framework for MAVLink communications. In this paper, MAVShield, AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, and Rabbit are integrated into four custom-built UAVs to establish secure communication links over RF and WiFi channels. Their performance is evaluated through flight experiments using a UAV swarm testbed. Encrypted telemetry data enable autonomous formation control and collision avoidance during flight. For collision avoidance, we develop a modified artificial potential field (APF) algorithm that computes attractive and repulsive forces directly in geodetic coordinates, eliminating Cartesian transformations and reducing trajectory oscillations while avoiding local-minimum trapping. CPU utilization, memory consumption, and packet delivery ratio (PDR) are measured for each encryption scheme. Results show that MAVShield achieves performance comparable to unencrypted communication while outperforming AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, and Rabbit in overall efficiency. Algebraic cryptanalysis and Wireshark-based traffic analysis demonstrate resistance to key-recovery attacks and protection of telemetry confidentiality. The results indicate that MAVShield is an efficient and secure solution for UAV swarm communication.

AI.tldr: MAVShield, a lightweight encryption framework for MAVLink, is tested on four custom UAVs in swarm flight experiments. It outperforms AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, and Rabbit in CPU, memory, and packet delivery efficiency while ensuring telemetry confidentiality. A modified APF algorithm using geodetic coordinates is also introduced for collision avoidance.
AI.motivation: UAV swarms depend on MAVLink for communication, but MAVLink lacks built-in encryption, making telemetry vulnerable to eavesdropping. Existing ciphers may impose excessive computational and memory overhead on resource-constrained UAV hardware, necessitating a lightweight yet secure alternative.
AI.method: MAVShield (the authors' prior work) and four other ciphers (AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, Rabbit) are integrated into four custom-built UAVs for encrypted communication over RF and WiFi. Performance is measured via CPU utilization, memory consumption, and packet delivery ratio (PDR) in flight experiments. A modified artificial potential field (APF) algorithm operating directly in geodetic coordinates is developed for collision avoidance. Security is evaluated through algebraic cryptanalysis and Wireshark traffic analysis.
AI.result: MAVShield achieves performance comparable to unencrypted communication and surpasses AES-CTR, Speck-CTR, ChaCha20, and Rabbit in overall efficiency. Encrypted telemetry supports autonomous formation control and collision avoidance. The modified APF algorithm reduces trajectory oscillations and avoids local-minimum trapping. Security analysis confirms resistance to key-recovery attacks and protection of telemetry confidentiality.
AI.conclusion: MAVShield is demonstrated to be an efficient and secure solution for UAV swarm communication, suitable for real-time coordination and safe autonomous flight.

title: The Inattentional Gap: Task-Conditioned Language and Vision Models Omit the Safety-Critical Signals They Can Otherwise Report
summary: AI safety is evaluated by how reliably a model detects the hazards it is told to find, yet accidents often arise from the hazard no one specified. We show that conditioning a language or vision model on a narrow task suppresses its reporting of co-present, safety-critical signals it can otherwise report, a machine analogue of human inattentional blindness arising from a different mechanism. Across radiology and driving text scenarios and chest-radiograph vision tasks, suppression appeared in every model tested, did not diminish with scale, persisted in a reasoning model, and varied more by model family than by size, while the same models reported these signals at substantially higher rates when unconstrained. We name this dissociation the Inattentional Gap and argue that it decouples measured benchmark safety from real-world safety: a system can score near-perfectly on the hazards an evaluation specifies while remaining blind to those that cause harm.

AI.tldr: Models conditioned on narrow tasks suppress reporting of co-present safety-critical signals they can otherwise detect — a phenomenon the authors term the "Inattentional Gap." This decouples benchmark safety from real-world safety, as systems can score near-perfectly on specified hazards while remaining blind to unspecified ones.
AI.motivation: AI safety evaluation typically measures how well a model detects hazards it is explicitly instructed to find. However, real-world accidents often stem from hazards that were never specified. The authors investigate whether task conditioning causes models to overlook safety-critical signals that are co-present but irrelevant to the assigned narrow task.
AI.method: The authors designed experiments across radiology and driving text scenarios, as well as chest-radiograph vision tasks. Models were tested under two conditions: (1) constrained — conditioned on a narrow task, and (2) unconstrained — asked open-ended questions. Reporting rates of co-present safety-critical signals were compared across conditions. Every model tested was evaluated, including models of varying scales and families, and a reasoning model.
AI.result: Suppression of safety-critical signal reporting appeared in every model tested. The effect did not diminish with model scale, persisted even in a reasoning model, and varied more by model family than by size. The same models reported these signals at substantially higher rates when unconstrained, revealing a dissociation between constrained and unconstrained performance.
AI.conclusion: The "Inattentional Gap" represents a fundamental decoupling between measured benchmark safety and real-world safety. A system can achieve near-perfect scores on specified hazard evaluations while remaining blind to the hazards that actually cause harm, challenging current safety evaluation paradigms.

title: Radical AI Interpretability
comment: Draft of manuscript to appear as Cambridge Element in the Philosophy of Artificial Intelligence
summary: We develop a framework for interpreting AI systems as agents, drawing on the philosophical tradition of radical interpretation and the tools of mechanistic interpretability. The core question is: given the computational facts about a system, how do we solve for its beliefs, desires, and meanings? This matters increasingly for safety. We want to be able to trust the systems we deploy, whether by understanding their goals or, more modestly, by reliably detecting deception. Interpretability researchers are building tools to read beliefs and desires off a model's internals, but there is no settled account of when such a tool has succeeded. This book supplies one. We propose criteria on both representationalist and interpretationist approaches, and tie each to tests current interpretability methods can carry out. A central lesson is that these attributions cannot be made piecemeal. Beliefs, desires, and the propositional structure they presuppose are jointly constrained, and a method that fixes one while measuring the others inherits whatever distortions that introduces. This holism becomes pressing for AI systems, which may not share the interpreter's concepts. However, it also provides leverage: a system's attitudes constrain its propositional structure, that structure constrains which attitudes can be attributed, and mechanistic interpretability can help us measure both.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework for interpreting AI systems as agents with beliefs and desires, combining radical interpretation philosophy with mechanistic interpretability. It argues that belief/desire attributions are holistically constrained — they cannot be made piecemeal — and provides criteria for validating interpretability tools, with implications for AI safety and deception detection.
AI.motivation: As AI systems become more capable, we need to trust them — either by understanding their goals or reliably detecting deception. Mechanistic interpretability researchers are developing tools to read beliefs and desires from model internals, but the field lacks a settled account of what constitutes success in such attributions. This paper aims to fill that gap by providing rigorous criteria for when an interpretability method has genuinely succeeded.
AI.method: The authors draw on the philosophical tradition of radical interpretation (Davidson, Quine) and integrate it with mechanistic interpretability. They propose criteria spanning both representationalist and interpretationist approaches, tie each to empirically testable procedures current interpretability methods can carry out, and analyze the joint constraints among beliefs, desires, and propositional structure.
AI.result: The central result is that belief, desire, and meaning attributions cannot be made piecemeal — they are holistically constrained. Fixing one element while measuring others introduces distortions. This holistic interdependence is especially pressing for AI systems that may not share human concepts, but it also provides leverage: a system's attitudes constrain its propositional structure, which in turn constrains attributable attitudes, and mechanistic interpretability can measure both.
AI.conclusion: A principled framework for agent interpretation must respect holistic constraints among beliefs, desires, and propositional structure. The paper supplies testable criteria for validating interpretability methods, advancing both the philosophical foundations and practical methodology of mechanistic interpretability for AI safety.

title: DualEval: Joint Model-Item Calibration for Unified LLM Evaluation
summary: Current LLM evaluation relies on two complementary but often disconnected signals: static benchmarks with objective correctness labels and arena-style preference data that better reflect open-ended user interactions. We introduce DualEval, a latent model-item calibration framework that represents models and evaluation items in a shared space, jointly estimating model ability together with item difficulty and sharpness. We apply DualEval across four domains: coding, math, miscellaneous domain-knowledge tasks, and generic everyday user queries. Our evaluation uses 18 frontier LLMs, static benchmark labels, and reward-model scores validated against held-out human preferences for open-ended model responses. Empirically, our framework produces reliable and balanced model rankings, and its learned item-level profiles support downstream applications such as benchmark compression for sample-efficient evaluation and anomaly detection for contamination or outlier analysis. Overall, DualEval unifies static and arena-style evaluation through joint model-item calibration, producing model rankings and item-level diagnostics that support more sample-efficient, interpretable, and auditable evaluation pipelines.

AI.tldr: DualEval introduces a latent model-item calibration framework that jointly estimates model ability, item difficulty, and item sharpness in a shared latent space, unifying static benchmarks and arena-style preference data. Applied across 18 frontier LLMs in four domains, it yields reliable rankings, enables benchmark compression, and supports anomaly detection.
AI.motivation: Current LLM evaluation is fragmented: static benchmarks provide objective correctness labels but lack ecological validity, while arena-style preference data capture open-ended user interactions but are noisy and lack absolute calibration. No existing framework unifies these two complementary signals into a single coherent evaluation pipeline.
AI.method: DualEval posits a joint latent space where both models and evaluation items are embedded. It simultaneously estimates three parameters: model ability (latent trait), item difficulty, and item sharpness (discrimination). The framework is applied across four domains — coding, math, miscellaneous domain-knowledge tasks, and generic user queries — using 18 frontier LLMs, static benchmark labels, and reward-model scores validated against held-out human preferences.
AI.result: DualEval produces reliable and balanced model rankings. The learned item-level profiles enable downstream applications including benchmark compression (identifying minimally sufficient item subsets for sample-efficient evaluation) and anomaly detection (flagging potential contamination or outlier behaviors).
AI.conclusion: DualEval successfully unifies static and arena-style evaluation through joint model-item calibration, yielding model rankings and item-level diagnostics that support more sample-efficient, interpretable, and auditable LLM evaluation pipelines.

title: Physical Layer Authentication With Channel Knowledge Maps in Indoor Environments
summary: Physical layer authentication (PLA) allows to authenticate the user by comparing measurements over time, assuming their time consistency or by modeling their evolution. However, these assumptions become problematic when devices are in motion and in indoor environments due to multipath propagation and obstructions. In this paper, we propose a PLA mechanism for moving devices in indoor environments, where multiple access points (APs) estimate the dominant channel tap path loss (PL) and angle of arrival (AoA) from the received signals and compare them with previously collected channel knowledge maps (CKMs). Specifically, the measurements are compared to those in the neighborhood of the previously known position obtained from CKMs. A comprehensive security analysis is conducted under both random and optimal attacks. Numerical results in a representative indoor scenario, with CKM obtained via ray tracing, validate the effectiveness of the proposed PLA approach.

AI.tldr: A physical layer authentication scheme for moving indoor devices is proposed, where multiple APs estimate dominant path loss and angle of arrival, then compare measurements against pre-collected channel knowledge maps around the device's previously known position. Security is analyzed under random and optimal attacks, and ray-tracing simulations confirm effectiveness.
AI.motivation: Traditional PLA relies on temporal consistency or evolution models of channel measurements, which break down when devices move indoors due to multipath and obstructions. There is a need for a PLA mechanism robust to indoor mobility.
AI.method: Multiple APs estimate the dominant channel tap's path loss and angle of arrival from received signals. These measurements are compared against previously constructed channel knowledge maps (CKMs), specifically using measurements in the spatial neighborhood of the device's last known position. Security is evaluated under random and optimal attack models, with CKMs generated via ray tracing in a representative indoor scenario.
AI.result: Numerical results in a representative indoor environment validate the effectiveness of the proposed PLA approach.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CKM-based PLA mechanism effectively authenticates moving devices in indoor environments, overcoming the limitations of conventional time-consistency assumptions.

title: \textsc{DiARC}: Distinguishing Positive and Negative Samples Helps Improving ARC-like Reasoning Ability of Large Language Models
summary: The Abstraction and Reasoning Corpus (ARC;~\citealp{chollet2019measure}) contains tasks that require summarizing patterns from limited grid samples and predicting output grids. Recently, many large language model based approaches have attempted to transform it into a text-based reasoning task. However, methods based on open-source models have generally yielded unsatisfactory results, while those relying on closed-source models are too costly. Current efforts mainly focus on data augmentation, constructing ARC-like data for more comprehensive supervised fine-tuning. In this work, we argue that solving ARC-like problems requires not only \textit{positive} sample supervision but also the ability to improve model reasoning by distinguishing \textit{negative} samples. To this end, we draw on the idea of preference alignment and propose \textsc{DiARC}, a method that constructs preference pairs to enable the model to distinguish between them. Specifically, we propose three ways to construct negative samples, including output-level visual transformations, DSL-level rule inversion, and task-specific rule editing. The resulting negative samples provide informative near-miss alternatives while keeping the observed demonstrations unchanged. Experimental results across multiple ARC-like benchmarks show that \textsc{DiARC} consistently improves performance over baseline models. The code is released at https://github.com/szu-tera/DiARC.

AI.tldr: DiARC proposes using preference alignment with constructed negative samples to improve LLM reasoning on ARC-like tasks, going beyond standard positive-sample supervision. Three negative-sample generation strategies — visual transformations, DSL rule inversion, and task-specific rule editing — create near-miss alternatives that help models learn to distinguish correct from incorrect patterns, yielding consistent improvements across benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing open-source LLM approaches for ARC-like tasks yield unsatisfactory results, while closed-source methods are costly. Current data augmentation efforts focus only on positive samples. The authors argue that learning to distinguish negative samples is equally crucial for solving ARC problems, motivating a preference-alignment approach.
AI.method: DiARC constructs preference pairs using three negative-sample generation strategies: (1) output-level visual transformations (perturbing correct outputs), (2) DSL-level rule inversion (inverting domain-specific language rules), and (3) task-specific rule editing (modifying rules to produce plausible but incorrect outputs). These near-miss negatives are paired with correct outputs while keeping input demonstrations unchanged, enabling preference-alignment training.
AI.result: Experimental results across multiple ARC-like benchmarks demonstrate that DiARC consistently improves performance over baseline models.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating negative sample supervision via preference alignment is an effective strategy for improving model reasoning on ARC-like tasks. The proposed negative-sample construction methods provide informative training signals beyond what positive samples alone can offer.

title: PMDformer: Patch-Mean Decoupling Information Transformer for Long-term Forecasting
summary: Long-term time series forecasting (LTSF) plays a crucial role in fields such as energy management, finance, and traffic prediction. Transformer-based models have adopted patch-based strategies to capture long-range dependencies, but accurately modeling shape similarities across patches and variables remains challenging due to scale differences. To address this, we introduce patch-mean decoupling (PMD), which separates the trend and residual shape information by subtracting the mean of each patch, preserving the original structure and ensuring that the attention mechanism captures true shape similarities. Futhermore, to more effectively model long-range dependencies and capture cross-variable relationships, we propose Trend Restoration Attention (TRA) and Proximal Variable Attention (PVA). The former module reintegrates the decoupled trend from PMD while calculating attention output. And the latter focuses cross-variable attention on the most relevant, recent time segments to avoid overfitting on outdated correlations. Combining these components, we propose PMDformer, a model designed to effectively capture shape similarity in long-term forecasting scenarios. Extensive experiments indicate that PMDformer outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in stability and accuracy across multiple LTSF benchmarks. The code is available at https://github.com/aohu1105/PMDformer.

AI.tldr: PMDformer introduces patch-mean decoupling to separate trend and shape in time series patches, combined with Trend Restoration Attention and Proximal Variable Attention, achieving state-of-the-art long-term forecasting accuracy.
AI.motivation: Transformer-based patch models struggle to capture true shape similarities across patches and variables due to scale differences, and cross-variable attention often overfits on outdated correlations.
AI.method: (1) Patch-Mean Decoupling (PMD): subtracts patch mean to isolate residual shape from trend. (2) Trend Restoration Attention (TRA): reintegrates decoupled trend during attention computation. (3) Proximal Variable Attention (PVA): restricts cross-variable attention to recent, relevant time segments to avoid outdated correlations.
AI.result: PMDformer outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods in both stability and accuracy across multiple LTSF benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Decoupling trend from shape via PMD, then separately handling them through TRA and PVA, provides a more effective framework for capturing genuine shape similarities in long-term time series forecasting.

title: Embedding Foundation Model Predictions in Discrete-Choice Models with Structural Guarantees
summary: Tabular foundation models achieve strong accuracy on choice prediction tasks, but their predictions often violate the economic logic those tasks require: raising a price can increase predicted demand, implied willingness-to-pay estimates are frequently negative or implausible, and unavailable alternatives receive nonzero probability. We propose a two-stage adapter that takes a foundation model's predicted choice probabilities as a precomputed feature and embeds them inside a multinomial logit's utility. In Stage 1, we fit the multinomial logit's structural coefficients by maximum likelihood with sign constraints; in Stage 2, we freeze those coefficients and fit a small neural correction operating on the foundation model's predictions. We prove that this composition exactly preserves the multinomial logit's marginal rate of substitution, so analytically computable value-of-time becomes a mathematical guarantee rather than an empirical accident. Across three datasets and two foundation models, the adapter gains 6.4 percentage points (pp) of test accuracy on average over the multinomial logit and up to 12.8 pp, maintains 100% cost monotonicity, and produces values of time within the published transportation-economics range on the transportation datasets. Performance degrades gracefully under foundation-model context restriction, retaining at least 6 pp of accuracy gain even at 10% of the original foundation-model context.

AI.tldr: Foundation models for choice prediction often violate economic rationality constraints (e.g., implausible willingness-to-pay). The paper proposes a two-stage adapter that embeds foundation model predictions inside a multinomial logit model, enforcing economic logic while retaining accuracy gains. The method guarantees valid marginal rates of substitution, achieves strong accuracy improvements, maintains 100% cost monotonicity, and produces economically plausible value-of-time estimates.
AI.motivation: Tabular foundation models achieve high accuracy on choice prediction tasks but frequently violate core economic logic: predicted demand can increase with price (violating downward-sloping demand), implied willingness-to-pay can be negative, and unavailable alternatives receive nonzero probability. These violations make such models unreliable for policy analysis and welfare estimation. The motivation is to retain the accuracy of foundation models while enforcing economic rationality constraints.
AI.method: A two-stage adapter: Stage 1 fits a multinomial logit (MNL) model's structural coefficients via maximum likelihood with sign constraints, using the foundation model's predicted choice probabilities as a precomputed feature embedded in the MNL utility function. Stage 2 freezes those structural coefficients and trains a small neural correction network on top of the foundation model's predictions. The composition provably preserves the MNL's marginal rate of substitution, guaranteeing analytically computable value-of-time.
AI.result: Across three datasets and two foundation models, the adapter achieves an average test accuracy gain of 6.4 percentage points (pp) over the multinomial logit baseline, up to 12.8 pp. It maintains 100% cost monotonicity. Produced value-of-time estimates fall within published transportation-economics ranges. Performance degrades gracefully under context restrictions, retaining at least 6 pp accuracy gain even at 10% of the original foundation-model context.
AI.conclusion: The proposed two-stage adapter successfully bridges the gap between high-accuracy foundation models and the economic rationality requirements of choice modeling. By embedding foundation model predictions within an MNL structure, it yields both strong predictive performance and theoretically guaranteed economic properties, making it suitable for practical policy and welfare analysis.

title: Type-based information flow analysis for $π$-calculus with a dynamically extensible security lattice
summary: We develop a type system for secure information flow where new security levels can be created and inserted into the security lattice dynamically, i.e., even in the middle of an execution of a system. Our system is formalized by extending Kobayashi's type-based secure information flow analysis for Milner's pi-calculus, which is one of the most expressive models (or "languages") supporting both sequential and concurrent computations, with concise syntax, reduction-based semantics, and bisimulation equivalence as a robust formalization of secrecy as non-interference. The development required careful treatment of extensions of lattices themselves as well as deliberate generalization from the simple 2-element lattice (consisting of only High and Low) in the original system.

AI.tldr: A type system for dynamic security level creation and lattice extension in the pi-calculus, extending Kobayashi's static information flow analysis to support runtime insertion of new security levels while preserving non-interference guarantees.
AI.motivation: Existing type-based secure information flow systems (like Kobayashi's for the pi-calculus) assume a fixed, static security lattice. In practice, systems may need to dynamically create new security levels during execution — for instance, when new principals, documents, or compartments emerge at runtime. This requires a formal framework that can safely extend the lattice without breaking non-interference.
AI.method: The authors extend Kobayashi's type system for the pi-calculus by: (1) formalizing dynamic lattice extension operations, allowing new security levels to be created and inserted mid-execution; (2) generalizing from the original 2-element {High, Low} lattice to richer lattice structures; and (3) preserving the reduction-based semantics and bisimulation-based non-interference guarantees of the original framework.
AI.result: A formally sound type system where security levels can be dynamically created and inserted into the lattice without violating non-interference. The system handles both sequential and concurrent computation within the expressive pi-calculus model.
AI.conclusion: Dynamic security lattice extension is feasible in a principled way within the pi-calculus framework, enabling more realistic secure information flow models where security policies can evolve at runtime while maintaining provable secrecy guarantees.

title: Erase-then-Delta Attention: Decoupling Erase and Write Addresses in Delta-Rule Linear Attention
summary: Delta-rule linear attention improves recurrent memory updates by correcting what is already stored at the current write address before writing new content. However, the active correction is still anchored to that same write address. As a result, stale information stored at a different address cannot be actively removed before new content is written elsewhere. We propose Erase-then-Delta Attention (EDA), a memory update rule that decouples where to erase from where to write. The key insight is that recurrent memory models should not only correct the current write, but also selectively suppress outdated memory at an independently chosen address. Concretely, our method first applies a targeted erase step along a learned erase direction, and then performs the standard delta-style corrective write along the current write direction. This preserves the corrective behavior of delta-rule updates while expanding their memory-management capacity. Language-model pretraining experiments across dense 2.5B and MoE 25B-A2.8B model families show that EDA performs best in both settings. The gain persists after 80B-token long-context midtraining of the MoE models, where EDA also performs best in long-context evaluations from 4k to 128k contexts. A compact update analysis and memory-state probes suggest why: EDA keeps the delta-rule corrective write intact while allocating an additional cleanup path most strongly when passive decay is weak. These results suggest that recurrent memory models should decide not only what to write, but also what stale information to erase and where.

AI.tldr: EDA proposes a two-step memory update rule for recurrent attention models: first erase stale information at a separately chosen address, then perform corrective delta-rule writing. This decoupling of erase and write addresses improves long-context performance in language model pretraining up to 128k tokens.
AI.motivation: Standard delta-rule linear attention only corrects memory at the current write address, leaving stale information stored at other addresses untouched. This limits the model's ability to actively manage and suppress outdated memories, especially critical for long-context processing.
AI.method: EDA introduces a two-phase memory update: (1) a targeted erase step along a learned erase direction at an independently chosen address, followed by (2) a standard delta-rule corrective write. This is tested on dense 2.5B and MoE 25B-A2.8B models, with long-context midtraining up to 80B tokens, evaluated across 4k–128k context lengths. Memory-state probes and update analyses are used to characterize the mechanism.
AI.result: EDA outperforms standard delta-rule attention across both dense and MoE model families. Gains persist after 80B-token long-context midtraining, with EDA achieving best results on long-context evaluations from 4k to 128k. Probe analyses show EDA adds a cleanup pathway that is most active when passive memory decay is weak.
AI.conclusion: Recurrent memory models benefit from decoupling erase and write decisions. EDA shows that explicitly choosing what and where to erase, before writing, enhances memory management and long-context modeling, suggesting a design principle for future recurrent architectures.

title: Explainable Ensemble-Based Machine Learning Models for Detecting the Presence of Cirrhosis in Hepatitis C Patients
summary: Hepatitis C is a liver infection caused by a virus, which results in mild to severe inflammation of the liver. Over many years, hepatitis C gradually damages the liver, often leading to permanent scarring, known as cirrhosis. Patients sometimes have moderate or no symptoms of liver illness for decades before developing cirrhosis. Cirrhosis typically worsens to the point of liver failure. Patients with cirrhosis may also experience brain and nerve system damage, as well as gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Treatment for cirrhosis focuses on preventing further progression of the disease. Detecting cirrhosis earlier is therefore crucial for avoiding complications. Machine learning (ML) has been shown to be effective at providing precise and accurate information for use in diagnosing several diseases. Despite this, no studies have so far used ML to detect cirrhosis in patients with hepatitis C. This study obtained a dataset consisting of 28 attributes of 2038 Egyptian patients from the ML Repository of the University of California at Irvine. Four ML algorithms were trained on the dataset to diagnose cirrhosis in hepatitis C patients: a Random Forest, a Gradient Boosting Machine, an Extreme Gradient Boosting, and an Extra Trees model. The Extra Trees model outperformed the other models achieving an accuracy of 96.92%, a recall of 94.00%, a precision of 99.81%, and an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 96% using only 16 of the 28 features.

AI.tldr: This study applies four machine learning algorithms to detect cirrhosis in hepatitis C patients using a dataset of 2,038 Egyptian patients with 28 attributes. The Extra Trees model achieved the best performance with 96.92% accuracy, 94.00% recall, 99.81% precision, and 96% AUC using only 16 features.
AI.motivation: Cirrhosis is a severe, often asymptomatic complication of hepatitis C that can lead to liver failure, neurological damage, and gastrointestinal hemorrhage. Early detection is critical to prevent disease progression. While ML has proven effective in diagnosing various diseases, no prior studies have applied ML specifically to detect cirrhosis in hepatitis C patients.
AI.method: The authors used a dataset of 28 attributes from 2,038 Egyptian patients (sourced from the UCI ML Repository). Four ensemble ML algorithms were trained: Random Forest, Gradient Boosting Machine, Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), and Extra Trees. Feature selection reduced the feature set to 16 attributes. Models were evaluated on accuracy, recall, precision, and AUC-ROC.
AI.result: The Extra Trees model outperformed all other algorithms, achieving 96.92% accuracy, 94.00% recall, 99.81% precision, and an AUC of 96% using only 16 of the 28 available features.
AI.conclusion: ML, particularly the Extra Trees algorithm, demonstrates strong potential for early and accurate diagnosis of cirrhosis in hepatitis C patients, which can aid in preventing severe complications through timely intervention.

title: Optimizing CUDA like a Human: Micro-Profiling Tools as Expert Surrogates for LLM-Based GPU Kernel Optimization
summary: We present KernelPro, a closed-loop multi-agent system that automatically generates, profiles, and iteratively optimizes GPU kernel code by integrating large language model (LLM) code generation with hardware profiler feedback and pluggable bottleneck detection tools. KernelPro introduces four contributions: (1) a semantic feedback operator that encodes expert heuristics as pluggable micro-profiling tools, transforming raw hardware metrics into actionable natural language guidance; (2) a two-stage tool invocation architecture where roofline-based bottleneck classification filters which specialized analysis tools execute, combining kernel-level (ncu), instruction-level (SASS), and system-level (nsys) profiling; (3) a domain-adapted MCTS with progressive widening, asymmetric branching, log-reward calibration, dead-end pruning, and search memory for cross-iteration learning; and (4) direct CuTe source-level code generation via autonomous code search over the CUTLASS/CuTe codebase. On KernelBench, KernelPro achieves geometric mean speedups of 2.42x/4.69x/5.30x on Levels 1/2/3, establishing state-of-the-art performance across all difficulty levels. On VeOmni's expert-optimized MoE training kernels, KernelPro achieves 1.23x over hand-tuned Triton by generating a from-scratch raw-CUDA+CuTe Hopper WGMMA kernel. Ablation studies demonstrate that each design component independently and significantly improves optimization quality: micro-profiling tools (p < 0.0001 vs raw metrics), MCTS search (26% higher geometric mean vs greedy, p = 0.004), and proactive tool orchestration (23% improvement, p = 0.035). Finally, KernelPro is the first CUDA kernel coding agent to optimize energy efficiency beyond the speed-only focus of prior systems, demonstrating an 11.6% measured energy reduction at matched speed.

AI.tldr: KernelPro is a multi-agent system that uses LLMs with hardware profiler feedback to iteratively optimize GPU kernels, achieving SOTA speedups on KernelBench and outperforming hand-tuned Triton kernels via CuTe code generation.
AI.motivation: Manual GPU kernel optimization is labor-intensive and requires deep hardware expertise. Prior LLM-based approaches lack systematic integration of hardware profiling feedback and struggle with complex kernel optimizations across difficulty levels.
AI.method: KernelPro employs a closed-loop multi-agent system with four key components: (1) semantic feedback operators that convert hardware metrics into natural language guidance via pluggable micro-profiling tools; (2) a two-stage tool invocation architecture using roofline-based bottleneck classification to selectively invoke kernel-level (ncu), instruction-level (SASS), and system-level (nsys) profilers; (3) a domain-adapted MCTS with progressive widening, asymmetric branching, log-reward calibration, dead-end pruning, and cross-iteration search memory; and (4) direct CuTe source-level code generation through autonomous search over the CUTLASS/CuTe codebase.
AI.result: On KernelBench, KernelPro achieves geometric mean speedups of 2.42x, 4.69x, and 5.30x on Levels 1/2/3 respectively, setting SOTA across all difficulty levels. On VeOmni's expert-optimized MoE training kernels, it achieves 1.23x over hand-tuned Triton via raw-CUDA+CuTe Hopper WGMMA kernels. Ablations confirm significant contributions: micro-profiling tools (p < 0.0001 vs raw metrics), MCTS search (26% higher geometric mean vs greedy, p = 0.004), and proactive tool orchestration (23% improvement, p = 0.035). It also achieves 11.6% measured energy reduction at matched speed.
AI.conclusion: KernelPro demonstrates that integrating LLM code generation with structured hardware profiling feedback and informed search yields substantial GPU kernel speedups, surpassing both prior automated methods and expert hand-tuned kernels, while also pioneering energy-aware optimization for CUDA kernel generation.

title: Inherited Circuits, Learned Semantics: How Fine-Tuning Creates Evasion Vulnerabilities Invisible to Standard Evaluation
summary: LLMs fine-tuned for security classification are usually evaluated on held-out examples from the same distribution as their training data. We show that this can miss vulnerabilities introduced by fine-tuning itself: models can learn token-level indicator semantics that preserve canonical accuracy while failing under behavior-preserving transformations such as PowerShell alias substitution, command reconstruction, string construction, execution indirection, and case mutation. We study Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct and its base model, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, on matched PowerShell classification cohorts. Causal interventions localize the classification circuit to a late-attention route inherited from Llama rather than created by fine-tuning. Fine-tuning concentrates and semantically specializes this inherited structure, improving baseline behavior while creating transformation-sensitive attack surfaces. A three-tier evasion benchmark finds Foundation-Sec misses on iwr substitution, Invoke-Expression reconstruction, and case-mutated Invoke-Expression/IEX variants that Llama does not share. We also derive a pre-deployment monitoring method: a linear probe at the classification boundary and an indicator-token sign test identify command families where canonical indicators change role after fine-tuning. These signals prioritize red-team variant generation using only canonical inputs, showing that security fine-tuning can improve task accuracy while expanding the evasion surface. These results caution against treating small task-specific fine-tunes as straightforwardly safer security classifiers: specialization can convert inherited model structure into brittle indicator rules that preserve held-out accuracy while expanding the evasion surface. Robust AI-enabled security will require specifying the full transformation space of the task and monitoring semantic drift through fine-tuning.

AI.tldr: Security fine-tuning of LLMs can introduce brittle, token-level indicator semantics that maintain held-out accuracy but fail under simple adversarial transformations (e.g., alias substitution, case mutation). The paper localizes this vulnerability to inherited attention circuits that fine-tuning concentrates and specializes, and proposes a pre-deployment monitoring method using linear probes and indicator-token sign tests to detect semantic drift.
AI.motivation: Standard evaluation of security-classification LLMs on held-out, in-distribution examples misses vulnerabilities introduced by fine-tuning itself. The authors aim to demonstrate that task-specific fine-tuning can create transformation-sensitive attack surfaces while preserving canonical accuracy, challenging the assumption that small fine-tuned security classifiers are straightforwardly safer.
AI.method: The authors study Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on matched PowerShell classification tasks. They use (1) causal intervention (activation patching) to localize the classification circuit to late-attention layers inherited from the base model; (2) a three-tier evasion benchmark testing transformations like PowerShell alias substitution (iwr), Invoke-Expression reconstruction, string construction, execution indirection, and case mutation; and (3) a pre-deployment monitoring method combining a linear probe at the classification boundary with an indicator-token sign test to identify command families where canonical indicators change role after fine-tuning.
AI.result: Fine-tuning concentrates and semantically specializes inherited late-attention structure from Llama rather than creating new circuits. Foundation-Sec misses on iwr substitution, Invoke-Expression reconstruction, and case-mutated Invoke-Expression/IEX variants that Llama correctly handles. The linear probe and sign test effectively identify command families with shifted indicator semantics, enabling prioritized red-team variant generation using only canonical inputs.
AI.conclusion: Security fine-tuning can improve task accuracy while simultaneously expanding the evasion surface by converting inherited model structure into brittle indicator rules. Robust AI-enabled security requires specifying the full transformation space of the task and monitoring semantic drift through fine-tuning, rather than treating small task-specific fine-tunes as inherently safer classifiers.

title: Zero-shot Tweet-Level Stance Detection Enhanced by External Knowledge and Reflective Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
summary: Zero-shot tweet-level stance detection confronts two primary challenges: (1) mitigating the context sparsity inherent in short texts, and (2) establishing the relevance between implicit targets and textual content. While existing methods primarily focus on incorporating external knowledge, they neglect the intrinsic semantic cues embedded within key intra-textual entities. Furthermore, current models exhibit limited capability in determining the relevance of unseen targets to the given text, thereby struggling to differentiate between "neutral" and "irrelevant" stance labels. To address these issues, we first construct a four-class, multi-topic Japanese tweet dataset. To our knowledge, this is the first Japanese tweet-level dataset for stance detection. We then propose KIRP, a zero-shot stance detection framework. It integrates external knowledge with entity reorganization for data augmentation and employs prompt chaining for reasoning. Specifically, the framework incorporates knowledge graphs to supplement and reorganize key textual entities, while reflective Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning extracts and validates implicit targets. To better distinguish "neutral" from "irrelevant" labels, we adopt stance-aware contrastive learning to capture discriminative features and design a three-layer iterative prototype network for fine-grained classification. Experimental results on SemEval-2016, WT-WT, and KIRP-D show that KIRP achieves state-of-the-art performance. KIRP obtains F1 scores of 84.05% (three-class) on SemEval-2016, and 84.99% and 79.18% (four-class) on WT-WT and KIRP-D, respectively.

AI.tldr: KIRP is a zero-shot stance detection framework that combines knowledge graph-enhanced entity reorganization with chain-of-thought reasoning and stance-aware contrastive learning. It introduces the first Japanese tweet-level stance detection dataset and achieves SOTA on SemEval-2016, WT-WT, and KIRP-D.
AI.motivation: Zero-shot tweet-level stance detection suffers from (1) context sparsity in short texts, (2) difficulty linking implicit targets to content, and (3) poor differentiation between "neutral" and "irrelevant" stance labels. Existing methods rely on external knowledge but overlook intrinsic semantic cues from key intra-textual entities and fail to model unseen target relevance effectively.
AI.method: The KIRP framework has three core components: (1) Knowledge graph integration with entity reorganization for data augmentation, enriching key textual entities; (2) Reflective Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning via prompt chaining to extract and validate implicit targets; (3) Stance-aware contrastive learning combined with a three-layer iterative prototype network for fine-grained classification, specifically targeting the neutral-vs-irrelevant distinction. The authors also construct KIRP-D, a four-class multi-topic Japanese tweet dataset.
AI.result: KIRP achieves state-of-the-art F1 scores: 84.05% (three-class) on SemEval-2016, 84.99% (four-class) on WT-WT, and 79.18% (four-class) on the newly introduced KIRP-D dataset.
AI.conclusion: KIRP effectively addresses zero-shot stance detection by synergizing external knowledge augmentation with intrinsic entity cues and reflective reasoning. The introduction of the first Japanese stance detection dataset (KIRP-D) fills a resource gap, and the strong empirical results across multiple benchmarks validate the framework's robustness and generalizability.

title: EvoOptiGraph: Weakness-Driven Coevolution via Graph-Based Structural Generation for Optimization Modeling
summary: Automating optimization modeling from natural language with large language models (LLMs) faces two key challenges. First, training corpora lack structural diversity. Second, data generation pipelines remain static and decoupled from model learning. To address these challenges, we propose EvoOptiGraph, a novel framework where data and model co-evolve, driven by model weaknesses. EvoOptiGraph represents each mixed-integer linear program (MILP) as an attributed bipartite graph and applies validity-preserving evolutionary operators to generate structurally diverse instances. The evolved graphs are converted into solver code and natural language via deterministic compilation and verified back-translation. Training proceeds in two stages: supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on an initial dataset, followed by reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), where graph-derived weakness signals guide the generation of new instances targeting the model's failures. This forms a closed loop that continuously updates the training distribution. Empirical results on six public datasets show that EvoOptiGraph significantly outperforms larger generalist models, agentic methods, and specialized baselines in accuracy, executability, and generalization. These results demonstrate that targeted data-model coevolution is an effective strategy for improving LLMs on optimization modeling tasks.

AI.tldr: EvoOptiGraph introduces a co-evolutionary framework where MILP instances represented as attributed bipartite graphs are mutated via validity-preserving operators, and model weaknesses from RLVR training guide targeted data generation, creating a closed-loop that significantly outperforms larger models and baselines on optimization modeling from natural language.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches to automating optimization modeling from natural language with LLMs suffer from two core limitations: (1) training corpora lack structural diversity in their MILP representations, and (2) data generation pipelines are static and decoupled from the model's learning process, meaning they cannot adapt to address specific model failures.
AI.method: EvoOptiGraph represents each MILP as an attributed bipartite graph (variables and constraints as nodes, edges for incidence). Validity-preserving evolutionary operators (crossover, mutation) generate structurally diverse graph instances while maintaining MILP feasibility. These graphs are deterministically compiled into solver code and back-translated into natural language descriptions. Training uses a two-stage pipeline: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on an initial dataset, then (2) reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), where graph-derived weakness signals identify failure modes and drive targeted generation of new training instances, forming a closed co-evolution loop between data and model.
AI.result: Experiments across six public datasets demonstrate that EvoOptiGraph significantly outperforms larger generalist models, agentic methods, and specialized baselines on accuracy, executability, and generalization metrics.
AI.conclusion: Targeted data-model co-evolution, where training data generation is dynamically guided by model weaknesses, is an effective strategy for improving LLM performance on optimization modeling tasks.

title: Finding the Time to Think: Learning Planning Budgets in Real-Time RL
summary: Deliberating takes time. In real-time settings, that time is not free. Standard reinforcement learning (RL) sidesteps this as the environment waits indefinitely for the agent's decision. Instead, we study real-time RL environments where the environment progresses while waiting for the agent's action. Building on prior real-time formalizations, we introduce variable-delay real-time RL, where the agent chooses how long to deliberate at each decision point since the environment progresses. For the planning agents we use, the right delay is state-dependent, and naively planning how long to plan can paralyze the agent. We instead approach this setting by training a lightweight gating policy on top of a planner to select state-dependent planning budgets. Across real-time Pac-Man, Tetris, Snake, Speed Hex, and Speed Go, our gating policy outperforms fixed-budget and heuristic baselines, and transfers to a real-time setup where the environment and agent run on two different GPUs.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces variable-delay real-time RL, where agents choose how long to deliberate while the environment progresses. A lightweight gating policy selects state-dependent planning budgets, outperforming fixed-budget and heuristic baselines across multiple real-time games.
AI.motivation: Standard RL assumes the environment waits indefinitely for agent decisions, which is unrealistic in real-time settings. Existing real-time RL formalizations use fixed deliberation budgets, but optimal deliberation time is state-dependent. The authors address the problem of learning *how long* to plan in environments that progress during deliberation, avoiding the paralysis that occurs when naively planning how long to plan.
AI.method: The authors formalize variable-delay real-time RL and propose training a lightweight gating policy on top of a planner.
