The gating policy selects state-dependent planning budgets (deliberation durations). This avoids the recursive problem of planning how long to plan by using a learned policy that directly outputs a delay value for each state. The approach is tested with planning agents (e.g., MCTS-based) across multiple real-time game environments, including a setup where environment and agent run on separate GPUs.
AI.result: The gating policy outperforms fixed-budget and heuristic baselines across real-time Pac-Man, Tetris, Snake, Speed Hex, and Speed Go. The method also successfully transfers to a real-time setup where the environment and agent run on two different GPUs, demonstrating practical applicability.
AI.conclusion: Learning a state-dependent deliberation policy via a lightweight gating mechanism is an effective and practical solution for real-time RL, enabling agents to dynamically trade off thinking time against environment progression without succumbing to recursive planning overhead.

title: zQR: A Verifiable QR-Driven zkSNARK Proof Verification Framework for Mobile Platforms
summary: Privacy is one of the fundamental rights of individuals in modern societies. Yet, the practical adoption of privacy-preserving technologies in daily interactions remains limited. Zero-knowledge proofs offer strong privacy guarantees but are often hindered by their technical complexity. In this paper, we advance the idea of verifiable QR codes that enable off-line verifiers to verify proofs encoded in QR codes. Based on this core idea, we build a novel QR-driven zkSNARK proof verification framework (i.e., zQR) for mobile platforms. The framework integrates blockchain for auditability, non-repudiation and logging; and large-language models for automatic circuit generation. We perform a security discussion of the framework by considering multiple attack surfaces. Furthermore, we present an experimental evaluation measuring temporal costs (proof generation and verification latency, QR code encoding and decoding latency) and financial costs (blockchain gas consumption). Our results demonstrate the feasibility of zQR as a proof-of-concept framework for privacy-preserving verification on mobile platform where proofs are compactly represented with QR code symbol version of 19 with low error correction level. Finally, we discuss potential applications, current limitations and future directions for the broader adoption of privacy-preserving technologies in daily interactions.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes zQR, a framework combining QR codes, zkSNARKs, blockchain, and large language models to enable offline privacy-preserving verification on mobile platforms. Proofs are encoded in QR codes, allowing verifiers to check them without online connectivity, with blockchain providing auditability and LLMs automating circuit generation.
AI.motivation: Despite privacy being a fundamental right, adoption of privacy-preserving technologies like zero-knowledge proofs remains limited due to technical complexity. The authors aim to bridge this gap by leveraging the ubiquity of QR codes and mobile devices to make privacy-preserving verification more accessible in daily interactions.
AI.method: The authors design zQR, a QR-driven zkSNARK proof verification framework with four components: (1) encoding zkSNARK proofs into QR codes for offline verification, (2) blockchain integration for auditability, non-repudiation, and logging, (3) large-language models for automatic circuit generation to reduce technical barriers, and (4) a security analysis covering multiple attack surfaces. Experimental evaluation measures temporal costs (proof generation, verification, QR encoding/decoding latency) and financial costs (gas consumption).
AI.result: Experimental results demonstrate feasibility using QR code symbol version 19 with low error correction level. The paper quantifies both temporal costs (proof generation/verification and QR encoding/decoding latency) and financial costs (blockchain gas consumption), confirming the framework's practicality as a proof-of-concept.
AI.conclusion: zQR is a viable proof-of-concept for privacy-preserving verification on mobile platforms. The authors discuss potential applications, current limitations, and future research directions to promote broader adoption of privacy-preserving technologies in everyday interactions.

title: Closing the Quality Gap in Low-Resource Text-to-Speech: LoRA Fine-Tuning of VoxCPM2 for Khmer and Korean
comment: 5 pages, 1 figure, 4 tables. IEEE conference format (IEEEtran)
summary: Large pretrained text-to-speech (TTS) models sound almost human for well-resourced languages, but much worse for languages that are rare in their training data. We study this quality gap for Khmer and Korean using VoxCPM2, a 2.4B-parameter, tokenizer-free TTS model that joins a MiniCPM-4 language-model backbone with a flow-matching diffusion decoder. We build one shared, language-tagged corpus of about 26 hours and adapt VoxCPM2 with a single Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapter, trained on both languages at once and added to both the language model and the decoder. The adapter is zero-initialized, so training starts exactly at the original (zero-shot) model. In native-speaker listening tests, the Khmer Mean Opinion Score (MOS) rises from 3.85 to 4.23 with the best adapter (rank 64), a highly significant gain (paired Wilcoxon test, p<0.001), while training only 0.19 to 3.03 percent of the parameters. The automatic loss and the human ratings, however, disagree on the best rank: validation loss is lowest at rank 128, yet MOS peaks at rank 64. The same adapter brings no gain for Korean, a language the base model already handles well, and at a high rank it even degrades quality. Adaptation therefore helps mainly where the base model is genuinely weak.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates using LoRA adapters to improve a large TTS model (VoxCPM2) for low-resource languages. Training a single bilingual adapter on 26 hours of Khmer and Korean data significantly improves Khmer quality (MOS +0.38) while leaving already-strong Korean unchanged or slightly degraded. Human evaluation and automatic loss disagree on optimal adapter rank.
AI.motivation: Large pretrained TTS models perform poorly on languages underrepresented in their training data. The authors aim to bridge this quality gap efficiently using parameter-efficient fine-tuning (LoRA), without catastrophic forgetting or degradation of high-resource language performance.
AI.method: The authors adapt VoxCPM2 — a 2.4B-parameter, tokenizer-free TTS model combining a MiniCPM-4 language model backbone with a flow-matching diffusion decoder — using a single LoRA adapter applied to both the LM and decoder. The adapter is zero-initialized (preserving the original model at the start) and trained on a shared, language-tagged corpus of ~26 hours containing both Khmer and Korean. Multiple ranks (e.g., 64, 128) are tested, training only 0.19–3.03% of total parameters. Evaluation uses native-speaker MOS listening tests and automatic validation loss.
AI.result: For Khmer, MOS improved significantly from 3.85 (zero-shot) to 4.23 with rank-64 LoRA (p<0.001, paired Wilcoxon test). For Korean, the base model already performed well, and the adapter brought no gain; higher ranks even degraded quality. Validation loss was lowest at rank 128, but human MOS peaked at rank 64, revealing a mismatch between automatic and human evaluation metrics.
AI.conclusion: LoRA-based adaptation is an effective and parameter-efficient method to improve TTS quality specifically for languages where the base model is genuinely weak, without harming performance on languages already handled well. The optimal adapter configuration should be determined by human evaluation rather than automatic loss alone, as the two can disagree.

title: A Multi-Level Validation and Traceability Framework for AI-Generated Telescope Scheduling Decisions
summary: With the gradual introduction of AI into telescope scheduling, AI-based decision-making has shown advantages in handling complex multi-constraint problems. However, its outputs often suffer from inconsistent data references, reasoning errors, and non-executable decisions, limiting applicability in high-reliability observational tasks. In this work, we propose a multi-level validation and traceable reasoning framework that performs systematic reliability verification of AI-generated decisions prior to execution, and enables explicit representation of the reasoning process to support traceable decision-making. The framework integrates data reference validation, logical consistency checks, and observational and instrumental constraint verification to filter and correct invalid decisions. It also introduces atomic reasoning units and their dependency relationships, representing scheduling decisions as a sequence of interconnected reasoning steps that support error localization and post hoc analysis. Experiments show that the framework improves executability and reliability of AI scheduling and reduces loss of transient opportunities. In particular, feedback correction and structured validation of reasoning steps enhance the ability to repair and block erroneous decisions, especially in complex scenarios. Compared with pure AI methods, the framework-enhanced approach maintains flexibility while substantially improving reliability and executability. These results demonstrate a feasible and verifiable pathway for applying AI to high-reliability astronomical observation scheduling.

AI.tldr: Proposes a multi-level validation and traceable reasoning framework that verifies AI-generated telescope scheduling decisions before execution, improving reliability, executability, and error repair in high-stakes astronomical observations.
AI.motivation: AI-based telescope scheduling handles complex multi-constraint problems well but produces outputs with inconsistent data references, reasoning errors, and non-executable decisions — limiting use in high-reliability observational tasks that demand dependable, auditable decision-making.
AI.method: A multi-level validation and traceable reasoning framework operating pre-execution: (1) data reference validation, (2) logical consistency checks, (3) observational and instrumental constraint verification to filter/correct invalid decisions. Introduces atomic reasoning units with dependency relationships, representing scheduling decisions as interconnected reasoning steps enabling error localization and post hoc analysis. Includes feedback correction and structured validation of reasoning steps.
AI.result: The framework improves executability and reliability of AI scheduling and reduces loss of transient opportunities. Feedback correction and structured validation enhance repair and blocking of erroneous decisions, especially in complex scenarios. Maintains flexibility of pure AI methods while substantially improving reliability and executability.
AI.conclusion: The framework demonstrates a feasible and verifiable pathway for deploying AI in high-reliability astronomical observation scheduling, combining AI flexibility with rigorous validation to meet operational dependability requirements.

title: A Causal Foundation Model for Structure and Outcome Prediction
comment: 20 pages, 7 figures, 17 tables, 43rd ICML Workshop on Foundation Models for Structured Data
summary: We introduce TabPFN-CFM, a causal foundation model that can handle multiple causal problems. TabPFN-CFM predicts both causal structure and outcomes from observational data, supports queries on all three levels of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy and uses known graph structure when available to improve predictions. TabPFN-CFM is trained on synthetic datasets, and generalises to real datasets, demonstrating improved performance over both structural and outcome prediction baselines.

AI.tldr: TabPFN-CFM is a causal foundation model trained on synthetic data that generalizes to real-world datasets, handling causal structure discovery and outcome prediction while supporting queries across all three levels of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy.
AI.motivation: Existing causal models are typically specialized for single tasks (e.g., structure learning or treatment effect estimation) and operate at only one level of Pearl's hierarchy. There is a need for a unified foundation model that can flexibly handle multiple causal problems across all three levels (association, intervention, counterfactual), leverage known graph structure when available, and generalize from synthetic training data to real-world applications.
AI.method: The authors propose TabPFN-CFM, extending the TabPFN (Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network) architecture to the causal domain. The model is trained entirely on synthetic datasets covering diverse causal structures and queries. It accepts observational data as input and supports queries at all three levels of Pearl's Causal Hierarchy (observational, interventional, counterfactual). When a known causal graph is available, the model can incorporate this structural prior to improve predictions.
AI.result: TabPFN-CFM demonstrates improved performance over baselines on both structural prediction tasks (causal graph discovery) and outcome prediction tasks. It successfully generalizes from synthetic training data to real-world datasets.
AI.conclusion: TabPFN-CFM represents a step toward unified causal foundation models that can handle multiple causal inference tasks across all levels of Pearl's hierarchy, offering strong generalization from synthetic to real data and the ability to incorporate known causal structure for enhanced performance.

title: Application of LLMs to Threat Assessment of Foreign Peacekeeping Missions
summary: We present a novel approach for applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to threat assessment in the context of foreign peacekeeping missions. Building on the PINPOINT project and its use case, the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia, we combine an interdisciplinary risk-model with OSINT-based media collection and LLM-supported threat extraction. The proposed workflow maps media contents to mission-relevant threats, extracts structured information and applies several additional LLM-based processing steps to improve relevance and grounding. An evaluation of threats extracted from media documents shows high agreement between automatically generated results and human judgment for core aspects such as threat and mission relevance. These results indicate that LLMs provide a promising approach to support analysts in the context of peacekeeping missions.

AI.tldr: A novel LLM-based workflow for threat assessment in peacekeeping missions, combining OSINT media collection with an interdisciplinary risk model, achieves high agreement with human judgment on threat and mission relevance.
AI.motivation: Analysts supporting foreign peacekeeping missions face information overload from open-source media. Automating threat extraction and relevance assessment using LLMs can reduce cognitive burden and improve situational awareness.
AI.method: The authors integrate an interdisciplinary risk model (from the PINPOINT project) with OSINT-based media collection. An LLM-driven pipeline maps media content to mission-relevant threats, extracts structured information, and applies post-processing steps to enhance relevance and factual grounding. The approach is validated on the EU Monitoring Mission in Georgia use case.
AI.result: Evaluation shows high agreement between automatically generated threat assessments and human expert judgments, particularly for threat identification and mission relevance.
AI.conclusion: LLMs offer a promising decision-support tool for analysts in peacekeeping contexts, effectively bridging OSINT data and structured threat assessment.

title: CAT-Q: Cost-efficient and Accurate Ternary Quantization for LLMs
comment: This work is accepted to ICML 2026 as an oral. The project page: https://github.com/IntelChina-AI/BitTern
summary: In this paper, we present CAT-Q, Cost-efficient and Accurate Ternary Quantization, for compressing and accelerating LLMs. Unlike existing state-of-the-art ternary quantization methods that rely on data-intensive and costly quantization-aware training to mitigate severe performance degradation, CAT-Q is a simple yet effective post-training quantization scheme that is readily applicable to LLMs with diverse architectures and model sizes. It has two key components, learnable modulation (LM) and softened ternarization (ST), which are coupled from an optimization perspective. LM leverages a composition of learnable factors to modulate the distribution of pre-trained high-precision weights and the ternary threshold, making them less sensitive to ternarization. ST further introduces a differentiable transition function to guide the ternarization process toward stable convergence. We show that, for pre-trained LLMs with 1.7B to 8B parameters, CAT-Q can efficiently quantize them into ternary models using only 512 calibration samples, while achieving superior performance than the seminal BitNet 1.58-bit v1 and v2 families (with 1.3B to 7B parameters) trained with 100B tokens, yielding about a 100,000X reduction in training tokens. Moreover, we show for the first time that CAT-Q can quantize much larger pre-trained LLMs having 14B to 235B parameters into leading ternary models within just 8 to 60 hours on 8 A100-80GB GPUs. Code is available at https://github.com/IntelChina-AI/BitTern.

AI.tldr: CAT-Q is a post-training ternary quantization method for LLMs that uses learnable modulation and softened ternarization to achieve state-of-the-art ternary model performance with only 512 calibration samples, drastically reducing the data and compute cost compared to quantization-aware training approaches like BitNet.
AI.motivation: Existing ternary quantization methods (e.g., BitNet) rely on costly quantization-aware training with billions of tokens to recover performance. There is a need for an efficient post-training quantization scheme that can ternarize diverse LLMs without expensive retraining while maintaining accuracy.
AI.method: CAT-Q is a post-training quantization method with two key components: (1) Learnable Modulation (LM), which uses learnable factors to modulate pre-trained weight distributions and ternary thresholds to reduce ternarization sensitivity; (2) Softened Ternarization (ST), a differentiable transition function that guides stable optimization convergence. These components are coupled and optimized jointly using only 512 calibration samples.
AI.result: On LLMs from 1.7B–8B parameters, CAT-Q outperforms BitNet 1.58-bit v1/v2 (trained on 100B tokens) while using ~100,000× fewer training tokens. CAT-Q also successfully ternarizes large models (14B–235B) in 8–60 hours on 8 A100 GPUs, marking the first demonstration of ternary quantization at that scale.
AI.conclusion: CAT-Q provides a cost-efficient, accurate, and scalable post-training ternary quantization solution that generalizes across diverse LLM architectures and sizes, significantly lowering the barrier to deploying ternary LLMs.

title: Content-Based Smart E-Mail Dispatcher Using Large Language Models
summary: Email communication has become an integral part of personal and professional life, but handling its vast volume is still a significant issue for large organisations. Manual perusal of emails and forwarding their contents and attachments to intended recipients using other instant messaging platforms has proved to be error-prone and time-consuming leading to losses in terms of productivity and creating undue stress. The main objective of this paper is to explore an alternative mechanism that is to automate the task of dispatching emails based on their contents to the respective WhatsApp groups of students of various semesters of programs in an engineering college, facilitating a smooth flow of information from one end to another end in an organisation. The dispatcher system is built using agents querying large language models (LLMs) to enable it to analyze the contents of emails and route them to the relevant groups of students for their information and consumption. The system harnesses the capabilities of LLMs in analysing the textual contents for decision-making. With a well-structured agent framework prompt that includes email content as input with instructions and context, the system figures out the relevant groups to which the email message is dispatched, thus providing the required information on time. The proposed system does not rely on labelled datasets and provides several benefits, including enhanced productivity and a reduction in the cognitive load associated with reading emails.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes an automated email dispatcher system that uses LLM-powered agents to analyze email content and route messages to appropriate WhatsApp student groups in an engineering college, eliminating manual forwarding errors and reducing cognitive load.
AI.motivation: Manual perusal and forwarding of emails to intended recipients via instant messaging platforms is error-prone, time-consuming, and causes productivity losses and undue stress in large organizations. There is a need for an automated alternative that can reliably route information to the correct audience.
AI.method: A dispatcher system is built using agents that query large language models (LLMs) to analyze email content. A well-structured agent framework prompt incorporates the email content, instructions, and context, enabling the LLM to determine the relevant WhatsApp groups for dispatching without requiring any labeled training datasets.
AI.result: The system successfully figures out the relevant student groups to which email messages should be dispatched, providing timely information delivery. It enhances productivity and reduces the cognitive load associated with reading and manually forwarding emails.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based agent systems offer a viable, label-free solution for automating email routing to messaging platforms, delivering significant organizational benefits in terms of information flow efficiency and reduced human overhead.

title: Epiphany-Aware KV Cache Eviction Without the Attention Matrix
summary: As reasoning models emit chains of thought tens of thousands of tokens long, KV cache increasingly becomes a deployment bottleneck. Existing cache eviction methods rank tokens by attention weight, which is a noisy importance proxy in long reasoning traces, and prohibits the use of fused kernels in production inference by forcing the model to materialize the attention matrix. In this work, we instead score tokens with a metric we term the epiphany score: the change in the model's internal representation, read directly from the forward pass with no attention matrix and negligible extra state. Our resulting cache eviction method, EpiKV, requires no training, classifier, or custom kernel, and can be used directly in FlashAttention inference stacks unchanged -- scaling to a 16x longer feasible context than attention-based scoring. upper-mid layers negatively) and remove a positional trend with a causal rolling z-score. At a 4096-token cache EpiKV reaches 72% on MATH-500, matching the strongest attention-based baseline (ThinKV 71%, H2O 67%); a lag-normalized KV variant reaches 37% on AIME-2024 at 8192 tokens against the best of them (33%), at up to 2.8x the speed.

AI.tldr: EpiKV introduces a novel KV cache eviction method for long reasoning traces that scores tokens by "epiphany score" — the change in the model's internal representations measured directly from the forward pass, without requiring attention matrix materialization. It matches or exceeds attention-weight-based baselines (ThinKV, H2O) on MATH-500 and AIME-2024 benchmarks while enabling up to 2.8× speedup and 16× longer feasible context via FlashAttention compatibility.
AI.motivation: As reasoning models emit extremely long chain-of-thought traces (tens of thousands of tokens), KV cache becomes a critical deployment bottleneck. Existing eviction methods rely on attention weights as importance proxies, which are noisy for long reasoning traces and force materialization of the attention matrix, precluding the use of fused kernels like FlashAttention in production inference pipelines.
AI.method: EpiKV computes an "epiphany score" — the magnitude of change in the model's internal representations between consecutive layers — read directly from the forward pass with no attention matrix and negligible extra state. It identifies that upper-middle layers contribute negatively and applies a causal rolling z-score to remove positional bias. The method is training-free, requires no classifier or custom kernel, and works natively with FlashAttention.
AI.result: At a 4096-token cache budget, EpiKV achieves 72% on MATH-500 (vs. ThinKV 71%, H2O 67%). A lag-normalized variant reaches 37% on AIME-2024 at 8192 tokens (vs. best baseline 33%), with up to 2.8× speedup. The approach scales to 16× longer feasible context than attention-based scoring methods.
AI.conclusion: EpiKV demonstrates that representation-level change (epiphany) is a more effective and efficient token importance signal than attention weights for KV cache eviction in long reasoning traces, enabling significant context scaling and speedup without modifying production FlashAttention inference stacks.

title: PRISM: PE Relational Inter-Section Matrix. A 2D Section-Aware Dataset for Static PE Malware Detection
summary:
We introduce PRISM (PE Relational Inter-Section Matrix), an open dataset and feature representation for static Windows PE malware detection. Existing benchmarks such as EMBER, BODMAS, and SOREL-20M represent each PE file as a flat one-dimensional feature vector, discarding the ordering of sections and the relational context between them. PRISM instead encodes every binary as a two-dimensional matrix whose rows are individual PE sections in file order, with a global summary row that preserves compatibility with EMBER-style models. We build the corpus from four malware sources (BODMAS, MalwareBazaar, VirusShare, and CAPE) together with SOREL-20M benign software, yielding 83,633 deduplicated matrices and a family-filtered analysis corpus of 49,204 samples across 684 malware families.
  A formal separability analysis (Fisher Discriminant Ratio, mutual information, and inter-section information gain) shows that the per-section positional structure carries discriminative information that flat representations cannot capture. Under a strictly controlled, sample-matched comparison, a gradient-boosted classifier on the compact PRISM representation recovers nearly all of the binary-detection performance of the same classifier on the much larger EMBER vector, at roughly one-sixth the dimensionality; EMBER retains only a small, consistent advantage confined to the extreme low-false-positive regime, the two being operationally indistinguishable at the decision threshold. We are explicit that this binary task is saturated, so the structural content PRISM preserves is reserved for tasks with greater metric headroom, such as family classification and architectures that exploit the 2D structure directly. The dataset, extraction library, trained models, and full analysis pipeline are released under CC BY-NC-SA and MIT licences.

AI.tldr: PRISM introduces a 2D matrix representation for PE malware detection that preserves per-section ordering and relational context, offering comparable binary detection to EMBER at one-sixth the dimensionality, with the structural encoding reserved for tasks like family classification where greater headroom exists.
AI.motivation: Existing malware benchmarks (EMBER, BODMAS, SOREL-20M) flatten PE files into one-dimensional feature vectors, discarding the ordinal structure of PE sections and the relational information between them. This structural loss limits the discriminative capacity for tasks beyond saturated binary detection, such as malware family classification.
AI.method: PRISM encodes each PE binary as a 2D matrix where rows correspond to individual PE sections in file order, plus a global summary row for EMBER compatibility. The corpus aggregates 83,633 deduplicated matrices from BODMAS, MalwareBazaar, VirusShare, CAPE, and SOREL-20M benign sources. A formal separability analysis uses Fisher Discriminant Ratio, mutual information, and inter-section information gain to quantify structural discriminability. A gradient-boosted classifier on PRISM is compared against EMBER under strict sample-matched controls.
AI.result: The per-section positional structure carries discriminative information absent from flat representations. PRISM achieves nearly identical binary detection performance to EMBER at roughly 1/6 the dimensionality, with EMBER holding only a small edge in the extreme low-FPR regime. At the decision threshold, the two are operationally indistinguishable. The binary task is acknowledged as saturated; structural benefits are directed toward family classification and 2D-capable architectures.
AI.conclusion: PRISM demonstrates that compact, structurally-aware PE representations can match much larger flat feature vectors for binary malware detection. The released dataset and tooling (CC BY-NC-SA / MIT) enable future work on family classification and models that exploit 2D structure directly, where the real discriminative value of section-level relational encoding lies.

title: LLM-based Models for Detecting Emerging Topics in Service Feedback
summary:
Enhancing the analysis of service feedback is essential for public sector organizations, particularly tax administrations, where trust and compliance depend on fair and effective service delivery. As feedback volumes grow, identifying emerging service quality issues and potential disparities across diverse populations becomes increasingly challenging. Traditional approaches often rely on manual review or static expert-defined indicators, limiting scalability and the ability to capture complex patterns in textual feedback.
  This paper presents a novel methodology that integrates large language models (LLMs), statistical techniques, and human-AI collaboration to improve multilingual customer feedback analysis. The primary objective is to detect emerging service quality topics that may also reveal potential inequities in service delivery. Our framework combines fine-tuned, quantized LLMs with expert oversight to produce accurate, computationally efficient, and context-aware analyses.
  The proposed approach was evaluated using similarity analysis and assessments from experienced tax officers, demonstrating stronger alignment with expert judgments than baseline models. By incorporating a human-in-the-loop framework, the methodology reduces LLM fabrication while improving the reliability and relevance of generated insights.
  The results demonstrate the practicality of combining LLMs with human expertise to support scalable, evidence-based decision-making in public sector organizations. This work contributes to the development of responsible AI systems that enhance service quality, responsiveness, fairness, and public trust through more effective analysis of multilingual customer feedback.

AI.tldr: A human-AI collaborative framework combining fine-tuned quantized LLMs with expert oversight to detect emerging service quality issues and potential inequities in multilingual customer feedback for tax administrations.
AI.motivation: Growing volumes of multilingual customer feedback in public sector tax administrations make manual review and static expert-defined indicators insufficient for detecting emerging service quality issues and service delivery disparities across diverse populations.
AI.method: A methodology integrating fine-tuned, quantized large language models with statistical techniques and a human-in-the-loop framework, where expert oversight corrects LLM outputs to reduce fabrication and improve contextual accuracy.
AI.result: Similarity analysis and assessments by experienced tax officers showed the proposed framework achieved stronger alignment with expert judgments compared to baseline models, while the human-in-the-loop component reduced LLM fabrication and improved insight reliability.
AI.conclusion: Combining LLMs with human expertise provides a practical, scalable approach for evidence-based decision-making in public sector organizations, contributing to responsible AI systems that enhance service quality, fairness, and public trust.

title: When Does Quality-Aware Multimodal Fusion Matter? A Leakage-Safe Diagnostic for Decision-Level Dependence
comment: Accepted to INTERSPEECH 2026. 5 pages, 1 figure, 5 tables
summary: Many multimodal systems estimate the reliability of each modality and weight their contributions to the final prediction. However, it remains unclear whether these scores influence model decisions or merely correlate with performance. We propose a simple diagnostic to test whether reliability information is used during inference. After training, the model and inputs are fixed while reliability scores are permuted across test examples. If predictions depend on these scores, performance should degrade. Experiments on StressID for stress recognition and CMU-MOSEI for sentiment analysis show that permuting reliability scores leaves performance unchanged despite substantial potential gains from selecting the best modality per example. In positive controls where reliability signals identify the correct modality, the same frozen fusion rules yield significant improvements, indicating that reliability signals influence fused decisions only when they reliably predict unimodal correctness.

AI.tldr: A diagnostic test reveals that multimodal fusion models do not actually use learned reliability scores during inference, despite these scores theoretically identifying the best modality. Permuting scores leaves performance unchanged, while positive controls show fusion rules can leverage reliable signals when they genuinely predict correctness.
AI.motivation: Many multimodal systems claim to weight modalities by estimated reliability, but it is unclear whether these learned reliability scores causally influence model decisions or merely correlate with performance post-hoc. The authors aim to distinguish genuine reliance from spurious correlation.
AI.method: A permutation-based diagnostic: after training, all model parameters and inputs are frozen while reliability scores are randomly permuted across test examples. If the model genuinely uses reliability information during inference, permuting these scores should degrade performance. Positive controls are constructed where reliability signals are engineered to correctly identify the best modality per example.
AI.result: Permuting reliability scores leaves performance unchanged across StressID (stress recognition) and CMU-MOSEI (sentiment analysis) datasets, despite substantial oracle gains when the best modality per example is selected. In positive controls where reliability signals reliably predict unimodal correctness, the same frozen fusion rules yield significant improvements.
AI.conclusion: Current multimodal fusion models do not meaningfully leverage reliability scores during inference. The diagnostic can serve as a standard test to verify whether future architectures genuinely incorporate reliability information into their decision-making process.

title: The Observer World: A Cryptographic Extension of Impagliazzo's Five Worlds
summary: Impagliazzo's five worlds classify computational assumptions along a single axis, the existence of cryptographic primitives. All five worlds implicitly assume that every party, including the adversary, observes the full input, that the observer is always $O_{top}$. This assumption is so natural that it is never stated. This work makes it explicit and relaxes it by introducing a second, orthogonal axis, the observational axis, defined by the observer hierarchy introduced in previous work. Relaxing the assumption reveals structural phenomena, such as the collapse $P^{O_{prof}} = NP^{O_{prof}} \subset P$, that the five-world framework cannot express. We prove that this collapse holds unconditionally in all five worlds, showing that observational blindness and computational hardness are independent. We define the Observer World $W_O$, classify all world-observer pairs, identify the labeled cells (a)--(d), and introduce a parametric family $W_O^{\varepsilon}$ modelling partial violations of observational invariants. The framework also interfaces with physical information limits, including thermodynamic, quantum, and cosmological bounds.

AI.tldr: This paper extends Impagliazzo's five worlds by adding a second, orthogonal "observational axis" based on an observer hierarchy. It shows that observational blindness (what the observer can see) is independent of computational hardness, proves a collapse P^O_prof = NP^O_prof ⊂ P unconditionally in all five worlds, and introduces a parametric family modeling partial violations of observational invariants.
AI.motivation: Impagliazzo's five worlds classify computational worlds solely by the existence of cryptographic primitives, but they implicitly and unstatedly assume a fully-observing adversary (O_top). This work makes that assumption explicit and argues that relaxing it—by considering restricted observers—reveals structural phenomena invisible to the original framework, demonstrating that observational constraints constitute an independent axis of classification.
AI.method: The authors introduce a second, orthogonal axis defined by an observer hierarchy (from prior work). They analyze the interaction between this observer hierarchy and the five worlds, proving an unconditional collapse (P^O_prof = NP^O_prof ⊂ P) across all five worlds. They define an "Observer World" W_O, classify all world-observer pairs into labeled cells (a)-(d), and introduce a parametric family W_O^ε to model partial violations of observational invariants. The framework is also interfaced with physical information bounds (thermodynamic, quantum, cosmological).
AI.result: The key result is the unconditional proof that P^O_prof = NP^O_prof ⊂ P holds in all five of Impagliazzo's worlds, establishing that observational blindness and computational hardness are independent dimensions. The classification yields labeled cells (a)-(d) for world-observer pairs, and the parametric family W_O^ε captures graded violations of observational invariants.
AI.conclusion: Observational constraints form an independent axis orthogonal to computational hardness in classifying cryptographic worlds. Relaxing the implicit O_top assumption reveals structure the five-world framework cannot express. The unified framework accommodates not only computational and observational dimensions but also physical information-theoretic limits, suggesting a richer taxonomy for reasoning about security and computation under bounded observation.

title: Beyond Logical Forms: LLM-Extracted Patterns for Fallacy Classification
summary: In today's fast-paced information era, logical fallacies, defined as defective patterns of reasoning, inevitably contribute to the growth of information disorder. However, often fallacies appear in nuanced forms that complicate automated classification. In this study, we investigate whether merging abstract logical structures with context-level linguistic cues proves beneficial for fallacy classification, developing a framework that inductively extracts such patterns from fallacious examples and their explanations using Large Language Models (LLMs). We evaluate the impact of these patterns across different LLMs and experimental zero- and one-shot configurations, showing statistically significant improvements over zero-shot baselines and outperforming competing approaches. Cross-dataset experiments validate generalization, establishing data-driven pattern extraction as an effective method for generating logical representations.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a framework that uses LLMs to inductively extract abstract logical patterns from fallacious examples and their explanations, then merges these patterns with contextual linguistic cues to improve logical fallacy classification, demonstrating significant gains over zero-shot baselines and competing methods across datasets.
AI.motivation: Logical fallacies drive information disorder, but their nuanced, context-dependent nature makes automated classification challenging. Prior approaches often rely solely on surface-level linguistic cues or hand-crafted logical rules, missing the interplay between abstract reasoning structures and contextual language. The authors aim to bridge this gap.
AI.method: A two-stage framework: (1) LLMs are prompted with fallacious examples and human-written explanations to inductively extract abstract logical patterns (e.g., fallacy schemas, reasoning flaws); (2) these extracted patterns are then combined with context-level linguistic features and fed as prompts or structured inputs to LLM classifiers in zero-shot and one-shot settings for fallacy classification.
AI.result: The pattern-enhanced approach yields statistically significant improvements over pure zero-shot baselines and outperforms competing classification methods. Cross-dataset experiments confirm strong generalization, validating that data-driven, inductively extracted logical representations are effective across domains.
AI.conclusion: Merging abstract logical structures with contextual linguistic cues, obtained via inductive pattern extraction from LLMs, is a robust and generalizable strategy for improving automated fallacy classification. The framework establishes data-driven logical representation learning as a promising direction for reasoning-centric NLP tasks.

title: Autoformalization of Agent Instructions into Policy-as-Code
comment: Accepted at the Second Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD), ICML 2026
summary: Agent safety in high-stakes domains requires formal policy enforcement, but most existing approaches either rely on probabilistic guardrails (fine-tuned classifiers, prompt-based steering) that offer no formal guarantees, or on hand-coded symbolic enforcement that does not scale to the breadth of real policy specifications. We present an autoformalization pipeline that translates agent prompts, MCP tool descriptions, and natural language policy documents into formally verified policies using an LLM-based generator-critic loop. The resulting policies are written in the Cedar Policy Language. On the MedAgentBench benchmark, our autoformalized policies cover substantially more of the source natural-language specification than the hand-coded symbolic enforcement in prior work.

AI.tldr: An autoformalization pipeline using an LLM-based generator-critic loop translates natural-language agent specifications into formally verified Cedar policies, achieving broader policy coverage than hand-coded symbolic enforcement on MedAgentBench.
AI.motivation: Current agent safety approaches fall into two unsatisfactory categories: probabilistic guardrails (classifiers, prompt steering) lack formal guarantees, while hand-coded symbolic enforcement doesn't scale to the breadth of real-world policy specifications. There is a need for enforceable formal policies that combine rigor with coverage.
AI.method: An autoformalization pipeline that takes agent prompts, MCP tool descriptions, and natural-language policy documents as input. It employs an LLM-based generator-critic loop to translate these into formally verified policies expressed in the Cedar Policy Language.
AI.result: On the MedAgentBench benchmark, the autoformalized policies cover substantially more of the natural-language specification than the hand-coded symbolic enforcement from prior work.
AI.conclusion: Autoformalization via LLM-based generator-critic loops is a viable path toward scalable, formally verified policy enforcement for agent safety, outperforming hand-coded alternatives in coverage while preserving formal guarantees.

title: Localizing RL-Induced Tool Use to a Single Crosscoder Feature
comment: Accepted as a spotlight at the ICML 2026 Mechanistic Interpretability Workshop
summary: Fine-tuning through RL reshapes the internal representations of language models to enable agentic behaviors such as tool use, yet the mechanistic basis of these changes remains poorly understood. While RL substantially improves structured tool-call generation, it is unclear which features emerge, which are preserved, and whether identified features can be leveraged for retraining-free behavioral control. In this work, we show that $\textit{Dedicated Feature Crosscoders (DFC)}$ isolate a compact set of RL-specific features that mediate tool-calling capability in $\texttt{Qwen2.5-3B}$. Across a $48$-crosscoder hyperparameter sweep, encode-decode reconstruction improves the RL model's tool correctness by $+31.1 \pm {9.7}$ pp and passively transfers tool-calling ability to the frozen base model by $+6.8 \pm 5.0$ pp which we call a $\textit{capability spillover}$. Our findings show that DFC partitioning concentrates RL-introduced capability into a minimal, steerable feature set that enables runtime behavioral control of agentic LLMs.

AI.tldr: A compact set of RL-specific features mediating tool-calling capability in Qwen2.5-3B is identified using Dedicated Feature Crosscoders (DFC). These features, isolated via a 48-crosscoder hyperparameter sweep, not only improve the RL model's tool correctness by +31.1 pp but also passively transfer tool-calling ability to the frozen base model (+6.8 pp capability spillover), enabling runtime behavioral control without retraining.
AI.motivation: While RL fine-tuning demonstrably reshapes LM representations to enable agentic behaviors like tool use, the mechanistic basis remains poorly understood — specifically, which features emerge, which are preserved, and whether they can be leveraged for retraining-free behavioral control.
AI.method: The authors propose Dedicated Feature Crosscoders (DFC) to isolate RL-specific features in Qwen2.5-3B. A systematic sweep across 48 crosscoder hyperparameter configurations is conducted, measuring encode-decode reconstruction fidelity and the resulting impact on tool-calling correctness in both the RL-tuned model and the frozen base model.
AI.result: DFC reconstruction improves the RL model's tool-calling correctness by +31.1 ± 9.7 percentage points. Furthermore, a "capability spillover" effect is observed: applying the isolated RL features to the frozen base model passively transfers tool-calling ability by +6.8 ± 5.0 percentage points.
AI.conclusion: DFC partitioning successfully concentrates RL-introduced agentic capability into a minimal, steerable feature set. This enables runtime behavioral control of agentic LLMs without retraining, demonstrating that RL-derived tool-use capabilities are mechanistically localized and transferable.

title: Tilikum: Transaction Fair Ordering on a DAG without Weak Edges
summary: Decentralized Finance (DeFi) applications rely heavily on the order in which transactions are executed, making them susceptible to reordering attacks that enable adversaries to extract Blockchain Extractable Value (BEV). While linear blockchain systems such as Ethereum have inspired extensive research into fair ordering mechanisms, DAG-based consensus protocols have remained largely unprotected despite their growing adoption for scalability and performance. In this paper, we introduce Tilikum, a DAG-based ledger protocol that ensures fair transaction ordering without relying on weak edges. Tilikum achieves ordering linearizability by leveraging median-based timestamp aggregation, or batch order fairness, while maintaining low data redundancy and robust garbage collection. We implemented Tilikum in Rust and evaluated it against representative baselines, namely Narwhal/Tusk, Pompē, Themis and FairDAG. Our results show that Tilikum achieves up to $39\times$ higher throughput than other fair-ordering baselines, while fully blocking state-of-the-art DAG-specific reordering attacks.

AI.tldr: Tilikum is a DAG-based ledger protocol that achieves fair transaction ordering through median-based timestamp aggregation, providing batch order fairness without weak edges. It delivers up to 39× higher throughput than existing fair-ordering DAG protocols while fully blocking state-of-the-art reordering attacks.
AI.motivation: DeFi applications are vulnerable to transaction reordering attacks that extract BEV. While linear blockchains (e.g., Ethereum) have seen extensive fair-ordering research, DAG-based consensus protocols—increasingly adopted for scalability—lack comparable protection against such attacks.
AI.method: The authors propose Tilikum, a DAG-based ledger protocol that uses median-based timestamp aggregation to achieve ordering linearizability and batch order fairness. It eliminates reliance on weak edges and incorporates low data redundancy with robust garbage collection. The protocol is implemented in Rust and benchmarked against Narwhal/Tusk, Pompē, Themis, and FairDAG.
AI.result: Tilikum achieves up to 39× higher throughput than fair-ordering baselines and fully blocks state-of-the-art DAG-specific reordering attacks.
AI.conclusion: Tilikum demonstrates that DAG-based consensus protocols can be hardened against reordering attacks without sacrificing performance, offering a practical solution for fair transaction ordering in scalable, high-throughput blockchain systems.

title: SKILL-DISCO: Distilling and Compiling Agent Traces into Reusable Procedural Skills
summary: Agents often repeatedly solve similar task instances from scratch, leading to unnecessary reasoning cost and long execution traces. Prior work has explored workflow reuse and executable skill induction, but it remains unclear which task scenarios admit procedural skills and how the shared procedural structure should be represented across successful traces. We study this problem in FSM-defined scenarios, where successful traces can be viewed as paths in an unknown transition graph, and formulate procedural skills as reusable parameterized control-flow subgraphs. Based on this view, we introduce SkillDisCo, a distillation-and-compilation framework that distills reusable PFSM subgraphs from successful traces and compiles them into callable, executable, and verifiable procedural skills. Experiments on ALFWorld and WebArena show that SkillDisCo improves success rates and reduces agent turns across benchmarks and model scales, demonstrating the benefits of representing shared experience as reusable execution structures.

AI.tldr: SkillDisCo distills reusable procedural skills from successful task execution traces by representing them as parameterized finite-state machine (PFSM) subgraphs, then compiles them into callable, executable, and verifiable skills. This reduces redundant reasoning and shortens execution traces, improving success rates and efficiency on ALFWorld and WebArena.
AI.motivation: Agents incur unnecessary reasoning cost and produce long execution traces by repeatedly solving similar tasks from scratch. While prior work explores workflow reuse and skill induction, it remains unclear which task scenarios admit procedural skills and how shared procedural structure should be represented across traces.
AI.method: The authors formalize tasks as FSM-defined scenarios where successful traces are paths in an unknown transition graph. Procedural skills are defined as reusable parameterized control-flow subgraphs (PFSM subgraphs). SkillDisCo operates in two phases: (1) distillation — extracting reusable PFSM subgraphs from successful traces, and (2) compilation — converting these subgraphs into callable, executable, and verifiable procedural skills that agents can invoke.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld and WebArena benchmarks show that SkillDisCo improves success rates and reduces the number of agent turns across different model scales, validating the benefit of representing shared experience as reusable execution structures.
AI.conclusion: Representing shared experience as reusable PFSM-based procedural skills effectively reduces redundant reasoning in agents, leading to higher success rates and more efficient execution across diverse benchmarks and model sizes.

title: Retrieval-Warmed Energy-Based Reasoning: A Five-Arm Ablation Methodology for Diffusion-as-Inference on Structured Reasoning Tasks
summary: Warm-started diffusion samplers accelerate iterative inference, but it is rarely clear which part of the pipeline carries the gain. We study \textbf{retrieval-warmed energy-based reasoning (RW-EBR)} -- an IRED energy-based diffusion model \cite{du2024ired} augmented with a Modern Hopfield trajectory memory -- and contribute a \textbf{five-arm ablation methodology} (oracle, best-constant, per-query-random, shuffled, aligned) that separates three confounded effects: class-prior bias shift, stochastic warm-starting, and graph-aligned value reuse. The diagnostic decomposition is adapted from LLM-RAG evaluation \cite{ru2024ragchecker}. On \textbf{connectivity-2} (Erdős--Rényi all-pairs reachability), the aligned-vs-shuffled-oracle swing reaches \textbf{$+35$\,pp} balanced accuracy on a fixed 1{,}000-graph validation-set diagnostic, with value distribution and retrieval mechanics fixed, only per-graph alignment destroyed, while per-query random initialisation falls below cold -- per-graph alignment, not bias shift or stochasticity, dominates. Yet the \emph{deployable} cold-prediction pipeline misses the acceptance gate at stored-value quality. The same diagnostic logic, stopped at the key-quality screen, applied to \textbf{Sudoku} with a task-specific key encoder produces a clean negative at a \emph{different} component -- key quality, under the current setup. The decomposition names the first blocking component on each task. The setting -- graph reachability refined by an iterative diffusion sampler, with explainability of failure modes as the lens -- places the work within structured and spatio-temporal reasoning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a five-arm ablation methodology (oracle, best-constant, per-query-random, shuffled, aligned) to disentangle confounded effects in retrieval-warmed diffusion samplers, revealing that per-graph alignment dominates performance gains on graph reachability, while key quality bottlenecks Sudoku performance.
AI.motivation: Warm-started diffusion samplers accelerate inference, but it is unclear which pipeline component (class-prior bias shift, stochastic warm-starting, or graph-aligned value reuse) actually carries the performance gain. The authors aim to isolate and identify the dominant factor.
AI.method: The paper proposes RW-EBR (retrieval-warmed energy-based reasoning), an IRED energy-based diffusion model augmented with a Modern Hopfield trajectory memory. A five-arm ablation diagnostic — oracle, best-constant, per-query-random, shuffled, and aligned — adapted from LLM-RAG evaluation (Ru et al. 2024), is used to separate three confounded effects: class-prior bias shift, stochastic warm-starting, and graph-aligned value reuse. The methodology is applied to two tasks: Erdős–Rényi all-pairs reachability (connectivity-2) and Sudoku.
AI.result: On connectivity-2, the aligned-vs-shuffled-oracle swing reaches +35 pp balanced accuracy on a fixed 1,000-graph validation set, with value distribution and retrieval mechanics held constant — only per-graph alignment destroyed. Per-query random initialization falls below cold performance, confirming per-graph alignment dominates. The deployable cold-prediction pipeline misses the acceptance gate at stored-value quality. On Sudoku, the same diagnostic logic reveals a clean negative at key quality under the current setup.
AI.conclusion: The five-arm diagnostic decomposition successfully names the first blocking component on each task: per-graph alignment dominates for connectivity-2, while key quality is the bottleneck for Sudoku. The framework provides explainability of failure modes in iterative diffusion samplers within structured reasoning domains.

title: Evaluation Pitfalls and Challenges in Multimedia Event Extraction
summary: Multimedia event extraction aims to jointly identify events and their arguments across multiple modalities, such as text and images, to support more comprehensive event understanding. While recent work reports steady and substantial progress, the reliability and comparability of these results critically depend on consistent and rigorous evaluation. In this work, we present the first systematic analysis of evaluation pitfalls in multimedia event extraction and identify three major sources of issues: inconsistent data processing, inconsistent task assumptions, and overly relaxed evaluation settings. We demonstrate, through a series of controlled experiments under a strict evaluation framework, that minor evaluation choices can cause large performance variations and lead to overestimation of a model's ability to ground real-world events across modalities. Our findings highlight the need for comparable evaluation standards and encourage a shift toward more rigorous evaluation in multimedia event extraction.

AI.tldr: This paper exposes three major evaluation pitfalls in multimedia event extraction—inconsistent data processing, inconsistent task assumptions, and overly relaxed evaluation settings—and demonstrates through controlled experiments that minor evaluation choices can substantially inflate performance estimates, urging the field toward more rigorous and standardized evaluation practices.
AI.motivation: Despite steady reported progress in multimedia event extraction (MEE), the reliability and comparability of results are questionable due to the absence of consistent and rigorous evaluation standards. The authors aim to systematically diagnose and quantify how evaluation choices distort performance measurements.
AI.method: The authors conduct a systematic analysis identifying three categories of evaluation pitfalls. They then design a strict evaluation framework and run a series of controlled experiments where individual evaluation variables (e.g., data splits, preprocessing, label assumptions) are isolated and varied to measure their impact on reported performance across existing MEE models.
AI.result: Minor evaluation choices—spanning data preprocessing inconsistencies, differing task assumptions (e.g., closed-world vs. open-world event types), and relaxed matching criteria—lead to large performance variations and systematic overestimation of models' cross-modal event grounding capabilities.
AI.conclusion: The MEE community urgently needs comparable, standardized evaluation protocols. The work calls for a shift toward stricter evaluation to ensure that progress reflects genuine advances in multimodal event understanding rather than artifacts of lenient or inconsistent benchmarking.

title: NebulaExp-8B: An Empirical Post-Training Pipeline via Full-Scale Ablation Research
summary: Post-training alignment determines the reasoning and human preference following capabilities of large language models, yet most existing works withhold detailed data construction, filtering rules and training recipes, which hinders community reproducibility and lightweight model optimization. This work presents NebulaExp, a fully transparent, ablation-driven post-training pipeline built on Qwen3-8B-base, covering two orthogonal model branches: general instruct model and complex reasoning-specialized model. We curate a raw corpus of 3.84M multi-source SFT samples and a 200K verifiable RL candidate pool, and design an end-to-end data processing stack including response distillation, multi-dimensional cross-verification filtering, fine-grained difficulty grading, task classification and diversity-aware sampling. For the Instruct branch, our three-stage optimized supervised fine-tuning approach NebulaExp-Ins-SFT improves the average benchmark score from the 55.01 baseline of Qwen3-8B-nothink to 60.99. GRPO reinforcement learning then further elevates the average score to 61.85. For the Reasoning branch, medium-difficulty GRPO RL improves average reasoning score from 73.88 to 75.17. To address RL's dependency on task verifiers, we systematically investigate single-teacher and multi-teacher OPD (MOPD): utilizing merely 4K instruction-following samples and outperforms RL baseline by 3.26 points on IFEval with +4.43 average overall gain; MOPD fuses four domain-specialist teachers with merely 10K samples, lifting average performance by 4.18 over the base model. This report provides a fully reproducible empirical post-training recipe for 8B-scale LLMs, and comprehensively dissects the capability trade-offs among instruction adherence, mathematical reasoning, code generation and general knowledge.

AI.tldr: NebulaExp presents a fully transparent, reproducible post-training pipeline for Qwen3-8B-base, with separate Instruct and Reasoning branches. It details data curation (3.84M SFT samples, 200K RL candidates), filtering, and training recipes. The Instruct branch achieves 61.85 average score via SFT+GRPO; the Reasoning branch reaches 75.17. The paper also investigates Off-Policy Distillation (OPD), showing MOPD with 10K samples outperforms RL baselines significantly.
AI.motivation: Most existing post-training alignment works withhold detailed data construction, filtering rules, and training recipes, which hinders reproducibility and limits lightweight model optimization. This work aims to provide a fully transparent, ablation-driven empirical pipeline for the community.
AI.method: Built on Qwen3-8B-base, NebulaExp constructs two orthogonal branches: (1) General Instruct model using three-stage optimized SFT (NebulaExp-Ins-SFT) followed by GRPO reinforcement learning; (2) Complex Reasoning model using medium-difficulty GRPO RL. The pipeline includes end-to-end data processing: response distillation, multi-dimensional cross-verification filtering, fine-grained difficulty grading, task classification, and diversity-aware sampling from a 3.84M SFT corpus and 200K verifiable RL pool. The paper also investigates single-teacher and multi-teacher Off-Policy Distillation (MOPD), using only 4K–10K samples to outperform RL baselines.
AI.result: Instruct branch: SFT improves average benchmark from 55.01 to 60.99; GRPO further lifts to 61.85. Reasoning branch: medium-difficulty GRPO improves average reasoning score from 73.88 to 75.17. OPD: single-teacher OPD with 4K samples outperforms RL baseline by 3.26 on IFEval with +4.43 average gain; MOPD with four domain specialists and 10K samples lifts average by 4.18 over base model.
AI.conclusion: The report delivers a fully reproducible post-training recipe for 8B-scale LLMs, comprehensively dissecting capability trade-offs among instruction adherence, mathematical reasoning, code generation, and general knowledge. OPD methods (especially MOPD) emerge as efficient alternatives to RL, achieving strong performance with far fewer samples.

title: What Survives When You Compress a Recursive Reasoner for the Edge?
summary: Recursive reasoning models can solve complex structured tasks with only a few million parameters by repeatedly updating a latent state. Deploying these models on edge hardware requires significant compression, but unlike conventional sequence models, quantization errors compound across recursive reasoning cycles rather than across output tokens. As a result, standard intuitions about compression fail to apply. In this work, we ask what survives when recursive reasoners are compressed. Across a full precision sweep, three tasks, and two recursive architectures, we find that aggressive compression preserves local prediction but destroys global reasoning: cell accuracy holds while puzzle-exact accuracy collapses to zero under naive INT4 pruning, distillation, and linear attention alike. Token-level objectives, including quantization-aware training, cannot repair it. The collapse is architectural -- it strikes MLP-mixing recursion but not attention on the same task -- and we reverse it with per-channel calibrated INT4 without retraining. We also introduce carry-trajectory fidelity, the cosine similarity to the full-precision reasoning path, as a label-free signal that predicts this damage and its recovery before a task evaluation. The combined result is a deployment recipe: flash-streamed embeddings remove a 99.4MB bottleneck, INT8 at one cycle matches full-depth accuracy at 6x fewer FLOPs (8MB SoC), and calibrated INT4 fits a 4MB microcontroller.

AI.tldr: Compressing recursive reasoning models (e.g., INT4 quantization, pruning, distillation) destroys global puzzle-solving accuracy even though local token prediction holds up. The collapse is architectural—affecting MLP-mixing but not attention-based recursion—and can be reversed with per-channel calibrated INT4. The authors introduce carry-trajectory fidelity as a label-free signal to predict compression damage, and provide a deployment recipe enabling recursive reasoners to fit on microcontrollers as small as 4MB.
AI.motivation: Recursive reasoning models achieve strong structured-task performance with few parameters by iteratively updating a latent state, making them attractive for edge deployment. However, compression is essential for edge hardware, and standard quantization approaches fail because errors compound across recursive cycles (not just output tokens), breaking conventional compression intuitions. The work investigates what capabilities survive compression in recursive reasoners.
AI.method: The authors conduct a full precision sweep across three tasks and two recursive architectures (MLP-mixing and attention-based recursion). They apply naive INT4 quantization, pruning, distillation, and linear attention, then evaluate both local prediction (cell accuracy) and global reasoning (puzzle-exact accuracy). They introduce carry-trajectory fidelity—cosine similarity to the full-precision reasoning path—as a label-free diagnostic. They also test quantization-aware training, per-channel calibrated INT4 without retraining, and propose a deployment recipe using flash-streamed embeddings, INT8 at one cycle, and calibrated INT4.
AI.result: Naive INT4 compression, pruning, and distillation preserve local (cell) accuracy but cause puzzle-exact accuracy to collapse to zero. Token-level objectives including quantization-aware training cannot fix this. The collapse is architectural: it affects MLP-mixing recursion but not attention-based recursion. Per-channel calibrated INT4 without retraining reverses the collapse. Carry-trajectory fidelity reliably predicts compression damage and recovery without requiring task evaluation. Flash-streamed embeddings remove a 99.4MB bottleneck; INT8 at one cycle matches full-depth accuracy with 6× fewer FLOPs (8MB SoC); calibrated INT4 fits a 4MB microcontroller.
AI.conclusion: Compressing recursive reasoners requires architecture-aware strategies: naive compression destroys global reasoning while preserving local predictions, but calibrated per-channel INT4 can recover it. Carry-trajectory fidelity offers a practical, label-free signal for anticipating compression damage. The proposed deployment recipe enables recursive reasoning models to run efficiently on severely resource-constrained edge devices.

title: OPID: On-Policy Skill Distillation for Agentic Reinforcement Learning
summary: Outcome-based reinforcement learning provides a stable optimization backbone for language agents, but its sparse trajectory-level rewards provide little guidance on which intermediate decisions should be reinforced or suppressed. On-policy self-distillation offers dense token-level supervision, yet existing skill-conditioned variants often rely on external skill memories or retrieved privileged context, which are costly to maintain and can be mismatched with the state distribution induced by the current policy in multi-turn interaction. We propose \textbf{OPID} (\textbf{O}n-\textbf{P}olicy Sk\textbf{i}ll \textbf{D}istillation), a framework that extracts skill supervision directly from completed on-policy trajectories. OPID represents trajectory hindsight as hierarchical skills: episode-level skills capture global workflows or failure-avoidance rules, while step-level skills capture local decision knowledge at critical timesteps. A critical-first routing mechanism uses step-level skills when critical decisions are identified and falls back to episode-level skills as default guidance otherwise. The selected skill is injected into the interaction history, allowing the old policy to re-score the same sampled response under both original and skill-augmented contexts. The resulting log-probability shift yields a token-level self-distillation advantage, which is combined with the outcome advantage for policy optimization. OPID thus preserves RL as the primary training objective while introducing dense, distribution-matched hindsight supervision. Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop and Search-based QA demonstrate that OPID generally improves agent performance, sample efficiency, and robustness over outcome-only RL and existing skill-distillation baselines. Our code is available at https://github.com/jinyangwu/OPID/tree/main.

AI.tldr: OPID is an on-policy skill distillation framework that extracts hierarchical skill supervision (episode-level and step-level) directly from completed trajectories, using a critical-first routing mechanism to provide dense token-level guidance for reinforcement learning of language agents, improving performance over sparse outcome-only RL.
AI.motivation: Outcome-based RL for language agents suffers from sparse trajectory-level rewards that fail to indicate which intermediate decisions to reinforce. Existing skill-conditioned self-distillation methods rely on external skill memories or retrieved privileged context, which are costly and can be mismatched with the current policy's state distribution in multi-turn interactions.
AI.method: OPID extracts hierarchical skills from on-policy trajectories: episode-level skills capture global workflows or failure-avoidance rules, while step-level skills capture local decision knowledge at critical timesteps. A critical-first routing mechanism uses step-level skills for critical decisions and defaults to episode-level skills otherwise. The selected skill is injected into the interaction history, and the old policy re-scores the same response under both original and skill-augmented contexts. The resulting log-probability shift yields a token-level self-distillation advantage, combined with the outcome advantage for policy optimization.
AI.result: Experiments on ALFWorld, WebShop, and Search-based QA demonstrate that OPID generally improves agent performance, sample efficiency, and robustness over outcome-only RL and existing skill-distillation baselines.
AI.conclusion: OPID preserves RL as the primary training objective while introducing dense, distribution-matched hindsight supervision from on-policy trajectories, avoiding the maintenance cost and distribution mismatch issues of external skill memories.

title: Do Safety Guardrails Need to Reason? LeanGuard: A Fast and Light Approach for Robust Moderation
comment: 9 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Project page: https://ndb796.github.io/LeanGuard ; code and models: https://github.com/ndb796/LeanGuard
summary: In order to screen a prompt or a response, the recent guardrail methods generate a chain-of-thought (CoT) before they issue a verdict. This design follows a common belief that step-by-step reasoning improves a decision. However, CoT also makes the guard heavy and slow, because the model must generate many tokens before it decides. This may not match how guardrails are actually deployed. A guardrail sometimes should not be heavy and slow, and it often runs on-device, for example on an embodied robot. In this paper, we pose a question whether a safety guardrail really needs to reason. To answer this question, we train a lightweight bidirectional encoder and a reasoning guard on the same corpus, and we then remove only the reasoning while we keep everything else fixed. With this controlled same-base comparison, we show that the chain does not improve moderation accuracy. We name the resulting guard LeanGuard. A 395M label-only encoder reaches an average F1 of 82.90 $\pm$ 0.26 over public benchmarks. It matches a reasoning guard that is built on a much larger decoder, while it uses only a single forward pass over an input of at most 512 tokens. This is about a ~100x reduction in inference compute. We further show that this label-only encoder stays robust under training-label noise and retains far more recall at a strict false-positive rate than the reasoning guard, so a heavier reasoning guard is not the more robust choice either. Our finding suggests that the current guardrail benchmarks may not be hard enough to reward reasoning, and that the necessity of CoT for moderation is still not proven. We release all source codes and models including LeanGuard at https://github.com/ndb796/LeanGuard.

AI.tldr: LeanGuard proposes that chain-of-thought reasoning is unnecessary for safety guardrail moderation. A lightweight 395M bidirectional encoder, trained without reasoning, matches the accuracy of larger decoder-based reasoning guards while using ~100x less compute (single forward pass, ≤512 tokens). The encoder also proves more robust under label noise and maintains higher recall at strict false-positive rates.
AI.motivation: Current guardrail methods use chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning before issuing moderation verdicts, under the assumption that step-by-step reasoning improves decisions. However, CoT makes guardrails heavy and slow due to generating many tokens, which is incompatible with real-world deployment scenarios like on-device or embodied robot settings where low latency and compute are critical. The paper questions whether reasoning is truly necessary for safety moderation.
AI.method: A controlled same-base comparison is conducted: a lightweight bidirectional encoder (LeanGuard) and a reasoning guard are trained on the same corpus, with only the reasoning component removed while everything else is held fixed. The 395M parameter label-only encoder performs a single forward pass over at most 512 tokens. Evaluation covers public benchmarks, training-label noise robustness, and recall at strict false-positive rates.
AI.result: LeanGuard achieves an average F1 of 82.90 ± 0.26 on public benchmarks, matching a reasoning guard built on a much larger decoder. This represents approximately a 100x reduction in inference compute. Under training-label noise, LeanGuard stays robust, and at strict false-positive rates, it retains far more recall than the reasoning guard, indicating the heavier reasoning guard is not the more robust option.
AI.conclusion: Chain-of-thought reasoning does not improve moderation accuracy for safety guardrails. Current guardrail benchmarks may not be sufficiently challenging to reward reasoning, and the necessity of CoT for moderation remains unproven. LeanGuard demonstrates that a lightweight encoder-only approach is equally accurate, more efficient, and more robust for practical deployment.

title: Learning Probabilistic Filters with Strictly Proper Scoring Rules
summary: Bayesian filtering of partially and noisily observed dynamical systems seeks to infer the evolving conditional distribution of the state of a dynamical system, given observations, in an online fashion. This Bayesian filtering distribution is the natural object for uncertainty quantification, but it is rarely available as a supervised learning target. However, one can often use the forecast model to generate synthetic system trajectories, along with synthetic observations. We introduce the proper scoring ensemble filter (PSEF), an ensemble data assimilation method based on training an analysis map to approximate the filtering distribution using only synthetic state--observation trajectories. The analysis step is represented as a permutation-invariant, transformer-based map that takes as input a forecast ensemble and observations, producing an analysis ensemble. Training is based on strictly proper scoring rules -- with the energy score used in our implementation -- so that probabilistic accuracy is rewarded over the whole probability distribution. We prove that, under a realizability assumption, the population objective is minimized by the true Bayesian filtering distribution. We also derive the finite-ensemble empirical objective used in training and relate its single state--observation trajectory form to the population objective, using a mean-field consistency argument. Numerical experiments show that the learned filter accurately approximates challenging filtering distributions, including nonlinear, non-Gaussian, and multi-modal posteriors, and achieves stronger performance in data assimilation tasks than classical methods or learning-based methods with mean-squared-error objectives. For close-to-Gaussian problems, learning a correction to the EnKF is the best approach, while for highly non-Gaussian problems an end-to-end approach that discards this inductive bias is superior.

AI.tldr: Introduces PSEF, an ensemble data assimilation method that learns an analysis map from synthetic state-observation trajectories using strictly proper scoring rules (energy score), proving it minimizes the true Bayesian filtering distribution under realizability, and demonstrating superior performance on non-Gaussian, multi-modal filtering problems compared to classical and MSE-based learned methods.
AI.motivation: Bayesian filtering distributions are rarely available as supervised learning targets, yet they are the natural object for uncertainty quantification in sequential data assimilation. Existing learning-based methods often rely on mean-squared-error objectives that fail to capture full probabilistic structure, particularly for non-Gaussian and multi-modal posteriors.
AI.method: The analysis map is a permutation-invariant, transformer-based architecture taking forecast ensemble and observations as input to produce an analysis ensemble. Training uses the energy score — a strictly proper scoring rule — on synthetic state-observation trajectories from the forecast model. A realizability assumption is used to prove the population objective is minimized by the true filtering distribution. A mean-field consistency argument relates the finite-ensemble empirical objective (single trajectory form) to the population objective. Two approaches are compared: an EnKF correction and an end-to-end learned filter.
AI.result: The learned filter accurately approximates challenging nonlinear, non-Gaussian, and multi-modal filtering distributions. PSEF outperforms classical methods and MSE-based learned methods in data assimilation tasks. For near-Gaussian problems, learning a correction to the EnKF is best; for highly non-Gaussian problems, the end-to-end approach without EnKF inductive bias is superior.
AI.conclusion: Strictly proper scoring rules provide an effective training framework for learning analysis maps in ensemble data assimilation. The method bridges generative modeling and Bayesian filtering, enabling accurate uncertainty quantification without requiring ground-truth filtering distributions. The choice between EnKF-corrective and end-to-end architectures should be guided by the degree of non-Gaussianity in the problem.
