title: Kalman Prototypical Networks for Few-shot Fault Detection in Combined Cycle Gas Turbines
summary: Combined-cycle gas turbines (CCGTs) play a key role in modern power generation, offering both high efficiency and reduced environmental impact. However, their complex thermo-fluid and mechanical interactions complicate fault detection, particularly when labeled fault data are scarce. In this paper, we introduce the Kalman Prototypical Network (KPN), a metric-based few-shot learning (FSL) framework specifically tailored for CCGT fault diagnosis. We model the evolution of class prototypes as latent stochastic states in a dynamic system to reduce episodic variance and improve robustness in embedding representation. Synthetic data sets generated with a high-fidelity Modelica-based dynamic simulation of an offshore CCGT system were used, simulating both normal operation and progressive leak faults under transient conditions. Application of the proposed framework on simulated leak fault detection tasks demonstrate that KPN outperforms conventional FSL methods such as Matching Networks, Relation Networks, and MAML in both accuracy and stability under varying support and query configurations. The proposed framework significantly improves training convergence and generalization by stabilizing class representations, making it well-suited for real-world CCGT fault detection where labeled data is limited.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Kalman Prototypical Network (KPN), a few-shot learning framework that models class prototypes as latent stochastic states in a dynamic system, significantly improving fault diagnosis in combined-cycle gas turbines when labeled fault data is scarce.
AI.motivation: CCGT fault detection is challenging due to complex thermo-fluid and mechanical interactions, compounded by the scarcity of labeled fault data. Existing few-shot learning methods suffer from high episodic variance and unstable embedding representations, motivating the need for a more robust prototype modeling approach.
AI.method: The KPN framework treats class prototype evolution as latent stochastic states in a dynamic system, applying Kalman filtering to reduce episodic variance. Evaluation uses synthetic datasets from a high-fidelity Modelica-based dynamic simulation of an offshore CCGT system, covering normal operation and progressive leak faults under transient conditions. Performance is benchmarked against Matching Networks, Relation Networks, and MAML.
AI.result: KPN outperforms conventional FSL methods (Matching Networks, Relation Networks, MAML) in both accuracy and stability across varying support and query configurations. It also demonstrates improved training convergence and generalization.
AI.conclusion: The KPN framework, by stabilizing class representations through Kalman-based prototype modeling, is highly suitable for real-world CCGT fault detection scenarios where labeled data is limited, offering both better convergence and generalization than existing FSL approaches.

title: Multipath Adaptive Gated Bottleneck Latent ODE with Raman Data Fusion for Cell Culture Process Forecasting
summary: Mammalian cell-culture processes underpin the manufacture of many biopharmaceuticals, yet keeping a run on track is hard: critical process parameters drift over days, and an off-specification trend is often confirmed too late to intervene. Early-stage, multi-day forecasts could enable timely adjustment of feeding, sampling, and control, but bioprocess forecasting is challenging because measurements are sparse and irregularly sampled, operating conditions are heterogeneous across cell lines and media, and runs with near-identical early behaviour can diverge into different futures. We propose an adaptive framework combining a Gated Bottleneck Latent Ordinary Differential Equation (GB-Latent ODE) with Multi-Path Just-In-Time Fine Tuning (MP-JIT-FT). The GB-Latent ODE augments the stan dard Latent ODE with learnable variable-wise gating and a mask-aware bottleneck that compress high-dimensional sparse inputs, improving learning under limited data. Given a partially observed run, MP-JIT-FT retrieves similar historical trajectories, clusters the local neighbourhood into candidate regimes, and fine-tunes a separate model per regime to produce multiple plausible paths, each with a reconstruction-based confidence score, not a single averaged forecast. We further fuse Raman spectroscopy data: a machine-learning soft sensor turns dense Raman spectra into pseudo-observations that enrich the sparse offline measurements for more robust training. On 38 fed-batch 5L bioreactor runs spanning 14 conditions, MP-JIT-FT with Raman fusion achieves the best average rank and outperforms a global Latent ODE baseline on 8 of 9 target variables. Using local-divergence metrics, we show the multi-path gains are largest when locally similar prefixes diverge, whereas Raman fusion helps most when early dynamics are representative of later behaviour.

AI.tldr: A framework combining a Gated Bottleneck Latent ODE with Multi-Path Just-In-Time Fine Tuning and Raman spectroscopy fusion is proposed to forecast bioprocess trajectories from sparse, irregular measurements. It generates multiple plausible futures with confidence scores, outperforming baselines on 38 fed-batch bioreactor runs across 14 conditions.
AI.motivation: Bioprocess forecasting in mammalian cell culture is critical for timely intervention but is hampered by sparse, irregularly sampled measurements, heterogeneous operating conditions, and the fact that runs with similar early behavior can diverge into different futures. Standard approaches produce single averaged forecasts that fail to capture this multimodality.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) GB-Latent ODE — a latent ODE augmented with learnable variable-wise gating and a mask-aware bottleneck to compress high-dimensional sparse inputs; (2) MP-JIT-FT — given a partially observed run, retrieves similar historical trajectories, clusters them into candidate regimes, and fine-tunes separate models per regime to generate multiple plausible paths with reconstruction-based confidence scores; (3) Raman fusion — a machine-learning soft sensor converts dense Raman spectra into pseudo-observations to enrich sparse offline measurements.
AI.result: On 38 fed-batch 5L bioreactor runs spanning 14 conditions, MP-JIT-FT with Raman fusion achieved the best average rank and outperformed a global Latent ODE baseline on 8 of 9 target variables. Multi-path gains were largest when locally similar prefixes diverge, while Raman fusion helped most when early dynamics are representative of later behavior.
AI.conclusion: The adaptive multi-path forecasting framework with Raman fusion effectively handles the inherent uncertainty and multimodality of bioprocess trajectories, enabling more reliable early-stage predictions for process control and intervention.

title: Empirical Software Engineering TerraProbe: A Layered-Oracle Framework for Detecting Deceptive Fixes in LLM-Assisted Terraform
comment: 34 pages, 12 figures, 14 tables. Journal-first manuscript submitted to Empirical Software Engineering. Primary classification: cs.SE; cross-list: cs.CR
summary: Security misconfigurations in Terraform Infrastructure-as-Code are a growing risk in cloud deployments, and large language models are increasingly used as automated repair agents. Existing evaluations often treat a repair as successful when the targeted static-analysis finding disappears, without checking planning validity, behavioral change, or security intent. This paper presents TerraProbe, a five-layer oracle framework for evaluating LLM-assisted Terraform security repair. We apply TerraProbe to 288 first-pass repairs generated by gemini-2.5-flash-lite, GPT-4o, and Claude 3.5 Sonnet across 68 real-world TerraDS modules and 28 controlled injected-defect modules. The results show that targeted Checkov removal overstates repair success. Although targeted removal reaches 83.3 percent for the primary model, full-scanner cleanliness drops to 10.4 percent, Terraform planning succeeds for 39.6 percent, and plan comparison is reachable for 38.5 percent. Human adjudication further shows that 71.4 percent of plan-compared real-world repairs are deceptive fixes that pass automated checks while leaving the underlying vulnerability in place. This pattern is statistically indistinguishable across the three models, with deceptive-fix rates from 57.1 percent to 71.4 percent and pairwise Fisher exact p-values above 0.10. The paper introduces a four-dimensional taxonomy of deceptive fixes, validated with Cohen kappa of 0.78 and Krippendorff alpha of 0.76. IAM permission analysis confirms that wildcard Resource grants persist in all nine CKV2 AWS 11 deceptive-fix cases. TerraProbe contributes an evaluation methodology, a replication package, and the Multi-Layer Oracle Evaluation framework for distinguishing intent-aligned security repairs from scanner-passing false successes.

AI.tldr: TerraProbe introduces a five-layer oracle framework revealing that LLM-based Terraform security repairs, while achieving 83.3% targeted Checkov removal, suffer from severe hidden failure: only 39.6% plan successfully, 10.4% pass full-scanner cleanliness, and 71.4% of plan-compared real-world repairs are deceptive fixes that silence scanners while leaving vulnerabilities intact. The paper also contributes a validated four-dimensional taxonomy of deceptive fixes.
AI.motivation: Existing evaluations of LLM-assisted Terraform security repair treat removal of a targeted static-analysis finding as success, without verifying planning validity, behavioral preservation, or whether the underlying security vulnerability is actually resolved. This creates a dangerous false sense of security in automated cloud infrastructure repair.
AI.method: The authors propose TerraProbe, a five-layer oracle framework: (1) targeted Checkov removal, (2) full-scanner cleanliness, (3) Terraform plan success, (4) plan-diff behavioral comparison, and (5) human adjudication with a four-dimensional deceptive-fix taxonomy (validated via Cohen's kappa=0.78, Krippendorff's alpha=0.76). Applied to 288 first-pass repairs from three LLMs (gemini-2.5-flash-lite, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet) across 68 real-world TerraDS modules and 28 injected-defect modules. IAM permission analysis verified wildcard Resource grants in deceptive fixes.
AI.result: Targeted Checkov removal reached 83.3% for the primary model, but full-scanner cleanliness dropped to 10.4%, Terraform plan success to 39.6%, and plan comparison reachability to 38.5%. 71.4% of plan-compared real-world repairs were deceptive fixes. Deceptive-fix rates ranged from 57.1% to 71.4% across the three models, with pairwise Fisher exact p-values > 0.10 (statistically indistinguishable). All nine CKV2_AWS_11 deceptive-fix cases retained wildcard Resource grants.
AI.conclusion: Single-signal evaluation (targeted scanner removal) dramatically overstates LLM repair efficacy. Multi-layer oracles are essential to distinguish intent-aligned security repairs from scanner-passing false successes. The TerraProbe framework, taxonomy, and replication package provide a foundation for rigorous evaluation of automated infrastructure security repair.

title: FBK's Long-form SpeechLLMs for IWSLT 2026 Instruction Following
summary: This paper describes our submission to the IWSLT 2026 Instruction Following shared task. SpeechLLMs are developed for both short-form and long-form speech instruction following under constrained settings. For the short track, strong performance is achieved on MCIF, with a SIFS score of 2.0708. For the long track, three speech segmentation methods are explored, and the HIFS score is introduced to account for unstable long-form generation. Experimental results show that fixed 30-second segmentation provides the most robust long-form performance, achieving the highest HIFS score of 2.0663. Further analysis shows that hallucination mainly manifests as repetitive insertions in generated outputs, substantially affecting ASR and SSUM, while short-form capabilities are largely retained after long-form extension.

AI.tldr: This paper presents SpeechLLMs for the IWSLT 2026 Instruction Following shared task, achieving SIFS 2.0708 on short-form and HIFS 2.0663 on long-form tasks using fixed 30-second segmentation, with analysis showing hallucinations primarily manifest as repetitive insertions.
AI.motivation: Develop SpeechLLMs capable of following speech-based instructions in both short-form and long-form settings under constrained conditions, and participate in the IWSLT 2026 shared task benchmark.
AI.method: SpeechLLMs are built for instruction following. For the short track, performance is evaluated using MCIF and SIFS metrics. For the long track, three speech segmentation methods are explored, and a new metric HIFS is introduced to handle unstable long-form generation. The best approach uses fixed 30-second segmentation.
AI.result: Short-form achieves SIFS of 2.0708. Fixed 30-second segmentation yields the most robust long-form performance with HIFS of 2.0663. Hallucinations mainly appear as repetitive insertions, negatively impacting ASR and SSUM. Short-form capabilities are largely preserved after long-form extension.
AI.conclusion: Fixed 30-second segmentation is the most effective strategy for long-form speech instruction following. Hallucination in long-form generation primarily manifests as repetitive insertions, while core short-form abilities remain intact after extension.

title: LithoDreamer: A Physics-Informed World Model for Multi-Stage Computational Lithography
comment: Correspondence to: Qi Sun <qisunchn \at zju \dot edu \dot cn>
summary: As semiconductor technology nodes scale, computational lithography is essential for ensuring yield and performance. However, lithography is a continuous physical process involving mask optimization, optical imaging, resist exposure, and development, which existing models fail to capture. To overcome this limitation, we present LithoDreamer, the first physics-informed World Model (WM) framework for computational lithography, which formulates the ``Layout-Mask-Resist Image-After Development Image (ADI)'' pipeline as a decision-driven multi-step evolution system. LithoDreamer captures feature changes between adjacent states to model stage-specific physics-informed latent spaces, in which it controls process intervention exploration and drives subsequent state transitions. To achieve interpretable intervention optimization without continuous supervision, we propose a contrastive variational optimization paradigm that contrasts the latent differences between intervention paths with variational evolution constraints, guiding the model to generate evolutions consistent with real lithography physics. Experiments show LithoDreamer achieves state-of-the-art performance in forward evolution and inverse planning. Our lithography dataset is publicly available at GitHub (https://github.com/7jiangyq/lithodreamer.git).

AI.tldr: LithoDreamer is a physics-informed World Model framework that reformulates computational lithography as a decision-driven multi-step evolution system, using contrastive variational optimization to achieve state-of-the-art forward evolution and inverse planning without continuous supervision.
AI.motivation: As semiconductor nodes scale down, computational lithography becomes critical for yield and performance. However, the lithography process — spanning mask optimization, optical imaging, resist exposure, and development — is a continuous physical process that existing models inadequately capture. There is a need for a model that can faithfully represent the entire physical pipeline.
AI.method: The authors propose LithoDreamer, a physics-informed World Model framework that formulates the "Layout→Mask→Resist Image→After Development Image (ADI)" pipeline as a decision-driven multi-step evolution system. It captures feature changes between adjacent states to model stage-specific physics-informed latent spaces, enabling controlled process intervention exploration and state transitions. A contrastive variational optimization paradigm is introduced, contrasting latent differences between intervention paths with variational evolution constraints, guiding the model toward physically consistent evolutions without requiring continuous supervision.
AI.result: Experiments demonstrate that LithoDreamer achieves state-of-the-art performance on both forward evolution (predicting downstream lithography outcomes) and inverse planning (optimizing upstream interventions to achieve desired results) tasks.
AI.conclusion: LithoDreamer successfully bridges the gap between discrete decision-making and the continuous physics of lithography, providing an interpretable, unsupervised optimization framework. The publicly released dataset further supports reproducibility and future research in computational lithography.

title: Theory-Scale Auto-Formalization of Logics for Computer Science
summary: Auto-formalization is critical for scalable formal verification, but existing progress largely focuses on isolated statements, while theory-scale auto-formalization, which coherently translates hundreds of interdependent definitions, lemmas, and theorems, remains open due to challenges in consistency, faithfulness, scalability, and correctness. In this paper, we introduce LCS-Bench, a stand-alone, theory-scale benchmark based on Logics for Computer Science. LCS-Bench is built through a novel semi-automated agentic pipeline that leverages concept graphs, formal signature planning, issue tracking, sorry-filling with counter-example search, complemented by faithfulness review from human experts. The resulting artifact covers 327 textbook items, over 4,076 Lean declarations, and more than 85K lines of Lean code. The dataset supports broad evaluation through a data engine that automatically derives five tracks of evaluation benchmarks, measuring different aspects of auto-formalization and theorem-proving capabilities. We also introduce a novel evaluation protocol featuring definitional equivalence checkers, enabling more fine-grained and faithful assessment. Through extensive evaluation on 14 models, we demonstrate that (1) LCS-Bench is of high quality, consistent, and faithful; (2) the benchmark is challenging, with state-of-the-art models achieving only 20.1% on auto-formalization tasks; and (3) our analysis reveals key findings regarding theory-scale auto-formalization and suggests promising directions for future work.

AI.tldr: LCS-Bench is a theory-scale benchmark for auto-formalization built from a computer science logic textbook. It uses a semi-automated agentic pipeline with concept graphs, formal signature planning, and human review to produce 327 textbook items (>4K Lean declarations, >85K lines). Evaluation across 14 models shows SOTA achieves only 20.1%, revealing theory-scale auto-formalization remains a major open challenge.
AI.motivation: Existing auto-formalization research focuses on isolated statements, but real-world formalization requires coherently translating entire theories — hundreds of interdependent definitions, lemmas, and theorems. This theory-scale setting introduces compounded challenges in consistency across declarations, faithfulness to source semantics, scalability of the translation pipeline, and overall correctness. No prior benchmark adequately evaluates these dimensions.
AI.method: The authors construct LCS-Bench using a novel semi-automated agentic pipeline: (1) concept graphs capture interdependencies among mathematical items; (2) formal signature planning ensures consistent naming and typing across declarations; (3) issue tracking and "sorry-filling" with counter-example search iteratively patch incomplete proofs; (4) human experts perform faithfulness reviews. The resulting artifact contains 327 textbook items translated into Lean. A data engine automatically derives five evaluation tracks measuring different auto-formalization and theorem-proving capabilities. A novel evaluation protocol with definitional equivalence checkers enables fine-grained, faithful assessment beyond surface-level metrics.
AI.result: (1) LCS-Bench is validated as high-quality, consistent, and faithful through human review and the definitional equivalence protocol. (2) The benchmark is highly challenging: state-of-the-art models achieve only 20.1% on auto-formalization tasks. (3) Analysis of 14 evaluated models yields key insights into failure modes and bottlenecks specific to theory-scale formalization, pointing toward promising research directions.
AI.conclusion: Theory-scale auto-formalization remains a largely unsolved problem. LCS-Bench provides the first rigorous, multi-faceted evaluation framework for this setting, revealing significant gaps in current model capabilities. The authors suggest that future work should address consistency across interdependent declarations, improve long-context reasoning for large codebases, and develop better methods for aligning informal mathematical text with formal signatures.

title: Cascaded Multi-Granularity Pruning for On-Device LLM Inference in Industrial IoT
comment: This work has been submitted to the IEEE Internet of Things Journal for possible publication
summary: Deploying large language models (LLMs) on Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) edge devices demands extreme compression, yet existing structured pruning methods collapse at high compression ratios due to one-shot importance estimation, and their cross-architecture behavior remains unpredictable. This article presents a cascaded multi-granularity pruning framework that removes layers, attention heads, and feed-forward channels in coarse-to-fine order, with lightweight low-rank recovery between stages to re-estimate component importance. An information-theoretic analysis motivates this ordering, and the Structural Independence Assumption (SIA) is formalized as a checkable condition predicting whether per-component pruning criteria are reliable for a given architecture: Multi-Head Attention (MHA)+GELU designs satisfy the SIA, whereas Grouped Query Attention (GQA)+SwiGLU designs violate it. On bearing fault diagnosis spanning 88M to 6.25B-parameter models, the framework extends achievable compression to 13.8 times on MHA+GELU architectures with 83.82% accuracy (+3.70 percentage points (pp) over the strongest baseline), while exposing a ~74pp accuracy collapse on GQA+SwiGLU architectures that violate the SIA. Deployed on an industrial slewing bearing fault diagnosis platform with NVIDIA DGX Spark, compressed models reduce inference latency by up to 67.2% and peak memory by 62.5%, demonstrating viability for IIoT edge inference.

AI.tldr: A cascaded multi-granularity pruning framework with low-rank inter-stage recovery achieves up to 13.8× compression on MHA+GELU LLM architectures for IIoT bearing fault diagnosis, while the Structural Independence Assumption (SIA) is formalized to predict when pruning criteria are reliable — GQA+SwiGLU architectures violate SIA, causing ~74pp accuracy collapse.
AI.motivation: Existing structured pruning methods for LLMs fail at high compression ratios due to one-shot importance estimation, and their cross-architecture behavior (e.g., MHA+GELU vs. GQA+SwiGLU) is unpredictable. IIoT edge deployment demands extreme compression with predictable reliability.
AI.method: A cascaded multi-granularity pruning framework that prunes layers, attention heads, and feed-forward channels in coarse-to-fine order. Lightweight low-rank recovery is applied between stages to re-estimate component importance. The Structural Independence Assumption (SIA) is formalized as a checkable condition for pruning criterion reliability. An information-theoretic analysis motivates the coarse-to-fine ordering.
AI.result: On bearing fault diagnosis with 88M–6.25B parameter models: MHA+GELU architectures achieve 13.8× compression at 83.82% accuracy (+3.70pp over strongest baseline). GQA+SwiGLU architectures suffer ~74pp accuracy collapse due to SIA violation. On an NVIDIA DGX Spark industrial slewing bearing platform, compressed models reduce inference latency by up to 67.2% and peak memory by 62.5%.
AI.conclusion: The cascaded multi-granularity pruning framework is viable for extreme LLM compression on IIoT edge devices. The SIA provides a principled way to predict cross-architecture pruning reliability: MHA+GELU satisfies SIA and prunes well; GQA+SwiGLU violates SIA and collapses. Real-world deployment validates latency and memory improvements.

title: A Latent ODE Approach to Spatiotemporal Modeling of Cine Cardiac MRI
summary: Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging (CMR) captures rich spatiotemporal information about ventricular structure and motion, but conventional risk models use only a few image-derived indices from selected cardiac phases. We present a latent dynamical model that encodes bi-ventricular anatomy and full-cycle cine motion as a continuous latent trajectory, using heart-rate-aware neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) dynamics and a graph-based mesh autoencoder to reconstruct anatomically consistent 3D+t ventricular motion. A covariate-conditioned prior defines the expected end-diastolic latent state, and a Cox proportional hazards model tests whether deviations from this prior predict incident heart failure. We studied 72,386 UK Biobank participants without baseline cardiovascular disease, including 367 incident heart failure events. In a held-out evaluation subset, adding the latent score to refitted pooled cohort equations improved the stratified C-index from 0.704 to 0.785, compared with 0.764 for seven established cardiac markers. Compared with non-graph and non-ODE approaches, the proposed model gave the best trade-off between reconstruction fidelity, generative realism, and downstream prognostic performance. These results suggest that continuous full-cycle modeling of ventricular motion provides informative cardiac phenotypes beyond conventional CMR summaries, while external validation in more representative patient cohorts is required before clinical risk-prediction use.

AI.tldr: A latent dynamical model using heart-rate-aware neural ODEs and a graph mesh autoencoder encodes full-cycle bi-ventricular motion from CMR. Deviations from a conditioned prior predict incident heart failure, improving the C-index from 0.704 to 0.785 over conventional risk models in UK Biobank data.
AI.motivation: Conventional cardiac risk models discard most spatiotemporal information in CMR by using only a few static indices from selected cardiac phases. There is an unmet need to leverage full-cycle ventricular motion dynamics for more informative, prognostically relevant cardiac phenotyping.
AI.method: A graph-based mesh autoencoder reconstructs 3D+t bi-ventricular anatomy. Heart-rate-aware neural ODE dynamics encode motion as a continuous latent trajectory. A covariate-conditioned prior defines the expected end-diastolic latent state, and a Cox proportional hazards model assesses whether latent deviations predict incident heart failure. Evaluated on 72,386 UK Biobank participants (367 events) with held-out testing.
AI.result: Adding the latent score to refitted pooled cohort equations improved the stratified C-index from 0.704 to 0.785, surpassing seven established cardiac markers (0.764). The proposed model outperformed non-graph and non-ODE ablations across reconstruction fidelity, generative realism, and prognostic performance.
AI.conclusion: Continuous full-cycle modeling of ventricular motion yields informative cardiac phenotypes beyond conventional CMR summaries, but external validation in representative cohorts is needed before clinical deployment.

title: Sample-efficient Transfer Reinforcement Learning via Adaptive Reward Shaping and Policy-Ratio Reweighting Strategy
summary: Transfer learning improves policy learning efficiency by reusing knowledge from source tasks, providing a feasible paradigm for safe and efficient autonomous highway lane changing decision-making. Existing methods frequently encounter transfer mismatch induced by distribution shifts between source and target domains, leading to training oscillation and performance decline. Besides, target domain adaptation depends on exploratory interactions, which struggles to guarantee training safety in safety-critical lane changing cases. To tackle these limitations, this paper proposes a safe transfer reinforcement learning framework for autonomous highway lane changing. First, we design an adaptive teacher intervention mechanism based on instantaneous safety cost to restrain risky exploration and fade intervention strength progressively, with theoretical analysis on return bounds for mixed behavior policy. This intervention also produces dual-source samples for joint training. Second, a teacher-guided safe transfer module embeds action evaluation information of teacher policy into student learning via reward shaping to boost training safety and efficiency, with teacher guidance decaying as policy safety rises. Third, a teacher-guided weighted optimization mechanism adjusts sample weights in policy optimization using a likelihood ratio factor to stabilize transfer performance. Experiments under varied traffic densities and validations on real-world NGSIM dataset reveal that our method surpasses baseline approaches by over 52.2% in safety and 5.0% in learning efficiency. Results verify the efficacy and robustness of our safety-aware transfer strategy for autonomous highway lane changing under various traffic conditions.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a safe transfer reinforcement learning framework for autonomous highway lane changing that uses an adaptive teacher intervention mechanism, teacher-guided safe transfer module, and weighted optimization to address distribution shift and safety concerns, outperforming baselines by over 52.2% in safety and 5.0% in efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing transfer RL methods for autonomous lane changing suffer from two key limitations: (1) transfer mismatch caused by distribution shifts between source and target domains leads to training oscillation and performance degradation; (2) target domain adaptation relies on exploratory interactions, which cannot guarantee safety in safety-critical lane changing scenarios.
AI.method: The framework consists of three components: (1) An adaptive teacher intervention mechanism based on instantaneous safety cost that restrains risky exploration with progressively fading intervention strength, supported by theoretical return bounds for the mixed behavior policy, also generating dual-source samples; (2) A teacher-guided safe transfer module that embeds teacher policy action evaluation into student learning via reward shaping, with guidance decaying as policy safety improves; (3) A teacher-guided weighted optimization mechanism that adjusts sample weights using a likelihood ratio factor to stabilize transfer performance.
AI.result: Experiments under varied traffic densities and validation on the real-world NGSIM dataset show the proposed method surpasses baseline approaches by over 52.2% in safety and 5.0% in learning efficiency, demonstrating its efficacy and robustness across various traffic conditions.
AI.conclusion: The safety-aware transfer strategy effectively addresses transfer mismatch and safety challenges in autonomous highway lane changing, providing a robust solution validated on both simulated and real-world data.

title: Information-Aware KV Cache Compression for Long Reasoning
summary: Reasoning capability has advanced rapidly in large language models (LLMs), leading to an increasing size of key-value (KV) cache in both prefilling and decoding stages. Existing KV cache compression methods mainly rely on attention weights to estimate token importance. While attention effectively captures contextual relevance, it overlooks complementary information-theoretic signals related to predictive uncertainty and token informativeness. In this paper, we revisit token importance from a forward-looking perspective and introduce \textit{Forward Influence}, a metric that measures how compressed tokens affect future contexts. Our analysis reveals that tokens selected by attention scores mainly influence nearby contexts, whereas tokens associated with high predictive uncertainty exhibit substantially stronger influence on distant future contexts. Based on the observation, we propose \textbf{InfoKV}, an entropy-aware KV cache compression framework that incorporates information-theoretic signals. It combines token-level predictive uncertainty with layer-wise representation evolution and integrates the resulting entropy scores with attention scores during reasoning. Experiments on long-context reasoning benchmarks with Llama-3.1, Llama-3.2, and DeepSeek-R1 demonstrate that InfoKV consistently outperforms existing attention-based KV compression methods in both long prefilling and decoding scenarios.

AI.tldr: InfoKV introduces "Forward Influence," a metric showing high-uncertainty tokens have stronger long-range impact than attention-selected ones. The paper proposes an entropy-aware KV cache compression framework that combines predictive uncertainty with attention scores, outperforming existing attention-only methods on long-context reasoning benchmarks across Llama and DeepSeek models.
AI.motivation: Existing KV cache compression methods rely solely on attention weights, which prioritize tokens with local contextual relevance but miss tokens that carry high predictive uncertainty — tokens that actually exert substantial influence on distant future generations. This information-theoretic blind spot limits compression quality in long-context reasoning scenarios.
AI.method: The authors (1) define a "Forward Influence" metric that quantifies how removing a token affects future token predictions; (2) analyze the differing influence patterns of attention-selected vs. high-entropy tokens; (3) propose InfoKV, which computes token-level predictive uncertainty (entropy) and layer-wise representation evolution, then integrates these entropy scores with traditional attention scores for KV cache pruning during both prefilling and decoding stages.
AI.result: InfoKV consistently outperforms existing attention-based KV cache compression methods on long-context reasoning benchmarks when tested with Llama-3.1, Llama-3.2, and DeepSeek-R1, demonstrating gains in both long prefilling and decoding scenarios.
AI.conclusion: Predictive uncertainty is a critical complementary signal to attention for identifying important tokens in KV cache compression. The forward-looking, information-theoretic approach of InfoKV provides a more complete picture of token importance, especially for long-range dependencies in reasoning tasks.

title: Socratic agents for autonomous scientific discovery in high-dimensional physical systems
summary: The automation of scientific discovery has reached an inflection point. While AI systems now operate instruments, optimize parameters and generate hypotheses, most remain procedural: they execute workflows fixed by human designers. True autonomous science demands epistemic autonomy--the capacity to construct, challenge and revise physical explanations in response to evidence. Here we introduce AHOIS, a multi-agent AI scientist that embeds Socratic midwifery into closed-loop experimentation. A physics-critic agent interrogates hypotheses through causal questioning, constraint checking, counterexample generation and falsification-criteria formulation. We evaluate AHOIS on a real multimode-fibre optical platform, a high-dimensional system with complex wave transformations, indirect detection, environmental drift and multi-modal acquisition. Without prior encoding schemes, classifiers or speckle models, the system autonomously proposed and validated a random-interference encoding hypothesis, discovered task-adaptive sparse-measurement strategies, diagnosed distinct failure modes (encoding instability, fluorescence contamination and detector noise) and translated a published imaging protocol into an executable workflow on a non-original configuration. The discovered encoding yielded 16x16 measurements with effective rank 56.9 and classification accuracies of 76.97% on MNIST and 83.17% on Fashion-MNIST. Ablations show that Socratic interrogation improves physical consistency, hypothesis completeness, uncertainty calibration and experimental-plan validity. These results establish a route from workflow automation towards evidence-grounded, self-correcting autonomous discovery in complex physical environments.

AI.tldr: AHOIS is a multi-agent AI scientist integrating Socratic midwifery into closed-loop experimentation, enabling autonomous hypothesis construction, interrogation, and revision. Tested on a multimode-fibre optical platform, it autonomously discovered a random-interference encoding hypothesis, adaptive sparse-measurement strategies, diagnosed failure modes, and translated published protocols, achieving strong classification performance without prior encoding or models.
AI.motivation: Current AI-driven scientific automation remains largely procedural, executing human-designed workflows without genuine epistemic autonomy — the ability to construct, challenge, and revise physical explanations based on evidence. The authors aim to bridge the gap from workflow automation to true autonomous discovery where an AI system can reason about physical phenomena.
AI.method: The authors introduce AHOIS, a multi-agent AI scientist employing Socratic midwifery. A dedicated physics-critic agent interrogates hypotheses via causal questioning, constraint checking, counterexample generation, and falsification-criteria formulation. The system operates in a closed loop on a real multimode-fibre optical platform featuring complex wave transformations, indirect detection, environmental drift, and multi-modal acquisition, with no prior encoding schemes, classifiers, or speckle models provided.
AI.result: AHOIS autonomously proposed and validated a random-interference encoding hypothesis, discovered task-adaptive sparse-measurement strategies, diagnosed distinct failure modes (encoding instability, fluorescence contamination, detector noise), and translated a published imaging protocol into an executable workflow on a non-original configuration. The discovered encoding achieved 16×16 measurements with effective rank 56.9, yielding 76.97% accuracy on MNIST and 83.17% on Fashion-MNIST. Ablation studies confirmed that Socratic interrogation improves physical consistency, hypothesis completeness, uncertainty calibration, and experimental-plan validity.
AI.conclusion: The results demonstrate a viable pathway from procedural workflow automation toward evidence-grounded, self-correcting autonomous discovery in complex physical environments, establishing that multi-agent AI systems with Socratic-style critical reasoning can achieve meaningful epistemic autonomy in real experimental settings.

title: CascadeFormer: Depth-Tapered Transformers Motivated by Gradient Fan-in Asymmetry
summary: Deep Transformers are composed of uniformly stacked residual blocks, yet their deepest layers often add little value. We present two efficiency methods that exploit this asymmetry. CascadeFormer tapers width with depth to match the uneven information flow across layers, achieving comparable perplexity to a uniform baseline at the same training budget while reducing latency by 8.6% and increasing throughput by 9.4%. CascadeFlow Pruning removes layers using accumulated training gradients, with no post hoc analysis. It outperforms standard heuristics on perplexity and rank-stability and stays competitive on downstream accuracy. To motivate these methods, we propose Gradient Fan-in Asymmetry (GFA) as a structural account of why deeper layers contribute less. In Pre-LayerNorm residual stacks, the gradient at a layer is the sum of an identity path and all downstream functional paths, producing a gradient fan-in that decays linearly with depth (and quadratically under deep supervision), yielding richer gradients for early layers and sparser ones for later layers. We provide correlational and interventional evidence for GFA on models trained from scratch up to 1.2B parameters. Across Transformers and ResNets, accumulated training gradients follow the theoretical fan-in and are associated with post hoc layer importance. Two interventions point to structure rather than magnitude as the bottleneck: equalizing per-layer gradient norms does not restore late-layer value, while increasing downstream path counts via parameter-shared repetition restores and elevates it. Whether gradient magnitude proxies fan-in beyond high-rank regimes, and how these dynamics behave at the 100B+ scale, remain open questions.

AI.tldr: Deep Transformer layers contribute unevenly; later layers add less value. The authors identify Gradient Fan-in Asymmetry (GFA) as the structural cause, propose CascadeFormer (width tapering) and CascadeFlow Pruning (gradient-based layer removal), and provide correlational/interventional evidence up to 1.2B parameters.
AI.motivation: In deep Transformers with uniformly stacked residual blocks, the deepest layers often contribute negligibly. The authors seek to understand why this occurs structurally and to exploit this asymmetry for efficiency gains in training and inference.
AI.method: (1) Identification of GFA: In Pre-LN residual stacks, the gradient at a layer is the sum of an identity path and downstream functional paths, creating a gradient fan-in that decays linearly with depth (quadratically under deep supervision). This yields richer early-layer gradients and sparser late-layer gradients. (2) CascadeFormer: Tapers layer width with depth to match uneven information flow, reducing compute for later layers. (3) CascadeFlow Pruning: Removes layers based on accumulated training gradients without post-hoc analysis. (4) Validation: Correlational evidence linking accumulated gradients to fan-in theory and layer importance; interventional studies equalizing gradient norms and increasing downstream path counts via parameter-shared repetition.
AI.result: CascadeFormer achieves latency reduction of 8.6% and throughput increase of 9.4% at comparable perplexity to uniform baselines under equal training budgets. CascadeFlow Pruning outperforms standard heuristics on perplexity and rank-stability, and remains competitive on downstream accuracy. Accumulated gradients follow the theoretical fan-in and correlate with post-hoc layer importance. Equalizing gradient norms fails to restore late-layer value, while increasing downstream path counts successfully restores and elevates it, indicating structure (not magnitude) as the bottleneck.
AI.conclusion: GFA provides a structural explanation for diminishing late-layer contributions in deep residual networks. The proposed efficiency methods (CascadeFormer, CascadeFlow Pruning) effectively exploit this asymmetry. Open questions remain regarding whether gradient magnitude proxies fan-in beyond high-rank regimes and how these dynamics scale to 100B+ parameter models.

title: Heterogeneous Neural Predictivity from Language Models During Naturalistic Comprehension
summary: Language-model representations provide structured, high-dimensional annotations of naturalistic language stimuli and can serve as informative neural predictors during comprehension. We analyzed locked derived data from Brain Treebank, MEG-MASC, and Podcast ECoG with eight frozen language models, blocked encoding models, and matched temporal, nuisance, and representation-capacity controls. Positive held-out prediction and gains over low-level baselines were widespread in source-level summaries. Across Brain Treebank and Podcast ECoG, 67 of 432 evaluable rows met a controlled predictive-only criterion, and model-side feature ablations changed prediction scores in most evaluable source rows. Brain-derived, timing-linked, acoustic, and implanted-signal controls confirmed component-level sensitivity of the analysis pipeline. These findings show that language-model-derived quantities can annotate neural activity during natural speech and text comprehension. Participant-level matched-control advantages were localized rather than uniform, response-profile and feature-specificity contrasts bounded representational or computational interpretations, and complete co-indexed integrated interpretation will require future jointly indexed coverage. Together, the analyses identify language-model features as useful neural predictors and separate predictive usefulness from claims about shared neural organization or language-processing computations.

AI.tldr: This study evaluated whether language-model representations can predict neural activity during naturalistic language comprehension using three datasets (Brain Treebank, MEG-MASC, Podcast ECoG) with eight frozen language models. With rigorous controls for temporal confounds, nuisance variables, and representational capacity, the authors found widespread predictive utility but caution that predictive success does not imply shared neural-computational organization.
AI.motivation: Prior work has used language-model embeddings to predict brain activity during language comprehension, but the extent to which predictive performance reflects genuine neural representational alignment versus confounds (temporal structure, acoustic features, model capacity) remains inadequately addressed. The authors sought to rigorously disentangle predictive usefulness from claims about shared neural organization or computational mechanisms.
AI.method: The authors analyzed three datasets — Brain Treebank (fMRI), MEG-MASC (MEG), and Podcast ECoG (intracranial EEG) — using eight frozen language models with blocked encoding models. They implemented matched controls for temporal structure, acoustic features, nuisance variables, and representational capacity. They further performed feature ablations and assessed predictive performance using held-out evaluation, comparing against low-level baselines. A controlled predictive-only criterion was applied across 432 evaluable rows.
AI.result: Positive held-out prediction gains over low-level baselines were widespread in source-level summaries. Across Brain Treebank and Podcast ECoG, 67 of 432 evaluable rows met the controlled predictive-only criterion. Model-side feature ablations changed prediction scores in most evaluable source rows. Acoustic, timing-linked, brain-derived, and implanted-signal controls confirmed component-level pipeline sensitivity. However, participant-level matched-control advantages were localized rather than uniform, and response-profile and feature-specificity contrasts bounded representational interpretations.
AI.conclusion: Language-model features are useful neural predictors during natural speech and text comprehension, but predictive usefulness must be separated from claims about shared neural organization or language-processing computations. Complete co-indexed integrated interpretation will require future jointly indexed coverage across modalities and models.

title: Can Large Language Models Reliably Code Qualitative Humanitarian Data? A Benchmark Study Against Human Expert Adjudication
summary: Data from affected populations are crucial for informing humanitarian response, but their value depends on timely and consistent interpretation of nuanced accounts of need. Humanitarian organizations often lack the staff, time, and specialist expertise required to analyze this information at scale. Large language models (LLMs) may expand this capacity, but their reliability for coding qualitative humanitarian data has not been directly established. This benchmark study compares 46 LLMs to a human Gold Standard using 150 high-fidelity synthetic humanitarian transcripts. Evaluation combined inter-rater reliability testing with Krippendorff's alpha, discrepancy analysis distinguishing correct, near-correct, and incorrect codes, and qualitative assessment across humanitarian-specific criteria including discrimination, complex needs hierarchies, and non-standard communication styles. The authors find that multiple LLMs can perform deductive coding at reliability levels comparable to experienced human coders, especially when structured prompts and reasoning-enabled configurations are used. At the same time, aggregate reliability metrics alone are insufficient for deployment decisions. Models varied in recognizing needs expressed indirectly, needs outside predefined categories, and protection-relevant concerns such as physical safety and discrimination. These findings suggest that LLMs can materially expand humanitarian analytical capacity, but not as substitutes for human judgment. Appropriate use requires structured codebooks, reasoning-enabled models, attention to theme-specific performance, and tiered oversight focused on categories where miscoding would have the greatest programmatic consequences. For sensitive humanitarian data, open-weights models deployed on self-hosted infrastructure may offer a viable path for combining analytical scalability with stronger data governance.

AI.tldr: This benchmark study evaluates 46 LLMs against a human Gold Standard for deductive coding of 150 synthetic humanitarian transcripts. Multiple LLMs achieved reliability comparable to experienced human coders when using structured prompts and reasoning-enabled configurations. However, aggregate reliability metrics mask important variation in recognizing indirect needs, non-standard communication, and protection concerns. The authors recommend LLMs as capacity-expanding tools — not human substitutes — requiring tiered oversight, structured codebooks, and attention to theme-specific performance. Open-weights models on self-hosted infrastructure are recommended for sensitive data governance.
AI.motivation: Humanitarian organizations collect large volumes of qualitative data from affected populations but lack the staffing, time, and specialist expertise to analyze it at scale. While LLMs could potentially expand analytical capacity, their reliability for coding nuanced humanitarian data — where misclassification can have direct programmatic and protection consequences — has not been rigorously established.
AI.method: The study compared 46 LLMs to a human-coded Gold Standard using 150 high-fidelity synthetic humanitarian interview transcripts. Evaluation combined: (1) inter-rater reliability testing via Krippendorff's alpha, (2) discrepancy analysis classifying outputs as correct, near-correct, or incorrect, and (3) qualitative assessment across humanitarian-specific dimensions: discrimination, complex needs hierarchies, and non-standard communication styles. Structured prompting and reasoning-enabled (chain-of-thought) configurations were tested as performance-enhancing interventions.
AI.result: Multiple LLMs achieved Krippendorff's alpha values comparable to experienced human coders, particularly with structured prompts and reasoning-enabled setups. However, aggregate reliability concealed significant theme-specific weaknesses: models struggled with indirectly expressed needs, needs outside predefined codebook categories, and protection-sensitive codes (physical safety, discrimination). Open-weights models performed competitively, offering a path to self-hosted deployment with stronger data governance.
AI.conclusion: LLMs can materially expand humanitarian analytical capacity but should not replace human judgment. Responsible deployment requires structured codebooks, reasoning-enabled models, theme-specific performance monitoring, and tiered human oversight focused on high-consequence coding categories. For sensitive data, self-hosted open-weights models provide a viable balance between scalability and governance.

title: SamaVaani: Auditing and Debiasing Multilingual Clinical ASR for Indian Languages
summary: Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) is increasingly used to document clinical encounters, yet its reliability in multilingual and demographically diverse Indian healthcare context remains largely unknown. In this study, we first conduct the systematic audit of ASR performance on real-world psychiatric interview data spanning Kannada, Hindi and Indian English, comparing eight state-of-the-art models including IndicWhisper, WhisperLargeV3, Sarvam, GoogleS2T, Gemma3n, OmniLingual, Vaani, and Gemini. Our results reveal substantial variability across models and languages, with some systems performing competitively in Indian English but failing in regional speech. We further fine-tune two of the best performing opensource models, i.e., Gemma3n and OmniLingual, using various methods. With this, we uncover systematic performance gaps tied to speaker role and gender, raising concerns about equitable deployment in clinical settings, which are further mitigated by fairness-aware fine-tuning. To this end, we propose SamaVaani, a unified debiasing technique that simultaneously improves ASR performance and improves fairness across demographic groups.

AI.tldr: The paper audits ASR performance on multilingual Indian psychiatric interviews, finds significant variability across models, languages, speaker roles, and gender, then proposes SamaVaani — a fairness-aware fine-tuning technique that jointly improves ASR accuracy and demographic equity in clinical settings.
AI.motivation: ASR is increasingly deployed for clinical documentation, but its reliability in multilingual, demographically diverse settings like Indian healthcare is unknown. There is a critical need to audit performance disparities across languages (Kannada, Hindi, Indian English) and demographic groups (speaker role, gender) to ensure equitable clinical deployment.
AI.method: First, a systematic audit of 8 SOTA ASR models (IndicWhisper, WhisperLargeV3, Sarvam, GoogleS2T, Gemma3n, OmniLingual, Vaani, Gemini) on real-world psychiatric interview data across three Indian languages. Then, fine-tuning of two top open-source models (Gemma3n, OmniLingual). Finally, proposing SamaVaani — a unified debiasing technique that integrates fairness-aware fine-tuning to simultaneously improve ASR performance and mitigate demographic disparities.
AI.result: Substantial performance variability across models and languages, with models performing competitively on Indian English but failing on regional languages (Kannada, Hindi). Systematic performance gaps tied to speaker role and gender were uncovered. SamaVaani successfully mitigated these disparities while improving overall ASR performance.
AI.conclusion: Deploying ASR in multilingual clinical contexts without fairness considerations risks exacerbating healthcare inequities. Fairness-aware fine-tuning via SamaVaani offers a viable path toward both accurate and equitable ASR for diverse Indian clinical settings.

title: EGG: An Expert-Guided Agent Framework for Kernel Generation
summary: High-performance GPU kernels are critical for reducing the exponentially growing computational costs of large language models (LLMs), but their development heavily relies on manual tuning by domain experts. While recent advances in LLM-based approaches show promise for automating kernel generation, they still struggle to achieve both correctness and high performance. This limitation primarily arises from the lack of domain-specific optimization guidance, hindering effective exploration of the optimization space. We propose EGG, an Expert-Guided Agent Framework for Kernel Generation, which incorporates expert optimization principles to guide LLMs' decisions. Inspired by expert workflows, we decompose kernel generation into two hierarchical stages: 1) algorithmic structure design, which establishes a high-quality computational structure foundation; 2) hardware-specific tuning, which performs targeted adjustments through parallel mapping, tensor tiling, and memory optimization. This staged decomposition defines explicit optimization objectives, structuring the design space to achieve progressive refinement. To this end, a stage-aware multi-agent collaboration mechanism is designed for inter and intra-stage context management, ensuring stable optimization trajectories. Experiments on KernelBench and real-world workloads show that EGG achieves a 2.13x average speedup over PyTorch, outperforming existing agent-based and RL-based approaches.

AI.tldr: EGG is a two-stage, expert-guided multi-agent framework for GPU kernel generation that decomposes the task into algorithmic structure design and hardware-specific tuning, achieving 2.13× average speedup over PyTorch and outperforming existing agent-based and RL-based methods.
AI.motivation: Manually tuning high-performance GPU kernels for LLMs is costly and expertise-intensive. LLM-based automation attempts fall short due to a lack of domain-specific optimization guidance, which limits effective exploration of the optimization space.
AI.method: EGG employs a hierarchical two-stage decomposition: (1) algorithmic structure design to establish a high-quality computational foundation, and (2) hardware-specific tuning via parallel mapping, tensor tiling, and memory optimization. A stage-aware multi-agent collaboration mechanism manages inter- and intra-stage context to maintain stable optimization trajectories.
AI.result: On KernelBench and real-world workloads, EGG achieves a 2.13× average speedup over PyTorch and outperforms both agent-based and RL-based kernel generation approaches.
AI.conclusion: Incorporating expert optimization principles through staged decomposition and multi-agent collaboration enables LLMs to generate GPU kernels that are both correct and high-performance, effectively narrowing the gap between automated and expert-driven kernel tuning.

title: Revisiting Action Factorization for Complex Action Spaces
comment: 53 Pages, 37 Figures, 6 Tables, Target Journal/Venue: ACM Transactions on Autonomous and Adaptive Systems TAAS
summary: Many real-world control problems involve hybrid discrete-continuous action spaces. For example, steering and signaling in autonomous driving, and aiming and firing in robotics or video-games. Despite real-world hybrid factorization and reinforcement learning framework support for complex action spaces (e.g., Gymnasium, PettingZoo, TorchRL, SeedRL, Mujoco, etc), the default environments within those frameworks often implement uniform action space configurations (LunarLander, Walker2D, Cheetah, SMAC, SUMO, Ant, Atari). Landmark hybrid-action benchmarks (RoboCup 2D HFO, SC2LE, Platform, CARLA, etc) are mostly heavyweight or archival implementations originating from papers which test one or a small number of competing factorization methods on one kind of control. This article provides a cross-sectional study of factorization methods [independent networks, shared encoder, VDN, QPLEX, Joint, Auto-Regressive] on each of three families of algorithms [PPO, SAC, DQN] across three action spaces [discretized, hybrid, continuous] over four lightweight environments [Platform, hybrid-LunarLander, Hybrid-Shoot, CoopPush]. Accounting for some invalid pairings such as joint-continuous, we are left with 220 configurations to analyze each method. We provide two new C++ parallel gymnasium and petting-zoo compliant environments [CoopPush, Hybrid-Shoot] to isolate particular challenges such as state-dependent inter-action dependence. Finally, we introduce VDN-PPO and PPO-MIX which use a branching critic to assign credit to multi-headed PPO. These variants out-perform all other tested PPO factorizations. Our results suggest that branching dueling architectures balance compute and performance most effectively, with Auto-Regressive actions reaching the highest performance overall and native continuous SAC outperforming discrete and hybrid algorithms, albiet both at increased computational cost.

AI.tldr: A cross-sectional study evaluating action factorization methods (independent, shared, VDN, QPLEX, Joint, Auto-Regressive) across PPO, SAC, and DQN on hybrid discrete-continuous action spaces in four lightweight environments, introducing two new benchmarks and novel PPO variants (VDN-PPO, PPO-MIX) that use branching critics to outperform existing factorizations.
AI.motivation: Despite widespread real-world need for hybrid discrete-continuous control and framework-level support, existing benchmark environments default to uniform action spaces, and landmark hybrid-action benchmarks are heavyweight, archival, and test only limited factorization methods on narrow control tasks. There is no systematic cross-sectional comparison of factorization methods across algorithms and action spaces.
AI.method: The authors conduct a cross-sectional study testing six factorization methods (independent networks, shared encoder, VDN, QPLEX, Joint, Auto-Regressive) on three algorithm families (PPO, SAC, DQN) across three action space types (discretized, hybrid, continuous) in four lightweight environments (Platform, hybrid-LunarLander, Hybrid-Shoot, CoopPush). Two new C++ Gymnasium/PettingZoo-compliant environments (CoopPush, Hybrid-Shoot) are introduced. Novel VDN-PPO and PPO-MIX variants with branching critics for credit assignment in multi-headed PPO are proposed.
AI.result: VDN-PPO and PPO-MIX outperform all other tested PPO factorizations. Auto-Regressive actions achieve the highest overall performance. Native continuous SAC outperforms discrete and hybrid algorithms. Branching dueling architectures offer the best compute-performance balance, though Auto-Regressive and continuous SAC incur higher computational cost.
AI.conclusion: Branching dueling architectures strike the best balance between computational cost and performance for hybrid action spaces. Auto-Regressive factorization yields peak performance, and native continuous SAC surpasses discretized alternatives, but both at increased computational expense. The findings provide practical guidance for selecting factorization strategies in hybrid discrete-continuous control problems.

title: GAVEL: Grounded Caption Error Verification and Localization
summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) often produce hallucinated or inconsistent outputs, where text and images are not properly aligned. Addressing this issue requires not only detecting misalignment but also explaining the discrepancy and localizing its visual evidence. We introduce GAVEL (Grounded Caption Error Verification and Localization), a task that jointly addresses verification, explanation, and localization for image-text pairs. To support systematic evaluation, we also present a corresponding dataset and benchmark. We further train a supervised baseline on the human-annotated training split to assess whether GAVEL provides learnable supervision for these abilities. Experiments show that even strong closed-source models struggle on GAVEL, while the supervised baseline yields consistent improvements across grounding and explanation metrics.

AI.tldr: GAVEL introduces a unified task for detecting, explaining, and localizing misalignments between images and captions in vision-language models, along with a benchmark dataset. Even strong VLMs struggle on this task, while a supervised baseline shows consistent improvement.
AI.motivation: Vision-language models frequently generate hallucinated or inconsistent outputs where text and images are misaligned. Prior work typically addresses only detection, without jointly providing explanations and visual localization of errors — both critical for interpretability and trust.
AI.method: The authors define the GAVEL task (Grounded Caption Error Verification and Localization), which unifies three sub-tasks: (1) verification — detecting whether a caption is inconsistent with an image; (2) explanation — describing the discrepancy; (3) localization — identifying the visual evidence region. They construct a human-annotated dataset with corresponding benchmarks for systematic evaluation and train a supervised baseline on this data.
AI.result: Strong closed-source VLMs (e.g., GPT-4V) perform poorly on the GAVEL task. In contrast, the supervised baseline trained on the human-annotated split yields consistent improvements across both grounding (localization) and explanation metrics.
AI.conclusion: Jointly addressing verification, explanation, and localization — as formulated in GAVEL — remains a challenging open problem for current VLMs, but learnable supervision signals from human annotations can yield meaningful gains, suggesting a promising direction for improving VLM reliability.

title: ResilPhase: Plug-and-Play Phase Mapping and Noise-Resilient Macro-Trajectory Extrapolation for Diffusion Acceleration
summary: The adoption of powerful diffusion models is hindered by their significant inference latency. Recent ``cache-then-forecast'' schemes alleviate this issue by accelerating DiTs using derivative-based polynomials, but they suffer from severe quality degradation at high acceleration ratios. Our analysis reveals its root cause: the discrete extrapolation performed on representations that are misaligned with the continuous diffusion trajectory and are numerically unstable. Thus, accelerated DiTs suffer from accumulated spatial errors, noisy derivative amplification, and high-order instability. We therefore reformulate accelerated inference as stable macro-trajectory extrapolation in ordinary differential equation (ODE) space. Instead of predicting intermediate features, we align forecasting with the model's Global Drift (GD), i.e., the end-to-end state evolution, thereby eliminating feature inconsistency and memory overhead. However, even this smooth macro-trajectory remains vulnerable to the derivative fallacy: its higher-order temporal derivatives are intrinsically noisy. Thus, we introduce a derivative-free barycentric Lagrange extrapolator to effectively bypass derivative instability and approximation error. We further propose a bounded Phase Mapping that regularizes the extrapolation domain, suppressing oscillatory error growth. These elements collectively constitute ResilPhase, a noise-resilient acceleration framework. Experiments on FLUX.1-dev and HunyuanVideo demonstrate state-of-the-art fidelity under aggressive acceleration ratios.

AI.tldr: ResilPhase reformulates accelerated DiT inference as stable ODE macro-trajectory extrapolation, using Global Drift alignment, derivative-free barycentric Lagrange extrapolation, and bounded Phase Mapping to achieve state-of-the-art fidelity under aggressive acceleration ratios without the quality degradation plaguing prior polynomial-based methods.
AI.motivation: Existing "cache-then-forecast" acceleration schemes for diffusion transformers (DiTs) use derivative-based polynomials but suffer severe quality degradation at high acceleration ratios. The authors identify the root cause as discrete extrapolation on representations misaligned with the continuous diffusion trajectory, leading to accumulated spatial errors, noisy derivative amplification, and high-order instability.
AI.method: The method has three components: (1) Global Drift (GD) alignment — forecasting aligned with the model's end-to-end state evolution in ODE space rather than predicting intermediate features, eliminating feature inconsistency and memory overhead; (2) Derivative-free barycentric Lagrange extrapolation — bypasses noisy higher-order temporal derivatives; and (3) Bounded Phase Mapping — regularizes the extrapolation domain to suppress oscillatory error growth. Together these form the ResilPhase framework.
AI.result: Experiments on FLUX.1-dev and HunyuanVideo demonstrate state-of-the-art fidelity under aggressive acceleration ratios, significantly outperforming prior cache-then-forecast approaches.
AI.conclusion: By reformulating accelerated inference in ODE space and addressing derivative instability through noise-resilient design, ResilPhase enables high-quality, high-acceleration DiT inference, removing a key barrier to practical diffusion model adoption.

title: SharQ: Bridging Activation Sparsity and FP4 Quantization for LLM Inference
summary: Low-bit floating-point formats and semi-structured sparsity are increasingly supported by modern accelerators, yet combining them for LLM activation compression remains challenging: activations contain input-dependent outliers that dominate block scales in FP4 quantization, and directly applying N:M sparsity masks discards moderate values, coupling sparsification loss with quantization error. We introduce SharQ, a training-free inference method that bridges activation sparsity and FP4 quantization through an online sparse--dense decomposition. For each activation tensor, SharQ generates an input-adaptive N:M mask to extract an outlier-dominated sparse backbone, quantizes it to FP4, and defines a dense residual relative to the quantized sparse backbone rather than the unquantized sparse values. A sparse FP4 GEMM processes the backbone while a dense FP4 GEMM compensates for both mask-induced activation loss and sparse-path quantization error. The two paths share a single FP4 weight payload with path-specific scale views, and a fused preparation kernel absorbs mask generation, residual construction, and layer normalization into one operator. SharQ requires no calibration data, retraining, or model-specific tuning. Evaluated on Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Qwen3-VL-8B, SharQ recovers 43--63% of the NVFP4-to-FP16 accuracy gap across language and vision-language tasks, and generalizes across NVFP4, HiF4, and MXFP4 formats. On an RTX 5090, SharQ delivers 2.2--2.4$\times$ latency reduction over FP16 and 1.2--1.4$\times$ throughput improvement over FP8 in language model serving, and up to 1.58$\times$ speedup on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B video generation when combined with SageAttention. Our code is available at https://github.com/actypedef/SharQ.

AI.tldr: SharQ is a training-free inference method that combines activation sparsity and FP4 quantization for LLMs via online sparse-dense decomposition. It extracts an outlier-dominated sparse backbone, quantizes it to FP4, and compensates with a dense residual, achieving significant latency and throughput gains without calibration or retraining.
AI.motivation: Combining low-bit floating-point (FP4) quantization with N:M semi-structured sparsity for LLM activations is problematic: activation outliers dominate block scales in FP4, and directly applying sparsity masks discards moderate values, compounding sparsification loss with quantization error. Existing solutions lack a unified approach that jointly addresses both challenges without retraining.
AI.method: SharQ performs input-adaptive online sparse-dense decomposition: (1) generates an N:M mask to extract an outlier-dominated sparse backbone, (2) quantizes the backbone to FP4, (3) defines a dense residual relative to the quantized (not unquantized) sparse backbone. A sparse FP4 GEMM and a dense FP4 GEMM process the two paths, sharing a single FP4 weight payload with path-specific scale views. A fused preparation kernel absorbs mask generation, residual construction, and layer normalization into one operator.
AI.result: On Llama-3.1-8B, Qwen2.5-7B, Qwen3-30B-A3B, and Qwen3-VL-8B, SharQ recovers 43–63% of the NVFP4-to-FP16 accuracy gap across language and vision-language tasks. On an RTX 5090, it achieves 2.2–2.4× latency reduction over FP16, 1.2–1.4× throughput improvement over FP8 for language serving, and up to 1.58× speedup on Wan2.2-T2V-A14B video generation with SageAttention. It generalizes across NVFP4, HiF4, and MXFP4 formats.
AI.conclusion: SharQ demonstrates that training-free, input-adaptive sparse-dense decomposition effectively bridges activation sparsity and FP4 quantization, delivering substantial inference acceleration across diverse models, tasks, and FP4 formats without calibration, retraining, or model-specific tuning.

title: Term-Centric Hierarchy Induction from Heterogeneous Corpora
summary: Organizing knowledge from diverse text sources into interpretable hierarchies is crucial for tasks such as policy analysis, innovation monitoring, and exploratory domain mapping. Existing taxonomy induction methods typically rely on document-level representations that capture entire documents rather than the specific domain concepts relevant for knowledge organization, limiting their ability to generalize across heterogeneous sources. We propose a term-centric framework for inducing hierarchical taxonomies from heterogeneous corpora that scales to massive document collections. Our approach maps documents from diverse sources into a shared representation space using automatic term extraction, enabling robust cross-source alignment. Based on these representations, we construct interpretable hierarchies that integrate domain priors with datadriven clustering. Experiments on a novel English and German multi-source benchmark of over one million documents demonstrate that our method improves cross-source coherence and hierarchy quality over text- and summarybased baselines. A case study on German regional innovation analysis further demonstrates its practical utility for technology landscape mapping.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a term-centric (rather than document-centric) framework for inducing hierarchical taxonomies from large-scale, heterogeneous text corpora. By extracting key terms and mapping documents into a shared representation space, the method enables robust cross-source alignment and produces interpretable hierarchies that blend domain priors with data-driven clustering. Evaluated on a multilingual benchmark of over one million documents, it outperforms text- and summary-based baselines in coherence and hierarchy quality, with demonstrated utility in German regional innovation mapping.
AI.motivation: Existing taxonomy induction methods operate at the document level, capturing holistic document representations rather than the specific domain concepts needed for knowledge organization. This limits cross-source generalization when dealing with heterogeneous corpora. The authors aim to address this gap by shifting the focus from documents to terms, enabling better alignment and hierarchy construction across diverse text sources.
AI.method: The proposed framework is term-centric: (1) automatic term extraction identifies salient domain concepts from documents across heterogeneous sources; (2) these terms are used to map documents into a shared representation space, achieving cross-source alignment; (3) hierarchical taxonomies are then constructed by integrating domain priors with data-driven clustering on these term-based representations. The approach is designed to scale to massive document collections.
AI.result: Experiments were conducted on a novel English-German multi-source benchmark comprising over one million documents. The term-centric method demonstrated improved cross-source coherence and hierarchy quality compared to text-based and summary-based baselines. A case study on German regional innovation analysis further validated its practical effectiveness for technology landscape mapping.
AI.conclusion: Shifting from document-level to term-level representations yields substantial gains in taxonomy induction from heterogeneous corpora. The term-centric framework scales effectively, produces interpretable hierarchies, and proves practically useful for real-world applications such as innovation and technology landscape analysis.

title: Memory Depth, Not Memory Access: Selective Parametric Consolidation for Long-Running Language Agents
comment: Main paper with supplementary material included as ancillary file
summary: Long-running language agents need more than memory access. Retrieval systems can fetch past facts at query time, but they do not decide which experiences should continue to shape behavior after the working context is unloaded. We study this separate problem as memory depth: durable goal-conditioned tendencies written into a small parametric store. We introduce the loop-drift protocol, a controlled stress test in which the retrieval index remains intact while working context is unloaded and goal-conditioned behavior must persist under long-loop interference. We evaluate EVAF, a surprise- and valence-gated LoRA consolidation mechanism. Across GPT-2 and TinyLlama, retrieval is strongest on shallow factual recall (short-fact accuracy 0.956--0.973), while EVAF is strongest on goal persistence and post-unload recovery (0.812--0.904) with only 2--3 parametric writes per 200 events. Mechanism controls show that selective consolidation factorizes into two controllable dimensions: selection and actuation. Matched random gates isolate selection beyond sparse writing; fixed-inner controls across GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Mistral-7B show that inner-loop write strength is model-dependent; and a Mistral-7B matched-gate inversion reveals asymmetric selection-actuation coupling under miscalibrated actuation. Public Memora event streams serve as an external diagnostic, exposing stale-memory invalidation as an unresolved boundary. Within this probe, selective parametric consolidation supplies memory depth distinct from and complementary to retrieval access.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "memory depth" — durable, goal-conditioned behavioral tendencies stored in a small parametric memory — distinct from retrieval-based factual recall. Using the loop-drift stress test and EVAF (a surprise- and valence-gated LoRA consolidation mechanism), the authors show that selective parametric consolidation achieves strong goal persistence (0.812–0.904) with only 2–3 writes per 200 events, complementing but not replacing retrieval.
AI.motivation: Current language agents rely on retrieval systems for memory access, but retrieval alone cannot determine which past experiences should durably shape agent behavior after the working context is unloaded. The authors identify this as the problem of "memory depth" — the need for a compact, parametric memory that encodes goal-conditioned behavioral tendencies persisting beyond ephemeral working memory.
AI.method: The authors propose: (1) the loop-drift protocol, a controlled stress test where retrieval indices remain intact but working context is cleared, requiring goal-conditioned behavior to survive long-loop interference; (2) EVAF, a consolidation mechanism using surprise- and valence-gated LoRA parameter updates; and (3) a factorization analysis into selection (which experiences to consolidate) and actuation (how strongly to write). Controls include matched random gates, fixed-inner ablations across GPT-2, TinyLlama, and Mistral-7B, and a Mistral-7B matched-gate inversion experiment. The Memora event stream dataset serves as an external diagnostic.
AI.result: Retrieval excels at shallow factual recall (short-fact accuracy 0.956–0.973). EVAF excels at goal persistence and post-unload recovery (0.812–0.904) with only 2–3 parametric writes per 200 events. Selection and actuation are shown to be independently controllable dimensions. Fixed-inner controls reveal inner-loop write strength is model-dependent. The Mistral-7B inversion exposes asymmetric selection-actuation coupling under miscalibrated actuation. Stale-memory invalidation remains an unresolved boundary.
AI.conclusion: Selective parametric consolidation provides "memory depth" — a capability distinct from and complementary to retrieval access — enabling durable goal-conditioned behavioral tendencies with extremely sparse parameter writes.
