The factorization into selection and actuation offers a principled framework for designing memory systems in long-running language agents.

title: RedVox: Safety and Fairness Gaps in Speech Models Across Languages
summary: Speech-capable models are increasingly deployed in real-world applications across languages. Yet their safety and fairness beyond English settings and under naturalistic conditions remain understudied. We survey safety reporting practices across state-of-the-art speech model releases, finding that only 8% document any multilingual analysis. To address this gap, we introduce RedVox, a multilingual safety and fairness benchmark for audio and speech built on real voices, covering unsafe and unfair stereotypical requests across five languages (English, French, Italian, Spanish, and German). Evaluating eight state-of-the-art models, we find that vulnerabilities persist even under non-adversarial conditions, worsen in non-English languages, and are amplified when the request comes from a spoken input. Finally, by surveying the participants who contributed to RedVox, we document the unique personal and privacy challenges of collecting speech data with human participants, pointing to broader sociotechnical challenges in naturalistic speech safety research.

AI.tldr: RedVox is a multilingual safety and fairness benchmark using real voices in five languages. The authors find that speech models exhibit safety vulnerabilities that worsen in non-English languages and with spoken input, and only 8% of model releases document multilingual safety analysis.
AI.motivation: Speech-capable models are widely deployed across languages, yet safety and fairness evaluations beyond English and under naturalistic conditions are largely absent. The authors aim to expose this gap and provide a systematic benchmark for multilingual speech safety.
AI.method: The authors (1) surveyed safety reporting practices across SOTA speech model releases; (2) built RedVox, a multilingual benchmark comprising unsafe and unfair stereotypical requests in English, French, Italian, Spanish, and German using real human voices; (3) evaluated eight SOTA models against this benchmark; and (4) surveyed RedVox contributors about the personal and privacy challenges of collecting speech data.
AI.result: Only 8% of model releases documented any multilingual safety analysis. Evaluations revealed persistent safety vulnerabilities under non-adversarial conditions, worse performance in non-English languages, and amplified risks when requests come as spoken rather than text input. Participant surveys highlighted significant privacy and personal challenges in naturalistic speech data collection.
AI.conclusion: Multilingual safety evaluation for speech models is critically under-addressed. Safety vulnerabilities are language-dependent and modality-dependent, and collecting naturalistic speech safety data raises sociotechnical challenges that the research community must confront.

title: KARLA: Knowledge-base Augmented Retrieval for Language Models
summary: We propose a new method that allows an LLM to automatically pull in factual knowledge from a knowledge base during token generation. This means that (1)~factual knowledge in the LLM output can be updated without retraining the LLM, (2)~facts in the LLM output can be traced to the knowledge base for transparency and explainability, and (3)~smaller models can achieve the same factual accuracy as larger models. Our core idea is to train the model to produce special tokens that trigger a query to the knowledge base. Our experiments show that our method improves factual grounding in both short and long-form generation, and allows factual revisions to take effect through KB edits rather than parameter updates.

AI.tldr: A method enabling LLMs to query a knowledge base during token generation via special trigger tokens, improving factual accuracy, transparency, and allowing knowledge updates without retraining.
AI.motivation: LLMs suffer from outdated factual knowledge, lack of explainability regarding source of facts, and the need for increasingly large models to achieve factual accuracy. The authors aim to decouple factual knowledge from model parameters.
AI.method: Train the LLM to emit special trigger tokens that invoke lookups to an external knowledge base during the token generation process. These queries pull in relevant factual information on-the-fly, grounding the generated output in the KB.
AI.result: The method improves factual grounding in both short-form and long-form generation tasks. Factual revisions can be achieved by simply editing the knowledge base rather than updating model parameters.
AI.conclusion: The proposed approach enables updatable, traceable, and size-efficient factual generation by interleaving KB queries with token generation, offering a compelling alternative to relying solely on parametric knowledge.

title: Sketched Linear Contrastive Learning: Approximation, Optimization, and Statistical Scaling
summary: Scaling laws describe how learning performance varies with model size, data size, and compute. While recent theoretical work has established scaling laws for sketched linear regression, much less is understood for contrastive representation learning. In this paper, we study a sketched linear model for contrastive learning under a paired Gaussian latent-variable setup. The learner observes only sketched views of two correlated variables and trains a bilinear contrastive score by full-batch empirical gradient descent. We analyze a Gaussian-negative quadratic contrastive surrogate under aligned power-law spectra and a contrastive source condition, where we derive a risk decomposition into irreducible risk, approximation error, GD bias, GD variance, and a cross term. The cross term is controlled by the bias and variance and therefore does not affect the upper-bound scaling. Our main theorem gives an explicit scaling law with respect to sketch dimension $M$, sample size $N$, and effective optimization horizon $L_{\mathrm{eff}}γ$. Compared with standard linear-regression scaling laws, the contrastive setting must learn interactions between two views, and this changes how optimization and finite-sample noise scale with model size, data, and training time. This provides a first theoretical step toward understanding scaling behavior in contrastive learning and gives guidance for balancing model size, data, and optimization compute.

AI.tldr: This paper derives explicit scaling laws for a sketched bilinear contrastive learning model under a Gaussian latent-variable setup. It decomposes risk into irreducible risk, approximation error, GD bias, GD variance, and a cross term, revealing how the interaction between two views fundamentally alters scaling behavior compared to standard linear regression.
AI.motivation: While scaling laws are well-established for standard supervised learning (e.g., sketched linear regression), theoretical understanding of how model size, data size, and compute jointly affect performance in contrastive representation learning remains largely unexplored. This gap motivates a rigorous analysis of scaling behavior in a tractable contrastive setting.
AI.method: The authors analyze a sketched linear model where the learner observes sketched views of two correlated Gaussian latent variables and trains a bilinear contrastive score via full-batch empirical gradient descent. They use a Gaussian-negative quadratic contrastive surrogate loss under aligned power-law spectra and a contrastive source condition. The risk is decomposed into five components: irreducible risk, approximation error, GD bias, GD variance, and a cross term (controlled by bias and variance, thus not affecting upper-bound scaling).
AI.result: The main theorem provides explicit scaling laws in terms of sketch dimension M, sample size N, and effective optimization horizon L_eff. Compared to standard linear regression scaling laws, the contrastive setting exhibits fundamentally different scaling behavior because the model must learn interactions between two views, which changes how optimization noise and finite-sample noise scale with model size, data, and training time.
AI.conclusion: This work represents a first theoretical step toward understanding scaling behavior in contrastive learning and offers practical guidance for balancing model size, data, and optimization compute in contrastive representation learning settings.

title: Auditing Framing-Sensitive Behavioral Instability in Large Language Models for Mental Health Interactions
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into mental health support tools and other psychologically sensitive conversational applications. In such settings, behavioral stability and consistency are important for trustworthy human-AI interaction. However, semantically similar concerns can be presented through different contextual framings, potentially eliciting different model responses. Such framing-sensitive variability may challenge user expectations regarding system behavior and complicate the assessment of AI reliability. While prior studies have primarily examined such effects at the behavioral level, less is known about how framing-related variation is reflected in the internal representations of aligned language models. In this work, we investigate these effects using controlled matched prompts spanning multiple contextual framing conditions across several instruction-tuned model families. Across architectures, framing systematically alters interpretive response tendencies. Layer-wise probing analyses show that behavior-associated information remains decodable throughout transformer depth, with architecture-dependent variation in decoding strength. Moreover, held-out framing probes remained consistently above chance across architectures despite strong lexical baselines. Activation steering experiments further suggest that framing-associated representational directions can partially modulate downstream behavioral outcomes. Finally, these findings indicate that robustness to contextual variation may represent an important consideration when evaluating the consistency and trustworthiness of conversational AI systems deployed in mental-health-oriented interactions.

AI.tldr: Semantically similar mental health queries framed differently elicit systematically varied responses from aligned LLMs. Internal representations encode framing-associated information throughout transformer layers, and activation steering along framing directions can partially modulate behavior, highlighting contextual robustness as a key trustworthiness metric.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in mental health support tools where behavioral consistency is critical for trust. Prior work has examined framing effects at the behavioral level, but little is known about how contextual framing variation manifests in the internal representations of aligned models. The authors aim to bridge this gap by investigating representational correlates of framing sensitivity.
AI.method: The study uses controlled matched prompts spanning multiple contextual framing conditions across several instruction-tuned model families. Layer-wise probing analyses decode behavior-associated information throughout transformer depth. Held-out framing probes are evaluated against strong lexical baselines. Activation steering experiments test whether framing-associated representational directions can causally modulate downstream behavioral outcomes.
AI.result: Framing systematically alters interpretive response tendencies across architectures. Behavior-associated information remains decodable at all transformer layers, with architecture-dependent variation in decoding strength. Held-out framing probes perform consistently above chance despite strong lexical baselines. Activation steering along framing directions partially modulates downstream behavioral responses.
AI.conclusion: Robustness to contextual framing variation should be considered an important dimension when evaluating the consistency and trustworthiness of conversational AI systems deployed in mental-health-oriented interactions.

title: Computational Analysis of Heart Rate Variability in Healthy Adults
summary: Heart Rate Variability (HRV) analysis is a key indicator of cardiac physiological state and aids in disease diagnosis. However, research on HRV parameters in healthy individuals remains limited, and no gold standard exists. This study evaluates HRV indices in 40 healthy adults (20 men, 20 women, aged 30-50) to improve HRV's clinical utility. Using computational methods for signal processing and data analysis, time, frequency, and nonlinear indices were analyzed to address five questions: (1) normality, (2) stability, (3) correlation, (4) reproducibility, and (5) consistency. Key findings: (1) Time-domain and nonlinear indices, particularly global and LF (low frequency), follow normal distributions, with gender differences noted. (2) Most indices are stable except HF (high frequency)-related ones. (3) High correlations in HF-related indices suggest redundancy, indicating only one is necessary in studies. (4) Comparisons with the Fantasia database revealed less than 10% error for most indices, except SD2 and SDNN in women (greater than 15%). (5) Time-domain and nonlinear indices show low inter-study variability, while frequency-domain indices exhibit high variability, limiting cross-study comparisons. The selected indices-ApEn and IRRR (global variability), HRVi and SD2 (LF), and MADRR or rMSSD (HF)-are best suited for accurately representing HRV components and enhancing its clinical and research relevance.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates HRV parameters in 40 healthy adults, assessing normality, stability, correlation, reproducibility, and consistency across time-, frequency-, and nonlinear domains. Key findings: time-domain and nonlinear indices are normally distributed and stable; HF-related indices are redundant; most indices show <10% error vs. Fantasia database; frequency-domain indices exhibit high inter-study variability. The authors recommend ApEn, IRRR, HRVi, SD2, and MADRR/rMSSD as optimal HRV indices for clinical and research applications.
AI.motivation: HRV analysis is a key cardiac physiological indicator, yet research on HRV parameters in healthy individuals remains limited, and no gold standard exists for which indices to use. This knowledge gap undermines HRV's clinical utility.
AI.method: Computational signal processing and data analysis were applied to HRV recordings from 40 healthy adults (20 men, 20 women, aged 30–50). Time-domain, frequency-domain, and nonlinear indices were systematically evaluated across five dimensions: (1) normality testing, (2) stability, (3) inter-index correlation, (4) reproducibility against the Fantasia database, and (5) inter-study consistency.
AI.result: (1) Time-domain and nonlinear indices plus LF follow normal distributions, with gender differences. (2) Most indices are stable except HF-related ones. (3) HF-related indices are highly correlated (redundant). (4) Compared to Fantasia, error was <10% for most indices, but SD2 and SDNN in women exceeded 15%. (5) Time-domain and nonlinear indices show low inter-study variability; frequency-domain indices show high variability, limiting cross-study comparisons.
AI.conclusion: A parsimonious subset of indices—ApEn and IRRR for global variability, HRVi and SD2 for LF, and MADRR or rMSSD for HF—is recommended. This selection accurately represents HRV components while minimizing redundancy, thereby enhancing HRV's clinical and research relevance. Frequency-domain indices are cautioned against for cross-study comparisons due to high variability.

title: Discovering Millions of Interpretable Features with Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for decomposing superposed language model representations into sparse and interpretable features. However, training SAEs is computationally expensive, and available open-source SAE models remain limited. In this work, we introduce \textbf{Qwen3-Instruct SAE}, a comprehensive suite of SAEs trained on the Qwen3 instruction-tuned model family, covering Qwen3-1.7B, Qwen3-4B, and Qwen3-8B. For Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B, we train layer-wise SAEs at three key activation sites: residual streams, MLP outputs, and attention outputs. For Qwen3-8B, we train SAEs on a subset of residual stream layers. We systematically evaluate these SAEs using both activation-level reconstruction metrics and model-level recovery metrics, revealing distinct sparsity--fidelity trade-offs across layers and components. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of Qwen3-Instruct SAE through a refusal-steering case study, showing that selected SAE features can causally steer instruction-tuned Qwen3 models toward refusal behavior. Our release provides a practical resource for studying sparse representations, feature-level mechanisms, and behavioral interventions in instruction-tuned language models

AI.tldr: The paper introduces Qwen3-Instruct SAE, a suite of sparse autoencoders trained on Qwen3 instruction-tuned models (1.7B, 4B, 8B) across multiple activation sites. It systematically evaluates sparsity-fidelity trade-offs and demonstrates causal steering capabilities through a refusal-steering case study.
AI.motivation: Training SAEs is computationally expensive, and open-source SAE models are scarce, particularly for instruction-tuned models. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a comprehensive, publicly available SAE suite for the Qwen3 model family to facilitate research on sparse representations and mechanistic interpretability.
AI.method: The authors train sparse autoencoders on three Qwen3 instruction-tuned model sizes (1.7B, 4B, 8B) at multiple activation sites: residual streams, MLP outputs, and attention outputs. For the smaller models, layer-wise SAEs are trained across all layers; for the 8B model, SAEs are trained on a subset of residual stream layers. Evaluation uses both activation-level reconstruction metrics (e.g., L2 loss, explained variance) and model-level recovery metrics (how well the SAE-reconstructed activations preserve downstream model behavior). A refusal-steering case study demonstrates causal intervention using selected SAE features.
AI.result: The evaluation reveals distinct sparsity-fidelity trade-offs that vary across layers and components (residual stream, MLP, attention). The refusal-steering experiment demonstrates that specific SAE features can causally steer instruction-tuned Qwen3 models toward refusal behavior, validating the practical utility of the learned features for behavioral interventions.
AI.conclusion: The Qwen3-Instruct SAE suite offers a valuable open-source resource for studying sparse representations, feature-level mechanisms, and behavioral interventions in instruction-tuned LMs. The work confirms that SAEs can capture causally meaningful features and highlights the layer- and component-dependent nature of sparsity-fidelity trade-offs.

title: ReaORE: Reasoning-Guided Progressive Open Relation Extraction Empowered by Large Reasoning Models
summary: Open Relation Extraction (OpenRE) requires a model to extract unseen relations between head and tail entities from unstructured text for real-world applications. The core challenge of OpenRE lies in achieving reliable generalization to unseen relation types. Current OpenRE approaches either employ clustering techniques, which cannot generate relation labels and suffer from poor generalization, or rely on direct relation label generation via Large Language Models (LLMs), which lack sufficient discriminative capacity to distinguish easily confused relations. To address these limitations, we propose Reasoning-guided progressive OpenRE (ReaORE), a framework for performing relation extraction through coarse-to-fine relation reasoning. Specifically, ReaORE consists of two key stages: (i) relation filtering, which reasons over multiple aspects to understand relations and instances, yielding an initial relation set, and further supplements and filters relations via embedding-based similarity to ensure the target relation is included; (ii) relation prediction, which aims to predict the target relations from the above set via fine-grained comparative reasoning to better distinguish easily confused relations. Extensive experiments on two widely used OpenRE datasets demonstrate that ReaORE outperforms existing baselines.

AI.tldr: ReaORE is a coarse-to-fine OpenRE framework combining multi-aspect relation filtering with embedding similarity, followed by fine-grained comparative reasoning to accurately predict relations, outperforming both clustering-based and LLM-based baselines.
AI.motivation: Existing OpenRE methods suffer from two key limitations: clustering approaches cannot generate explicit relation labels and generalize poorly, while LLM-based direct generation lacks discriminative power to distinguish easily confused relations. A framework is needed that can both generate relation labels and discriminate similar relations.
AI.method: ReaORE operates in two stages: (1) Relation Filtering — reasons over multiple semantic aspects to produce an initial relation set, then supplements and filters candidates using embedding-based similarity to ensure recall of the target relation; (2) Relation Prediction — performs fine-grained comparative reasoning over the filtered candidate set to precisely identify the target relation and resolve confusion among similar relations.
AI.result: ReaORE outperforms all existing baselines on two widely-used OpenRE datasets, demonstrating superior generalization to unseen relations.
AI.conclusion: The coarse-to-fine reasoning paradigm of ReaORE effectively addresses the dual challenges of label generation and relation discrimination in OpenRE, establishing a new state-of-the-art approach.

title: The Capability Frontier: Benchmarks Miss 82% of Model Performance
summary: Existing benchmarks typically report accuracy for a single model on a single run. This systematically understates real-world LLM capabilities, particularly under heterogeneous data distributions: (i) different models get different questions correct according to their specializations, and (ii) given a budget, multiple generations can be sampled and selectively retained. To quantify this gap, we introduce the Capability Frontier: a Pareto frontier over a set of models that characterizes the best achievable performance at each cost level under optimal selection across models and generations (i.e., via an oracle). Our construction corrects for two opposing biases: underestimation from single-model evaluation and overestimation from taking maxima over noisy samples. We study 21 LLMs across 16 widely used benchmarks spanning coding, reasoning, medicine, factuality, instruction following, and agentic tasks, comparing Capability Frontier performance at matched cost to each benchmark's top-performing model. Correcting for single-model evaluation yields a 54% error rate reduction; additionally correcting for single runs yields an 82% improvement, with SOTA accuracy matched at 85% cost reduction. Complementing these empirical results, we use controlled probabilistic simulations to show that higher query topic entropy produces a near-monotonic increase in the performance gap between oracle routing and the best single model. Our findings suggest collective LLM capabilities are substantially underestimated, with implications for evaluation and deployment in data-heterogeneous, multi-domain settings.

AI.tldr: Introduces the Capability Frontier—a Pareto frontier over multiple LLMs and generations—revealing that single-model, single-run evaluation underestimates collective LLM performance by up to 82%, with SOTA accuracy achievable at 85% lower cost via oracle selection.
AI.motivation: Standard benchmark evaluation (single model, single run) systematically underestimates real-world LLM capabilities. In heterogeneous data distributions, different models excel on different queries, and budget-constrained sampling with selective retention can boost performance. Prior work fails to quantify the gap between reported and achievable performance under optimal model/generation selection, while naive max-over-samples introduces overestimation bias.
AI.method: Constructs a Capability Frontier—a Pareto frontier over a set of models characterizing optimal accuracy at each cost level, using an oracle that selects the best response across models and multiple generations per query. This corrects both underestimation (single-model evaluation) and overestimation (noisy maxima). Empirical evaluation covers 21 LLMs across 16 benchmarks (coding, reasoning, medicine, factuality, instruction following, agentic tasks). Controlled probabilistic simulations analyze how query topic entropy affects the oracle-to-best-single-model performance gap.
AI.result: Correcting single-model evaluation yields 54% error rate reduction; additionally correcting single-run evaluation yields 82% improvement. SOTA accuracy is matched at 85% cost reduction. Higher query topic entropy produces a near-monotonic increase in the oracle routing vs. best single model performance gap.
AI.conclusion: Collective LLM capabilities are substantially underestimated by standard evaluation paradigms. The Capability Frontier framework offers a more accurate characterization of achievable performance under optimal model selection, with significant implications for multi-domain LLM evaluation and cost-efficient deployment.

title: From Weights to Features: SAE-Guided Activation Regularization for LLM Continual Learning
summary: Weight-space regularization methods such as Elastic Weight Consolidation (EWC) are the standard approach to catastrophic forgetting in continual learning. However, those methods tend to underperform when applied to large language models. We argue that such underperformance can be partly explained by the ``polysemantic'' nature of large language models: per-weight importance estimates utilized by EWC-style regularization are too coarse and cannot isolate the knowledge that needs protection. In this paper, we propose regularizing instead in the model's activation space, using pretrained Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) as a monosemantic feature dictionary. From the perspective of constrained optimization, we derive a new loss function that uses the SAE feature dictionary to explicitly balance stability and plasticity, and show that EWC is a special case in the one-sided weight-space penalty setting. Unlike replay-based methods that store or revisit examples from earlier tasks, our method requires no previous-task data after mask construction: current-task data is used to compute a compact SAE feature mask, and only this mask is retained for later training. Further, since the feature space has significantly lower dimensionality than the parameter space, the proposed method is more memory efficient. On the TRACE and MedCL continual learning benchmarks, the method achieves the strongest result among approaches without introducing task-specific architectural components, also surpassing traditional weight-space regularization methods like EWC. Beyond performance comparisons, we provide empirical evidence for the polysemanticity thesis: task-relevant representations are linearly separable in the SAE feature basis but indistinguishable from chance in the weight basis, and weight-space protection is nearly non-selective at the concept level.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a continual learning method that regularizes in activation space using Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) as a monosemantic feature dictionary, rather than in weight space like EWC. The method derives a loss function balancing stability and plasticity, requires storing only compact SAE feature masks rather than previous-task data, and is more memory efficient due to lower feature space dimensionality. It achieves state-of-the-art results on TRACE and MedCL benchmarks without task-specific architectural components, and provides empirical evidence that LLM polysemanticity explains EWC's underperformance.
AI.motivation: Weight-space regularization methods like EWC underperform on large language models. The authors argue this is because LLMs are "polysemantic" — individual weights encode multiple unrelated concepts, making per-weight importance estimates too coarse to isolate and protect specific knowledge. A more targeted, monosemantic approach is needed.
AI.method: The method regularizes in activation space instead of weight space, using pretrained Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) as a monosemantic feature dictionary. From constrained optimization, a new loss function is derived that explicitly balances stability and plasticity using SAE features. During training on a new task, a compact SAE feature mask is computed from current-task data and retained. In subsequent training, only this mask is used — no previous-task data is stored or replayed. EWC is shown to be a special case with a one-sided weight-space penalty.
AI.result: On TRACE and MedCL continual learning benchmarks, the method achieves the strongest results among approaches that do not introduce task-specific architectural components, surpassing EWC and other weight-space regularization methods. Empirical analysis supports the polysemanticity thesis: task-relevant representations are linearly separable in the SAE feature basis but indistinguishable from chance in the weight basis, and weight-space protection is nearly non-selective at the concept level.
AI.conclusion: Activation-space regularization via SAE feature masks is a more effective and memory-efficient strategy for continual learning in LLMs than weight-space methods like EWC. The polysemantic nature of LLM weights fundamentally limits EWC-style approaches, and monosemantic feature representations offer a principled solution.

title: Where Do Models Find Happiness? Emotion Vectors in Open-Source LLMs
summary: Recent work identified emotion vectors in Claude Sonnet 4.5, which are internal representations that encode emotion concepts, causally influence behavior, and exhibit geometry mirroring human psychological structure. We test the generality of these findings in two open-weight models, Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509 and Gemma-4-E4B-it, extracting emotion contrast vectors across all layers, using two model-generated corpora. We recover valence geometry for both models, with peak PC1--valence correlations of $r = 0.76$ and $r = 0.83$, approaching the $r = 0.81$ reported for Claude.Beyond replication, we observe notable differences in how valence representations emerge across model depth. In Gemma-4-E4B-it, valence is strongly encoded in early layers but collapses towards later layers, whereas Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509 exhibits the opposite pattern, with valence representations absent in early layers, but emerging at mid depths. Arousal encoding, in contrast, is sensitive to the extraction corpus: both models show stronger PC2--arousal alignment with Gemma-generated stories ($r$ up to $0.45$) than Apertus-generated ones ($r \leq 0.21$), suggesting arousal-relevant cues are unevenly distributed across generated corpora. We open-source our experiment code and dataset for reproducible investigation of emotion representations across language model architectures.

AI.tldr: This paper tests whether emotion vectors previously found in Claude Sonnet 4.5 generalize to open-weight models (Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509 and Gemma-4-E4B-it). Both models exhibit valence geometry similar to Claude, but the layer-wise emergence of valence differs markedly between architectures. Arousal encoding is corpus-dependent, appearing stronger with Gemma-generated text.
AI.motivation: Prior work discovered emotion vectors in the proprietary Claude Sonnet 4.5 — internal representations encoding emotion concepts that causally shape behavior and reflect human psychological structure. This paper aims to test the generality and robustness of these findings by replicating the analysis in open-weight models, which allows full access to internal representations and facilitates reproducibility across different architectures.
AI.method: The authors extract emotion contrast vectors across all layers of two open-weight models (Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509 and Gemma-4-E4B-it) using two model-generated text corpora (one from each model). They apply PCA to the extracted vectors and measure alignment between principal components and psychological dimensions of valence and arousal, comparing results to the previously reported findings from Claude Sonnet 4.5.
AI.result: Both models recover valence geometry: peak PC1–valence correlations reach r=0.76 (Apertus) and r=0.83 (Gemma), comparable to Claude's r=0.81. However, valence representations emerge differently across layers — Gemma encodes valence strongly in early layers that collapses later, while Apertus shows absent early-layer valence that emerges mid-depth. Arousal encoding (PC2) is corpus-sensitive: both models show stronger alignment with Gemma-generated stories (r up to 0.45) than Apertus-generated ones (r ≤ 0.21).
AI.conclusion: Emotion vectors and valence geometry generalize beyond Claude Sonnet 4.5 to open-weight models, supporting the robustness of the phenomenon. However, architectural differences produce distinct layer-wise profiles of valence emergence, and arousal representation quality depends on the corpus used for extraction. The authors release code and data for reproducibility.

title: Target-Aware Bandit Allocation for Scalable Surrogate Optimization in Chemical Space
summary: Identifying high-utility candidates from massive discrete spaces under expensive evaluations is a recurring challenge across the sciences, with structure-based drug discovery as a prominent example. While surrogate-based optimization can increase sample efficiency by reducing the number of expensive evaluations, modern molecular libraries have reached billions to trillions of compounds, making full-library surrogate inference itself a major computational bottleneck. We introduce BOBa, a bandit-guided surrogate optimization framework that eliminates full-library inference by adaptively allocating computation across partitions of the action space. By treating partitions as arms in a multi-armed bandit, BOBa concentrates inference and evaluations on empirically promising partitions while maintaining principled exploration. Experiments on real-world synthesis-on-demand libraries demonstrate that optimism-under-uncertainty bandits, combined with meaningful action space partitioning, are essential for effective allocation of inference and evaluations. Our findings reveal a tunable tradeoff between screening performance and surrogate inference cost, which supports practical optimization over current libraries, and establishes a viable route to ultra-large library virtual screening.

AI.tldr: BOBa is a bandit-guided surrogate optimization framework that partitions massive discrete action spaces and uses multi-armed bandits to adaptively allocate surrogate inference and expensive evaluations, eliminating the need for full-library surrogate inference in ultra-large virtual screening.
AI.motivation: Modern molecular libraries contain billions to trillions of compounds, making full-library surrogate inference computationally prohibitive. Existing surrogate-based optimization methods require inference over the entire library, creating a major bottleneck for structure-based drug discovery and other high-throughput screening applications.
AI.method: BOBa partitions the discrete action space into subsets and treats each partition as an arm in a multi-armed bandit. An optimism-under-uncertainty (Upper Confidence Bound) bandit strategy adaptively allocates both surrogate inference and expensive evaluations to the most promising partitions. This concentrates computational resources on empirically promising regions while maintaining principled exploration across partitions, avoiding exhaustive inference over the full library.
AI.result: Experiments on real-world synthesis-on-demand molecular libraries show that optimism-under-uncertainty bandits with meaningful partitioning significantly outperform naive allocation strategies. The framework reveals a tunable tradeoff between screening performance (quality of candidates identified) and surrogate inference cost.
AI.conclusion: BOBa establishes a viable route to ultra-large library virtual screening by decoupling surrogate inference cost from library size. The approach supports practical optimization over billion-scale compound libraries and provides a principled way to navigate the performance-efficiency tradeoff in massive discrete space optimization.

title: MinGram: A Minimalist Unigram Tokenizer with High Compression and Competitive Morphological Alignment
summary: The Unigram tokenizer uses an elegant representation which makes it straightforward to edit vocabularies, but its training is comparatively heavy and complex. We introduce MinGram (Minimalist Unigram), which keeps the token-list representation but simplifies training using a BPE-derived seed vocabulary, Hard EM on a minimum-token path, and a single flat score-pruning step. This removes the suffix array, the forward-backward pass, and the iterative prune loop, leaving a procedure that requires little beyond tokenizer inference itself. By making token count the primary objective and using a Unigram score only as a tiebreak, MinGram keeps the compression of pure token-count methods while retaining much of the morphological alignment and downstream quality of probabilistic ones. Across six languages, MinGram compresses better than both BPE and standard Unigram, and a compression-oriented variant matches the strongest token-count compressors while retaining substantially higher morphological alignment. In controlled downstream language-model training, Unigram-family tokenizers, with MinGram among the best, consistently beat BPE in bits-per-byte.

AI.tldr: MinGram simplifies Unigram tokenizer training by using BPE-derived seed vocabulary, Hard EM on minimum-token paths, and single-step score pruning, achieving better compression than BPE and standard Unigram while maintaining morphological alignment and downstream LM quality.
AI.motivation: Standard Unigram tokenizer training is heavy and complex (involving suffix arrays, forward-backward passes, iterative pruning). The goal is to preserve the elegant Unigram vocabulary representation while drastically simplifying training, maintaining or improving compression and morphological alignment.
AI.method: MinGram uses: (1) a BPE-derived seed vocabulary instead of a suffix-array seed; (2) Hard EM optimization on a minimum-token path (minimizing token count as primary objective, Unigram score as tiebreaker); and (3) a single flat score-pruning step, eliminating iterated pruning. This removes suffix arrays, forward-backward passes, and iterative loops.
AI.result: Across six languages, MinGram compresses better than both BPE and standard Unigram. A compression-oriented variant matches top token-count compressors while having substantially higher morphological alignment. In LM training, Unigram-family tokenizers (MinGram among the best) consistently beat BPE in bits-per-byte.
AI.conclusion: MinGram preserves the Unigram token-list representation's editability while making training nearly as simple as tokenizer inference, achieving state-of-the-art compression and strong downstream performance.

title: LCAi: Life Cycle Assessment with big data fusion and retrieval-augmented generation-assisted interpretation
comment: 23 pages, 14 figures, 6 tables. Includes Supplementary Information
summary: The interpretation phase of life cycle assessment often lacks structured mechanisms for translating quantified improvement opportunities addressing environmental hotspots into actionable strategic pathways under technological, social, and policy uncertainty. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a perspective-conditioned retrieval-augmented generation framework for LCA interpretation, where a multi-perspective retrieval and controlled synthesis is incorporated in the artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted LCA. To operationalise large language models in LCA interpretation, a perspective fusion RAG architecture was developed, covering academic, industry, public discourse, and European union (EU) funding datasets. Our approach comprises three steps: (1) a scenario anchor defining system boundaries and decarbonization targets, (2) a set of perspective-specific micro-queries with constrained retrieval, and (3) a neutral synthesis step integrating only ledger-stored outputs without further retrieval. The framework is demonstrated through a hydrogen-enabled diesel reduction use case in an Italian apple production facility using GPT-5 nano as the reasoning model. Overall, the structured retrieval and constrained synthesis are designed to mitigate the risk of hallucination while preserving cross-domain diversity. The approach presented can support more disciplined translation of impact results into strategic pathways and opens up new avenues for the use of advanced AI tools in LCA studies, particularly those focused on technologies that could be deployed at scale. This proof-of-concept demonstrates how AI-assisted, evidence-grounded interpretation can support implementation-oriented decision-making beyond conventional LCA studies.

AI.tldr: Proposes a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework with multi-perspective fusion to improve LCA interpretation, translating environmental hotspots into actionable strategies while mitigating hallucination risks, demonstrated via a hydrogen-diesel reduction case study in Italian apple production.
AI.motivation: Current LCA interpretation lacks structured mechanisms to translate quantified improvement opportunities into actionable strategic pathways under technological, social, and policy uncertainty. There is a gap in connecting hotspot identification to implementation-oriented decision-making.
AI.method: A perspective-conditioned RAG architecture with three steps: (1) scenario anchor defining system boundaries and decarbonization targets; (2) perspective-specific micro-queries with constrained retrieval across academic, industry, public discourse, and EU funding datasets; (3) neutral synthesis integrating only ledger-stored outputs. Demonstrated using GPT-5 nano on a hydrogen-enabled diesel reduction use case in Italian apple production.
AI.result: The structured retrieval and constrained synthesis successfully mitigated hallucination risk while preserving cross-domain diversity. The proof-of-concept showed that AI-assisted, evidence-grounded interpretation can support implementation-oriented decision-making beyond conventional LCA.
AI.conclusion: The perspective-fusion RAG framework enables more disciplined translation of LCA impact results into strategic pathways and opens new avenues for advanced AI tools in LCA studies, particularly for scalable technologies.

title: Zero-Shot Size Transfer for Neural ODEs on Sparse Random Graphs: Graphon Limits and Adjoint Convergence
summary: Graph Neural Differential Equations (GNDEs) model continuous-time graph dynamics by parameterizing Neural ODE velocity fields with Graph Neural Networks. Their local, size-independent filters suggest a zero-shot size-transfer principle: train on a small graph and deploy on larger, similar graphs without retraining. We develop a quantitative theory for this principle on sparse random graphs sampled from graphons. We consider Graphon Neural Differential Equations (Graphon-NDEs) and adjoint Graphon-NDEs as the infinite-node limits of the forward and adjoint GNDE systems, and establish well-posedness. For an $n$-node random graph with sparsity parameter $α_n$, we prove trajectory-wise convergence of GNDE solutions to Graphon-NDE solutions at rate $O((α_n n)^{-1/2})$, up to logarithmic factors, with high probability. We also establish uniform-in-time convergence bounds for adjoint systems governing hidden-state and parameter gradients. We further study discretize-then-optimize (DTO) and optimize-then-discretize (OTD) training. Under explicit Euler discretization with $M$ steps, we show that DTO and OTD are asymptotically consistent, with hidden-state and local parameter-gradient discrepancies of orders $O(1/M)$ and $O(1/M^2)$, respectively, up to sparsity and logarithmic factors. Experiments on HSBM and tent graphons support the theoretical rates, while zero-shot transfer experiments across four graphon classes demonstrate accurate deployment of learned GNDEs on larger independently sampled graphs.

AI.tldr: Develops a quantitative theory for zero-shot size transfer in Graph Neural Differential Equations (GNDEs) on sparse random graphs sampled from graphons. Establishes well-posedness of infinite-node Graphon-NDE limits, proves trajectory convergence at rate O((α_n n)^{-1/2}), analyzes DTO vs OTD training consistency, and validates results experimentally.
AI.motivation: GNDEs use local, size-independent filters, suggesting they can be trained on small graphs and deployed on larger ones without retraining ("zero-shot size transfer"). However, this empirical observation lacks theoretical foundation. The authors aim to develop a rigorous quantitative theory explaining when and how fast this transfer principle holds.
AI.method: The authors formalize the problem using graphon theory. They define Graphon Neural Differential Equations (Graphon-NDEs) as infinite-node continuum limits of GNDEs and prove their well-posedness. For n-node random graphs with sparsity α_n sampled from a graphon, they derive high-probability trajectory-wise convergence bounds at rate O((α_n n)^{-1/2}). They extend this to adjoint systems (for gradient computation), establishing uniform-in-time convergence. They further analyze two training paradigms — discretize-then-optimize (DTO) and optimize-then-discretize (OTD) — under explicit Euler discretization, proving asymptotic consistency with error rates O(1/M) and O(1/M²) for hidden-state and parameter-gradient discrepancies.
AI.result: Key theoretical results: (1) GNDE solutions converge to Graphon-NDE solutions at rate O((α_n n)^{-1/2}) (up to log factors) with high probability. (2) Adjoint state and parameter gradient convergence holds uniformly in time. (3) DTO and OTD are asymptotically consistent; hidden-state discrepancy is O(1/M) and local parameter-gradient discrepancy is O(1/M²). Experiments on HSBM and tent graphons validate the theoretical rates, and zero-shot transfer across four graphon classes shows accurate deployment on larger independently sampled graphs.
AI.conclusion: The paper provides the first rigorous theoretical framework for zero-shot size transfer in GNDEs, confirming that local, permutation-equivariant filters enable generalization from small to large graphs sampled from the same graphon. The theory covers both forward dynamics and gradient computation via adjoints, and clarifies the relationship between DTO and OTD training. This bridges continuous-depth graph learning and graphon theory, with practical implications for scalable graph model deployment.

title: Improving General Role-Playing Agents via Psychology-Grounded Reasoning and Role-Aware Policy Optimization
summary: Building general-purpose role-playing agents that faithfully portray any character from a natural-language profile remains challenging. The dominant paradigm -- supervised fine-tuning -- encourages behavioral mimicry without deep, human-like internal thought processes, resulting in poor out-of-distribution generalization. Therefore, we propose \textbf{Psy-CoT}, a psychology-grounded chain-of-thought framework that decomposes pre-response reasoning into three role-specific steps -- \emph{Interaction Perception}, \emph{Psychological Empathy}, and \emph{Logical Construction} -- so that the model \emph{thinks dynamically} from the profile rather than merely mimicking surface patterns. While structured reasoning provides a foundation, it alone is insufficient; reinforcement learning is essential to further align the model with character fidelity. However, we observe that under LLM-based reward models, both generic phrases that hack the reward model and genuinely role-specific phrases receive identical gradient signals -- this hacking accumulates over training, misleading the model into treating both as equally optimal choices. To address this, we propose \textbf{Role-Aware Policy Optimization (RAPO)}, which uses profile--token mutual information to weight gradients asymmetrically -- amplifying role-specific tokens under positive advantage while attenuating them under negative advantage. Experiments on CoSER, CharacterBench, and CharacterEval demonstrate that Psy-CoT outperforms existing role-playing CoT methods, and RAPO consistently surpasses GRPO across multiple model scales.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Psy-CoT, a psychology-grounded chain-of-thought reasoning framework for role-playing agents, and RAPO, a reinforcement learning method that uses profile–token mutual information to asymmetrically weight gradients, preventing reward hacking. Both methods together improve character fidelity over existing approaches.
AI.motivation: Supervised fine-tuning for role-playing agents encourages surface-level mimicry rather than deep internal reasoning, leading to poor generalization. Additionally, LLM-based reward models in RL fail to distinguish between genuinely role-specific phrases and generic phrases that hack the reward, causing both to receive identical gradient signals and misleading optimization.
AI.method: Psy-CoT decomposes pre-response reasoning into three steps: Interaction Perception, Psychological Empathy, and Logical Construction, enabling dynamic thinking from character profiles. RAPO employs profile–token mutual information to weight policy gradients asymmetrically, amplifying role-specific tokens under positive advantage and attenuating them under negative advantage, relative to a GRPO baseline.
AI.result: Experiments on CoSER, CharacterBench, and CharacterEval show that Psy-CoT outperforms existing role-playing CoT methods, and RAPO consistently surpasses GRPO across multiple model scales.
AI.conclusion: Combining structured psychological reasoning (Psy-CoT) with role-aware reinforcement learning (RAPO) yields role-playing agents with superior character fidelity and generalization, addressing both the shallow mimicry problem and the reward hacking problem inherent in prior approaches.

title: PersistentKV: Page-Aware Decode Scheduling for Long-Context LLM Serving on Commodity GPUs
summary: Autoregressive large language model (LLM) serving is increasingly limited by key-value (KV) cache movement rather than dense matrix multiplication. Modern paged-attention systems reduce KV-cache fragmentation and mature kernels such as FlashInfer provide highly optimized native-paged decode attention. However, the best single-kernel implementation is not always the best serving schedule: low-active long-context decode can under-utilize commodity GPUs, while mixed sequence lengths introduce a tension between many exact-length launches and coarse padded batches. We present PersistentKV, a native block-table decode attention engine and page-aware scheduling study for grouped-query attention (GQA). PersistentKV maps work by KV-head group, is designed to reuse K,V tiles across grouped query heads, supports native page tables, and adds a compact workqueue schedule that executes only non-empty row-KV-head-sequence-split tasks. On an RTX 3060 with FP16, page size 16, Hq=32, Hkv=8, d=128, and identical correctness tolerance against FlashInfer, a calibrated adaptive policy selects FlashInfer for small active batches, PersistentKV sequence splitting for B1 long-context steps, and PersistentKV workqueue scheduling for B8 long-context steps. With thresholds and split counts fixed on calibration traces, one held-out trace seed improves synchronized wall throughput by 1.063-1.265x on B8 bimodal, uniform, and Zipf-like workloads and by 1.399x on a B1 bucketed trace. On the B4 bimodal boundary case, the policy avoids the PersistentKV regression by selecting FlashInfer. These results identify a concrete systems niche for adaptive page-aware decode scheduling and show that work assignment, not only attention math, is a decisive serving-system variable.

AI.tldr: PersistentKV introduces a native block-table decode attention engine with adaptive page-aware scheduling for GQA-based LLM serving. It proposes two scheduling modes—sequence splitting and workqueue scheduling—and demonstrates that a calibrated adaptive policy selecting between PersistentKV and FlashInfer yields 1.063–1.399× throughput improvements across diverse workload patterns on commodity GPUs.
AI.motivation: KV-cache movement, not dense matmul, increasingly bottlenecks autoregressive LLM serving. Existing systems face two problems: (1) low-active long-context decode under-utilizes GPUs, and (2) mixed sequence lengths create tension between exact-length kernel launches (high overhead) and coarse padded batches (wasted compute). The authors argue that work assignment strategy—not just attention kernel math—is a decisive serving-system variable that has been underexplored.
AI.method: PersistentKV is a native block-table decode attention engine targeting grouped-query attention (GQA). It maps work by KV-head group, reuses K/V tiles across grouped query heads, and supports native page tables. Two scheduling modes are proposed: (1) sequence splitting for B1 long-context steps, which splits individual sequences to expose parallelism, and (2) workqueue scheduling for B8 long-context steps, which executes only non-empty row-KV-head-sequence-split tasks via a compact workqueue. A calibrated adaptive policy selects between FlashInfer (small active batches), PersistentKV sequence splitting (B1 long-context), and PersistentKV workqueue scheduling (B8 long-context), with thresholds and split counts fixed on calibration traces. Evaluation uses an RTX 3060 with FP16, page size 16, Hq=32, Hkv=8, d=128.
AI.result: On held-out traces, the adaptive policy improves synchronized wall throughput by 1.063–1.265× on B8 bimodal, uniform, and Zipf-like workloads and by 1.399× on a B1 bucketed trace. On the B4 bimodal boundary case, the policy correctly avoids PersistentKV regression by selecting FlashInfer.
AI.conclusion: PersistentKV identifies a concrete systems niche for adaptive page-aware decode scheduling in LLM serving. The results demonstrate that work assignment strategy is a decisive serving-system variable distinct from attention math optimization, and that adaptive kernel selection can yield meaningful throughput gains across diverse workloads.

title: NuclearQAv2: A Structured Benchmark for Evaluating Domain-Science Competence in Large Language Models
summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of tasks, but ensuring their reliability in highly technical domains remains a significant challenge. In nuclear engineering, problem solving often requires not only factual knowledge but also quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding. To address the need for systematic evaluation in this domain, we introduce NuclearQAv2, a benchmark for assessing LLMs on nuclear engineering knowledge. The benchmark comprises approximately 1,240 question-answer pairs spanning three categories: boolean, numeric, and verbal. NuclearQAv2 is constructed using a hybrid pipeline that combines expert-authored questions, existing datasets, and LLM-assisted generation from domain-specific technical corpora. By leveraging structured prompting for both automated question generation and response evaluation, the proposed framework enables scalable benchmark construction and evaluation. We evaluate a diverse set of LLMs using NuclearQAv2 and observe substantial performance differences across task types. While the models generally perform well on factual questions, quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding remain considerably more challenging. These results highlight the importance of multi-faceted evaluation frameworks and establish NuclearQAv2 as a scalable benchmark for assessing LLM capabilities in technical domains.

AI.tldr: NuclearQAv2 is a benchmark of ~1,240 QA pairs (boolean, numeric, verbal) for evaluating LLMs on nuclear engineering. Built via a hybrid pipeline combining expert-authored questions, existing datasets, and LLM-assisted generation, it reveals that while LLMs handle factual questions well, they struggle with quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding in this technical domain.
AI.motivation: LLMs perform well broadly but their reliability in highly technical, domain-specific settings — particularly nuclear engineering, which demands factual knowledge, quantitative reasoning, and conceptual understanding — remains uncertain. A systematic, scalable evaluation framework for this domain is lacking.
AI.method: The authors introduce NuclearQAv2, a benchmark with ~1,240 QA pairs across boolean, numeric, and verbal categories. Construction uses a hybrid pipeline: expert-authored questions, existing datasets, and LLM-assisted generation from domain-specific technical corpora, guided by structured prompting for both question generation and response evaluation. A diverse set of LLMs is evaluated on this benchmark.
AI.result: Substantial performance differences emerged across task types. Models generally performed well on factual (boolean/verbal) questions but struggled considerably on quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding tasks.
AI.conclusion: Multi-faceted evaluation frameworks are critical for assessing LLMs in technical domains. NuclearQAv2 establishes a scalable benchmark that exposes weaknesses in quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding, underscoring the gap between factual recall and deeper domain competence.

title: TAVR-VLM: Risk-Conditioned Causal Grounding for Hallucination-Resistant Report Generation
summary: Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement (TAVR) planning requires meticulous multimodal reasoning. However, adapting Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) to this high-stakes domain is severely impeded by diagnostic hallucinations, where generated text lacks anatomical grounding. To address this, TAVR-VLM is introduced: a novel framework featuring Risk-Conditioned Causal Grounding Attention (R-CGA) that instantiates a model-internal ``Risk $\rightarrow$ Region $\rightarrow$ Word'' structural grounding pathway. R-CGA compresses multimodal inputs into a causal risk bottleneck, purifying dense visual features into a global risk mask. During autoregressive generation, a support-projected causal consistency objective constrains token-level grounding within the risk-defined support mask. Evaluated on $\text{M}^3\text{TAVR}$, a comprehensive 1,482-patient cohort, TAVR-VLM establishes a new state-of-the-art. It achieves an AUROC of 0.896, boosts CIDEr to 0.936, and drastically reduces the hallucination rate to 8.1\%, thereby improving interpretability for evidence-based surgical AI.

AI.tldr: TAVR-VLM introduces Risk-Conditioned Causal Grounding Attention (R-CGA) to combat diagnostic hallucinations in multimodal LLMs for TAVR planning, achieving AUROC 0.896, CIDEr 0.936, and 8.1% hallucination rate on a 1,482-patient cohort.
AI.motivation: Adapting MLLMs to high-stakes TAVR planning is severely hindered by diagnostic hallucinations — generated text that lacks anatomical grounding. Existing models fail to provide the evidence-based, anatomically faithful reasoning required for clinical decision-making in transcatheter aortic valve replacement.
AI.method: TAVR-VLM proposes Risk-Conditioned Causal Grounding Attention (R-CGA), which establishes a "Risk → Region → Word" structural grounding pathway. It compresses multimodal inputs into a causal risk bottleneck, purifying dense visual features into a global risk mask. During autoregressive generation, a support-projected causal consistency objective constrains token-level grounding within the risk-defined support mask.
AI.result: Evaluated on M³TAVR, a comprehensive 1,482-patient cohort, TAVR-VLM achieves state-of-the-art performance: AUROC of 0.896, CIDEr score of 0.936, and a drastically reduced hallucination rate of 8.1%.
AI.conclusion: TAVR-VLM effectively mitigates diagnostic hallucinations through anatomically grounded causal attention, significantly improving interpretability and establishing a new benchmark for evidence-based surgical AI in TAVR planning.

title: Algorithmic Foundations of Deep Learning: Complexity-Theoretic Rates and a Characterization of Universal Approximation
summary:
Feedforward neural network (NN) expressivity is typically studied by emulating optimal basis-expansion schemes. While powerful, this perspective is incomplete: it primarily captures complexity through regularity, and therefore does not distinguish intuitively simple and complicated objects with comparable regularity, such as the square-root function and a typical Brownian path.
  The guiding message is that neural networks should be viewed not only as flexible basis functions, but also as models of computation. If a function is computable by a real-valued circuit over a prescribed elementary gate language, then it can be computed to comparable accuracy by an NN with explicit depth, width, and non-zero-parameter bounds controlled by the depth, width, gate count, and gate structure. Thus, neural-network complexity is not governed by regularity alone, but also by algorithmic complexity. We then show that any definable NN model satisfying a natural parallelization condition, allowing possibly multivariate non-linearities such as attention or layer normalization, is a universal approximator if and only if it contains a non-affine nonlinearity.
  The scope of our theory is illustrated by deducing universal approximation guarantees for continuous functions, minimax-optimal approximation guarantees for Besov classes, logarithmic-error complexity for holomorphic functions, and by showing that NNs can emulate numerical algorithms such as Newton-Raphson root finding and power iteration without architecture-specific arguments. Its precision is illustrated by shortest-path computation on $k$-vertex graphs: compiling the tropical dynamic-programming circuit yields NNs with O(log(1/ε)) non-zero parameters, exponentially improving in 1/ε over the generic $O(ε^{-c k^2})$ Lipschitz-approximation scale, for a constant c>0.

AI.tldr: Neural network expressivity should be understood through algorithmic complexity, not just functional regularity. The paper shows that functions computable by real-valued circuits can be approximated by NNs with tight resource bounds, establishes a universal approximation criterion (any parallelizable model containing a non-affine nonlinearity is universal), and demonstrates exponential improvements in parameter efficiency for algorithmic tasks like shortest-path computation.
AI.motivation: Traditional basis-expansion perspectives on NN expressivity fail to distinguish between functions of similar regularity but vastly different intuitive complexity (e.g., square-root vs. Brownian path). The authors argue that NNs should additionally be viewed as models of computation, with complexity governed by algorithmic structure rather than smoothness alone.
AI.method: The authors develop a circuit-to-NN compilation framework: any function computable by a real-valued circuit over elementary gates can be approximated by an NN with depth, width, and non-zero-parameter counts explicitly controlled by the circuit's structure. They establish a parallelization condition for definable NN models (allowing multivariate nonlinearities like attention or layer normalization) and prove that containing a non-affine nonlinearity is both necessary and sufficient for universal approximation. The framework is applied to compile algorithmic procedures (Newton-Raphson, power iteration, tropical dynamic programming) into NN architectures.
AI.result: Key results include: (1) universal approximation guarantees for continuous functions and Besov classes; (2) logarithmic-error complexity for holomorphic functions; (3) NNs emulating numerical algorithms without architecture-specific arguments; (4) for shortest-path computation on k-vertex graphs, tropical DP compilation yields NNs with O(log(1/ε)) non-zero parameters, exponentially improving over the generic O(ε^{-c k²}) Lipschitz-approximation scale.
AI.conclusion: NN complexity is governed by both regularity and algorithmic complexity. The circuit-computation perspective provides tighter, more meaningful complexity bounds, explains why some functions are efficiently learnable despite low regularity, and unifies approximation theory across diverse NN architectures through a simple universal-approximation criterion (presence of any non-affine nonlinearity in a parallelizable model).

title: Towards Explainable Adjudicative Variance: Quantifying Judicial Discretion via Gated Multi-Task Learning
comment: 17 pages (8 pages main text), 5 figures, 9 tables. Accepted to the AI for Law Workshop at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), Seoul, South Korea
summary: Legal outcome prediction must disentangle objective case facts from adjudicative context. Merit-based rulings rely on factual evidence while technical disposals may hinge on judicial discretion. We propose a Judge-Aware Gated Multi-Task Learning architecture that explicitly models this distinction. We introduce a fine-grained outcome taxonomy to supervise the encoder, enforcing a structural regularization that disentangles distinct semantic pathways. This granular legal curriculum enables our Gated Fusion mechanism to dynamically modulate reliance on judge identity. We evaluate our approach on 13,937 UK Employment Tribunal decisions. We benchmark our design against supervised fine-tuning (SFT) of a Gemma-4 26B-A4B backbone, in which judge identity and the taxonomy are injected as prompt tokens or autoregressive output targets. The two contextual signals compose only weakly when forced through a single autoregressive channel. In contrast, coupling a LoRA-adapted Gemma-4 encoder with our gated architecture defines a new state of the art on this benchmark while requiring an order of magnitude fewer trainable parameters than the generative SFT baselines, with gains concentrated on the most ambiguous and rarest outcome classes. Beyond accuracy, the architecture is interpretable; learned judge embeddings and calibration profiles localize the cases where adjudicative context drives the prediction. These results indicate that, for identity-conditioned classification of legal outcomes, the choice of conditioning interface dominates scale: differentiable structured composition yields more accurate, more parameter-efficient models than prompt-based composition over a substantially larger backbone.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a Judge-Aware Gated Multi-Task Learning architecture for legal outcome prediction that disentangles factual evidence from judicial discretion. Using a fine-grained outcome taxonomy and a gated fusion mechanism, the model dynamically modulates reliance on judge identity. Evaluated on 13,937 UK Employment Tribunal decisions, the approach outperforms much larger generative baselines (Gemma-4 26B-A4B) while using far fewer parameters, and offers interpretability through learned judge embeddings and calibration profiles.
AI.motivation: Legal outcome prediction requires separating objective case facts from adjudicative context. Merit-based rulings depend on evidence, while technical disposals may reflect judicial discretion. Existing approaches that inject judge identity and outcome taxonomy as prompt tokens into a single autoregressive pipeline force these distinct signals to compose weakly. The authors argue that a structured, differentiable composition interface is needed to properly disentangle these semantic pathways.
AI.method: The authors propose a Judge-Aware Gated Multi-Task Learning architecture with three key components: (1) a fine-grained outcome taxonomy used to supervise the encoder, enforcing structural regularization that disentangles fact-based and context-based semantic pathways; (2) a Gated Fusion mechanism that dynamically modulates reliance on judge identity embeddings; (3) a LoRA-adapted Gemma-4 encoder coupled with the gated architecture. This is benchmarked against supervised fine-tuning (SFT) baselines using a Gemma-4 26B-A4B backbone where judge identity and taxonomy are injected as prompt tokens or autoregressive output targets.
AI.result: The proposed architecture achieves state-of-the-art performance on a benchmark of 13,937 UK Employment Tribunal decisions while using an order of magnitude fewer trainable parameters than generative SFT baselines. Performance gains are concentrated on the most ambiguous and rarest outcome classes. The architecture is also interpretable: learned judge embeddings and calibration profiles localize cases where adjudicative context drives prediction.
AI.conclusion: For identity-conditioned classification of legal outcomes, the choice of conditioning interface dominates scale. Differentiable structured composition yields more accurate and parameter-efficient models than prompt-based composition over substantially larger backbones. This suggests that architectural design—specifically how contextual signals are composed—matters more than raw model size in this domain.

title: A Pipeline for Generating Longitudinal Synthetic Clinical Notes Using Large Language Models
summary: Synthetic data is increasingly used to enable the development and evaluation of AI systems in domains where access to real-world data is restricted. In healthcare, clinical documentation presents particular challenges due to its sensitivity. This work introduces a synthetic clinical notes pipeline and dataset designed to support the development of clinical AI tools while avoiding the privacy risks associated with real patient data. The dataset is generated using a modular pipeline that combines structured patient generation, semi-structured patient journey simulation, and unstructured clinical note generation using large language models. The pipeline is designed to prioritise internal consistency across longitudinal patient records, while also capturing variation in writing style, note structure, and clinical detail. Additional mechanisms, including LLM-based validation and augmentation steps, are used to improve faithfulness, realism, and diversity of the generated notes. We release a dataset of 70 synthetic patients, each associated with 20-50 clinical notes spanning a full hospital journey. The dataset is provided at multiple levels of validation, enabling users to balance realism and scalability depending on their use case. This dataset supports the development, testing, and evaluation of clinical AI systems, including summarisation tools, coding models, and decision support systems, without reliance on real patient data.

AI.tldr: A modular pipeline generates synthetic, longitudinal clinical notes (70 patients, 20–50 notes each) using LLMs, with built-in validation and augmentation to ensure consistency, realism, and diversity, enabling privacy-safe development of clinical AI tools.
AI.motivation: Real clinical data is highly sensitive and access-restricted, hindering development and evaluation of clinical AI systems. Synthetic data offers a privacy-preserving alternative, but generating realistic, internally consistent longitudinal patient records with natural variation in style and detail is challenging.
AI.method: A three-stage modular pipeline: (1) structured patient generation, (2) semi-structured patient journey simulation across a full hospital stay, (3) unstructured clinical note generation via large language models. LLM-based validation and augmentation steps enhance faithfulness, realism, and diversity. The dataset is released at multiple validation levels for flexible use.
AI.result: A released dataset of 70 synthetic patients, each with 20–50 longitudinal clinical notes covering complete hospital journeys, provided at multiple validation tiers to allow users to trade off realism against scalability.
AI.conclusion: The pipeline and dataset enable development, testing, and evaluation of clinical AI systems—including summarization, coding, and decision support tools—without reliance on real patient data, mitigating privacy risks while maintaining clinical fidelity.

title: HyperDFlash: MHC-Aligned Block Speculative Decoding with Gated Residual Reduction
summary: We present HyperDFlash, a block-parallel speculative decoding framework tailored to the novel multi-hyper-connection (MHC) architecture proposed by DeepSeek-V4. Despite the strong initial-token drafting performance of the native Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) module in DeepSeek-V4, its draft accuracy degrades sharply at later positions, as error accumulation from unverified intermediate tokens harms acceptance rates. Although the original DFlash method supports efficient one-pass block drafting, it cannot be seamlessly adapted to the MHC paradigm, since the multi-path residual stream of DeepSeek-V4 induces feature misalignment with conventional drafting designs. To resolve this mismatch, we propose two model-aligned optimizations for MHC residual streams. First, we adopt pre-collapse residual states as the exclusive conditioning signal, preserving multi-path structural information and aligning the drafter with the native prediction pathway of the target model. Second, we replace the heavy generic linear compressor with a lightweight gated residual reducer, whose parameters are inherited from the built-in hyper-connection head. This design yields input-aware path aggregation with three orders of magnitude fewer parameters while maintaining architectural alignment. We further enhance training via a targeted KL distillation loss applied to the LM-head, which regularizes predictions against the full target probability distribution and improves draft quality at early training stages. Experiments across math reasoning, code synthesis, and conversational benchmarks show that HyperDFlash consistently outperforms both the native MTP baseline and vanilla DFlash adaptation. It achieves substantial gains in average accepted draft length and decoding speedup, validating the effectiveness of MHC alignment, gated reduction, and targeted distillation for high-performance speculative decoding.

AI.tldr: HyperDFlash is a speculative decoding framework optimized for DeepSeek-V4's multi-hyper-connection (MHC) architecture, using pre-collapse residual states, a lightweight gated residual reducer, and targeted KL distillation to improve draft accuracy, acceptance rates, and decoding speedup over MTP and vanilla DFlash baselines.
AI.motivation: DeepSeek-V4's native Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) module drafts well for the initial token but suffers from error accumulation at later positions, degrading acceptance rates. The existing DFlash method supports efficient one-pass block drafting but cannot be directly applied to the MHC architecture due to feature misalignment caused by the multi-path residual stream.
AI.method: HyperDFlash introduces three key techniques: (1) using pre-collapse residual states as the exclusive conditioning signal to preserve multi-path structural information and align with the target model's prediction pathway; (2) replacing a heavy linear compressor with a lightweight gated residual reducer whose parameters are inherited from the built-in hyper-connection head, enabling input-aware path aggregation with ~1000× fewer parameters; and (3) a targeted KL distillation loss applied to the LM-head to regularize draft predictions against the full target distribution, especially beneficial during early training.
AI.result: HyperDFlash consistently outperforms both the native MTP baseline and vanilla DFlash adaptation across math reasoning, code synthesis, and conversational benchmarks, achieving substantial gains in average accepted draft length and decoding speedup.
AI.conclusion: MHC alignment via pre-collapse residuals, gated reduction for parameter-efficient path aggregation, and targeted distillation are all effective and complementary strategies for enabling high-performance speculative decoding on the DeepSeek-V4 MHC architecture.

title: The Riddle Riddle: Testing Flexible Reasoning in Large Language Models and Humans
summary: Humans flexibly adapt their reasoning strategies to the requirements of a given problem. Large language models (LLMs) have performed well on many cognitive tasks, however, it is unclear whether this accuracy is a result of pattern matching from training data or flexible reasoning. Here, we introduce a novel paradigm to test this question: the riddle riddle paradigm. Riddle riddles are word problems written to mimic popular riddles, but altered so their answers only require literal interpretations. Identifying correct answers requires looking past the structure of each question and flexibly apply different reasoning strategies based on the content. If LLMs respond to surface features, such as form, a riddle-like structure should cause models to use an inventive reasoning strategy even when a literal interpretation suffices. Alternatively, if LLMs reason based on content, they should flexibly switch strategies when appropriate. Across two experiments with nine state-of-the-art LLMs and 100 human participants, we show humans and LLMs fail on this paradigm in opposite directions. LLMs were far more accurate on genuine riddles than on riddle riddles (84.9% vs. 50.7%); whereas humans showed the reverse effect (50.5% vs. 80.5%). Error analysis shows that 90.8% of LLM errors on riddle riddles (the condition where they show diminished performance) were due to inappropriate use of inventive reasoning while only 57.6% of human errors on genuine riddles were due to overextending literal reasoning. Thus, while both groups make mistakes, reasoning mistakes are made more often by LLMs than by humans. Overall, LLMs' strong performance on genuine riddles may reflect memory retrieval rather than flexible strategy selection, and without stimuli designed to elicit this contrast, it becomes easy to conflate LLM-generated outputs that look like reasoning with genuine reasoning.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces the "riddle riddle" paradigm to test whether LLMs rely on flexible reasoning or surface-level pattern matching. Findings show LLMs excel at genuine riddles but fail on riddle riddles (requiring literal interpretation) due to overusing inventive reasoning, while humans show the opposite pattern. This suggests LLM performance reflects memory retrieval rather than genuine flexible reasoning.
AI.motivation: To determine whether LLMs' strong performance on cognitive tasks reflects genuine flexible reasoning or merely pattern matching from training data, and to develop a method that can distinguish between these two accounts.
AI.method: The authors created "riddle riddles" — problems mimicking the surface structure of popular riddles but whose answers require only literal interpretation.
