They tested nine state-of-the-art LLMs and 100 human participants on both genuine riddles and riddle riddles, comparing accuracy patterns and conducting error analysis to identify whether errors stemmed from inventive reasoning or literal reasoning strategies.
AI.result: LLMs showed higher accuracy on genuine riddles (84.9%) than riddle riddles (50.7%), while humans showed the reverse (50.5% vs. 80.5%). Error analysis revealed that 90.8% of LLM errors on riddle riddles involved inappropriate inventive reasoning, compared to only 57.6% of human errors on genuine riddles involving overextended literal reasoning. Both groups make mistakes, but reasoning mistakes are more frequent in LLMs.
AI.conclusion: LLMs' strong performance on genuine riddles likely reflects memory retrieval rather than flexible strategy selection. Without carefully designed stimuli that contrast surface form with required reasoning strategy, LLM outputs that resemble reasoning can easily be mistaken for genuine reasoning.

title: Generative Retrieval via Diffusion Transformer with Metric-Ordered Sequence Training and Hybrid-Policy Preference Optimization
summary: Embedding-based retrieval ranks items by their similarity to a query in a shared vector space and usually aims to return the highest-scoring items. In many production settings this is not what is wanted: given a seed set that expresses a fine-grained pattern, one needs more items that both satisfy a target attribute and stay within that pattern. We formalize this as pattern-preserving attribute retrieval. The two goals pull against each other: averaging the seeds preserves the pattern but stays in a low-attribute region, while global attribute retrieval drifts to unrelated patterns. We approach the task with continuous generative retrieval, where a model reads a sequence of item embeddings and generates query embeddings for nearest-neighbor search. We propose MO-DiT+HPPO, a staged framework with raw-sequence pretraining, multi-domain metric-ordered continuation pretraining, tail-centroid fine-tuning, and HPPO. Metric-ordered training turns sparse online retrieval labels into in-pattern trajectories ordered from low to high predicted attribute density, teaching one model the metric-improvement direction across domains. HPPO aligns the generated query distribution with the true online objective by labeling a hybrid candidate pool with the online intersection metric and applying reference-anchored preference optimization. A Pareto pair filter keeps only winner pairs that do not lower same-pattern purity, raising the attribute metric without sacrificing the pattern. Across four attribute domains under item- and pattern-holdout protocols, metric-ordered DiT improves the intersection metric over a pretrained generative retriever, and HPPO improves it further, with significant gains on seven of eight domain-split cells and a marginal tie on the hardest split. Metric-predictor validation, order ablations, CPT/SFT comparisons, and a candidate-policy ablation show where the gains come from.

AI.tldr: The paper formalizes "pattern-preserving attribute retrieval," where given a seed set expressing a fine-grained pattern, the goal is to retrieve items that both satisfy a target attribute and stay within that pattern. The authors propose MO-DiT+HPPO, a staged framework combining metric-ordered pretraining, tail-centroid fine-tuning, and a hybrid preference optimization method, achieving significant gains across multiple attribute domains.
AI.motivation: Standard embedding-based retrieval maximizes similarity to a query, but in production settings, users often need to retrieve items that match a specific attribute while preserving the nuanced pattern of a seed set. Averaging seed embeddings preserves pattern but yields low attribute scores; global attribute retrieval drifts to unrelated patterns. No existing method formalizes or solves this dual-objective retrieval problem.
AI.method: The authors propose MO-DiT+HPPO, a staged framework: (1) raw-sequence pretraining on item embedding sequences; (2) multi-domain metric-ordered continuation pretraining that transforms sparse online retrieval labels into trajectories ordered from low to high predicted attribute density, teaching a single model the metric-improvement direction across domains; (3) tail-centroid fine-tuning; and (4) HPPO (Hybrid Pareto Preference Optimization), which aligns generated query distributions with the online objective by labeling a hybrid candidate pool with an online intersection metric and applying reference-anchored preference optimization. A Pareto pair filter retains only winner pairs that maintain same-pattern purity.
AI.result: Across four attribute domains under item- and pattern-holdout protocols, metric-ordered DiT improves the intersection metric over a pretrained generative retriever, and HPPO yields further gains. Significant improvements are observed on seven of eight domain-split cells, with a marginal tie on the hardest split. Ablations on metric-predictor validation, training order, CPT/SFT comparisons, and candidate-policy design confirm the source of gains.
AI.conclusion: The MO-DiT+HPPO framework effectively balances pattern preservation and attribute retrieval, with metric-ordered training providing a strong signal for learning metric-improvement directions and HPPO aligning generated queries with the true online intersection objective without sacrificing pattern purity.

title: Structure Before Collapse: Transient semantic geometry in next-token prediction
summary: Neural Collapse predicts that balanced one-hot classification pushes model representations to be equally far from each other; a symmetric configuration that depends only on the output label and ignores any semantic similarity in the inputs. This creates a puzzle: next-token prediction language models are trained predominantly (as context length increases) with one-hot labels: the same context is very unlikely to appear twice in training with different labels. However, they clearly learn latent structural features. That is, despite the one-hot training regime, a language model's contextual embeddings represent the fact that the next word in ''Mary broke the ___'' is likely to be filled by tokens in the latent classes of a) medium-sized, b) rigid, c) inanimate nouns. How does gradient descent find such categorical semantic structure when co-occurrence statistics collapse to one-hot sparsity, eliminating any shared next-tokens among different contexts? To investigate this tension we identify three synthetic controlled settings where inputs have latent semantic factors but are mapped to distinct one-hot labels. We find that semantic geometry emerges early in training, and that representations cluster by shared attributes despite receiving no explicit supervision to do so. This structure is transient: with sufficient capacity and time, the model eventually reaches the predicted symmetric state where all representations are equally separated. We study this phase transition through Gram matrix analysis and propose a preliminary modification to the commonly used unconstrained features model to capture the emergent semantic geometry.

AI.tldr: Language models trained with one-hot next-token prediction labels nonetheless develop semantic structure in their representations, clustering by latent categorical attributes. This semantic geometry emerges early in training but is transient—eventually collapsing to the symmetric, equally-separated state predicted by Neural Collapse theory. The authors study this phase transition via Gram matrix analysis and propose a modified features model.
AI.motivation: Neural Collapse theory predicts that one-hot classification training drives representations to an equiangular, symmetric configuration that ignores input semantics. Yet language models trained with one-hot next-token labels clearly learn latent semantic structure (e.g., knowing that "Mary broke the ___" expects inanimate, rigid, medium-sized objects). This creates a tension: with near-infinite contexts and one-hot labels, co-occurrence statistics collapse to sparsity, eliminating shared labels across different contexts. How does gradient descent recover categorical semantics under such supervision?
AI.method: The authors construct three synthetic controlled settings where inputs possess latent semantic factors but are mapped to distinct one-hot labels. They track the evolution of learned representations over training, analyzing when and how semantic clustering emerges. They use Gram matrix analysis to characterize the phase transition from semantically structured representations to the symmetric Neural Collapse configuration. They also propose a modification to the unconstrained features model to account for the emergent semantic geometry.
AI.result: Semantic geometry emerges early in training: representations spontaneously cluster by shared latent attributes despite no explicit supervision to do so. This structure is transient—given sufficient model capacity and training time, representations eventually converge to the predicted symmetric state where all points are equally separated, consistent with Neural Collapse.
AI.conclusion: Gradient descent on one-hot classification objectives can transiently recover latent semantic structure before ultimately converging to the symmetric Neural Collapse solution. This explains how language models learn meaningful representations despite sparse one-hot labels. The phase transition from semantic to symmetric geometry represents an important training dynamic warranting further theoretical and empirical study.

title: Forecasting With LLMs: Improved Generalization Through Feature Steering
summary: Successful forecasting involves identifying patterns between historical and future states of the world which generalize to future observations. We apply LLMs to a variety of forecasting tasks and inspect their internal states using sparse autoencoders to understand whether they appear to rely on time-specific pieces of knowledge versus generalizable patterns. Our analyses identify features associated with both time-aware reasoning and look-ahead-biased reasoning. We then apply the LLMs to an entirely different domain and intervene on these features. We find that amplifying time-awareness features substantially reduces look-ahead bias on forecasting prompts while preserving general reasoning performance. In contrast, steering the candidate look-ahead-bias features does not produce an effect. These results suggest that interpretable temporal features can be used to causally shift LLMs toward more historically grounded reasoning.

AI.tldr: LLMs harbor interpretable temporal features that causally influence forecasting behavior. Sparse autoencoders reveal both time-aware and look-ahead-biased features; amplifying time-awareness features reduces look-ahead bias without harming general reasoning, enabling more historically grounded predictions.
AI.motivation: LLMs should ideally rely on generalizable patterns rather than time-specific knowledge when making forecasts, yet they may exhibit look-ahead bias — using information from a future point relative to a forecast's supposed timestamp. Understanding and mitigating this bias is crucial for reliable LLM-based forecasting.
AI.method: The authors apply LLMs to diverse forecasting tasks and probe internal representations using sparse autoencoders to isolate interpretable features. They identify candidate features for time-aware reasoning and look-ahead-biased reasoning. They then perform causal intervention experiments — amplifying or steering these features — and evaluate effects on forecasting accuracy, look-ahead bias, and general reasoning performance, including on an out-of-domain task.
AI.result: Amplifying time-awareness features significantly reduces look-ahead bias on forecasting prompts while preserving general reasoning performance. In contrast, steering candidate look-ahead-bias features fails to produce a comparable effect. This asymmetry suggests time-awareness features causally ground LLM reasoning in appropriate temporal context.
AI.conclusion: Interpretable temporal features discovered via sparse autoencoders can be leveraged to causally steer LLMs toward more historically grounded forecasting, offering a promising direction for improving reliability and reducing anachronistic biases in model predictions.

title: Learning to Recover Task Experts from a Multi-Task Merged Model
summary: Multi-task model merging aims to consolidate several task-specific experts into a unified model, yet static merging consistently suffers from parameter interference. While dynamic merging models aim to bridge this gap, many works rely on the costly storage and loading of redundant expert components at inference. In this work, from the perspective of task expert, we view parameter interference as parameter perturbation introduced to each expert during merging process. We show that such parameter perturbations can be modeled as affine transformation, which can be approximated as additive offsets. Motivated by these, we propose Recover Task eXpert (ReTeX), a framework that predicts those offsets, in order to undo parameter interference and recover task-expert performance from a single merged checkpoint. To recover the appropriate expert when task identity is unknown, we introduce a router-free task identifier based on SVD subspace signatures computed offline before inference. At inference, the identifier selects the task whose subspace yields the smallest projection residual for a given input. As a result, ReTeX recovers over 95% of individual-expert performance in both vision and NLP domains, while significantly improving generalization to unseen tasks. Crucially, we also show that the parameter offset prediction leads to emergent adaptive interpolation of expert knowledge for out-of-distribution (OOD) tasks. ReTeX adaptively interpolates seen expert knowledge to handle unseen tasks. Our code is available at https://github.com/BAIKLAB/ReTeX

AI.tldr: ReTeX is a multi-task model merging framework that treats parameter interference during merging as affine transformations approximated by additive offsets. It recovers task-specific expert performance from a single merged checkpoint by predicting these offsets, uses SVD subspace signatures for task identification without a router, and achieves over 95% expert performance recovery while enabling adaptive interpolation for unseen OOD tasks.
AI.motivation: Static multi-task model merging suffers from parameter interference; dynamic merging avoids this but requires costly storage and loading of redundant expert components at inference. The authors aim to recover individual task-expert performance from a single merged checkpoint without storing multiple experts, while also handling unknown task identities.
AI.method: The authors model parameter interference as affine transformations during merging, approximated as additive offsets. ReTeX predicts these offsets to recover task experts from a single merged checkpoint. For task identification when task identity is unknown, they introduce a router-free method using SVD subspace signatures computed offline: at inference, the task whose subspace yields the smallest projection residual for a given input is selected. The framework also supports emergent adaptive interpolation of expert knowledge for OOD tasks.
AI.result: ReTeX recovers over 95% of individual-expert performance in both vision and NLP domains and significantly improves generalization to unseen tasks. It also demonstrates emergent adaptive interpolation of seen expert knowledge for out-of-distribution tasks.
AI.conclusion: ReTeX provides an effective and efficient alternative to dynamic merging by recovering task experts from a single merged checkpoint via predicted additive offsets, eliminating the need for storing multiple expert components. The SVD-based task identifier further reduces inference overhead, and the framework generalizes well to unseen tasks through adaptive interpolation.

title: Batch-Invariant Spectral Intelligence for Robust and Explainable Insect Authentication
comment: 20 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables (excluding supplementary materials, submitted to journal
summary: Edible insects offer an efficient source of alternative protein, requiring less land, water and emitting less greenhouse gas than conventional livestock. However, their successful integration into the food supply chain demands reliable species authentication to control allergen exposure, prevent adulteration, and meet regulatory standards. Near-infrared spectroscopy provides a rapid analytical tool, but its performance drops when applied to production batches unseen during training due to batch-to-batch variation in spectral measurements. We introduce the Batch-Invariant Spectral Network (BISN), an end-to-end framework that combines a learnable preprocessing module, initialised with Savitzky-Golay filtering, with an entropy-regularised adversarial objective to suppress batch-specific spectral variation. In contrast to Domain-Adversarial Neural Networks, which enforce domain adaptation only after feature extraction, BISN suppress batch-effects before species-specific features are learned. Using 2,700 spectra from three species (Acheta domesticus, Hermetia illucens, and Tenebrio molitor) collected across three independent production batches, BISN achieves a mean leave-one-batch-out accuracy of 0.93 (standard deviation 0.04), outperforming the strongest baseline by four percent. Further insights gained by using explainable AI confirm that model decisions consistently rely on the lipid and protein absorption regions across all folds, connecting predictive performance to known insect biochemistry. BISN addresses both cross-batch robustness and biochemical interpretability for automated insect species authentication under realistic industrial conditions. The source code and dataset are publicly available at https://github.com/majharB/bisn.

AI.tldr: BISN introduces a learnable preprocessing adversarial network that suppresses batch-specific spectral variation before feature extraction, achieving 93% cross-batch accuracy for edible insect species authentication using NIR spectroscopy, outperforming Domain-Adversarial Neural Networks by 4%.
AI.motivation: Edible insects are a promising alternative protein source, but reliable species authentication is needed for allergen control, adulteration prevention, and regulatory compliance. NIR spectroscopy is rapid and scalable, yet batch-to-batch spectral variation severely degrades model performance when applied to unseen production batches, limiting real-world deployment.
AI.method: The authors propose the Batch-Invariant Spectral Network (BISN), an end-to-end framework with three key components: (1) a learnable preprocessing module initialized with Savitzky-Golay filtering coefficients, (2) an entropy-regularized adversarial objective that removes batch-specific variation prior to feature extraction, and (3) a species classifier trained on batch-invariant representations. Unlike Domain-Adversarial Neural Networks (DANN) which apply domain adaptation post-feature-extraction, BISN suppresses batch effects earlier in the pipeline. Explainable AI (XAI) is used to validate that predictions rely on biochemically relevant spectral regions (lipids, proteins).
AI.result: On 2,700 NIR spectra from three insect species (Acheta domesticus, Hermetia illucens, Tenebrio molitor) across three independent production batches, BISN achieves a mean leave-one-batch-out accuracy of 0.93 (SD 0.04), surpassing the strongest baseline by 4 percentage points. XAI analysis confirms consistent reliance on lipid and protein absorption bands across all cross-validation folds.
AI.conclusion: BISN effectively addresses both cross-batch robustness and biochemical interpretability for automated insect species authentication under realistic industrial conditions. The learnable preprocessing combined with early adversarial batch suppression proves superior to post-feature-extraction domain adaptation approaches.

title: Syntactic Belief Update as the Driver of Garden Path Processing Difficulty
summary:
Garden path sentences present a processing difficulty for humans -- the sentence prefix leads the listener towards one interpretation, until the listener hears a critical word that shows that the initial interpretation was wrong. Lexical surprisal, a measure that usually predicts sentence processing difficulty quite well, fails to provide good predictions for garden path sentences.
  We propose an alternative that actively predicts a probability distribution over syntactic trees (its syntactic belief) and updates that distribution after each new word. If a processor is led down a garden path, syntactic beliefs will be wrong and will require a large update at the critical word. The magnitude of the update is measured with a generalized Rényi divergence. Crucially, this metric is dependent on lexical items, but is fully independent of the probability of lexical items. This Syntactic Belief Update provides a better fit to the human reading time data on garden path sentences. This suggests a new research direction examining purely non-lexical alternatives to surprisal for psycholinguistics.

AI.tldr: Lexical surprisal fails to predict processing difficulty in garden path sentences. The authors propose Syntactic Belief Update, a non-lexical metric using generalized Rényi divergence to measure how much a processor's syntactic belief distribution shifts at the critical word, providing better fit to human reading time data.
AI.motivation: Garden path sentences consistently challenge standard lexical surprisal models, which otherwise predict sentence processing difficulty well. There is a need for a metric that captures the structural reanalysis cost when initial syntactic expectations are violated, independent of lexical probability.
AI.method: A probabilistic syntactic processor actively maintains a distribution over syntactic trees (syntactic beliefs) and incrementally updates this distribution word-by-word. When the critical word disambiguates the garden path, the magnitude of belief revision is quantified using generalized Rényi divergence. This metric is lexical-item-dependent but fully independent of lexical-item probability.
AI.result: The Syntactic Belief Update metric provides a significantly better fit to human reading time data on garden path sentences compared to lexical surprisal.
AI.conclusion: The findings suggest a promising new research direction in psycholinguistics: exploring purely non-lexical alternatives to surprisal for modeling sentence processing difficulty, with syntactic belief updating as a viable candidate.

title: Diagnosing Task Insensitivity in Language Agents
summary: Large language models can serve as capable long-horizon agents, but their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains weak. We identify a key source of this failure as task insensitivity: when faced with similar but distinct tasks, models might apply patterns learned during training and fail to solve the task at hand. We show that models often continue with actions aligned with the original task even when the instruction is semantically corrupted and cannot be directly answered. We further find that, when we replace the task description in a trained prompt with another similar but distinct task, the model may still output the same action. This behavior is accompanied by a consistent training-time attention drift away from task tokens and toward local observations, suggesting an optimization bias toward shortcuts. To mitigate this problem, we propose Task-Perturbed NLL Optimization, a lightweight contrastive regularizer that explicitly encourages action dependence on the task instruction. Extensive evaluations show that our intervention improves task sensitivity and OOD generalization while preserving more stable attention to task tokens.

AI.tldr: Language models acting as agents fail at OOD generalization due to task insensitivity—they follow learned action patterns even when instructions are corrupted or changed. The authors identify an attention drift from task tokens to observations during training, and propose a contrastive regularizer (Task-Perturbed NLL) that restores task sensitivity and improves generalization.
AI.motivation: LLM-based agents exhibit poor OOD generalization. The authors diagnose that this stems from task insensitivity: models latch onto spurious action patterns from training and ignore the actual task instruction, especially when faced with semantically similar but distinct tasks.
AI.method: The authors first demonstrate task insensitivity via two experiments: (1) semantic instruction corruption and (2) task description replacement, both showing models persist with original actions. They trace this to an attention drift phenomenon—during training, attention steadily shifts away from task tokens toward local observations, indicating a shortcut-learning optimization bias. To address this, they propose Task-Perturbed Negative Log-Likelihood (NLL) Optimization, a contrastive regularizer that penalizes the model when its action distribution is insensitive to task perturbations, thereby enforcing task-conditional action generation.
AI.result: The proposed regularizer improves task sensitivity metrics, enhances OOD generalization across multiple benchmarks, and yields more stable attention allocation to task tokens throughout training.
AI.conclusion: Task insensitivity is a key failure mode in LLM agents, driven by an optimization bias toward shortcut features. The Task-Perturbed NLL regularizer is a lightweight, effective intervention that restores task-conditional behavior and improves OOD robustness.

title: Escaping Iterative Parameter-Space Noise: Differentially Private Learning with a Hypernetwork
summary: Differentially private (DP) training of neural networks is often hindered by the large amount of noise required by gradient-based methods such as DP-SGD, which repeatedly inject high-dimensional noise in parameter space throughout training. In this paper, we propose a new framework for DP learning that avoids iterative optimization in parameter space. Instead of updating the target model using privatized gradients, we employ a hypernetwork trained on public datasets to map a private dataset to the parameters of the target model. Specifically, each example is embedded into a low-dimensional representation, the embeddings are aggregated and perturbed to obtain a DP dataset embedding, and the hypernetwork generates the target model parameters from this noisy embedding. Because privacy noise is injected only once into a low-dimensional dataset representation, our approach can significantly reduce the adverse effect of noise. We theoretically show in a synthetic setting that, under a fixed privacy budget, models produced by our approach achieve higher utility than those trained with DP-SGD. Moreover, we apply our approach to LoRA fine-tuning of diffusion models and show that it achieves lower FID than LoRA models trained with DP-SGD and other public-data-guided methods.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a DP learning framework that replaces iterative DP-SGD with a hypernetwork trained on public data. Private dataset examples are embedded into low-dimensional vectors, aggregated and perturbed once to obtain a DP embedding, then a hypernetwork generates target model parameters from this embedding — significantly reducing noise impact compared to per-iteration gradient perturbation.
AI.motivation: DP-SGD injects high-dimensional noise repeatedly throughout training, severely degrading model utility. The authors aim to reduce this noise burden by shifting privacy perturbation from the parameter/gradient space (high-dimensional, iterative) to a one-time injection in a low-dimensional dataset representation space.
AI.method: The framework uses (1) a per-example encoder to map private data into low-dimensional embeddings, (2) DP aggregation of these embeddings (with noise injected once) to produce a DP dataset embedding, and (3) a hypernetwork (pre-trained on public data) that maps the noisy embedding to target model parameters. The approach is also applied to LoRA fine-tuning of diffusion models.
AI.result: Theoretical analysis in a synthetic setting shows higher utility than DP-SGD under a fixed privacy budget. Empirical results on LoRA fine-tuning of diffusion models demonstrate lower FID scores compared to both DP-SGD-trained LoRA and other public-data-guided DP methods.
AI.conclusion: Shifting DP noise injection from iterative high-dimensional gradient perturbation to a single low-dimensional dataset embedding perturbation enables better privacy-utility trade-offs, validated both theoretically and empirically on generative model fine-tuning tasks.

title: Paved with True Intents: Intent-Aware Training Improves LLM Safety Classification Across Training Regimes
summary: We argue that safety classifiers should model user intent as an explicit signal between the prompt and the final label. To study this, we introduce AIMS, a human-annotated dataset of 1,724 difficult safety prompts, each paired with an intent description and harm label. We use AIMS to evaluate intent-aware training across supervised fine-tuning, preference learning, reasoning distillation, and reinforcement learning. Despite its size, AIMS enables competitive safety classifiers across training regimes: DPO from model-generated intent errors improves over SFT, and intent-conditioned distillation outperforms reasoning-only distillation in most teacher-student pairs. Most notably, directly rewarding intent faithfulness with GRPO yields the strongest average performance across five external safety benchmarks, while our intent-aware models form the inference latency-F1 Pareto frontier. These results show that faithful intent modeling is a compact, high-quality supervision signal for more robust safety classifiers.

AI.tldr: AIMS introduces a 1,724-sample dataset pairing safety prompts with explicit user intent descriptions, demonstrating that modeling intent as an intermediate signal improves safety classifiers. Intent-aware training—especially GRPO-based intent faithfulness rewards—achieves state-of-the-art performance across five external benchmarks while forming the latency-F1 Pareto frontier.
AI.motivation: Existing safety classifiers typically map prompts directly to harm labels, ignoring the user's underlying intent. The authors argue that explicitly modeling user intent as an intermediate signal can produce more robust and interpretable safety classifications, especially for ambiguous or difficult prompts where surface-level features may be misleading.
AI.method: The authors introduce AIMS, a human-annotated dataset of 1,724 safety prompts with intent descriptions and harm labels. They evaluate intent-aware training across four paradigms: (1) supervised fine-tuning (SFT), (2) preference learning via DPO using model-generated intent errors, (3) reasoning distillation where intent-conditioned distillation is compared against reasoning-only distillation across teacher-student pairs, and (4) reinforcement learning with GRPO directly rewarding intent faithfulness.
AI.result: DPO from model-generated intent errors outperforms SFT. Intent-conditioned distillation surpasses reasoning-only distillation in most teacher-student configurations. GRPO with direct intent-faithfulness rewards achieves the strongest average performance across five external safety benchmarks. Intent-aware models define the inference latency-F1 Pareto frontier, demonstrating both accuracy and efficiency.
AI.conclusion: Faithful intent modeling provides a compact, high-quality supervision signal that yields more robust safety classifiers. Explicitly incorporating user intent as an intermediate representational layer consistently improves classification performance across diverse training paradigms, suggesting a promising direction for future safety systems.

title: Where Do CoT Training Gains Land in LLM based Agents?
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is widely used in language-model agents, but prior work has shown that verbalized CoT is not always faithful and may instead reflect post-hoc reasoning, which means the model already knows the answer before reasoning. We therefore ask what CoT training is actually improving: is the model getting better at changing its action through generated reasoning, or is it getting better at predicting the action directly from the prompt? We study this question by comparing \emph{prompt actions} (predicting action without CoT) with CoT actions (predicting action with CoT). Across checkpoints, prompt-action quality improves substantially. While interacting with the environment, the relative advantage of CoT actions over prompt actions remains similar, showing that CoT training does not widen the advantage of CoT reasoning, and it helps to improve the quality of prompt actions. We further find that later checkpoints are less likely to revise the action in response to CoT, suggesting greater reliance on the prompt. Motivated by these patterns, we selectively mask action-token supervision on a fraction of training examples. This intervention improves out-of-domain generalization.

AI.tldr: CoT training improves the model's ability to predict actions directly from the prompt (without reasoning), not just its ability to reason through CoT. Later checkpoints rely more on prompt-based action prediction and are less likely to revise actions in response to CoT. Masking action-token supervision on some training examples improves out-of-domain generalization.
AI.motivation: Prior work has shown that verbalized chain-of-thought reasoning is not always faithful and may reflect post-hoc rationalization rather than genuine step-by-step reasoning. This raises the question: what is CoT training actually improving — the model's ability to change its actions through generated reasoning, or its ability to predict actions directly from the prompt?
AI.method: The authors compare "prompt actions" (predicting action without CoT) against "CoT actions" (predicting action with CoT) across different training checkpoints. They evaluate both action quality and the model's tendency to revise actions in response to CoT. They further conduct an intervention where action-token supervision is selectively masked on a fraction of training examples.
AI.result: Prompt-action quality improves substantially across checkpoints. The relative advantage of CoT actions over prompt actions remains stable, indicating CoT training does not widen the CoT advantage. Later checkpoints are less likely to revise actions in response to CoT, showing increased reliance on the prompt. Selectively masking action-token supervision improves out-of-domain generalization.
AI.conclusion: CoT training improves the model's direct action-prediction capability from the prompt, not just its reasoning ability. This suggests a form of "internalization" where reasoning patterns are absorbed into direct prompt-to-action mappings, and the selective masking intervention provides a practical method to leverage this insight for better generalization.

title: Reproducibility Study of "AlphaEdit: Null-Space Constrained Knowledge Editing for Language Models"
summary: Fang et al. (2025) introduced a null-space constrained projection, named AlphaEdit, for locate-then-edit knowledge editing methods, theoretically guaranteeing that edits do not disrupt previously preserved knowledge, and reports substantial gains over existing editing methods on LLaMA3, GPT2-XL, and GPT-J. In this work, we present a reproducibility study of AlphaEdit, reproducing its reported results under the original experimental setup and extending the evaluation along three axes: new model architectures, additional downstream benchmarks, and substantially longer sequential editing horizons. We successfully reproduce AlphaEdit's reported metrics across the original models, though we identify a discrepancy in the reported fluency and consistency metric. Extending AlphaEdit to newer model families, we find that its advantage does not generalize uniformly, which we trace to architectural assumptions in the locate-then-edit paradigm that are violated by these newer models. We further stress-test AlphaEdit's central sequential-editing claim by extending the number of edits well beyond those evaluated in the original paper, and find that performance, which is stable at the originally reported scale, degrades as edits reach a much higher count, indicating that the null-space projection's protection against catastrophic forgetting is bounded rather than unconditional. Finally, we extend evaluation of edited models on three extra benchmarks, namely, BoolQ, HellaSwag, and XSTest, and we find that large-scale sequential editing degrades both general downstream task competence and safety-relevant refusal behavior. Our results confirm that AlphaEdit performs as reported within its original scope, while showing that its core theoretical guarantees are sensitive to model architecture and editing scale in ways that have practical implications for its deployment.

AI.tldr: A reproducibility study of AlphaEdit confirms its original results but reveals that its null-space projection guarantees are architecture-dependent and bounded under extensive sequential editing, with degradation in downstream task performance and safety behavior at larger editing scales.
AI.motivation: AlphaEdit claims to theoretically guarantee preservation of previously stored knowledge during locate-then-edit operations via null-space constrained projection. The authors seek to verify these claims through reproduction and to stress-test the method's limits beyond the original paper's scope.
AI.method: The study reproduces AlphaEdit on original models (LLaMA3, GPT2-XL, GPT-J) under the original setup, then extends evaluation along three axes: (1) newer model architectures, (2) three additional downstream benchmarks (BoolQ, HellaSwag, XSTest), and (3) substantially longer sequential editing horizons to stress-test the null-space projection's capacity.
AI.result: Original metrics were successfully reproduced, though a fluency/consistency discrepancy was identified. AlphaEdit's advantage did not generalize uniformly to newer model architectures due to violated architectural assumptions. Performance degraded at high edit counts despite stability at originally reported scales, and large-scale sequential editing impaired both downstream task competence and safety refusal behavior.
AI.conclusion: AlphaEdit performs as reported within its original scope, but its theoretical guarantees are sensitive to model architecture and editing scale, with practical implications for real-world deployment, indicating that the null-space protection against catastrophic forgetting is bounded rather than unconditional.

title: Compositionality and the lexicon in evolutionary semantics
summary: Formal semantics has shown that sentence meanings arise by recursively composing lexical meanings, yet much of the literature on semantic universals models either lexicons with fixed signal structures or holistic composition without interpretable lexical parts. We introduce a framework that integrates this fundamental insight of formal semantics in evolutionary modeling, by allowing lexical meanings and a composition function to co-evolve under pressures for conceptual simplicity and communicative accuracy. We apply this framework to the evolution of quantificational meaning. Analyzing the Pareto frontier, we find that the most well-known semantic universal, conservativity, emerges as an efficient system-wide abstraction. The account is sensitive to syntactic structure and helps reconcile tensions between empirical evidence on quantifier learnability and prior evolutionary models. More broadly, the results demonstrate that the picture of sentential meaning developed in formal semantics can be productively combined with evolutionary modeling. The framework offers a template for studying universals that involve global compression within a grammatical category, semantic specialization of syntactic arguments, and the co-evolution of lexical and compositional meaning.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes a co-evolutionary framework where lexical meanings and a composition function evolve jointly under pressures for simplicity and communicative accuracy. Applied to quantificational semantics, it shows that the semantic universal of conservativity emerges naturally as a Pareto-efficient abstraction, reconciling formal semantics with evolutionary modeling.
AI.motivation: Formal semantics treats sentence meaning as arising from recursive composition of lexical meanings, but semantic universals research typically models either holistic communication without lexical parts or fixed-signal lexicons, neglecting compositionality. The authors aim to bridge this gap by integrating compositional structure into evolutionary models of meaning.
AI.method: The authors introduce an evolutionary framework where lexical meanings and a composition function co-evolve under multi-objective optimization: conceptual simplicity and communicative accuracy. The model is applied to quantificational meanings, and the Pareto frontier is analyzed to identify which semantic properties emerge as efficient solutions under these competing pressures.
AI.result: Conservativity—the most well-known semantic universal for quantifiers—emerges as an efficient system-wide abstraction along the Pareto frontier. The model is sensitive to syntactic structure and helps reconcile tensions between empirical learnability findings and prior evolutionary accounts of quantifier universals.
AI.conclusion: The picture of sentential meaning from formal semantics can be productively combined with evolutionary modeling. The framework provides a template for studying universals involving global compression within grammatical categories, semantic specialization of syntactic arguments, and the co-evolution of lexical and compositional meaning.

title: Look-Before-Move: Narrative-Grounded World Visual Attention in Dynamic 3D Story Worlds
summary: As embodied AI and world models increasingly operate in dynamic 3D environments, visual perception must move beyond passively interpreting given observations toward actively deciding what to observe. We study this problem through camera planning in dynamic 3D story worlds, where the camera must not only generate smooth motion, but also decide what visual evidence should be acquired before it moves. We formulate this capability as Narrative-Grounded World Visual Attention, where the camera acts as an embodied observer that determines what to observe, how to compose the observation, and how to shift attention over time under narrative intent and physical 3D constraints. To realize this capability, we propose Look-Before-Move, a camera planning framework that separates observation specification from motion execution. It first builds a Semantic Observation Contract to convert directorial intent into executable visual constraints, then performs Monte Carlo Viewpoint Search to find narrative-compliant and geometrically feasible viewpoints, and finally applies Semantic Trajectory Grounding to connect selected viewpoints into continuous, collision-aware, and temporally coherent camera motion. We further construct a dynamic 3D Story World Benchmark based on StoryBlender, covering 50 stories, 457 scenes, and 1585 shots with animated characters, semantic scene configurations, and executable 3D environments. Experiments show that our framework improves subject perception, intent consistency, and trajectory quality over representative baselines, demonstrating the importance of organizing visual attention before generating camera motion.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "Look-Before-Move," a camera planning framework for dynamic 3D story worlds that decouples observation specification from motion execution. It formulates the problem as Narrative-Grounded World Visual Attention, using a Semantic Observation Contract, Monte Carlo Viewpoint Search, and Semantic Trajectory Grounding to generate narrative-compliant, collision-free camera trajectories. A new benchmark (StoryBlender-based) with 50 stories, 457 scenes, and 1585 shots validates improvements in subject perception, intent consistency, and trajectory quality.
AI.motivation: Existing visual perception in embodied AI passively interprets given observations. In dynamic 3D story worlds, a camera must actively decide what to observe, how to compose shots, and how to shift attention over time — all under narrative intent and physical 3D constraints. No prior framework explicitly separates the "what to observe" decision from the "how to move" execution, motivating a planning-before-motion paradigm.
AI.method: The Look-Before-Move framework has three stages: (1) Semantic Observation Contract — converts directorial/narrative intent into executable visual constraints (subject framing, composition rules); (2) Monte Carlo Viewpoint Search — samples and evaluates candidate viewpoints for narrative compliance and geometric feasibility (collision, occlusion); (3) Semantic Trajectory Grounding — connects selected viewpoints into continuous, temporally coherent, collision-aware camera motion paths.
AI.result: Evaluated on the new StoryBlender-based Dynamic 3D Story World Benchmark (50 stories, 457 scenes, 1585 shots with animated characters and executable environments). The framework outperforms representative baselines on three axes: subject perception quality, narrative intent consistency, and trajectory quality (smoothness, collision avoidance, temporal coherence).
AI.conclusion: Organizing visual attention before generating camera motion is crucial for embodied perception in dynamic 3D story worlds. The Look-Before-Move framework demonstrates that decoupling observation specification from motion execution yields superior narrative-aligned, physically valid camera trajectories, advancing the intersection of embodied AI, world models, and dynamic visual storytelling.

title: AIGP: An LLM-Based Framework for Long-Term Value Alignment in E-Commerce Pricing
comment: Accepted by KDD 2026 Applied Data Science Track (Oral presentation)
summary: Traditional dynamic pricing models in large-scale e-commerce suffer from limited interpretability, poor utilization of unstructured information, and misalignment with long-term business objectives such as cumulative Gross Merchandise Value (GMV), Return on Investment (ROI) and milestone achievement. We propose AIGP, a novel framework that leverages a Large Language Model (LLM) prompted with domain knowledge, structured data and textual context to make interpretable, knowledge-aware pricing decisions. For efficient deployment while maintaining high-quality outputs, we employ supervised fine-tuning for knowledge distillation. Central to AIGP is the Long-Term Value Estimator (LTVE), trained via offline reinforcement learning on historical data, which serves as a reward model to score candidate pricing actions and select preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), thereby aligning the pricing policy with long-term business objectives. Extensive offline evaluations and large-scale online A/B tests on Tao Factory demonstrate that AIGP achieves significant improvements: +13.21% in GMV, +7.59% in ROI, and +8.20% in milestone achievement rate over 14 days compared to the production baseline, while simultaneously providing interpretable and transparent pricing rationales.

AI.tldr: AIGP is an LLM-based dynamic pricing framework that combines domain knowledge, structured data, and textual context with a Long-Term Value Estimator trained via offline RL to align pricing decisions with long-term business objectives (GMV, ROI, milestone achievement). Deployed on Tao Factory, it achieved +13.21% GMV, +7.59% ROI, and +8.20% milestone achievement over 14 days.
AI.motivation: Traditional dynamic pricing models for large-scale e-commerce have three key limitations: (1) limited interpretability of pricing decisions, (2) poor utilization of unstructured/textual information (e.g., product descriptions, market context), and (3) misalignment with long-term business objectives like cumulative GMV, ROI, and milestone achievement, as opposed to short-term revenue optimization.
AI.method: The AIGP framework uses an LLM prompted with domain knowledge, structured data, and textual context to generate interpretable pricing decisions. For efficient deployment, supervised fine-tuning is used for knowledge distillation. The core innovation is the Long-Term Value Estimator (LTVE), trained via offline reinforcement learning on historical data, which acts as a reward model to score candidate pricing actions. These scores are used to select preference pairs for Direct Preference Optimization (DPO), aligning the policy with long-term objectives.
AI.result: In offline evaluations and large-scale online A/B tests on Tao Factory, AIGP achieved: +13.21% improvement in GMV, +7.59% improvement in ROI, and +8.20% improvement in milestone achievement rate over a 14-day period compared to the production baseline, while providing interpretable pricing rationales.
AI.conclusion: AIGP demonstrates that LLM-based pricing agents, when augmented with a long-term value estimator and aligned via DPO, can outperform traditional pricing models on both short-term and long-term business metrics while offering interpretability — a critical practical advantage for real-world e-commerce deployment.

title: CARVE: Content-Aware Recurrent with Value Efficiency for Chunk-Parallel Linear Attention
comment: 27 pages, 2 figures, multiple tables. Submitted to arXiv. Primary category: cs.LG; cross-list: cs.CL
summary:
Recurrent models must forget in order to remember, yet the state of the art decides what to erase without consulting what is stored -- the gate sees only the arriving token, not the memory it is about to modify. This memory-blind gating is one of three coupled defects in the leading delta-rule architecture (GDN-2): the value-axis erase mask wastes parameters at the scale of the value projection, and -- as we prove -- mathematically prevents the WY-form triangular chunk solver that makes recurrent training competitive with Transformers.
  We introduce CARVE (Content-Aware Recurrent with Value Efficiency), which resolves all three problems through one principle: erase only on the key axis. This is provably necessary and sufficient for the WY-form solver to remain valid. Within it, CARVE reuses the recurrent output tensor -- already written to GPU memory -- as a free content signal for the erase gate, and replaces the per-value write-gate projection with a single scalar per head. At initialisation CARVE is bit-identical to GDN-2; any quality difference emerges from what the content gate learns.
  At 1.3B parameters trained on 100B tokens, CARVE achieves WikiText perplexity 15.72 (minus 0.18 vs. GDN-2, a 4.5-sigma effect), leads every recurrent baseline on nine common-sense reasoning benchmarks, and sets state of the art on every RULER retrieval probe -- at 0.4% throughput overhead, 13% lower peak memory, and 19% fewer parameters. Six formal theorems cover memory capacity, Lyapunov stability, gradient flow, expressivity separation, Pareto-optimal chunk size, and hybrid optimality.

AI.tldr: CARVE introduces a content-aware gating mechanism for recurrent models that erases only on the key axis, fixing three defects in GDN-2: memory-blind gating, wasteful value-axis erase masks, and incompatibility with the WY-form chunk solver. The result is better perplexity, superior reasoning and retrieval benchmarks, and improved efficiency at 1.3B scale.
AI.motivation: Existing state-of-the-art recurrent architectures (specifically GDN-2) suffer from three coupled defects: (1) the erase gate is memory-blind — it decides what to forget based only on the incoming token, not the stored memory; (2) the value-axis erase mask wastes parameters at the scale of the value projection; (3) this design mathematically prevents use of the WY-form triangular chunk solver, which is critical for making recurrent training competitive with Transformers. Addressing all three through a unified principle is the central motivation.
AI.method: CARVE enforces a single principle: erase only on the key axis. This is proven necessary and sufficient for the WY-form solver to remain valid. Within this constraint, CARVE (1) reuses the recurrent output tensor (already in GPU memory) as a content signal for the erase gate, making gating content-aware at zero extra memory cost; and (2) replaces the per-value write-gate projection with a single scalar per head, eliminating parameter waste. At initialization, CARVE is bit-identical to GDN-2; all differences emerge purely from learned content-aware gating.
AI.result: At 1.3B parameters trained on 100B tokens, CARVE achieves WikiText perplexity of 15.72 (−0.18 vs. GDN-2, a 4.5σ effect), leads all recurrent baselines on nine common-sense reasoning benchmarks, and sets state of the art on every RULER retrieval probe. It accomplishes this with only 0.4% throughput overhead, 13% lower peak memory, and 19% fewer parameters. Six formal theorems are provided covering memory capacity, Lyapunov stability, gradient flow, expressivity separation, Pareto-optimal chunk size, and hybrid optimality.
AI.conclusion: The single design principle of erasing only on the key axis is provably necessary and sufficient to resolve the three intertwined defects in GDN-2. Making the erase gate content-aware via the recurrent output tensor yields statistically significant and practically meaningful improvements across language modeling, reasoning, and long-range retrieval, while simultaneously reducing parameter count and memory usage — all with negligible throughput cost.

title: Einstein World Models
summary: Does intelligence require the ability to reason about phenomena beyond direct experience? It is natural to suspect that some complex thought cannot be captured through language alone. However, of particular concern to this work, is whether visualising counterfactual events can complement language as a mechanism for complex thought. We ask whether LLMs can be trained to utilise such visualisation mechanisms, in a way that benefits their reasoning abilities. Motivated by this question, we propose Einstein World Models. EWMs are a blueprint for LLM-based reasoning systems that place visual-temporal rollouts inside the reasoning trace, allowing them to reason in ways that text alone may not support well. In an EWM, the LLM calls a world-module (not to be confused with a world model), to produce short rollouts of scenes under consideration. The returned rollout is treated not as the answer, but as an inspectable hypothesis that can support later reasoning. Einstein World Models extend the capability of LLMs for tool calling (such as web search or code execution), into the domain of visual thought experiments.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes Einstein World Models (EWMs), a blueprint for LLM-based reasoning systems that integrate visual-temporal rollouts into the reasoning trace, enabling models to visualize counterfactual events as inspectable hypotheses that complement language-based reasoning.
AI.motivation: The authors are motivated by the question of whether complex reasoning requires abilities beyond language — specifically, whether visualizing counterfactual scenarios can complement text-based thought. They investigate whether LLMs can be trained to utilize visual imagination mechanisms to enhance their reasoning capabilities beyond what text alone supports.
AI.method: EWMs place a world-module (distinct from a world model) within the LLM reasoning trace. The LLM calls this module to generate short visual-temporal rollouts of scenes under consideration. Critically, the returned rollout is treated as an inspectable hypothesis rather than a final answer, allowing it to inform subsequent reasoning steps. This extends existing LLM tool-calling paradigms (e.g., web search, code execution) into the domain of visual thought experiments.
AI.result: The abstract does not report specific empirical results; it presents the EWM blueprint as a conceptual framework and architectural proposal for future LLM-based reasoning systems.
AI.conclusion: Visualising counterfactual events can serve as a complementary mechanism to language for complex reasoning. EWMs provide a structured approach for integrating such visual imagination into LLM reasoning pipelines, extending tool-use capabilities into visual thought experiments.

title: Reasoning Quality Emerges Early: Data Curation for Reasoning Models
summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on a small, high-quality set of long reasoning traces is an effective approach for eliciting strong reasoning capabilities in Large Language Models (LLMs). However, existing methods for curating high-quality SFT data rely heavily on strong reasoning models to filter examples based on diversity and difficulty, making the curation process costly while often yielding suboptimal data quality. In this work, we show that diverse and challenging reasoning examples can be identified using only the initial reasoning tokens. Specifically, we demonstrate that difficult problems can be reliably detected based on the loss of the first 100 reasoning tokens evaluated at a randomly perturbed checkpoint of the pretrained model. We further show that examples exhibiting similar loss patterns over their first 1k reasoning tokens across a small number of perturbed checkpoints extrapolating along the fine-tuning trajectory provably induce similar gradients. We validate our approach through extensive experiments on fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B models on the M23K medical reasoning and OpenThoughts-Math datasets. Our method outperforms existing baselines by up to 1.7% while being 91% more token efficient.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a cost-efficient method for selecting high-quality SFT reasoning data using only the initial reasoning tokens' loss patterns, rather than relying on expensive strong reasoning models for filtering. By analyzing losses on the first 100–1k tokens at perturbed checkpoints, they identify diverse and challenging examples that outperform existing baselines by up to 1.7% with 91% greater token efficiency.
AI.motivation: Existing SFT data curation methods depend on strong reasoning models (e.g., GPT-4) to filter examples based on diversity and difficulty, which is expensive and often yields suboptimal data quality. The authors aim to find a cheaper, more effective alternative that does not require external reasoning models.
AI.method: The method identifies challenging reasoning examples using only initial reasoning tokens: (1) difficulty is detected via the loss of the first 100 reasoning tokens evaluated at a randomly perturbed checkpoint of the pretrained model; (2) diversity is captured by comparing loss patterns over the first 1k reasoning tokens across a small number of perturbed checkpoints extrapolated along the fine-tuning trajectory, where similar loss patterns provably induce similar gradients. Experiments are conducted fine-tuning Qwen2.5-7B and Llama3.1-8B on M23K (medical reasoning) and OpenThoughts-Math datasets.
AI.result: The proposed method outperforms existing baselines by up to 1.7% on reasoning benchmarks while being 91% more token-efficient, all without requiring access to strong external reasoning models for data filtering.
AI.conclusion: Diverse and challenging reasoning examples can be effectively identified using only initial reasoning tokens and perturbed checkpoints, enabling more efficient and cost-effective SFT data curation that rivals or surpasses methods relying on expensive strong reasoning models.

title: Bridging Talk and Thought: Understanding Dialogue Dynamics Across Collaborative Problem-Solving Contexts
summary: We present a conceptual framework for analyzing dialogue in collaborative problem-solving contexts, with an emphasis on the emerging dynamics of human-AI and multi-agent collaboration. As intelligent systems become active agents capable of autonomous reasoning and strategic cooperation, understanding the dialogic interaction during collaborative problem solving is increasingly important for optimizing and evaluating such partnerships. Our framework addresses key limitations in current analytical approaches through a hierarchical two-layer coding scheme that integrates cognitive and non-cognitive problem solving with metacognitive regulatory mechanisms. We demonstrate its effectiveness and generalizability across nine datasets spanning multiple domains, and provide insights into how humans and agents coordinate their knowledge, skills, and efforts to solve complex problems, showing in particular that metacognitive regulation can be an essential discriminator of deeper collaboration.

AI.tldr: A hierarchical two-layer coding framework is proposed to analyze dialogue in collaborative problem-solving, integrating cognitive/non-cognitive dimensions with metacognitive regulation. Tested across nine datasets, it reveals metacognition as a key discriminator of deep collaboration, particularly for human-AI and multi-agent settings.
AI.motivation: Current analytical approaches for dialogue in collaborative problem-solving lack the capacity to capture emerging dynamics in human-AI and multi-agent collaborations. As intelligent systems become autonomous collaborative partners, a framework is needed that can evaluate and optimize these interactions by accounting for both problem-solving content and regulatory processes.
AI.method: The authors propose a conceptual framework with a hierarchical two-layer coding scheme: one layer captures cognitive and non-cognitive problem-solving processes, while the second layer captures metacognitive regulatory mechanisms. The framework is validated across nine datasets from multiple domains to test generalizability.
AI.result: The framework effectively generalizes across diverse datasets and domains. Analysis reveals how humans and agents coordinate knowledge, skills, and efforts during complex problem-solving. Metacognitive regulation emerges as a critical discriminator distinguishing deeper, more effective collaboration from shallower interactions.
AI.conclusion: The two-layer coding framework offers a robust, generalizable tool for analyzing collaborative problem-solving dialogue. It highlights that metacognitive regulation is essential for understanding and fostering deeper human-AI and multi-agent collaboration.

title: Adaptive Utility driven Resource Orchestration for Resilient AI (AURORA-AI)
comment: Accepted at IEEE Research and Technologies for Society and Industry 2026 conference
summary: Modern AI systems are increasingly deployed under non-stationary computational, demographic, and operational conditions in which static resource allocation strategies degrade both predictive performance and human-centric properties such as fairness and explainability. This paper presents AURORA-AI, an Adaptive Utility-driven Resource Orchestration framework for Resilient AI that unifies Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman feedback control, Lyapunov-based stability monitoring, and a fairness-aware composite utility into a single closed-loop policy.The framework continuously redistributes computational budget across a population of heterogeneous AI models so that the global utility, defined jointly over predictive performance, demographic parity, cost, latency, robustness, and interpretability, remains maximised under disruption. The framework is evaluated in a stress-rich discrete-time simulation that concurrently injects demographic bias shocks, gradual concept drift, and abrupt black-swan disruptions, and is compared against five established controllers including Static, Round Robin, Greedy, LinUCB, and a deep reinforcement-learning agent based on Proximal Policy Optimisation. AURORA-AI achieves immediate recovery from the black-swan event compared to eighty-eight time steps for the Static baseline and twenty-two for Proximal Policy Optimisation, lifts the alpha-quantile and the super-quantile by twenty-nine and twenty-five percent respectively, simultaneously reduces the mean and maximum demographic parity gap, and increases the fraction of Lyapunov-stable operating steps. These results indicate that fairness-aware adaptive orchestration grounded in stability theory is a practical and theoretically motivated path toward resilient human-centric AI deployment.

AI.tldr: AURORA-AI is a closed-loop resource orchestration framework that uses Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman control and Lyapunov stability monitoring to continuously allocate computational budget across heterogeneous AI models, jointly optimizing predictive performance, fairness, cost, latency, robustness, and interpretability under non-stationary conditions. It significantly outperforms five baseline controllers in recovery speed, utility quantiles, demographic parity, and stability.
AI.motivation: Modern AI deployments face non-stationary computational, demographic, and operational conditions where static resource allocation degrades both predictive performance and human-centric properties (fairness, explainability). Existing controllers lack a unified approach that jointly addresses performance, fairness, stability, and resilience under concurrent disruptions such as demographic bias shocks, concept drift, and black-swan events.
AI.method: AURORA-AI integrates three components: (1) Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) feedback control for optimal dynamic resource allocation, (2) Lyapunov-based stability monitoring to ensure system stability, and (3) a fairness-aware composite utility function that jointly captures predictive performance, demographic parity, cost, latency, robustness, and interpretability. Evaluation uses a stress-rich discrete-time simulation with three concurrent disruption types — demographic bias shocks, gradual concept drift, and abrupt black-swan events — benchmarked against Static, Round Robin, Greedy, LinUCB, and PPO-based deep RL controllers.
AI.result: AURORA-AI achieves immediate (0-step) recovery from black-swan events vs. 88 steps for Static and 22 for PPO; lifts α-quantile by 29% and super-quantile by 25%; reduces both mean and maximum demographic parity gap; and increases the fraction of Lyapunov-stable operating steps.
AI.conclusion: Fairness-aware adaptive orchestration grounded in stability theory offers a practical and theoretically principled path toward resilient human-centric AI deployment, outperforming both classical and learning-based controllers across utility, fairness, and stability metrics.

title: Quantization in Federated Learning: Methods, Challenges and Future Directions
summary: Federated Learning (FL) has become a foundational paradigm for privacy-preserving distributed intelligence, yet its scalability remains fundamentally constrained by communication bottlenecks, device heterogeneity, and the challenges of training under statistically non-IID data. Quantization is one of the most effective mechanisms for mitigating these limitations, reducing both uplink/downlink payloads and on-device computation. This paper provides the first FL-centric systematic review of quantization, introducing a novel taxonomy organized around FL-specific dimensions, including client heterogeneity, aggregation consistency, communication-scheduling adaptation, non-IID robustness, privacy/security integration, and hardware/energy co-optimization. Beyond cataloging existing methods, we analyze how quantization interacts with core FL behaviors such as client drift, partial participation, convergence stability, secure aggregation, and differential privacy. We further identify cross-method insights, open research gaps, and design guidelines for practitioners deploying quantized FL on mobile, IoT, and edge platforms. This survey thus establishes quantization not merely as a compression technique, but as a fundamental systems component shaping the performance, robustness, and practicality of modern FL.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first systematic review of quantization techniques specifically tailored for Federated Learning (FL), introducing a novel FL-centric taxonomy. It analyzes how quantization interacts with core FL challenges—client drift, non-IID data, partial participation, secure aggregation, and differential privacy—and provides design guidelines, identifies research gaps, and frames quantization as a fundamental systems component rather than merely a compression tool.
AI.motivation: FL scalability is severely constrained by communication overhead, device heterogeneity, and non-IID data distributions. While quantization is a proven remedy, existing surveys lack an FL-specific lens. This work fills that gap by systematically examining quantization through dimensions unique to FL: aggregation consistency, client heterogeneity, communication scheduling, non-IID robustness, privacy/security integration, and hardware/energy co-optimization.
AI.method: The authors conduct a comprehensive literature review and propose a novel taxonomy organized around six FL-centric dimensions: (1) client heterogeneity, (2) aggregation consistency, (3) communication-scheduling adaptation, (4) non-IID robustness, (5) privacy/security integration, and (6) hardware/energy co-optimization. They then analyze the interplay between quantization and core FL phenomena (client drift, partial participation, convergence stability, secure aggregation, differential privacy) and synthesize cross-method insights, open problems, and practical design guidelines.
AI.result: The survey catalogs and categorizes a wide range of quantization methods, revealing that quantization significantly impacts—and is impacted by—FL-specific dynamics. Key findings include the tension between quantization error and client drift under non-IID data, the need for quantization-aware secure aggregation protocols, and the importance of hardware-aware quantization for heterogeneous edge devices. The paper identifies open gaps such as joint optimization of quantization with differential privacy, adaptive bit-width allocation across heterogeneous clients, and energy-quantization trade-offs on resource-constrained platforms.
AI.conclusion: Quantization should be viewed as a fundamental systems component in FL, not merely a compression afterthought. It shapes convergence, robustness, privacy guarantees, and energy efficiency. The survey provides practitioners with actionable design guidelines and charts a research roadmap emphasizing adaptive, heterogeneity-aware, and privacy-integrated quantization strategies for real-world FL deployments on mobile, IoT, and edge platforms.

title: LMs as Task-Specific Knowledge Bases: An Interpretability Analysis
summary: Language models (LMs) capture large amounts of factual knowledge applicable to a wide range of tasks, motivating the view of their parameters as a knowledge base. An important property of knowledge bases is that different queries for the same fact return consistent results, drawing on a single source of truth. We investigate whether LMs satisfy this property through behavioral and mechanistic analyses. Our results suggest that they encode knowledge in a task-specific manner. Behaviorally, facts acquired on one task frequently fail to co-emerge on others during training. Parameter localization experiments suggest a mechanistic explanation, revealing distinct parameter subsets underlying different tasks for the same fact. Finally, we show that chain-of-thought reasoning draws part of its effectiveness from engaging task-specific parameters beyond those tied to the evaluation task. Our findings suggest that what the model knows and how it is asked are intertwined in parameter space, undermining the "knowledge base" analogy and carrying implications for the reliability and controllability of factual knowledge in LMs.

AI.tldr: LMs encode factual knowledge in a task-specific rather than task-agnostic manner, undermining the "parameters as knowledge base" analogy. Different queries for the same fact activate distinct parameter subsets, and facts learned on one task often fail to transfer to others.
AI.motivation: To investigate whether language models satisfy the knowledge base property of consistency — that different queries for the same fact should draw on a single source of truth and return consistent results.
AI.method: Behavioral analysis tracking whether facts acquired on one task co-emerge on other tasks during training; mechanistic parameter localization experiments identifying parameter subsets responsible for different tasks on the same fact; analysis of chain-of-thought reasoning's engagement of task-specific parameters.
AI.result: Facts acquired on one task frequently fail to co-emerge on others during training. Distinct parameter subsets underlie different tasks for the same fact. Chain-of-thought reasoning derives part of its effectiveness from engaging task-specific parameters beyond those tied to the evaluation task.
AI.conclusion: What an LM knows and how it is asked are intertwined in parameter space. This challenges the knowledge base analogy and has implications for the reliability and controllability of factual knowledge in LMs.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Learning for Parametric Prophet Inequalities
summary: We study learning in prophet inequalities with i.i.d. rewards drawn from an exponential-type parametric family with an unknown parameter $θ$, a class that includes exponential, Pareto, and bounded-support power-family distributions. We first characterize the optimal full-information asymptotic competitive ratio for this family. In the unbounded-support case, the limit is $ {\left(θ/({θ-c_+})\right)^{c_+/θ}}/ {Γ(1-c_+/θ)},$ while in the bounded-support case, the limit is $1$. We then propose a confidence-based dynamic-programming policy for online learning. By exploiting the explicit parametric structure, the policy achieves the same optimal asymptotic competitive ratio using only online observations, without external offline samples. We further derive distribution-specific convergence rates for canonical examples. Finally, numerical experiments on synthetic instances illustrate the performance of our algorithm.

AI.tldr: This paper studies online learning for prophet inequalities with i.i.d. rewards from exponential-type parametric families with unknown parameter θ. It characterizes the optimal full-information asymptotic competitive ratio, then proposes a confidence-based dynamic programming policy that achieves the same ratio using only online observations, without offline samples.
AI.motivation: Classical prophet inequality results assume known reward distributions, which is unrealistic in many applications. The authors aim to bridge the gap by studying online learning in prophet inequalities where the reward distribution belongs to a parametric family with an unknown parameter, enabling data-driven decision-making without prior knowledge.
AI.method: The authors first derive the optimal full-information asymptotic competitive ratio for exponential-type families (exponential, Pareto, bounded power-family) as the number of arrivals grows. For the online learning setting, they design a confidence-based dynamic programming (CB-DP) policy that constructs confidence intervals around the unknown parameter θ from sequential observations and solves an optimistic dynamic program to make stopping decisions, exploiting the explicit parametric structure.
AI.result: The optimal asymptotic competitive ratio is characterized: for unbounded-support distributions it is (θ/(θ-c₊))^{c₊/θ} / Γ(1-c₊/θ), and for bounded-support it is 1. The proposed CB-DP policy achieves these same optimal ratios using only online observations. Distribution-specific convergence rates are derived for canonical examples, and numerical experiments validate the theoretical findings.
AI.conclusion: The paper demonstrates that for exponential-type parametric families, it is possible to achieve the optimal full-information asymptotic competitive ratio in an online learning setting without offline samples, by leveraging the parametric structure through a confidence-based dynamic programming approach.

title: How Surprising Is Historical Italian to Language Models? Tokenization Tax, Comprehension Tax, and a Simple Mitigation
comment: The 22nd Conference on Information and Research Science Connecting to Digital and Library Science
summary:
Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly critical to digital library workflows, yet their ability to process historical language remains poorly understood. Historical difficulty is typically treated as a monolithic barrier, conflating orthographic variation, linguistic distance, and pretraining exposure. In this paper, we propose a diagnostic framework that decomposes this difficulty into four distinct dimensions: tokenization cost, predictive uncertainty (surprisal), semantic robustness, and context sensitivity.
  We evaluate this framework on three datasets spanning three centuries: (1) a newly curated corpus of 17th-century Italian texts (1610-1689) digitized from original page images; (2) canonical 19th-century Italian "I Promessi Sposi" serving as a high-exposure control; and (3) 18th-century Russian civil print books as a contrastive orthographic stress test.
  Our results reveal a distinct dissociation between encoding cost and comprehension. While Russian and early modern Italian incur comparable tokenization penalties (25-30% inflation), their predictive difficulty diverges sharply. 17th-century Italian is on average 2.4 times more surprising than its modern equivalent - with academic prose reaching 3.2 times - whereas Russian shows only a modest increase. But predictive uncertainty does not imply representational degradation: embedding similarity remains robust (> 0.85) across all datasets, confirming that models can represent historical meaning even when generation is unstable.
  Finally, we demonstrate that a minimal temporal context prompt reduces historical surprisal by approximately 60%, offering a simple, model-agnostic mitigation. These findings suggest that while historical text imposes a consistent encoding tax, digital libraries can safely deploy LLMs for semantic retrieval tasks, provided that generative applications are carefully adapted.

AI.tldr: Proposes a four-dimensional diagnostic framework to decompose LLM difficulty with historical text into tokenization cost, surprisal, semantic robustness, and context sensitivity. Testing on 17th-c Italian, 19th-c Italian, and 18th-c Russian reveals that encoding cost and comprehension dissociate: tokenization penalties are comparable across languages, but surprisal diverges sharply. Semantic representations remain robust, and a minimal temporal context prompt reduces surprisal by ~60%.
AI.motivation: LLMs are increasingly deployed in digital library workflows, yet historical language difficulty is poorly understood and typically treated as a monolithic barrier. The authors aim to disentangle the distinct factors (orthography, linguistic distance, pretraining exposure) that contribute to this difficulty, enabling informed deployment decisions for retrieval vs. generative tasks.
