AI.method: A diagnostic framework with four dimensions: (1) tokenization cost (subword segmentation inflation), (2) predictive uncertainty (surprisal via language modeling), (3) semantic robustness (embedding similarity between historical and modern paraphrases), and (4) context sensitivity (effect of temporal context prompting). Evaluated on three datasets: a newly curated 17th-c Italian corpus (1610–1689), 19th-c Italian literary text as a high-exposure control, and 18th-c Russian civil print as an orthographic stress test.
AI.result: Russian and 17th-c Italian both incur 25–30% tokenization inflation. However, 17th-c Italian surprisal is 2.4× modern Italian (3.2× for academic prose), while Russian shows only a modest increase. Embedding similarity remains >0.85 across all datasets, indicating robust semantic representation despite generation instability. A temporal context prompt reduces historical surprisal by approximately 60%.
AI.conclusion: Historical text imposes a consistent "encoding tax" on LLMs, but semantic representation remains robust. Digital libraries can safely deploy LLMs for semantic retrieval tasks; generative applications require careful adaptation. Temporal context prompting offers a simple, model-agnostic mitigation strategy.

title: How to evaluate clustering with ground truth?
comment: Preprint of a book chapter to appear: P. Fränti, "How to evaluate clustering with ground truth?", In Center-based clustering, Springer Nature, 2026
summary: External indexes can be used for cluster evaluation when ground truth is available. We review the most common external validity indexes focusing on set-matching-based measures. We recommend centroid index (CI), because it is an intuitive cluster-level measure with an explainable result. If we need a more fine-tuned, point-level measure, there are more choices. Pair-set index (PSI) provides a normalized score which is not biased by cluster sizes. If all points should matter equally, then clustering accuracy (ACC) or any other set-matching measure is suitable.

AI.tldr: The paper reviews external cluster validity indexes based on set-matching, recommending the Centroid Index (CI) as an intuitive cluster-level measure and the Pair-Set Index (PSI) for normalized point-level evaluation unbiased by cluster size.
AI.motivation: To guide practitioners in selecting appropriate external cluster validation measures when ground truth is available, by systematically reviewing set-matching-based indexes and clarifying the trade-offs between cluster-level and point-level measures.
AI.method: The paper reviews and compares common external validity indexes, focusing on set-matching-based measures such as the Centroid Index (CI), Pair-Set Index (PSI), and Clustering Accuracy (ACC), analyzing their properties, biases, and interpretability.
AI.result: CI is recommended as an intuitive, cluster-level measure with explainable output. PSI offers a normalized, cluster-size-unbiased point-level alternative. ACC and similar set-matching measures are appropriate when every point should contribute equally to the evaluation.
AI.conclusion: The choice of external cluster validity index should be driven by the evaluation objective: CI for interpretable cluster-level assessment, PSI for normalized fine-grained evaluation, and ACC for uniform point-level measurement.

title: GEOALIGN: Geometric Rollout Curation for Robust LLM Reinforcement Learning
comment: Accepted as a conference paper at ICML 2026
summary: Online reinforcement learning is widely used to align large language models (LLMs) with reward signals, yet training can be unstable under noisy or misspecified rewards. We identify a failure mode we call directional inconsistency: within a batch, a small set of high-reward rollouts induces representation-space preference directions that sharply disagree with the batch majority, resulting in high-variance and destabilizing updates. We propose geoalign, a lightweight plug-in for rollout curation in iterative policy optimization. Geoalign (i) forms within-prompt preference pairs, (ii) learns an online projector on per-rollout hidden states to concentrate reward-ordered displacement directions, and (iii) detects directionally inconsistent rollouts via their angular deviation from a batch consensus prototype and rectifies them with within-prompt stable alternatives. Geoalign is forward-pass only and adds negligible overhead. Across dialogue alignment with a learned reward model and mathematical reasoning with binary verified rewards, Geoalign improves final performance and reduces training oscillation, outperforming PF-PPO, PAR, PODS, and Seed-GRPO. These results suggest latent directional consensus as an effective reliability signal for online LLM RL.

AI.tldr: Geoalign is a lightweight rollout curation method for online RL alignment of LLMs that detects and corrects "directionally inconsistent" rollouts via latent-space angular deviation from a batch consensus prototype, improving training stability and final performance.
AI.motivation: Online RL for LLM alignment suffers from training instability under noisy or misspecified rewards. The authors identify "directional inconsistency" — a failure mode where high-reward rollouts in a batch produce representation-space preference directions that sharply disagree with the batch majority, causing high-variance, destabilizing updates.
AI.method: Geoalign operates in three steps during iterative policy optimization: (i) forms within-prompt preference pairs from rollouts, (ii) learns an online projector on per-rollout hidden states to concentrate reward-ordered displacement directions, and (iii) detects directionally inconsistent rollouts via angular deviation from a batch consensus prototype, then rectifies them using within-prompt stable alternatives. The method is forward-pass only with negligible computational overhead.
AI.result: Across dialogue alignment (learned reward model) and mathematical reasoning (binary verified rewards), Geoalign improves final performance and reduces training oscillation compared to PF-PPO, PAR, PODS, and Seed-GRPO.
AI.conclusion: Latent directional consensus serves as an effective reliability signal for online LLM RL, and lightweight rollout curation via Geoalign successfully mitigates directional inconsistency to stabilize training.

title: Multilingual Reasoning Cascades Need More Context
summary: Translation cascades for reasoning translate the query from another language to English, reason in English, and translate the answer back to the original language. This is a competitive approach to multilingual reasoning, but structurally lossy, since each stage discards information later stages may need, including cues for cultural grounding, register, and disambiguation. We examine the benefits of a simple and training-free intervention: a context-aware translation cascade, which additionally provides the original question, the English translated question, and the reasoning trace to the context of the final translation module. We evaluate gains across nine multilingual benchmarks including various task types, three backbone models, and 285 high-, mid-, and low-resource languages, and demonstrate strong gains for open-ended generation across models and resource regimes. We show that the original language question carries most of the beneficial context. Our study emphasizes the need to better design information flow in machine translation cascades for mitigating error propagation, and provides a simple and actionable default strategy: preserve the original user question until the end of the pipeline.

AI.tldr: Translation cascades for multilingual reasoning lose information at each stage. The authors propose a simple, training-free fix: providing the original question, English translation, and reasoning trace as context to the final translation module. This context-aware cascade yields strong gains across 9 benchmarks, 3 models, and 285 languages, with the original-language question carrying most of the benefit.
AI.motivation: Standard translation cascades (translate→reason in English→translate back) are structurally lossy: each stage discards information that later stages may need, such as cultural grounding, register, and disambiguation cues. The authors aim to quantify and mitigate this information loss without requiring additional training.
AI.method: A context-aware translation cascade that preserves the original question, the English-translated question, and the full reasoning trace as context for the final back-translation module. This is a training-free intervention applicable to any existing cascade pipeline. The approach is evaluated across nine multilingual benchmarks spanning diverse task types, three backbone models, and 285 languages across high-, mid-, and low-resource regimes.
AI.result: The context-aware cascade demonstrates strong gains for open-ended generation across all models and resource regimes. Ablation reveals that the original language question carries most of the beneficial context, suggesting that simply preserving the user's original query until the pipeline's end is the key actionable insight.
AI.conclusion: Better information flow design in machine translation cascades is critical for mitigating error propagation in multilingual reasoning. The recommended default strategy is simple and actionable: preserve the original user question until the end of the pipeline.

title: Joint Learning of Experiential Rules and Policies for Large Language Model Agents
summary: For LLM agents in multi-step interactive environments, a key challenge is to make effective use of accumulated interaction experience. Existing work has typically separated two uses of such experience: keeping it outside the model as natural-language rules for later prompting, or using trajectories and feedback to update the model parameters. The former is easy to interpret but can fall out of sync with the evolving policy; the latter improves the policy more broadly but provides only limited correction for local mistakes in sparse-reward settings. We present Joint Learning of Experiential Rules and Policies for LLM Agents (JERP), which updates a long-term experiential-rule pool and the policy from the same interaction trajectories. At decision time, JERP retrieves task-relevant rules and conditions the agent on them together with the interaction history. After each episode, it uses the collected trajectories both to optimize the policy and to revise the rule pool by comparing current rollouts with reference successful trajectories. This coupling keeps the rule pool aligned with the evolving policy while allowing stable and effective behaviors to be gradually absorbed into the model itself. Experiments on AlfWorld and WebShop show that JERP yields consistent gains in decision performance for complex interactive tasks.

AI.tldr: JERP proposes a framework that jointly updates both a long-term experiential rule pool and the LLM agent's policy from the same interaction trajectories, coupling rule-based guidance with policy optimization to improve decision-making in sparse-reward interactive environments.
AI.motivation: Existing approaches split the use of interaction experience into two disconnected paradigms: external natural-language rules (interpretable but drift-prone as the policy evolves) and parameter updates from trajectories (broad improvement but poor at correcting local mistakes in sparse-reward settings). Neither achieves both alignment with the evolving policy and effective local correction.
AI.method: JERP maintains a long-term experiential-rule pool. At decision time, it retrieves task-relevant rules and conditions the agent on them alongside interaction history. After each episode, it uses collected trajectories to both optimize the policy (via parameter updates) and revise the rule pool — comparing current rollouts against reference successful trajectories to add, modify, or remove rules. This coupling ensures the rule pool stays aligned with the evolving policy, while stable behaviors are gradually absorbed into the model.
AI.result: Experiments on AlfWorld and WebShop demonstrate consistent gains in decision performance for complex interactive tasks.
AI.conclusion: Jointly learning experiential rules and policy parameters from the same trajectories effectively combines the interpretability and local correction of rule-based methods with the broad improvement of policy optimization, leading to better performance in multi-step interactive environments.

title: Decision-Aligned Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification
summary: Uncertainty estimates in machine learning are typically evaluated using generic metrics such as the negative log-likelihood and expected calibration error, yet good performance on such metrics does not necessarily imply high utility in downstream decisions. We introduce decision-alignment, a criterion that reveals which evaluation metrics meaningfully align with downstream utilities. Applying this framework, we show that many widely used uncertainty metrics are either misaligned with common decision problems or encode pathological prior beliefs about the downstream task. We then propose prior-weighted utility metrics, a special class of proper scoring rules that provides decision-aligned uncertainty evaluation. Across benchmark experiments and real-world case studies, our metrics consistently align with realized decision utility, while conventional metrics do not. Our results surface flaws in the current UQ evaluation protocol and offer a principled extension of existing metrics toward decision-relevant UQ evaluation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces "decision-alignment," a framework showing that standard uncertainty quantification metrics (NLL, ECE) often fail to correlate with downstream decision utility. The authors propose prior-weighted utility metrics—a class of proper scoring rules—that consistently align with realized decision utility, offering a principled extension to current UQ evaluation protocols.
AI.motivation: Standard UQ evaluation metrics like negative log-likelihood and expected calibration error do not necessarily reflect how useful uncertainty estimates are for downstream decision-making. This disconnect means practitioners may select models that appear well-calibrated but perform poorly in real-world decisions.
AI.method: The authors develop a decision-theoretic framework centered on "decision-alignment," which assesses whether an evaluation metric correlates with downstream decision utility. They analyze existing proper scoring rules through this lens, revealing misalignment or embedded pathological priors, and then derive prior-weighted utility metrics—a subclass of proper scoring rules explicitly designed to align evaluation with the utility of downstream decisions.
AI.result: Benchmark experiments and real-world case studies demonstrate that prior-weighted utility metrics consistently correlate with realized decision utility, whereas conventional metrics like NLL and ECE do not. The analysis also exposes that many widely used uncertainty metrics implicitly encode unreasonable prior beliefs about the downstream task.
AI.conclusion: Current UQ evaluation protocols are flawed because they rely on metrics misaligned with decision utility. The proposed prior-weighted utility metrics provide a principled, decision-relevant extension of proper scoring rules, enabling more meaningful evaluation of predictive uncertainty in practical applications.

title: Beyond Surface Forms: A Comprehensive, Mechanism-Oriented Taxonomy of Indirect Linguistic Encoding for LLM-Based Coded Language Detection
comment: Submitted for review in ARR for EMNLP 2026
summary: To avoid moderation and surveillance on social media, some users routinely invent indirect linguistic expressions (ILE) that camouflage sensitive meanings. Such expressions surface as algospeak, euphemisms, and adversarial obfuscation, depending on intent and context, and they involve recurring encoding mechanisms. We propose a comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy of ILE that abstracts away from communicative goals and instead categorizes the underlying operations through which meaning is encoded and recovered. We evaluate the taxonomy by incorporating it into LLM prompts and comparing it with four existing taxonomies and a no-taxonomy baseline, using 2,000 manually annotated TikTok and Bluesky posts. The proposed taxonomy attains the strongest document- and span-level performance across the three LLMs, achieving an improvement of 4.7% in accuracy and 5.4% in F1 over the best-performing benchmark. The empirical results reveal the importance of a comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy as a stable scaffold for detecting emerging coded language and a useful input to content moderation. Disclaimer: This paper contains content that may be profane, vulgar, or offensive.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a mechanism-oriented taxonomy for indirect linguistic expressions (ILEs) used to evade social media moderation, and demonstrates that this taxonomy improves LLM-based detection of algospeak, euphemisms, and adversarial obfuscation, outperforming four existing taxonomies and a no-taxonomy baseline by 4.7% accuracy and 5.4% F1.
AI.motivation: Social media users increasingly employ indirect linguistic expressions (ILEs) — including algospeak, euphemisms, and adversarial obfuscation — to evade content moderation and surveillance. Existing taxonomies are fragmented, goal-oriented, and fail to capture the shared underlying encoding mechanisms across these phenomena. A unified, mechanism-focused framework is needed to improve automatic detection of emerging coded language.
AI.method: The authors develop a comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy of ILEs that categorizes the fundamental encoding and decoding operations (e.g., phonetic substitution, semantic shift, character-level obfuscation) independent of communicative intent. The taxonomy is evaluated by incorporating it into LLM prompts and benchmarking against four existing taxonomies and a no-taxonomy baseline. Evaluation uses 2,000 manually annotated posts from TikTok and Bluesky, tested across three LLMs at both document-level and span-level.
AI.result: The proposed mechanism-oriented taxonomy achieves the best document- and span-level performance across all three LLMs tested. It yields a 4.7% improvement in accuracy and a 5.4% improvement in F1 over the best-performing existing taxonomy baseline.
AI.conclusion: A comprehensive, mechanism-oriented taxonomy provides a stable and effective scaffold for detecting evolving coded language on social media. It serves as a valuable input for content moderation systems. The paper includes a disclaimer about potentially offensive content.

title: OpenRCA 2.0: From Outcome Labels to Causal Process Supervision
summary: Root cause analysis (RCA) poses a holistic test of LLM agentic capabilities, such as long-context understanding, multi-step reasoning, and tool use. However, existing datasets suffer from a fundamental gap: they label only the root cause, not the propagation path connecting it to the observed symptom, which largely simplifies the task to naive pattern matching. To support rigorous evaluation, we introduce PAVE, a step-wise labeling protocol that leverages known interventions from fault injection to reconstruct causal propagation paths. The mechanism is forward verification: reasoning from cause to effect rather than inferring backward from symptoms. Applying PAVE yields OpenRCA 2.0 (500 instances), the first cross-system RCA benchmark with step-wise causal annotations for LLM agents. Across 11 frontier LLMs, recovering the exact root-cause set succeeds in only 20.7% of cases on average. To locate where this difficulty lies, we relax the criterion and find what we call the ungrounded diagnosis: agents identify at least one correct root-cause service in 76.0% of cases, but ground that service in a verified causal propagation path to the observed symptom in only 61.5%. Outcome-only evaluation hides this failure mode; step-wise causal ground truth is the missing piece for trustworthy LLM-based RCA agents.

AI.tldr: PAVE introduces a step-wise labeling protocol using fault injection to reconstruct causal propagation paths, producing OpenRCA 2.0—the first cross-system RCA benchmark with full causal annotations. Evaluating 11 LLMs reveals a critical gap: agents often identify the correct root-cause service (76%) but fail to ground it in a verified causal path (61.5%), a failure mode hidden by outcome-only evaluation.
AI.motivation: Existing RCA benchmarks only label the root cause, omitting the causal propagation path from cause to observed symptom. This reduces RCA—which inherently demands long-context understanding, multi-step reasoning, and tool use—to naive pattern matching, preventing rigorous evaluation of LLM agentic capabilities.
AI.method: PAVE (a step-wise labeling protocol) leverages known interventions from fault injection to perform forward verification: reasoning from cause to effect to reconstruct causal propagation paths, rather than inferring backward from symptoms. This yields OpenRCA 2.0, a 500-instance cross-system benchmark with step-wise causal annotations.
AI.result: Across 11 frontier LLMs, exact root-cause set recovery achieves only 20.7% on average. A relaxed evaluation reveals "ungrounded diagnosis": agents identify at least one correct root-cause service in 76.0% of cases, but ground it in a verified causal propagation path in only 61.5% of cases.
AI.conclusion: Outcome-only evaluation masks the ungrounded diagnosis failure mode. Step-wise causal ground truth is essential for developing and evaluating trustworthy LLM-based RCA agents, and OpenRCA 2.0 provides the necessary benchmark infrastructure.

title: Uncertainty quantification via conformal prediction in data assimilation
comment: Submitted to Quarterly Journal of the Royal Meteorological Society
summary: Quantifying the evolution of uncertainty is critical to both probabilistic forecasting and data assimilation in numerical weather prediction. In this study, we investigate the applicability of conformal prediction (CP), a recent machine learning (ML) method, to quantify uncertainty in a controlled, idealized setting. We use the one dimensional modified shallow water model, designed to mimic the convective process. CP provides a set of possible outcomes with a chosen confidence level. Here, we compare and evaluate the average empirical coverage, the average interval length, miss low, miss high and average interval score loss (AISL) for three variants of CP, namely a) Standard CP, b) Normalized CP and c) Conformalized Quantile Regression. We further compare these CP-based uncertainty estimates with traditional ensemble-based measures such as standard deviation intervals and ensemble spread. In addition, we investigate the integration of CP-derived uncertainty within the data assimilation cycle through CP perturbations. Our results highlight the strengths and limitations of each approach, providing insight into the effectiveness of CP to complement common ensemble-based uncertainty quantification in simplified atmospheric models.

AI.tldr: This study evaluates conformal prediction (CP) for uncertainty quantification in a 1D modified shallow water model that mimics atmospheric convection. Three CP variants (Standard CP, Normalized CP, Conformalized Quantile Regression) are compared against traditional ensemble-based uncertainty measures, and CP perturbations are integrated into data assimilation cycles.
AI.motivation: Uncertainty quantification is crucial for probabilistic forecasting and data assimilation in numerical weather prediction. The authors seek to explore whether conformal prediction, a recent ML-based framework, can complement or improve upon traditional ensemble-based uncertainty quantification methods in simplified atmospheric models.
AI.method: The study employs a one-dimensional modified shallow water model that mimics convective processes as an idealized testbed. Three CP variants are evaluated: (a) Standard CP, (b) Normalized CP, and (c) Conformalized Quantile Regression (CQR). These are benchmarked against traditional ensemble-based uncertainty measures (standard deviation intervals, ensemble spread) using metrics: average empirical coverage, average interval length, miss-low rate, miss-high rate, and average interval score loss (AISL). Additionally, CP-derived perturbations are integrated into the data assimilation cycle to assess operational viability.
AI.result: The results highlight distinct strengths and limitations for each CP variant and for traditional ensemble methods. No single approach uniformly dominates across all metrics; trade-offs exist between coverage, interval sharpness, and calibration. CP-based perturbation within data assimilation shows promise but also reveals challenges in this idealized setting.
AI.conclusion: Conformal prediction offers a viable framework for uncertainty quantification in simplified atmospheric models and can complement traditional ensemble-based approaches. The choice of CP variant involves trade-offs that depend on the specific forecasting or assimilation objective. Further investigation in more complex, operational-scale models is warranted.

title: LLM-Based Examination of Eligibility Criteria from Securities Prospectuses at the German Central Bank
summary: Verifying the eligibility of securities as collateral is a key responsibility of the German Central Bank. However, manually verifying these assets against legal and financial criteria within lengthy, semi-structured, and often bilingual prospectuses is a resource-intensive task. While previous efforts utilized traditional Named Entity Recognition (NER) for information extraction, these methods can struggle with OCR noise, linguistic variance, and rigid span-based constraints, and the need for manually annotated training data for each relevant annotation type. In this paper, we present the first case study applying Large Language Models (LLMs) to the eligibility examination process, shifting the paradigm toward a generative Information Extraction pipeline. Our approach decomposes the task into extraction, normalization, and interpretation, allowing for greater flexibility in handling noisy text and interleaved German-English content. We further introduce a value-based evaluation methodology using LLM-as-a-judge, which offers a more semantic assessment than location-based metrics. Our results demonstrate that LLM-based systems achieve high precision (up to 91%) in document-level eligibility, exhibiting a conservative operating profile that minimizes false acceptance.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a case study on using Large Language Models (LLMs) for automating the German Central Bank's collateral eligibility verification, shifting from traditional NER to a generative IE pipeline with extraction, normalization, and interpretation stages. It introduces LLM-as-a-judge for semantic evaluation and achieves up to 91% precision with a conservative error profile.
AI.motivation: Manually verifying securities collateral eligibility against legal/financial criteria in lengthy, semi-structured, bilingual (German-English) prospectuses is resource-intensive. Traditional NER approaches struggle with OCR noise, linguistic variance, rigid span constraints, and require costly manual annotation for each entity type.
AI.method: A generative Information Extraction pipeline using LLMs, decomposing the task into three stages: extraction (retrieving relevant information), normalization (standardizing values), and interpretation (applying eligibility rules). Evaluation uses a novel LLM-as-a-judge methodology for value-based semantic assessment rather than traditional location-based (span-matching) metrics.
AI.result: LLM-based systems achieve up to 91% precision in document-level eligibility classification. The system exhibits a conservative operating profile — prioritizing minimization of false acceptance (incorrectly approving ineligible collateral) over false rejection.
AI.conclusion: LLMs are viable for regulatory document processing tasks like collateral eligibility verification, offering flexibility with noisy, multilingual text. The generative IE paradigm and LLM-as-a-judge evaluation framework provide practical advantages over traditional span-based NER approaches in real-world financial compliance settings.

title: TOPS: First-Principles Visual Token Pruning via Constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets for Efficient MLLM Inference
summary: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong multimodal reasoning capabilities, but their efficiency is limited by the large number of visual tokens, which introduces substantial computational overhead. Visual token pruning offers a natural solution, yet existing methods are imperfect: attention-based criteria tend to retain redundant tokens, while diversity-based criteria are often agnostic to user instructions. Even methods that combine multiple criteria still lack a principled formulation of the intrinsic objective of token pruning. In this paper, we revisit visual token pruning from a first-principles perspective and formulate it as constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets. Through a top-down information-theoretic analysis, we identify three fundamental principles for effective token selection: Task Relevance, Information Coverage, and Semantic Diversity. Based on these principles, we propose TOPS, a training-free and model-agnostic pruning module that can be applied to various MLLMs. Extensive experiments on 7 MLLM backbones and 14 benchmarks demonstrate that TOPS outperforms prior methods under diverse pruning settings. Notably, on LLaVA-NeXT, TOPS removes 77.8% of visual tokens while preserving 100.0% and 100.6% performance on its 7B and 13B models, respectively, suggesting that pruning redundant visual tokens can sometimes mitigate hallucination and inspire future lightweight MLLM design.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes TOPS, a training-free, model-agnostic visual token pruning method for MLLMs grounded in three information-theoretic principles: Task Relevance, Information Coverage, and Semantic Diversity. TOPS removes up to 77.8% of visual tokens while maintaining or exceeding baseline performance.
AI.motivation: MLLMs suffer from high computational overhead due to large numbers of visual tokens. Existing pruning methods are suboptimal: attention-based criteria retain redundant tokens, diversity-based criteria ignore user instructions, and hybrid methods lack a principled formulation of the pruning objective.
AI.method: The authors frame token pruning as constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets. Through top-down information-theoretic analysis, they derive three principles: (1) Task Relevance — tokens must be relevant to the user query; (2) Information Coverage — selected tokens should collectively cover salient visual information; (3) Semantic Diversity — retained tokens should be non-redundant. TOPS operationalizes these principles into a training-free, model-agnostic module applicable to any MLLM.
AI.result: Experiments across 7 MLLM backbones and 14 benchmarks show TOPS outperforms prior methods. On LLaVA-NeXT, pruning 77.8% of visual tokens achieves 100.0% and 100.6% performance retention on 7B and 13B models, respectively. Notably, pruning sometimes mitigates hallucination, suggesting redundant visual tokens may contribute to errors.
AI.conclusion: TOPS demonstrates that principled visual token pruning, guided by Task Relevance, Information Coverage, and Semantic Diversity, can dramatically reduce computational cost without sacrificing performance. The finding that pruning can even reduce hallucination opens avenues for designing more efficient MLLMs with fewer but higher-quality visual tokens.

title: A Generalization Theory for JEPA-Based World Models
summary: Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for world modeling by learning predictive dynamics in a latent space rather than generating future observations at the input level. Despite their empirical success, the theoretical understanding of JEPA-based world models remains limited. In this paper, we develop the first generalization theory for JEPA-based world models. We formulate JEPA pretraining as a conditional spectral graph learning problem and show that the JEPA objective is equivalent to a low-rank factorization of an action-conditioned co-occurrence matrix. Building on this characterization, we establish a connection between JEPA pretraining error and downstream planning regret, leading to a finite-sample generalization bound for JEPA-based world models. Our analysis reveals an inherent trade-off between approximation and sample errors with respect to the latent dimension, providing theoretical insights into the advantages and limitations of latent predictive models compared with input-level predictive approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes the first generalization theory for JEPA-based world models, framing JEPA pretraining as conditional spectral graph learning equivalent to low-rank factorization of an action-conditioned co-occurrence matrix, and derives a finite-sample generalization bound linking pretraining error to downstream planning regret while revealing an approximation-sampling trade-off with respect to latent dimension.
AI.motivation: Despite the empirical success of Joint Embedding Predictive Architectures (JEPAs) for world modeling, their theoretical underpinnings remain unexplored. The authors aim to fill this gap by providing a rigorous understanding of why and how JEPA-based world models generalize, and what theoretical advantages or limitations they possess compared to input-level predictive approaches.
AI.method: The paper formulates JEPA pretraining as a conditional spectral graph learning problem, proving equivalence between the JEPA objective and low-rank factorization of an action-conditioned co-occurrence matrix. Using this characterization, the authors connect JEPA pretraining error to downstream planning regret and derive a finite-sample generalization bound via spectral analysis and learning-theoretic techniques.
AI.result: The analysis yields a finite-sample generalization bound for JEPA-based world models and reveals an inherent trade-off between approximation error and sample error as a function of the latent dimension. This trade-off provides theoretical insights into when latent predictive models outperform or underperform input-level predictive approaches.
AI.conclusion: JEPA-based world models admit rigorous generalization guarantees derived from their spectral structure as conditional co-occurrence matrix factorizations. The latent dimension serves as a critical parameter controlling the approximation-sample error trade-off, offering principled guidance for model design and highlighting both the strengths and limitations of learning predictive dynamics in latent space.

title: Empowering GUI Agents via Autonomous Experience Exploration and Hindsight Experience Utilization for Task Planning
summary: Multimodal web agents can assist humans in operating repetitive GUI tasks, where effective task planning is essential for decomposing complex tasks into executable actions. While small open source MLLMs are cost efficient and privacy preserving compared with commercial large models, they suffer from weak planning and limited cross website generalization. To address these limitations, we introduce the planning experience exploration and utilization (PEEU) method, which autonomously explores environments to discover experiences and utilizes hindsight experience to synthesize strictly aligned, high level training data. To quantitatively analyze the generalization behaviors driving this performance, we propose the task decomposition hierarchical analysis framework (TDHAF) to systematically study compositional generalization across three task granularities: low, middle and high levels. Our analysis reveals that mastering low level atomic skills does not guarantee high level planning competence, while high level task training yields stronger OOD generalization. Experiments on real world benchmarks demonstrate PEEU's superior effectiveness: our 7B model achieves 30.6% accuracy, outperforming the much larger Qwen2.5-VL-32B model. These demonstrate constructing hindsight high level tasks and leveraging experiences is crucial for OOD planning abilities of small MLLMs.

AI.tldr: PEEU is a method that lets small MLLMs autonomously explore GUI environments and synthesize hindsight-based high-level training data, significantly improving out-of-distribution task planning. A 7B model trained this way surpasses the 32B Qwen2.5-VL. The paper also introduces TDHAF to analyze compositional generalization across task granularities, showing that high-level training drives stronger OOD generalization.
AI.motivation: Small open-source MLLMs for GUI agents are cost-efficient and privacy-preserving but suffer from weak planning and poor cross-website generalization. The paper aims to bridge this gap without relying on large proprietary models.
AI.method: Two main contributions: (1) **PEEU (Planning Experience Exploration and Utilization)** — autonomously explores environments to discover experiences, then uses hindsight experience replay to synthesize strictly aligned, high-level training data for fine-tuning. (2) **TDHAF (Task Decomposition Hierarchical Analysis Framework)** — systematically studies compositional generalization at low (atomic skills), middle, and high task granularities.
AI.result: A 7B model trained with PEEU achieves 30.6% accuracy on real-world benchmarks, outperforming the much larger Qwen2.5-VL-32B model. Analysis via TDHAF shows that mastering low-level atomic skills does not ensure high-level planning competence, whereas high-level task training yields superior OOD generalization.
AI.conclusion: Constructing hindsight high-level tasks and leveraging planning experiences are crucial for developing out-of-distribution planning abilities in small MLLMs. This approach offers a viable path to strong GUI agents without dependence on large commercial models.

title: A Process Harness for Uplifting Legacy Workflows to Agentic BPM: Design and Realization in CUGA FLO
summary: We introduce the process harness, a new mechanism for uplifting legacy workflows into Agentic Business Process Management (Agentic BPM) without replacing the underlying workflow engine. A process harness places a policy-governed agentic layer around a deterministic workflow engine, intercepting designated control points to contribute reasoning, adaptation, and oversight while the engine retains structural authority over the process. To define the process harness rigorously, we develop the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model, specifying both its data schema and its execution semantics. TDF decomposes LLM reasoning across three policy-governed agent types: a TaskAgent for knowledge-intensive task execution, a DecisionAgent for per-case gateway routing, and a FlowAgent that governs runtime flow adaptation through a principled hook mechanism. Each agent reasons within an explicit policy drawn from the process FRAME, the aggregate policy set governing all LLM calls in the system. We then present CUGA FLO as the design and implementation realization of the TDF model, and demonstrate it on a loan approval workflow that exercises all three agent types and hook-driven regulatory override. The process harness uniquely reconciles imperative requirements, realized through deterministic workflow execution that enforces structural compliance, with normative requirements, realized through policy-framed agentic autonomy invoked at designated control points wherever the process demands it.

AI.tldr: Introduces the "process harness," a mechanism that layers policy-governed LLM agents around existing deterministic workflow engines to enable Agentic BPM without engine replacement. Formalized via the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model and implemented as CUGA FLO, it reconciles imperative structural compliance with normative, adaptive agent reasoning.
AI.motivation: Legacy BPM workflows are rigid and deterministic, making them ill-suited for knowledge-intensive, adaptive, or exception-handling scenarios. Replacing the underlying workflow engine is costly and risky. There is a need for a non-invasive mechanism that augments existing workflows with LLM-based reasoning, adaptation, and oversight while preserving the engine's structural authority.
AI.method: Proposes the process harness: a policy-governed agentic layer wrapped around a deterministic workflow engine. Intercepts designated control points via hooks. Develops the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model with formal data schema and execution semantics, decomposing LLM reasoning across three agent types (TaskAgent, DecisionAgent, FlowAgent), each governed by policies from a unified FRAME policy set. Implements the approach as CUGA FLO and demonstrates on a loan approval workflow.
AI.result: CUGA FLO successfully demonstrates all three agent types and hook-driven regulatory override on a loan approval workflow. The process harness effectively reconciles imperative requirements (deterministic structural compliance) with normative requirements (policy-framed agentic autonomy), showing that agentic capabilities can be added without replacing the existing workflow engine.
AI.conclusion: The process harness and TDF model provide a principled, non-disruptive path to upgrading legacy BPM systems with agentic AI capabilities, balancing the need for deterministic process control with the flexibility of LLM-driven reasoning, all governed by explicit policies.

title: Just how sure are you? Improving Verbalized Uncertainty Calibration in Medical VQA
summary:
Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) applied to Medical Visual Question Answering (VQA) tend to produce overconfident outputs regardless of actual correctness, and existing verbalized confidence calibration methods, developed primarily for text only LLMs, do not account for the multimodal nature of medical image understanding.
  This work proposes a training based framework that finetunes MLLMs to improve their calibration using a composite loss function combining a Brier style calibration term, an anchor regularizer that prevents confidence collapse toward extreme values, a contrastive image text alignment term, and a KL based model stabilization term. The alignment signal is derived from a $2 \times 2$ factorial perturbation design that crosses image presence with text integrity, probing the reliance of the model on visual modality input versus language priors. Finally, a top K KL divergence regularizer is used to protect the answering ability of the model during finetuning.
  Across three Medical VQA benchmarks and two architectures (MedGemma 4B IT and Qwen2 VL 7B Instruct), our method reduces calibration error by 60% or more, and improves discrimination by 26% or more, while preserving predictive accuracy. On average across benchmarks, the technique outperforms prompting based, sampling based, and training based approaches, and ablation experiments confirm that each component of the loss function is indeed necessary for improving the calibration. All code for the experiments is publicly available.

AI.tldr: MLLMs exhibit overconfidence in Medical VQA. This work proposes a finetuning framework using a composite loss (Brier calibration, anchor regularization, contrastive image-text alignment, KL stabilization) with a factorial perturbation design. Results show ≥60% calibration error reduction and ≥26% discrimination improvement across benchmarks while preserving accuracy.
AI.motivation: Multimodal LLMs applied to Medical Visual Question Answering produce overconfident predictions regardless of correctness. Existing confidence calibration methods are designed for text-only LLMs and fail to account for the multimodal nature of medical image understanding, particularly the interplay between visual and textual modalities.
AI.method: A training-based calibration framework that finetunes MLLMs using a composite loss function with four components: (1) a Brier-style calibration term for proper scoring, (2) an anchor regularizer to prevent confidence collapse toward extremes, (3) a contrastive image-text alignment term derived from a 2×2 factorial perturbation design crossing image presence with text integrity to probe visual vs. language prior reliance, and (4) a top-K KL divergence regularizer to preserve answering ability during finetuning.
AI.result: Across three Medical VQA benchmarks and two architectures (MedGemma 4B IT, Qwen2 VL 7B Instruct), the method reduces calibration error by ≥60%, improves discrimination by ≥26%, and preserves predictive accuracy. It outperforms prompting-based, sampling-based, and other training-based approaches. Ablation studies confirm all loss components are necessary.
AI.conclusion: The proposed composite-loss finetuning framework effectively calibrates MLLMs for Medical VQA, substantially reducing overconfidence while maintaining accuracy. The factorial perturbation design successfully captures multimodal alignment signals, and the method generalizes across architectures and benchmarks. Code is publicly available.

title: Mapping Political-Elite Networks in Europe with a Multilingual Joint Entity-Relation Extraction Pipeline
summary: Whether political elites organise into rent-seeking coalitions that capture public resources or civic networks that sustain governance is a central question in comparative politics. Yet observing these complex, informal, and adversarial ties at scale has historically required intensive manual coding, while automated text-as-data methods have largely been limited to simple co-occurrence. Recent large language model (LLM) approaches offer a path forward but often rely on proprietary APIs, lack cross-lingual capability, and struggle with scalable entity resolution. We present a modular, fully open-weight pipeline for multilingual joint entity-relation extraction that builds signed, temporal knowledge graphs from massive unstructured news corpora. It combines span-based named-entity recognition (NER) with a three-stage linking cascade mapping mentions to language-independent Wikidata identifiers; a high-throughput, ontology-constrained mixture-of-experts model then uses guided decoding to extract directed, signed relationships grounded in a domain ontology. A full-coverage spot-check against a 3491-relation gold standard shows high textual correctness (68.2% strict to 93.7% lenient). Two large-scale case studies validate the pipeline against the public record. In Austria, it reconstructs a political party's complete lifecycle, dating internal fractures and tracking personnel into successor factions and court convictions. In a Polish corpus, it uncovers the overlapping economic and governance networks of state-enterprise patronage, alongside the structurally balanced, signed conflict network of the polarized Civic Platform (Platforma Obywatelska, PO)--Law and Justice (Prawo i Sprawiedliwość, PiS) duopoly. By bridging raw multilingual text and structured relational data, our framework provides a robust, replicable foundation for cross-national empirical computational social science.

AI.tldr: An open-weight, multilingual pipeline extracts signed, temporal knowledge graphs from news corpora by combining NER, Wikidata entity linking, and ontology-constrained mixture-of-experts relation extraction. Validated on Austrian and Polish cases, it reconstructs party lifecycles, patronage networks, and polarized conflict structures.
AI.motivation: Capturing elite rent-seeking coalitions versus civic networks at scale has been hampered by manual coding costs and limitations of simple co-occurrence text-as-data methods. Existing LLM approaches rely on proprietary APIs, lack cross-lingual capability, and face entity resolution challenges. A fully open, scalable method is needed.
AI.method: A modular, fully open-weight pipeline: (1) span-based multilingual NER; (2) three-stage linking cascade mapping mentions to language-independent Wikidata IDs; (3) high-throughput, ontology-constrained mixture-of-experts model with guided decoding for directed, signed relation extraction, producing signed temporal knowledge graphs.
AI.result: Spot-check against a 3,491-relation gold standard yields 68.2% strict and 93.7% lenient textual correctness. In Austria, the pipeline reconstructs a party's full lifecycle including internal fractures and court convictions. In Poland, it reveals state-enterprise patronage networks and the structurally balanced signed conflict network of the PO-PiS duopoly.
AI.conclusion: The framework bridges raw multilingual text and structured relational data, providing a robust, replicable foundation for cross-national empirical computational social science without reliance on proprietary systems.

title: Vulnerability of Natural Language Classifiers to Evolutionary Generated Adversarial Text
summary: Deep learning models have achieved impressive performance across various fields but remain vulnerable to adversarial inputs, particularly in NLP, where such attacks can have significant real-world consequences. Adversarial attacks often involve small, semantically similar token replacements to fool NLP models, and recent methods have become more precise by targeting specific vulnerable words, often by exploiting some level of access to the model's internal structure. This paper proposes GAversary, a hybrid Genetic Algorithm (GA) to generate adversarial attacks on natural language models. The GA is able to treat the target model as a black box, requiring only the logit value output by the model to guide the search. GAversary differs from GAs previously proposed for this problem by using GloVe embeddings to propose word replacements (the mutation operator) to improve the semantic similarity of the adversarial examples. GAversary is applied to several benchmark data sets and well-known target models. GAversary is able to substantially reduce the target model's accuracy on test data compared to the BAE and A2T attacks compared against (in the best case, reducing a 76.8% accuracy to 5.8%, compared to BAE's 27.6%). The trade-off is that GAversary perturbs just under twice as many words as the other two methods, with a slightly lower semantic similarity to the original text and around a 5% increase in run-time.

AI.tldr: GAversary is a black-box genetic algorithm attack using GloVe-based mutations that dramatically reduces NLP model accuracy (76.8% → 5.8%) at the cost of more word perturbations and marginally lower semantic similarity.
AI.motivation: Deep learning NLP models are vulnerable to adversarial attacks using semantically similar token replacements. Existing precise attacks often require access to model internals (white-box). There is a need for effective black-box attacks that only use model outputs while maintaining semantic similarity.
AI.method: GAversary: a hybrid Genetic Algorithm that treats the target model as a black box, using only logit outputs to guide search. Mutation uses GloVe embeddings to propose semantically similar word replacements, distinguishing it from prior GA-based approaches.
AI.result: GAversary reduced target model accuracy from 76.8% to 5.8% (vs. BAE's 27.6% and A2T). Trade-offs: nearly 2× more word perturbations, slightly lower semantic similarity, and ~5% increase in runtime compared to baselines.
AI.conclusion: GAversary demonstrates that black-box genetic algorithms with embedding-guided mutations can achieve stronger adversarial attacks than existing methods like BAE and A2T, albeit with a trade-off in perturbation rate, semantic fidelity, and runtime.

title: Symplectic Neural Networks for learning Generalized Hamiltonians
summary: Hamiltonian Neural Networks (HNNs) integrate physical priors into neural models by learning a system's Hamiltonian, improving generalization and sample efficiency. Identifying the system Hamiltonian from noisy observations of state variables is a challenging task. For simulations to faithfully reflect the long-term behavior of Hamiltonian systems, especially energy conservation, it is essential to use symplectic integrators, which preserve the system's geometric structure. This fidelity comes at a cost: implicit symplectic integrators are more computationally intensive and make backpropagation through the ODE solver non-trivial. However, by leveraging the fact that symplectic discretizations of the adjoint system yield the same sensitivities associated by backpropagation, we obtain an efficient method of training the Neural Network parameters. In our work, we explore this alternate method of HNN training under noisy observation of trajectories with our HNN model based on an implicit symplectic integrator. Computationally, a predictor-corrector based ODE solver and fixed point iteration help to mitigate the computational cost of the implicit timestepping, resulting in more efficient generation of gradient updates. We showcase the numerical advantage, in experiments, in system identification and energy preservation on a range of non-separable, chaotic systems and the efficient computation and memory complexity of our method. We also observe that the post-processing of the learned Hamiltonian using backward error analysis yields a modified Hamiltonian that is a more accurate approximation of the true Hamiltonian without the need to use more accurate discretizations of the flow map.

AI.tldr: HNNs are trained with implicit symplectic integrators using an efficient backpropagation method based on adjoint sensitivity analysis. A predictor-corrector solver with fixed-point iteration reduces computational cost, and backward error analysis yields a modified Hamiltonian that more accurately approximates the true Hamiltonian. The method is demonstrated on non-separable chaotic systems with noisy observations, showing improved energy preservation and system identification.
AI.motivation: Training Hamiltonian Neural Networks from noisy trajectory observations is challenging. Implicit symplectic integrators are essential for long-term fidelity and energy conservation in Hamiltonian systems, but they are computationally intensive and complicate backpropagation through the ODE solver. The authors seek an efficient training method that retains the benefits of implicit symplectic integration while mitigating its computational drawbacks.
AI.method: The authors leverage the property that symplectic discretizations of the adjoint system yield the same sensitivities as backpropagation, enabling efficient gradient computation. They employ a predictor-corrector ODE solver with fixed-point iteration to reduce the cost of implicit timestepping. Additionally, post-processing via backward error analysis produces a modified Hamiltonian that serves as a more accurate approximation of the true Hamiltonian without requiring finer discretizations.
AI.result: The proposed method demonstrates numerical advantages in system identification and energy preservation on non-separable, chaotic Hamiltonian systems under noisy observations. It achieves efficient computation and memory complexity. The backward error analysis post-processing yields a modified Hamiltonian that is a more accurate approximation of the true Hamiltonian than the directly learned one.
AI.conclusion: Training HNNs with implicit symplectic integrators via adjoint-based backpropagation is both efficient and accurate. The combination of predictor-corrector solvers, fixed-point iteration, and backward error analysis enables robust learning of Hamiltonian structure from noisy data, with strong energy preservation and improved Hamiltonian recovery on chaotic, non-separable systems.

title: Ask, Don't Judge: Binary Questions for Interpretable LLM Evaluation and Self-Improvement
comment: Acceepted to the Second Workshop on Compositional Learning at ICML 2026, Seoul, South Korea
summary: Evaluating LLM outputs remains a major bottleneck in NLP: human evaluation is expensive and slow, lexical metrics correlate poorly with human judgments on open-ended generation, and holistic LLM judges often produce opaque scores that are hard to debug. We propose BINEVAL, a framework that decomposes evaluation criteria into atomic binary questions and aggregates the resulting verdicts into interpretable, multi-dimensional scores. Given a task prompt, a meta-prompt generates fine-grained evaluation questions, and an LLM answers them independently for each output, yielding transparent question-level feedback together with calibrated overall scores. This decomposition makes evaluation easier to inspect, easier to diagnose, and directly usable for prompt improvement. Across SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS, BINEVAL matches or outperforms strong baselines including UniEval and G-Eval, with especially strong results on factual consistency benchmarks such as QAGS. Beyond competitive correlation with human judgments, BINEVAL better matches human score distributions and avoids the ceiling effects common in prior LLM judges, leading to better discrimination between borderline and clearly flawed outputs. We further show that the same question-level feedback supports iterative prompt optimization, improving evaluator prompts on summarization and generation prompts on IFBench under both self-update and cross-model update settings. Overall, BINEVAL provides a task-agnostic, training-free, and interpretable evaluation framework that combines strong empirical performance with practical diagnostic and optimization value.

AI.tldr: BINEVAL decomposes LLM output evaluation into atomic binary questions with aggregated scores, providing interpretable multi-dimensional assessment that matches or outperforms existing evaluators while enabling prompt optimization.
AI.motivation: LLM output evaluation suffers from three key problems: human evaluation is expensive and slow, lexical metrics (BLEU, ROUGE) correlate poorly with human judgment on open-ended tasks, and holistic LLM judges produce opaque scores that are hard to debug. A transparent, fine-grained, interpretable evaluation framework is needed.
AI.method: BINEVAL uses a two-stage framework: (1) a meta-prompt generates task-specific atomic binary evaluation questions from the original task prompt, decomposing evaluation criteria into fine-grained, answerable yes/no questions; (2) an LLM answers these questions independently for each generated output. The binary verdicts are then aggregated into interpretable multi-dimensional scores. No training is required, and the framework is task-agnostic. The question-level feedback also supports iterative prompt optimization via self-update and cross-model update settings.
AI.result: On SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS benchmarks, BINEVAL matches or outperforms strong baselines (UniEval, G-Eval). It shows especially strong results on factual consistency (QAGS). Beyond correlation with human judgments, BINEVAL better matches human score distributions, avoids ceiling effects common in prior LLM judges, and better discriminates borderline from clearly flawed outputs. The question-level feedback also improves summarization evaluator prompts and IFBench generation prompts under both self-update and cross-model update settings.
AI.conclusion: BINEVAL provides a task-agnostic, training-free, interpretable evaluation framework combining strong empirical correlation with human judgments, practical diagnostic transparency via atomic binary questions, and direct utility for iterative prompt optimization.

title: State Representation Matters in Deep Reinforcement Learning: Application to Energy Trading
summary: Energy trading decisions depend not only on current market prices, but also on expected future market conditions, and operational constraints. This makes the state representation given to a reinforcement learning agent an important design choice. We study this in HydroDam, a pumped-storage arbitrage environment, using a fixed Double DQN agent. The environment, action space, reward function, network, and training protocol are kept fixed; only the market features are changed. We compare absolute price/calendar features, relative features that compare current prices with recent market history, forecast features, and all combinations of these three feature families. Policies are trained and selected using 2007--2011 Belgian day-ahead prices and evaluated on two test settings: a later same-market test set from 2012--2025 and 39 other ENTSO-E market zones. Absolute features only reaches 28.8% on the test set and a median 5.7% across zones. Relative-only and forecast-only states also stay below a rolling price-score heuristic in the cross-zone median. Combining feature families is much stronger: absolute + relative reaches 49.9% on the test set and a 39.8% cross-zone median, while absolute + relative + forecast reaches 55.6% and 47.5%. These results suggest that state representation is not a minor preprocessing choice in storage-trading RL, but a central part of the policy design: robust transfer requires combining price scale, recent relative price context, and short-horizon forecast information, rather than relying on any single feature family.

AI.tldr: State representation is critical in RL-based energy storage trading. Using a fixed Double DQN agent on a pumped-storage arbitrage task, the study shows that combining absolute price, relative (historical context), and forecast features dramatically improves performance (55.6% vs. 28.8% for absolute-only) and cross-market transferability, suggesting feature design is a central—not peripheral—policy design choice.
AI.motivation: Energy trading decisions depend on current prices, expected future conditions, and operational constraints, making state representation a crucial but underexamined design choice in RL-based storage arbitrage. The paper aims to systematically quantify how different market feature families affect agent performance and transferability.
AI.method: A fixed Double DQN agent is trained in the HydroDam pumped-storage arbitrage environment. Only market features vary across experiments. Three feature families are compared: (1) absolute price/calendar features, (2) relative features comparing current prices to recent history, and (3) short-horizon forecast features—plus all combinations. Training uses 2007–2011 Belgian day-ahead prices; evaluation uses a same-market holdout (2012–2025) and 39 other ENTSO-E zones for transfer testing. A rolling price-score heuristic serves as baseline.
AI.result: Absolute features alone achieve 28.8% on the same-market test set and median 5.7% across zones. Relative-only and forecast-only states both underperform the heuristic baseline in cross-zone median. Combining feature families yields strong gains: absolute+relative reaches 49.9% test / 39.8% cross-zone median; absolute+relative+forecast reaches 55.6% test / 47.5% cross-zone median.
AI.conclusion: State representation is not a minor preprocessing choice but a central element of policy design for storage-trading RL. Robust cross-market transfer requires integrating price scale, recent relative context, and short-horizon forecasts; relying on any single feature family severely limits performance and generalization.

title: EO-WM: A Physically Informed World Model for Probabilistic Earth Observation Forecasting
summary: Earth Observation (EO) forecasting aims to predict future Earth surface dynamics from satellite observations under changing meteorological conditions. In this paper, we view this task as a partially observed, weather-driven world modeling problem, in which weather acts as a conditioning signal, while forecasting remains uncertain due to sparse observations and unobserved land-surface states. However, existing methods do not fully capture this setting: deterministic models collapse uncertainty into a single future prediction, while diffusion-based methods typically treat weather variables as undifferentiated conditioning signals, and existing benchmarks focus mainly on reconstruction accuracy rather than whether forecasts respond correctly to changed weather forcing.We introduce EO-WM, a video diffusion transformer for multispectral EO forecasting. EO-WM incorporates a physically informed conditioning framework that represents meteorological forcing through a climatological baseline, weather anomalies, and cumulative physical stress signals. Specifically, it separates baseline and anomaly through distinct conditioning pathways, and accumulates anomalous forcing over time to capture sustained heat and drought stress. To evaluate weather-response behavior beyond standard metrics, we introduce two diagnostic benchmarks: an Extreme Summer Benchmark for severity-aware prediction of vegetation degradation under extreme weather, and a Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark for testing response fidelity under changed weather forcing. Experiments show that EO-WM reduces the error in predicted Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) decline amplitude by a relative 5.63% and improves directional hit rate by a relative 7.80%, while remaining competitive on standard pixel-level metrics. The benchmarks and model will be made open-source at https://github.com/Luo-Z13/EO-WM.

AI.tldr: EO-WM is a video diffusion transformer for multispectral Earth observation forecasting that uses physically informed weather conditioning (climatological baseline, anomalies, and cumulative stress) to improve prediction of vegetation response under extreme weather, demonstrated via two novel diagnostic benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Existing EO forecasting methods either collapse uncertainty (deterministic models) or treat weather as undifferentiated conditioning signals (standard diffusion models), failing to capture whether forecasts respond correctly to changed weather forcing. Current benchmarks also neglect weather-response behavior in favor of reconstruction accuracy.
AI.method: A video diffusion transformer with a physically informed conditioning framework comprising three components: (1) a climatological baseline pathway, (2) a weather anomaly pathway — separated via distinct conditioning streams, and (3) cumulative physical stress signals that accumulate anomalous forcing over time to model sustained heat and drought stress. Two new evaluation benchmarks are introduced: the Extreme Summer Benchmark (severity-aware vegetation degradation prediction) and the Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark (response fidelity under changed weather forcing).
AI.result: EO-WM achieves a relative 5.63% reduction in NDVI decline amplitude error and a relative 7.80% improvement in directional hit rate on the proposed benchmarks, while remaining competitive on standard pixel-level metrics.
AI.conclusion: Explicitly modeling weather as baseline, anomaly, and cumulative stress within a diffusion framework improves physically meaningful EO forecasting, and diagnostic benchmarks reveal weather-response fidelity that standard metrics miss.

title: Finding Stationary Points by Comparisons
comment: 41 pages, 4 figures. To appear in the Forty-Third International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026)
summary: We study the problem of finding stationary points of non-convex functions when access to the objective is provided only through a comparison oracle that, given two points, outputs which has the larger function value. For a twice differentiable $f\colon\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R$ with Lipschitz gradient and Hessian, we develop an algorithm that visits an $ε$-stationary point using $\widetilde O(n^2/ε^{1.5})$ queries. Our approach uses a subroutine that estimates the normalized Hessian to accuracy $δ$ using $\widetilde O(n^2\log(1/δ))$ queries. We further study this problem with a quantum comparison oracle model where queries can be made in superpositions, and develop the first quantum algorithm that finds an $ε$-stationary point, which takes $\widetilde O(n/ε^{1.5})$ queries.

AI.tldr: For non-convex optimization with only a comparison oracle, the authors give a classical algorithm finding ε-stationary points in Õ(n²/ε^1.5) queries and the first quantum algorithm achieving Õ(n/ε^1.5) queries, using a key subroutine that estimates the normalized Hessian via comparisons.
AI.motivation: Classical optimization typically assumes access to function values or gradients. However, in many practical settings (e.g., preference-based learning, human feedback, hyperparameter tuning), only pairwise comparisons are available. The paper aims to understand the query complexity of finding stationary points when only a comparison oracle — answering "which point has larger function value?" — is available, for both classical and quantum settings.
AI.method: The authors consider twice differentiable f with Lipschitz gradient and Hessian. The core classical algorithm relies on a subroutine that estimates the normalized Hessian (direction of most negative curvature) to accuracy δ using Õ(n² log(1/δ)) comparison queries. This subroutine is then used within a broader optimization framework to locate an ε-stationary point using Õ(n²/ε^1.5) total queries. For the quantum setting, they exploit superposition queries to a quantum comparison oracle, achieving a quadratic speedup in the dimension dependence: Õ(n/ε^1.5) queries.
AI.result: Classically: Õ(n²/ε^1.5) comparison queries suffice to find an ε-stationary point. The key building block estimates the normalized Hessian using Õ(n² log(1/δ)) queries. Quantumly: the first quantum algorithm for this problem achieves Õ(n/ε^1.5) queries, improving the n-dependence from n² to n.
AI.conclusion: Comparison-based non-convex optimization is tractable with query complexity polynomial in dimension and 1/ε. A quadratic quantum speedup in dimension is achievable. The normalized Hessian estimation subroutine is a fundamental primitive enabling these results.

title: Simulation-based inference for rapid Bayesian parameter estimation in epidemiological models: a comparison with MCMC
summary: Mechanistic epidemiological models are widely used to support infectious disease forecasting and public-health decision making. Bayesian calibration of such models is commonly performed using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which can become computationally expensive for high-dimensional nonlinear systems and repeated near-real-time analyses. Here, we investigate simulation-based inference (SBI) using neural posterior estimation as a scalable alternative for Bayesian calibration of a mechanistic SECIR epidemiological model using COVID-19 intensive care unit (ICU) occupancy data from Germany during 2020. We compared SBI and MCMC across multiple epidemic phases using both 31-day inference windows and a substantially more challenging 201-day reconstruction problem involving multiple transmission change points. Posterior agreement was evaluated quantitatively using Wasserstein distances and Kullback-Leibler divergences together with posterior predictive checks. Across the 31-day windows, SBI recovered posterior distributions in strong agreement with MCMC while accurately reproducing observed ICU trajectories. In the 201-day setting, SBI preserved the dominant posterior structure despite increased uncertainty. SBI, by combining CPU and GPU resources, substantially reduced computational runtime compared with MCMC, which was restricted to running on CPUs. Whereas MCMC required approximately 1000 seconds for the 31-day inference problems, SBI achieved comparable posterior and predictive performance in approximately 60-70 seconds on a single GPU. For the 201-day inference problem, SBI required an average of 157 seconds, while the MCMC runs took over 19,000 seconds. Our results demonstrate that SBI provides a rapid and computationally efficient framework for Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models, supporting repeated near-real-time inference and rapid outbreak analysis.

AI.tldr: SBI via neural posterior estimation matches MCMC accuracy for calibrating a mechanistic SECIR epidemiological model on COVID-19 ICU data from Germany, while reducing runtime from ~1000s to ~60-70s (31-day windows) and from ~19,000s to ~157s (201-day window), enabling rapid near-real-time outbreak analysis.
AI.motivation: Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models using MCMC becomes computationally prohibitive for high-dimensional nonlinear systems and repeated near-real-time analyses. A scalable, faster alternative is needed without sacrificing posterior accuracy.
AI.method: The authors applied simulation-based inference (SBI) with neural posterior estimation to a SECIR compartmental model, calibrating against COVID-19 ICU occupancy data from Germany in 2020. They compared SBI against MCMC across multiple epidemic phases using 31-day inference windows and a challenging 201-day reconstruction with multiple transmission change points. Evaluation used Wasserstein distances, Kullback-Leibler divergences, and posterior predictive checks.
AI.result: SBI posteriors strongly agreed with MCMC across 31-day windows and accurately reproduced ICU trajectories. In the 201-day setting, SBI preserved dominant posterior structure despite increased uncertainty. Runtime comparisons: 31-day — SBI ~60-70s (1 GPU) vs. MCMC ~1000s (CPU); 201-day — SBI ~157s vs. MCMC >19,000s.
AI.conclusion: SBI offers a rapid, computationally efficient framework for Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models, well-suited for repeated near-real-time inference and rapid outbreak analysis, with posterior quality comparable to MCMC.

title: Data-Free Reservoir Features for Efficient Long-Horizon Cold-Start Continual Learning
summary: Cold-start exemplar-free class-incremental learning requires learning a growing set of classes without replay, external pretraining, or a large initial task. Existing cold-start methods typically either train the backbone throughout the stream and compensate for semantic drift, or freeze a backbone after the first task, producing features biased toward the initial classes. These choices also create a computational tension: drift-compensation methods require repeated backbone training and increasingly expensive updates as the task horizon grows, while frozen-backbone methods are cheap but weak under cold start. We study a third option: a feature extractor that is never fit to image data at all. We propose CIRCLE, a class-incremental classifier built from fixed bidirectional two-dimensional reservoir features, adapted from BiRC2D for image classification, and streaming linear discriminant analysis heads. CIRCLE groups multiple random reservoir instantiations into feature ensembles and averages the softmax outputs of independent SLDA heads, yielding a tunable bias-variance tradeoff between richer random features and prediction-level ensembling. Because the feature extractor is fixed and the head admits streaming closed-form updates, CIRCLE performs sample-wise training without replay, task-boundary information, or backbone backpropagation. On CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, ImageNet-Subset, and ImageNet-1k, CIRCLE is competitive at 10-20 task splits and substantially outperforms strong CS-EFCIL baselines at 50, 100, and 500 task splits, while training much faster than trained-backbone drift-compensation methods. Ablations show that the BiRC2D-style extractor, SLDA head, and balanced feature/prediction ensembling each contribute to the final performance.

AI.tldr: CIRCLE introduces a cold-start exemplar-free class-incremental learning method using a fixed, never-trained 2D reservoir feature extractor combined with streaming LDA heads in an ensemble, achieving strong performance without replay, backbone training, or large initial tasks—especially excelling at extreme task splits (50–500).
AI.motivation: Existing cold-start EFCIL methods face a tradeoff: drift-compensation approaches retrain the backbone continually, incurring escalating computational cost as tasks grow, while frozen-backbone methods are cheap but produce features biased toward early classes. The authors explore a third path—a feature extractor never fit to image data—to eliminate semantic drift and backbone training costs entirely.
AI.method: CIRCLE uses fixed bidirectional 2D reservoir computing features (adapted from BiRC2D) as an untrained feature extractor, paired with streaming linear discriminant analysis (SLDA) heads. Multiple independent reservoir instantiations form feature ensembles, and softmax outputs from independent SLDA heads are averaged, creating a tunable bias-variance tradeoff. The extractor is static and SLDA admits closed-form streaming updates, enabling sample-wise training without replay, task boundaries, or backpropagation.
AI.result: On CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, ImageNet-Subset, and ImageNet-1k, CIRCLE is competitive at 10–20 task splits and significantly outperforms strong CS-EFCIL baselines at 50, 100, and 500 task splits, while training substantially faster than trained-backbone drift-compensation methods. Ablations confirm that the BiRC2D extractor, SLDA head, and balanced feature/prediction ensembling each contribute to performance.
AI.conclusion: A completely untrained, fixed reservoir-based feature extractor paired with streaming closed-form classifiers offers a computationally efficient and performant alternative for cold-start EFCIL, particularly under extreme incremental learning scenarios with many task splits.

title: Prompt Injection in Automated Résumé Screening with Large Language Models: Single and Multi-Injection Settings
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to screen and rank job applicants, creating incentives for candidates to strategically manipulate algorithmic hiring systems. We study prompt injection in automated résumé screening, defined as subtle self-promotional text that introduces no new qualifications but is designed to influence LLM evaluations. Using controlled experiments, we show that prompt injection reliably improves applicant rankings when résumé quality is homogeneous and few candidates inject. However, its effectiveness rapidly diminishes as more candidates inject, collapsing when manipulation becomes widespread. When candidate quality is heterogeneous, prompt injection is less effective on average, but can occasionally allow lower-quality candidates to outrank higher-quality ones, raising fairness concerns. Overall, LLM-based screening is most vulnerable when manipulation is rare and candidate quality differences are small. Code and resources are publicly available at: https://github.com/preetb1199/Prompt_Injection_ACL26

AI.tldr: Prompt injection in LLM-based résumé screening boosts rankings when manipulation is rare and candidate quality is homogeneous, but its effectiveness collapses under widespread use. In heterogeneous pools, injection occasionally lets weaker candidates outrank stronger ones, raising fairness issues.
AI.motivation: As LLMs are increasingly deployed for automated job applicant screening, candidates have strong incentives to strategically manipulate these systems. The authors aim to systematically study the vulnerability of LLM-based résumé screening to "prompt injection" — subtle, non-qualification-altering text designed to sway algorithmic evaluations — and understand how its effectiveness varies under different conditions of prevalence and candidate quality distribution.
