AI.method: Controlled experiments using LLMs to screen synthetic résumés. The authors vary two key dimensions: (1) the prevalence of prompt injection among candidates (rare to widespread), and (2) the homogeneity vs. heterogeneity of candidate quality. They measure how prompt injection affects applicant rankings under these conditions.
AI.result: Prompt injection reliably improves rankings when résumé quality is homogeneous and few candidates inject. Effectiveness diminishes rapidly as injection becomes widespread, collapsing entirely under universal manipulation. When quality is heterogeneous, injection is less effective on average but can occasionally enable lower-quality candidates to outrank higher-quality ones, raising fairness concerns. The system is most vulnerable when manipulation is rare and quality differences are small.
AI.conclusion: LLM-based hiring systems are susceptible to strategic manipulation via prompt injection, but the threat is context-dependent — most acute when manipulation is rare and candidates are similarly qualified. The findings highlight fairness risks and suggest that the effectiveness of such attacks is self-limiting, as widespread adoption negates their advantage.

title: Transformer-Based Classification of Bacterial Raman Spectra with LOOCV
summary: Transformer-based models have recently attracted increasing attention for Raman spectral classification. In this study, a transformer-based approach was systematically evaluated using a nested leave-one-replicate-out cross-validation framework and compared with conventional machine-learning pipelines combining PCA or ICA with LDA, SVM, and Random Forest classifiers. A bacterial Raman dataset comprising 5,417 single-cell spectra from six bacterial species and nine independent measurement replicates was used. The transformer consistently achieved the highest classification performance across independent test replicates and significantly outperformed all conventional approaches. Analysis of the learned latent feature space revealed improved class separation compared with PCA- and ICA-based representations. Furthermore, the transformer maintained superior performance when applied directly to raw Raman spectra without preprocessing, demonstrating robust behavior across measurement replicates. These findings highlight the potential of transformer-based models for robust Raman spectral classification and emphasize the importance of replicate-aware validation for realistic model evaluation.

AI.tldr: This study systematically evaluates a transformer-based model for Raman spectral classification of bacteria, demonstrating it significantly outperforms conventional PCA/ICA + classifier pipelines. Using a replicate-aware nested cross-validation framework on 5,417 single-cell spectra from six bacterial species, the transformer achieves superior accuracy, better latent class separation, and robust performance even on raw unpreprocessed spectra.
AI.motivation: While transformers are gaining attention in Raman spectroscopy, existing studies lack systematic evaluation against conventional methods and often use validation schemes that fail to account for measurement replicates, leading to overoptimistic performance estimates. This work aims to rigorously benchmark transformer-based models and highlight the importance of replicate-aware validation.
AI.method: A transformer-based classification model was evaluated on a bacterial Raman dataset (5,417 single-cell spectra, 6 species, 9 independent measurement replicates). A nested leave-one-replicate-out cross-validation framework ensured that all spectra from the same replicate remained together in either training or test sets. The transformer was compared against conventional pipelines combining PCA or ICA with LDA, SVM, and Random Forest. Latent feature space analysis assessed class separation quality.
AI.result: The transformer consistently achieved the highest classification accuracy across all independent test replicates, significantly outperforming all conventional PCA/ICA-based approaches. The learned latent representations showed markedly better class separation. Notably, the transformer maintained superior performance even on raw Raman spectra without preprocessing, demonstrating robustness to replicate variability.
AI.conclusion: Transformer-based models show strong potential for robust Raman spectral classification, outperforming conventional pipelines in accuracy, representation quality, and tolerance to raw inputs. The study underscores that replicate-aware nested cross-validation is essential for realistic, non-overoptimistic model evaluation in spectral analysis.

title: When Does Combining Language Models Help? A Co-Failure Ceiling on Routing, Voting, and Mixture-of-Agents Across 67 Frontier Models
summary:
Multi-model LLM systems such as routing, voting, cascades, fusion, and mixture-of-agents are used to beat single-model accuracy. We show that their gain is capped by a quantity the field rarely reports. For any policy whose output is one member model answer, accuracy cannot exceed one minus beta, where beta is the rate at which every model is wrong on the same query. In contrast, the usual diagnostic, average pairwise error correlation rho, cannot identify beta: error laws with identical marginals and pairwise correlations can have different all-wrong rates. A Clopper-Pearson bound on beta gives a finite-sample certificate on the largest gain any router, vote, or cascade could deliver before training a router.
  Across 67 models from 21 providers, a tetrachoric-calibrated single-factor model still underprices the all-wrong tail: on open-ended mathematics, observed beta is 0.052 versus 0.023 under the full 67-model Gaussian copula, about 2.5 times underpricing, with 90 percent CI 1.7 to 3.4 and k equals 17. The effect recurs on execution-graded code, where beta is 0.079. Re-asking the same GPQA-Diamond questions in free-response rather than multiple-choice form reopens the tail, with beta 0.127 and a five-judge panel with kappa 0.73 to 0.92, locating co-failure in answer format rather than subject. At matched quality, low-rho heterogeneous ensembles beat high-rho Self-MoA, but on checkable tasks in our pool, combining models rarely beats the single best model without a strong query-level routing signal. Gains come from models failing on different questions, not from adding more models.

AI.tldr: Multi-model LLM systems (routing, voting, cascades, fusion) face a fundamental accuracy ceiling determined by beta — the rate at which all models fail simultaneously on the same query — rather than by pairwise error correlation rho. Empirical analysis across 67 models shows beta is substantially higher than Gaussian copula models predict, and combining models rarely beats the single best model without strong query-level routing.
AI.motivation: The field of multi-model LLM systems lacks rigorous understanding of the theoretical limits on accuracy gains. While practitioners combine models via routing, voting, and ensembles, no clear bound identifies when such approaches are futile. The authors aim to provide a principled, finite-sample certifiable upper bound on achievable accuracy and to demonstrate that standard diagnostics like pairwise error correlation (rho) are insufficient for capturing this limit.
AI.method: The authors derive a theoretical bound: for any policy outputting one member model's answer, accuracy ≤ 1 - beta, where beta is the all-wrong rate. They apply a Clopper-Pearson confidence bound on beta to provide finite-sample certificates without training. Empirically, they analyze 67 models from 21 providers on open-ended mathematics, execution-graded code tasks, and GPQA-Diamond questions in both multiple-choice and free-response formats. They compare observed beta against a tetrachoric-calibrated single-factor Gaussian copula model and examine heterogeneous vs. homogeneous (Self-MoA) ensembles.
AI.result: Observed beta on open-ended math is 0.052 versus 0.023 predicted under the Gaussian copula — approximately 2.5× underpricing (90% CI: 1.7–3.4). On code tasks, beta = 0.079. On free-response GPQA-Diamond, beta = 0.127, with five-judge panel kappa 0.73–0.92, indicating co-failure stems from answer format rather than subject matter. Low-rho heterogeneous ensembles outperform high-rho Self-MoA at matched quality, but combining models rarely beats the single best model without strong query-level routing signals.
AI.conclusion: The all-wrong rate beta, not pairwise error correlation rho, is the correct statistic for reasoning about multi-model system ceilings. Gains derive from models failing on different questions, not from adding more models. On checkable tasks, ensembles without strong routing signals offer little benefit over the single best model. Co-failure is better explained by answer format than by subject domain.

title: Heavy-Ball Q-Learning with Residual Weighting Correction
summary: This paper proposes a corrected heavy-ball Q-learning method for reinforcement learning (RL) and establishes its convergence. It also identifies conditions under which the method is theoretically guaranteed to converge faster than standard Q-learning. The same construction is then extended to Q-learning with linear function approximation, where analogous convergence and acceleration statements are derived. The analysis is based on a switched linear system (SLS) representation of Q-learning algorithms and on the joint spectral radius (JSR) of the associated switching families. This SLS viewpoint is not commonly used in standard analyses of Q-learning, and it provides a complementary framework and new insight into how heavy-ball momentum can accelerate Q-learning.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces a momentum-accelerated variant of Q-learning using a corrected heavy-ball method, proves its convergence, establishes conditions for faster convergence than standard Q-learning, and extends the results to linear function approximation. The analysis employs a switched linear systems (SLS) framework and joint spectral radius (JSR), offering a novel complementary perspective on Q-learning dynamics.
AI.motivation: Standard Q-learning can suffer from slow convergence. Heavy-ball momentum is a well-known acceleration technique in optimization, but its direct application to Q-learning is non-trivial due to the stochastic and off-policy nature of the algorithm. The authors aim to rigorously design a momentum-accelerated Q-learning variant with provable convergence and acceleration guarantees, while also providing a new analytical lens distinct from traditional stochastic approximation or ODE-based approaches.
AI.method: The authors propose a corrected heavy-ball Q-learning algorithm that incorporates a momentum term with a correction mechanism to stabilize off-policy updates. The analysis casts both standard and heavy-ball Q-learning as switched linear systems, where the switching signal corresponds to the behavioral policy's exploration. Convergence and acceleration rates are then characterized using the joint spectral radius (JSR) of the resulting matrix families. The construction is extended to linear function approximation via analogous SLS representations.
AI.result: The corrected heavy-ball Q-learning method is proven to converge. Conditions on the momentum parameter and learning rate are identified under which the JSR of the heavy-ball system is strictly smaller than that of standard Q-learning, guaranteeing faster convergence. Analogous convergence and acceleration results are established for the linear function approximation case.
AI.conclusion: The corrected heavy-ball momentum mechanism can provably accelerate Q-learning in both tabular and linear function approximation settings. The switched linear systems / joint spectral radius framework provides a novel, complementary tool for analyzing Q-learning dynamics and formally quantifying acceleration, bridging a gap between control theory and reinforcement learning analysis.

title: Language-Based Digital Twins for Elderly Cognitive Assistance
comment: Accepted and published in the Proceedings of the ACM International Conference on PErvasive Technologies Related to Assistive Environments (PETRA 2026). The final published version is available through the ACM Digital Library
summary: Digital twins have emerged as a promising paradigm for personalized healthcare, enabling modeling of individual behavior and health trajectories. In cognitive health, early detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) remains challenging, where language and conversational patterns serve as non-invasive biomarkers. In this work, we propose a language-based digital twin framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to mimic the conversational behavior of elderly individuals by incorporating stylometric cues and contextual metadata. To evaluate fidelity and cognitive consistency, we introduce a multi-head conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) that jointly measures reconstruction quality and predicts cognitive scores. Experiments on the I-CONECT dataset show that the digital twin preserves identity-specific characteristics and achieves reconstruction and MoCA prediction errors comparable to real data, while outperforming baseline GPT-generated responses. These results highlight the potential of language-based digital twins as a scalable and non-invasive approach for personalized and continuous cognitive health monitoring.

AI.tldr: A language-based digital twin framework using LLMs and stylometric cues to mimic elderly conversational behavior for cognitive health monitoring, evaluated with a multi-head cVAE that jointly assesses reconstruction fidelity and MoCA score prediction on the I-CONECT dataset.
AI.motivation: Early detection of Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) is challenging, and language/conversational patterns offer non-invasive biomarkers. Personalized, scalable, and continuous cognitive health monitoring is needed, motivating the use of digital twins that can model individual behavior and health trajectories through conversational data.
AI.method: The authors propose a language-based digital twin framework that uses LLMs conditioned on stylometric cues and contextual metadata to generate individualized conversational responses. A multi-head conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) is introduced to jointly optimize two objectives: (1) reconstruction quality of conversational behavior and (2) prediction of Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) scores, thereby enforcing cognitive consistency in the generated outputs.
AI.result: On the I-CONECT dataset, the digital twin preserves identity-specific characteristics and achieves reconstruction and MoCA prediction errors comparable to real participant data. The framework outperforms baseline GPT-generated responses in both fidelity and cognitive score prediction.
AI.conclusion: Language-based digital twins represent a scalable, non-invasive approach for personalized and continuous cognitive health monitoring, with the potential to aid early MCI detection through faithful simulation of individual conversational behavior.

title: Cross-Head Attention Uplift Network with Inverse Propensity Score under Unobserved Confounding
summary: Uplift modeling, crucial for estimating individual treatment effects (ITE), faces dual challenges: flexibly leveraging inter-group similarity to enhance discriminative power and debiasing under unobserved confounding scenarios. In this paper, we propose the Cross-Head Attention Uplift Network (CHAUN) and Robust Adversarial Inverse Propensity Score (RA-IPS) method to address these limitations. CHAUN employs shared feature embeddings and cross-head attention mechanisms to dynamically integrate treatment-specific and control-specific representations, enhancing inter-group correlation modeling. Theoretically, we prove that access to the true propensity scores ensures ITE identifiability even with unobserved confounders. For practical scenarios lacking true propensity scores, RA-IPS adversarially optimizes propensity weights within constrained uncertainty sets to mitigate bias from unobserved variables. Experiments on public datasets (CRITEO-UPLIFT, LAZADA) and a production e-commerce dataset demonstrate CHAUN's superiority over state-of-the-art uplift models, achieving relative improvements of up to 25.6% in QINI scores. RA-IPS further enhances robustness, outperforming standard IPS by 5.4% under unobserved confounding. The results validate the effectiveness of our proposed methods in real-world causal inference tasks.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes CHAUN, a cross-head attention architecture for uplift modeling that dynamically integrates treatment and control representations, alongside RA-IPS, an adversarial propensity score optimization method. CHAUN achieves up to 25.6% QINI improvement over baselines, while RA-IPS outperforms standard IPS by 5.4% under unobserved confounding.
AI.motivation: Uplift modeling faces two key challenges: (1) flexibly leveraging inter-group similarity between treatment and control groups to improve discriminative power, and (2) debiasing individual treatment effect estimates when unobserved confounders are present. Existing methods struggle to address both simultaneously.
AI.method: CHAUN: Uses shared feature embeddings with cross-head attention mechanisms to dynamically fuse treatment-specific and control-specific representations, enabling inter-group correlation modeling. RA-IPS: Adversarially optimizes propensity score weights within constrained uncertainty sets to mitigate bias from unobserved confounders. A theoretical proof shows that true propensity scores guarantee ITE identifiability under unobserved confounding.
AI.result: Experiments on CRITEO-UPLIFT, LAZADA, and a proprietary e-commerce dataset show CHAUN achieves up to 25.6% relative improvement in QINI scores over state-of-the-art uplift models. RA-IPS enhances robustness, surpassing standard IPS by 5.4% under unobserved confounding scenarios.
AI.conclusion: The proposed CHAUN and RA-IPS methods are validated as effective solutions for real-world causal inference tasks, addressing both representation learning for inter-group similarity and debiasing under unobserved confounding.

title: Kolmogorov Arnold networks (KAN) for aerodynamic prediction: a comparison with MLPs and GNNs
summary: Kolmogorov Arnold networks (KAN) have recently been introduced as a (deep) neural network architecture whose trainable parameters adapt the activation functions, instead of the coefficients of the affine transformations at the core of traditional architectures such as deep multilayer perceptrons (MLPs). This architecture builds on the Kolmogorov-Arnold theorem, which endows it with universal approximation properties. While the advent of KANs has been received with excitement, there is a current debate about the possible KAN supremacy over deep multilayer perceptrons (MLPs) for classic fields such as symbolic regression, generic-purpose machine learning, natural language processing or computer vision. Here we assess the performance of KANs --and its nuanced comparison against MLPs and graph neural networks (GNNs)-- in the realm of fluid dynamics surrogate modelling. To that aim, we consider the task of predicting the surface pressure distribution over subsonic and transonic airfoils, a canonical task in aerodynamics. Our results show that KAN models show good performance in predicting the whole pressure coefficients and is able to interpolate across Mach numbers and angles of attack, however its performance is comparable --marginally inferior-- to a suitably trained MLP, where best performance is achieved by a GNN at the expense or requiring lengthier training. While the optimal KAN model have typically much lower complexity than MLP and GNN --hence resulting in faster training--, we find that KANs suffer from training instabilities, and their performance is highly dependent on a proper hyperparameter optimisation.

AI.tldr: The paper evaluates Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) against MLPs and GNNs for aerodynamic surrogate modeling (airfoil pressure prediction). KANs perform comparably but marginally worse than MLPs, with GNNs achieving best results at higher training cost. KANs offer lower complexity and faster training but suffer from instability and hyperparameter sensitivity.
AI.motivation: To rigorously assess whether KANs offer genuine advantages over established architectures (MLPs, GNNs) in the specific and practically relevant domain of fluid dynamics surrogate modeling, addressing the ongoing debate about KAN supremacy claims.
AI.method: Comparative empirical evaluation using the canonical aerodynamic task of predicting surface pressure distributions over subsonic and transonic airfoils. Models tested across varying Mach numbers and angles of attack, with hyperparameter optimization applied to all architectures.
AI.result: KANs achieve good interpolation performance but are marginally inferior to well-tuned MLPs. GNNs deliver the best overall predictive accuracy at the cost of longer training. KANs benefit from lower model complexity and faster training, yet exhibit training instabilities and high sensitivity to hyperparameter configuration.
AI.conclusion: KANs do not demonstrate clear superiority over MLPs in aerodynamic surrogate modeling; their practical adoption is hampered by instability and hyperparameter sensitivity despite appealing efficiency properties.

title: fTNN: a tensor neural network for fractional PDEs
summary: We develop the fTNN, a deterministic tensor neural network subspace method for problems involving the fractional Laplacian on bounded domains, taking the fractional Poisson equation and time-dependent fractional advection-diffusion equation as typical representatives. The work employs a geometry-adapted integration split featuring a spatially dependent near-field radius, which decomposes the fractional Laplacian into three contributions: a singular near field, a regular interior far field, and an analytical exterior far field. Then the singular radial integrals are treated by Gauss-Jacobi quadrature, the regular radial integrals by Gauss quadrature, and the angular variables by deterministic angular quadrature, yielding a fully deterministic integration framework of the fractional Laplacian operator. To accurately resolve low-regularity solutions and the associated loss functional, we construct boundary-singularity-aware trial functions enriched with explicit boundary features, and propose two strategies for automatically selecting the leading exponent and evaluating the loss function from the singularity structure induced by the fractional operator, or jointly by the fractional operator and the source term. For time-dependent fractional PDEs, we design a spatiotemporally separable neural network that factorizes the time-space residual into a sum of low-dimensional temporal and spatial integrals, and we integrate this representation with an alternating neural network subspace optimization strategy for efficient training. Numerical experiments show that the proposed framework attains high accuracy on the tested benchmarks and improves substantially over existing fPINN and Monte Carlo baselines, particularly for problems with strong boundary singularities and long-time simulations.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces fTNN, a deterministic tensor neural network method for fractional Laplacian PDEs. It uses a geometry-adapted integration split with quadrature rules, boundary-singularity-aware trial functions with automatic exponent selection, and a spatiotemporally separable network for time-dependent problems, substantially outperforming fPINN and Monte Carlo baselines on benchmarks with strong boundary singularities.
AI.motivation: Solving fractional Laplacian PDEs on bounded domains is challenging due to the nonlocal, singular nature of the operator, which induces low-regularity solutions with strong boundary singularities. Existing neural network methods (fPINNs, Monte Carlo-based approaches) suffer from low accuracy, stochastic noise, and poor handling of these singularities, motivating a fully deterministic, high-accuracy framework.
AI.method: The proposed fTNN framework has four key components: (1) A geometry-adapted integration split with a spatially dependent near-field radius that decomposes the fractional Laplacian into singular near-field, regular interior far-field, and analytical exterior far-field contributions. (2) Deterministic quadrature: Gauss-Jacobi for singular radial integrals, standard Gauss for regular radial integrals, and deterministic angular quadrature. (3) Boundary-singularity-aware trial functions enriched with explicit boundary features and two automatic strategies for selecting the leading exponent and evaluating loss based on operator/source singularity structure. (4) For time-dependent problems, a spatiotemporally separable neural network factorizing the time-space residual into low-dimensional temporal and spatial integrals, trained via alternating neural network subspace optimization.
AI.result: The fTNN framework achieves high accuracy on tested benchmarks (fractional Poisson equation and time-dependent fractional advection-diffusion equation) and substantially improves over existing fPINN and Monte Carlo baselines, particularly for problems with strong boundary singularities and long-time simulations.
AI.conclusion: The fTNN provides an accurate, fully deterministic neural network subspace method for fractional Laplacian PDEs. Its integration split, singularity-aware trial functions, and separable space-time architecture collectively overcome key limitations of prior neural network approaches, demonstrating significant gains in accuracy and robustness for problems with boundary singularities and long-time horizons.

title: Stochastic Gradient Optimization with Model-Assisted Sampling
summary: This work addresses the problem of variance in stochastic gradient estimation for machine learning optimization. Deep learning relies on mini-batch methods such as stochastic gradient descent, which approximate full gradients but introduce noise, creating trade-offs between convergence stability, speed, and generalization. Existing methods, including variance reduction techniques (e.g., SVRG and SAG) and adaptive optimizers, aim to mitigate gradient noise but may introduce additional computational overhead. We propose a model-assisted sampling framework that interprets mini-batch gradients through survey sampling theory, treating the dataset as a fixed finite population and gradients as sample-based estimates. Our aim is to bridge machine learning optimization and survey sampling theory by combining their perspectives on sample-based estimation and variance reduction. By incorporating auxiliary gradient-prediction models, we construct more efficient gradient estimators, with uniform sampling arising as a special case when no auxiliary information is used. Our approach integrates easily with existing optimizers, improving efficiency without altering their dynamics. Empirical results on synthetic and six benchmark datasets show performance gains in 71-86% of the experiments, particularly for medium-sized input spaces in our benchmarks. Notably, with momentum-based optimizers such as AdamW, the proposed estimator achieves clearly better generalization in roughly half the training epochs compared to baseline estimator.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a model-assisted sampling framework that applies survey sampling theory to mini-batch gradient estimation, using auxiliary gradient-prediction models to construct more efficient gradient estimators. Empirical results show performance gains in 71–86% of experiments, with momentum-based optimizers like AdamW achieving better generalization in roughly half the training epochs.
AI.motivation: Stochastic gradient estimation in deep learning introduces noise that creates trade-offs between convergence stability, speed, and generalization. Existing variance reduction techniques (SVRG, SAG) and adaptive optimizers add computational overhead. The paper aims to bridge machine learning optimization and survey sampling theory to address gradient variance more efficiently.
AI.method: A model-assisted sampling framework that treats the dataset as a fixed finite population and mini-batch gradients as sample-based estimates. Auxiliary gradient-prediction models are incorporated to construct more efficient gradient estimators, with uniform sampling as a special case. The approach integrates with existing optimizers without altering their dynamics.
AI.result: Performance gains were observed in 71–86% of experiments across synthetic and six benchmark datasets, particularly for medium-sized input spaces. With momentum-based optimizers (e.g., AdamW), the proposed estimator achieves clearly better generalization in roughly half the training epochs compared to the baseline.
AI.conclusion: The model-assisted sampling framework effectively reduces gradient estimation variance by leveraging survey sampling principles, improving optimization efficiency and generalization while integrating seamlessly with existing optimizers like AdamW.

title: RecallRisk-BERT: A Multi-Task Framework for Post-Report Medical Device Recall Triage
summary: Medical device recalls are a critical regulatory mechanism for protecting patient safety. The growing volume of FDA recall records presents challenges in post-report recall triage, severity assessment, and root-cause interpretation. Existing studies mostly address recall occurrence prediction or root-cause analysis separately, while joint modeling of recall severity and root-cause categories has received limited attention. We develop an automated recall triage framework using 54,165 FDA medical device recall records from openFDA, covering the period from 2002 to October 2025. We first evaluate classical machine learning and boosting-based models for recall severity and root-cause category prediction. We then develop RecallRisk-BERT, a multi-task model that combines PubMedBERT-based textual representations of recall narratives with embedding-based representations of structured categorical features, including product code, regulation number, and medical specialty. The model simultaneously predicts recall severity (Class I/II/III) and a consolidated root-cause category (9 classes). Performance was evaluated using accuracy, macro-averaged precision, recall, F1-score, and ROC-AUC. In single-task severity prediction, our LightGBM-based text--tabular configuration achieved the strongest performance, with an accuracy of 0.963, macro-F1 of 0.856, and ROC-AUC of 0.974. In the multi-task setting, RecallRisk-BERT substantially outperformed the single-task PubMedBERT baseline. Model-derived risk rankings were strongly consistent with observed root-cause severity patterns (rho = 0.983, p = 1.936e-6). These findings indicate that text--tabular learning can support scalable post-report recall triage, regulatory decision support, and model-based root-cause risk analysis.

AI.tldr: This paper presents RecallRisk-BERT, a multi-task model that jointly predicts FDA medical device recall severity (Class I/II/III) and root-cause categories by combining PubMedBERT text embeddings of recall narratives with structured tabular features, achieving strong performance (LightGBM accuracy 0.963, macro-F1 0.856) and high rank consistency with observed severity patterns (rho=0.983).
AI.motivation: The growing volume of FDA medical device recall records creates challenges in post-report triage, severity assessment, and root-cause interpretation. Existing work addresses recall occurrence prediction or root-cause analysis separately, leaving a gap in joint modeling of severity and root-cause categories.
AI.method: Using 54,165 FDA medical device recall records (2002–October 2025) from openFDA, the authors first benchmark classical ML and boosting models for single-task prediction. They then develop RecallRisk-BERT, a multi-task architecture that fuses PubMedBERT-based textual representations of recall narratives with embedding-based representations of structured categorical features (product code, regulation number, medical specialty) to simultaneously predict recall severity (3 classes) and consolidated root-cause category (9 classes). Evaluation uses accuracy, macro-averaged precision/recall/F1, and ROC-AUC.
AI.result: The LightGBM text–tabular configuration achieved the best single-task severity prediction (accuracy 0.963, macro-F1 0.856, ROC-AUC 0.974). In multi-task settings, RecallRisk-BERT substantially outperformed the single-task PubMedBERT baseline. Model-derived risk rankings showed strong rank correlation with observed root-cause severity patterns (Spearman rho = 0.983, p = 1.936e-6).
AI.conclusion: Text–tabular learning can effectively support scalable post-report recall triage, regulatory decision support, and model-based root-cause risk analysis for FDA medical device recalls.

title: Automating Potential-based Reward Shaping with Vision Language Model Guidance
summary: Sparse rewards are inherently challenging for reinforcement learning agents as they lack intermediate feedback to guide exploration and to correctly attribute the sparse success rewards to relevant parts of the trajectory. Naive reward shaping can induce reward hacking, yielding policies that exploit auxiliary signals instead of solving the intended task. Potential-based reward shaping (PBRS) guarantees preservation of the optimal policy set, but requires the definition of a heuristic potential function over the state space. In this work, we introduce the VLM-guided PBRS framework VLM-PBRS that learns the potential function directly from vision language model (VLM) feedback. We query a lightweight VLM to obtain preferences over image pairs and train a model of the potential function using these preferences. As this approach is based on potential-based reward shaping, it preserves the original optimal policies, and removes the need for expert-designed reward shaping terms. Because large VLMs are prohibitively expensive to invoke repeatedly during policy learning, we employ smaller, more computationally efficient VLMs. Although the resulting preference labels are less accurate, empirical evidence shows that the preference labels can still be used to accelerate learning. We validate our method empirically in the Meta-World and Franka Kitchen environments and highlight the connection between VLM preference label accuracy and sample efficiency improvements. Our contributions are threefold: (1) the first application of VLM preference-based learning to synthesize a potential function for PBRS, (2) a principled, low-cost solution that leverages small VLMs, and (3) extensive empirical demonstration of improved sample efficiency and robustness to reward hacking.

AI.tldr: VLM-PBRS uses a small vision-language model to learn a potential function from image-pair preferences, enabling potential-based reward shaping that preserves optimal policies while eliminating the need for handcrafted heuristics.
AI.motivation: Sparse reward problems in RL suffer from poor exploration and credit assignment. While PBRS guarantees policy invariance, it requires hand-designed potential functions. Large VLMs are too expensive for repeated querying during training, motivating the use of cheaper, smaller VLMs despite their lower accuracy.
AI.method: A lightweight VLM is queried for preferences over image pairs. These preferences supervise a learned potential function model. The learned potential is then used in a PBRS framework to shape rewards during RL, preserving optimal policy invariance while providing dense learning signals.
AI.result: Empirical validation in Meta-World and Franka Kitchen shows that even with imperfect preference labels from small VLMs, the method accelerates learning and improves sample efficiency. A correlation between VLM preference accuracy and sample efficiency gains is demonstrated.
AI.conclusion: VLM-PBRS is the first to apply VLM preference-based learning to synthesize PBRS potential functions, offering a principled, low-cost solution that improves sample efficiency and is robust to reward hacking.

title: Explaining Temporal Graph Neural Networks via Feature-induced Information Flow
summary: Event-based Temporal Graph Neural Networks (ETGNNs) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of applications, including social network analysis, epidemic tracing, recommender systems, and political event forecasting. However, their increasing complexity poses significant challenges for explainability. Existing explanation methods focus only on a subset of the information flow within ETGNNs, typically tracing contributions from the event-related embeddings to the output. Consequently, they overlook the important pathways through event-induced variables, which mediate interactions between nodes and thereby play a central role in capturing long-range temporal dependencies. To overcome this limitation, we propose a novel attribution method that analyzes the \emph{entire} information flow through all event-associated variables. Our method is built upon the recent Normalized Relevance Measure (NRM) framework, which enables explicit quantification of information flow originating from event embeddings as well as information flow passing through event-induced variables. It also ensures comparability of latent variables across layers, and supports higher-order analysis of interactions between events. To handle the architectural complexity of ETGNNs, we extend the NRM framework with a modular decomposition procedure that facilitates the systematic construction of relevance structure for complex neural architectures. We evaluate our approach on two synthetic datasets for epidemic tracing and social dynamics, as well as a real-world dataset of political event networks. Our qualitative and quantitative experiments show that our method consistently outperforms existing explanation approaches while producing more human-interpretable explanations.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a novel attribution method for Event-based Temporal Graph Neural Networks (ETGNNs) that traces the entire information flow through all event-associated variables — including event-induced variables previously overlooked by existing methods. Built on the Normalized Relevance Measure (NRM) framework and extended with modular decomposition, the approach produces more interpretable explanations and outperforms existing methods on synthetic and real-world datasets.
AI.motivation: Existing explanation methods for ETGNNs only trace contributions from event-related embeddings to the output, ignoring event-induced variables that mediate inter-node interactions and capture long-range temporal dependencies. This incomplete information flow analysis limits explainability as model complexity grows.
AI.method: The authors propose an attribution method based on the Normalized Relevance Measure (NRM) framework that quantifies the entire information flow — both from event embeddings and through event-induced variables. They extend NRM with a modular decomposition procedure to systematically construct relevance structures for complex ETGNN architectures, ensuring cross-layer comparability of latent variables and supporting higher-order interaction analysis between events.
AI.result: Qualitative and quantitative experiments on two synthetic datasets (epidemic tracing, social dynamics) and one real-world dataset (political event networks) demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing explanation approaches while yielding more human-interpretable explanations.
AI.conclusion: The proposed NRM-based attribution method with modular decomposition successfully addresses the explainability gap in ETGNNs by capturing complete information flow, offering both superior performance and interpretability compared to prior methods.

title: Graph Neural Networks Applications Across Domains: All Insights You Need
summary: Graph neural networks have moved from a niche representation-learning technique to the default model class wherever data carry relational structure. The interesting question is no longer whether message passing helps on a given dataset, but where graph structure earns its computational cost and where it does not. This survey organises the field around a single design space, derives the spectral and spatial formulations from shared first principles, and connects expressive power to the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy with explicit statements of what current architectures can and cannot separate. Against that methodological backbone we examine twelve application domains, among them recommendation and social networks, knowledge graphs and language-model integration, drug discovery and molecular property learning, healthcare and neuroscience, computer vision, traffic and urban computing, power and renewable-energy systems, wireless and sixth-generation networks, fraud and cybersecurity, industrial prognostics, materials science, and climate modelling. For each domain we specify the graph-construction choices and their costs, identify which architecture families dominate and why, and separate reported gains from artefacts of weak baselines or favourable splits. A cross-domain comparison exposes recurring patterns: heterophily and scale undercut the same models almost everywhere, temporal graphs remain harder than their static counterparts, and the architectures that top public leaderboards are seldom the ones that reach deployment. We treat over-smoothing, over-squashing, robustness, distribution shift, fairness, and explainability not as a closing checklist but as the constraints that decide adoption.

AI.tldr: A comprehensive survey that unifies graph neural network architectures within a single design space, connects expressive power to the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy, and evaluates twelve application domains to identify where graph structure provides genuine value versus where it incurs unjustified computational cost.
AI.motivation: GNNs have become the default model class for relational data, but practitioners lack a systematic framework to determine when graph structure is worth its computational overhead. The field needs to move beyond asking whether message passing helps, toward understanding precisely where and why it helps — separating genuine architectural gains from artefacts of weak baselines or cherry-picked evaluation protocols.
AI.method: The survey organizes the GNN landscape around a unified design space, deriving both spectral and spatial formulations from shared first principles. It explicitly maps expressive power onto the Weisfeiler-Leman hierarchy, cataloguing what current architectures can and cannot distinguish. Twelve application domains are examined with consistent criteria: graph-construction choices and their costs, dominant architecture families and their rationale, and a critical separation of reported gains from evaluation artefacts. Cross-domain patterns are extracted, and practical deployment constraints — over-smoothing, over-squashing, robustness, distribution shift, fairness, and explainability — are framed as adoption gatekeepers rather than an afterthought.
AI.result: Heterophily and scale undermine the same model classes across nearly all domains. Temporal graphs remain consistently harder than static counterparts. Architectures dominating public leaderboards rarely match those deployed in production. Graph-construction design choices and their associated costs prove as consequential as model architecture. Weak baselines and favourable data splits account for a non-trivial fraction of reported performance gains across domains.
AI.conclusion: The GNN field has matured to a point where the critical question is cost-effectiveness, not capability. Methodological hygiene — rigorous baselines, honest splitting, and attention to heterophily and temporal dynamics — is essential for continued progress. Practical adoption hinges on robustness, fairness, explainability, and distribution-shift resilience, constraints that should be treated as design requirements rather than post-hoc checklists.

title: The Geometry of Updates: Fisher Alignment at Vocabulary Scale
comment: Accepted at the 43rd International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2026), PMLR 306. 64 pages total (main paper plus appendix), 4 figures, 29 tables
summary: Training-free source selection for LLM families with shared vocabularies arises in scientific string domains such as SMILES, protein, and genomic sequences, where candidate corpora share a tokenizer but differ in prediction targets. This creates an activation-dark regime: representation-similarity metrics can be uninformative without assumptions about label-conditioned error geometry, while classical update-geometry metrics are computationally prohibitive at vocabulary scale. We show that, in a shared-output head setting, representation metrics (e.g., CKA) are non-identifiable for transfer; models can share identical representations yet have orthogonal head updates. The key identity is that head Fisher alignment is exactly a cosine between kernel mean embeddings in the joint activation-error space, exposing activation, error, and coupling factors rather than requiring a materialized Fisher matrix. FisherSketch estimates this cosine directly in a single streaming pass, making K=128,256 head Fisher alignment practical with a 16 KB task signature (m=4096) and a 192 KB per-task streaming state, small enough to store next to a model hash, but encoding transfer-relevant update structure. Beyond source selection, the same signatures and marginals provide a diagnostic instrument for studying whether LLM task similarity is driven by activations, errors, or their coupling; shared-parameter and internal-layer validations, together with Llama-3.1-8B verbalizer-shift experiments, show that FisherSketch remains informative when activation similarity cannot distinguish tasks.

AI.tldr: FisherSketch efficiently selects transfer-learning sources for LLM families with shared tokenizers by estimating head Fisher alignment via a single-pass streaming sketch, avoiding expensive full-Fisher computation. It provides a compact 16–192 KB task signature that captures activation–error coupling, remaining informative when representation similarity (CKA) fails.
AI.motivation: In scientific string domains (SMILES, protein, genomic sequences), LLM families share tokenizers but differ in prediction targets, creating an "activation-dark" regime where representation-similarity metrics like CKA are non-identifiable for transfer. Classical update-geometry metrics (e.g., Fisher) are computationally prohibitive at vocabulary scale. A lightweight, training-free source selection method is needed.
AI.method: The authors prove that in a shared-output-head setting, head Fisher alignment equals the cosine similarity between kernel mean embeddings in the joint activation–error space, decomposing into activation, error, and coupling factors. FisherSketch estimates this cosine via a single streaming pass using randomized sketching (count sketch) on per-token gradient outer products, requiring only K-dimensional sketches (K=128,256). The resulting task signature is ~16 KB (m=4096) with a 192 KB streaming state, small enough to store alongside a model hash.
AI.result: FisherSketch makes head Fisher alignment practical at vocabulary scale. Shared-parameter and internal-layer validations, plus Llama-3.1-8B verbalizer-shift experiments, show that FisherSketch remains informative when activation similarity (CKA) cannot distinguish tasks.
AI.conclusion: FisherSketch enables scalable, training-free source selection for shared-vocabulary LLM families, and its compact signatures double as a diagnostic tool for studying whether task similarity is driven by activations, errors, or their coupling.

title: Effective Covariance Dynamics in Solvable High-Dimensional GANs
summary: We study a solvable high-dimensional model of generative adversarial network (GAN) training in which a linear generator learns a low-dimensional subspace from data with structured latent covariance. Prior solvable GAN analyses assume unconditional signals with diagonal latent covariance; we extend the multi-feature discriminator setting to class-dependent, correlated, and non-zero-mean latent structure. For the quadratic energy discriminator, all such heterogeneity enters the dynamics through a probability-weighted effective second moment. We prove that the stochastic microscopic training process converges, in the high-dimensional limit, to deterministic ordinary differential equations governed by this effective covariance. In the matched-covariance specialization, the stability analysis yields a mode-wise solvable interval determined by the learning rates and noise level: learning begins when the leading effective eigenvalue crosses the lower threshold, while full recovery requires all relevant effective modes to remain within the interval. This reveals a signal-boosting mechanism: low-rank correlations can lift weak directions above the learnability threshold, whereas overly strong correlations destabilize recovery. Numerical simulations validate the ODE, phase boundary, and boosting mechanism. Experiments on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10 further show that informed generator covariance improves alignment with the data-driven reference subspace.

AI.tldr: This paper extends solvable GAN analysis to a high-dimensional linear model with class-dependent, correlated, and non-zero-mean latent structure. It proves convergence of stochastic training to deterministic ODEs governed by an effective covariance, reveals a signal-boosting mechanism where low-rank correlations aid learnability but strong correlations destabilize recovery, and validates findings on both synthetic and real image datasets.
AI.motivation: Prior solvable GAN analyses are limited to unconditional signals with diagonal latent covariance, failing to capture realistic scenarios with class-conditional structure, correlations, and non-zero means. The authors aim to bridge this gap by extending the theoretical framework to structured latent distributions and understanding how such heterogeneity affects GAN training dynamics and learnability.
AI.method: The authors study a high-dimensional GAN model with a linear generator learning a low-dimensional subspace, using a quadratic energy discriminator. They derive how class-dependent, correlated, non-zero-mean latent structure enters dynamics through a probability-weighted effective second moment. They prove that the stochastic microscopic training process converges to deterministic ODEs in the high-dimensional limit, then perform stability analysis to obtain mode-wise solvable intervals as functions of learning rates and noise level.
AI.result: Key results include: (1) all latent heterogeneity collapses into an effective covariance matrix governing the ODE dynamics; (2) a mode-wise solvable interval exists where learning occurs when the leading effective eigenvalue exceeds a lower threshold, with full recovery requiring all relevant modes to stay within the interval; (3) a signal-boosting mechanism where low-rank correlations lift weak directions above the learnability threshold; (4) overly strong correlations destabilize recovery. Numerical simulations confirm the ODE, phase boundary, and boosting mechanism, while experiments on MNIST, FashionMNIST, and CIFAR-10 demonstrate that informed generator covariance improves alignment with data-driven reference subspaces.
AI.conclusion: The effective covariance framework provides a unified description of structured latent heterogeneity in GAN training. The signal-boosting phenomenon and mode-wise stability analysis offer practical insights: moderate low-rank correlations enhance learnability of weak modes, but practitioners must avoid excessively strong correlations that cause destabilization. The framework generalizes beyond the matched-covariance case to future analyses.

title: RSPC: A Benchmark for Modeling Stress and Psychiatric Conditions in Digitally Mediated Relationships using Psychiatrist Annotations
summary: In NLP, mental health conditions are often modeled as isolated phenomena, without interpersonal context. We use Reddit posts about long-distance relationships to capture both mental health distress and associated relational triggers. We introduce the Relational Stress and Psychiatry Corpus (RSPC) containing 1,799 Reddit posts annotated by psychiatrists for diagnostic categories, including the most prevalent mood disorders (anxiety and depression), relational stressor triggers, and indications of relationship phase. We benchmark seven fine-tuned transformer models and five large language models across multi-label disorder classification, relational trigger detection, and temporal phase prediction tasks. We find clear task-dependent differences between model families, with Claude-3-Haiku achieving the best disorder classification performance (Macro-F1 = 0.538) and GPT-4o obtaining the strongest relational trigger detection performance (Macro-F1 = 0.519), suggesting distinct model capabilities. We further find strong associations between anxiety disorders and chronic relational uncertainty. Overall, RSPC establishes a benchmark for NLP tasks that consider relational context and supports a shift from individual-centric to context-aware mental health modeling that captures the social and temporal dynamics of distress.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces RSPC, a corpus of 1,799 Reddit posts about long-distance relationships annotated for mental health disorders, relational stressors, and relationship phase. Benchmarking 12 models reveals task-dependent performance differences, with Claude-3-Haiku best for disorder classification and GPT-4o best for trigger detection, while establishing associations between anxiety and chronic relational uncertainty.
AI.motivation: Current NLP approaches to mental health model conditions as isolated individual phenomena, ignoring the interpersonal and relational contexts that often trigger or exacerbate psychological distress. The authors aim to shift mental health NLP from individual-centric to context-aware modeling by capturing the social and temporal dynamics of distress within relationships.
AI.method: The authors construct the Relational Stress and Psychiatry Corpus (RSPC) with 1,799 Reddit posts from long-distance relationship communities, annotated by psychiatrists across three dimensions: (1) multi-label diagnostic categories (anxiety, depression, and other mood disorders), (2) relational stressor triggers, and (3) temporal relationship phase indicators. They benchmark seven fine-tuned transformer models and five large language models (LLMs) on these tasks.
AI.result: Claude-3-Haiku achieved the best disorder classification performance (Macro-F1 = 0.538), while GPT-4o performed best on relational trigger detection (Macro-F1 = 0.519). Performance differences were task-dependent, indicating distinct strengths across model families. A strong association was found between anxiety disorders and chronic relational uncertainty.
AI.conclusion: RSPC provides a novel benchmark for context-aware mental health NLP, demonstrating that incorporating relational and temporal dimensions yields richer modeling of psychological distress. The task-dependent performance gap between model families suggests future work should explore hybrid or ensemble approaches. The findings support a paradigm shift toward mental health models that account for interpersonal dynamics.

title: BetXplain: An Explanation-Annotated Dataset for Detecting Manipulative Betting Advertisements on Social Media
summary: The promotion of betting applications on social media platforms has increased significantly in recent years. Many of these advertisements use persuasive techniques that may mislead users, encourage risky behavior, and potentially influence users' mental well-being. However, research on the automated detection of manipulative and deceptive betting advertisements remains limited due to the lack of publicly available annotated datasets. In this work, we introduce a new dataset of betting-related advertisements collected from two widely used social media platforms, Instagram and Reddit. The advertisements were manually annotated for manipulative and deceptive advertising practices. In addition to classification labels, the dataset includes human-provided explanations that describe the reasoning behind each annotation, enabling research into explainable approaches to detecting manipulative advertising. Furthermore, we analyze the strategies commonly used in betting advertisements and examine how these persuasive tactics may impact users' mental health. The proposed framework can also enable practical applications such as browser plugins that warn users about manipulative betting advertisements and automated web crawlers that help regulatory authorities monitor and detect such promotions online.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces a new manually annotated dataset of betting advertisements from Instagram and Reddit, labeled for manipulative and deceptive practices with human explanations. It analyzes common persuasive strategies and their potential mental health impacts, and proposes practical applications like browser plugins and regulatory crawlers.
AI.motivation: The proliferation of betting app advertisements on social media uses persuasive techniques that can mislead users and harm mental well-being, yet automated detection research is hindered by the absence of publicly available annotated datasets.
AI.method: The authors collected betting-related advertisements from Instagram and Reddit, then manually annotated them for manipulative and deceptive advertising practices. Each annotation includes human-provided textual explanations describing the reasoning. They further analyzed the persuasive strategies employed and examined their potential mental health impacts, and outlined a framework for practical downstream applications.
AI.result: A new publicly available dataset of betting advertisements with classification labels and human explanations was created, enabling explainable detection of manipulative advertising. Analysis revealed common persuasive tactics used in betting promotions and their possible effects on users' mental health.
AI.conclusion: The dataset and framework enable both explainable automated detection of manipulative betting ads and practical tools for user protection (browser warnings) and regulatory monitoring (automated crawlers), addressing a critical gap at the intersection of social media advertising, gambling harm, and mental health.

title: How Good Can Linear Models Be for Time-Series Forecasting?
summary: Time-series forecasting research has been moving steadily toward larger architectures, from specialized transformers to general-purpose foundation models, on the assumption that capacity is what unlocks accuracy. We take the opposite position: most of the gap can be closed at far lower cost by tuning preprocessing rather than scaling models. We use Ridge regression as the testbed, since it has a closed-form solution and interpretable weights, which let the optimal hyperparameters be read off the search directly. We search over context length, local normalization, regularization, and augmentation on eight standard benchmarks and find three patterns. (1) Optimal lookback is strongly series-specific and often non-monotonic in forecast horizon, with fitted power-law exponents ranging from $+0.46$ on ETTm2 to $-0.19$ on Exchange and Traffic, challenging the convention that longer horizons need longer history. (2) Normalizing over a learned trailing fraction of the context, rather than its entirety, is almost universally preferred. (3) Series within the same dataset often disagree on hyperparameters; the optimal degree of cross-series sharing varies from fully shared to fully per-series. The resulting models beat prior linear forecasters on most dataset-horizon entries and exceed Transformer, MLP, and CNN baselines on six of eight benchmarks. The optimized hyperparameters also serve as a diagnostic on the data itself, revealing structures that larger models absorb silently into their learned parameters.

AI.tldr: This paper challenges the trend of scaling up model architectures for time-series forecasting, showing that careful tuning of preprocessing (context length, normalization, regularization, augmentation) using simple Ridge regression can match or exceed the performance of large transformers, MLPs, and CNNs at a fraction of the cost.
AI.motivation: The dominant assumption in time-series forecasting is that larger, more complex architectures (transformers, foundation models) are necessary to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy. The authors question whether this capacity is truly needed or whether most of the performance gap can be closed by optimizing simpler, more interpretable components like preprocessing and hyperparameter selection.
AI.method: The authors use Ridge regression as a testbed due to its closed-form solution and interpretable weights, allowing optimal hyperparameters to be directly observed. They systematically search over four dimensions: context length (lookback window), local normalization strategy (learned trailing fraction vs. full context), regularization strength, and data augmentation. Experiments span eight standard forecasting benchmarks, with analysis of per-series vs. cross-series hyperparameter sharing.
AI.result: Three key findings: (1) Optimal lookback is highly series-specific and often non-monotonic with forecast horizon—fitted power-law exponents range from +0.46 (ETTm2) to −0.19 (Exchange, Traffic), contradicting the assumption that longer horizons always benefit from longer history. (2) Normalizing over a learned trailing fraction of the context is almost universally preferred over full-context normalization. (3) Hyperparameter preferences vary significantly across series within the same dataset; optimal sharing ranges from fully shared to fully per-series. The resulting ridge models outperform prior linear forecasters on most dataset-horizon combinations and exceed Transformer, MLP, and CNN baselines on six of eight benchmarks.
AI.conclusion: Capacity is not the primary bottleneck in time-series forecasting—preprocessing choices matter more. The optimized hyperparameters also serve as a diagnostic tool for understanding dataset structure, revealing patterns that larger models silently absorb into their learned parameters without making them interpretable.

title: Recovering Governing Equations from Solution Data: Identifiability Bounds for Linear and Nonlinear ODEs
summary: Learning governing equations from observed solution data is a fundamental challenge in scientific machine learning \cite{bruntonDiscoveringGoverningEquations2016,kovachkiNeuralOperatorLearning2023,longPDENetLearningPDEs2018,rudyDatadrivenDiscoveryPartial2017,raonicConvolutionalNeuralOperators2023}, yet the theoretical conditions under which a ground-truth ODE can be uniquely and stably identified from multiple solution observations remain largely undeveloped, and no quantitative analysis of the sample complexity of such learning tasks exists in the literature. To address this gap, we introduce the Hausdorff distance on solution sets as the natural metric for comparing differential equations, since it captures the worst-case separation between two equations over all admissible initial conditions and thus encodes the minimax structure of the identification problem. We establish identifiability bounds for governing ODEs across a wide class of structure equations--ranging from linear ODEs to nonlinear classes with Lipschitz (Hölder)-continuous vector fields--characterizing precisely when two distinct equations can be distinguished from solution data. Using this metric, we derive metric entropy estimates for the relevant ODE classes and analyze sample complexity bounds, quantifying how many solution observations are needed to reliably recover the governing equation.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces the Hausdorff distance on solution sets as a natural metric for comparing ODEs, establishes identifiability bounds across diverse ODE classes, and derives metric entropy estimates to quantify the sample complexity of learning governing equations from solution observations.
AI.motivation: Current literature lacks theoretical conditions for unique and stable identification of ground-truth ODEs from multiple solution observations, and no quantitative sample complexity analysis exists for such learning tasks.
AI.method: The authors propose the Hausdorff distance on solution sets as the metric for comparing differential equations, capturing worst-case separation over all admissible initial conditions. They then establish identifiability bounds for classes ranging from linear ODEs to nonlinear systems with Lipschitz/Hölder-continuous vector fields, and derive metric entropy estimates to bound sample complexity.
AI.result: Identifiability bounds are established across a wide class of structure equations, precisely characterizing when two distinct equations can be distinguished from solution data. Metric entropy estimates and sample complexity bounds are derived, quantifying the number of solution observations required for reliable recovery.
AI.conclusion: The Hausdorff distance framework provides a principled foundation for analyzing the theoretical limits of ODE identification from solution data, offering the first quantitative sample complexity guarantees for this class of scientific machine learning problems.

title: Designing Reward Signals for Portable Query Generation: A Case Study in Industrial Semantic Job Search
comment: Accepted to KDD 2026 Workshop on AI Agent for Information Retrieval (Agent4IR)
summary:
Job-search platforms rely on low-bandwidth query interfaces that often fail to capture the high-dimensional complexity of candidate profiles. We present an end-to-end RLAIF (Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback) framework to generate \emph{portable} job search queries, terms that abstract away seeker-specific identifiers while preserving generalizable qualifications. This task introduces a highly adversarial reward surface where policy optimization frequently exploits flaws in LLM-as-judge rubrics, resulting in degenerate verbatim-copying behaviors.
  We conducted comprehensive empirical experiments to isolate the impact of optimization mechanics against structured reward engineering. Our results demonstrate that for critic-free optimizers, performance is overwhelmingly dictated by robust reward shaping, rendering the specific choice of algorithm largely immaterial. While critic-free per-rollout baseline methods (RLOO and REINFORCE++) natively resist reward-hacking, the group-relative advantage normalization in GRPO appears uniquely sensitive to spurious reward signals, making it disproportionately susceptible to exploitation. We show that introducing a deterministic, rule-based reward floor to correct for rewards assigned to verbatim copying mitigates this failure mode, resulting in a substantial $+0.147$ quality improvement on a cross-family evaluation judge. Ultimately, we show that the training-time reward model inflates performance gains by $2.4\times$, confirming that the training success is fundamentally dependent on enforcing reward-shaping disciplines rather than selecting alternative optimizers.

AI.tldr: RLAIF-based job search query generation suffers from reward hacking (verbatim copying). The paper shows reward shaping, not optimizer choice, dominates performance; GRPO is uniquely vulnerable to spurious rewards, mitigated by a rule-based reward floor (+0.147 improvement). Training-time reward models inflate gains 2.4×.
AI.motivation: Job-search platforms use low-bandwidth query interfaces that fail to capture the high-dimensional complexity of candidate profiles. The authors aim to generate "portable" queries that abstract away personally identifiable seeker-specific identifiers while preserving generalizable qualifications, but this creates an adversarial reward surface where policy optimization easily exploits LLM-as-judge rubrics through degenerate behaviors like verbatim copying.
AI.method: An end-to-end RLAIF (Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback) framework for generating portable job search queries. The study isolates optimization mechanics from reward engineering through comprehensive empirical experiments comparing critic-free optimizers (RLOO, REINFORCE++, GRPO). Key intervention: introducing a deterministic, rule-based reward floor to correct for spurious rewards assigned to verbatim-copying behaviors. Cross-family evaluation judges assess quality improvements.
AI.result: For critic-free optimizers, performance is overwhelmingly dictated by robust reward shaping — the choice of algorithm is largely immaterial. RLOO and REINFORCE++ natively resist reward-hacking, but GRPO's group-relative advantage normalization makes it disproportionately susceptible to exploiting spurious reward signals. The rule-based reward floor mitigates this failure mode, yielding a +0.147 quality improvement. The training-time reward model inflates performance gains by 2.4×, confirming training success depends on reward-shaping discipline rather than optimizer selection.
AI.conclusion: Training success fundamentally depends on enforcing reward-shaping disciplines rather than selecting alternative optimizers. GRPO's sensitivity to spurious rewards can be corrected via a simple rule-based reward floor. Reward model scores during training dramatically overstate true performance (2.4× inflation), underscoring the need for robust, cross-family evaluation.

title: A Multi-Fidelity Convolutional Autoencoder-Transfer Learning Framework for Guided-Wave-Based Damage Diagnosis Using Large Simulated and Limited Experimental Datasets
summary: Guided wave-based structural health monitoring (GWSHM) with onboard transducers offers significant potential for the early diagnosis of damage in engineering structures. However, the practical deployment of deep learning models is often hindered by the limited availability of labelled experimental data and the high computational cost of generating large-scale high-fidelity simulation datasets. This study presents a multifidelity transfer learning framework that integrates lightweight physics-based simulations, convolutional autoencoder (CAE)-based deep feature learning, a feed-forward neural network, and limited experimental measurements for accurate damage localisation and sizing in plate-like structures instrumented with piezoelectric transducers. A computationally efficient one-dimensional time-domain spectral element model is employed to generate a large synthetic dataset for pretraining, while transfer learning adapts the model to experimental domains using only a small amount of labelled data. The CAE-based transfer learning framework significantly outperforms its CNN-based counterpart in damage localisation accuracy. The model achieves excellent predictive performance with $R^2$ scores exceeding 0.93 for damage localisation and 0.99 for damage sizing. Its generalisation capability is demonstrated on previously unseen data, showing high prediction accuracy for damage scenarios not represented during pretraining or fine-tuning. The results establish the proposed framework as an accurate, computationally efficient, and practically viable solution for real-world GWSHM applications.

AI.tldr: A multifidelity transfer learning framework combining lightweight physics-based simulations, convolutional autoencoders, and limited experimental data achieves high-accuracy damage localisation (R²>0.93) and sizing (R²>0.99) in plate-like structures for guided wave SHM.
AI.motivation: Deep learning for GWSHM is constrained by scarce labelled experimental data and the prohibitive computational cost of generating large-scale high-fidelity simulation datasets. A practical solution is needed that bridges the simulation-to-experiment gap efficiently.
AI.method: A computationally efficient 1D time-domain spectral element model generates a large synthetic dataset for pretraining a convolutional autoencoder (CAE) for deep feature learning, coupled with a feed-forward neural network. Transfer learning then adapts the model to the experimental domain using minimal labelled experimental data, outperforming CNN-based counterparts.
AI.result: The CAE-based transfer learning framework achieved R² scores exceeding 0.93 for damage localisation and 0.99 for damage sizing, with strong generalisation to previously unseen damage scenarios not represented during pretraining or fine-tuning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed framework offers an accurate, computationally efficient, and practically viable solution for real-world guided wave SHM, effectively overcoming data scarcity and computational barriers through multifidelity transfer learning.

title: Blackwell Approachability and Gradient Equilibrium are Equivalent
comment: 30 pages, 1 figure, accepted for presentation at COLT 2026
summary: Gradient equilibrium (GEQ) is a recently introduced online optimization framework that generalizes first-order stationarity from offline optimization and abstracts problems like online conformal prediction. While GEQ has curious similarities with known online learning frameworks, namely regret minimization, prior work has shown that GEQ error and regret are incomparable objectives, leaving open a precise understanding of how GEQ fits into the broader online learning landscape. In this work, we show that GEQ is equivalent to Blackwell approachability in the algorithmic sense. That is, a Blackwell approachability problem can always be solved using queries to a black-box GEQ oracle, with no asymptotic loss in the oracle's error rate, and vice versa. Taken together with known equivalences between approachability, regret minimization, and calibration, these results imply that GEQ is equivalent to these frameworks, as well. Our reductions are efficient and can be used to transfer refined guarantees, such as optimism and strong adaptivity, from regret minimization to GEQ. Along the way, we also identify necessary and sufficient conditions for GEQ, and establish reductions between different notions of GEQ with unconstrained and constrained decision sets.

AI.tldr: The paper establishes that Gradient Equilibrium (GEQ) is algorithmically equivalent to Blackwell approachability, and by extension to regret minimization and calibration, thereby positioning GEQ firmly within the broader online learning landscape. The authors provide efficient reductions that transfer guarantees like optimism and adaptive bounds between these frameworks.
AI.motivation: Prior work introduced GEQ as a generalization of first-order stationarity but left its relationship to standard online learning frameworks unclear — GEQ error and regret were known to be incomparable as objectives. The paper seeks to resolve this by precisely characterizing how GEQ fits into the online learning ecosystem.
AI.method: The authors prove bidirectional algorithmic reductions: (1) any Blackwell approachability problem can be solved via black-box GEQ oracle queries with no asymptotic loss in error rate, and (2) vice versa. These reductions are efficient and preserve refined guarantees. They also leverage known equivalences between approachability, regret minimization, and calibration to extend the equivalence transitively. Additionally, they derive necessary and sufficient conditions for GEQ and reductions between constrained and unconstrained GEQ variants.
AI.result: GEQ is algorithmically equivalent to Blackwell approachability, regret minimization, and calibration. The reductions enable transferring guarantees like optimism and strong adaptivity from regret minimization to GEQ. Necessary and sufficient conditions for GEQ are identified, along with reductions connecting different GEQ formulations with constrained/unconstrained decision sets.
AI.conclusion: GEQ is not a separate, incomparable paradigm but rather equivalent to well-established online learning frameworks. This unification allows cross-pollination of algorithmic techniques and theoretical guarantees across GEQ, approachability, regret minimization, and calibration.

title: Beyond the Hard Budget: Sparsity Regularizers for More Interpretable Top-k Sparse Autoencoders
summary: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have become a leading tool for interpreting the representations of vision foundation models, decomposing their polysemantic activations into a larger set of sparse, more monosemantic features. The Top-$k$ SAE, a now-standard variant, enforces sparsity architecturally through its activation function, retaining only the $k$ most active latents per input. Because it was designed precisely to avoid the $\ell_1$ penalty used by earlier SAEs and its known drawbacks, it has not been combined with an explicit sparsity regularizer, despite retaining limitations of its own, such as a budget $k$ that is fixed regardless of input complexity and a tendency to overfit to the training value of $k$. We introduce two sparsity regularizers compatible with the Top-$k$ architecture, both acting on the activations before the Top-$k$ selection: an $\ell_1$ penalty on the unselected (off-support) units, and a scale-invariant $\ell_1/\ell_2$-ratio penalty that concentrates the code onto fewer effective units. Both penalties are applied only to the batch-active units, those selected by the Top-$k$ operator at least once within the batch. Across two datasets, three vision foundation models, and a range of $k$, both regularizers consistently improve monosemanticity at no cost to reconstruction quality. The $\ell_1/\ell_2$ penalty further concentrates information into fewer latents, making reconstruction more robust to the inference-time choice of $k$ and improving small-budget linear probing. Our central finding is that hard architectural sparsity and soft sparsity regularization are complementary rather than mutually exclusive.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces two sparsity regularizers (an ℓ₁ penalty on off-support units and a scale-invariant ℓ₁/ℓ₂ ratio penalty) that are compatible with Top-k SAEs. The key insight is that architectural (hard) sparsity and soft regularization are complementary: applying these regularizers before Top-k selection consistently improves feature monosemanticity without harming reconstruction, and the ℓ₁/ℓ₂ penalty additionally makes reconstruction more robust to inference-time k and improves linear probing.
AI.motivation: Top-k SAEs enforce sparsity architecturally but suffer from two limitations: (1) the fixed budget k is applied uniformly regardless of input complexity, and (2) the model tends to overfit to the training value of k. Prior work avoided combining Top-k SAEs with explicit sparsity regularization because the architecture was designed to circumvent the drawbacks of ℓ₁-based SAEs. The authors challenge this assumption, hypothesizing that soft regularization can complement hard architectural sparsity.
AI.method: The authors propose two regularizers applied to activations before Top-k selection: (1) an ℓ₁ penalty on unselected (off-support) units to suppress them, and (2) a scale-invariant ℓ₁/ℓ₂ ratio penalty that concentrates representation onto fewer effective latents.
