Both penalties are applied only to batch-active units (those selected by Top-k at least once in a batch). Experiments span two datasets, three vision foundation models (CLIP, DINOv2, SAM), and multiple k values, evaluating monosemanticity, reconstruction quality, robustness to inference-time k, and linear probing performance.
AI.result: Both regularizers consistently improve monosemanticity with no degradation in reconstruction quality. The ℓ₁/ℓ₂ penalty further (1) concentrates information into fewer latents, (2) makes reconstruction more robust to inference-time choice of k, and (3) improves small-budget linear probing. These benefits hold across all tested models, datasets, and k values.
AI.conclusion: Hard architectural sparsity (Top-k selection) and soft sparsity regularization are complementary rather than mutually exclusive. Combining them yields SAEs with better monosemanticity, more efficient code concentration, and greater robustness to k, without sacrificing reconstruction fidelity.

title: Hallucination in World Models is Predictable and Preventable
comment: Interactive paper, live demo, code, dataset, and models: https://www.nicklashansen.com/mmbench2
summary:
Modern generative world models render increasingly realistic action-controllable futures, yet they frequently hallucinate: rollouts remain visually fluent while drifting from the ground-truth dynamics. We hypothesize that hallucination concentrates in low-coverage regions of the state-action space, where lightweight data-centric signals can both detect it and guide mitigation. To test this, we introduce MMBench2, a 427-hour, 210-task dataset for visual world modeling with ground-truth actions, rewards, and live simulators, and train a 350M-parameter world model on it. We identify three distinct hallucination modes: perceptual, action-marginalized, and scene-diverging -- each anchored to a different stage of the pipeline, and develop three signals that accurately predict where the model will fail. To close coverage gaps at training time, we develop a coverage-aware sampling technique; to close them online, our hallucination predictors serve as curiosity rewards for targeted data collection, yielding a data-efficient finetuning recipe that adapts the pretrained world model to entirely unseen environments with as few as 50 real environment trajectories. Overall, our findings reveal that hallucination in world models is inherently a data coverage issue, and that the same signals used to detect it can also be used for mitigation.
  An interactive web version of our paper is available at https://www.nicklashansen.com/mmbench2

AI.tldr: World models hallucinate in low-coverage regions of state-action space; the paper introduces MMBench2 (427h, 210-task dataset), identifies three hallucination modes, develops detection signals, and proposes coverage-aware sampling plus curiosity-driven finetuning to mitigate hallucination with as few as 50 trajectories in unseen environments.
AI.motivation: Generative world models produce visually fluent but dynamically inaccurate (hallucinated) rollouts. The authors hypothesize that hallucination is fundamentally a data coverage problem — concentrated in low-density regions of state-action space — and that lightweight, data-centric signals can both detect and mitigate it.
AI.method: (1) MMBench2: a 427-hour, 210-task benchmark with ground-truth actions, rewards, and live simulators. (2) A 350M-parameter world model trained on it. (3) Identification of three hallucination modes: perceptual, action-marginalized, and scene-diverging, each tied to a pipeline stage. (4) Three predictive signals for failure detection. (5) Coverage-aware sampling at training time. (6) Online hallucination predictors used as curiosity rewards for targeted data collection, enabling finetuning to unseen environments with ~50 trajectories.
AI.result: The three signals accurately predict where the world model will fail. Coverage-aware sampling closes coverage gaps at training time. The curiosity-driven finetuning recipe adapts the pretrained world model to entirely unseen environments in a data-efficient manner (as few as 50 real environment trajectories).
AI.conclusion: Hallucination in world models is inherently a data coverage issue. The same signals used to detect hallucination can also guide mitigation, enabling robust adaptation to new environments with minimal data.

title: Error-Conditioned Neural Solvers
summary: Neural surrogate models offer fast approximate mappings from PDE parameters to solutions, but they typically treat solving as a purely statistical task: once trained, they struggle to correct their own constraint violations and extrapolate beyond the training distribution. Recent hybrid methods promote physical correctness by targeting the PDE residual via gradient descent or Gauss--Newton steps, but inherit the compute cost and instability of the underlying classical optimizers. We show, theoretically and empirically, that numerically minimizing the PDE residual can be an unreliable proxy for reconstruction accuracy in ill-conditioned systems, explaining why these methods often do not make accurate predictions despite achieving low residuals. We propose error-conditioned Neural Solvers (ENS), built on a different principle: rather than an optimization target, the PDE residual field is passed as a direct input to the network at each iteration, enabling it to read the spatial structure of its own errors and learn an update policy to iteratively correct its predictions. Across four PDE families, ENS attains the highest prediction accuracy in the large majority of settings, with gains reaching $10\times$ on turbulent Kolmogorov flow, while avoiding the expensive compute cost of hybrid methods. ENS's learned correction policy generalizes under distribution shift, including zero-shot parameter changes and cross-equation transfer, where its relative advantage is largest in the ill-conditioned regimes where residual minimization is least reliable. Project website: https://neuralsolver.github.io/.

AI.tldr: ENS proposes feeding the PDE residual field directly as input to a neural solver at each iteration, enabling the network to learn an iterative correction policy by reading its own error structure, outperforming both pure statistical surrogates and residual-minimizing hybrid methods, especially in ill-conditioned regimes.
AI.motivation: Neural surrogate models for PDEs lack mechanisms to correct their own errors and generalize poorly. Hybrid methods that minimize PDE residuals via gradient-based optimization inherit high computational cost and instability. Moreover, the authors identify a fundamental problem: low PDE residual does not imply high reconstruction accuracy in ill-conditioned systems, making residual minimization an unreliable proxy.
AI.method: Error-Conditioned Neural Solvers (ENS) take a fundamentally different approach: instead of treating the PDE residual as an optimization target, ENS passes the residual field as a direct input channel to the neural network at each iteration. This allows the network to perceive the spatial structure of its prediction errors and learn a learned update policy (correction operator) that iteratively refines solutions. The architecture conditions on residual fields rather than minimizing them.
AI.result: ENS achieves the highest prediction accuracy across four PDE families in most settings, with up to 10× improvement on turbulent Kolmogorov flow. It avoids the expensive compute of hybrid methods. The learned correction policy generalizes under distribution shift, including zero-shot parameter changes and cross-equation transfer, with the largest relative gains in ill-conditioned regimes where residual minimization fails most.
AI.conclusion: Conditioning on the residual field rather than minimizing it is a more effective paradigm for neural PDE solving, particularly for ill-conditioned systems. ENS provides a computationally efficient, generalizable alternative that decouples accuracy from residual magnitude.

title: Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators
summary: Efficient sampling of molecular systems at thermodynamic equilibrium is a hallmark challenge in statistical physics. This challenge has driven the development of Boltzmann Generators (BGs), which allow rapid generation of uncorrelated equilibrium samples by combining a generative model with exact likelihoods and an importance sampling correction. However, modern BGs predominantly rely on normalizing flows (NFs), which either suffer from limited expressivity due to strict invertibility constraints (discrete time) or computationally expensive likelihoods (continuous time). In this paper, we propose Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators (ArBG) -- a novel autoregressive modelling framework -- that overcomes these limitations by departing from the flow-based BG paradigm. ArBG circumvents the topological constraints of flows and enables sequential inference-time interventions, while offering enhanced scalability by leveraging architectures effective in Large Language Models. We empirically demonstrate that ArBG leads to significant improvements over flow-based models across all benchmarks, but particularly in larger peptide systems such as the 10-residue Chignolin. Furthermore, we introduce Robin, a 132 million parameter transferable model trained with the ArBG framework which improves over the previous state-of-the-art, reducing the zero-shot energy error, E-W$_2$, on 8-residue systems by over 60$\%$. The code can be found at the following link: https://github.com/danyalrehman/autobg.

AI.tldr: ArBG introduces an autoregressive framework for Boltzmann Generators that overcomes invertibility constraints of normalizing flows, enabling better scalability and inference-time interventions, with state-of-the-art results on peptide systems.
AI.motivation: Normalizing-flow-based Boltzmann Generators face a fundamental trade-off: discrete-time flows suffer limited expressivity due to strict invertibility constraints, while continuous-time flows incur computationally expensive likelihoods. There is a need for a generative framework that escapes these limitations while maintaining exact likelihood computation.
AI.method: The authors propose Autoregressive Boltzmann Generators (ArBG), which model molecular distributions autoregressively (factorizing the joint distribution into conditional distributions) rather than via invertible flows. This is combined with importance sampling for unbiased equilibrium sampling. They also introduce Robin, a 132M-parameter transferable model leveraging LLM-style architectures.
AI.result: ArBG significantly outperforms flow-based models across all benchmarks, especially on larger systems like 10-residue Chignolin. The transferable Robin model improves zero-shot energy error (E-W₂) on 8-residue systems by over 60% compared to the previous state-of-the-art.
AI.conclusion: Moving beyond the flow-based paradigm via autoregressive modeling yields substantial gains in expressivity, scalability, and performance for equilibrium molecular sampling, with promising transferable capabilities.

title: Reinforcement Learning without Ground-Truth Solutions can Improve LLMs
summary: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for training LLMs typically rely on ground-truth answers to assign rewards, limiting their applicability to tasks where the ground-truth solution is unknown. We introduce a \textbf{R}anking-\textbf{i}nduced \textbf{VER}ifiable framework (RiVER) that trains LLMs on score-based optimization tasks without ground-truth solutions, using deterministic execution feedback as continuous-valued supervision. When applying group-relative RL to such continuous rewards, we identify two key challenges: \emph{scale dominance}, where uncalibrated score magnitudes across test instances distort policy updates, and \emph{frequency dominance}, where repeatedly sampled suboptimal solutions can outweigh rare but stronger candidates. RiVER addresses these challenges with calibrated reward shaping that uses instance-wise comparisons and emphasizes top-ranked solvers while retaining bounded feedback for other valid solutions. We train on 12 AtCoder Heuristic Contest tasks and evaluate on Algorithm Engineering Benchmark (ALE-Bench), LiveCodeBench, and USACO. RiVER advances Qwen3-8B and GLM-Z1-9B-0414 by 8.9\% and 9.4\% in ALE rating rank. More importantly, despite training exclusively on score-based tasks without any ground-truth solutions, RiVER also improves the backbones across exact-solution benchmarks such as LiveCodeBench and USACO by an absolute average improvement of 2.4\% and 3.5\%. By contrast, baselines trained with raw execution scores improve ALE rating but fail to transfer to exact-solution benchmarks. These results suggest that score-based optimization tasks, combined with proper reward calibration, can serve as effective training environments for general coding ability without ground-truth solutions.

AI.tldr: RiVER introduces a ranking-induced framework for training LLMs on score-based optimization tasks without ground-truth answers, using calibrated reward shaping to overcome scale and frequency dominance issues in continuous RL, achieving strong transfer to exact-solution benchmarks.
AI.motivation: Standard RLVR requires ground-truth answers for reward assignment, limiting applicability to open-ended optimization tasks. The authors aim to unlock score-based tasks (e.g., heuristic optimization) as training environments for general coding ability, where only continuous execution scores — not binary correctness — are available.
AI.method: RiVER uses deterministic execution feedback as continuous-valued supervision and applies group-relative RL. It addresses two identified failure modes: (1) scale dominance, mitigated via instance-wise score normalization/calibration, and (2) frequency dominance, mitigated by emphasizing top-ranked solutions while retaining bounded feedback for others. Training is conducted on 12 AtCoder Heuristic Contest tasks. Evaluation spans ALE-Bench, LiveCodeBench, and USACO.
AI.result: RiVER improves Qwen3-8B and GLM-Z1-9B-0414 by 8.9% and 9.4% in ALE rating rank. Despite no ground-truth training, it transfers to exact-solution benchmarks: +2.4% on LiveCodeBench and +3.5% on USACO (absolute average). Baselines using raw execution scores improve ALE but fail to transfer.
AI.conclusion: Score-based optimization tasks, when paired with proper reward calibration, can serve as effective training environments for general coding ability without requiring ground-truth solutions. This broadens the applicability of RLVR beyond tasks with known answers.
